title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Binary mask
B(x) = 1 (object) where I(x) > t, else 0 (background)


Histogram
h_i = number of pixels with grey level i (or in bin i)


Normalised histogram
p_i = h_i / N, N = number of pixels; \sum_i p_i = 1


Cumulative histogram
P(t) = \sum_{i \le t} p_i: the fraction of pixels a threshold at t calls background


Mask area
1 - P(t)


Percentile threshold
the t with P(t) = 1 - q: keep the brightest fraction q


Ground truth
the true mask (known for synthetic images, drawn by hand for real ones)

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
By hand
B1. A 5 \times 5 image with grey levels 0–7: I = \begin{bmatrix} 0&1&1&2&1\\ 1&6&7&6&2\\ 1&7&5&6&1\\ 2&6&6&3&0\\ 1&2&1&0&4 \end{bmatrix} (a) Draw the histogram h_i, the normalised histogram p_i and the cumulative histogram P(t). (b) Threshold at t = 3 and at t = 4 (object where I > t). How many object pixels does each give, and which pixels change? Why is the change small? (c) Compare t = 1 with t = 2. Which threshold would you trust more, and why?
B2. A 256 \times 256 image: background grey level 50 (75 % of the pixels), objects 110 (25 %), plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation \sigma_n = 20. The threshold is t = 80. (a) Which fraction of the background pixels ends up above t, and of the object pixels below t? How many wrong pixels is that in total? (A normal variable lies more than 1.5 standard deviations above its mean with probability 0.0668.) (b) The image is smoothed first with a 3 \times 3 mean. What is the noise now, and roughly how many wrong pixels remain? (More than 4.5 standard deviations: probability 3.4 \cdot 10^{-6}.) (c) Which pixels does (b) ignore, that will in fact be wrong after smoothing?
B3. A 12-bit camera stores its images in a 16-bit container (grey levels 0–4095 out of 0–65 535). (a) You make a histogram with 256 equal bins over 0–65 535. How many bins contain data? (b) Suggest two better choices of bins.
B4. In a 512 \times 512 fluorescence image, spots cover about 2 % of the pixels. The cumulative histogram gives P(100) = 0.950, P(110) = 0.968, P(120) = 0.980, P(130) = 0.988. (a) Which threshold keeps the brightest 2 %? How many pixels is that? (b) In the next image of the series the cells are more active and spots cover 4 %. What does the same percentile rule do now?
B5. In the demo’s synthetic image (25 % objects) the mask area is 25.8 % at t = 100 and 22.3 % at t = 130. After adding strong noise (\sigma_n = 35) it is 33.8 % and 20.5 %. (a) How many pixels per thousand change label per grey level of t in each case? (b) Which image’s segmentation depends more on the exact choice of t, and by what factor? What does that tell you about its histogram between 100 and 130?
B6. A 3 \times 3 window of a dark background contains one hot pixel: 50, 52, 48, 51, 250, 49, 50, 53, 47 (the 250 in the centre). (a) Compute the mean and the median of the window. (b) The image is thresholded at t = 60 after a 3 \times 3 mean. What happens around the hot pixel? And after a 3 \times 3 median?
B7. You shuffle the pixels of an image to random positions. Which of these change: the histogram, the mask area at t = 100, the shape of the mask, the best threshold according to a method that uses only the histogram?






Solutions





B1. (a) Counts h = (3, 8, 4, 1, 1, 1, 5, 2) for grey levels 0–7 (sum 25). Normalised: p = (0.12, 0.32, 0.16, 0.04, 0.04, 0.04, 0.20, 0.08). Cumulative: P = (0.12, 0.44, 0.60, 0.64, 0.68, 0.72, 0.92, 1.00). (b) t = 3: the 9 pixels with grey level 4–7 (the 3 \times 3 bright block except the 3, plus the 4 in the bottom-right corner). t = 4: 8 pixels; only the single 4 in the corner changes. The change is small because there is only one pixel at grey level 4: t moves inside the valley of the histogram (levels 3, 4, 5 have one pixel each). (c) t = 1 gives 14 object pixels, t = 2 gives 10: the four 2s change, the edge of the dark peak. A threshold in the valley (3 or 4) is more trustworthy: moving it by one changes one pixel, not four.
B2. (a) 80 is 1.5 standard deviations from both means: 6.68 % of each class is wrong. That is 0.0668 \cdot 49\,152 = 3284 background pixels and 0.0668 \cdot 16\,384 = 1095 object pixels: about 4378 wrong pixels, scattered as salt and pepper. (b) The mean of 9 independent noise values has \sigma = 20/3 = 6.7. Now 80 is 4.5 standard deviations away: 3.4 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 65\,536 \approx 0.2, so essentially no pixel inside the objects or the background is wrong. (c) The pixels near the edges: their 3 \times 3 window contains both object and background, so their mean lies between 50 and 110 (partial volume). Those near 80 can go either way; the boundary becomes less precise.
B3. (a) The bin width is 65\,536/256 = 256, so 0–4095 fall into the first 4096/256 = 16 bins; the other 240 bins are empty. The histogram has 16 coarse bars: any valley is invisible. (b) One bin per grey level over 0–4095 (4096 bins), or 256 bins over the actual range of the data [\min, \max] (width 16 for the full 12-bit range). With few pixels per bin, prefer fewer bins.
B4. (a) P(t) = 1 - 0.02 = 0.98 at t = 120. That keeps 0.02 \cdot 262\,144 \approx 5243 pixels. (b) It still keeps the brightest 2 %, i.e. about half of the spot pixels: the threshold rises into the spots. The percentile rule assumes the object fraction, so it is only safe when that fraction is known and stable.
B5. (a) Clean: (25.8 - 22.3)\,\% / 30 = 0.117\,\%, i.e. 1.2 pixels per thousand per grey level. Noisy: (33.8 - 20.5)\,\% / 30 = 0.443\,\%, i.e. 4.4 per thousand. (b) The noisy one, 3.8 times as sensitive. The change of the area per grey level is the histogram at t: the clean histogram has a deep valley between 100 and 130, the noisy one has pixels everywhere there.
B6. (a) Mean 650/9 = 72.2, median 50. (b) After the mean, every window that contains the hot pixel (the 9 windows around it) has a mean near 72: a 3 \times 3 object appears around the hot pixel. The mean spreads the outlier instead of removing it. After the median every window gives about 50: the hot pixel disappears.
B7. Unchanged: the histogram (the same grey levels), hence the mask area at any t and the threshold of any histogram method. Changed: the shape of the mask, which becomes scattered pixels instead of blobs.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that \sigma^2 = \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - \mu^2. Compute \mu and \sigma^2 for the image of B1.
B9. (math) Noise values n_1, \dots, n_n are independent with variance \sigma^2, and \bar n = \sum_k w_k n_k with \sum_k w_k = 1. Show that \operatorname{Var}(\bar n) = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2, and that among all weights with \sum_k w_k = 1 the equal weights w_k = 1/n make it smallest.
B10. (math) Let A(t) = 1 - P(t) be the mask area. Show that A(t) - A(t + 1) = p_{t+1}, and for continuous grey levels with density p(x) that A'(t) = -p(t). Use it to explain B5.






Solutions (math)





B8. Expand: \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - 2\mu \sum_i i\,p_i + \mu^2 \sum_i p_i = \sum_i i^2 p_i - 2\mu^2 + \mu^2. For B1: \mu = \sum_i i\,p_i = 72/25 = 2.88; \sum_i i^2 p_i = 352/25 = 14.08; \sigma^2 = 14.08 - 2.88^2 = 5.79.
B9. For independent variables the variances add: \operatorname{Var}(\sum_k w_k n_k) = \sum_k w_k^2 \operatorname{Var}(n_k) = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2. Minimise \sum_k w_k^2 subject to \sum_k w_k = 1: the Lagrange condition 2w_k = \lambda makes all weights equal, w_k = 1/n, with \sum_k w_k^2 = 1/n. (Or by Cauchy–Schwarz: 1 = (\sum_k w_k)^2 \le n \sum_k w_k^2.)
B10. A(t) = \sum_{i > t} p_i, so A(t) - A(t + 1) = \sum_{i > t} p_i - \sum_{i > t + 1} p_i = p_{t+1}. Continuously, A(t) = \int_t^\infty p(x)\,dx and A'(t) = -p(t) by the fundamental theorem of calculus. In B5 the average slope between 100 and 130 is the average histogram height there: 1.2 per thousand per grey level for the clean image, 4.4 for the noisy one.

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Explore
The demo shows an image (left) with the mask in orange, its histogram (top right) and the mask area 1 - P(t) as a function of t (bottom right). Drag the threshold on either plot, or use the slider. The synthetic image has bright blobs covering exactly 25 % of the pixels on a dark background; its ground truth is known, so the readout gives the Dice coefficient (1 = the mask is perfect; defined in the evaluation unit). noise σ adds Gaussian noise; median 3×3 and blur σ smooth the image before the histogram is made; bins sets the number of histogram bins; P(t) adds the cumulative histogram to both plots; dark objects makes the mask I \le t.



E1. Preset clean bimodal. Read the mask area and Dice at t = 120. Move t to 100 and to 130: how much do the mask area and Dice change? Find the t with the highest Dice.
E2. Tick P(t). Where does the cumulative curve rise steeply, and where is it flat? Relate this to the peaks and the valley of the histogram.
E3. Preset noise fills the valley. Where is the valley now? Read Dice at t = 110, and find the best t. Then preset blur restores it: Dice at t = 110? Instead of the blur, try median 3×3 (blur σ = 0), then blur σ = 3. Which works best, and why is σ = 3 worse than σ = 1.5?
E4. Preset too few bins (8 bins). Can you see two peaks? Raise the bins to 32 and 256. Which number of bins shows the structure best for this 256 \times 256 image? Tick log scale: what does it reveal?
E5. Preset percentile: brightest 25 % (noise 35). Which t does it choose, and how does its Dice compare with the best you found in E3? Why does this work here, and when would it fail?
E6. Preset the micrograph (an electron micrograph: the cell is darker than the empty background, so dark objects is on). Describe the histogram. Is there a clear valley? What does the mask contain at t = 150?






Solutions





E1. At t = 120: mask area 23.7 % (truth: 25 %), Dice 0.974. At t = 100: 25.8 %, Dice 0.983; at t = 130: 22.3 %, Dice 0.942. Thirty grey levels move only 3.5 % of the pixels, because t is in the valley. The best Dice is 0.991 at t = 108.
E2. P(t) rises steeply through each peak (most steeply in the background peak around 60, where 75 % of the pixels sit) and is almost flat in the valley between about 90 and 140 and above 190. Its slope is the histogram, and the mask area is its mirror image 1 - P(t).
E3. With noise 35 the two peaks merge into one broad hump with a shoulder; there is no valley. Dice at t = 110 is 0.813; the best is 0.823 at t = 119. After a Gaussian blur with σ = 1.5 the valley is back and Dice at t = 110 is 0.970. The 3 \times 3 median gives 0.960, a bit worse here (the noise is Gaussian, which averaging handles best). With σ = 3 the best Dice falls to 0.949 (0.936 at t = 110): the blur now smears the edges of the blobs over several pixels, and these partial-volume pixels fill the valley again.
E4. With 8 bins (width 32) the histogram is a staircase: a big bar for the background and a falling tail, with no visible second peak. With 32 bins both peaks and the valley appear; 256 bins also show them, but more ragged (about 256 pixels per bin on average). 32–64 bins are a good compromise here. The log scale makes small counts visible: the long tails of the peaks and the few pixels in the valley.
E5. It chooses t = 119 (the smallest t with P(t) \ge 0.75), with Dice 0.823, the same as the best threshold of E3. It works because the objects really cover 25 % of this image. In an image with a different object fraction it would keep the wrong number of pixels, however clear the valley is.
E6. The histogram is broad: it rises from about 50 to a plateau between 100 and 200 and has a peak near 240, the empty background. There is no deep valley; the cell (cytoplasm, nucleus, dark membranes) spreads over most grey levels. At t = 150 the mask holds 39.7 % of the pixels: the cell, its dark membranes and the dark material outside it, with a ragged boundary where texture crosses the threshold. A single threshold cannot pick out the nucleus: it has the same grey levels as the cytoplasm.

title: Exercise: histograms and a global threshold
text:
Where this leads
So far t was chosen by eye. The next unit chooses it from the histogram: Otsu’s method makes the two classes as tight as possible, and the minimum-error threshold models the histogram as two normal distributions and puts t where they cross.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: a threshold t splits the histogram into background and object, and a good t sits in a valley. Now the computer chooses t from the histogram alone.

Otsu: make both classes as tight as possible; equivalently, push their means apart.
Isodata: two means and their midpoint, repeated; 1D k-means.
Minimum error: model the histogram as two normal distributions and put t where they cross (Bayes).
Which method is biased when one class is small or wide, and in which direction.
Briefly: the triangle and maximum-entropy methods, and three classes.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Two classes

A threshold t splits the grey levels into class 0 (background, i \le t) and class 1 (object, i > t). Each class has

a weight \omega_0, \omega_1: the fraction of pixels in it (\omega_0 = P(t), \omega_1 = 1 - \omega_0),
a mean \mu_0, \mu_1 and a variance \sigma_0^2, \sigma_1^2 of its grey levels.

Worked example (8 grey levels, 20 pixels): h = (2, 5, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2), mean \mu = 3.3, variance \sigma_T^2 = 5.81. At t = 3: \omega_0 = 0.55, \mu_0 = 1.27, \mu_1 = 5.78.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Otsu: tight classes, far apart
Otsu (1979): a good split makes each class tight around its own mean.

Measure the spread within the classes: \sigma_W^2 = the weighted average of the two class variances. Choose t to make it smallest.
The total spread of all pixels, \sigma_T^2, does not depend on t. It splits into within + between: the spread of the pixels around their class mean, plus the spread of the class means around the overall mean.
So making the classes tight is the same as making the class means far apart: maximise the between-class variance \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2.
\sigma_B^2 is large when the means are far apart and both classes are substantial: a class with 1 % of the pixels contributes little, however far away it is.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: within + between
With p_i the normalised histogram, class 0 = \{i \le t\}: \sigma_T^2 = \sum_i (i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_{k=0}^{1}\sum_{i \in k} \big((i - \mu_k) + (\mu_k - \mu)\big)^2 p_i . Expand the square. The cross term 2(\mu_k - \mu)\sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)p_i vanishes, because the deviations from a class’s own mean sum to zero. What remains: \sigma_T^2 = \underbrace{\omega_0\sigma_0^2 + \omega_1\sigma_1^2}_{\sigma_W^2} + \underbrace{\omega_0(\mu_0 - \mu)^2 + \omega_1(\mu_1 - \mu)^2}_{\sigma_B^2}. \sigma_T^2 is fixed, so \arg\min_t \sigma_W^2 = \arg\max_t \sigma_B^2. With \mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1: \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1) and \mu_1 - \mu = \omega_0(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1^2(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 + \omega_1\omega_0^2(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 .

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: The math: one pass over the histogram
text:
The math: one pass over the histogram
With the running sums P(t) = \sum_{i \le t} p_i and M(t) = \sum_{i \le t} i\,p_i of the last unit: \omega_0 = P, \mu_0 = M/P, \mu_1 = (\mu - M)/(1 - P), and \mu_1 - \mu_0 = \frac{\mu P - M}{P(1 - P)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sigma_B^2(t) = \frac{\big(\mu\,P(t) - M(t)\big)^2}{P(t)\,\big(1 - P(t)\big)} .

Build the histogram: O(N) for N pixels. Then one pass over the L grey levels evaluates \sigma_B^2 at every t: O(L).
For 256 grey levels the search is free; even for 16-bit data it is 65 536 evaluations.
Undefined where a class is empty (P = 0 or 1).

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Try it: Otsu by hand




The bars are the worked example; drag a bar to change its count, move t with the slider or by clicking a row. The stacked bar under the plot shows total = within + between: the total stays at 5.81 while t moves. Tour: move t from 0 to 6 and watch the star (best t) and the stacked bar. “isodata step” from 5.5: 4.17 → 3.75 → 3.53, the same split as Otsu. “two equal peaks”: t* = 3 by symmetry. “isodata stuck”: three groups of levels; isodata from 6.5 stops at 4.58 (split 4, σ_B² = 3.33) while Otsu’s best is t = 0 (4.05).

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Isodata: two means and their midpoint
text:
Isodata: two means and their midpoint
Ridler & Calvard (1978): start with any t, then repeat

split at t and compute the two class means \mu_0, \mu_1;
move t to their midpoint (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2;

until t stops moving.

Every pixel joins the nearer mean, then the means are recomputed: this is k-means with k = 2 in one dimension.
The worked example from t = 5.5: 4.17 \to 3.75 \to 3.53, which splits at 3, the same as Otsu.
It can stop at a different fixed point: with three groups of grey levels (levels 0, 3–4 and 7), isodata from 6.5 stops at 4.58 (split \{0, 3, 4\} vs \{7\}), while Otsu’s best split is \{0\} vs the rest. Isodata finds a local optimum; Otsu searches all t.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: The math: Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point
text:
The math: Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point
Continuous grey levels with density p(x): P' = p(t), M' = t\,p(t). Write D = \mu P - M = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = D^2 / (P(1 - P)) and D' = (\mu - t)\,p(t). Setting the derivative to zero (with p(t) \ne 0, D \ne 0): 2(\mu - t)\,P(1 - P) = D(1 - 2P) \;\Longrightarrow\; t = \mu - \tfrac12 (1 - 2P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0). Insert \mu = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1: t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2}. Every stationary point of \sigma_B^2(t), the maximum included, is a fixed point of isodata. The converse fails: a fixed point can be a local maximum or even a minimum of \sigma_B^2.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Two classes as probabilities: Bayes
Treat the grey level x of a pixel as random. Class k has prior probability \omega_k (its share of the pixels) and a distribution f_k(x) of grey levels.

Bayes’ rule: the probability that a pixel with grey level x is object is proportional to \omega_1 f_1(x); that it is background, to \omega_0 f_0(x). “Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.”
Decide object where \omega_1 f_1(x) > \omega_0 f_0(x): this rule makes the fewest errors.
For a threshold t: the errors are the background tail above t plus the object tail below t. Moving t trades one tail for the other; the total is smallest where the two weighted curves cross.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Where the curves cross

Background \mu_0 = 50 (90 % of the pixels), objects \mu_1 = 150 (10 %), both with \sigma = 20.

The crossing is at 108.8, not at the midpoint 100: the rarer class gets less room. Error 0.35 %, against 0.62 % at the midpoint.
Shaded: the two tails that a threshold at the crossing gets wrong.
Equal variances, equal weights: the crossing is the midpoint, as in isodata.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: the minimum-error threshold
The error of the rule “object if x > t”: E(t) = \omega_0 \int_t^\infty f_0(x)\,dx + \omega_1 \int_{-\infty}^t f_1(x)\,dx, \qquad E'(t) = -\omega_0 f_0(t) + \omega_1 f_1(t) = 0 . For normal f_k take logarithms: \ln\omega_0 - \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{(t - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} = \ln\omega_1 - \ln\sigma_1 - \frac{(t - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}.

Equal variances: the t^2 terms cancel, and t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\,\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1} . Example: 100 + \frac{400}{100}\ln 9 = 108.8.
Unequal variances: a quadratic in t with up to two roots. The wider class wins in both tails: far out on either side its density is larger.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Minimum error from the histogram
We do not know \omega_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k. Kittler & Illingworth (1986): for every candidate t,

fit a normal distribution to each side of the split (weight, mean and variance of the pixels on that side),
measure how well the two fitted curves explain the histogram,
keep the t with the best fit, and threshold there.

When the histogram really is two normal peaks, this lands near the crossing, even for unequal weights or widths. When it is not (clipped values, a long tail, three groups), the fit can go badly wrong.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
The math: Kittler–Illingworth
The criterion is the average negative log-likelihood of the pixels under the fitted mixture, with each pixel assigned to its side of t: J(t) = -\sum_i p_i \ln\big(\omega_{k(i)}\, f_{k(i)}(i)\big) = \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \tfrac12 + \sum_k \omega_k \ln\sigma_k - \sum_k \omega_k \ln\omega_k , using \sum_{i \in k} p_i (i - \mu_k)^2 = \omega_k\sigma_k^2. Dropping constants and doubling: J(t) = 1 + 2(\omega_0\ln\sigma_0 + \omega_1\ln\sigma_1) - 2(\omega_0\ln\omega_0 + \omega_1\ln\omega_1), \qquad t^* = \arg\min_t J(t). Like Otsu, one pass with running sums (now also \sum_{i \le t} i^2 p_i). A class with almost zero variance gives \ln\sigma \to -\infty: guard against empty or one-level classes.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Who is biased, and which way
text:
Who is biased, and which way
Otsu and isodata use only the means. In effect they assume equal variances and similar weights.

Small object class (10 % of the pixels): Otsu moves into the larger class. On the curves above it chooses 98.5 instead of 108.8; at 3 % objects it falls to 60.5, inside the background peak.
Much wider background: Otsu again moves into the wider class.
Minimum error follows the crossing as long as the two-Gaussian model fits.
Heavy overlap: every threshold has a large error; the grey level alone cannot decide. Neighbours must help (graph cuts, day 13).

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Try it: two Gaussians, six thresholds
text:
Try it: two Gaussians, six thresholds




The image (right) is drawn from the mixture: blob-shaped objects with fraction ω₁, each pixel’s grey level sampled from its class. Top: histogram (grey), weighted densities (blue, orange), every method’s threshold (dashed); the selected one is solid, its error tails shaded. Below: its criterion curve. Table: threshold and error rate under the model. Tour: “equal, well separated”: all at 125 except the triangle. “unequal weights” (ω₁ = 0.1): Otsu 85 with 19.9 % error, Bayes 114.6 (3.4 %), min-error 123 (4.1 %). “unequal variances”: two Bayes crossings, 40.8 and 105.4. “small object (3 %)”: Otsu 62 (40.6 %), triangle 91, Kapur 93, min-error 98, Bayes 94.1, all about 1.4 %. “heavy overlap”: the best possible error is 21.9 %. Shrink the image to 32² to see how noisy small histograms make every method.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Other criteria: triangle and maximum entropy
text:
Other criteria: triangle and maximum entropy

Triangle (Zack et al., 1977): draw a line from the histogram’s peak to the far end of its long tail; the threshold is where the histogram lies farthest below that line. Made for a unimodal histogram with a few bright object pixels (fluorescent spots), where there is no valley and Otsu fails.
Maximum entropy (Kapur et al., 1985): choose t so that the grey levels within each class are as spread out as possible (the entropies H_0 + H_1 of the two class distributions p_i/\omega_k are largest).
Another criterion, another answer: there is no single “correct” threshold. The choice is a choice of model of the histogram.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Three classes: multi-level Otsu
\sigma_B^2 = \sum_k \omega_k(\mu_k - \mu)^2 for K classes; for three, try all pairs t_1 < t_2 (about 32 000 for 256 levels).




The micrograph with three-class Otsu: t₁ = 120, t₂ = 188 (dark material in purple, the middle grey levels in orange, the bright background unmarked). Two-class Otsu (untick “3 classes”) gives 163 with η = σ_B²/σ_T² = 0.76. The middle class mixes cytoplasm and nucleus: their grey levels overlap, so no threshold separates them.

title: Choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Summary

Otsu: total variance = within + between; minimise the within-class variance \Leftrightarrow maximise \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2. One pass over the histogram.
Isodata: t \leftarrow (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2, repeated; 1D 2-means. Otsu’s optimum is one of its fixed points; it may stop at another.
Bayes / minimum error: decide object where \omega_1 f_1 > \omega_0 f_0; the best threshold is where the weighted densities cross. Equal variances: midpoint shifted by \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}.
Kittler–Illingworth fits two Gaussians at every t and keeps the best fit.
Otsu and isodata are biased into the larger or wider class; triangle for a unimodal histogram with a tail; three classes by multi-level Otsu.

title: Quiz: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Class 0 is background (i \le t), class 1 is object; \omega_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2 are the class weights, means and variances.

Q1. Why is minimising the within-class variance the same as maximising the between-class variance?






Hint





What happens to the total variance when t moves?









Answer





Total = within + between, and the total variance of all pixels does not depend on t. Whatever the within part loses, the between part gains.




Q2. Two splits have class means 40 and 200. In split A the classes hold 50 % and 50 % of the pixels; in split B 99 % and 1 %. Which has the larger \sigma_B^2, and by how much?






Hint





\sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2.









Answer





A: 0.25 \cdot 160^2 = 6400. B: 0.0099 \cdot 160^2 = 253. A is about 25 times larger: Otsu prefers splits where both classes are substantial.




Q3. One isodata step: the current split has class means 60 and 140. Where does the threshold go next? When does isodata stop?






Hint





Midpoint.









Answer





To (60 + 140)/2 = 100. It stops when the new midpoint gives the same split as before: every pixel is then nearer to its own class mean (a fixed point, as in k-means with k = 2).




Q4. Objects are rare (5 % of the pixels) and both classes have the same spread. Is the minimum-error threshold above or below the midpoint of the two means?






Hint





At the midpoint, which class is more likely for a pixel?









Answer





Above (towards the object mean). At the midpoint both densities are equal, but background is 19 times more common, so a pixel there is probably background. The boundary moves towards the rarer class until the weighted densities are equal.




Q5. Why can the minimum-error rule with unequal variances label a pixel object when it is darker than the background mean?






Hint





Compare the tails of a narrow and a wide normal curve.









Answer





If the object class is much wider, its density decays more slowly than the narrow background peak, so far below the background mean the object density is larger again. The weighted curves cross twice, and the Bayes rule says “object” in both tails. (In practice that dark tail holds very few pixels.)




Q6. A fluorescence image has a huge dark background peak and a faint tail of a few bright spots, with no valley. Which method would you try first, and why does Otsu fail?






Hint





Otsu needs both classes to be substantial.









Answer





The triangle method (or maximum entropy): it is made for a unimodal histogram with a long tail and puts t where the peak ends. Otsu’s \sigma_B^2 barely rewards separating a 1 % class, so it splits the background peak instead.




Q7. Two classes overlap so much that the best possible threshold misclassifies 20 % of the pixels. Will a cleverer histogram method do better?






Hint





What information does any histogram method use?









Answer





No. The Bayes threshold is already the best rule that looks at one grey level at a time. To do better you need more information than the grey level of a single pixel: its neighbours (smoothing, graph cuts) or other features.




Q8. (math) Show that \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1).






Hint





\mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1 and \omega_0 = 1 - \omega_1.









Answer





\mu_0 - \mu = \mu_0 - (1 - \omega_1)\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1\mu_0 - \omega_1\mu_1 = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1).

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute Otsu’s threshold by hand from a small histogram, and check that total = within + between,
run isodata by hand, and recognise when it stops at a different split than Otsu,
find the minimum-error (Bayes) threshold of two normal classes, and say which way it moves from the midpoint,
predict from the shape of a histogram which method is biased, and in which direction.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the three demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Background







Symbol
Meaning




Class 0, class 1
grey levels i \le t (background) and i > t (object)


\omega_0, \omega_1
class weights: fractions of the pixels; \omega_0 = P(t)


\mu_0, \mu_1; \sigma_0^2, \sigma_1^2

\sigma_W^2

where \omega_0 f_0(t) = \omega_1 f_1(t); equal variances: t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
By hand
The worked example of the lecture: grey levels 0–7 with counts h = (2, 5, 3, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2), N = 20, \mu = 3.3, \sigma_T^2 = 5.81.
B1. Otsu’s table. (a) Compute \omega_0, \mu_0, \mu_1 and \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2 for t = 2, t = 3 and t = 4. (b) Given \sigma_B^2 = 1.21, 3.60, \cdot, \cdot, \cdot, 3.94, 1.52 for the other t, which t does Otsu choose? Which pixels are object?
B2. Isodata on the same histogram. (a) Start at t = 5.5 (class 0 = levels 0–5). Compute \mu_0, \mu_1 and the new t. Do one more step. (b) Where does it stop? Compare with B1.
B3. Three groups: counts h = (9, 0, 0, 8, 7, 0, 0, 5) for levels 0–7 (29 pixels). (a) Run isodata from t = 6.5. Where does it stop? (b) Compute \sigma_B^2 for the split \{0\} \mid \{3, 4, 7\} and for \{0, 3, 4\} \mid \{7\}. Which one does Otsu choose? (c) Run isodata from t = 0.5. What does this tell you about isodata?
B4. Two classes with normal grey levels: background \mu_0 = 50, objects \mu_1 = 150, both \sigma = 20; objects are 10 % of the pixels. (a) Compute the Bayes threshold. Does it lie above or below the midpoint 100? Explain in words why. (b) What is the threshold when the objects are 50 % of the pixels? (c) Isodata and Otsu ignore the weights. Which way would you expect them to err for 10 % objects, and why?
B5. Unequal widths: background \mu_0 = 80, \sigma_0 = 12; objects \mu_1 = 150, \sigma_1 = 40, \omega_1 = 0.4. The weighted densities cross at 40.8 and 105.4. (a) Sketch the two weighted curves. Which class wins (has the larger weighted density) below 40.8, between 40.8 and 105.4, and above 105.4? (b) Is a single threshold the best possible rule here? What is the best rule?
B6. For each histogram shape, name a method that suits it and one that fails: (a) two well-separated peaks of similar size and width; (b) a large dark background peak and a small, long bright tail (a few fluorescent spots); (c) three peaks (background, cytoplasm, nucleus); (d) two peaks that overlap so much that there is no dip between them.






Solutions





B1. (a) t = 2: class 0 has 2 + 5 + 3 = 10 pixels with sum 0 + 5 + 6 = 11: \omega_0 = 0.50, \mu_0 = 1.10; class 1 has 10 pixels with sum 66 - 11 = 55: \mu_1 = 5.50; \sigma_B^2 = 0.5 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 4.4^2 = 4.84. t = 3: 11 pixels, sum 14: \omega_0 = 0.55, \mu_0 = 1.27; class 1: 9 pixels, sum 52, \mu_1 = 5.78; \sigma_B^2 = 0.55 \cdot 0.45 \cdot 4.51^2 = 5.02. t = 4: 12 pixels, sum 18: \omega_0 = 0.60, \mu_0 = 1.50; class 1: 8 pixels, sum 48, \mu_1 = 6.00; \sigma_B^2 = 0.6 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 4.5^2 = 4.86. (b) The largest is 5.02 at t^* = 3: object = grey levels 4–7, 9 pixels.
B2. (a) Class 0 = levels 0–5: 14 pixels, sum 28, \mu_0 = 2.00; class 1 = levels 6–7: 6 pixels, sum 38, \mu_1 = 6.33; new t = 4.17. Next: class 0 = levels 0–4: 12 pixels, \mu_0 = 1.50; class 1: \mu_1 = 6.00; t = 3.75. (b) Then class 0 = levels 0–3: \mu_0 = 1.27, \mu_1 = 5.78, t = 3.53, which gives the same split again: it stops at 3.53, the split \{0..3\} \mid \{4..7\}, the same as Otsu.
B3. (a) From 6.5: class 0 = \{0, 3, 4\}: 24 pixels, sum 0 + 24 + 28 = 52, \mu_0 = 2.17; class 1 = \{7\}: \mu_1 = 7; t = 4.58. The split is the same, so it stops at 4.58. (b) \mu = (24 + 28 + 35)/29 = 3.00. Split \{0\} \mid rest: \omega_0 = 9/29 = 0.31, \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 87/20 = 4.35: \sigma_B^2 = 0.31 \cdot 0.69 \cdot 4.35^2 = 4.05. Split \{0, 3, 4\} \mid \{7\}: \omega_0 = 24/29 = 0.83, \sigma_B^2 = 0.83 \cdot 0.17 \cdot (7 - 2.17)^2 = 3.33. Otsu chooses \{0\} \mid \{3, 4, 7\}. (c) From 0.5: class 0 = \{0\}, \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 4.35, t = 2.17; the split is the same, so it stops at 2.17, the Otsu split. Isodata finds a fixed point near its start: a local optimum. With two clear groups there is only one; with three groups there are several.
B4. (a) t = 100 + \frac{20^2}{100}\ln\frac{0.9}{0.1} = 100 + 4 \cdot 2.197 = 108.8, above the midpoint. Near the midpoint, a grey level is equally far from both means, but a random pixel is 9 times more likely to be background; the boundary moves towards the rarer class until the two weighted densities are equal. (b) \ln 1 = 0: t = 100, the midpoint. (c) They put t near the middle of the two class means, or lower: the large background class dominates, and a split that cuts into its tail barely changes \mu_0. They err towards the background (too low t), so many background pixels become object. (On these curves Otsu chooses 98.5.)
B5. (a) Below 40.8 the wide object class wins (its tail decays much more slowly than the narrow background peak), between 40.8 and 105.4 the background wins, above 105.4 the objects win. (b) No. The Bayes rule labels object both below 40.8 and above 105.4. A single threshold at 105.4 misses the (tiny) object tail below 40.8; in practice that tail is so small that the single threshold is nearly as good, but the rule is an interval, not a threshold.
B6. (a) Otsu, isodata and minimum error all work and agree; nothing fails badly (the triangle method is not made for this and lands lower). (b) Triangle or maximum entropy (or minimum error if the tail is roughly normal); Otsu and isodata fail, dragged into the big peak. (c) Multi-level Otsu with three classes; any two-class method has to merge two of the classes. (d) Every histogram method fails: the grey level alone cannot separate the classes. Smooth first, or use neighbours (graph cuts).




Math questions
B7. (math) Prove \sigma_T^2 = \sigma_W^2 + \sigma_B^2 (add and subtract the class mean inside the square), and then \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1)^2. Check both at t = 3 in the worked example (\sigma_0^2 = 0.744, \sigma_1^2 = 0.840).
B8. (math) With P = P(t) and M = M(t), show that \mu_1 - \mu_0 = (\mu P - M)/(P(1 - P)) and hence \sigma_B^2(t) = (\mu P - M)^2/(P(1 - P)).
B9. (math) Show that for continuous grey levels every stationary point of \sigma_B^2(t) satisfies t = (\mu_0 + \mu_1)/2 (Otsu’s optimum is an isodata fixed point).
B10. (math) Derive the equal-variance minimum-error threshold t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1} from E'(t) = 0. Then show that for unequal variances the condition is a quadratic equation in t.
B11. (math) Show that the average negative log-likelihood of the pixels, each assigned to its own side of t with a fitted normal distribution, is \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \tfrac12 + \sum_k\omega_k\ln\sigma_k - \sum_k\omega_k\ln\omega_k (the Kittler–Illingworth criterion up to constants).






Solutions (math)





B7. \sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu)^2 p_i = \sum_{i \in k}\big((i - \mu_k) + (\mu_k - \mu)\big)^2 p_i = \sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)^2 p_i + 2(\mu_k - \mu)\sum_{i \in k}(i - \mu_k)p_i + (\mu_k - \mu)^2\sum_{i \in k}p_i. The middle sum is \omega_k\mu_k - \mu_k\omega_k = 0. Summing over k: \sigma_T^2 = \sum_k \omega_k\sigma_k^2 + \sum_k\omega_k(\mu_k - \mu)^2. With \mu = \omega_0\mu_0 + \omega_1\mu_1 and \omega_0 + \omega_1 = 1: \mu_0 - \mu = \omega_1(\mu_0 - \mu_1), \mu_1 - \mu = \omega_0(\mu_1 - \mu_0), so \sigma_B^2 = \omega_0\omega_1^2 d^2 + \omega_1\omega_0^2 d^2 = \omega_0\omega_1 d^2 with d = \mu_0 - \mu_1. At t = 3: \sigma_W^2 = 0.55 \cdot 0.744 + 0.45 \cdot 0.840 = 0.787, \sigma_B^2 = 5.023, sum 5.81 = \sigma_T^2.
B8. \mu_0 = M/P and \mu_1 = (\mu - M)/(1 - P) (the total first moment is \mu). Then \mu_1 - \mu_0 = \frac{P(\mu - M) - M(1 - P)}{P(1 - P)} = \frac{\mu P - M}{P(1 - P)}, and \sigma_B^2 = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2 = \frac{(\mu P - M)^2}{P(1 - P)}.
B9. With density p: P' = p(t), M' = t\,p(t), D = \mu P - M, D' = (\mu - t)p(t). \frac{d}{dt}\frac{D^2}{P(1 - P)} = \frac{2DD'P(1 - P) - D^2(1 - 2P)p}{P^2(1 - P)^2} = 0 gives (for p(t) \ne 0, D \ne 0) 2(\mu - t)P(1 - P) = D(1 - 2P). With D = P(1 - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0): t = \mu - \frac12(1 - 2P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0), and inserting \mu = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1 gives t = P\mu_0 + (1 - P)\mu_1 - \frac12(\mu_1 - \mu_0) + P(\mu_1 - \mu_0) = \frac12(\mu_0 + \mu_1).
B10. E'(t) = -\omega_0 f_0(t) + \omega_1 f_1(t) = 0. With normal densities, take logs: \ln\omega_0 - \ln\sigma_0 - \frac{(t - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2} = \ln\omega_1 - \ln\sigma_1 - \frac{(t - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}. For \sigma_0 \ne \sigma_1 the t^2 terms have different coefficients: a quadratic at^2 + bt + c = 0 with a = \frac1{2\sigma_1^2} - \frac1{2\sigma_0^2}. For \sigma_0 = \sigma_1 = \sigma they cancel: (t - \mu_1)^2 - (t - \mu_0)^2 = (\mu_0 - \mu_1)(2t - \mu_0 - \mu_1) = 2\sigma^2\ln\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_0}, so t = \frac{\mu_0 + \mu_1}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_1 - \mu_0}\ln\frac{\omega_0}{\omega_1}.
B11. -\sum_i p_i\ln\big(\omega_k f_k(i)\big) = -\sum_k\sum_{i \in k}p_i\Big(\ln\omega_k - \ln\sigma_k - \tfrac12\ln 2\pi - \frac{(i - \mu_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2}\Big). Use \sum_{i \in k}p_i = \omega_k and \sum_{i \in k}p_i(i - \mu_k)^2 = \omega_k\sigma_k^2: = -\sum_k\omega_k\ln\omega_k + \sum_k\omega_k\ln\sigma_k + \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \sum_k\frac{\omega_k\sigma_k^2}{2\sigma_k^2}, and the last sum is \tfrac12.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Explore: Otsu by hand
The eight bars are a histogram; drag a bar up or down to change its count (0–9). The threshold t (slider, or click a row of the table) colours class 0 blue and class 1 orange; the dots under the bars are the class means. The table lists \omega_0, \mu_0, \mu_1 and \sigma_B^2 for every t (★ = Otsu). The bar below the plot splits the total variance into within and between. isodata step moves the isodata threshold (dashed) to the midpoint of the class means.



P1. Preset the worked example. Check your B1 table. Move t from 0 to 6: what happens to the total, the within and the between part?
P2. Press isodata step three times and compare with B2. Then preset isodata stuck: press isodata step until it stops, and compare with B3.
P3. Preset two equal peaks. Where is Otsu’s threshold, and why? Now drag the bar at level 7 up to 9. Does t^* move?
P4. Preset a tiny object class: the objects are the 2 pixels at level 7. Which split does Otsu choose? Is that the split you want? What does isodata give from 5.5?






Solutions





P1. The table matches B1: t^* = 3 with \sigma_B^2 = 5.02. The total stays at 5.81 for every t; the within part is smallest (0.79) exactly where the between part is largest (5.02), and both trade off as t moves.
P2. From 5.5: 4.17, 3.75, 3.53, then it stops at the split of t = 3, as in B2. Stuck: 6.5 → 4.58, and then 4.58 again: it stops at split 4 with \sigma_B^2 = 3.33, while the star (Otsu) is at t = 0 with 4.05 (the rows t = 0, 1, 2 tie, because levels 1 and 2 are empty).
P3. t^* = 3, with \sigma_B^2 = 3.27: the histogram (1, 4, 6, 2, 2, 6, 4, 1) is symmetric about 3.5, so the best split is in the middle. Raising h_7 to 9 makes the histogram asymmetric, but t^* stays at 3 (\sigma_B^2 = 4.29, just ahead of 4.26 at t = 4): the extra bright pixels raise \mu_1 for every split, and the middle remains the best place to cut.
P4. Otsu splits at t = 3: levels 4–7 (6 pixels: three 4s, one 5 and the two 7s) are called object. It cuts into the tail of the big peak, because a class of 2 pixels out of 32 contributes little to \sigma_B^2 (at t = 6, \sigma_B^2 = 1.45 against 1.84 at t = 3). Isodata from 5.5 goes to 4.52 and stops at 4.13 (split 4): also inside the big peak.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
section: Explore: two Gaussians and six thresholds
text:
Explore: two Gaussians and six thresholds
The image (right) is drawn from a two-class model: a blob-shaped object mask covering a fraction \omega_1 of the pixels, and for each pixel a grey level drawn from its class’s normal distribution \mathcal N(\mu_k, \sigma_k^2). Top left: the histogram of the image (grey), the weighted class densities \omega_0 f_0 (blue) and \omega_1 f_1 (orange), and the thresholds of Otsu, isodata, min-error (Kittler–Illingworth), triangle, Kapur (maximum entropy) and the Bayes boundary of the true model (dashed; the selected method solid). The shaded areas are the selected method’s errors: orange = object pixels it calls background, blue = background pixels it calls object. Below: the selected method’s criterion as a function of t. The table gives each method’s threshold and its error rate under the model; the caption above the image gives the wrong pixels in this image.



E1. Preset equal, well separated. Which methods agree, and on what threshold? Which one does not, and why?
E2. Preset unequal weights (\omega_1 = 0.1). Read Otsu’s threshold and error, and the Bayes threshold and error. Which way did Otsu move, and how does that match B4? Which histogram method comes closest to Bayes? Now raise \omega_1 to 0.3 and 0.5.
E3. Preset unequal variances. Where are the two Bayes crossings? Select min-error and Otsu: compare their thresholds and errors.
E4. Preset small object (3 %). Is the histogram bimodal? Compare the errors of Otsu, triangle, Kapur and min-error with Bayes. Select triangle and look at its criterion curve.
E5. Preset heavy overlap. What is the smallest possible error? What do the masks look like?
E6. Back to unequal weights: set the image size to 32² (1024 pixels) and to 256². Which methods change their threshold, and by how much?






Solutions





E1. Otsu, isodata and min-error choose 125 and Kapur 124, all at the Bayes threshold 125.0 (error 0.1 %). The triangle method chooses 109 (error 1.2 %): it draws its line from the background peak to the end of the histogram and assumes a unimodal histogram with a tail, which this is not.
E2. Otsu: 85 with an error of 19.9 %; Bayes: 114.6 with 3.4 %. Otsu moved down, into the large background class, by about 30 grey levels, as predicted in B4. Min-error chooses 123 (4.1 %), Kapur 108 (3.9 %), triangle 105 (4.5 %): Kapur is closest in error here, min-error is the only one on the correct side of Bayes. At \omega_1 = 0.3: Otsu 97 (7.5 %) against Bayes 105.6 (6.0 %); at \omega_1 = 0.5 every method except the triangle chooses 100, the Bayes threshold (6.7 %).
E3. The weighted densities cross at 40.8 and 105.4; below 40.8 the wide object class wins again (B5). Min-error chooses 112 (7.2 %), close to the Bayes error of 6.2 %; Otsu chooses 125 (10.8 %): it ignores that the object class is wide and puts the threshold too far into it.
E4. No: the 3 % object class is a small shoulder on the right of one big peak. Otsu chooses 62, inside the background peak, with a disastrous 40.6 % error; isodata 64 (34.4 %). Triangle 91, Kapur 93 and min-error 98 all have about 1.4–1.5 %, close to Bayes (94.1, 1.4 %). The triangle criterion is the distance below the line from the peak to the end of the tail; it is largest where the background peak ends and the object tail begins.
E5. Bayes: 120.4 with 21.9 % error, the best any threshold can do: more than a fifth of the pixels are wrong whatever t is. Otsu and isodata (113, 23.2 %) and Kapur (123, 22.1 %) are close to it; min-error (173) and triangle (149) fail badly because the histogram is one hump. Every mask is speckled: the grey level of a single pixel simply does not tell the classes apart. Neighbouring pixels must help (smoothing, or graph cuts).
E6. At 32² the histogram is ragged: Otsu stays at 85, isodata 85, but the triangle method jumps from 105 to 85 (19.9 %), Kapur from 108 to 103 and min-error from 123 to 121. At 256² the curves are smooth: Otsu 84, triangle 114 (3.4 %), Kapur 107, min-error 123. Methods that look at the shape of the histogram (triangle, Kapur) need many pixels; Otsu’s means are stable even for small images (but biased).

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Explore: Otsu on the micrograph
The same demo as in the last unit, now with Otsu’s criterion \eta(t) = \sigma_B^2(t)/\sigma_T^2 (between 0 and 1) on the lower plot, and the option of three classes (two thresholds t and t_2; multi-level Otsu).



C1. Untick 3 classes and press t = Otsu. What is Otsu’s threshold for the micrograph, and how large is \eta there? What does the mask separate?
C2. Tick 3 classes and press t = Otsu. Give t_1 and t_2. What do the three classes contain? Can any threshold separate the nucleus from the cytoplasm?
C3. Untick 3 classes, choose synthetic blobs, set noise σ to 20, and press t = Otsu. Compare Otsu’s Dice with the best Dice you can find by hand.






Solutions





C1. t^* = 163 with \eta = 0.76: the split explains 76 % of the grey-level variance. It separates the bright empty background (above 163) from everything else (45.2 % of the pixels are at or below 163): the cell and the dark material around it.
C2. t_1 = 120, t_2 = 188. Darkest class (purple): membranes, dense granules and the darkest parts of the cell; middle class (orange): cytoplasm and nucleus together; brightest: empty background. The nucleus and the cytoplasm have overlapping grey levels, so no threshold separates them; their difference is texture and position, which the histogram does not see.
C3. Otsu chooses t = 106 with Dice 0.946; the best threshold is about 112 with Dice 0.951. With 25 % objects Otsu is slightly biased into the background, but the loss is small when the peaks are well separated.

title: Exercise: choosing the threshold from the histogram
text:
Where this leads
Every method here looks at one pixel at a time and at one global histogram. The next unit drops both assumptions: the threshold may vary over the image (local thresholds), and a pixel’s decision may depend on its neighbours (hysteresis). The Bayes two-class model returns in graph cuts (day 13): its data term is exactly this unit’s -\log(\omega_k f_k), with a smoothness term added.

title: Decision trees
text:
About this lecture
The first day of learning from examples. So far we wrote every rule by hand: a threshold, a filter, an energy. Now the rule is learned from examples that someone has labelled.

Classification = colouring a feature space: each pixel or object is a point.
A decision tree asks yes/no questions about one feature at a time.
It is grown greedily: the question that makes the two groups purest.
A tree grown too far memorises the training data: overfitting.
Training, validation and test data, and cross-validation: how to measure honestly.
Regression trees: the same idea for numbers.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This day owns the classification basics for the whole course: feature space, training/validation/test data, overfitting, cross-validation. Later days (neural networks, evaluation, SVM, mixtures) recall them from here. The next unit makes forests from many trees; unit 3 classifies objects from measurements; unit 4 classifies pixels.

title: Decision trees
text:
Classification: colour the feature space

Measure a few numbers per pixel or per object: its features (intensity, local variance, area, …).
Each pixel or object is then a point, one axis per feature.
Training data: points whose class someone knows (nucleus / background, mitotic / not).
The classifier must colour the whole plane: every new point gets a class from where it lands.

The simplest way: give a new point the class of its nearest training point (nearest neighbour). Trees do it with a few questions instead.

Draw two clouds on the board, a new point between them. Nearest neighbour is mentioned only as the obvious baseline; it needs all training points at prediction time and depends on the units of the axes (a tree does not, see later).

title: Decision trees
text:
A decision tree

Eight pixels, two features: intensity I and local variance V (texture). Each node asks “is feature \le t?”; each leaf holds a class (or the class proportions). Every question cuts the plane along an axis: a tree is a set of axis-aligned rectangles. A tree with one question is a stump.

Read the tree: V ≤ 4.5 → background (3 smooth, dim pixels). Otherwise ask I ≤ 55: the left leaf still holds one of each, the right leaf three nuclei. The plane on the left is the same tree. Prediction is a handful of comparisons.

title: Decision trees
text:
Growing a tree

Take all training points in a node.
For every feature and every threshold between two neighbouring values: split the points into “≤” and “>”.
Keep the split whose two children are purest.
Repeat in each child (recursive partitioning), until a stopping rule says no.

This is greedy: each question is the best one now. The best first question is not always part of the best tree. With four quadrants coloured like a chessboard (XOR), no single cut helps, yet two cuts solve it.

The XOR preset in the demo shows this: the split scan at the root is almost flat (best impurity decrease 0.024 of a possible 0.5), but after three splits the training error is 1 of 120. Finding the best tree overall is computationally hopeless, hence greedy.

title: Decision trees
section: Impurity: how mixed is a node?
text:
Impurity: how mixed is a node?

0 when the node holds a single class; largest when the classes are equally mixed.
Gini impurity: the chance that two points drawn at random from the node (with replacement) have different classes. For two classes with shares p and 1 - p: 2p(1-p), at most 0.5.
Entropy: how many yes/no questions are still needed, on average, to name the class (at most 1 for two classes). It chooses almost the same splits; the full story is on the compression day.
A split is good when the weighted impurity of the children is much lower than the parent’s: the impurity decrease.

title: Decision trees
section: The math: impurity and its decrease
text:
The math: impurity and its decrease
Class shares p_k in a node. Gini, entropy and misclassification: G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2 = \sum_{k \ne l} p_k p_l, \qquad H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k, \qquad M = 1 - \max_k p_k .
A split of n points into n_L and n_R: \Delta = I(\text{parent}) - \tfrac{n_L}{n}\, I(L) - \tfrac{n_R}{n}\, I(R) \;\ge\; 0 \quad\text{for concave } I . (The parent’s shares are the weighted mean of the children’s; Jensen’s inequality.) With H, \Delta is called the information gain.
M is a poor criterion: it is only piecewise linear, so many useful splits give \Delta = 0. Example: 400 + 400 points split into (300, 100) | (100, 300) or into (200, 400) | (200, 0). Both have \Delta M = 0.25; Gini prefers the second, which has a pure child (\Delta G = 0.167 against 0.125).

title: Decision trees
text:
Try it: grow a tree




Left: points (click to add, drag to move), the tree’s rectangles behind them, the split lines on top. Right: the tree, and for the selected node the split scan: impurity decrease against the threshold for a cut along x (blue) and y (green); click on a curve to force that cut. Tour: “two blobs”: one stump at x ≤ 0.48, best decrease 0.48, 1 of 100 training points wrong. “XOR”: the scan at the root is flat (0.024): next split three times, error drops to 1/120. “diagonal”: grow fully, a staircase of 13 leaves. “one mislabelled point”: a deep tree draws a thin sliver around it; min leaf size 3 removes it. “noisy overlap” with the error-vs-depth view: training error falls to 0.5 %, test error is lowest at depth 3 (20.9 %) and ends at 28.9 %.

title: Decision trees
text:
When to stop: overfitting

Grown until every leaf is pure, a tree memorises the training points: zero training error, jagged boundaries, a sliver around every mislabelled point.
Stopping rules: maximum depth, minimum points per leaf, minimum impurity decrease (or grow fully, then prune).
Training error falls with depth; test error on new data first falls, then rises: the U-shaped curve.
A deep tree is unstable: move a few points and you get a completely different tree (high variance). The next unit turns this weakness into a strength.


Numbers from the “noisy overlap” preset (200 training points, 1000 test points from the same two overlapping clouds): depth 1: 22.5 % / 22.8 %; depth 3: 17.5 % / 20.9 %; depth 12: 0.5 % / 28.9 %.

title: Decision trees
text:
Training, validation and test data

Training set: fits the model (grows the tree).
Validation set: chooses the settings (depth, leaf size) by comparing their errors.
Test set: touched once, at the very end, to report the error. If you choose anything with it, it has become a validation set and the reported error is optimistic.

Few labelled examples? k-fold cross-validation reuses them:

title: Decision trees
text:
Images are not independent samples

Neighbouring pixels in one painted stroke are near copies of each other; cells in one image share its staining and its illumination.
A random split by pixel puts near copies on both sides: the validation error looks far better than it will be on a new image.
Rule: split by image (or by region, or by stroke), never by pixel.

The pixel-classification unit shows the effect; the evaluation and statistics day treats data leakage in full.

title: Decision trees
text:
Regression trees: steps

Leaves hold a number (the mean of their points) instead of a class.
Splits reduce the spread: the sum of squared differences from the mean.
The fit is a staircase: a piecewise-constant function. Across a cell edge, a depth-2 tree gives four plateaus.
A small neural network (the neural-networks day) fits the same profile with bends instead of steps.

title: Decision trees
section: Try it: steps across a cell edge
text:
Try it: steps across a cell edge




The profile: 60 samples across a blurred, noisy edge from 40 to 160. Depth 1: one step at x = 0.449, means 46 and 155, training MSE 262.8. Depth 2: four plateaus 40, 75, 129, 158, training MSE 124.7, test MSE 141.4. The test error is lowest at depth 3 (130.1) and rises again (224.2 at depth 6): overfitting looks the same for numbers.

title: Decision trees
section: The math: search cost and regression
text:
The math: search cost and regression

Sort each feature once; sweep the thresholds from left to right, updating the class counts of the left child: O(d\, n \log n) per node for d features and n points.
Finding the tree with the fewest errors at a given size is NP-hard: hence the greedy growth.
Regression: a leaf predicts \bar y_{\text{leaf}}; the split criterion is the decrease of the sum of squared errors, \Delta = \sum_{i \in P}(y_i - \bar y_P)^2 - \sum_{i \in L}(y_i - \bar y_L)^2 - \sum_{i \in R}(y_i - \bar y_R)^2 , i.e. the variance reduction times n.

title: Decision trees
text:
What trees are good at

No scaling: only the order of a feature’s values matters. Measure area in µm² or in pixels, apply a logarithm: the same tree (with moved thresholds).
Mixed units: intensities, areas, ratios and yes/no features side by side.
Fast: a prediction is a handful of comparisons.
Readable, when small.

Weak points: axis-aligned staircases for oblique boundaries, and the instability of deep trees.

title: Decision trees
text:
Summary

Classification colours a feature space; training points are examples with known class.
A tree asks one-feature questions; its leaves are axis-aligned rectangles.
Grow greedily by the largest impurity decrease (Gini; entropy is almost the same).
Deep trees overfit: low training error, higher test error, unstable.
Choose settings on validation data or by cross-validation; report the test error once; split images, not pixels.
Regression trees fit steps.

title: Quiz: decision trees
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A tree has three questions: “x \le 0.5?”, then on both sides “y \le 0.3?”. Into how many regions does it cut the plane, and what shape are they?






Hint





Each question cuts one region in two, along an axis.









Answer





Four regions (one per leaf), all axis-aligned rectangles: left-bottom, left-top, right-bottom, right-top. Here both sides happen to use the same threshold on y, so the four rectangles form a 2 \times 2 grid.




Q2. A node holds 6 nuclei and 2 background pixels. What is its Gini impurity? What would a pure node have?






Hint





G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2.









Answer





G = 1 - 0.75^2 - 0.25^2 = 0.375. A pure node (one class only) has G = 0; the most mixed two-class node has G = 0.5.




Q3. Why does the split search only try thresholds between neighbouring values of a feature?






Hint





What changes when the threshold moves between two neighbouring values?









Answer





Moving the threshold between two neighbouring values does not move any training point from one side to the other, so the split and its impurity stay the same. Only n - 1 distinct splits exist per feature for n distinct values; taking the midpoint is a convention.




Q4. A tree grown until every leaf is pure has 0 % training error. Why is that not good news?






Hint





What does it do with a mislabelled or noisy training point?









Answer





It has memorised the training data, including its noise: every mislabelled point gets its own small region. On new data those regions are wrong, so the test error is higher than for a shallower tree. Zero training error says nothing about new data.




Q5. You tried ten depths and chose the one with the smallest test error. What is wrong with reporting that test error?






Hint





What role did the test set play in the choice?









Answer





The test set was used to choose a setting, so it has become a validation set and its error is optimistic (the best of ten noisy numbers). Choose on a validation set or by cross-validation, then evaluate once on a test set that played no role in any choice.




Q6. In 5-fold cross-validation, how often is each training example used for validation, and how many trees are grown per setting?






Hint





Each fold takes its turn.









Answer





Each example is validated exactly once (when its fold is held out) and used for training in the other 4 rounds. Five trees are grown per setting, one per round; their 5 validation errors are averaged.




Q7. One feature is an area in µm², another an intensity from 0 to 4095. Do you have to rescale them before growing a tree?






Hint





Does a split depend on the size of the numbers or on their order?









Answer





No. A split only depends on the order of the values along one feature; rescaling (or any increasing transformation) moves the thresholds but keeps the same splits. Methods based on distances (nearest neighbour, the SVM) do need comparable scales.




Q8. A regression tree with 4 leaves is fitted to a smooth intensity ramp. What does the fit look like?






Hint





What does a leaf predict?









Answer





A staircase of 4 flat steps: each leaf predicts the mean of its points, so the fit is piecewise constant. A smooth ramp needs many leaves to be approximated well.




Q9. (math) Show that for two classes the Gini impurity is 2p(1-p), where p is the share of one class.






Hint





p_1 = p, p_2 = 1 - p.









Answer





G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 1 - p^2 - 1 + 2p - p^2 = 2p - 2p^2 = 2p(1-p). Equivalently \sum_{k \ne l}p_kp_l = p(1-p) + (1-p)p.

title: Exercise: decision trees
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature space
one axis per feature; each pixel or object is a point


Decision tree
nodes ask “feature j \le t?”; leaves hold a class (or class shares)


Gini impurity
G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2: chance that two random points of the node have different classes


Entropy
H = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k (almost the same splits as Gini)


Impurity decrease
\Delta = I(\text{parent}) - \tfrac{n_L}{n}I(L) - \tfrac{n_R}{n}I(R); the best split has the largest \Delta


Overfitting
training error keeps falling with depth, test error rises again


Validation / test
the validation set chooses settings; the test set is used once, at the end


k-fold cross-validation
k rounds, each fold validates once; average the k errors


Regression tree
leaves hold the mean; splits reduce the sum of squared errors









The math: why the impurity decrease is never negative





The parent’s class shares are the weighted mean of the children’s: p_k = \tfrac{n_L}{n}p_k^L + \tfrac{n_R}{n}p_k^R. Gini and entropy are concave functions of the shares, so (Jensen) I(\text{parent}) \ge \tfrac{n_L}{n}I(L) + \tfrac{n_R}{n}I(R), i.e. \Delta \ge 0. Equality holds when both children have the parent’s shares: such a split is useless.

Solutions (math)





B8. 1 = (\sum_k p_k)^2 = \sum_k p_k^2 + \sum_{k \ne l} p_k p_l. Two classes: G = 1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1 - p), derivative 2 - 4p = 0 at p = 1/2, maximum G = 0.5. H = -p\log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p), derivative \log_2\frac{1-p}{p} = 0 at p = 1/2, maximum H = 1 bit. Both are 0 at p = 0 and p = 1.
B9. With w = n_L/n, the parent’s shares are \mathbf p = w\,\mathbf p^L + (1 - w)\,\mathbf p^R. Concavity of I gives I(\mathbf p) \ge w\,I(\mathbf p^L) + (1-w)\,I(\mathbf p^R), i.e. \Delta \ge 0. For a strictly concave I (Gini, entropy) equality holds only if \mathbf p^L = \mathbf p^R: both children have the parent’s class mix.
B10. Parent: M = 0.5, G = 0.5. Split 1: both children have M = 0.25, so \Delta M = 0.5 - 0.25 = 0.25; G = 2 \cdot 0.75 \cdot 0.25 = 0.375 each, \Delta G = 0.125. Split 2: M(200, 400) = 1/3, M(200, 0) = 0; \Delta M = 0.5 - \tfrac34 \cdot \tfrac13 - 0 = 0.25. G(200, 400) = 4/9, \Delta G = 0.5 - \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac49 = 0.167. M cannot tell them apart; Gini prefers split 2, which makes a pure child that needs no further questions. M is piecewise linear (not strictly concave), so it misses such progress, and in a node where every candidate child keeps the parent’s majority class it gives \Delta M = 0 for every split and the growth stops too early.
B11. Write S = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2. With \bar y = (n_L\bar y_L + n_R\bar y_R)/n, the split of the total sum of squares gives S_P = S_L + S_R + n_L(\bar y_L - \bar y)^2 + n_R(\bar y_R - \bar y)^2. Since \bar y_L - \bar y = \frac{n_R}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R) and \bar y_R - \bar y = -\frac{n_L}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R), the last two terms are \frac{n_L n_R^2 + n_R n_L^2}{n^2}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R)^2 = \frac{n_L n_R}{n}(\bar y_L - \bar y_R)^2. B6: \frac{3 \cdot 3}{6}(11 - 31)^2 = 600 = 604 - 4.

title: Exercise: decision trees
text:
Explore
Left: points of two or three classes in a square (two features, x and y). Click to add a point of the chosen class, drag points to move them, remove points to delete. The tree’s rectangles are coloured behind the points; the split lines are drawn on top, the last one thicker. next split grows the most useful open node (largest impurity decrease, weighted by its number of points), grow fully grows until the depth or leaf-size limit, reset goes back to the root. Right: the tree (click a node to select it) and either the split scan of the selected node (impurity decrease against the threshold, for a cut along x and along y; click on a curve to force that cut) or the error vs depth curve (each depth grown fully). show test points draws a hidden test set from the same source as open circles and reports the test error.



E1. Preset two blobs: one stump. Which question does the root ask, with which impurity decrease? What is the best cut along y, and why does the tree not use it? How many training points are wrong? Press grow fully: how many leaves, and what happens to the training and test errors (tick show test points)?
E2. Preset XOR: first split looks useless. Read the best impurity decrease along x and y at the root and compare with the decrease in E1. Press next split four times and note the training error after each. What does this say about greedy growth?
E3. Preset diagonal: staircase. How many leaves does the full tree have? Tick show test points: what is the test error? Set min leaf size to 5: leaves and test error now? Why can a tree only approximate this boundary?
E4. Preset one mislabelled point. Find the point of class 2 inside the class-1 cloud. How does the full tree handle it? Set min leaf size to 3. What changes in the picture, in the training error and in the test error?
E5. Preset noisy overlap: error vs depth. Read the training and test errors at depth 1, 3 and 12 from the curve. Which depth would you choose, and how would you choose it without a test set?
E6. Back to two blobs, choose misclass. and press grow fully. How many splits does the tree make now, and why does it stop? Compare with Gini.
E7. Preset regression: a cell edge. Read the leaf means of the depth-2 tree. Using the error-vs-depth curve, give the training and test MSE at depths 1, 2, 3 and 6. Which depth fits the edge best?






Solutions





E1. The root asks x \le 0.48, with impurity decrease 0.480 (of a possible 0.5: the children are almost pure). The best cut along y is y \le 0.475 with decrease 0.328: the blobs overlap more in y. 1 of 100 training points is wrong. Grown fully: 3 splits, 4 leaves, depth 3, training error 0, but the test error rises from 2.5 % (stump) to 3.5 %: the two extra splits only chase one point.
E2. Root: best decrease 0.024 along x (at 0.453) and 0.013 along y, against 0.48 in E1: no single cut separates a chessboard. Training errors: 47/120 after one split, 20/120 after two, 1/120 after three, 0 after four. A useless-looking first question can be the start of a perfect tree; greedy growth works here only because it keeps going.
E3. 13 leaves (depth 7), training error 0, test error 7.7 %. With min leaf size 5: 7 leaves (depth 4), training error 2.7 %, test error 10.0 %. Each split is horizontal or vertical, so a diagonal line can only be approximated by a staircase; finer steps need many leaves and many points.
E4. The point at (0.27, 0.40) belongs to class 2 but sits among class 1. The full tree (4 leaves, depth 3) cuts a thin horizontal strip around it: training error 0, test error 1.0 %. With min leaf size 3 a leaf may not hold a single point, the strip disappears, the point is simply misclassified (training error 1/81 = 1.2 %), and the test error drops to 0.8 %.
E5. Depth 1: training 22.5 %, test 22.8 %. Depth 3: 17.5 % and 20.9 % (the lowest test error). Depth 12: 0.5 % and 28.9 %. Choose depth 3 (or 4, 21.0 %). Without a test set: cross-validation on the training points, or a separate validation set; the test set is then used once to report the error.
E6. With misclassification the tree stops after 1 split (training error 1/100). The further splits under Gini isolate a single point inside a child where the other class is the large majority; the majority class of each child does not change, so the misclassification impurity does not decrease (\Delta M = 0) and the growth stops. Gini still sees the purer child (as in B10).
E7. Depth 2: four plateaus with means 40, 75, 129 and 158 (left to right). MSE (training / test): depth 1: 262.8 / 264.8; depth 2: 124.7 / 141.4; depth 3: 88.0 / 130.1; depth 6: 31.8 / 224.2. Depth 3 has the lowest test error; deeper trees follow the noise of the training samples.

title: Exercise: decision trees
text:
Where this leads
One deep tree is unstable: small changes of the data give a different tree. The next unit grows many trees on slightly different data and lets them vote: bagging and random forests. Later units use forests on tables of object measurements and on stacks of filtered images.

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

describe pixels and objects as points in a feature space,
run k-means (Lloyd’s algorithm) by hand on a few points, and compute J at every step,
explain why k-means always stops, why it can stop in a local minimum, and how k-means++ and restarts help,
predict where k-means fails: elongated groups, groups of different sizes, features in different units.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Feature space
one axis per measured number (intensity, colour channels, position, area, …); every pixel or object is a point


Centre \mathbf m_k
the representative point of group k


Assign step
every point goes to its nearest centre (Voronoi cells)


Update step
every centre moves to the mean of its points


J
\sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2, the within-cluster sum of squares


k-means++
next centre drawn with probability \propto D(\mathbf x)^2, the squared distance to the nearest centre so far

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
By hand
B1. Points 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10 on a line, K = 2, start \mathbf m = (1, 2). (a) Run k-means to convergence. After every assign step give the groups and J; after every update step the centres. (b) Where is the boundary between the two groups at the end? (c) Start instead from \mathbf m = (4, 7). Where does it end?
B2. Points 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11, K = 3, start \mathbf m = (0, 1, 8). (a) Do one assign and one update step. Show that nothing changes any more. What is J? (b) Compute J for the groups \{0, 1\}, \{5, 6\}, \{10, 11\}. (c) Explain in one sentence why no single step of k-means can get from (a) to (b).
B3. k-means++ on the points of B2, with the first centre at 0. (a) Give the probability of each point being chosen as the second centre. What is the probability that it is 10 or 11? (b) Suppose the second centre is 10. Give the probabilities for the third centre. How likely is a start with one centre in each group?
B4. Six points in 2D: (0, 0), (0, 2), (1, 1), (6, 0), (6, 2), (7, 1), K = 2, start \mathbf m_1 = (0, 0), \mathbf m_2 = (1, 1). Run k-means to convergence and give J after each assign step.
B5. Predict, with a sketch, what k-means with K = 2 does with (a) two long parallel cigar-shaped groups, close together; (b) a large, widely spread group of 120 points next to a tight group of 30 points; (c) two groups that differ only in y, when y is measured in units 10 times smaller (so the numbers in y are 10 times larger).
B6. For the points of B2 the smallest possible J for K = 1, \dots, 6 is 101.5, 26.5, 1.5, 1.0, 0.5, 0. (a) Why can the best J never increase with K? (b) Draw J against K. Which K would you choose, and why?






Solutions





B1. (a)









step

1
