Halfway between the centres: (2.33 + 8.67)/2 = 5.5.
Assign \{1, 2, 4\}, \{7, 9, 10\} at once; update to (2.33, 8.67): the same answer, after one iteration.

B2. (a) Distances from 5: to 1 is 4, to 8 is 3, so 5 goes to 8, and so do 6, 10, 11. Groups \{0\}, \{1\}, \{5, 6, 10, 11\}; the update gives 0, 1 and (5 + 6 + 10 + 11)/4 = 8: unchanged. J = 0 + 0 + 9 + 4 + 4 + 9 = 26. (b) 6 \times 0.5^2 = 1.5. (c) To reach (b), the centre at 1 would have to move to 5.5 and the centre at 0 to 0.5; but the centre at 1 owns only the point 1, so its mean is 1; and 5 is closer to 8 than to 1. Every single step keeps the configuration.
B3. (a) D^2 = 0, 1, 25, 36, 100, 121, sum 283. Probabilities 0, 0.004, 0.088, 0.127, 0.353, 0.428; for 10 or 11: 221/283 = 0.78. (b) Now D^2 = \min(distance to 0, distance to 10)^2 = 0, 1, 25, 16, 0, 1, sum 43. P(5 \text{ or } 6) = 41/43 = 0.95. Working through the other second centres in the same way (11: 50/52; 5: 61/63; 6: 41/43; 1: always a bad start, since the pair \{0, 1\} already holds two centres) and weighting by their probabilities from (a) gives 0.95 for a start with one centre in each pair. Random points as centres are much worse: of the \binom{6}{3} = 20 triples only 2^3 = 8 have one point in each pair, probability 0.4 (some bad starts still recover when k-means runs).
B4. Assign 1: (0, 0) to \mathbf m_1, the other five to \mathbf m_2: J = 0 + 2 + 0 + 26 + 26 + 36 = 90. Update: \mathbf m_1 = (0, 0), \mathbf m_2 = (4, 1.2). Assign 2: \{(0,0), (0,2), (1,1)\} and \{(6,0), (6,2), (7,1)\}, J = 25.12. Update: \mathbf m_1 = (0.33, 1), \mathbf m_2 = (6.33, 1). Assign 3: unchanged, J = 5.33. Converged.
B5. (a) It cuts across both cigars: a straight boundary through their middle, one centre near each end. Halving the length of a long group lowers J more than separating two close parallel groups. (b) The boundary is the bisector between the two centres, halfway between them. The spread-out group has points beyond that line: they are given to the small group, which ends up too big (the demo: 108 and 42 instead of 120 and 30). (c) With y numbers 10 times larger, differences in y dominate the squared distances (by a factor 100): the groups that differ in y are found easily. In the opposite case (y numbers 10 times smaller), y is ignored and k-means splits along x, even if that means nothing. Units are a choice; k-means takes them literally.
B6. (a) With one more centre you can always keep the old solution and put the new centre on one of the points: J cannot go up, and usually goes down. (b) J drops from 101.5 to 26.5 to 1.5, then hardly changes (1.0, 0.5, 0). The elbow is at K = 3: the three pairs. Beyond that, every extra centre only splits a pair.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that for a fixed set of points \mathbf x_1, \dots, \mathbf x_n the sum \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m\rVert^2 is smallest for \mathbf m = \bar{\mathbf x}, the mean. Show also that \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m\rVert^2 = \sum_i\lVert\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}\rVert^2 + n\lVert\mathbf m - \bar{\mathbf x}\rVert^2.
B8. (math) Show that the set of points equally far from \mathbf m_1 and \mathbf m_2 is the hyperplane through (\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2)/2 with normal \mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1.
B9. (math) Prove that the assign step and the update step each cannot increase J, and conclude that k-means terminates after finitely many iterations.
B10. (math) Multiply feature 2 of every point by s > 0. Is the k-means result (the groups) the same for every s? Give a two-point-per-group example in 2D where the answer changes between s = 1 and s = 10.






Solutions (math)





B7. f(\mathbf m) = \sum_i\lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m\rVert^2 has gradient -2\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m), zero at \mathbf m = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i; f is a convex quadratic (Hessian 2nI), so this is the minimum. For the identity, write \mathbf x_i - \mathbf m = (\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}) + (\bar{\mathbf x} - \mathbf m) and expand: the cross term 2(\bar{\mathbf x} - \mathbf m)^\top\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x}) is zero because the deviations from the mean sum to zero.
B8. \lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_2\rVert^2 \iff 2\mathbf x^\top(\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1) = \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2. This is a hyperplane with normal \mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1. Inserting \mathbf x = (\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2)/2: (\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2)^\top(\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1) = \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2, true.
B9. Assign: J = \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2, and each term is replaced by \min_k\lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_k\rVert^2 \le the old term. Update: J = \sum_k \sum_{i \in G_k}\lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_k\rVert^2, and by B7 each inner sum is smallest at the group mean. So J is non-increasing. If an assign step changes some c(i) (with ties broken consistently, only when the new centre is strictly nearer), J decreases strictly. J after the update depends only on the partition, and there are at most K^n partitions; a strictly decreasing sequence cannot revisit one, so the assignments stop changing after finitely many iterations.
B10. No. Distances become \sqrt{(\Delta x_1)^2 + s^2(\Delta x_2)^2}, so the groups depend on s. Example: points (0, 0), (0, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1), K = 2. At s = 1: split by x_1, \{(0,0), (0,1)\} and \{(3,0),(3,1)\} with J = 4 \times 0.25 = 1, while the split by x_2 gives J = 4 \times 2.25 = 9. At s = 10 the second coordinates are 0 and 10: the split by x_2 has J = 9 and the split by x_1 has J = 4 \times 25 = 100, so the best groups are now \{(0,0),(3,0)\} and \{(0,1),(3,1)\}.

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
Explore
The demo shows points (grey until assigned, then coloured by their group) and the centres as large crossed circles, with the Voronoi cell of each centre shaded. assign colours every point by its nearest centre; update moves every centre to the mean of its points (the dashed trail shows where it came from); step does both; run repeats until nothing changes. The plot shows J after every assign step; 100 restarts runs k-means from 100 different starts and draws a histogram of the final J. Click to add points, drag points or centres, choose the start (random points, k-means++, or by hand), K, and a stretch of the y axis.



E1. Preset by hand (1D). Press assign and update alternately. Compare the centres and J with your table in B1. Then drag the two centres to 4 and 7 (B1c) and run again.
E2. Preset three blobs (k-means++). Press run. How many updates are needed, and what is the final J? Now choose random points and press 100 restarts. How many of the 100 runs reach the best J, and what do the others look like? Repeat with k-means++.
E3. Preset stuck: two centres in one group. Check B2: what is J, and does anything change when you press step? Press 100 restarts (random points). What fraction reaches J = 1.5? Then preset k-means++ avoids it: where are the three seeds?
E4. Preset elongated: cut across. Run. Describe the groups. Is k-means wrong, or is it doing what it was asked? (The true split into the two cigars has J = 5.51.)
E5. Preset big and small group. Run. Where is the boundary, compared with the gap between the groups? Count roughly how many points of the big group end up in the small one.
E6. Preset rescale the y axis (two horizontal bands). Run at y \times 1. Then drag the y-axis slider to 1.5 and run again. Explain the change with B5(c).






Solutions





E1. Centres (1, 6.4), (1.5, 7.5), (2.33, 8.67); J = 142, 26.84, 15.50, 9.33, as in B1. From 4 and 7 the first assignment is already final and the run ends at the same centres.
E2. Two updates: J goes 3.478 → 1.814 → 1.811 (in the units of the unit square). With random points as starts, 94 of 100 runs reach J = 1.811; the other 6 stop between 7.6 and 8.4, with two centres in one blob and one centre between the other two blobs. With k-means++: 99 of 100.
E3. J = 26 and step changes nothing (B2). With random starts, 80 of 100 runs reach 1.5 and 20 stop at 26. The k-means++ seeds land at 10, 0 and 5, one per pair, and one update gives J = 1.5.
E4. Each group gets one end of both cigars: the boundary is a straight line across them, and only 125 of the 160 points are grouped as in the two cigars. The final J is 3.08, lower than 5.51 for the true split. k-means did what it was asked: the true groups simply do not minimise J. A model with elongated groups is needed (units 2–3).
E5. The boundary is halfway between the two centres, which is inside the spread of the big group, not in the gap. The groups come out as 108 and 42 points instead of 120 and 30: about 12 points of the big group are given to the small one.
E6. At y \times 1 k-means splits the bands into a left and a right half (73 of 140 points agree with the bands, i.e. chance level): the bands are long in x, and cutting them across lowers J most. At y \times 1.5 the vertical gap between the bands counts 2.25 times more in the squared distances, and k-means separates the two bands (all 140 points). Nothing in the data changed, only the units.

title: Exercise: feature spaces and k-means
text:
Where this leads
k-means draws straight boundaries between round groups of equal size, and every point belongs to exactly one group. The next unit replaces each group by a Gaussian with its own shape (covariance), size and weight, and gives every point a probability of belonging to each group. Unit 3 fits that model with EM, which turns out to be a “soft” k-means.

title: 3D images
text:
About this lecture
So far every image was 2D. CT and MRI scanners, confocal and light-sheet microscopes and electron microscopes all deliver 3D images: stacks of slices.

A volume is a 3D array plus its voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), often with \Delta z > \Delta x.
Voxel ↔︎ world: one 4 \times 4 matrix turns an index into a position in µm or mm, and back.
Trilinear interpolation, orthogonal and oblique slices, resampling: inverse mapping one dimension up.
Anisotropy in practice: filter sizes and neighbourhoods in physical units.
A first maximum-intensity projection, and what it hides.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the course’s unit on 3D images. The rest of this day (marching squares and cubes, measuring surfaces), the 3D-graphics day, and the 3D remarks on the labelling, morphology, skeleton, measurement, FFT-registration and moments days all point back here. Prerequisites: the “Images as arrays” unit (inverse mapping, bilinear interpolation) and a 4 × 4 matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates (one line of linear algebra). Timing: about 45 minutes of lecture, 45 of exercise.

title: 3D images
text:
Where 3D images come from








Instrument
Typical voxel size
Shape of the voxel




CT (X-ray tomography)
0.5 mm
about a cube


MRI
1 mm, slices often 3–5 mm
flat in plane, long across slices


Confocal microscope
0.1 µm in x, y, 0.3–0.5 µm in z
elongated along z


Light-sheet microscope
0.3–0.5 µm in x, y, 1–2 µm in z
elongated along z


Electron microscopy (serial sections)
5 nm in x, y, 30–50 nm in z
elongated along z




Microscopes take one 2D image per focus position: the stack. The step between images is \Delta z.
Why \Delta z is usually larger: the blur of a microscope is several times longer along the optical axis than across it (the elongated PSF of the image formation day), so finer steps in z would add little detail.

title: 3D images
section: A volume is an array plus its spacing
text:
A volume is an array plus its spacing





Values I[z, y, x]: slice z, row y, column x (as in images/: x right, y down, z along the stack).
Voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) in µm or mm: the distance between neighbouring voxel centres.
The array alone does not know its spacing. Drawn with \Delta z = \Delta x, a round nucleus becomes a flat pancake; its volume and surface come out wrong.


Always carry the spacing with the array, and do every measurement in physical units.

title: 3D images
section: From a voxel index to a position
text:
From a voxel index to a position
Voxel (i, j, k) = column i, row j, slice k. Its centre in the world (in µm):

step i times along the voxel’s x axis (length \Delta x), j times along y, k times along z,
starting from the position of voxel (0, 0, 0), the origin (e.g. the stage position).

Example: spacing (0.5, 0.5, 2) µm, origin (10, 20, 5) µm. Voxel (2, 3, 1) is at
(10 + 2 \cdot 0.5,\; 20 + 3 \cdot 0.5,\; 5 + 1 \cdot 2) = (11,\; 21.5,\; 7)\ \text{µm}.
Backwards, the world point (12.125, 21.75, 8.5) µm lies at voxel (4.25, 3.5, 1.75): between voxels, so we will need to interpolate.

title: 3D images
section: The math: the voxel → world matrix
text:
The math: the voxel → world matrix
In homogeneous coordinates one 4 \times 4 matrix does it:
\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = A \begin{bmatrix} i \\ j \\ k \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} R\,\mathrm{diag}(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}.

The columns of A are the three voxel axes (scaled by the spacing) and the origin \mathbf o. R is a rotation, when the axes of the scanner are tilted against the world (a tilted head in MRI); in a microscope R = I.
Spacing alone: A = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta x & 0 & 0 & o_x \\ 0 & \Delta y & 0 & o_y \\ 0 & 0 & \Delta z & o_z \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
World → voxel: A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathrm{diag}(1/\Delta)\,R^\top & -\mathrm{diag}(1/\Delta)\,R^\top\mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
Medical file formats store this matrix (or its parts) in their header. Warning: their axis conventions differ (which way x and y point, whether k counts up or down), so check with a known landmark.

title: 3D images
text:
Trilinear interpolation
To read the volume between voxels, interpolate in x, then in y, then in z: trilinear interpolation, the 3D version of bilinear interpolation from images/.

The point lies in a cube of 8 voxels. Its fractional position (f_x, f_y, f_z) in that cube sets the weights.
Example at (4.25, 3.5, 1.75): along x (f_x = 0.25) the four pairs 10, 20 \;\to\; 12.5; 30, 60 \to 37.5; 50, 50 \to 50; 90, 70 \to 85. Along y (f_y = 0.5): 25 and 67.5. Along z (f_z = 0.75): 25 + 0.75 \cdot 42.5 = 56.875.
The order (x first or z first) does not matter.

title: 3D images
text:
The math: trilinear weights
With f_x, f_y, f_z \in [0, 1] the position inside the cube and I_{abc} the corner values (a, b, c \in \{0, 1\}):
I(f_x, f_y, f_z) = \sum_{a,b,c \in \{0,1\}} I_{abc}\; w_a(f_x)\, w_b(f_y)\, w_c(f_z), \qquad w_0(f) = 1 - f,\; w_1(f) = f.

The 8 weights are \ge 0 and sum to 1: a weighted average of the corners.
It is linear along every line parallel to an axis, but not along other lines: on the diagonal f_x = f_y = f_z = t it is a cubic in t. (This is why level sets of the interpolant are curved, which matters in the next units.)
It reproduces exactly every function a + bx + cy + dz + exy + fyz + gxz + hxyz.

title: 3D images
text:
Slices: orthogonal and oblique

Orthogonal slices (xy, xz, yz) are array indexing: fix one index. Draw them with their physical aspect ratio (xz is n_x\Delta x wide and n_z\Delta z high).
An oblique slice is a plane at any angle: a centre \mathbf c and two orthogonal unit directions \mathbf u, \mathbf w in the world. For each output pixel (p, q):

world point \mathbf x = \mathbf c + p\,s\,\mathbf u + q\,s\,\mathbf w (pixel size s),
voxel position A^{-1}\mathbf x,
trilinear interpolation there.

This is inverse mapping from images/, one dimension up: loop over the output, ask where it comes from.
Resampling to isotropic voxels is the same loop over a new grid with spacing (\Delta x, \Delta x, \Delta x). It does not add detail along z; it only makes later steps simpler.

title: 3D images
section: Try it: slices of a stack
text:
Try it: slices of a stack




Synthetic nuclei stack: 64 × 64 × 20 voxels of 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.5 µm, origin (10, 20, 4) µm. Nuclei A and B overlap in x–y but sit at z = 2.8 and 7.2 µm; C is an elongated cell tilted 35° in the x–z plane; D is small. Tour: move the z slice and the y slice (j = 31 passes through A and B). Click a voxel in the xy slice and read its world position; check it against the matrix (row 1: 0.2 i + 10). “Ignored z spacing”: the header says Δz = 0.2, the box flattens and C’s tilt in the xz slice drops from 35° to 15.6°. “Oblique slice through the tilted cell”: a plane tilted −35° about y through C’s centre shows its full length, 7.2 µm. “Resample to isotropic”: 64 × 64 × 50 voxels, the matrix becomes 0.2 on the whole diagonal, and the slices look the same as before.

title: 3D images
text:
Anisotropy in practice
Work in physical units, convert to voxels per axis:

A Gaussian blur of \sigma = 0.4 µm in every direction is \sigma = 2 voxels in x and y but 0.8 voxels in z (spacing 0.2, 0.2, 0.5 µm). An “isotropic” \sigma = 2 voxels would blur 1 µm along z.
Derivatives (gradients, Sobel from kernels/): divide each difference by its own spacing.
Neighbourhoods: in 3D a voxel has 6 face neighbours, 18 with the edges, 26 with the corners (the 3D connectivities of the labelling day). With \Delta z \gg \Delta x the “neighbour” above is much further away than the one beside.
Distances: the distance transform and every size measure need the spacing.

title: 3D images
text:
The math: per-axis scale
A physical length \ell along axis a covers \ell / \Delta a voxels, so
\sigma_x^{\text{vox}} = \frac{\sigma}{\Delta x},\quad \sigma_y^{\text{vox}} = \frac{\sigma}{\Delta y},\quad \sigma_z^{\text{vox}} = \frac{\sigma}{\Delta z}, \qquad \frac{\partial I}{\partial z} \approx \frac{I[k+1] - I[k-1]}{2\,\Delta z}.

The 3D Gaussian is separable: blur along x, then y, then z, each with its own \sigma^{\text{vox}}; 3 passes of length \sim 6\sigma instead of one (6\sigma)^3 kernel.
With the gradient divided by voxels instead of µm, the z component is \Delta z / \Delta x times too large: the direction of \nabla I (and every normal computed from it) tilts.

title: 3D images
section: A first look: the maximum-intensity projection
text:
A first look: the maximum-intensity projection




MIP: for every (x, y), the largest value along z. One 2D image that shows every bright object, which is why microscopy figures use it.
What it hides:

Overlaps: nuclei at different depths merge into one blob.
Sizes: areas in the MIP are areas of the shadow, not of a section.
Depth: nothing tells you which object is in front.


Rule: look at MIPs, measure in 3D.

In the demo’s nuclei stack, thresholding at 100 finds 3 objects in the z-MIP (A and B merged) and 4 in 3D (26-connected labelling). Projections as a rendering method (MIP from any direction, volume rendering) are taught on the 3D-graphics day.

title: 3D images
text:
Slice by slice, or in 3D?

2D, slice by slice: segment each xy image on its own, then link the pieces across slices. Simple, but every slice decides alone: an object can break between slices, and two objects touching in one slice get merged.
3D: filters, thresholds, connected components, watershed and the rest work on the whole volume with 3D neighbourhoods; sizes and shapes are measured in 3D with the spacing.
With very coarse z (MRI slices of 5 mm), 2D per slice plus linking can be the honest choice: there is little 3D information to use.
Showing results: slices, projections, or a surface around each object. Surfaces are the rest of this day.

title: 3D images
text:
Summary

A 3D image = an array I[z, y, x] plus voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) and an origin; in microscopy usually \Delta z > \Delta x.
One 4\times4 matrix maps voxel indices to world positions; its inverse maps back.
Trilinear interpolation: a weighted average of 8 voxels. Oblique slices and resampling are inverse mapping + trilinear.
Blur, derivatives, neighbourhoods and measurements: in physical units, per axis.
The MIP is for looking, not for measuring: it merges objects at different depths.

title: Quiz: the DP principle
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Paths go from the top row to the bottom row of a cost image, one row down per step and at most one column sideways; M(i, j) is the cost of the cheapest path to pixel (i, j).

Q1. State the principle of optimality for minimal paths in one sentence. Why does it let us keep only one number per pixel?






Hint





What could you do if a part of the best path were not the best way to its end pixel?









Answer





Every part of an optimal path is itself optimal: if the best path to the bottom passes through p, its part up to p is the cheapest path to p (otherwise we could swap in the cheaper part). So for continuing paths only the cheapest way to reach p matters, and one number per pixel, M(p), is enough.




Q2. Three cells above pixel (i, j) have M = 12, 9, 15, and C(i, j) = 4. What is M(i, j), and where does its pointer point?






Answer





M(i, j) = 4 + \min(12, 9, 15) = 13; the pointer points to the middle cell (straight up), the one with 9.




Q3. Why does the greedy path (cheapest first pixel, then always the cheapest pixel below) usually fail?






Answer





It decides each step by looking only at the next pixel. A cheap step can lead into an expensive region that cannot be left in time, because a path moves at most one column per row. DP avoids this by not committing to any step before the whole table is filled: the path is chosen from the end.




Q4. An image gets twice as many rows (same width). Roughly what happens to the number of paths, and to the work of DP?






Hint





About m \cdot 3^{n-1} paths, about 3nm operations.









Answer





The number of paths is roughly squared (divided by m): 3^{2n-1} instead of 3^{n-1}, so astronomically more. The DP work only doubles: it grows linearly with the number of pixels.




Q5. You need only the cost of the best path, not the path. How much memory does DP need? And if you need the path?






Answer





For the cost, one row of M is enough: each row is computed from the previous one only. For the path, you also need the pointers of every cell (or the whole table M), to backtrack from the end.




Q6. In the two-label chain of the graph-cut day (E = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\,\#\{\text{label changes}\}), what are the stages, the states and the cost of a step? What is the “path”?






Answer





Stages: the pixels along the line. States: the two labels. Each pixel-and-label pays its data cost D_p(\ell), and a step that changes the label pays \lambda. The “path” is the labelling: one label per pixel. The same table, with 2 columns instead of m.




Q7. Why is one raster-order pass of the distance transform not enough, while one row-by-row pass is enough for monotone paths?






Answer





A monotone path only ever comes from above, so when row i is filled, everything it needs (row i-1) is final. For the distance transform, the shortest way to the nearest background pixel may come from below or from the right, which a top-to-bottom, left-to-right pass has not seen yet. Each pass is DP with a fixed order; neither order covers all paths.




Q8. (math) Paths go from the top-left to the bottom-right cell with steps right, down, or diagonally right-down. Write the recursion for M, and say in which order the table can be filled.






Answer





M(0, 0) = C(0, 0) and M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j),\ M(i, j-1),\ M(i-1, j-1)\big), with M = \infty outside the grid. Row by row, left to right (or column by column): all three cells on the right-hand side come earlier. This is the table that aligns two signals (dynamic time warping).

title: Quiz: 3D images
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Volumes are stored I[z, y, x] with voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z).

Q1. A confocal stack has \Delta x = \Delta y = 0.1 µm and \Delta z = 0.4 µm. A program shows the xz slice with square pixels. What does a round nucleus look like, and why?






Hint





How many rows does the nucleus span in z compared with columns in x?









Answer





Flattened by a factor 4: a nucleus 4 µm across spans 40 columns but only 10 slices, and with square pixels those 10 rows are drawn as tall as 10 columns. The slice must be drawn 4 times taller per row (its physical aspect ratio), or resampled.




Q2. Voxel (0, 0, 0) is at (100, 50, 0) µm and the spacing is (0.2, 0.2, 1) µm. Where is voxel (10, 20, 3)?






Hint





Start at the origin and step along each axis by index × spacing.









Answer





(100 + 10 \cdot 0.2,\; 50 + 20 \cdot 0.2,\; 0 + 3 \cdot 1) = (102, 54, 3) µm.




Q3. How many voxel values does trilinear interpolation use, and what is the result exactly halfway between all of them?






Hint





The point lies in a cube.









Answer





8 (the corners of the surrounding cube). At the centre every weight is \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac18: the mean of the 8 values.




Q4. To compute an oblique slice, why do we go from each output pixel to the volume, and not from each voxel to the plane?






Hint





How many voxels lie exactly on a tilted plane?









Answer





Inverse mapping: every output pixel asks where it comes from and gets one interpolated value. Pushing voxels onto the plane would hit only a few output pixels (almost no voxel lies exactly on the plane), leaving holes. The same reasoning as for rotating a 2D image.




Q5. You want to smooth a stack with \Delta x = 0.2 µm and \Delta z = 0.6 µm by the same physical amount in all directions, \sigma = 0.6 µm. What \sigma in voxels do you use along x and along z?






Hint





Divide the physical \sigma by the spacing of each axis.









Answer





0.6/0.2 = 3 voxels along x (and y), 0.6/0.6 = 1 voxel along z.




Q6. In a MIP along z you count 12 nuclei. Is the true number at most 12, at least 12, or neither?






Hint





What happens to two nuclei at different depths in the projection? Can one nucleus become two?









Answer





Usually at least 12: nuclei at different depths that overlap in x–y merge into one blob in the MIP, so the projection can only undercount by merging. (A strongly curved cell could in principle appear as two blobs, but that is rare; merging is the common error.) Count in 3D.




Q7. Does resampling a stack with \Delta z = 0.5 µm to isotropic voxels of 0.1 µm improve the resolution along z?






Hint





Where do the new values come from?









Answer





No. The new slices are interpolated from the old ones; nothing between the original slices was measured. Resampling makes later steps simpler (cubic voxels, equal neighbourhoods), but costs memory (5 times more voxels here) and adds no detail.




Q8. (math) Write the 4 \times 4 voxel → world matrix for spacing (0.2, 0.2, 0.5) µm and origin (10, 20, 4) µm, and its inverse.






Hint





Spacing on the diagonal, origin in the last column; for the inverse, undo the translation, then the scaling.









Answer





A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0.2 & 0 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 & -50 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & -100 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

fill the DP table of a minimal path by hand, and recover the path by backtracking,
explain why greedy choices fail and why trying all paths is hopeless,
count the operations of DP and the number of paths,
recognise the same recursion in the two-label chain (graph-cut day) and the distance transform (morphology day),
(math) prove the principle of optimality and count paths and operations in general.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Cost image C
one number per pixel; a path pays the sum of its pixels


Monotone path
one pixel per row, from the top row to the bottom row; each step goes one row down and at most one column sideways (↙ ↓ ↘)


Table M
M(i, j) = cost of the cheapest path from the top row to pixel (i, j)


Recursion
M(0, j) = C(0, j); M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j-1), M(i-1, j), M(i-1, j+1)\big)


Pointer
which of the cells above gave the minimum


Backtracking
start at the smallest M of the last row and follow the pointers up


Tie rule (demo)
on a tie, straight wins, then left, then right



Pixels are written (row, column), counting from 0; row 0 is the top.

Fill the 5 \times 5 table M and draw the pointers.
Find the cheapest path and its cost by backtracking.
The greedy path starts at the cheapest pixel of the top row and always steps to the cheapest of the (up to) three pixels below. Which path is that, and what does it cost? Where does it go wrong?

B2. Counting. (a) How many monotone paths does a 5 \times 5 image have? (Count them with the same kind of table: the number of paths that reach each cell.) Compare with m \cdot 3^{n-1}. (b) How many candidate evaluations (one addition and one comparison each) does filling the table of B1 take? (c) For a 100 \times 100 image: roughly how many paths, and how many evaluations? If a computer checks 10^9 paths per second, how long would trying them all take? (The age of the universe is about 4 \cdot 10^{17} s.)

The path, top to bottom, has columns 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 and costs 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 10. (a) Counting paths with the table N(0, j) = 1, N(i, j) = \sum N(\text{cells above}): the rows are (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), (2, 3, 3, 3, 2), (5, 8, 9, 8, 5), (13, 22, 25, 22, 13), (35, 60, 69, 60, 35): 259 paths. m \cdot 3^{n-1} = 5 \cdot 81 = 405 overestimates, because the border cells have only 2 cells above. (b) Rows 1–4 each have 3 interior cells with 3 candidates and 2 border cells with 2: 4 \cdot (9 + 4) = 52 evaluations. (c) About 1.5 \cdot 10^{49} paths, against 99 \cdot 298 = 29\,502 evaluations. At 10^9 paths per second: 1.5 \cdot 10^{40} s, about 4 \cdot 10^{22} times the age of the universe.
B3. (a) Stages = the pixels p = 1, \dots, 5; states = the labels 0 and 1; the “cost of a pixel” of the path is the data cost D_p(\ell); a step that keeps the label costs 0, a step that changes it costs \lambda. It is a minimal path through a grid with 5 rows and 2 columns, with a penalty \lambda on the sideways step. (b) D(0) = 9, 9, 1, 9, 0 and D(1) = 0, 0, 4, 0, 9. M_1 = (9, 0); M_2(0) = 9 + \min(9, 0 + 2) = 11, M_2(1) = 0 + \min(0, 9 + 2) = 0; M_3 = (1 + \min(11, 2),\ 4 + \min(0, 13)) = (3, 4); M_4 = (9 + \min(3, 6),\ 0 + \min(4, 5)) = (12, 4); M_5 = (0 + \min(12, 6),\ 9 + \min(4, 14)) = (6, 13). Minimum energy 6, with L_5 = 0; backtracking: L_5 = 0 came from L_4 = 1 (6 = 0 + 4 + 2), L_4 = 1 from L_3 = 1, L_3 = 1 from L_2 = 1, L_2 = 1 from L_1 = 1: the labelling 11110, the same as the graph-cut day’s B3.
B4. (a) After one pass, column 3 is 0, 1, 2 (correct), but all of columns 0–2 are still \infty: their nearest background pixel lies to the right, and the pass only looks up and left, so the information never reaches them. The true distances (city block) are \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 5 & 4 & 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. (b) The reverse raster order (bottom to top, right to left), looking down and right: D(i, j) \leftarrow \min\big(D(i, j), D(i+1, j) + 1, D(i, j+1) + 1\big). After it, all values are correct. Each pass is a Bellman recursion with its own fixed order; neither order alone covers paths that go both ways.
B5. Only entries that depend on (0, 4) can change: M(0, 4) becomes 1, and below it only cells whose minimum came through (0, 4). M(1, 4) = 2 + \min(8, 1) = 3 and M(1, 3) = 8 + \min(8, 8, 1) = 9; but row 2 then gives M(2, 4) = 8 + 3 = 11, M(2, 3) = 6 + \min(7, 9, 3) = 9, and the cheapest bottom value stays M(4, 1) = 10 (the right part of rows 2–4 is expensive). The best path does not change. Greedy starts at the same pixel as before and pays 1 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 = 17: still worse.




Math questions
B6. (math) Prove the principle of optimality for minimal monotone paths: if j_0, \dots, j_{n-1} is a cheapest path and 0 \le k < n-1, then j_0, \dots, j_k is a cheapest path from the top row to (k, j_k). Use it to prove by induction that the recursion gives M(i, j) = the cost of the cheapest path to (i, j).
B7. (math) (a) Show that the number of evaluations to fill an n \times m table (m \ge 2) is exactly (n-1)(3m-2). Check it for B2. (b) Show that the number of monotone paths P satisfies m \cdot 2^{n-1} \le P \le m \cdot 3^{n-1}.
B8. (math) Paths from the top-left to the bottom-right cell with steps right or down only. (a) Write the recursion for M and the order of filling. (b) Show that there are \binom{n + m - 2}{n - 1} such paths in an n \times m grid, and evaluate it for 5 \times 5.
B9. (math) Allow steps of up to \delta columns sideways with a penalty \alpha |d| for a step of d columns. Write the recursion and its cost in operations. Why does a large \alpha give straighter paths?






Solutions (math)





B6. Suppose j_0, \dots, j_k is not cheapest: some path j'_0, \dots, j'_k with j'_k = j_k costs less. Then j'_0, \dots, j'_k, j_{k+1}, \dots, j_{n-1} is a valid path (the step from j_k to j_{k+1} is unchanged) and costs less than the original, a contradiction. Induction: M(0, j) = C(0, j) is correct. If M(i-1, \cdot) is correct, a cheapest path to (i, j) passes through some (i-1, j+d), |d| \le 1, and by the principle its first part costs M(i-1, j+d); so the cheapest cost is C(i, j) + \min_d M(i-1, j+d), which is the recursion.
B7. (a) Rows 1, \dots, n-1 each have m - 2 interior cells with 3 candidates and 2 border cells with 2: 3(m-2) + 4 = 3m - 2 per row. For 5 \times 5: 4 \cdot 13 = 52. (b) With N(i, j) the number of paths to (i, j): every cell has at least 2 and at most 3 cells above it (for m \ge 2), so by induction 2^i \le N(i, j) \le 3^i. Summing over the m cells of the last row gives the bounds.
B8. (a) M(0, 0) = C(0, 0), M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j), M(i, j-1)\big), with M = \infty outside the grid; fill row by row, left to right (both right-hand cells come earlier in this order). (b) A path makes n - 1 down-steps and m - 1 right-steps in some order: choose which n - 1 of the n + m - 2 steps go down. For 5 \times 5: \binom{8}{4} = 70.
B9. M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min_{|d| \le \delta} \big(M(i-1, j+d) + \alpha|d|\big): 2\delta + 1 candidates per cell, about (2\delta+1)nm operations. A large \alpha makes every sideways step expensive, so the path changes column only where the costs of the image make it worth it: straighter, smoother paths. (\alpha = 0 and \delta = 1 is the case of B1.)

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Explore
The demo shows the cost image C (left; light = cheap) and the table M (right). step fills one cell: the candidates in the row above are outlined in blue, the chosen minimum is shaded green and an arrow points back to it (show pointers keeps all arrows). next stage fills a whole row, fill all the table, backtrack follows the arrows from the best cell of the last row; the last frame adds the greedy path (red “g”). The readout counts cells, operations and paths. Click the upper half of a cost cell to raise it by 1, the lower half to lower it. moves → ↓ switches to paths from the top-left to the bottom-right cell.



E1. Preset by-hand exercise grid. Step through the first two rows and compare every entry and arrow with your table from B1. Then fill all and backtrack. What are the operations and the number of paths at the end?
E2. Preset greedy fails. Before stepping, guess the best path. Then end: what do the optimal and the greedy path cost, and why does greedy fail here?
E3. Preset two equal optima. Which path does the demo report? Find the second path with the same cost. Why does the table report only one of them, and how would you change the backtracking to find both?
E4. Preset a detour. The cheap channel of 1s runs down, right, up, right and down again. What does the best monotone path cost, and where does it go? Find a cheaper path by hand if you are allowed to move up, down, left and right. Why can no row-by-row table find it?
E5. Back to by-hand exercise grid, now with moves → ↓. What does the cheapest path from the top-left to the bottom-right cost, how many paths are there, and how many operations does the table take? Check the path count with B8.
E6. Back to by-hand exercise grid (moves ↙ ↓ ↘). Predict first, then check: raise C(0, 1) from 4 to 9 (five clicks on its upper half). Which path is now the cheapest, and what does it cost? Does the greedy path change?






Solutions





E1. The table and arrows match B1. At the end: 25 of 25 cells filled, 52 operations, 259 paths; optimal cost 10, greedy 19.
E2. Optimal 9: straight down the right column, 3 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1. Greedy 20: it starts at the 1 in column 2 (the cheapest first pixel), then takes 2, and is then surrounded by 8s and 9s: 1 + 2 + 8 + 8 + 1. The cheapest first step leads into the most expensive region.
E3. The demo reports (0,2), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), (4,2): cost 1 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 9. Its mirror image (0,2), (1,3), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2) also costs 9. At (4, 2) the two candidates M(3, 1) = M(3, 3) = 8 tie, and the pointer stores only one (left wins). To find all optimal paths, store all tied predecessors (a set of pointers per cell) and backtrack along every branch.
E4. The best monotone path costs 24: down the channel in column 1 to row 5 (six 1s), then through two 9s and out at the bottom left: (0,1), \dots, (5,1), (6,0), (7,0). Following the channel costs 19 (nineteen cells of cost 1): down column 1, right along row 5 to column 3, up column 3 to row 2, right along row 2 to column 6, and down column 6 to the bottom. A row-by-row table only allows one cell per row and moves downwards, so it cannot represent a path that goes back up; and even if it could, M of a cell in row 2 would depend on cells in row 5, which are filled later. There is no fixed row order: the live-wire unit solves this with Dijkstra’s algorithm.
E5. Cost 32, along (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (2,1), (3,1), (3,2), (3,3), (3,4), (4,4); 70 paths, 40 operations (every cell except the first row and column has 2 candidates: 16 \cdot 2 + 8 \cdot 1 = 40). \binom{8}{4} = 70, as in B8.
E6. The old path loses its cheap start (it would now cost 15). The new optimum is 13: columns 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, that is 7 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2: it starts at the 7 and joins the old path in row 1. Greedy is unchanged (it starts at the 3 in the top-right corner): 19. Only the cells whose cheapest path ran through (0, 1) change in M (most of the table); the right column, whose paths never touch (0, 1), is unchanged.

title: Exercise: the DP principle
text:
Where this leads
The table filled row by row works because a monotone path has a natural order. The next unit turns the table sideways: a closed boundary around a nucleus becomes a path through a polar image, with one radius per angle. After that, the live-wire unit drops the fixed order altogether (Dijkstra’s algorithm), and the fast marching unit makes the path continuous.

title: Exercise: 3D images
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Volume
values I[z, y, x]: slice z, row y, column x


Voxel spacing
(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z): distance between neighbouring voxel centres (µm, mm)


Voxel → world
voxel (i, j, k) is at (o_x + i\,\Delta x,\; o_y + j\,\Delta y,\; o_z + k\,\Delta z); in general a 4\times 4 matrix A


World → voxel
\big((x - o_x)/\Delta x,\; (y - o_y)/\Delta y,\; (z - o_z)/\Delta z\big), i.e. A^{-1}


Trilinear
interpolate along x (4 pairs), then y (2 pairs), then z (1 pair)


Oblique slice
output pixel → world point on the plane → A^{-1} → trilinear


MIP
for every (x, y): the maximum over z









The math: the voxel → world matrix





\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf x \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = A \begin{bmatrix} i \\ j \\ k \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad A = \begin{bmatrix} R\,D & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad D = \mathrm{diag}(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), with R a rotation (R = I for a microscope stack) and \mathbf o the world position of voxel (0, 0, 0). Trilinear interpolation at fractional position (f_x, f_y, f_z) in a cube with corner values I_{abc}: I = \sum_{a,b,c \in \{0,1\}} I_{abc}\; w_a(f_x)\,w_b(f_y)\,w_c(f_z),\qquad w_0(f) = 1 - f,\ w_1(f) = f.

B4. The stack of B1 is to be smoothed with a Gaussian of \sigma = 1 µm in every direction. (a) What is \sigma in voxels along x, y and z? (b) A colleague uses \sigma = 2 voxels along all three axes. What is the physical \sigma along z then? What does that do to a thin, horizontal structure?
B5. A spherical nucleus of diameter 5 µm is imaged with spacing (0.2, 0.2, 0.5) µm. (a) How many slices does it cover? (b) The software ignores the spacing and treats the voxels as cubes of 0.2 µm. How tall does the nucleus appear, and by what factor is its volume underestimated? Give both volumes.
B6. An oblique slice of a stack with spacing (0.2, 0.2, 0.5) µm and origin (0, 0, 0) is defined by its centre \mathbf c = (6, 6, 5) µm, the in-plane directions \mathbf u = (1, 0, 0) and \mathbf w = (0, \cos 30°, \sin 30°), and a pixel size of 0.2 µm. Output pixel (p, q) lies at \mathbf c + 0.2\,p\,\mathbf u + 0.2\,q\,\mathbf w. (a) Where in the world is the output pixel (p, q) = (5, 10)? (b) At which voxel position must the stack be interpolated for it? (c) Why do we loop over the output pixels and not over the voxels?






Solutions





B1. (a) A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. (b) (10 + 2 \cdot 0.5,\; 20 + 3 \cdot 0.5,\; 5 + 1 \cdot 2) = (11, 21.5, 7) µm. (c) \big((12.125 - 10)/0.5,\; (21.75 - 20)/0.5,\; (8.5 - 5)/2\big) = (4.25, 3.5, 1.75). The surrounding voxels are i \in \{4, 5\}, j \in \{3, 4\}, k \in \{1, 2\}, and (f_x, f_y, f_z) = (0.25, 0.5, 0.75).
B2. (a) Along x with f_x = 0.25: 10 \to 20 gives 12.5; 30 \to 60 gives 37.5; 50 \to 50 gives 50; 90 \to 70 gives 85. Along y with f_y = 0.5: (12.5 + 37.5)/2 = 25 (slice k = 1) and (50 + 85)/2 = 67.5 (slice k = 2). Along z with f_z = 0.75: 25 + 0.75 \cdot (67.5 - 25) = 56.875. (b) The nearest voxel is (4, 4, 2) (rounding 4.25 \to 4, 3.5 \to 4 by rounding half up, 1.75 \to 2): 90. Nearest neighbour jumps; here it is far from the interpolated 56.9. (c) Yes: at (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) every weight is \tfrac18, so the value is the mean, (10 + 20 + 30 + 60 + 50 + 50 + 90 + 70)/8 = 47.5.
B3. (a) The MIP:

One object: the 9-block, the 8-block and the 7-pixels touch in the projection.
In 3D the 9-block (slice 0) and the 8-block (slice 2) are separated by the empty slice 1. The 7-pixels (slice 1, rows 3–4) touch the 8-block only diagonally: voxel (row 3, column 4, slice 1) and voxel (row 3, column 3, slice 2) differ by one column and one slice, an edge neighbour. With 6-connectivity: 3 objects; with 26-connectivity (and 18): 2.
Not the MIP’s 1. Between 2 and 3 we need the physical scale: whether two blobs that touch only diagonally across slices are one cell. With \Delta z much larger than \Delta x, a diagonal step across slices is a long way; 6-connectivity, or a size/shape check, is safer.

B4. (a) 1/0.5 = 2 voxels in x and y, 1/2 = 0.5 voxels in z. (b) 2 \cdot 2 = 4 µm along z: four times the intended blur. A thin horizontal structure (a membrane in the xy plane) is smeared over several slices and its contrast drops.
B5. (a) 5/0.5 = 10 slices. (b) 10 slices of 0.2 µm: it appears 2 µm tall, a flat ellipsoid with semi-axes 2.5, 2.5, 1 µm. True volume \tfrac43\pi\,2.5^3 = 65.45 µm³; apparent \tfrac43\pi \cdot 2.5 \cdot 2.5 \cdot 1 = 26.18 µm³, a factor 0.2/0.5 = 0.4.
B6. (a) (6, 6, 5) + 1 \cdot (1, 0, 0) + 2 \cdot (0, 0.866, 0.5) = (7, 7.732, 6) µm. (b) (7/0.2,\; 7.732/0.2,\; 6/0.5) = (35, 38.66, 12): between rows 38 and 39 of slice 12; interpolate (here only along y). (c) Looping over the output gives every output pixel exactly one value. Looping over voxels and pushing each to the plane would leave holes (most voxels do not lie on the plane) and needs a rule for collisions. It is inverse mapping, as in images/.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the inverse of A = \begin{bmatrix} RD & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} (R a rotation, D diagonal with positive entries) is \begin{bmatrix} D^{-1}R^\top & -D^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Check it on B1(c).
B8. (math) (a) Show that the 8 trilinear weights are non-negative and sum to 1. (b) Show that the interpolant is linear along every line parallel to a coordinate axis, but cubic in t along the diagonal (t, t, t). (c) Show that trilinear interpolation reproduces every function a + bx + cy + dz + exy + fyz + gxz + hxyz exactly, and that these 8 functions are as many as there are corners.
B9. (math) The nuclei stack of the demo has 64 \times 64 \times 20 voxels of 0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.5 µm. (a) How many voxels does it have after resampling to isotropic voxels of 0.2 µm? (b) Show that resampling a function that is linear in z along z reproduces it exactly, and give an example of what resampling cannot recover.






Solutions (math)





B7. Multiply: \begin{bmatrix} RD & \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} D^{-1}R^\top & -D^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} RDD^{-1}R^\top & -RDD^{-1}R^\top\mathbf o + \mathbf o \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} I & \mathbf 0 \\ \mathbf 0^\top & 1 \end{bmatrix}, using RR^\top = I. For B1, R = I: D^{-1}(\mathbf x - \mathbf o) = \big(2.125/0.5,\; 1.75/0.5,\; 3.5/2\big) = (4.25, 3.5, 1.75).
B8. (a) Each weight is a product of three factors in [0, 1]. The sum factorises: \sum_{a,b,c} w_a(f_x)w_b(f_y)w_c(f_z) = \big(w_0(f_x) + w_1(f_x)\big)\big(w_0(f_y)+w_1(f_y)\big)\big(w_0(f_z)+w_1(f_z)\big) = 1 \cdot 1 \cdot 1. (b) With f_y, f_z fixed, every term is (1 - f_x) or f_x times a constant: linear in f_x. On the diagonal each weight is a product of three factors t or 1 - t, e.g. w_1w_1w_1 = t^3: a cubic. (c) Each of the 8 functions is a product of factors that are linear along each axis separately; trilinear interpolation is exact for 1, x, y, z along each axis and the product structure carries this over (check xyz: corner values abc, interpolant \sum abc\,w_a w_b w_c = f_x f_y f_z). The interpolant is determined by its 8 corner values, and these 8 functions are linearly independent, so they span all trilinear interpolants.
B9. (a) z: 20 \cdot 0.5/0.2 = 50 slices, so 64 \cdot 64 \cdot 50 = 204\,800 voxels instead of 81\,920 (2.5 times more). (b) Along z the resampling is linear interpolation between neighbouring slices, which is exact for a linear function. It cannot recover detail between the original slices: a structure thinner than 0.5 µm that fell between two slices stays missing, and the axial blur of the microscope stays.

text:
Explore: the volume viewer
The demo shows a synthetic stack of nuclei: 64 \times 64 \times 20 voxels of 0.2 \times 0.2 \times 0.5 µm, origin (10, 20, 4) µm, grey values about 10 (background) to 200. Nuclei A and B overlap in x–y at different depths, C is an elongated cell tilted in the x–z plane, D is a small nucleus. The 3D view (drag to rotate) shows the box with the xy slice, the xz slice and the oblique plane; the 2D panels show the slices with their physical aspect ratio and the MIP along z. Click the xy or xz slice to read a voxel. Δz in the header is the spacing the software believes (the true value is 0.5 µm). The readout shows the voxel → world matrix and the number of objects above 100 in the MIP and in 3D.



E1. Preset slices. Set the z slice to k = 6 and click the centre of the large nucleus (near column 23, row 30). Read the world position and check it with the matrix by hand. Which row of A gives the z coordinate?
E2. Preset two nuclei merge in the MIP, not in 3D. How many objects does the readout count in the MIP and in 3D? Which two nuclei merge? Use the xz slice (j = 31) and the oblique panel (here a vertical plane) to see why. At what depths (in µm) are their centres?
E3. Preset ignored z spacing squashes the cell. What changes in the matrix, in the box and in the xz slice? The cell C is tilted by 35° in the true geometry: estimate its tilt in the squashed xz slice, and explain the number with \tan.
E4. Now set Δz in the header to 1.0 µm (too large). What happens to the shape of the box and to the tilt of C?
E5. Preset an oblique slice through the tilted cell. The plane is tilted by −35° about y and passes through C’s centre. How long and how wide is C in this slice (count pixels: the oblique slice has pixels of 0.22 µm)? Move tilt about y to 0°: why does C look shorter?
E6. Preset resample to isotropic. How many voxels does the volume have now, and what does the matrix look like? Do the slices show more detail than before?






Solutions





E1. Voxel (23, 30, 6) has the value 198 (a nucleus) and lies at (10 + 23 \cdot 0.2,\; 20 + 30 \cdot 0.2,\; 4 + 6 \cdot 0.5) = (14.6, 26, 7) µm. The third row of A, (0, 0, 0.5, 4), gives z = 0.5\,k + 4.
E2. MIP 3 objects, 3D 4 objects (threshold 100). Nuclei A and B merge in the MIP: they overlap in x–y, but in the xz slice A sits higher (centre at z = 2.8 µm above the origin, slice 5.6) and B lower (z = 7.2 µm, slice 14.4), with background between them. In the 3D labelling they are separate objects.
E3. The third diagonal entry of A drops from 0.5 to 0.2, the box becomes 4 µm deep instead of 10, and every structure is flattened by 0.4 along z. The cell’s tilt in the xz slice drops from 35° to about 16°: a slope \tan 35° = 0.70 becomes 0.70 \cdot 0.2/0.5 = 0.28, i.e. \arctan 0.28 = 15.6°. Angles, lengths, areas and volumes measured in this geometry are all wrong.
E4. The box becomes 20 µm deep (twice the truth); C now looks steeper: \arctan(0.70 \cdot 1.0/0.5) = 54.5°.
E5. About 33 pixels long and 11 wide, i.e. about 7.2 µm by 2.4 µm: the full length 2 \cdot 3.6 µm and width 2 \cdot 1.2 µm of the cell. At 0° the plane is an xy plane through C’s centre: it cuts the tilted cell at an angle, through its narrow direction, so the section is only about 3.8 µm long (17 pixels).
E6. 64 \times 64 \times 50 = 204\,800 voxels; the matrix has 0.2 on the whole diagonal and the same origin. The slices look the same, slightly smoother along z: resampling interpolates between existing slices and adds no information.

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
About this lecture
Many image problems ask for the cheapest path: a boundary along dark pixels, a seam through an image, an alignment of two signals. There are far too many paths to try them all. Dynamic programming (DP) finds the best one exactly, with a table and a few additions.

The question: the cheapest path from the top row to the bottom row of a cost image.
Why trying all paths fails, and why the greedy choice fails.
The key idea: an optimal path is made of optimal sub-paths.
Fill a table row by row, then backtrack to read off the path.
The general recipe, and two old friends that are the same recursion: the two-label chain of the graph-cut day and the distance transform.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This is the first unit of the dynamic-programming day (elective group “Curves and energies”, after snakes and level sets). Everything here is sums, minima and a table; no probability. The next units turn the same table sideways (closed boundaries in polar coordinates), drop the fixed order (Dijkstra, live-wire), and go continuous (fast marching).

The cost of a path is the sum of its five pixels. Try to guess the best path before the next slide.

Give the class a minute. Most people start at the 3 in the top right (the cheapest first pixel) or look for the column of small numbers. The answer is 10, along columns 1, 0, 1, 1, 1; the “start at the cheapest pixel and keep going downhill” path costs 19.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Why not try all paths?

From each pixel there are 3 ways down (2 at the image border). A path through n rows has n - 1 steps, so there are about m \cdot 3^{n-1} paths in an image with m columns.
5 \times 5: 259 paths (405 without the border effect). Still possible by hand, barely.
100 \times 100: about 1.5 \cdot 10^{49} paths.
256 \times 256: about 10^{124} paths, more than the roughly 10^{80} atoms in the observable universe.

Trying them all is hopeless. We need a way to reuse work: the paths overlap almost everywhere.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Greedy fails
The obvious shortcut: start at the cheapest pixel of the top row and always step to the cheapest of the three pixels below.

In the example: start at 3 (top right), then 2, 6, 2, 6: 19.
The best path costs 10: 4, 2, 1, 1, 2. Its first pixel (4) is not the cheapest one.

A cheap first step can lead into an expensive region. To decide the first step well, we must know what comes later. Dynamic programming turns this around: it works out the best way to reach every pixel, so no decision is made too early.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The key idea: optimal sub-paths
Suppose the best path to the bottom passes through pixel p. Then its part from the top to p must be the best path to p: if there were a cheaper way to reach p, we could swap it in and get a cheaper path to the bottom.
So we only ever need to remember one number per pixel:

M(p) = the cost of the cheapest path from the top row to p.

and, for pixel p in row i, it is known as soon as row i - 1 is known:

M(p) = cost of p + the smallest M among the (up to) three pixels above it.

This is Bellman’s principle of optimality (1957).
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The math: the Bellman recursion
Cost image C(i, j), rows i = 0, \dots, n-1, columns j = 0, \dots, m-1. A path is j_0, j_1, \dots, j_{n-1} with |j_{i} - j_{i-1}| \le 1, cost \sum_i C(i, j_i).
M(0, j) = C(0, j), \qquad M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min_{d \in \{-1, 0, 1\}} M(i-1, j+d) \quad (i \ge 1),
with M = \infty outside the image. Store the minimising d as a pointer B(i, j). The optimal cost is \min_j M(n-1, j); the path follows the pointers back from that cell.
Why it is correct (by induction on i): every path to (i, j) comes from one of the three cells above, and its cost is C(i, j) plus the cost of its part up to row i - 1, which is at least M(i-1, j+d). The recursion takes the best of these lower bounds, and it is reached by extending the optimal path to that cell.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Filling the table, then backtracking


Row 0 of M copies the costs. Row 1: M(1,0) = 2 + \min(7, 4) = 6; M(1,1) = 9 + \min(7, 4, 8) = 13; …
Each cell also remembers which cell above gave the minimum: a pointer.
At the end, the smallest M in the last row is 10. Follow the pointers back up: columns 1, 0, 1, 1, 1.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Try it: the table step by step
text:
Try it: the table step by step




Left: the costs; right: the table M. “step” fills one cell: the candidates in the row above are outlined, the chosen minimum is shaded green and an arrow points back to it. “next stage” fills a whole row, “fill all” the table, “backtrack” follows the arrows from the best cell of the last row; the last frame adds the greedy path (red “g”). Tour: by-hand grid (10 against greedy 19; 52 operations against 259 paths). “greedy fails”: 9 against 20. “two equal optima”: both mirror paths cost 9; the table keeps one pointer per cell (on a tie: straight, then left, then right), so it reports one of them. “a detour”: the cheap channel turns back upwards; no monotone path can follow it (cost 24). That is the cliffhanger for the live-wire unit. Click the upper half of a cost cell to raise it, the lower half to lower it.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
What it costs

Each cell looks at (at most) 3 cells above: one addition and one comparison each. An n \times m image needs about 3nm operations.
5 \times 5: 52 operations instead of 259 paths. 256 \times 256: about 195 000 operations instead of 10^{124} paths.
Memory: the whole table and the pointers to recover the path; if only the cost is wanted, the previous row is enough.

The trick is the overlap: the cheapest way to each pixel is computed once and reused by every path that continues from it.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: The math: counting paths and operations
text:
The math: counting paths and operations
Let N(i, j) be the number of paths from row 0 to (i, j). Then N(0, j) = 1 and N(i, j) = \sum_{d} N(i-1, j+d): the same recursion with (+, \text{sum}) in place of (+, \min).

Every cell has between 2 and 3 cells above it (for m \ge 2), so m \cdot 2^{n-1} \le \sum_j N(n-1, j) \le m \cdot 3^{n-1}: exponential in n.
The table needs one candidate per (cell, step): (n-1)(3m - 2) evaluations (the two border cells of each row have 2 candidates). Linear in the number of pixels.
With 2\delta + 1 allowed steps instead of 3: O(nm\delta) work, about m(2\delta+1)^{n-1} paths.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
The recipe
Dynamic programming in four steps:

Stages and states: here the rows are the stages and the column of the path is the state.
A recursion: the best value of a state from the best values of the previous stage.
An order in which every right-hand side is known before it is needed: here, row by row.
Backtracking: store where each minimum came from, and follow it back from the best final state.

Step 3 is the condition that matters later: if no such order exists, plain DP does not work (the live-wire unit).
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Same recursion, other states: the two-label chain
text:
Same recursion, other states: the two-label chain
Recall from the graph-cut day (unit Segmentation as energy minimisation): the best labelling of a 1D profile, E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\,\#\{p : L_p \ne L_{p+1}\}, solved exactly by DP.

Stage = pixel p, state = its label 0 or 1. The table has two numbers per pixel.
Transition cost \lambda when the label changes: a “path” through a 2-column grid with a step penalty.
This is the Viterbi algorithm; the same idea decodes signals and aligns speech.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Try it: the two-label chain




The demo is the graph-cut day’s own demo, embedded unchanged. Only make the link: two states per stage instead of m, and a penalty λ on a “sideways” step. The exercise (B3) fills the two-state table for the graph-cut day’s 1 × 5 example.

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Same recursion, other steps
The recursion does not care what the steps are, as long as each one goes back in the filling order.

One row down, up to \delta columns sideways, with a penalty \alpha |d| for a step of d columns: smoother paths. The next unit uses this for closed boundaries.
Right or down (top-left to bottom-right): M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j),\ M(i, j-1)\big). Fill row by row, left to right. In the demo: moves → ↓. Adding the diagonal step gives the table used to align two signals (dynamic time warping).
Seams through an image (seam carving) are the ↙↓↘ case on an energy image.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
section: Same recursion, other order: the distance transform
text:
Same recursion, other order: the distance transform
Recall from the morphology day: the two-pass (chamfer) distance transform. Its first pass is
D(i, j) = \min\big(D(i, j),\ D(i-1, j) + 1,\ D(i, j-1) + 1\big)
in raster order: a Bellman recursion where the “previous stage” is the pixel above and the pixel to the left.

One pass is not enough: a pixel whose nearest background lies below or to the right gets the wrong value. A second pass in the opposite order fixes this case.
So what happens when the best path may go up, down, left and right, and no fixed order works at all? That is the live-wire unit: let the algorithm discover the order.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
When is DP exact?

DP is exact when the problem is a chain (one state per stage, each stage talks only to the next) or a tree, so that there is an order in which everything needed is already known.
A 2D labelling with neighbours in both directions is not a chain: the grid has loops. The graph-cut day solves binary 2D labellings exactly in another way (max-flow, for submodular energies).
A boundary that can be written as one value per stage (one column per row, one radius per angle) is a chain, so DP finds the global optimum, however many local minima the image has.
crumbs: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid

title: The DP principle: minimal paths on a grid
text:
Summary

The cheapest path through a cost image cannot be found by trying all paths (\sim 10^{124} for 256 \times 256) or greedily.
Principle of optimality: the best path to the end is made of best paths to its intermediate pixels.
Fill the table M = cost + the smallest M above, row by row; store pointers; backtrack from the best final cell.
About 3nm operations, exact.
The recipe (stages, states, recursion, order, backtracking) also gives the two-label chain (Viterbi) and the passes of the distance transform.

title: Quiz: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Local field u_p = J\sum_{q \sim p}s_q + h; p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{neighbours}) = 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T}); J = 1, h = 0 unless stated.

Q1. Why can a sampler update one pixel without knowing Z?






Hint





Compare the two states that differ only in that pixel.









Answer





The update only needs the ratio of the probabilities of two states that differ in one pixel, e^{-\Delta E/T}, and Z cancels in a ratio. \Delta E involves only the pixel and its neighbours.




Q2. A pixel’s four neighbours are all +1. At T = 2, what is the probability that the Gibbs sampler sets it to -1?






Hint





u_p = 4.









Answer





1 - 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 1/(1 + e^{4}) = 0.018. Rare, but it happens: at T = 2 an aligned region still has a few isolated flipped pixels.




Q3. In Metropolis, a proposed flip raises the energy. Is it always rejected? Why does that matter?






Hint





What would the algorithm do if it only went downhill?









Answer





No: it is accepted with probability e^{-\Delta E/T}. Without uphill moves the chain would only descend and stop in the nearest local minimum (that is ICM, next unit); with them it visits states in proportion to their Gibbs probability.




Q4. What is detailed balance, in words?






Hint





Think of traffic between two states after the chain has run for a long time.









Answer





In the long run, the chain moves from state a to state b exactly as often as from b to a: \pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_bP_{ba}. A chain built this way keeps \boldsymbol\pi unchanged, so if it converges at all, it converges to \boldsymbol\pi. Metropolis is built so that this holds for the Gibbs distribution.




Q5. A sampler is started from a noisy image. Why do we throw away the first sweeps, and why are 1000 kept sweeps worth less than 1000 independent samples?






Hint





Where does the chain start, and how much does one sweep change?









Answer





The start is not a typical state of the distribution; the first sweeps (the burn-in) still remember it. And consecutive states share most pixels: they are strongly correlated, so averages over them converge more slowly than over independent samples.




Q6. Describe a typical state of a large 2D Ising lattice below, at and above T_c \approx 2.27.






Hint





Think of domain sizes and of |m|.









Answer





Below: one sign dominates, with small islands of the other (|m| near 1). At T_c: clusters of all sizes, a fractal-looking pattern. Above: fine-grained noise with small clusters (m \approx 0).




Q7. Why is a 1D chain never ordered at T > 0, while a 2D lattice is below T_c?






Hint





What does it cost to cut a domain in two?









Answer





In 1D one disagreeing pair (cost 2J) splits a chain into two domains, and there are many places to put it: at any T > 0 walls appear with a finite density and the signs average out. In 2D a wall around a domain costs energy proportional to its length; below T_c that cost beats the number of ways to draw the wall, and large domains are stable.




Q8. Simulated annealing is cooled too fast (a quench). What typically goes wrong?






Hint





What can the lattice still do at very low T?









Answer





Domains form everywhere at once and freeze: at low T only downhill flips are accepted, so walls that would need an uphill flip to move stay forever. The result is a local minimum, not the ground state.




Q9. (math) Show that the Metropolis rule satisfies detailed balance for the Gibbs distribution when E_b > E_a and the proposal is symmetric.






Answer





P_{ab} = q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T} and P_{ba} = q (downhill is always accepted). Then \pi_aP_{ab} = \frac{e^{-E_a/T}}{Z}q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T} = \frac{e^{-E_b/T}}{Z}q = \pi_bP_{ba}.

title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the local conditional probability of a pixel given its neighbours,
carry out one Gibbs and one Metropolis update by hand,
set up the transition matrix of a two-state chain, find its long-run distribution and check detailed balance,
describe the phase transition of the 2D Ising model from a simulation, and critical slowing down,
explain why simulated annealing must cool slowly, and what a quench does.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.
