title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Local field
u_p = J\sum_{q \sim p}s_q + h: the neighbours’ vote for +1


Local conditional
p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{neighbours}) = 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T})


Energy change of a flip
\Delta E = 2s_pu_p (s_p = the value before the flip)


Gibbs sampler
set s_p = +1 with the local conditional probability, else -1


Metropolis
flip if \Delta E \le 0; otherwise flip with probability e^{-\Delta E/T}


Sweep
one update of every pixel


Stationary distribution
\boldsymbol\pi with \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi (row vector, P_{ab} = probability a \to b)


Detailed balance
\pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_bP_{ba} for every pair of states


Critical temperature
T_c = 2J/\ln(1 + \sqrt2) \approx 2.27 for the square lattice



Unless stated otherwise: J = 1, h = 0, 4-neighbours.

title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
By hand
B1. A pixel has neighbours (+, +, +, -). (a) Compute u_p and p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{neighbours}) at T = 1, T = 2 and T = 4. (b) The same with neighbours (+, +, -, -), and with (+, +, +, +) at T = 2. (c) Add a field h = 0.5 to (b)’s first case. What changes?
B2. Metropolis. The same pixel is +1 with neighbours (+, +, +, -). (a) What is \Delta E of flipping it to -1? With which probability is the flip accepted at T = 2, and at T = 0.5? (b) The pixel is -1 with the same neighbours. What is \Delta E of flipping it to +1, and the acceptance probability?
B3. Gibbs or Metropolis. For the pixel of B2 at T = 2: (a) After one Gibbs update, what is the probability that it is +1, if it was +1 before? If it was -1 before? (b) The same for one Metropolis update. (c) Which of the two changes the pixel more often? Show that in both cases the long-run fraction of time at +1 (with the neighbours held fixed) is the same, and give it.
B4. A two-state chain. Two states a and b with energies E_a = 0, E_b = 1, T = 1. Metropolis proposes the other state at every step. (a) Write the transition matrix P. (b) Find \boldsymbol\pi = (\pi_a, \pi_b) with \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi and \pi_a + \pi_b = 1. (c) Check detailed balance, and that \boldsymbol\pi is the Gibbs distribution. (d) Start in a. What is the probability of being in a after 1, 2 and 3 steps? How fast does it approach \pi_a?
B5. Predict. Sketch what a typical state of a large lattice looks like at T = 1, T = 2.27 and T = 5 (h = 0). What is |m| roughly in each case? What does a small field h = 0.05 change at T = 1.8, and at T = 5?
B6. Cooling. (a) A geometric schedule should go from T_0 = 4 to T = 0.5 in 100 sweeps. What is the factor r per sweep? (b) With the logarithmic schedule T_k = 4/\ln(k + 2), after how many sweeps is T = 0.5? And T = 0.1? (c) Why does a quench to T = 0.5 from random spins usually not reach the ground state of a large lattice?






Solutions





B1. (a) u_p = 1 + 1 + 1 - 1 = 2. T = 1: 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 0.982; T = 2: 1/(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.881; T = 4: 1/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.731. (b) (+, +, -, -): u_p = 0, probability \tfrac12 at every T. (+, +, +, +): u_p = 4, at T = 2: 1/(1 + e^{-4}) = 0.982. (c) u_p = 0 + 0.5 = 0.5: 1/(1 + e^{-0.5}) = 0.622 at T = 2. The field breaks the tie.
B2. (a) \Delta E = 2s_pu_p = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 = 4: accepted with e^{-2} = 0.135 at T = 2 and e^{-8} = 0.00034 at T = 0.5. (b) \Delta E = 2 \cdot (-1) \cdot 2 = -4: downhill, always accepted.
B3. (a) Gibbs ignores the old value: +1 with probability 0.881 either way. (b) Metropolis from +1: stays +1 unless the flip is accepted: 1 - 0.135 = 0.865. From -1: always flips to +1: probability 1. (c) Gibbs changes the value with probability 0.119 (from +1) or 0.881 (from -1); Metropolis with 0.135 or 1: Metropolis changes it more often. Long run, Metropolis: balance \pi_+ \cdot 0.135 = \pi_- \cdot 1 gives \pi_+ = 1/(1 + 0.135) = 0.881, the same as Gibbs, and equal to the local conditional.
B4. (a) From a: uphill by 1, accept e^{-1} = 0.368. From b: downhill, always. P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.632 & 0.368 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}. (b) \pi_a = 0.632\pi_a + \pi_b gives \pi_b = 0.368\pi_a; with \pi_a + \pi_b = 1: \boldsymbol\pi = (0.731, 0.269). (c) \pi_aP_{ab} = 0.731 \cdot 0.368 = 0.269 = \pi_bP_{ba} = 0.269 \cdot 1. Gibbs: e^{0}/(e^0 + e^{-1}) = 0.731. The same. (d) After 1 step: 0.632; after 2: 0.632^2 + 0.368 \cdot 1 = 0.768; after 3: 0.768 \cdot 0.632 + 0.232 \cdot 1 = 0.717. The distance to 0.731 is 0.269 \cdot 0.368^k with alternating sign: -0.099, +0.036, -0.013. It shrinks by a factor 0.368 per step.
B5. T = 1: almost all spins equal; |m| \approx 1 (0.999). T = 2.27: clusters of every size, ragged; |m| fluctuates and is small for a large lattice. T = 5: noise with tiny clusters; |m| \approx 0. At T = 1.8, below T_c, the lattice has to choose a sign; a small field decides which, quickly and for the whole lattice. At T = 5 the field only shifts m slightly towards +.
B6. (a) r = (0.5/4)^{1/100} = 0.125^{0.01} = 0.979. (b) 4/\ln(k + 2) = 0.5: \ln(k + 2) = 8, k = e^8 - 2 = 2979 sweeps. T = 0.1: \ln(k + 2) = 40, k \approx 2.4 \cdot 10^{17} sweeps: hopeless. (c) Domains form everywhere at once. Their walls shrink only by flips that do not raise the energy; a straight wall across the whole (periodic) lattice cannot move without uphill flips, which at T = 0.5 are accepted with tiny probability. The lattice is stuck in a local minimum.




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive the local conditional p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{rest}) = 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T}) from the Gibbs distribution, and show that it depends on the rest only through the neighbours of p.
B8. (math) Show that detailed balance \pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_bP_{ba} implies \boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi. Show that the single-pixel Gibbs update satisfies detailed balance with respect to the Gibbs distribution.
B9. (math) For the chain of B4, find both eigenvalues of P and explain the factor 0.368 in B4(d).
B10. (math) In a long 1D chain at temperature T (no field), the fraction of disagreeing neighbour pairs is 1/(1 + e^{2J/T}). Evaluate it at T = 1 and T = 0.5. Use it to argue that a chain has no ordered phase at any T > 0.






Solutions (math)





B7. States \mathbf s^\pm differ only at p. Terms of E without s_p cancel in E(\mathbf s^-) - E(\mathbf s^+) = 2J\sum_{q \sim p}s_q + 2h = 2u_p. So p(\mathbf s^+)/p(\mathbf s^-) = e^{2u_p/T}, and p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{rest}) = p(\mathbf s^+)/(p(\mathbf s^+) + p(\mathbf s^-)) = 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T}). Only u_p appears: the neighbours.
B8. \sum_a\pi_aP_{ab} = \sum_a\pi_bP_{ba} = \pi_b\sum_aP_{ba} = \pi_b. Gibbs update at p: for \mathbf s^+ \ne \mathbf s^- (differing at p), P_{\mathbf s^-\mathbf s^+} = \pi(\mathbf s^+)/(\pi(\mathbf s^+) + \pi(\mathbf s^-)), so \pi(\mathbf s^-)P_{\mathbf s^-\mathbf s^+} = \pi(\mathbf s^-)\pi(\mathbf s^+)/(\pi(\mathbf s^+) + \pi(\mathbf s^-)), which is symmetric in the two states. A sweep is a sequence of such updates, each leaving \boldsymbol\pi stationary.
B9. Rows sum to 1, so \mu_1 = 1 (right eigenvector (1, 1)). The trace is 0.632 + 0 = 0.632, so \mu_2 = 0.632 - 1 = -0.368. Writing the start as \boldsymbol\pi plus a multiple of the other eigenvector, each step multiplies that part by \mu_2 = -0.368: the deviation shrinks by 0.368 and changes sign each step. The closer |\mu_2| is to 1, the slower the chain mixes.
B10. T = 1: 1/(1 + e^2) = 0.119; T = 0.5: 1/(1 + e^4) = 0.018. A chain of n pixels therefore has about 0.018n walls at T = 0.5 and 0.119n at T = 1: domains of typical length 55 and 8. However low T is, a long enough chain contains walls, and the two signs occupy equal shares on average: m = 0 for an infinite chain. (Derivation: with the transfer matrix, \langle s_is_{i+1}\rangle = \mu_2/\mu_1 = \tanh(J/T), and the fraction of disagreeing pairs is (1 - \tanh(J/T))/2 = 1/(1 + e^{2J/T}).)

title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Explore: sampling the 3 \times 3 lattice
The demo of the previous unit, in sample mode. One step updates one randomly chosen site (circled; dashed if it did not change) by Gibbs or Metropolis. The red dots are the fraction of all steps so far spent in each energy level (or magnetisation), the bars the exact probabilities.



S1. Preset sample: converges (T = 3, Gibbs). Use 1 step a few times: which values does the readout’s “seen” take, and why is it so far from p? Then play at 100 and 1000 steps per frame. After about how many steps do the dots sit on the bars? Compare the dot and the bar of the lowest level after 1000 and after 100 000 steps.
S2. Preset sample: low T, stuck (T = 1, Metropolis, magnetisation tab). Play at 1000 steps per frame. What do the dots show after 100 000 steps? Is the chain wrong? Switch to the energy tab: does the energy histogram look right?
S3. In the same preset, set T = 2 and restart (choose Metropolis again). What changes, and why?






Solutions





S1. After a few steps “seen” is 0 or a large fraction such as 0.5: the chain has visited only a handful of states. After 100 steps the dots are still far off (the lowest level has 0.19 against 0.377 exact); after 1000 steps 0.346, after 100 000 steps 0.385. Thousands of steps are needed for a few per cent of accuracy: the samples are correlated.
S2. All the mass sits at m = +1 and nearby; m = -1 never appears (the exact bars give both 0.498). The chain is correct but has not mixed: to reach the other ground state it would need to pass through states of much higher energy, starting with a flip of \Delta E = 8 (accepted with e^{-8} = 0.0003). The energy histogram nevertheless looks right (the two ground states have the same energy), which is why checking one statistic can hide a mixing problem.
S3. At T = 2 the chain switches sign every few hundred steps (a run started from all +1 switched 418 times in 100 000 steps), and both sides fill in. Uphill moves are far more likely (e^{-4} = 0.018 for \Delta E = 8).

title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Explore: a large lattice
A 256 \times 256 periodic lattice (choose 64^2 or 128^2 for speed), animated with Metropolis or Gibbs sweeps. Orange is +1, blue -1. The plots show the magnetisation m and the energy per spin E/n over the last 400 sweeps. Cool to 0.5 lowers T geometrically over the chosen number of sweeps; quench sets T = 0.5 at once. The T-scan tab runs its own 64 \times 64 lattice from T = 4 down to T = 1 and plots the average |m| against T with Onsager’s exact curve.



E1. Presets hot: noise, cold: domains coarsen and at T_c: all scales. Describe each lattice after a few hundred sweeps, and read m and E/n. Compare E/n at T_c with the exact -\sqrt2 = -1.414.
E2. In cold: domains coarsen, watch the domains. Do they all keep their size? What happens to E/n and why?
E3. Preset a small field decides (T = 1.8, h = 0.05). How quickly does m approach its final value? Set h = 0 and press random start: what happens now? Then try h = 0.05 at T = 4.
E4. Open the T-scan tab and run it. Where does \langle|m|\rangle follow Onsager’s curve, and where not? Why is it not 0 above T_c?
E5. Preset critical slowing down (128^2, T = 2.3, start all +1). How does m behave? Restart at T = 3 and at T = 2.5 (button all +1). Compare.
E6. Preset quench, then slow cooling (both 128^2). Compare the final states and their E/n. Which one is a local minimum, and why can it not escape at T = 0.5?






Solutions





E1. Hot (T = 5): noise, m \approx 0, E/n \approx -0.42. Cold (T = 1.5): domains of each sign that grow; with this seed one sign takes over (m = 0.986 after 1000 sweeps, E/n = -1.95). At T_c: ragged clusters of every size, from single pixels to most of the lattice; m wanders near 0 and E/n is -1.40 after 1000 sweeps, close to -1.414 (the small difference is the finite lattice and the remaining relaxation).
E2. Small domains shrink and vanish, large ones grow (coarsening): a domain wall costs energy per unit length, so the lattice lowers its energy by shortening walls. The number of disagreeing pairs falls from 9740 after 10 sweeps to 3396 after 100 and 1618 after 1000, and E/n falls accordingly (from -1.70 to -1.95).
E3. With h = 0.05: m = 0.82 after 20 sweeps and 0.96 after 50; it stays there. With h = 0 the lattice coarsens without a winner for a long time (m = -0.21 after 400 sweeps). At T = 4 the same field only shifts m to about 0.05 (average over sweeps 100–400): above T_c there is no order for the field to choose.
E4. Below T_c the points lie on Onsager’s curve (e.g. T = 2.0: 0.912 against 0.911; T = 2.2: 0.782 against 0.785). Above T_c the exact value for an infinite lattice is 0, but the 64 \times 64 lattice gives 0.03–0.13: a finite lattice always has some net magnetisation by chance (about 1/\sqrt{\text{cluster count}}), largest close to T_c where clusters are big (0.36 at T = 2.3).
E5. At T = 2.3, m falls from 1 to about 0.5 within 100 sweeps and then lingers there for hundreds of sweeps, although its long-run value is near 0: it reaches |m| < 0.1 only after 1580 sweeps. At T = 3 it takes 6 sweeps, at T = 2.5 29. Near T_c the large clusters must be taken apart pixel by pixel.
E6. Quench: domains form and coarsen, but with this seed the lattice ends in two stripes across the whole torus (m \approx 0.1, E/n \approx -1.966) and stays there. Slow cooling (from 3.5 to 0.5 over 300 sweeps): one domain, m = -1 (a ground state, apart from rare thermal flips). The stripes are a local minimum: their straight walls can only move by flips that raise the energy by 4 first (accepted with e^{-8} = 0.0003 at T = 0.5), so they effectively never do. With other seeds a quench may also reach one domain, and slow cooling may also end in stripes; slower cooling makes stripes rarer.

title: Exercise: sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Where this leads
So far the field h was the same for every pixel. In the next unit the field comes from a noisy image: the Ising model becomes a prior for the clean image, and sampling, annealing and the exact minimum cut become tools for Bayesian denoising.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
About this lecture
A threshold gives a ragged, leaky outline. Often we want something else: one smooth closed curve that sits on the edges of the object. An active contour, or snake (Kass, Witkin & Terzopoulos, 1988), is such a curve that moves by itself until it settles there.

A closed chain of beads: springs between neighbours, plus a pull towards edges.
The beads move downhill on an energy: internal (smooth, short) plus image (on edges).
The force on one bead, by hand: the neighbours’ midpoint, and a straightening term.
What the knobs do: elasticity \alpha, rigidity \beta, smoothing \sigma, step \tau.
What goes wrong: shrinking away, cut corners, stuck on noise, too far away, explosion.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Find the boundary of this nucleus
text:
Find the boundary of this nucleus


Left: a snake starts as a circle (dashed) around a noisy disk and shrinks onto its edge. Middle: the edge map, bright where the image changes. Right: the same on a micrograph.
A threshold would label pixels; the snake gives a curve: a list of points, smooth, closed, one object. Perimeter, curvature and shape come for free.


Right panel: the nucleus of the course micrograph (128 × 128), start circle centre (74, 57), radius 44, σ = 3, 500 steps: the outline runs along the dark nuclear envelope, with a short cut across at the lower left. The disk: radius 30, start radius 45; after 300 steps the mean radius is 29.79.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Recall: segmentation as energy minimisation
On the graph cuts day (seg-energy/) a segmentation was the labelling with the lowest energy: a data term (fit the image) plus \lambda times a smoothness term (short boundaries).
A snake uses the same recipe with a different unknown:









graph cut
snake




unknown
a label per pixel
the positions of n points on a closed curve


image term
grey level fits the label
the curve lies on edges


smoothness
boundary length, weight \lambda
stretching (\alpha) and bending (\beta)


minimised by
one max-flow, exact
moving the points downhill, step by step, locally



The snake finds a local minimum near where it starts. That is both its weakness (it needs a start) and its strength (it follows what you point it at).

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
A closed chain of beads
The curve is a polygon of n points \mathbf x_0, \dots, \mathbf x_{n-1}; after the last comes the first again.

Elastic springs between neighbours (weight \alpha): stretching costs energy. Each bead is pulled towards the midpoint of its two neighbours. A chain with springs alone contracts to a point.
Stiffness (weight \beta): bending costs energy. Each bead is pushed to make the chain locally straight; corners are expensive.
The image: low energy on edges. Each bead is pulled uphill on the edge map, towards the nearest strong edge, if there is one nearby.

The snake stops where the three forces balance at every bead.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Try it: a snake on a disk
text:
Try it: a snake on a disk




Disk of radius 30 (noise 0.05), start circle radius 45, n = 40, α = 0.1, β = 0.05, σ = 2, w = 2, semi-implicit τ = 1. Press play: the circle shrinks slowly (the elastic force is weak on a smooth circle): mean radius 39.7 after 50 steps, 34.9 after 100; then the edge catches it, and after 200 steps it sits at 29.78 and stays. The energy plot: the internal energy falls from 100.95 to 44.27, the image energy drops from about 0 to −70.9 when the snake reaches the edge. Switch the forces on (default) and the “edge map” view. Drag on the image to place a new circle. Then the presets: “α too large” (α = 1: the springs win, radius 0.2 after 500 steps), “β too large” (square, β = 2: rounded corners), “σ too small” (noise 0.25, σ = 0.5: stuck at radius 37–44), “too far” (α = 0.01: after 300 steps still at radius 53.4), “τ too large” (explicit step, explodes after 55 steps).

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: The forces on a square, by hand
text:
The forces on a square, by hand
Four beads at (1, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1), (1, -1), no image.

Elastic (\alpha = 1): bead (1, 1) has neighbours (-1, 1) and (1, -1), midpoint (0, 0). The force is \alpha \times (sum of the neighbours -\,2\times the bead) = (-1,1) + (1,-1) - 2(1,1) = (-2, -2): twice the way to the midpoint.
One step of size \tau = 0.1: (1, 1) + 0.1\,(-2, -2) = (0.8, 0.8). All four beads do the same: the square shrinks to 0.8 and stays a square.
Rigid (\beta = 1): the straightening force at the corner is (-4, -4) (math slide). With \alpha = \beta = 1: (-6, -6), and the step lands at (0.4, 0.4).

On a fine polygon, the elastic force at a bead is the difference with its neighbours: the same [1, -2, 1] as the second-derivative kernel of Filtering & convolution.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: The math: the snake energy and its force
text:
The math: the snake energy and its force
E = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \Big[\tfrac12\alpha\,|\mathbf x_{i+1} - \mathbf x_i|^2 + \tfrac12\beta\,|\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1}|^2 + E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x_i)\Big], \qquad \text{indices mod } n.
E is an ordinary function of 2n numbers. The force on bead i is -\partial E/\partial \mathbf x_i. Point \mathbf x_i appears in two elastic terms and three rigid terms:
-\frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathbf x_i} = \underbrace{\alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1})}_{\text{elastic}} \;\underbrace{-\,\beta(\mathbf x_{i-2} - 4\mathbf x_{i-1} + 6\mathbf x_i - 4\mathbf x_{i+1} + \mathbf x_{i+2})}_{\text{rigid}} \;-\, \nabla E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x_i).

[1, -2, 1] is the discrete second derivative; [1, -4, 6, -4, 1] = [1, -2, 1] * [1, -2, 1] is the fourth.
Square, \beta = 1, corner (1, 1): \mathbf x_{i\pm2} is the opposite corner (-1,-1), so -\big[(-1,-1) - 4(1,-1) + 6(1,1) - 4(-1,1) + (-1,-1)\big] = (-4, -4).
The internal forces sum to zero over all beads: moving the whole snake costs nothing.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The image term
The snake should sit where the image changes most. Smooth the image with a Gaussian of size \sigma, take the gradient (Filtering & convolution), and square its length: the edge map
f = |\nabla (G_\sigma * I)|^2, \qquad E_\text{ext} = -w\,f \quad (\text{low on edges}).

The image force on a bead is w\,\nabla f: it points uphill on the edge map, towards the ridge of the nearest edge.
Far from any edge f is flat and the force is zero: the snake does not feel the object. How far the pull reaches, the capture range, is a few \sigma.
Small \sigma: sharp, accurate edges, but noise makes its own little edges. Large \sigma: a wide pull, but blurred and slightly shifted edges.


1D check (exercise B5): an edge map f(x) = exp(−(x − 10)²/8) (edge at x = 10, width 2). Its slope f′ is +0.30 at x = 8 (push right, towards the edge), −0.30 at x = 12, and −0.00001 at x = 20: a bead 10 pixels away feels nothing. In the demo the largest inward image force on the disk is 0.69 (w = 2, σ = 2), at radius 31.5.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The math: the continuous snake (Euler–Lagrange)
Let the number of beads grow: a curve \mathbf x(s), s \in [0, L), closed. The sums become integrals:
E[\mathbf x] = \int_0^L \tfrac12\alpha\,|\mathbf x'(s)|^2 + \tfrac12\beta\,|\mathbf x''(s)|^2 + E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x(s))\;ds.
Change the curve a little, \mathbf x + \varepsilon\mathbf h. For the elastic term, integrate by parts (the curve is closed, so the boundary terms cancel):
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int \tfrac12\alpha|\mathbf x' + \varepsilon\mathbf h'|^2 ds\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = \int \alpha\,\mathbf x'\cdot\mathbf h'\,ds = -\int \alpha\,\mathbf x''\cdot\mathbf h\,ds.
The rigid term, integrated by parts twice, gives +\beta\mathbf x''''. A minimum needs the change to vanish for every \mathbf h: the Euler–Lagrange equation
-\alpha\,\mathbf x'' + \beta\,\mathbf x'''' + \nabla E_\text{ext}(\mathbf x) = 0:\qquad \text{internal force} + \text{image force} = 0.

The discrete stencils are exactly these derivatives with spacing 1. Circle \mathbf x(s) = r(\cos s, \sin s): \alpha\mathbf x'' = -\alpha\mathbf x, a force of size \alpha r towards the centre.

title: Active contours (snakes)
section: Moving the snake: one step at a time
text:
Moving the snake: one step at a time
Start from a curve near the object and repeat: compute the force on every bead, move every bead a little along it.
\text{new position} = \text{position} + \tau \times \text{force}

\tau (the step) small: the snake creeps downhill on the energy and stops where the forces balance.
\tau slightly too large: beads overshoot, the next force overshoots back, and a zig-zag grows until the snake explodes. With \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05 this happens above \tau \approx 1.67.
The image force is read at each bead’s (non-integer) position by bilinear interpolation.

Why exactly 1.67, and a step that never explodes: the next unit.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
The math: gradient descent
Stack all bead positions into one vector \mathbf x \in \mathbb R^{2n}. The update is gradient descent on E:
\mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t - \tau\,\nabla E(\mathbf x_t) = \mathbf x_t + \tau\,\mathbf F(\mathbf x_t).

For small enough \tau, E(\mathbf x_{t+1}) < E(\mathbf x_t) unless \nabla E = 0 (Taylor: E(\mathbf x - \tau\nabla E) = E - \tau|\nabla E|^2 + O(\tau^2)).
“Small enough” depends on how curved E is: the internal part has curvature up to \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta, and the step is stable while \tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2. For \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05: \lambda_\text{max} = 1.2, \tau < 1.67.
A fixed point is a solution of the discrete Euler–Lagrange equation: internal + image force = 0 at every bead.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Try it: what goes wrong




“concavity: cannot enter the U”: n = 100, α = 0.03, β = 0.01, resample every 10. The snake wraps the outside of the U and bridges the slot: after 800 steps its deepest point in the slot is at y = 15.6 (the slot ends at y = 77.5). The edge force inside the slot points sideways, at the slot walls, never down into it. Unit 2 fixes this with GVF. “two blobs”: one snake wraps both blobs and bridges the gap (half-height of the bridge 12.6 pixels at the centre): a snake has one outline, whatever the number of objects. “micrograph”: σ = 3, n = 60.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Not covered here, but close

Point spacing: the beads slide along the curve and bunch up in some places. The demo can resample the curve to equal spacing every k steps.
Searching instead of sliding: the greedy snake (Williams & Shah) tries a few positions around each bead and keeps the best. The dynamic-programming snake (Amini et al.) finds the exact best positions within a window for all beads at once: on the dynamic programming day.
Curves that split and merge: an explicit chain of beads cannot. Level sets represent the curve implicitly and can: on the level set day.

title: Active contours (snakes)
text:
Summary

A snake is a closed polygon that moves downhill on an energy: elastic (short), rigid (straight) and image (on edges) terms.
Force on a bead: \alpha pulls it towards its neighbours’ midpoint, \beta straightens, the image pulls it uphill on the edge map |\nabla(G_\sigma * I)|^2.
Balance at every bead = a local minimum = the Euler–Lagrange equation -\alpha\mathbf x'' + \beta\mathbf x'''' + \nabla E_\text{ext} = 0.
Failure modes: shrinks (\alpha), cuts corners (\beta), noise (small \sigma), capture range (too far), explodes (large \tau), concavities, one outline only.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
About this lecture
A binary image was corrupted by noise. We want the clean image back, using what we know about noise (the likelihood) and about images (the Ising prior).

Bayes: posterior \propto likelihood \times prior; its negative log is an energy.
Two answers: the single most probable image (MAP) and the most probable value of each pixel (MPM).
Four ways to compute them: ICM, simulated annealing, mean field, and the exact minimum cut.
What goes wrong: local minima, and a prior weight \lambda that is too large.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

From this unit on the prior weight is λ (= 2J), as on the graph-cut day; J appears only in the math slides that connect to units 1–2. The demo is mrfdenoise: a 128 × 128 binary image, noise, six methods, and an energy plot.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The problem


Truth \mathbf x: a binary image (here a disc, a square, a 1-pixel and a 3-pixel line, a small square).
Observed \mathbf y: each pixel flipped with probability \varepsilon = 0.2. Taking \mathbf y as the answer leaves 3321 of 16 384 pixels wrong.
Right: two estimates from this unit. The exact best image under the model has 242 wrong pixels, but the 1-pixel line is gone. Why, and what else could we have done?

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Recall: Bayes’ rule and energies
From the thresholding day (the two-class Bayes rule) and the graph-cut day (seg-energy/, “the probabilistic view”):
\underbrace{p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y)}_{\text{posterior}} \;\propto\; \underbrace{p(\mathbf y \mid \mathbf x)}_{\text{likelihood: the noise}}\;\underbrace{p(\mathbf x)}_{\text{prior: what images look like}}

Taking -\log turns the product into a sum: posterior energy = data term + prior term.
Most probable image = lowest energy. That is the graph-cut day’s energy minimisation, now with a probabilistic meaning for every term.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The model: noise + Ising prior
Labels L_p \in \{0, 1\} (1 = object), as on the graph-cut day:
E(L \mid \mathbf y) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q]

Data term from the noise. With flip noise, a label that disagrees with y_p costs \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon} more than one that agrees: \log 4 = 1.39 for \varepsilon = 0.2. Rare flips make disagreeing expensive.
Prior from the Ising model: every disagreeing neighbour pair costs \lambda (= 2J).
\lambda = 0 is thresholding: every pixel keeps its observed value.
With Gaussian noise on two grey levels (the camera-noise model of cameranoise/, day 3), D_p(\ell) = (y_p - \mu_\ell)^2/2\sigma_n^2: grey values near the middle are uncertain, values far out are sure.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The math: likelihood, field and posterior
text:
The math: likelihood, field and posterior
Flip noise, independent per pixel: p(y_p \mid x_p) = 1 - \varepsilon if y_p = x_p, else \varepsilon. In spins (x_p, y_p = \pm 1):
\log p(y_p \mid x_p) = \tfrac12\log\big(\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)\big) + h\,x_py_p, \qquad h = \tfrac12\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.
With the Ising prior p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp(J\sum x_px_q) the posterior is again an Ising model, with a pixel-dependent field h_p = h\,y_p:
E(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = -J\sum_{(p,q)}x_px_q - \sum_p h_px_p \;(+\text{ const}), \qquad p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) \propto e^{-E(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y)}.
In label form (unit 1): D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h_p, \lambda = 2J. Gaussian noise with levels \mu_0, \mu_1: D_p(\ell) = (y_p - \mu_\ell)^2/2\sigma_n^2, so h_p = \frac{D_p(0) - D_p(1)}{2} is linear in y_p (the squares y_p^2 cancel). The model’s own temperature is T = 1; a T in an algorithm below is a knob of the algorithm.

With \lambda < 0.69 two boundaries would be cheaper, and the MAP would keep \mathbf y.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Two answers: MAP and MPM
The posterior is a distribution over images. Which single image do we report?

MAP (maximum a posteriori): the one most probable image = the lowest energy. All pixels are decided jointly.
MPM (maximum of the posterior marginals; Marroquin, Mitter & Poggio, 1987): for each pixel separately, the value it has in most of the posterior’s probability mass.
MPM gets, on average, the fewest wrong pixels. MAP is the best guess of the whole image.
Marginals come from sampling at T = 1: run a Gibbs sampler, count how often each pixel is 1. The marginal is also an uncertainty map: 0.5 = don’t know.
Three pixels: p(L_2 = 1) = 0.64, p(L_1 = 1) = 0.75, so MPM is also 111, but with a clear warning that the middle pixel is uncertain.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The math: which estimate minimises which loss?
text:
The math: which estimate minimises which loss?
For an estimate \hat{\mathbf x} and the unknown truth \mathbf x (distributed as the posterior):

0–1 loss (“right only if every pixel is right”): \mathbb E[1 - [\hat{\mathbf x} = \mathbf x]] = 1 - p(\hat{\mathbf x} \mid \mathbf y), minimised by the MAP.
Number of wrong pixels: \mathbb E\sum_p[\hat x_p \ne x_p] = \sum_p\big(1 - p(x_p = \hat x_p \mid \mathbf y)\big). Each term depends on one pixel: minimised pixel by pixel by \hat x_p = \arg\max_v p(x_p = v \mid \mathbf y), the MPM.

The marginal p(x_p = v \mid \mathbf y) = \sum_{\mathbf x: x_p = v}p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) sums over 2^{n-1} images: no closed form. A Gibbs sampler at T = 1 estimates it as the fraction of samples (after burn-in) with x_p = v.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Finding the MAP: ICM
Iterated conditional modes (Besag, 1986): the Gibbs sampler at T = 0.

Visit the pixels in turn; give each the label with the lower energy given its neighbours. Repeat until nothing changes.
Fast (a few sweeps), and the energy never increases.
But it stops in the nearest local minimum, and the result depends on the order of visits.
Three pixels from \mathbf y = (1, 0, 1), left to right: pixel 1 sees a background neighbour and switches to 0 (1.39 < 2); pixel 2 stays 0, pixel 3 switches for the same reason: 000, energy 2.77, a local minimum. Visiting the middle pixel first gives 111, the MAP.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Annealing and mean field

Simulated annealing (unit 2): Gibbs sampling while T falls from T_0 towards 0, then ICM. Slow cooling approaches the lowest energy; a quench behaves like ICM.
Mean field: replace each neighbour by its average value and iterate: every pixel holds a number between 0 and 1 instead of a label. Deterministic and smooth; an approximation of the marginals (often over-confident). Thresholded at 0.5, it gives an estimate.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
The math: mean field
In spin form, keep for each pixel a mean m_p \in [-1, 1] and replace the neighbours in the local field by their means:
m_p \leftarrow \tanh\Big(\frac{J\sum_{q \sim p}m_q + h_p}{T}\Big), \qquad p(x_p = +1) \approx \frac{1 + m_p}{2}.

This is the mean of the local conditional p(x_p \mid \text{neighbours}) (unit 2) with the neighbours frozen at their means. Iterated pixel by pixel, it reaches a fixed point.
It is exact when the pixels are independent (J = 0: m_p = \tanh(h_p/T)). Otherwise it ignores correlations between neighbours and tends to be too sure.
Mean field minimises a “free energy” over factorised distributions (variational inference, also behind the VAE day): pointer only.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: The exact MAP: one minimum cut
text:
The exact MAP: one minimum cut
For binary labels and \lambda \ge 0 this energy is the graph-cut day’s segmentation energy. One max-flow gives its exact minimum (Greig, Porteous & Seheult, 1989; recalled from maxflow/ and graphcut-seg/).

In the demo it is computed once per parameter change (128 \times 128: about 50 ms) and drawn as the dashed reference line.
So for binary images the optimiser is not the problem: we can always compare with the true minimum.
For more labels the exact MAP is in general NP-hard (graph-cut day, α-expansion).

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
section: Try it: denoising a binary image
text:
Try it: denoising a binary image




Panels: noisy input, current estimate, and truth / errors (red: false object, blue: missed object, grey: correct object) / marginal p(object). Energy plot: log sweep axis, dashed = exact minimum (min-cut). Tour, ε = 0.2: “ICM: fast, stuck” (λ = 0.8): 14 sweeps, energy 5171.6 against the exact 5121.2; 427 wrong pixels against 242. “Slow cooling” (1000 sweeps): energy 5124.2, 235 wrong: annealing almost reaches the min-cut energy. “Quench” (10 sweeps): 5161.2, like ICM. “MAP vs MPM” (λ = 1.2): Gibbs at T = 1 for 300 sweeps; MPM 276 wrong, MAP 314; switch the third panel to p(object): uncertain pixels along every edge and on the 3-pixel line. “λ too large” (λ = 3): the exact MAP removes both lines and the small square: 602 wrong. “the exact MAP is not the best image” (λ = 1.6): exact 469 wrong, ICM 401, mean field 207.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Lessons from the comparison

ICM is fast but stuck: its energy stays clearly above the minimum. Slow annealing gets close to the min-cut energy; a quench does not.
The exact MAP is not always the best image. Greig et al. (1989) found that for large \lambda the exact MAP was worse than approximate solutions. In the demo at \lambda = 1.6: exact MAP 469 wrong pixels, ICM 401, mean field 207. The fault is the prior (it charges for every boundary pixel, so thin structures are “improbable”), not the optimiser.
The posterior’s best image and the true image are different things. Compare methods by energy to judge the optimiser, and by errors against a known truth to judge the model.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Choosing \lambda

Too small: noise survives. An isolated wrong pixel has 4 disagreeing neighbours; it is removed only if 4\lambda > \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}: \lambda > 0.35 for \varepsilon = 0.2. Below that, the MAP is the thresholded image.
Too large: structures vanish, thin ones first. A clean line of width k is removed once 2\lambda > k \log\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} (two boundaries against k data costs per unit length): the shrinking bias of the graph-cut day.
\varepsilon can be estimated from the noise (e.g. in a flat region); \lambda by trial on a synthetic image with known truth, or by pseudo-likelihood (Besag, 1974): named only.

title: Bayesian image denoising with an Ising prior
text:
Summary

Posterior energy = data term from the noise model + \lambda\cdot(number of disagreeing neighbours). \lambda = 0 is thresholding.
MAP: the most probable image (lowest energy). MPM: per pixel, the most probable value; fewest expected wrong pixels; comes with an uncertainty map from sampling.
ICM is greedy and gets stuck; annealing gets close to the minimum if cooled slowly; mean field is a fast deterministic approximation; the minimum cut gives the exact MAP for binary images.
A better optimiser does not fix a poor prior: for large \lambda the exact MAP loses thin lines and small objects.

title: Quiz: active contours (snakes)
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A snake is a closed polygon \mathbf x_0, \dots, \mathbf x_{n-1} with elasticity \alpha, rigidity \beta and an image term from the edge map f = |\nabla(G_\sigma * I)|^2.

Q1. What does a snake give you that a threshold does not?






Answer





One closed, smooth curve around one object, as a list of points: no holes, no stray pixels, no leaks through small gaps. Its smoothness is controlled (\alpha, \beta), and the outline directly gives perimeter, curvature and shape. The price: it needs a starting curve near the object, and it finds a local, not a global, best.




Q2. A bead sits at (4, 2); its neighbours are at (2, 4) and (4, 0). With \alpha = 0.5 and \beta = 0, what is the elastic force on it?






Hint





\alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1}).









Answer





0.5\big((2, 4) + (4, 0) - 2(4, 2)\big) = 0.5\,(-2, 0) = (-1, 0). The neighbours’ midpoint is (3, 2): the force points there, with \alpha times twice the distance.




Q3. A snake is placed in an empty image (no edges at all), with \alpha > 0. What happens?






Answer





It shrinks towards a point (its centroid stays put): every bead is pulled towards the midpoint of its neighbours and nothing pulls back. That is why a snake must start around the object (or be inflated by a balloon force, next unit).




Q4. Which parameter would you increase if the snake follows the object well but has small wiggles from noise along its outline: \alpha, \beta or \sigma? Which side effect do you expect?






Answer





\beta (rigidity) removes wiggles directly, at the price of rounding real corners; increasing \sigma also helps, by smoothing the noise out of the edge map, at the price of blurred and slightly shifted edges. Increasing \alpha shortens the curve but also pulls it off the edge.




Q5. A bead is 15 pixels away from the nearest edge, with \sigma = 1.5. Why does the image force not move it, and name one way to fix that.






Answer





The edge map f is only non-zero within a few \sigma of the edge; 15 pixels away it is flat, so its slope, the image force, is (almost) zero: the bead is outside the capture range. Fixes: a larger \sigma (coarse to fine), a start closer to the object, or a force that reaches further (balloon force, gradient vector flow: next unit).




Q6. The snake zig-zags and explodes after a few dozen steps. What do you change?






Answer





The step \tau is too large for the explicit (gradient-descent) update: make it smaller (below 2/\lambda_\text{max}, \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta), or use the semi-implicit update, which is stable for any \tau (next unit).




Q7. Why can a snake started around a U-shaped object not follow it into the U?






Answer





Inside the U the image force points sideways, to the walls, and nowhere into the opening; the beads across the mouth feel no pull inwards, and the springs keep them on a straight line. The edge force only pulls towards nearby edges.




Q8. (math) Show that for a closed curve the elastic force \alpha\mathbf x'' on the circle \mathbf x(s) = r(\cos s, \sin s) points to the centre with size \alpha r.






Answer





\mathbf x'(s) = r(-\sin s, \cos s), \mathbf x''(s) = -r(\cos s, \sin s) = -\mathbf x(s). So \alpha\mathbf x'' = -\alpha\mathbf x: towards the centre, of length \alpha|\mathbf x| = \alpha r. (It is the first-variation term -\alpha\mathbf x'' of the Euler–Lagrange equation, with the sign of a force.)




Q9. (math) Which kernel do you get by applying the second difference [1, -2, 1] twice, and which term of the snake force uses it?






Answer





[1, -2, 1] * [1, -2, 1] = [1, -4, 6, -4, 1], a discrete fourth derivative. It is the rigid (bending) force: -\beta(\mathbf x_{i-2} - 4\mathbf x_{i-1} + 6\mathbf x_i - 4\mathbf x_{i+1} + \mathbf x_{i+2}).

title: Quiz: Bayesian image denoising
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Posterior energy E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q]; with flip noise \varepsilon, a label that disagrees with the observed pixel costs \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.

Q1. Where do the two terms of the posterior energy come from?






Hint





Bayes’ rule, then -\log.









Answer





p(L \mid \mathbf y) \propto p(\mathbf y \mid L)\,p(L). The data term is -\log of the likelihood (the noise model); the smoothness term is -\log of the Ising prior (images have few disagreeing neighbours). -\log turns the product into a sum.




Q2. Flip noise with \varepsilon = 0.01 versus \varepsilon = 0.3: in which case does the data term weigh more, and why does that make sense?






Hint





Compute \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}.









Answer





\varepsilon = 0.01: \log 99 = 4.6; \varepsilon = 0.3: \log(7/3) = 0.85. With rare flips an observed pixel is very likely right, so overriding it is expensive; with frequent flips the prior must do more of the work.




Q3. What is the difference between the MAP and the MPM estimate? Which one makes fewer wrong pixels on average?






Hint





One decides the whole image jointly, the other each pixel separately.









Answer





MAP: the single most probable image (lowest energy). MPM: for each pixel, its more probable value under the posterior marginal. The MPM minimises the expected number of wrong pixels; the MAP maximises the chance that the whole image is right.




Q4. Why does ICM get stuck, and why does annealing not?






Hint





What moves does each method allow?









Answer





ICM only makes single-pixel changes that lower the energy, so it stops as soon as no single change helps: a local minimum (e.g. a small clump of noise pixels that support each other). Annealing samples at T > 0, which also accepts uphill moves; if cooled slowly it can leave such minima before T gets low.




Q5. How is the marginal p(L_p = 1 \mid \mathbf y) obtained in practice, and what is it good for besides the MPM?






Hint





Unit 2.









Answer





Run a Gibbs sampler on the posterior at T = 1, discard the burn-in, and count the fraction of sweeps in which L_p = 1. It is an uncertainty map: values near 0.5 mark pixels the model cannot decide, typically along edges and in thin structures.




Q6. For binary denoising, the exact MAP can be computed with one minimum cut. Why then compare ICM, annealing and mean field at all?






Hint





Think of other models, and of the MPM.









Answer





The cut works only for binary labels with \lambda \ge 0; for more labels or other priors the iterative methods are what is available. And the exact MAP is not always the best image: with a large \lambda it removes thin structures that approximate methods (or the MPM) keep. The cut is the reference for judging optimisers, not the answer to every question.




Q7. You increase \lambda. In which order do a disc of radius 20, a 3-pixel-wide line and a 1-pixel line disappear from the MAP?






Hint





Gain grows with area, cost with boundary length.









Answer





The 1-pixel line first (two boundaries per unit length against one pixel of data gain), then the 3-pixel line (two boundaries against three pixels), the disc last (its area grows faster than its perimeter). This is the shrinking bias of the graph-cut day.




Q8. (math) For flip noise in spin form, what is the field h_p of the posterior Ising model?






Answer





h_p = \tfrac12\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}\,y_p: the observed spin, weighted by half the log-odds of a correct observation. \log p(y_p \mid x_p) = \text{const} + h\,x_py_p.

title: Exercise: active contours (snakes)
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Snake
a closed polygon \mathbf x_0, \dots, \mathbf x_{n-1}; after \mathbf x_{n-1} comes \mathbf x_0


Elastic force (weight \alpha)
\alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1}): towards the midpoint of the two neighbours


Rigid force (weight \beta)
-\beta(\mathbf x_{i-2} - 4\mathbf x_{i-1} + 6\mathbf x_i - 4\mathbf x_{i+1} + \mathbf x_{i+2}): straightens the chain


Edge map
f = \lvert\nabla(G_\sigma * I)\rvert^2: large on edges


Image force
w\,\nabla f: uphill on the edge map, towards the nearest edge


One step
new position = position + \tau\,\times (elastic + rigid + image force)

title: Exercise: active contours (snakes)
text:
By hand
B1. Four beads at (1, 1), (-1, 1), (-1, -1), (1, -1) (in this order), no image, \alpha = 1, \beta = 0. (a) Compute the elastic force on each bead. Where does it point? (b) Take one step with \tau = 0.1. Where are the beads now? Is it still a square? (c) The elastic energy is \tfrac12\alpha\sum_i|\mathbf x_{i+1} - \mathbf x_i|^2. Compute it before and after the step. (d) What happens after many steps?
B2. Same square, now with \beta = 1. (a) For the corner (1, 1), which bead is \mathbf x_{i-2} and which is \mathbf x_{i+2}? Compute the rigid force there. (b) With \alpha = \beta = 1: total force and the position after one step with \tau = 0.1.
B3. A regular octagon: 8 beads on the unit circle, at angles 0°, 45°, \dots, 315°; \alpha = 1, \beta = 0. (a) Compute the elastic force on the bead at (1, 0). (Its neighbours are at (\cos 45°, \pm\sin 45°).) (b) After one step with \tau = 0.1, what is the radius of the octagon? Compare with the square of B1. (c) With more and more beads on the same circle, does the elastic force per bead grow or shrink? What does that mean for a snake with many points?
B4. The edge map along a line across an edge at x = 10 is f(x) = e^{-(x - 10)^2/8}. (a) Compute the slope f'(x) at x = 8, 9, 10, 11, 14 and 20. In which direction does the image force w f'(x) push a bead at each position? (b) A bead starts at x = 20. What happens to it if there are no internal forces? (c) How would you make the image force reach further? What is the price?
B5. Force balance. A snake of n = 40 beads lies on a circle of radius r around a bright disk. (a) The beads of a regular polygon satisfy \mathbf x_{i-1} + \mathbf x_{i+1} = 2\cos(2\pi/n)\,\mathbf x_i (centre at the origin). Show that the elastic force has size \alpha r (2 - 2\cos(2\pi/n)) and points to the centre. Compute it for r = 28.5. (b) In the demo’s disk image (\sigma = 2, w = 2) the edge can push a bead outwards with at most about 0.67 (at radius 28.5). Above which \alpha can the edge no longer hold the snake?
B6. Predict, in one sentence each, what the snake on a noisy disk does when (a) \alpha is ten times too large, (b) \beta is very large and the object is a square, (c) \sigma is very small, (d) the start circle lies far outside the disk and \alpha is tiny, (e) the step \tau is too large.






Solutions





B1. (a) Bead (1, 1): neighbours (-1, 1) and (1, -1), force (-1, 1) + (1, -1) - 2(1, 1) = (-2, -2). By symmetry every bead gets -2 times its own position: (2, -2) at (-1, 1), (2, 2) at (-1, -1), (-2, 2) at (1, -1). All point to the centre (the midpoint of each bead’s neighbours is (0, 0)). (b) (1, 1) + 0.1(-2, -2) = (0.8, 0.8), and likewise: the square (\pm0.8, \pm0.8). Still a square, 0.8 times the size. (c) Each side has length 2: \tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 2^2 = 8. After the step the sides are 1.6: \tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 1.6^2 = 5.12. (d) It shrinks by 0.8 every step, towards its centre: springs alone contract the snake to a point.
B2. (a) For bead i at (1, 1) with neighbours \mathbf x_{i-1} = (1, -1) and \mathbf x_{i+1} = (-1, 1), both \mathbf x_{i-2} and \mathbf x_{i+2} are the opposite corner (-1, -1) (with 4 beads, two steps back is two steps forward). Rigid force: -\big[(-1,-1) - 4(1,-1) + 6(1,1) - 4(-1,1) + (-1,-1)\big] = -(4, 4) = (-4, -4). (b) (-2, -2) + (-4, -4) = (-6, -6); after one step (1, 1) + 0.1(-6, -6) = (0.4, 0.4). On a square the straightening force also points inwards: a 4-bead “square” is as bent as a closed polygon can be.
B3. (a) (\cos 45°, \sin 45°) + (\cos 45°, -\sin 45°) - 2(1, 0) = (2\cos 45° - 2, 0) = (-0.586, 0): size 0.586, towards the centre. (b) Radius 1 - 0.1 \cdot 0.586 = 0.941, against 0.8 for the 4-bead square (whose corners are at radius \sqrt2, but the factor is what counts: 1 - 0.1\cdot 2 = 0.8). (c) It shrinks: the force is (2 - 2\cos(2\pi/n))\,r \approx (2\pi/n)^2 r, so doubling n makes it four times weaker. A snake with many points shrinks slowly in flat regions, and \alpha must be read together with n.
B4. (a) f'(x) = -\tfrac{x - 10}{4}e^{-(x-10)^2/8}: f'(8) = 0.303, f'(9) = 0.221, f'(10) = 0, f'(11) = -0.221, f'(14) = -0.135, f'(20) = -0.0000093. Left of the edge the force pushes right, right of it left: always towards the edge, zero on it. (b) Practically nothing: the force at x = 20 is 10^{-5} times the force at x = 8. The bead is outside the capture range and stays where it is. (c) Smooth more (larger \sigma): the edge map becomes wider and the pull reaches further. The price: neighbouring edges merge, corners round off, and the ridge of f can move away from the true edge.
B5. (a) \alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} + \mathbf x_{i+1} - 2\mathbf x_i) = \alpha(2\cos(2\pi/n) - 2)\mathbf x_i: a negative multiple of \mathbf x_i, so towards the centre, with size \alpha r(2 - 2\cos 9°) = 0.0246\,\alpha r. For r = 28.5: 0.702\,\alpha. (b) The edge holds while 0.702\,\alpha < 0.67, i.e. up to \alpha \approx 0.95. Above that the springs pull the snake through the edge and it shrinks to a point.
B6. (a) It shrinks off the edge towards a point. (b) It cuts the corners: a rounded square inside the true one. (c) It stops on the first speckles of noise it meets: a ragged outline away from the edge. (d) It hardly moves: no image force reaches it, and the springs are too weak to bring it in. (e) The beads overshoot, a zig-zag grows, and the snake explodes.




Math questions
B7. (math) For the discrete energy E_\text{int} = \sum_j \tfrac12\alpha|\mathbf x_{j+1} - \mathbf x_j|^2 + \tfrac12\beta|\mathbf x_{j-1} - 2\mathbf x_j + \mathbf x_{j+1}|^2, compute \partial E_\text{int}/\partial\mathbf x_i and show that minus it is the elastic plus rigid force of the table above.
B8. (math) Show that the internal forces on all beads add up to zero, and explain why that had to be so. Show that [1, -4, 6, -4, 1] is the convolution of [1, -2, 1] with itself.
B9. (math) Continuous snake \mathbf x(s), s \in [0, 2\pi), closed. (a) Show by integration by parts that the first variation of \int\tfrac12\alpha|\mathbf x'|^2 ds in the direction \mathbf h is -\int\alpha\,\mathbf x''\cdot\mathbf h\,ds. (b) For the circle \mathbf x(s) = r(\cos s, \sin s), compute the internal force \alpha\mathbf x'' - \beta\mathbf x''''. In which direction does it point, and how large is it? Compare with B3 and B5.
B10. (math) For a one-dimensional quadratic energy E(x) = \tfrac12\lambda x^2 (\lambda > 0), write the gradient-descent step x_{t+1} = x_t - \tau E'(x_t). For which \tau does x_t go to 0? What happens for \tau\lambda slightly above 2?






Solutions (math)





B7. \mathbf x_i appears in the elastic terms j = i - 1 and j = i: \partial/\partial\mathbf x_i gives \alpha(\mathbf x_i - \mathbf x_{i-1}) - \alpha(\mathbf x_{i+1} - \mathbf x_i) = -\alpha(\mathbf x_{i-1} - 2\mathbf x_i + \mathbf x_{i+1}). Write \mathbf d_j = \mathbf x_{j-1} - 2\mathbf x_j + \mathbf x_{j+1}; \mathbf x_i appears in \mathbf d_{i-1} (coefficient 1), \mathbf d_i (-2) and \mathbf d_{i+1} (1), so the derivative of \tfrac12\beta\sum|\mathbf d_j|^2 is \beta(\mathbf d_{i-1} - 2\mathbf d_i + \mathbf d_{i+1}) = \beta(\mathbf x_{i-2} - 4\mathbf x_{i-1} + 6\mathbf x_i - 4\mathbf x_{i+1} + \mathbf x_{i+2}). Minus these are the two forces.
B8. Summed over i (indices mod n), each \mathbf x_j appears with total coefficient 1 - 2 + 1 = 0 in the elastic sum and 1 - 4 + 6 - 4 + 1 = 0 in the rigid one. It had to be so: the internal energy depends only on differences of positions, so translating the whole snake by \mathbf c leaves it unchanged, and the derivative in that direction, \sum_i \partial E/\partial\mathbf x_i\cdot\mathbf c, is zero for every \mathbf c. Convolution: [1, -2, 1] * [1, -2, 1] = [1, -2-2, 1+4+1, -2-2, 1] = [1, -4, 6, -4, 1].
B9. (a) \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\int\tfrac12\alpha|\mathbf x' + \varepsilon\mathbf h'|^2 = \int\alpha\,\mathbf x'\cdot\mathbf h' at \varepsilon = 0; integrating by parts, = [\alpha\,\mathbf x'\cdot\mathbf h]_0^{2\pi} - \int\alpha\,\mathbf x''\cdot\mathbf h, and the bracket vanishes because \mathbf x and \mathbf h are periodic. (b) \mathbf x'' = -r(\cos s, \sin s) = -\mathbf x and \mathbf x'''' = \mathbf x, so the internal force is -\alpha\mathbf x - \beta\mathbf x = -(\alpha + \beta)\mathbf x: towards the centre, size (\alpha + \beta)r. With n beads the parameter step is 2\pi/n instead of 1, which gives the factor (2\pi/n)^2 of B3: 2 - 2\cos(2\pi/n) \approx (2\pi/n)^2.
B10. x_{t+1} = x_t - \tau\lambda x_t = (1 - \tau\lambda)x_t, so x_t = (1 - \tau\lambda)^t x_0. It goes to 0 when |1 - \tau\lambda| < 1, i.e. 0 < \tau < 2/\lambda. For \tau\lambda slightly above 2 the factor is slightly below -1: x changes sign every step and grows, an oscillation that explodes. The snake’s zig-zag is this, for the stiffest pattern of the polygon (next unit).

title: Exercise: active contours (snakes)
text:
Explore
The demo shows a 128 \times 128 image with a snake (yellow, orange beads). Drag on the image to place a new start circle (or choose drag: draw and draw a closed curve). Play, step and +10 move the snake; reset goes back to the start. Blue arrows: the internal force on each bead, red: the image force (both \times 10). field shows the image force on a grid; edge map shows f instead of the image. The plot gives the internal, image and total energy per iteration; the readout gives \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta and, for the explicit step, \tau\lambda_\text{max}. n points changes the number of beads, resample every re-spaces them evenly. Leave the update on semi-implicit unless a question says otherwise (the explicit step is plain gradient descent; the next unit explains the difference).



E1. Preset fits the disk. Play for about 300 iterations. How do the internal and the image energy change, and when? Why does the internal energy not fall to zero? Look at the arrows at the end: what balances what?
E2. Preset α too large: shrinks away (\alpha = 1). Lower \alpha with the slider (press reset after each change) and find, roughly, the largest \alpha at which the snake stays on the edge. Compare with B5.
E3. Preset β too large: rounds the square (\beta = 2). Describe the result. Then set \beta = 0, reset and play. What changes at the corners? Why does \beta affect the corners and hardly the straight sides?
E4. Preset σ too small: stuck on noise (noise 0.25, \sigma = 0.5). Switch to the edge map view: what does the snake see? Raise \sigma to 1, 1.5, 2 and 4 (reset each time). From which \sigma does the snake find the edge? What happens to the result at \sigma = 4?
E5. Preset too far: does not move (\alpha = 0.01). Tick field: why does the snake hardly move? Now set \alpha = 0.1 and reset: what happens, and why? Would that help if the start circle were inside the disk, or beside it?
E6. Preset τ too large: explodes (explicit update, \tau = 2). Step through the first 40 iterations: what pattern grows? Find the largest \tau for which the explicit snake still settles, and compare with the readout \tau\lambda_\text{max}. Then switch to semi-implicit with \tau = 2.
E7. Presets concavity: cannot enter the U and two blobs: one snake bridges them. Describe each result and explain it with the image force (tick field). Which of the two problems could a better image force fix, and which not?
E8. Preset micrograph: nucleus. Where does the snake follow the nuclear envelope, and where not? Try \sigma = 1, and draw your own start curve close to the envelope.






Solutions





E1. The internal energy falls steadily from 101.0 while the circle shrinks (78.7 at iteration 50, 60.6 at 100); the image energy stays near 0 until the snake reaches the edge region, then drops quickly, between iterations 100 (−0.8) and 200 (−70.9). At the end the snake sits at radius 29.8 with internal energy 44.3 and image energy −70.9 (total −26.6). The internal energy cannot reach zero while the snake keeps its size: a circle of radius 30 has stretched springs. At the end the blue arrows (inward, elastic) and the red ones (image force, outward on the inner flank of the edge ridge) cancel at every bead.
E2. On the demo’s image the snake holds up to about \alpha = 0.80 and shrinks away from \alpha = 0.85 (after 500 iterations: radius 28.5 at 0.80, 7.5 at 0.85, and 0.2 at 1). B5 predicted 0.95 for a clean edge; the noise weakens the image force at some beads (along one ray of the noisy image the largest outward force is only 0.56, which gives 0.80), and the snake gives way at its weakest bead.
E3. With \beta = 2 the corners are cut off: the snake is a rounded square whose corner lies about 10.4 pixels from the true corner, and it sits up to 9 pixels inside the square near the corners. With \beta = 0 (only \alpha = 0.1) it follows the square much more closely; the corners are still slightly rounded (5.8 pixels from the true corner) because the edge map itself is blurred there (\sigma = 2). The rigid force is proportional to the change of the second difference: zero on a straight side, large where the direction changes, so only the corners pay.
E4. In the edge map at \sigma = 0.5 the noise makes bright speckles everywhere: the snake stops on the first ones (radius between 37 and 44 after 500 iterations). At \sigma = 1 it gets through most of the speckles but is still caught in places (radius 28.6 to 36). From \sigma = 1.5 it finds the edge (mean radius 29.9). At \sigma = 4 it is smooth but slightly too small (mean radius 29.6): strong blurring moves the ridge of the edge map of a curved edge inwards.
E5. All beads are more than 20 pixels from the edge, where the image force is practically zero (the field shows dots, not arrows), and the springs at \alpha = 0.01 shrink the circle very slowly: radius 56.4 after 100 iterations, 53.4 after 300. With \alpha = 0.1 the springs bring the snake in (radius 45.2 after 100 iterations) until the edge catches it: radius 29.8 after 300. This only works because the start encloses the object, so shrinking happens to move towards it. A circle inside the disk would shrink away from the edge, and one beside the disk would shrink to a point next to it.
E6. A zig-zag: alternate beads move in and out, more every step (radius between 40.5 and 40.9 at iteration 20, between 10.9 and 137 at iteration 40), and at iteration 55 the snake has exploded. \lambda_\text{max} = 4 \cdot 0.1 + 16 \cdot 0.05 = 1.2: the explicit step is stable for \tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2, i.e. \tau < 1.67. In the demo \tau = 1.65 (\tau\lambda_\text{max} = 1.98) does not explode, but the beads keep wobbling (after 400 iterations they still lie between radius 22.9 and 31.6); \tau = 1.7 (2.04) explodes after 284 iterations. The semi-implicit update with \tau = 2 settles at radius 29.8 like \tau = 1.
E7. The U: the snake closes over the mouth of the slot and never enters it (after 800 iterations its deepest point in the slot is at y = 15.6, the slot goes down to y = 77.5). The field shows why: inside the slot the image force points sideways, to the two walls, and nowhere down into it; a bead at the mouth sees no reason to go in, and the springs pull it straight. Two blobs: one snake wraps both blobs and bridges the gap between them. A better image force (gradient vector flow, next unit) fixes the concavity. The two blobs it cannot fix: one snake is one closed curve, and it cannot split into two.
E8. The snake runs along the dark envelope on the right and the top, but cuts across at the lower left and the left, where the cytoplasm next to the nucleus is just as dark and the envelope gives a weaker edge. With \sigma = 1 the texture of the cytoplasm catches it (from the same start it ends far outside, from x = 33 to 119). A start drawn close to the envelope does much better: the snake refines a good guess, it does not find the object on its own.

title: Exercise: active contours (snakes)
text:
Where this leads
The explicit step explodes when \tau is too large, and the image force reaches only a few pixels. The next unit writes the internal forces as a matrix, shows which patterns of the curve explode and why, introduces the semi-implicit step that never does, and extends the capture range with balloon forces and gradient vector flow.

title: Exercise: Bayesian image denoising
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

turn a noise model into a data term, and add the Ising prior to get the posterior energy,
find the MAP of a tiny image by listing its energies, and the MPM from its marginals,
run ICM by hand and show that it can get stuck, depending on the order of visits,
predict which structures a too large prior weight \lambda removes,
compare ICM, annealing, sampling, mean field and the exact minimum cut on a real-size image.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:
