title: Exercise: Bayesian image denoising
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Labels
L_p \in \{0, 1\}, 1 = object; observed binary image \mathbf y


Flip noise
each pixel flipped independently with probability \varepsilon


Data term (flip noise)
0 if L_p = y_p, \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon} if not


Data term (Gaussian noise)
D_p(\ell) = (y_p - \mu_\ell)^2/2\sigma_n^2, grey levels \mu_0, \mu_1


Posterior energy
E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}[L_p \ne L_q], posterior \propto e^{-E}


MAP
the labelling with the lowest energy


Marginal
p(L_p = 1 \mid \mathbf y): the summed probability of all labellings with L_p = 1


MPM
L_p = 1 where the marginal exceeds 0.5


ICM
visit pixels in turn, give each its cheaper label given its neighbours, until nothing changes

title: Exercise: Bayesian image denoising
text:
By hand
B1. Data costs. Compute \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon} for \varepsilon = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.45. What happens to the data term as \varepsilon \to 0.5, and what does that mean?
B2. Three pixels. \mathbf y = (1, 0, 1), \varepsilon = 0.2, \lambda = 2. (a) Compute the energy of all 8 labellings. Which is the MAP? (b) Turn the energies into probabilities (e^{-E}, normalised). (c) For which \lambda would the MAP be \mathbf y itself?
B3. ICM. Same image and \lambda, start from \mathbf y. (a) Run ICM visiting pixels 1, 2, 3 (repeat until nothing changes). Where does it stop, and with which energy? (b) Run it again visiting 2, 1, 3. Where does it stop now? (c) Is the result of (a) a local minimum? In what sense?
B4. MPM. From B2(b), compute p(L_1 = 1) and p(L_2 = 1). What is the MPM labelling? Does it agree with the MAP? What does p(L_2 = 1) tell you that the MAP does not?
B5. Choosing \lambda (flip noise, 4-neighbours). (a) A single wrong pixel in a large uniform region: above which \lambda does the MAP correct it? Evaluate for \varepsilon = 0.2 and \varepsilon = 0.1. (b) A long, clean line of width k pixels: above which \lambda is it cheaper to remove it? Evaluate for k = 1 and k = 3 at \varepsilon = 0.2. (c) Can \lambda be chosen to remove all single-pixel noise and keep a 1-pixel line at \varepsilon = 0.2?
B6. Gaussian noise. Grey levels \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 1, \sigma_n = 0.5. Compute D_p(0) - D_p(1) for y_p = 0.2, 0.5 and 0.9. Which pixel gives no evidence at all? Which gives the strongest?






Solutions





B1. 2.197, 1.386, 0.847, 0.201. As \varepsilon \to 0.5 the cost goes to 0: a pixel’s observed value says nothing about its true value, and only the prior decides.
B2. (a) Data cost 1.386 per pixel that differs from \mathbf y, plus 2 \times the number of boundaries:












labelling
111
000
001, 100
101
011, 110
010




energy
1.386
2.773
3.386
4.000
4.773
8.159


probability
0.601
0.150
0.081 each
0.044
0.020 each
0.0007



The MAP is 111. (b) In the table (\sum e^{-E} = 0.416). (c) \mathbf y = 101 costs 2\lambda, 111 costs 1.386: \mathbf y is the MAP for \lambda < 0.693.
B3. (a) Pixel 1 (neighbour 0): label 1 costs 0 + 2 = 2, label 0 costs 1.386: switch to 0. Pixel 2 (neighbours 0 and 1): label 0 costs 0 + 2, label 1 costs 1.386 + 2: stays 0. Pixel 3 (neighbour 0): switch to 0. Next sweep: no changes. Result 000, energy 2.773. (b) Pixel 2 first (neighbours 1 and 1): label 1 costs 1.386, label 0 costs 0 + 4: switch to 1. Pixels 1 and 3 are now happy. Result 111, energy 1.386: the MAP. (c) Yes: no single pixel change lowers the energy of 000 (100, 010, 001 cost 3.386, 8.159, 3.386), but changing all three at once does. ICM only looks at one pixel at a time.
B4. p(L_1 = 1) = 0.601 + 0.081 + 0.044 + 0.020 = 0.747 (labellings 111, 100, 101, 110). p(L_2 = 1) = 0.601 + 0.020 + 0.020 + 0.0007 = 0.643. MPM: 111, the same as the MAP here. But the marginal 0.64 says the middle pixel is far from certain: the MAP alone does not show that.
B5. (a) Correcting it saves 4 boundaries (4\lambda) and costs \log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}: \lambda > 1.386/4 = 0.35 (\varepsilon = 0.2) and \lambda > 2.197/4 = 0.55 (\varepsilon = 0.1). Rarer noise is more trusted, so it needs a larger \lambda to override. (b) Per unit length, keeping the line costs 2 boundaries (2\lambda); removing it costs k \cdot 1.386. Removed for \lambda > 0.69 (k = 1) and \lambda > 2.08 (k = 3). (c) Barely: any \lambda between 0.35 and 0.69 does both for a clean line. But the line pixels are noisy too (a fifth of them are flipped), which makes the line cheaper to remove; in the demo the 1-pixel line is already partly lost at \lambda = 0.6.
B6. D_p(0) - D_p(1) = \big(y_p^2 - (y_p - 1)^2\big)/(2 \cdot 0.25) = 2(2y_p - 1): -1.2 (evidence for 0), 0 (no evidence), +1.6 (evidence for 1, the strongest). The data term is linear in y_p.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that for flip noise, in spin form (x_p, y_p = \pm 1), \log p(y_p \mid x_p) = \text{const} + h\,x_py_p with h = \tfrac12\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}. Hence show that the posterior is an Ising model with field h_p = h\,y_p and J = \lambda/2.
B8. (math) Show that the expected number of wrong pixels, \mathbb E\big[\sum_p[\hat x_p \ne x_p] \,\big|\, \mathbf y\big], is minimised by the MPM estimate, and that the probability of getting the whole image right is maximised by the MAP.
B9. (math) Mean field on B2 in spin form: J = 1, h_p = 0.693\,y_p, T = 1. Start from m_p = \tanh(h_p) and update m_p \leftarrow \tanh(J\sum_{q\sim p}m_q + h_p) in the order 1, 2, 3. Give m after one sweep. The fixed point is m = (0.905, 0.807, 0.905): compare (1 + m_p)/2 with the exact marginals of B4.






Solutions (math)





B7. p(y_p \mid x_p) = (1 - \varepsilon)^{(1 + x_py_p)/2}\varepsilon^{(1 - x_py_p)/2}, so \log p = \tfrac12\log(\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)) + \tfrac12 x_py_p\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}. Summing over pixels and adding the log-prior J\sum x_px_q: \log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = J\sum x_px_q + \sum_p h\,y_px_p + \text{const} = -E_{\text{Ising}}(\mathbf x) with h_p = h\,y_p. In labels (unit 1): \lambda = 2J and D_p(1) - D_p(0) = -2h_p = -y_p\log\frac{1 - \varepsilon}{\varepsilon}, as in the table.
B8. \mathbb E\sum_p[\hat x_p \ne x_p] = \sum_p\big(1 - p(x_p = \hat x_p \mid \mathbf y)\big). Each term depends on \hat x_p only, so choose \hat x_p to maximise p(x_p = \hat x_p \mid \mathbf y): the MPM. P(\hat{\mathbf x} = \mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = p(\hat{\mathbf x} \mid \mathbf y) is maximised by the most probable image: the MAP.
B9. Start m = (0.6, -0.6, 0.6). Pixel 1: \tanh(-0.6 + 0.693) = 0.093. Pixel 2: \tanh(0.093 + 0.6 - 0.693) = -0.0003. Pixel 3: \tanh(-0.0003 + 0.693) = 0.600. After one sweep m = (0.093, -0.0003, 0.600). At the fixed point (1 + m)/2 = (0.95, 0.90, 0.95), against the exact (0.75, 0.64, 0.75): the same decisions (111), but far too confident. Mean field ignores that neighbours fluctuate together.

title: Exercise: Bayesian image denoising
text:
Explore
A 128 \times 128 binary image (test shapes: a disc, a square, a 1-pixel and a 3-pixel line, a small square; or the micrograph, blurred and thresholded to make a binary “truth”), corrupted by flip noise \varepsilon or Gaussian noise \sigma_n on the grey levels 0 and 1. Choose the prior weight \lambda and a method; play runs it sweep by sweep. Panels: the noisy input, the current estimate, and the truth / the errors (red: false object, blue: missed object) / the marginal p(object) for Gibbs and mean field. The plot shows the energy against sweeps for every method run so far, and the exact minimum (min-cut) dashed. Changing the image, the noise or \lambda starts afresh.



E1. Preset ICM: fast, stuck (\varepsilon = 0.2, \lambda = 0.8). How many sweeps does ICM take? Compare its energy and its wrong pixels with the exact MAP. Where are ICM’s extra errors?
E2. Preset slow cooling (annealing over 1000 sweeps), then quench (10 sweeps). Compare the final energies and wrong pixels with ICM and the exact MAP. What does the energy curve of annealing do in the first sweeps, and why?
E3. Preset MAP vs MPM (\lambda = 1.2; Gibbs sampling at T = 1 for 300 sweeps after 20 sweeps of burn-in). Compare the MPM’s wrong pixels with the MAP’s. Show p(object): where is the model uncertain? Is the MPM’s energy higher or lower than the MAP’s, and is that a contradiction?
E4. Choose exact MAP and raise \lambda from 0.4 to 3 in steps. In which order do the structures disappear? Relate the \lambda values to B5.
E5. Preset λ = 0 is thresholding. Check that the exact MAP and the thresholded image are the same. Then raise \lambda slowly from 0: at which \lambda does the MAP first change? Compare with B5(a).
E6. Preset exact MAP not the best image (\lambda = 1.6). Compare wrong pixels and energies of exact MAP, ICM and mean field. Which has the lowest energy, which the fewest errors? What does this say about the prior?
E7. Preset Gaussian noise, micrograph (\sigma_n = 0.8, \lambda = 1). Compare thresholding, ICM, mean field and the exact MAP (wrong pixels). Then try \lambda = 0.5 and \lambda = 2 for the exact MAP.






Solutions





E1. ICM stops after 14 sweeps (the last one changes nothing), at energy 5171.6 against the exact minimum 5121.2, with 427 wrong pixels against 242 (thresholding: 3321). ICM keeps small clumps of noise pixels that support each other (224 false object pixels in 60 clumps, and 203 missed pixels in 43 holes; the exact MAP has only 71 false object pixels): flipping any single pixel of a clump raises the energy, so ICM never removes it.
E2. Slow cooling: energy 5124.2, only 3 above the minimum, and 235 wrong pixels (by chance even 7 fewer than the exact MAP). Quench: 5161.2 and 381 wrong, close to ICM. At the start (T_0 = 4) annealing raises the energy far above the noisy image’s: at high T the sampler moves almost freely, and only as T falls does the energy come down.
E3. MPM 276 wrong pixels, MAP 314. The marginal is uncertain (grey) along all edges and especially on the 3-pixel line, which the MAP removes in part (184 of its 312 pixels kept) while the MPM keeps more of it (250). The MPM’s energy (5434.3) is higher than the MAP’s (5384.0): no contradiction, the MPM does not aim at low energy, it aims at few expected wrong pixels.
E4. At \lambda = 0.4 much noise survives (2106 wrong). The 1-pixel line goes first (partly at 0.6, completely by 0.8), then the 3-pixel line (between 1.2 and 1.6), then the small 12 \times 12 square (between 2 and 3). The disc and the large square stay. The order follows B5(b): the cost of keeping a structure grows with its boundary, the gain with its area. Noise in the structures lowers the gain, so they go earlier than the clean-line estimates.
E5. At \lambda = 0 both have 3321 wrong pixels. The MAP stays equal to the thresholded image up to \lambda \approx 0.35 (at 0.3 still 3321 wrong; at 0.4, 2106): the threshold of B5(a), \log 4/4 = 0.347, where isolated wrong pixels start to be corrected.
E6. Exact MAP: lowest energy (5581.8) but 469 wrong pixels. ICM: energy 5931.9 but 401 wrong. Mean field: 5660.6 and only 207 wrong. The lowest energy is not the most correct image: at this \lambda the prior says that thin lines are improbable, and the exact optimiser obeys it fully. Approximate methods that stop earlier happen to keep more of the lines. Greig, Porteous and Seheult (1989) found the same.
E7. Thresholding: 4378 wrong (at \sigma_n = 0.8 about a quarter of the pixels fall on the wrong side of 0.5); ICM: 793; mean field: 256; exact MAP: 260. With \lambda = 0.5 the exact MAP has 739 wrong, with \lambda = 2 365: the best \lambda is somewhere in between. Note the “truth” here is itself a thresholded micrograph.

title: Exercise: Bayesian image denoising
text:
Where this leads
The binary prior counts disagreeing neighbours. For grey values, the natural prior penalises differences between neighbours: squared differences (a Gaussian MRF, solved by one linear system) or absolute differences (total variation, which keeps edges). That is the next unit. For more than two labels (several tissues) the same model is the Potts model; its exact MAP is no longer a single cut.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
About this lecture
So far the pixels were binary. Now they are grey values, and the prior says “neighbours have similar values”. How we measure “similar” decides whether edges survive.

Quadratic prior (a Gaussian MRF): one linear system with the graph Laplacian; a low-pass filter; it blurs edges.
Total variation (TV): absolute differences; keeps edges, but makes staircases and shrinks small features.
Huber: in between.
What samples from these priors look like, and where TV comes back in the course.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Demo: mrf1d (1D profiles, so everything can be seen and solved exactly). The forward model here is the identity (denoising only); deblurring with the same priors is on the deconvolution day.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
From labels to grey values
Observed y_p = x_p + \text{noise}, Gaussian with standard deviation \sigma_n (the camera-noise model of cameranoise/, day 3). We want \mathbf x.
E(\mathbf x) = \underbrace{\tfrac12\sum_p (x_p - y_p)^2}_{\text{stay close to the data}} \;+\; \lambda\underbrace{\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q)}_{\text{neighbours similar}}

\rho is the penalty on a difference between neighbours: \rho(d) = d^2/2 (quadratic), |d| (TV), or Huber.
\lambda weighs the prior against the data, as before; \lambda = 0 returns \mathbf y.
The noise level is absorbed in \lambda (math slide): more noise, larger \lambda.
Same structure as the binary energy: data term + \lambda\cdot(neighbour penalty). The binary [L_p \ne L_q] is now a function of the size of the difference.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Quadratic smoothing, by hand
\mathbf y = (0, 3, 0), quadratic penalty, \lambda = 1:
E = \tfrac12\big(x_1^2 + (x_2 - 3)^2 + x_3^2\big) + \tfrac12\big((x_1 - x_2)^2 + (x_2 - x_3)^2\big).
Setting each partial derivative to zero gives one linear equation per pixel: each x_p is pulled towards its data and towards its neighbours:
2x_1 - x_2 = 0, \qquad -x_1 + 3x_2 - x_3 = 3, \qquad -x_2 + 2x_3 = 0.
Solution: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.75, 1.5, 0.75). The peak is halved and spread to its neighbours; the total 0.75 + 1.5 + 0.75 = 3 is preserved.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: The math: one sparse linear system
text:
The math: one sparse linear system
With \rho(d) = d^2/2 the smoothness term is \frac\lambda2\sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 = \frac\lambda2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x, with the graph Laplacian L = D - W (from ncut/, graph-cut day; on a path: 1, 2, …, 2, 1 on the diagonal, -1 beside it). The gradient of E is (\mathbf x - \mathbf y) + \lambda L\mathbf x, so the minimum solves
(I + \lambda L)\,\mathbf x = \mathbf y, \qquad \text{on a path: } \begin{bmatrix} 1 + \lambda & -\lambda & & \\ -\lambda & 1 + 2\lambda & -\lambda & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots \\ & & -\lambda & 1 + \lambda\end{bmatrix}\mathbf x = \mathbf y.

Tridiagonal in 1D (solved in O(n) by elimination); in 2D a sparse system with 5 non-zeros per row. I + \lambda L is symmetric positive definite: one unique minimum.
Probabilistically: the posterior \propto \exp\big(-\frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\|\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 - \frac{\lambda'}2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x\big) is Gaussian (a Gaussian MRF). Multiply by \sigma_n^2: our \lambda = \lambda'\sigma_n^2. Its MAP, its mean and its MPM coincide.
L is the matrix form of the image Laplacian \nabla^2 of kernels/ (with a minus sign).

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: Quadratic smoothing is a low-pass filter
text:
Quadratic smoothing is a low-pass filter
On a long signal (or a ring) the same weighted averaging happens everywhere: the solution is a convolution of \mathbf y with a fixed kernel. In frequency space each frequency is multiplied by a gain:
\text{gain}(\omega) = \frac{1}{1 + \lambda\,(2 - 2\cos\omega)}

Constant signals (\omega = 0) pass unchanged; the fastest oscillation (\omega = \pi, +1, -1, +1, \dots) is divided by 1 + 4\lambda: by 5 at \lambda = 1, by 41 at \lambda = 10.
At \lambda = 10 the gain is \tfrac12 at 0.05 cycles per sample: details shorter than about 20 samples are halved.
An edge contains all frequencies: removing the high ones blurs it. A quadratic prior cannot tell an edge from noise.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: The math: the DFT diagonalises I + \lambda L
text:
The math: the DFT diagonalises I + \lambda L
On a ring of n samples, L is circulant: (L\mathbf x)_p = 2x_p - x_{p-1} - x_{p+1}, a convolution with (-1, 2, -1). Every circulant matrix has the Fourier vectors f_p = e^{i\omega p}, \omega = 2\pi k/n, as eigenvectors (fourier/: the DFT is a change of basis):
(L\mathbf f)_p = (2 - e^{-i\omega} - e^{i\omega})\,e^{i\omega p} = (2 - 2\cos\omega)\,f_p.
So in the Fourier basis (I + \lambda L) is diagonal with entries 1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega), and solving the system divides each Fourier coefficient by it. For small \omega, 2 - 2\cos\omega \approx \omega^2: gain \approx 1/(1 + \lambda\omega^2), a smooth low-pass.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Why squares blur edges
How expensive is a step of height 3 for each prior?




one jump of 3
three steps of 1
thirty steps of 0.1




quadratic \sum d^2/2
4.5
1.5
0.15


absolute \sum \lvert d\rvert (TV)
3
3
3




The quadratic prior prefers ramps: spreading a jump over many small steps makes it almost free. Edges get smeared.
With absolute values, a monotone transition costs its height, however it is spread. The data term then decides, and the data say “sharp”.
(Prior samples: a quadratic prior is a random walk with normal steps; it has no notion of an edge.)

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Total variation
E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}|x_p - x_q| \qquad\text{(Rudin, Osher \& Fatemi, 1992)}
By hand: \mathbf y = (0, 0, 3, 3), \lambda = 1:

Moving the left plateau up by \delta and the right one down by \delta costs 2 \cdot 2 \cdot \tfrac12\delta^2 = 2\delta^2 in data and saves 2\delta in TV (3 - 2\delta instead of 3). Best: \delta = 0.5.
\hat{\mathbf x} = (0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5): the step stays sharp, the two plateaus move towards each other by \lambda/\text{width} = 0.5. Energy 0.5 + 2 = 2.5, against 3 for \mathbf y itself.
The quadratic prior on the same data: (0.43, 0.86, 2.14, 2.57): a ramp.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: The math: what the TV solution looks like
text:
The math: what the TV solution looks like
\rho(d) = |d| is convex but has a kink at 0. At the minimum, for every sample the subgradient contains 0:
x_p - y_p + \lambda\,(g_{p-1} - g_p) = 0, \qquad g_p \in \operatorname{sign}(x_{p+1} - x_p), \; g_p \in [-1, 1] \text{ where } x_{p+1} = x_p.
Sum this over a plateau (a run of equal values c from a to b): the inner g’s cancel and
\sum_{p=a}^b(y_p - c) = \lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c = \bar y_{[a,b]} - \frac{\lambda\,(g_{a-1} - g_b)}{b - a + 1}.

Each plateau sits at the mean of its data, shifted by \lambda/\text{width} for each neighbouring plateau that is higher or lower: up from a local minimum, down from a local maximum, 2\lambda/\text{width} for a peak with two lower neighbours; no net shift between a lower and a higher neighbour.
Plateaus merge when the shift would overshoot their neighbour. Exact 1D algorithms find all plateaus directly (Condat, 2013: linear time in practice).
\mathbf y = (0, 3, 0): the peak would drop by 2\lambda and the sides rise by \lambda: (\lambda, 3 - 2\lambda, \lambda) for \lambda \le 1, then all equal to the mean 1.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: The price of TV: staircases and lost contrast
text:
The price of TV: staircases and lost contrast

Staircasing: a ramp has no single cheapest shape under TV; with noise, the minimum breaks it into flat steps. (The demo’s ramp at \lambda = 3: about a dozen steps.)
Small features lose contrast: a plateau of width w that sticks out on both sides is lowered by about 2\lambda/w. Narrow peaks shrink first, then vanish. \mathbf y = (0, 3, 0) at \lambda = 0.5: (0.5, 2, 0.5); at \lambda = 1: flat (1, 1, 1).
Huber penalty: quadratic for small differences |d| \le \delta (smooth ramps, no stairs), linear for large ones (edges stay): a compromise.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: Try it: quadratic, Huber and TV
text:
Try it: quadratic, Huber and TV




200 samples: a step at 40 (0 → 2), a ramp from 2 to 0 over 80–140, a 4-sample peak of height 2 at 166–169; Gaussian noise σn = 0.3 (seed 1); noisy data RMSE 0.291. Tour: “quadratic blurs the step” (λ = 10): noise gone, but the step spreads over about 15 samples and the peak drops to 0.90; RMSE 0.240. Lower λ to 1.2 (its best, 0.190): the noise comes back. “TV keeps the step” (λ = 1): the step stays within two samples, RMSE 0.137; the peak is lowered to 1.36. “TV staircases the ramp” (λ = 3): steps on the ramp. “TV shrinks the narrow peak” (λ = 2): peak 0.86, at λ = 3 0.36. “Huber in between” (λ = 5, δ = 0.1): smooth ramp, sharp step, peak 1.72, RMSE 0.128. Tabs: “prior samples” and “the matrix” (I + λL and the gain curve).

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
What do the priors believe?
Draw samples from the priors themselves (no data): p(\mathbf x) \propto e^{-\lambda\sum\rho(x_{p+1} - x_p)} makes each step x_{p+1} - x_p independent: a random walk.

Quadratic: normal steps. TV: Laplace steps \propto e^{-\lambda|d|}: more very small steps and more large jumps than a normal distribution with the same spread.
But TV samples do not look piecewise constant: they are rough random walks too. The flat plateaus of the TV estimate come from taking the minimum (the MAP), not from what the prior’s typical samples look like.
Lesson (as with the exact MAP of the binary model): an estimate can have properties that typical images of the model do not have.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
TV elsewhere in the course

Level sets (elective): the Chan–Vese length term is the total variation of an indicator function (a 0/1 image); the binary Ising energy counts the same boundary length on the pixel grid.
Relaxing labels: TV of a soft (0…1) labelling is a convex relaxation of graph-cut segmentation: pointer only.
Deconvolution (day 5): the same quadratic (Tikhonov) and TV priors with a blurring forward model. Here the forward model is the identity.
Radon (algebraic reconstruction) and wavelets (shrinkage) recall TV from here as a regulariser.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Summary

Grey-value denoising: E = \frac12\sum(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum\rho(x_p - x_q).
Quadratic \rho (Gaussian MRF): one sparse linear system (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y; a low-pass filter with gain 1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega)); blurs edges because ramps are cheaper than jumps.
Total variation \rho = |d|: a monotone transition costs its height, so edges stay sharp; plateaus move by \lambda/\text{width}; ramps become staircases, small features lose contrast.
Huber: quadratic for small differences, linear for large ones.
Prior samples are random walks; the piecewise-constant look of TV is a property of the minimum, not of the prior.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the Gibbs distribution p(\mathbf s) \propto e^{-E(\mathbf s)/T}, and why its normaliser Z is out of reach for an image. Today: we draw samples anyway, one pixel at a time.

The local rule: a pixel given its neighbours is a coin flip with a known bias.
Two samplers: Gibbs (redraw the pixel) and Metropolis (propose a flip, maybe accept).
Why they work: a random walk whose long-run distribution is the Gibbs distribution.
What samples of a large lattice look like: the phase transition at T_c \approx 2.27.
Simulated annealing: sample while cooling, to find low energies.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Notation as in unit 1: spins ±1, coupling J, field h, temperature T; neighbours are the 4-neighbours; the large lattice is periodic (a torus), so every site has 4 neighbours. The demos: isingenum (the 3 × 3 lattice, now in sample mode) and isinglattice (256 × 256).

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
section: A sample is the best picture of a distribution
text:
A sample is the best picture of a distribution

Each panel is one random state of a 128 \times 128 Ising lattice (J = 1, h = 0), drawn by the methods of this unit (500 sweeps from random spins).

We cannot list 2^{16384} probabilities, but a few typical states tell us what the model believes.
Cold: large regions that agree. Hot: noise. In between, at T_c: clusters of every size.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
section: One pixel at a time: no Z needed
text:
One pixel at a time: no Z needed
Change only pixel p. Its two possible values give two states that differ in s_p alone; their energy difference involves only p and its neighbours.

The neighbours “vote”: the local field u_p = J\cdot(\text{sum of the 4 neighbouring spins}) + h.
Given its neighbours, the pixel is +1 with probability p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{neighbours}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2u_p/T}} a logistic curve in the vote.
Example: neighbours (+, +, +, -), J = 1, h = 0: u_p = 2. At T = 2: 1/(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.88. At T = 1: 0.98; at T = 4: 0.73.
Markov property: given its neighbours, a pixel does not care about the rest of the image. Hence “Markov random field”.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
The math: the local conditional
Write \mathbf s^+ and \mathbf s^- for the state with s_p = +1 and s_p = -1, everything else fixed. Every term of E that does not contain s_p is the same in both, so
E(\mathbf s^-) - E(\mathbf s^+) = 2J\sum_{q \sim p}s_q + 2h = 2u_p.
The ratio of probabilities needs no Z:
\frac{p(\mathbf s^+)}{p(\mathbf s^-)} = e^{2u_p/T} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p(s_p = +1 \mid \text{rest}) = \frac{e^{2u_p/T}}{e^{2u_p/T} + 1} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-2u_p/T}}.
It depends on the rest of the image only through the neighbours (via u_p): the Markov property. Flipping p changes the energy by \Delta E = 2s_pu_p.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Two samplers
Visit the pixels one after the other (a sweep visits each once).

Gibbs sampler (heat bath; Geman & Geman, 1984): draw the pixel anew from its local conditional, i.e. set +1 with probability 1/(1 + e^{-2u_p/T}).
Metropolis (Metropolis et al., 1953): propose to flip the pixel. Compute \Delta E:

\Delta E \le 0 (downhill): always accept;
\Delta E > 0 (uphill): accept with probability e^{-\Delta E/T}.


Uphill moves are what make it a sampler and not a minimiser. A flip with \Delta E = 4 is accepted with probability e^{-2} = 0.14 at T = 2, but only e^{-8} = 0.0003 at T = 0.5.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Try it: sampling the 3 \times 3 lattice




Sample mode: one step = one randomly chosen site, updated by Gibbs or Metropolis; the circled site is the last one visited (dashed: rejected / unchanged). The red dots are the fraction of steps spent at each energy level, the bars the exact values from enumeration. Tour: “sample: converges” (T = 3, Gibbs), play at 10 steps per frame, then 100 and 1000: after 100 steps the dots are far off (total-variation distance 0.35), after 1000 close (0.07), after 100 000 within 0.01. Then “sample: low T, stuck” (T = 1, Metropolis, magnetisation tab): the energy histogram looks right, but the chain never leaves the m = +1 side, although m = −1 has the same probability. Leaving needs a flip with ΔE = 8: e^−8 = 0.0003 per try, and then many more uphill steps.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
section: Why does this work? A random walk on states
text:
Why does this work? A random walk on states
The sampler moves from state to state at random: a Markov chain. Two states, a (energy 0) and b (energy 1), T = 1, Metropolis:

From a: propose b, uphill by 1: go with probability e^{-1} = 0.37, else stay.
From b: propose a, downhill: always go.

P = \begin{bmatrix} 0.63 & 0.37 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad (\text{row} = \text{from}, \text{column} = \text{to})

Run long: the fraction of time in a and b settles at \boldsymbol\pi = (0.73, 0.27), whatever the start.
That is exactly the Gibbs distribution: 1/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.73.
Balance: in the long run, traffic a \to b (0.73 \cdot 0.37 = 0.27) equals traffic b \to a (0.27 \cdot 1).

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
section: The math: stationary distribution and detailed balance
text:
The math: stationary distribution and detailed balance
A Markov chain with transition matrix P (P_{ab} = probability to go from a to b; rows sum to 1) moves a distribution \boldsymbol\pi (a row vector) to \boldsymbol\pi P. A stationary distribution satisfies
\boldsymbol\pi P = \boldsymbol\pi: \quad \boldsymbol\pi \text{ is a left eigenvector of } P \text{ with eigenvalue } 1.
If every state can reach every other (and the chain is not periodic), it is unique and the chain converges to it from any start.
Detailed balance: \pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_bP_{ba} for all pairs. Summing over a: \sum_a\pi_aP_{ab} = \pi_b\sum_aP_{ba} = \pi_b, so detailed balance implies stationarity.
Metropolis with a symmetric proposal and E_b > E_a: P_{ab} = q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T}, P_{ba} = q. Then
\pi_aP_{ab} = \frac{e^{-E_a/T}}{Z}\,q\,e^{-(E_b - E_a)/T} = \frac{e^{-E_b/T}}{Z}\,q = \pi_bP_{ba}.
The Gibbs sampler satisfies it too (it is a Metropolis–Hastings move that is always accepted). Note: Z never had to be computed.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
In practice: burn-in and mixing

Burn-in: the chain starts somewhere arbitrary (the noisy image, random spins). The first sweeps are not yet samples of the Gibbs distribution: discard them.
Correlated samples: consecutive states differ in a few pixels. 1000 sweeps are worth far fewer than 1000 independent samples.
Mixing: at low T the chain can stay in one region of states for a very long time. On the 3 \times 3 lattice at T = 1 it never leaves “mostly +1” in 100 000 steps, although “mostly -1” is as probable.
No convergence proofs here: in practice, run longer, start from several states, and check that the answers agree.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
The phase transition
On a large lattice (here 256 \times 256, periodic, h = 0) the samples change character at the critical temperature T_c = 2/\ln(1 + \sqrt2) \approx 2.27 (for J = 1; Onsager, 1944):

Below T_c: domains grow and one sign takes over the lattice: a magnetisation |m| well above 0 (0.91 at T = 2).
Above T_c: noise with small clusters; m \approx 0.
At T_c: clusters of all sizes, from single pixels to the whole lattice.

The model has no preferred sign, but below T_c the lattice picks one: spontaneous symmetry breaking. A tiny field h decides which.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Try it: a large lattice




256 × 256 periodic lattice, checkerboard Metropolis sweeps (about 2.5 ms per sweep in the browser, so several per frame). Tour: “cold: domains coarsen” (T = 1.5 from random spins): domains grow, the domain-wall length falls (9740 disagreeing pairs after 10 sweeps, 1618 after 1000) and with this seed one sign wins (m = 0.986 at sweep 1000). “hot: noise” (T = 5): m stays near 0, E/n ≈ −0.42. “at T_c”: clusters of all sizes; E/n approaches −1.40 (the exact value for the infinite lattice is −√2 = −1.414). “a small field decides” (T = 1.8, h = 0.05): m = 0.82 after 20 sweeps, 0.96 after 50; with h = 0 the lattice is still undecided after 400 sweeps (m = −0.21). T-scan tab: run it, ⟨|m|⟩ against T follows Onsager’s curve below T_c (0.912 against 0.911 at T = 2) and is small but not zero above it (a finite lattice).

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
The math: Onsager’s results
For the infinite square lattice with h = 0 (Onsager 1944; Yang 1952):
T_c = \frac{2J}{\ln(1 + \sqrt2)} \approx 2.269\,J, \qquad |m| = \Big(1 - \sinh(2J/T)^{-4}\Big)^{1/8} \text{ for } T < T_c, \quad 0 \text{ above}.
Energy per spin at T_c: -\sqrt2\,J.
No transition in 1D. For a chain, the transfer matrix of unit 1 gives the free energy per spin -T\ln\mu_1 with \mu_1 = 2\cosh(J/T) (for h = 0): a smooth function of T for every T > 0. A single disagreeing pair cuts a chain into two domains at a finite energy cost 2J, so at any T > 0 such walls appear with density about e^{-2J/T} and destroy long-range order. In 2D a wall around a domain costs energy proportional to its length, which wins against the entropy of the wall below T_c.

title: Sampling, temperature and the phase transition
text:
Critical slowing down
Near T_c local updates become slow: big clusters must be dismantled one pixel at a time.
Start a 128 \times 128 lattice with all spins +1 and count the sweeps until |m| < 0.1 (the true value above T_c is 0):
