B has mean 5/3 and deviations (-\tfrac23, \tfrac43, -\tfrac23). At t = 1 the pixels of A are B itself: NCC = 1. At t = 5, (2, 6, 2) = 2B: the same deviations times 2, NCC = 1. At t = 3, (1, 0, 2) has mean 1 and deviations (0, -1, 1); the sum of products of deviations is 0 - \tfrac43 - \tfrac23 = -2, the squared lengths are \tfrac{24}{9} and 2, so NCC = -2/\sqrt{48/9} = -0.866. (The others: -0.189 at t = 0, 2, 4.)
CC chooses t = 5 (22 against 11 for the exact copy): it prefers the bright copy. SSD chooses t = 1 (0 against 11). NCC scores both copies 1. For tiles with different exposure, NCC: a change of gain or offset does not matter to it, while SSD would penalise the true shift.

B2. (a) CC = 1, 0, 0, 5, 5: the maximum (5) is in the bright region at t = 3 and 4, while the copy of B is at t = 0 (CC 1, SSD 0). (b) At t = 4 the pixels of A are (5, 5, 5): flat, with zero spread, so NCC is 0/0, undefined. Flat regions carry no pattern; NCC cannot (and should not) say they match. Implementations return 0 or skip them.
B3. SSD = 2^2 + 3^2 + 4^2 = 29. B = 2A + 1, so NCC = 1: the same pattern with more contrast and an offset. SSD says “different”, NCC says “same pattern”.
B4. (a) All shifts of two N-pixel images cost about N^2: (2048^2)^2 = 1.8 \cdot 10^{13} multiply-adds, about 4.9 hours. (b) 41^2 = 1681 shifts of about 205 \cdot 2048 = 4.2 \cdot 10^5 pixels: 7 \cdot 10^8 (exactly 6.7 \cdot 10^8, counting the slightly smaller overlaps of the shifted strips), less than a second. (c) If the stage is worse than you assumed, the true shift is outside the window, and the best score in the window is a wrong shift. Check the score: a low NCC means “not found”, not “found here”.
B5. At every shift that is a multiple of 12 away from the true one: if the true shift is 9, at -39, -27, -15, -3, 9, 21, 33, 45. A defect or the edge of the grating inside the overlap, or the nominal stage position (take the peak nearest to it), decides.
B6. (a) NCC about 1 (a gain does not matter). (b) Lower: the template sees only part of the big cell, a bright patch filling most of the window; NCC is positive but well below 1, and the best position may be off-centre. (c) Undefined or close to 0: no pattern (in practice the noise gives small random values). (d) Close to −1: the same pattern with the contrast inverted. A detector keeps the positive peaks above a threshold.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that over the overlap \Omega_t, \mathrm{SSD}(t) = E_A(t) + E_B(t) - 2\,\mathrm{CC}(t) with E_A(t) = \sum_{\Omega_t} f(x+t)^2 and E_B(t) = \sum_{\Omega_t} g(x)^2. For a template that always lies completely inside A, which of the two energies depends on t? What does that mean for SSD vs CC?
B8. (math) (a) Show that |\mathrm{NCC}| \le 1, with equality exactly when g = af + b on the overlap (a \ne 0). (b) Show that NCC does not change when g is replaced by ag + b with a > 0. What happens for a < 0?
B9. (math) Show that all shifts of two signals of length N (every shift with a non-empty overlap) cost N^2 multiply-adds in total, and that a window |t| \le w costs (2w+1)N - w(w+1). Give the 2D versions for N \times N images.






Solutions (math)





B7. Expand (f - g)^2 = f^2 + g^2 - 2fg and sum over \Omega_t. For a template inside A, \Omega_t is always the whole template, so E_B is a constant; but E_A(t) is the energy of the part of A under the template and changes with t. SSD = E_A(t) + \text{const} - 2\,\mathrm{CC}(t): minimising SSD is maximising \mathrm{CC}(t) - E_A(t)/2, which punishes bright regions. Maximising CC alone rewards them (B2).
B8. (a) Let \mathbf u, \mathbf v be the mean-free overlap vectors of f and g. NCC = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v / (\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|), and Cauchy–Schwarz gives |\mathbf u \cdot \mathbf v| \le \|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|, with equality iff \mathbf v = a\mathbf u, i.e. g - \bar g = a(f - \bar f), g = af + b. (b) ag + b has mean a\bar g + b, so its mean-free vector is a\mathbf v: numerator and denominator both scale by |a| up to the sign of a, NCC becomes \operatorname{sign}(a)\,NCC. For a < 0 (inverted contrast) NCC changes sign: a perfect match scores −1.
B9. Shift t overlaps N - |t| samples. \sum_{t=-(N-1)}^{N-1}(N - |t|) = N + 2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}k = N + N(N - 1) = N^2. For the window: \sum_{|t| \le w}(N - |t|) = (2w+1)N - 2\cdot\frac{w(w+1)}{2} = (2w+1)N - w(w+1). In 2D the overlap (N - |t_x|)(N - |t_y|) is a product, so the double sum is the square of the 1D sum: N^4 for all shifts, \big((2w+1)N - w(w+1)\big)^2 for the window; for N = 1024, w = 32: 65504^2 = 4.29 \cdot 10^9.

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Explore: sliding and scoring
Image A (blue, 64 samples) and image B (red) placed at the shift t; the shaded band is the overlap. Below, the score of every shift: SSD (red), CC (green) and NCC (blue), each scaled to its own range in all three mode; the bold part has been “visited” by B so far, the dots mark each score’s best shift, the dotted green line the true shift. SSD and CC are averaged over the overlap (so that long and short overlaps compare fairly); the readout gives the sums and counts the multiply-adds. gain, offset and ramp change B’s brightness; min. overlap limits the shifts.



E1. Preset by hand: (1,3,1). Move the shift from 0 to 5 and check your table of B1. Which shift does each score choose?
E2. Preset a matching bump: B is a 16-sample piece of A. Slide B from left to right. Which shift does each score choose? How many multiply-adds did the whole search cost?
E3. Preset brighter copy: SSD fails (B as long as A, gain 1.6, offset 40). Where are the best shifts of SSD, CC and NCC? Compare SSD per pixel at the true shift and at SSD’s best shift. Set the gain back to 1 and the offset to 0: what changes?
E4. Preset bright blob: CC fails. Where does CC put its peak, and why there? Do SSD and NCC agree with the truth?
E5. Preset periodic: many peaks, score NCC. List the shifts where NCC reaches 1. Which one does the readout report as best, and why that one?
E6. Preset tiny overlap: NCC noisy (noise 15, overlaps down to 2 samples). Where is NCC’s best shift, and how large is the overlap there? Raise min. overlap to 16. What does NCC choose now, and what is its value at the true shift?
E7. Preset micrograph profile: A is a row of the course micrograph. Which score fails here? Look at the profile: why?






Solutions





E1. The readout gives the sums of B1: CC 6, 11, 6, 3, 12, 22; SSD 9, 0, 9, 10, 27, 11; NCC −0.189, 1, −0.189, −0.866, −0.189, 1. Best: SSD 1, CC 5, NCC 1 (both copies score 1; the first one is reported).
E2. All three find the true shift 22. The search covers 65 shifts (min. overlap 8) and costs 968 multiply-adds.
E3. SSD chooses 48 (wrong), CC 10 (one off), NCC 9 (the truth, NCC 1.000). SSD per pixel is 9462.6 at the truth but only 1598.3 at 48, where B’s bright parts happen to lie on bright parts of A. With gain 1 and offset 0 B is an exact copy, SSD is 0 at the truth and all three agree.
E4. CC puts its peak at 42, where B lies on the bright blob: the products are large because A is large there. SSD and NCC find the truth, 12.
E5. NCC is 1 at -39, -27, -15, -3, 9, 21, 33, 45: every 12 samples. The readout reports −3, the first of the equal maxima from the left: the choice between equal peaks is arbitrary. (The true shift is 9.)
E6. NCC’s best is at 62, where the overlap is only 2 samples: two pairs of numbers always have a correlation of ±1. With min. overlap 16 NCC chooses 9, the true shift, with NCC 0.874 (less than 1 because of the noise).
E7. CC chooses −28; SSD and NCC find 9. The micrograph is bright (around 170) with dark structures: CC is largest where B’s bright parts lie on bright parts of A, not where the dark structures match.

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Explore: template matching
Drag the yellow template box over the image. The right panel shows the NCC of the template at every position (top-left corner of the box; red positive, blue negative, grey where the template does not fit). Cyan boxes mark the local maxima above the threshold.



E8. Preset dark granules: a 20 \times 20 template on a dark granule of the micrograph. What is the NCC at the template’s own position, and how high are the next best matches? Lower the threshold to 0.3: what kind of places are added?
E9. Preset nuclei (synthetic): 18 nuclei, a 32 \times 32 template on the one at the top left. How many matches are there at threshold 0.5? Which nuclei are missed, and what do they have in common? Lower the threshold to 0.3: how many nuclei are found now?






Solutions





E8. NCC is 1.00 at (99, 59), the template’s own position (it is a copy of itself). The next best are (203, 10), (225, 162) and (79, 207), all with NCC about 0.5: dark specks with some likeness, but no real copies of the granule. At 0.3 many more dark or textured places pass the threshold: NCC rewards any similar local pattern, so the threshold sets the trade-off between missed and false matches.
E9. At 0.5 there are 14 matches, one on each of 14 nuclei (NCC from 1.00 for the template itself down to 0.57). Three of the four missed nuclei touch a neighbour, so the template window also contains part of the other nucleus; the fourth, at the bottom edge, is cut by the border and the template cannot be centred on it. At 0.3 there are 16 matches, on 16 of the 18 nuclei. Of the last two, one (touching its neighbour at the bottom left) scores only 0.27; the other, at the right (NCC 0.35), lies within half a template of a better match on its touching neighbour, and the search keeps only the higher of two nearby maxima. Template matching assumes isolated objects of one size and shape; touching and elongated objects score lower.

title: Exercise: finding a shift by sliding and scoring
text:
Where this leads
Trying every shift costs about N^2 operations for two images of N pixels. The next unit computes the cross-correlation for all shifts at once with three FFTs, at a cost of about N \log N. After that, normalising the spectrum turns the broad CC peak into a sharp spike: phase correlation.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Explore: gradient descent on a landscape
text:
Explore: gradient descent on a landscape
The colours show a loss over two parameters (a, b) in bands (darker = lower; the white dot is the minimum). Each loss is the average over 40 training examples, so a mini-batch gradient is a real noisy estimate. Click to start a path (up to three), then 1 step or run 50 steps. The small plot shows the loss above the minimum, on a log scale.



G1. Presets too small and just right (the same start). Run each until the loss is within 0.001 of the minimum (0.092). How many steps does each need?
G2. Still on the bowl, raise \eta step by step from 0.3 (click the same start, or use diverges for \eta = 0.8). Above which \eta does the path diverge?
G3. Preset zig-zag across a narrow valley (\eta = 0.6). Describe the path. Then lower \eta to 0.03: what happens? Finally preset momentum in the valley (\eta = 0.03 with momentum).
G4. Preset SGD noise (batches of 4, \eta = 0.1). Compare the path with the full batch (set the batch size to 40, same \eta). Where does the mini-batch path end up after 200 steps? What changes with a smaller \eta?
G5. Preset two starts, two minima. Where does each path end, and with which loss?
G6. Preset one neuron’s real loss: the cross-entropy of one neuron p = \text{sigmoid}(ax + b) on 40 points of two overlapping classes. Describe the landscape. How many steps does \eta = 2 need, and \eta = 0.5?






Solutions





G1. \eta = 0.02: 192 steps; \eta = 0.3: 11 steps.
G2. \eta = 0.6 still converges (8 steps, with a small overshoot); at \eta = 0.8 the path jumps from side to side further each time and the loss explodes. The limit lies near \eta = 0.75: stability needs \eta < 2/\lambda_\text{max}, and the steepest curvature of this bowl is \lambda_\text{max} = 2.67, so 2/2.67 = 0.75.
G3. With \eta = 0.6 the path bounces from one wall of the valley to the other while it creeps along the valley floor; it gets within 0.001 of the minimum after 67 steps. With \eta = 0.03 there is no zig-zag, but progress along the flat floor is very slow: after 200 steps the loss is still 0.19 (minimum 0.064). With momentum, the same \eta = 0.03 gets there in 115 steps: the velocity builds up along the floor, while the back-and-forth across the valley cancels out. (The valley’s curvatures differ by a factor of about 40.)
G4. The mini-batch path wanders: each step uses only 4 of the 40 examples. It gets near the minimum about as fast as the full batch (within 0.001 after about 40 steps against 37), but it never settles: after 200 steps it is still jiggling around the minimum (loss 0.0924 against 0.0921). A smaller \eta makes the jiggle smaller but the approach slower (with \eta = 0.02 the loss is still 0.096 after 200 steps). In practice \eta is lowered during training for this reason.
G5. The left start (a = -0.3) ends in the deeper minimum at a = -1.03 (loss -0.254), the right start (a = +0.3) in the shallower one at a = 0.97 (loss +0.246). Gradient descent finds the bottom of the valley it starts in, not the deepest one.
G6. A long, flat, curved valley; the minimum is at (a, b) = (2.34, -0.61) with loss 0.325 (the classes overlap, so the loss cannot reach 0). Far from the minimum it rises steeply on one side and flattens on the other. \eta = 2 gets within 0.001 in 21 steps, \eta = 0.5 in 89. The real losses of networks have exactly this kind of flat and curved valleys, in millions of dimensions.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Explore: overfitting and its cures
The point classifier of the previous unit, now with the training controls: learning rate, batch size, validation share (hollow points are held out for validation and never used for training), weight decay \lambda and dropout. The plot shows the training loss (blue) and the validation loss (red); the readout gives the step with the lowest validation loss.



E1. Preset overfitting: 8+8 units, 60 noisy points (30 for training, 30 for validation). Train for about 2000 steps. Where is the validation loss lowest? What do the two losses do after that? Look at the decision boundary: how does it treat the noisy training points?
E2. Preset weight decay smooths it (\lambda = 0.003). Train again and compare both curves and the boundary with E1.
E3. Preset dropout (probability 0.4). What does the training curve look like, and why? What happens to the validation loss?
E4. Preset more data cures it (300 points). Compare the gap between the two curves with E1.
E5. Preset mini-batches of 8 (200 points, 100 for training). How many steps are one epoch? Compare the curves with the full batch (move the batch size slider to “all”).
E6. Presets learning rate too large (\eta = 1.5) and dead network (\eta = 5). Describe the loss curves and the hidden-unit thumbnails. What has happened?






Solutions





E1. The validation loss is lowest at step 126 (0.169, validation accuracy 90 %). After that the training loss falls towards zero (0.002 at step 2000) while the validation loss rises (0.72 at step 500, 0.38 at step 2000): the boundary bends around single noisy training points, making small islands that are wrong for new points. Early stopping would keep the step-126 network.
E2. The training loss stops at about 0.164 (it cannot go to zero: large weights are penalised), and the validation loss stays near 0.31 instead of climbing to 0.7. The boundary is smooth, without islands. (Its lowest validation loss, 0.185 at step 183, is not better than early stopping here; the gain is that it no longer matters much when you stop.)
E3. The training curve is noisy and stays high (about 0.23–0.32): every step trains a different random half-silenced network. The validation loss (computed with all units) stays low much longer: 0.18 after 2000 steps, against 0.38 without dropout.
E4. With 150 training points the two curves stay close (at step 1000: training 0.20, validation 0.18; at 4000: 0.13 and 0.24); the network cannot memorise 150 points with its 105 weights as easily as 30. More data is the most reliable cure.
E5. 100 training points in batches of 8: 12.5 steps per epoch. The mini-batch curve is jagged, the full-batch curve smooth; per step the full batch gets lower faster (at step 1000: 0.18 against 0.22 training loss), but each mini-batch step costs 1/12 as much.
E6. \eta = 1.5: the loss jumps up and down during the first steps (0.79, 0.65, 0.55, 0.45, 0.41, 0.44, 0.38, 0.39, 0.47, 0.56, …) and then gets stuck near 0.38; 14 of the 16 hidden units are dead (off for every training point; their thumbnails are blank). \eta = 5: after a few huge jumps (up to 6.4) again 14 of the 16 units are dead, the network outputs probability one half everywhere, and the loss sits at 0.693 = \ln 2 for ever: almost no gradient reaches the hidden weights any more.

title: Exercise: convolutional networks
text:
Explore: receptive fields
Bottom row: input pixels along one line of the image; every row above is a layer (no padding, so each layer is a little shorter). Click a unit: the units it depends on light up in all layers below, and the bracket shows its receptive field. The square on the right shows that field in 2D next to a 20-pixel nucleus; the readout lists the field, the jump and the weights (for 16 channels in and out) of every layer.



F1. Presets three 3×3 layers = 7 and one 7×7 layer. Compare the field and the total weights. Check B6.
F2. Preset with pooling. Read the field after every layer. Click a unit in the second layer: why does it light up two input pixels more than a unit of the first layer, but a unit in the fourth layer four more than the third?
F3. Preset how deep to see a whole nucleus? Check B4. Remove layers one by one from the top: at which depth does the field drop below 20 pixels?
F4. Preset dilated: 1, 2, 4. What is the field after each layer? Why is dilation an alternative to pooling for growing the field?






Solutions





F1. Both see 7 pixels. Weights: three 3 \times 3 layers 6960 in total (2320 each), one 7 \times 7 layer 12,560.
F2. Fields 3, 4, 8, 10, 18 (jumps 1, 2, 2, 4, 4). The first pooling adds 1 pixel (r = 3 + 1 \cdot 1) but doubles the jump: after it, neighbouring units are 2 input pixels apart, so each further 3 \times 3 layer adds 2 \times 2 = 4 pixels instead of 2. After the second pooling the jump is 4, and the last convolution adds 8.
F3. 32 pixels after all 8 layers. Removing the top layer gives 24 (still enough), removing one more gives 16 (after conv, conv, pool, conv, conv, pool): too small for a 20-pixel nucleus. So 7 layers are needed, as in B4.
F4. 3, 7, 15: dilation d spreads the 3 taps d pixels apart, so the layer adds 2d pixels. The field doubles with each layer, as with pooling, but the maps keep their full resolution (useful for segmentation, the next unit).

title: Exercise: convolutional networks
text:
Explore: inside a trained network
A small convolutional network (conv 3 \times 3 with 8 kernels → pool → conv 3 \times 3 with 16 kernels → pool → dense → softmax, 9,098 weights) was trained on 60,000 handwritten digits (MNIST). Pick a digit or draw one; rotate and shift it. You see the 8 learned layer-1 kernels, the layer-1 and layer-2 feature maps and the class probabilities. Click a layer-2 map to see the 9 test-image patches (its receptive field, 8 \times 8) that excite it most. occlusion map covers each part of the input in turn with a 6 \times 6 black square and marks in red where this lowers the probability of the predicted class. Weight sets: trained with rotation augmentation (random rotations up to ±45°), training snapshots after 0, 1 and 3 epochs, and a network for cell masks (round, elongated, dividing, protrusion).



V1. Pick a few digits. Which layer-1 maps light up for horizontal strokes, which for vertical ones? Click two layer-2 maps and describe their favourite patches.
V2. Preset shifted digit (the 6, shifted 4 pixels right). What do the maps do, and what is the prediction? Now shift by 6 pixels left or right, or up or down. Is the network shift-invariant? Which part of it is not?
V3. Preset rotation 30°, no augmentation, then rotation 30°, with augmentation. Compare the predictions. Then rotate the 6 step by step with both weight sets: over which range of angles does each still say 6? The readout gives the test accuracy on digits rotated by 45°: compare.
V4. Preset a 6 rotated to a 9. What does the network say? Is it wrong? Would full rotation augmentation (any angle) be a good idea for digits?
V5. Choose the weight sets epoch 0, epoch 1, epoch 3 and the final one. What do the layer-1 kernels look like at epoch 0? How does the test accuracy develop?
V6. Preset what is the network looking at? (a 4, with the occlusion map). Where is the red region? Imagine the 4 with that part missing: which digit could it then be?
V7. Choose cell masks. Pick the four example shapes, then rotate the protrusion cell by 90° and 180°. Why is this network not troubled by rotation?






Solutions





V1. Different maps respond to different edges of the strokes: kernels 4 and 8 (positive above, negative below) light up along the lower edges of horizontal strokes, kernel 6 along diagonal edges, kernel 2 (all positive) on the ink itself. Layer-2 maps respond to combinations: their favourite patches show, for example, the end of a stroke, a curve, a corner where two strokes meet, or a short horizontal bar, each at the centre of the 8 \times 8 patch.
V2. The maps of both layers shift with the input (by 4 pixels in layer 1, by 2 in layer 2, which is pooled once); the prediction stays 6 with probability 1.00 for shifts of 4 left or right. At 6 pixels it breaks: shifted 6 left the network says 2 (0.53), 6 right 1 (0.79), 6 down 2 (0.50), 6 up 8 (0.99). The convolutional layers are equivariant and pooling adds a little tolerance, but the final dense layer has a separate weight for each position of the 7 \times 7 maps: it has only seen digits that are centred.
V3. At 30°, the network without augmentation says 4 (0.55), the one with augmentation 6 (1.00). Without augmentation the 6 stays a 6 from −75° to +20°; with augmentation from −85° to +50° (steps of 5°). On test digits rotated by 45°: 46.9 % correct without augmentation, 92.9 % with (at 0°: 98.7 % and 97.2 %; the augmented network pays a little on upright digits).
V4. It says 9 (probability 0.98; the augmented network 0.80). That is right: a 6 rotated by 180° is a 9. Rotation invariance is not wanted for digits; full rotation augmentation would make 6 and 9 (and partly 2 and 5) the same class. Augment only with changes that keep the label.
V5. Epoch 0: random kernels (noise patterns of small numbers), every digit gets about 10 % for every class, test accuracy 9.8 %. After one epoch (469 gradient steps) the kernels have structure and the accuracy is 94.4 %; after 3 epochs 97.4 %; after 10 epochs 98.7 %. Most of the learning happens in the first epoch.
V6. The red region lies at the upper right, where the right arm of the 4 starts above the crossbar (rows 8–13, columns 16–21 of the 28 \times 28 image). Covering it lowers the probability of 4 from 0.98 to 0.007; the network then says 5 (0.57): without that part, the remaining strokes (left arm, bar, lower stem) look more like a 5. The network bases its decision on a few key strokes, not on the whole shape.
V7. All four examples are classified correctly (protrusion with probability 1.00), and the protrusion cell rotated by 90° or 180° is still a protrusion (1.00). The training masks were generated in every orientation, so rotation was already “augmented” by the data: the network has learned the invariance from examples. Test accuracy 99.0 %.

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
About this lecture
k-means describes a group by one point and cuts the space with straight lines. Now each group gets a shape, a size and a weight: a Gaussian.

One Gaussian in 2D: a hill whose contour lines are ellipses, set by the covariance matrix \Sigma.
Mahalanobis distance: “how many standard deviations away”, in the direction you are going.
Covariance types: spherical, diagonal, full, tied.
The mixture as a recipe for making data; the hidden component of each point; responsibilities (soft labels) by Bayes’ rule.
The likelihood of a data set, and why one Gaussian is easy to fit and a mixture is not.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
From one dimension to two
In 1D the normal density is a bell: centre \mu, width \sigma. What matters is how many standard deviations x is from \mu: (x - \mu)/\sigma.
In 2D (two features per pixel) the density is a hill over the plane.

Its contour lines (points of equal density) are ellipses around the centre \boldsymbol\mu.
Round hill: both features vary equally and independently. Stretched hill: one direction varies more. Tilted hill: the features are correlated (bright in one channel, bright in the other).
All of this is in one 2 \times 2 matrix, the covariance \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \sigma_1^2 & c \\ c & \sigma_2^2 \end{pmatrix}: variances on the diagonal, covariance c off it.

Notation: \Sigma for the covariance of a model component, S for a covariance computed from data.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Reading an ellipse: an example




\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, centred at \mathbf 0.

Eigenvalues \lambda_1 = 6, \lambda_2 = 1; eigenvectors \mathbf v_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt5, \mathbf v_2 = (-1, 2)/\sqrt5.
The 1σ ellipse: half-axis \sqrt6 = 2.45 along (2, 1), half-axis 1 across it. Tilted by 26.6°.
Check: \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = 7 = 5 + 2 (the trace), \lambda_1\lambda_2 = 6 = 5 \cdot 2 - 2^2 (the determinant).

The points P = (2, 1) and Q = (-1, 2) are both \sqrt5 = 2.24 from the centre. Is either of them unusual?
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Mahalanobis distance
Euclidean distance ignores the shape of the cloud. The Mahalanobis distance measures in standard deviations along the direction you are going:
d_M(\mathbf x)^2 = (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu).

In 1D: d_M = |x - \mu|/\sigma, the familiar “how many sigmas”.
The 1σ ellipse is exactly d_M = 1; the 2σ ellipse d_M = 2.
In the example: P lies along the long axis, d_M(P) = \sqrt{5/6} = 0.91, inside the 1σ ellipse. Q lies along the short axis, d_M(Q) = \sqrt5 = 2.24: more than 2σ out. Same Euclidean distance, very different.

Use: “is this pixel (or object) unusual for this class?” (unit 4: anomalies).
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: the density and its ellipses
text:
The math: the density and its ellipses
\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d/2}\,|\Sigma|^{1/2}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12 (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)\right)
In 1D the exponent is -\tfrac12 (x - \mu)^2/\sigma^2; \Sigma^{-1} replaces 1/\sigma^2.

\Sigma is symmetric positive definite: \Sigma = Q\Lambda Q^\top with orthonormal eigenvectors in Q and \Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_d). In the rotated coordinates \mathbf y = Q^\top(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu): d_M^2 = \sum_i y_i^2/\lambda_i.
So the density factorises into independent 1D normals with variances \lambda_i along the eigenvectors, and d_M = 1 is the ellipse with half-axes \sqrt{\lambda_i}. |\Sigma| = \prod_i\lambda_i.
Sampling: with \mathbf z standard normal (d independent \mathcal N(0, 1)), \mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu + Q\Lambda^{1/2}\mathbf z has covariance Q\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{1/2}Q^\top = \Sigma. (Any L with LL^\top = \Sigma, e.g. the Cholesky factor, works too.)
Example: \Sigma^{-1} = \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{pmatrix}; d_M(P)^2 = \frac16(8 - 8 + 5) = \frac56; d_M(Q)^2 = \frac16(2 + 8 + 20) = 5.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Try it: one Gaussian




Preset “same Euclidean distance, different Mahalanobis”: Σ = [5 2; 2 2]. The readout gives λ1 = 6, λ2 = 1, the angle 26.6°, and for P = (2, 1): Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 0.91, density 0.043; for Q = (−1, 2): Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 2.24, density 0.005. Drag the square handles: the ellipse turns and stretches; the samples (300, fixed seed) follow. Switch Σ to “spherical”: circles, Mahalanobis = Euclidean / σ. “diagonal”: axis-aligned ellipses only.

More freedom fits better, but needs more data and can overfit (unit 3).

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: A mixture is a recipe for data
text:
A mixture is a recipe for data
A Gaussian mixture with K components makes one data point like this:

pick a component k at random, with probability \pi_k (the weights, summing to 1);
draw \mathbf x from that component’s Gaussian \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k).

The density of the result is a weighted sum of hills:
p(\mathbf x) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k).
Image example: a pixel is background (weight 0.6, dark), cytoplasm (0.3, grey) or nucleus (0.1, bright), and its value scatters around the class mean.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
The labels are hidden
We see the points, not which component made each one: the component is a hidden (latent) variable.

With colours (labels), fitting is easy: each class’s mean and covariance separately (this is supervised learning).
Without them, the clouds overlap and we must recover the recipe from the uncoloured points: unsupervised.
Fitting a mixture = finding \pi_k, \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k that could have produced the data (unit 3).

In the demo: tick hide colours: this is what an algorithm gets.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Responsibilities: soft labels
Given the parameters, which component made \mathbf x? Bayes’ rule, as on the thresholding day:
r_k(\mathbf x) = P(k \mid \mathbf x) = \frac{\pi_k\,\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k)}{p(\mathbf x)}.

A soft label: “70 % component 1, 30 % component 2”. The r_k sum to 1.
The hard label is the component with the largest r_k.
1D example: \pi = (0.7, 0.3), \mu = (100, 160), \sigma = 20 for both. At x = 130 (halfway) the two densities are equal, so r_1 = 0.7: the weights decide. At x = 120: r_1 = 0.91; at x = 140: r_1 = 0.34.
The boundary (r_1 = r_2) is at 135.6, not at the midpoint 130: the more frequent class gets more room.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Bayes boundaries: straight or curved
Where two components are equally probable, \pi_1\mathcal N_1(\mathbf x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(\mathbf x):

same covariance (tied): the boundary is a straight line (a plane), shifted by the weights. k-means’ bisector is the special case of equal weights and round, equal components.
different covariances: a curved boundary (a conic: ellipse, parabola or hyperbola). The wider component wins far away on both sides.
1D: \mathcal N(0, 1) and \mathcal N(3, 2^2), equal weights: the narrow component wins only for -3.42 < x < 1.42. Far to the left the wide one wins again.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: tied covariances give straight boundaries
text:
The math: tied covariances give straight boundaries
Take logs of \pi_1\mathcal N_1(\mathbf x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(\mathbf x) with \Sigma_1 = \Sigma_2 = \Sigma:
\log\pi_1 - \tfrac12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_1)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_1) = \log\pi_2 - \tfrac12(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_2)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu_2).
The normalising constants are equal and cancel; so does \mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x:
\mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2) = \tfrac12\left(\boldsymbol\mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_2\right) + \log\frac{\pi_2}{\pi_1}:
linear in \mathbf x. With \Sigma_1 \ne \Sigma_2 the term \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top(\Sigma_2^{-1} - \Sigma_1^{-1})\mathbf x survives: a quadratic boundary. In 1D with equal variances: x = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}, the thresholding day’s equal-variance threshold. Example: 130 + \frac{400}{60}\log\frac{0.7}{0.3} = 135.6.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Try it: a mixture




Preset “two overlapping components”: weights 0.6 and 0.4. The samples are coloured by the component that produced them; tick “hide colours”: that is what an algorithm sees. P at (0.3, 0.3): responsibilities 75 % / 25 %. Move the weight sliders: the bar changes although nothing moved. “same covariance: straight boundary” with the background “most probable component”: a straight line; change one weight and it shifts parallel. “different covariances: curved boundary”: the narrow component’s region is an island; the wide one wins on both sides.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The likelihood of a data set
text:
The likelihood of a data set
How well do parameters \theta explain the data? The likelihood: the probability density of the observed points, treated as a function of \theta:
p(\mathcal D \mid \theta) = \prod_i p(\mathbf x_i \mid \theta), \qquad \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta) = \sum_i \log p(\mathbf x_i \mid \theta).

Maximum likelihood: choose the parameters that make the observed data most probable.
For one Gaussian the answer is in closed form: \boldsymbol\mu = the sample mean, \Sigma = the sample covariance S (divided by n).
For a mixture, \log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_i \log \sum_k \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i): a log of a sum, and no closed form. If we knew the hidden labels, each component would be fitted by its own mean and covariance. That chicken-and-egg problem is unit 3.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
section: The math: maximum likelihood for one Gaussian
text:
The math: maximum likelihood for one Gaussian
\log p(\mathcal D) = -\frac{nd}{2}\log 2\pi - \frac n2\log|\Sigma| - \frac12\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu).

Gradient in \boldsymbol\mu: \Sigma^{-1}\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu) = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i.
In \Sigma^{-1} =: P (using \partial\log|P|/\partial P = P^{-1} and \partial\,\mathbf a^\top P\mathbf a/\partial P = \mathbf a\mathbf a^\top): \frac n2 P^{-1} - \frac12\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})^\top = 0 \Rightarrow \hat\Sigma = \frac1n\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})(\mathbf x_i - \hat{\boldsymbol\mu})^\top = S.
With known labels the mixture splits into K such problems, plus \hat\pi_k = n_k/n. With hidden labels the \log\sum_k couples everything.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Generative and discriminative
The same 2D point cloud, two ways of learning from it:

With labels (random-forests day, SVM elective): learn a boundary between the classes directly. Discriminative: says nothing about where points come from.
Without labels (this day): learn a model of how the points were made, a mixture. Generative: it gives a density p(\mathbf x), can draw new points, can say “this point is unlikely under every class”, and its Bayes boundaries come for free.

Generative models need more assumptions (here: Gaussian groups). When the assumptions hold, few data suffice; when they do not, a discriminative boundary is usually more accurate.
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Summary

A 2D Gaussian is a hill with elliptical contours: axes = eigenvectors of \Sigma, half-lengths \sqrt{\lambda_i} (1σ).
Mahalanobis distance d_M^2 = (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu): standard deviations in the direction of \mathbf x.
Covariance types: spherical, diagonal, full, tied: more freedom, more parameters.
A mixture: pick a component with probability \pi_k, then draw from its Gaussian; the component is hidden.
Responsibilities r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x): soft labels; boundaries straight for tied covariances, curved otherwise.
Likelihood \sum_i\log p(\mathbf x_i): one Gaussian has a closed-form fit; a mixture does not (next unit).
crumbs: The multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model

title: Quiz: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Energy E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q) with \rho(d) = d^2/2 (quadratic) or \lvert d\rvert (TV).

Q1. Why is quadratic smoothing “just a linear system”, while TV is not?






Hint





Differentiate the energy.









Answer





With \rho(d) = d^2/2 every derivative of E is linear in \mathbf x: setting the gradient to zero gives (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. With \lvert d\rvert the derivative is \pm1 (and undefined at 0), so the optimality conditions are not linear; TV needs a special algorithm (in 1D an exact one).




Q2. A noisy image has a sharp edge of height 100. Why does quadratic smoothing blur it, while TV keeps it sharp?






Hint





Compare the prior cost of one jump with many small steps.









Answer





A quadratic prior charges d^2: one jump of 100 costs \tfrac12 \cdot 10^4, the same rise in 10 steps of 10 costs \tfrac12 \cdot 1000: ten times less. So it spreads the edge into a ramp. TV charges the total height (100) however it is spread, so nothing is gained by blurring and the data, which say “sharp”, win.




Q3. In what sense is quadratic smoothing a low-pass filter?






Hint





What does the solution do to a wave +1, -1, +1, \dots, and to a constant?









Answer





On a long signal it multiplies each frequency \omega by 1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega)): 1 for a constant, 1/(1 + 4\lambda) for the fastest oscillation. High frequencies (noise, but also the sharp part of edges) are damped, low ones pass.




Q4. What are staircasing and contrast loss in TV denoising?






Hint





What shapes do TV solutions consist of?









Answer





TV solutions are made of flat runs. A smooth ramp in noisy data is therefore turned into a series of flat steps (staircasing). Each run is pulled towards its neighbours by about \lambda/\text{width}, so small or narrow features (a thin bright line, a small spot) lose contrast and eventually vanish.




Q5. When would you prefer the Huber penalty over TV?






Hint





Huber is quadratic for small differences.









Answer





When the image has both smooth gradients and sharp edges. Huber treats small differences quadratically, so ramps stay smooth (no staircases), and large differences linearly, so edges are not blurred.




Q6. Samples from the TV prior look like rough random walks, not like flat plateaus. Why then are TV estimates piecewise constant?






Hint





Which single image does the estimate pick from the posterior?









Answer





The estimate is the minimum of the energy (the MAP), not a typical sample. The kink of \lvert d\rvert at 0 makes “exactly equal neighbours” a common place for the minimum to sit, although typical samples almost never have equal neighbours. The look of the estimate is a property of the optimisation, not of what the prior believes images look like.




Q7. How does the noise level enter the quadratic smoothing system?






Hint





Start from the posterior with noise standard deviation \sigma_n.









Answer





The posterior energy is \frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\sum(x_p - y_p)^2 + \frac{\lambda'}2\sum(x_p - x_q)^2; multiplying by \sigma_n^2 gives our form with \lambda = \lambda'\sigma_n^2. More noise means a larger effective \lambda: the data are trusted less and the image is smoothed more.




Q8. (math) Why does (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y always have exactly one solution?






Answer





\mathbf x^\top(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \|\mathbf x\|^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 > 0 for every \mathbf x \ne 0 (with \lambda \ge 0): the matrix is positive definite, hence invertible. Equivalently the energy is strictly convex.

title: Quiz: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A Gaussian has mean \boldsymbol\mu and covariance \Sigma; a mixture has weights \pi_k; responsibilities r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x).

Q1. A 2D Gaussian has \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}. Describe its 1σ ellipse.






Hint





A diagonal matrix: the eigenvectors are the coordinate axes.









Answer





Axis-aligned, with half-axis \sqrt4 = 2 along x and \sqrt1 = 1 along y: twice as wide as tall.




Q2. What does a positive off-diagonal entry of \Sigma do to the ellipse, and what does it mean for the two features?






Hint





Think of two colour channels.









Answer





It tilts the ellipse towards the diagonal y = x direction: the features are positively correlated, so a pixel that is high in one tends to be high in the other.




Q3. Two points are both at Euclidean distance 3 from the mean of a Gaussian that is long in the x direction (σ = 3) and narrow in y (σ = 1). One lies at (3, 0), the other at (0, 3) relative to the mean. Give their Mahalanobis distances. Which is the outlier?






Hint





For a diagonal covariance, d_M^2 = \sum_j (x_j - \mu_j)^2/\sigma_j^2.









Answer





(3, 0): d_M = 3/3 = 1, on the 1σ ellipse, quite typical. (0, 3): d_M = 3/1 = 3, three standard deviations out across the narrow direction: the outlier.




Q4. A mixture of 4 components in 2D with full covariances. How many numbers must be estimated?






Hint





Weights (they sum to 1), means, and d(d+1)/2 numbers per covariance.









Answer





3 weights + 4 \times 2 means + 4 \times 3 covariance numbers = 23.




Q5. Describe in words how a Gaussian mixture “makes” one data point. What is hidden when we only see the data?






Hint





Two random choices.









Answer





First pick a component k with probability \pi_k, then draw the point from that component’s Gaussian. In the data we see the point but not which component was picked: the component label is hidden (latent).




Q6. Two 1D components with equal variances have \mu_1 = 100 and \mu_2 = 160. A pixel has value 130. What is r_1 if the weights are (0.5, 0.5)? If they are (0.9, 0.1)?






Hint





At the midpoint the two Gaussian densities are equal.









Answer





The densities are equal, so r_1 = \pi_1/(\pi_1 + \pi_2): 0.5, and 0.9 with the unequal weights. At the midpoint only the prior weights decide.




Q7. Two components have the same covariance matrix. What shape is the boundary between the regions where each is most probable? And if one is much wider than the other?






Hint





Which terms cancel when you compare the two log-densities?









Answer





Same covariance: a straight line (plane), shifted towards the less frequent component when the weights differ. Different widths: a curved boundary; the narrow component’s region is a closed island, and the wide component wins far away on all sides.




Q8. Why can one Gaussian be fitted in closed form (sample mean and covariance), while a mixture cannot?






Hint





Look at the log of the density of one point.









Answer





For one Gaussian, \log p(\mathbf x_i) is a quadratic in \mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu, and setting the gradient of the sum to zero gives the mean and covariance directly. For a mixture, \log p(\mathbf x_i) = \log\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i): the log of a sum couples all components, and the equations have no closed-form solution. If the labels were known it would split into separate one-Gaussian fits.




Q9. (math) Show that \mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu + L\mathbf z, with \mathbf z standard normal and LL^\top = \Sigma, has mean \boldsymbol\mu and covariance \Sigma.






Hint





E[\mathbf z] = \mathbf 0 and E[\mathbf z\mathbf z^\top] = I.









Answer





E[\mathbf x] = \boldsymbol\mu + LE[\mathbf z] = \boldsymbol\mu. E[(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top] = LE[\mathbf z\mathbf z^\top]L^\top = LL^\top = \Sigma. (A linear transformation of a Gaussian vector is Gaussian, so \mathbf x \sim \mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma).)

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

set up and solve the linear system of quadratic (Gaussian MRF) smoothing for a few pixels,
explain with numbers why a quadratic prior blurs edges and total variation keeps them,
solve small TV problems by hand with the plateau rule, and predict staircasing and contrast loss,
read quadratic smoothing as a low-pass filter,
choose between quadratic, Huber and TV for a given kind of image.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the interactive part. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Energy
E(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12\sum_p(x_p - y_p)^2 + \lambda\sum_{(p,q)}\rho(x_p - x_q), neighbours on a line or grid


Quadratic
\rho(d) = d^2/2; minimum solves (I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y


Path Laplacian L
diagonal 1, 2, …, 2, 1; -1 for each neighbour pair


Gain
quadratic smoothing multiplies frequency \omega by 1/(1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega))


Total variation (TV)
\rho(d) = \lvert d\rvert


Plateau rule (TV, 1D)
the solution is made of flat runs; each sits at the mean of its data, moved by \lambda/\text{width} towards each neighbouring run that is higher or lower


Huber
\rho(d) = d^2/2 for \lvert d\rvert \le \delta, \delta(\lvert d\rvert - \delta/2) beyond

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
By hand
B1. Quadratic, three pixels. \mathbf y = (0, 3, 0). (a) Write I + \lambda L for \lambda = 1 and solve (I + L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. (b) Repeat for \lambda = 2. What happens to the sum x_1 + x_2 + x_3? (c) Compute the energy of your solution for \lambda = 1, and of \mathbf y itself and of (1, 1, 1). Is the solution really the best of the three?
B2. Ramps and jumps. A signal must go from 0 to 3. Compute the prior cost \sum\rho(d) of doing it in one jump, in 3 equal steps, and in 30 equal steps, for the quadratic and the absolute penalty. Which shape does each prior prefer? What does this predict for an edge in a noisy image?
B3. TV, a step. \mathbf y = (0, 0, 3, 3). (a) Use the plateau rule to find the TV solution for \lambda = 1. Check that its energy is lower than that of \mathbf y. (b) For which \lambda does the step disappear completely? What is the solution then? (c) Compare with quadratic smoothing at \lambda = 1: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.43, 0.86, 2.14, 2.57). Describe the difference in words.
B4. TV, a narrow peak. \mathbf y = (0, 3, 0). (a) Find the TV solution for \lambda = 0.5 and for \lambda = 1. (b) A peak of width w samples and height a on a flat background: about how much does TV lower it? For which \lambda does it vanish, roughly? Which features of an image does TV therefore remove first?
B5. Low-pass. For quadratic smoothing: (a) Compute the gain at \omega = \pi (the pattern +1, -1, +1, \dots) for \lambda = 1 and \lambda = 10. (b) For \lambda = 10, at which frequency (in cycles per sample, \omega/2\pi) is the gain \tfrac12? (c) Why does any low-pass filter blur a step edge?
B6. Which prior? Choose quadratic, Huber or TV, and explain: (a) a fluorescence image of cells with flat interiors and sharp boundaries; (b) an estimate of the slowly varying illumination of a microscope; (c) a gel image with smooth gradients and sharp bands.






Solutions





B1. (a) I + L = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}. By symmetry x_1 = x_3 = a, x_2 = b: 2a - b = 0, -2a + 3b = 3, so b = 1.5, a = 0.75. (b) I + 2L: 3a - 2b = 0, -4a + 5b = 3: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.857, 1.286, 0.857). The sum stays 3: quadratic smoothing preserves the mean (the rows of L sum to 0). (c) E(\hat{\mathbf x}) = \tfrac12(0.75^2 + 1.5^2 + 0.75^2) + \tfrac12(0.75^2 + 0.75^2) = 1.6875 + 0.5625 = 2.25. E(\mathbf y) = 0 + \tfrac12(9 + 9) = 9. E(1, 1, 1) = \tfrac12(1 + 4 + 1) + 0 = 3. Yes, 2.25 is the lowest.
B2. Quadratic: \tfrac12 \cdot 9 = 4.5; 3 \cdot \tfrac12 = 1.5; 30 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 0.01 = 0.15. Absolute: 3 in all three cases. The quadratic prior strongly prefers spreading the change over many small steps (a ramp); TV is indifferent to how a monotone change is spread. Prediction: under a quadratic prior an edge is smeared out; under TV the data decide, and they say the edge is sharp.
B3. (a) Two plateaus of width 2, data means 0 and 3. The left one has a higher neighbour: up by \lambda/2 = 0.5; the right one down by 0.5: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 2.5). Energy: data 4 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot 0.25 = 0.5, TV \lambda \cdot 2 = 2: total 2.5, against 0 + 3 = 3 for \mathbf y. (b) The plateaus meet at the mean 1.5 when \lambda/2 = 1.5: \lambda = 3. For \lambda \ge 3 the solution is (1.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.5). (c) TV keeps one sharp jump, just smaller (2 instead of 3): contrast is lost but the edge stays where it is and stays sharp. Quadratic smoothing replaces the jump by a ramp over all four samples.
B4. (a) The peak (width 1, two lower neighbours) drops by 2\lambda, each side (width 1, one higher neighbour) rises by \lambda: \lambda = 0.5: (0.5, 2, 0.5). At \lambda = 1 they would meet at 1: (1, 1, 1), the mean. (b) It is lowered by about 2\lambda/w (a little less in practice, because the background rises too). It disappears for \lambda around aw/2. Small and narrow features lose contrast first and then vanish, even if they are bright: TV shrinks small structures.
B5. (a) \omega = \pi: 2 - 2\cos\pi = 4; gain 1/5 = 0.2 (\lambda = 1) and 1/41 = 0.024 (\lambda = 10). (b) 1 + 10(2 - 2\cos\omega) = 2: \cos\omega = 0.95, \omega = 0.318, i.e. 0.051 cycles per sample (a period of about 20 samples). (c) A step is a sum of waves of all frequencies (its Fourier transform falls off only like 1/\omega); damping the high frequencies removes the parts that make it sharp. A linear filter cannot distinguish a high frequency belonging to an edge from one belonging to noise.
B6. (a) TV: flat regions with sharp boundaries are exactly what its solutions look like (some contrast loss at small cells). (b) Quadratic (and a large \lambda): illumination has no edges, and the linear system is fast. (c) Huber: quadratic for the small differences of smooth gradients (no staircases), linear for the large jumps at bands (no blurring).




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 = \mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x, that the gradient of E for the quadratic prior is (\mathbf x - \mathbf y) + \lambda L\mathbf x, and that I + \lambda L is positive definite, so the minimum is unique.
B8. (math) On a ring of n samples, show that \mathbf f with f_p = e^{i\omega p}, \omega = 2\pi k/n, is an eigenvector of L with eigenvalue 2 - 2\cos\omega, and derive the gain of B5.
B9. (math) Derive the plateau rule for 1D TV from the optimality condition x_p - y_p + \lambda(g_{p-1} - g_p) = 0, g_p \in \operatorname{sign}(x_{p+1} - x_p) (with g_p \in [-1, 1] where x_{p+1} = x_p, and g = 0 beyond the ends).
B10. (math) With Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n and the prior p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp(-\frac{\lambda'}2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x), show that the posterior is Gaussian, that its MAP solves (I + \lambda'\sigma_n^2L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y, and that MAP and posterior mean coincide.






Solutions (math)





B7. \mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x = \sum_pd_px_p^2 - \sum_{p,q}W_{pq}x_px_q = \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p^2 + x_q^2 - 2x_px_q) = \sum_{(p,q)}(x_p - x_q)^2 (each edge once). \nabla\tfrac12\|\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 = \mathbf x - \mathbf y and \nabla\frac\lambda2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x = \lambda L\mathbf x (L symmetric). \mathbf x^\top(I + \lambda L)\mathbf x = \|\mathbf x\|^2 + \lambda\sum(x_p - x_q)^2 > 0 for \mathbf x \ne \mathbf 0: positive definite, so E is strictly convex with one minimum.
B8. (L\mathbf f)_p = 2e^{i\omega p} - e^{i\omega(p-1)} - e^{i\omega(p+1)} = (2 - e^{-i\omega} - e^{i\omega})e^{i\omega p} = (2 - 2\cos\omega)f_p; on the ring p \pm 1 wraps around, which works because e^{i\omega n} = 1. Then (I + \lambda L)\mathbf f = (1 + \lambda(2 - 2\cos\omega))\mathbf f, and solving the system divides the \mathbf f-component of \mathbf y by this number: the gain.
B9. On a plateau x_a = \dots = x_b = c with different values outside, add the conditions for p = a, \dots, b: the terms \lambda(g_{p-1} - g_p) telescope to \lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b), so \sum_{p=a}^b(c - y_p) = -\lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b) and c = \bar y_{[a,b]} - \lambda(g_{a-1} - g_b)/(b - a + 1). g_{a-1} = +1 if the left neighbour is lower (-1 if higher), g_b = +1 if the right neighbour is higher (-1 if lower). A higher neighbour on one side and a lower one on the other: g_{a-1} = g_b, no shift. A local maximum: g_{a-1} = 1, g_b = -1, shift -2\lambda/w. A plateau at the end of the signal with one higher neighbour: +\lambda/w.
B10. -\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = \frac1{2\sigma_n^2}\|\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{\lambda'}2\mathbf x^\top L\mathbf x + \text{const}, a quadratic form in \mathbf x with Hessian A = I/\sigma_n^2 + \lambda'L (positive definite): the posterior is Gaussian with covariance A^{-1}. Gradient zero: (\mathbf x - \mathbf y)/\sigma_n^2 + \lambda'L\mathbf x = 0, i.e. (I + \lambda'\sigma_n^2L)\mathbf x = \mathbf y. A Gaussian has its maximum at its mean, and each marginal is a Gaussian centred at the same point: MAP = mean = MPM.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Explore
A profile of 200 samples with Gaussian noise (fixed seed): step · ramp · peak (a step at 40, a ramp from 2 down to 0 over 80–140, a 4-sample peak of height 2 at 166–169), plateaus, or a line across the micrograph. Choose the prior and \lambda (and \delta for Huber). The plot shows the noisy data (grey dots), the truth (dashed) and the estimate; the readout splits the energy into data and prior terms and gives the error (RMSE) against the truth. Tabs: prior samples (five random walks from the quadratic and from the TV prior, with the same step variance, and the two step distributions), and the matrix (I + \lambda L for 10 samples, and the gain of quadratic smoothing against frequency).



E1. Preset quadratic blurs the step (\lambda = 10). Read the RMSE of the estimate and of the noisy data. Over how many samples is the step spread? How high is the peak? Now find the \lambda with the smallest RMSE for the quadratic prior. What do you see at that \lambda?
E2. Preset TV keeps the step (\lambda = 1). Compare the step, the RMSE and the energy split with E1. What happened to the ramp and to the peak?
E3. Preset TV staircases the ramp (\lambda = 3, zoomed on the ramp). Describe the estimate on the ramp. Is the RMSE better or worse than at \lambda = 1?
E4. Preset TV shrinks the narrow peak (\lambda = 2, zoomed on the peak). Read the peak height of the estimate at \lambda = 1, 2 and 3 and compare with B4(b) (w = 4, a = 2).
E5. Preset Huber in between (\lambda = 5, \delta = 0.1). Compare step, ramp, peak and RMSE with the best quadratic and the best TV result (find the best \lambda for TV).
E6. Choose the plateaus profile. Compare quadratic (\lambda = 10) and TV (\lambda = 1). Why does TV do especially well here?
E7. Tab prior samples. Which draws look more like the profiles we denoise: the quadratic or the TV ones? Do the TV draws have flat plateaus? Compare the two step distributions in the lower plot.
E8. Tab the matrix. For \lambda = 10, read the entries of I + \lambda L and compare with the Background table. Read the gain at 0.05 and at 0.5 cycles per sample, and check with B5.






Solutions





E1. RMSE 0.240 against 0.291 for the noisy data. The step rises from 10 % to 90 % over about 15 samples, and the peak reaches only 0.90 (true height 2). The best quadratic \lambda is about 1.2 (RMSE 0.190): the step is a little sharper (about 13 samples) and the peak higher (1.53), but much of the noise is back. Quadratic smoothing trades noise against blur and cannot win both.
E2. The step stays sharp (from 0.25 to 2.04 within two samples), RMSE 0.137, energy 7.30 (data) + 6.81 (prior). The ramp is cut into flat steps (staircasing), and the peak is lowered to 1.36.
E3. The ramp becomes a staircase of about a dozen flat steps. RMSE 0.268, worse than at \lambda = 1 (0.137): the plateaus also lose more contrast (the peak is down to 0.36).
E4. Peak 1.36 (\lambda = 1), 0.86 (\lambda = 2), 0.36 (\lambda = 3). The rule 2\lambda/w = \lambda/2 predicts 1.5, 1.0, 0.5: the same trend, each a bit lower because the noise and the rising background also count. It vanishes around \lambda = aw/2 = 4.
E5. Huber (\lambda = 5, \delta = 0.1): sharp step, smooth ramp without stairs, peak 1.72, RMSE 0.128. The best quadratic gets 0.190 (\lambda \approx 1.2), the best TV 0.125 (\lambda \approx 0.55; small noise plateaus remain in the flat parts, and the ramp is still a staircase). Huber and TV are about equally good by RMSE; Huber looks better on the ramp.
E6. Plateaus: quadratic RMSE 0.227, TV 0.104. The profile is piecewise constant, which is exactly the shape of a TV solution: TV’s prior assumption is right here, so it removes noise without blurring the jumps.
E7. Neither looks like a profile with steps: both are rough random walks drifting up and down. The TV draws have no flat plateaus. Their step distribution (Laplace) has a sharper peak at 0 and heavier tails than the normal one: more tiny steps and more big ones. The flat plateaus of TV estimates come from minimising the energy, not from the prior’s typical samples.
E8. Diagonal 1 + 10 = 11 at the two ends and 1 + 20 = 21 inside, -10 next to the diagonal, zeros elsewhere: tridiagonal. Gain 0.505 at 0.05 cycles per sample and 1/41 = 0.024 at 0.5: as in B5.

title: Exercise: quadratic smoothing and total variation
text:
Where this leads
The same two priors return when the image is also blurred: the deconvolution day adds a point-spread function to the data term (Tikhonov = quadratic, and TV). In 2D, TV denoising keeps object boundaries in microscopy images, and its binary cousin, the boundary length, is the smoothness term of graph cuts, of the Ising model and of the Chan–Vese level-set model.

title: Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Covariance \Sigma
variances on the diagonal, covariances off it; symmetric, positive definite


1σ ellipse
points with d_M = 1: axes along the eigenvectors of \Sigma, half-lengths \sqrt{\lambda_1}, \sqrt{\lambda_2}


Mahalanobis distance
d_M^2 = (\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu)


Mixture
p(\mathbf x) = \sum_k \pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k), weights \pi_k \ge 0 summing to 1


Responsibility
r_k(\mathbf x) = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x)/p(\mathbf x)


Covariance types
spherical (\sigma_k^2I), diagonal, full, tied (one \Sigma for all)

title: Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
By hand
B1. \Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}, \boldsymbol\mu = \mathbf 0. (a) Find the eigenvalues and unit eigenvectors. (Check: they must add up to the trace and multiply to the determinant.) (b) Sketch the 1σ and 2σ ellipses. What are the half-axes, and at what angle is the long axis?
B2. Same Gaussian. The inverse is \Sigma^{-1} = \frac16\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 5\end{pmatrix}. (a) Compute the Euclidean and the Mahalanobis distance of P = (2, 1) and of Q = (-1, 2). (b) Which of the two would you call unusual? Explain with your sketch from B1.
B3. You fit a mixture with K = 3 components to colour pixels (d = 3). Count the parameters for spherical, diagonal, full and tied covariances. Which would you try first with 500 pixels? With 50 000?
B4. A 1D mixture of two components: \pi = (0.7, 0.3), \mu = (100, 160), \sigma = (20, 20). (a) Compute r_1 at x = 120, 130 and 140. (b) Where is the boundary r_1 = r_2? Why is it not at 130? (c) What happens to the boundary if \pi = (0.5, 0.5)?
B5. Four points: (0, 0), (2, 2), (1, 3), (3, 1). (a) Compute the maximum-likelihood mean and covariance (divide by n = 4). (b) Give the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of your covariance and sketch the 1σ ellipse over the points.
B6. Predict, with a sketch, the boundary between two equally weighted 2D components when (a) both have \Sigma = I; (b) both have the same tilted, elongated \Sigma; (c) one is a small circle and the other a large circle around a nearby centre.
B7. A microscope image contains 70 % background pixels (dark), 25 % cytoplasm (grey) and 5 % nuclei (bright). (a) Write down the mixture that could have produced the grey values, in words and as a formula. (b) A grey value lies exactly halfway between the cytoplasm and nucleus means, and both components have the same σ. Which label does Bayes’ rule give it, and why?






Solutions





B1. (a) \det(\Sigma - \lambda I) = (5 - \lambda)(2 - \lambda) - 4 = \lambda^2 - 7\lambda + 6 = 0: \lambda_1 = 6, \lambda_2 = 1 (sum 7 = trace, product 6 = determinant). For \lambda = 6: (5 - 6)v_1 + 2v_2 = 0, so \mathbf v_1 = (2, 1)/\sqrt5; \mathbf v_2 = (-1, 2)/\sqrt5. (b) 1σ: half-axes \sqrt6 = 2.45 along \mathbf v_1 and 1 along \mathbf v_2; 2σ: twice that (4.90 and 2). The long axis is at \arctan(1/2) = 26.6°.
B2. (a) Both have Euclidean distance \sqrt5 = 2.24. d_M(P)^2 = \frac16(2 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 + 5 \cdot 1) = \frac56, d_M(P) = 0.91. d_M(Q)^2 = \frac16(2 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 + 5 \cdot 4) = 5, d_M(Q) = 2.24. (b) Q: it lies along the short axis, beyond the 2σ ellipse. P lies along the long axis and inside the 1σ ellipse: in the direction the data spread most, 2.24 units is less than one standard deviation.
B3. Weights 2 and means 9 in every case. Covariances: spherical 3, diagonal 9, full 18, tied 6. Totals: 14, 20, 29, 17. With 500 pixels, all are well determined, but full covariances with 29 numbers are already fine; with very few pixels per component (say 20), spherical or tied is safer. With 50 000 pixels, full covariances are no problem, and they can describe correlated channels (shadows, stains). (Unit 3 gives a criterion: BIC.)
B4. (a) r_1 = 0.91, 0.70, 0.34 at 120, 130, 140. At 130 the two densities are equal, so r_1 = 0.7/(0.7 + 0.3). (b) x = 130 + \frac{20^2}{60}\ln\frac{0.7}{0.3} = 130 + 5.65 = 135.6. The more frequent component wins near the midpoint, so the boundary moves towards the rarer one. (c) It moves to the midpoint, 130.
B5. (a) Mean (1.5, 1.5). Centred: (-1.5, -1.5), (0.5, 0.5), (-0.5, 1.5), (1.5, -0.5). S_{11} = (2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25)/4 = 1.25, S_{22} = 1.25, S_{12} = (2.25 + 0.25 - 0.75 - 0.75)/4 = 0.25. (b) \lambda_1 = 1.25 + 0.25 = 1.5 along (1, 1)/\sqrt2, \lambda_2 = 1 along (1, -1)/\sqrt2. A slightly elongated ellipse along the diagonal, half-axes 1.22 and 1.
B6. (a) The perpendicular bisector of the two means (as in k-means). (b) Still a straight line through the midpoint, but in general no longer perpendicular to the line joining the means: its normal is \Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2), not \boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2. (c) A closed curve (a circle) around the small component; outside it, on all sides, the large component wins.
B7. (a) Pick background with probability 0.70, cytoplasm 0.25, nucleus 0.05; then draw the grey value from that class’s Gaussian: p(x) = 0.70\,\mathcal N(x \mid \mu_b, \sigma_b^2) + 0.25\,\mathcal N(x \mid \mu_c, \sigma_c^2) + 0.05\,\mathcal N(x \mid \mu_n, \sigma_n^2). (b) Cytoplasm: at the midpoint the two densities are equal, and cytoplasm is five times more frequent (r = 0.25/0.30 = 0.83). The boundary to “nucleus” lies further up, towards the nucleus mean.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that the 1σ ellipse \{\mathbf x : d_M(\mathbf x) = 1\} has its axes along the eigenvectors of \Sigma with half-lengths \sqrt{\lambda_i}. (Write \Sigma = Q\Lambda Q^\top and change coordinates.)
B9. (math) Derive the maximum-likelihood mean of one Gaussian with known \Sigma from n points: set the gradient of \sum_i\log\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu, \Sigma) to zero.
B10. (math) Show that two Gaussians with the same covariance \Sigma and weights \pi_1, \pi_2 have a linear Bayes boundary. Give its 1D form and check it against B4(b).
B11. (math) Show that |\Sigma| = \lambda_1\lambda_2, and explain why the peak height of a 2D Gaussian is 1/(2\pi\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2}). What happens to the peak height when the ellipse collapses to a line (\lambda_2 \to 0)?






Solutions (math)





B8. \Sigma^{-1} = Q\Lambda^{-1}Q^\top. With \mathbf y = Q^\top(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu) (a rotation: coordinates along the eigenvectors), d_M^2 = \mathbf y^\top\Lambda^{-1}\mathbf y = y_1^2/\lambda_1 + y_2^2/\lambda_2. d_M = 1 is the standard ellipse y_1^2/\lambda_1 + y_2^2/\lambda_2 = 1 in these coordinates: half-axes \sqrt{\lambda_1} and \sqrt{\lambda_2} along \mathbf v_1, \mathbf v_2.
B9. \sum_i\log\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i) = \text{const} - \frac12\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu). Its gradient in \boldsymbol\mu is \Sigma^{-1}\sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu); since \Sigma^{-1} is invertible this is zero iff \sum_i(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu) = 0, i.e. \hat{\boldsymbol\mu} = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i. The function is concave in \boldsymbol\mu (Hessian -n\Sigma^{-1}), so this is the maximum.
B10. Equal \pi_1\mathcal N_1 = \pi_2\mathcal N_2, take logs; the constants -\frac d2\log2\pi - \frac12\log|\Sigma| cancel, and so does -\frac12\mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf x, leaving \mathbf x^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2) = \frac12(\boldsymbol\mu_1^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_1 - \boldsymbol\mu_2^\top\Sigma^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_2) + \log(\pi_2/\pi_1), linear in \mathbf x. In 1D: x(\mu_1 - \mu_2)/\sigma^2 = (\mu_1^2 - \mu_2^2)/(2\sigma^2) + \log(\pi_2/\pi_1), i.e. x = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}. B4: 130 + \frac{400}{60}\ln\frac73 = 135.6.
B11. The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues (\det Q\Lambda Q^\top = \det\Lambda). At \mathbf x = \boldsymbol\mu the exponent is 0, so the density is 1/((2\pi)^{d/2}|\Sigma|^{1/2}) = 1/(2\pi\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2}) for d = 2. As \lambda_2 \to 0 the peak height goes to infinity: the same total probability is squeezed onto a line. (This is how a mixture component “collapses” in unit 3.)

title: Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Explore
The demo shows one Gaussian (or a mixture of 2–3) with draggable handles: the circle moves the mean, the squares are the ends of the two 1σ half-axes (they rotate and stretch the ellipse). Drawn: the 1σ (solid), 2σ and 3σ (dashed) ellipses and 300 samples with a fixed seed. The probes P and Q can be dragged; the readout gives \Sigma, its eigenvalues and the angle, and the Euclidean and Mahalanobis distances of the probes. Σ restricts the shape (spherical, diagonal, full). In a mixture, the samples are coloured by the component that made them (hide colours removes that), the background shows the density or the most probable component, and the bar gives the responsibilities of P.



E1. Preset same Euclidean distance, different Mahalanobis. Check your answers to B1 and B2 in the readout. Drag P along the long axis until d_M = 1: where is it? Then drag Q onto the 2σ ellipse: what does the readout say?
E2. Preset tilted cigar. Read \Sigma, the eigenvalues and the angle. Now choose diagonal. What happens to the ellipse, and which entry of \Sigma is forced to zero? Choose spherical: what is left?
E3. Preset circle. For a spherical Gaussian with σ = 1.5, what is the relation between the Euclidean distance and the Mahalanobis distance of P? Check it.
E4. Preset two overlapping components: the hidden labels. Read the responsibilities of P. Tick hide colours: could you still tell which sample came from which component? Move the weight of component 1 from 0.6 to 0.3: how do the responsibilities of P change, although P did not move?
E5. Preset same covariance: straight boundary (background: most probable component). Describe the boundary. Where is P, and what are its responsibilities? Change one weight: what happens to the boundary?
E6. Preset different covariances: curved boundary. Describe the region of the narrow component. Drag P from (0, 0) to the left along the x axis, through the narrow component and beyond: how does the bar change? Explain with Q7 of the quiz.






Solutions





E1. The readout gives \lambda_1 = 6.00, \lambda_2 = 1.00, angle 26.6°; P: Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 0.91; Q: Euclidean 2.24, Mahalanobis 2.24. Along the long axis, d_M = 1 is at the end of the half-axis, about (2.19, 1.10), where the orange square is. Q on the 2σ ellipse shows Mahalanobis 2.00, whatever direction.
E2. \Sigma = [4.78\ 2.55;\ 2.55\ 1.83], \lambda_1 = 6.25, \lambda_2 = 0.36 (half-axes 2.5 and 0.6), angle 30°. Diagonal: the ellipse snaps to the axes (\Sigma_{12} = 0), keeping its half-axes: it can no longer describe the correlation. Spherical: a circle with one radius (the geometric mean of the two half-axes, \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 0.6} = 1.22).
E3. d_M = d_{\text{Euclid}}/\sigma: P has Euclidean 2.24 and Mahalanobis 2.24/1.5 = 1.49.
E4. P = (0.3, 0.3): 75 % component 1, 25 % component 2. With hidden colours the two clouds merge into one blob with a slightly irregular outline: you cannot tell which point came from which component, only that the density has two bumps. With weights 0.3 and 0.4 (normalised 0.43 and 0.57), P’s responsibility for component 1 drops to about 60 %: the responsibility combines the density at P with how frequent each component is.
E5. A straight line through the midpoint (0, 0), almost vertical (about 94°). The perpendicular bisector of the two means, which k-means would use, would be tilted at about 117°: the shared, tilted ellipse turns the boundary. P at (0, 0), halfway, has responsibilities 50 % / 50 %. Changing one weight shifts the line parallel to itself, away from the more frequent component.
E6. The narrow component (σ = 0.6) owns a closed, roughly circular island around its mean; the wide component (half-axes 2.2 and 1.4) owns everything else. At (0, 0), P is 57 % narrow. Moving left, the narrow share rises to about 100 % near its centre, then falls again: 77 % at x = -2.5, 37 % at x = -3 and almost 0 at x = -4. Far away, the wide Gaussian’s tails are heavier, so it wins on both sides: a curved (closed) boundary.

title: Exercise: the multivariate Gaussian and the mixture model
text:
Where this leads
We can now describe each group by a Gaussian and say how likely each point is to belong to it, if we know the parameters. Unit 3 finds the parameters from unlabelled data with the EM algorithm: guess soft labels, refit the Gaussians, repeat.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
About this lecture
So far a colour image was “an M \times N \times 3 array”. Today: what the three numbers mean, and why there are three.

Light is a spectrum: power at every wavelength, far more than three numbers.
The eye (or a camera) reduces it to three responses: a linear map with a large blind spot.
Different spectra with the same three numbers: metamers. They are why screens work, and why cameras and eyes disagree.
CIE XYZ and the chromaticity diagram: a map of all colours; mixtures lie on straight lines; a display reaches a triangle.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Linear algebra used: matrix–vector product, rank, null space, change of basis, and (math slides only) the projector onto a null space. The demos assume an sRGB screen; a projector rarely is one, so every swatch in the demos comes with its numbers. Say this once at the start.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Colour is not in the light alone
text:
Colour is not in the light alone

Two lamps look the same white, yet a red apple looks different under them.
Two fabrics look identical to us, but different in a photo.
A colour-blind colleague cannot tell two cables apart that you can.

In each case different light gives the same colour to one observer and not to another. To understand why, follow the light from the lamp to the three numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Light is a spectrum
The light reaching a point of the eye or the sensor is a spectrum s(\lambda): power at each wavelength from about 380 nm (violet) to 730 nm (deep red).

Daylight: smooth, power everywhere. A light bulb (a hot filament): rises towards the red. A white LED: a sharp blue peak plus a broad yellow hump. A laser: one line.
A surface reflects a fraction r(\lambda) of each wavelength; what we see from it is s(\lambda)\,r(\lambda): lamp times reflectance.
Sample the spectrum every 10 nm: 36 numbers. Real spectra need that many, or more.

So the input is a vector with 36 (or more) entries. The output of the eye is three numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Three cone types




The retina has three kinds of cones: L (long), M (medium), S (short wavelengths).

Each cone adds up the light, weighted by its sensitivity curve: L = \sum_\lambda s(\lambda)\,\bar l(\lambda), and so on.
The curves are broad and overlap: L and M are almost the same.
A camera does the same with three filters R, G, B; its curves are different.



The cone curves here are the Hunt–Pointer–Estévez combination of the CIE colour-matching functions (right), so they are exactly a change of basis of them; real measured cone fundamentals look very similar. Each curve is scaled to peak 1 on the left. Point at 450–500 nm: S and M both respond; at 600 nm L and M both respond, L more.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: colour vision is a 3 × 36 matrix
text:
The math: colour vision is a 3 × 36 matrix
Sample at 10 nm, \lambda_j = 380, 390, \dots, 730: a spectrum is \mathbf s \in \mathbb R^{36}, and
\mathbf c = \begin{pmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \end{pmatrix} = A\,\mathbf s, \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix} \bar l(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar l(\lambda_{36}) \\ \bar m(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar m(\lambda_{36}) \\ \bar s(\lambda_1) & \cdots & \bar s(\lambda_{36}) \end{pmatrix} \Delta\lambda .

The integral \int s(\lambda)\,\bar l(\lambda)\,d\lambda becomes a dot product of two vectors: row 1 of A times \mathbf s.
A is 3 \times 36 of rank 3: the eye is a linear map \mathbb R^{36} \to \mathbb R^3.
A camera: \mathbf c_\text{cam} = A_\text{cam}\,\mathbf s, another 3 \times 36 matrix. A surface under a lamp: \mathbf c = A\,\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf e)\,\mathbf r, lamp \mathbf e, reflectance \mathbf r.
