title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Try it: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Try it: from a spectrum to three numbers




Top: the spectra (drag to draw). Middle: the three cone curves; the shaded areas are spectrum × sensitivity for A, whose sums are the numbers. Right: the colours and the numbers (each relative to daylight, so daylight gives 1, 1, 1). Tour: “daylight vs LED”: two very different spectra (the LED has a peak of 245 at 450 nm and almost nothing below 420), both 1.000, 1.000, 1.000 for the eye, and chromaticity 0.313, 0.329. Click “camera”: the LED becomes 0.905, 0.962, 0.900, the match is gone. Then “make a metamer” several times: B changes wildly, the numbers stay 1.022, 0.931, 0.591. Then “metameric failure under tungsten” (surfaces): click “daylight” (match), back to “tungsten” (0.602, 0.545, 0.353 against 0.589, 0.555, 0.302).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Metamers
Many spectra give the same three numbers: they are metamers, and they look identical.

36 numbers in, 3 out: the eye throws away almost everything. Any change of the spectrum that all three cones are blind to goes unnoticed.
Those invisible changes form a huge set: wiggles that add a bit of light at some wavelengths and remove the same “cone-weighted” amount at others.
Why screens work: a display has only three primaries, yet it can produce a metamer of the light from (most) real scenes. The spectrum on the screen is nothing like the scene’s.
Constraint: a spectrum cannot be negative. A metamer must stay \ge 0 everywhere.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: metamers live in the null space
text:
The math: metamers live in the null space
A\mathbf s_1 = A\mathbf s_2 \iff A(\mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1) = \mathbf 0 \iff \mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1 \in \ker A.

Rank–nullity: \dim\ker A = 36 - 3 = 33. Every spectrum has a 33-dimensional family of metamers (cut down by \mathbf s_2 \ge \mathbf 0).
Projector onto \ker A (for A of full row rank): P = I - A^\top (AA^\top)^{-1} A. Check: AP = A - AA^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A = 0.
Making a metamer: take any vector \mathbf v, then \mathbf s_2 = \mathbf s_1 + t\,P\mathbf v, with t as large as the constraint \mathbf s_2 \ge \mathbf 0 allows. This is the demo’s make a metamer button.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
When metamers break
A match holds for one observer under one light:

A different observer. A camera has A_\text{cam} \ne A, with a different blind set: a pair that matches for the eye differs in the photo.
A colour-blind observer. A deuteranope has no M cones: two numbers instead of three. More pairs match: everything that only the M cones could tell apart.
A different lamp (metameric failure). Two fabrics match in daylight; under a light bulb the lamp re-weights the wavelengths, and they no longer match.

Metamerism is the reason colour in images is never “the” colour of an object: it is the colour for this camera, under this light.

These are the demo presets “the camera disagrees”, “a dichromat sees more matches” (for the deuteranope 0.955, –, 0.812 for both; the eye sees M 0.972 vs 0.693) and “metameric failure under tungsten”. White balance, next unit, tries to undo the lamp; metameric failure shows why it can never be perfect.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Colour matching: how the eye was measured
text:
Colour matching: how the eye was measured
Before cones could be measured, the eye was characterised by matching (Wright and Guild, 1920s):

An observer sees a test light on one half of a field and adjusts three primary lights (red, green, blue) on the other half until the two halves look the same.
Done for every wavelength: three colour-matching functions \bar r(\lambda), \bar g(\lambda), \bar b(\lambda), the amounts needed.
Surprise: for many test wavelengths no match is possible. One primary must be moved to the test side: a negative amount.

Three numbers per wavelength again: the matching functions describe the same three-dimensional information as the cones, in another basis.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
CIE XYZ: a standard basis
The CIE (1931) chose a new basis of the same three-dimensional space with two convenient properties:

the three functions \bar x, \bar y, \bar z are never negative, so every real light has X, Y, Z \ge 0;
\bar y is the eye’s brightness sensitivity, so Y is the luminance: how bright the light looks.

The price: the XYZ “primaries” are not real lights. XYZ is a coordinate system for colours, the common reference for every device.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: XYZ is a change of basis
text:
The math: XYZ is a change of basis
Cones, colour-matching functions and \bar x \bar y \bar z are three bases of the same row space of A:
\begin{pmatrix} \bar l \\ \bar m \\ \bar s \end{pmatrix} = T \begin{pmatrix} \bar x \\ \bar y \\ \bar z \end{pmatrix} \;\Rightarrow\; \begin{pmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \end{pmatrix} = T \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix}, \quad T = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4002 & 0.7076 & -0.0808 \\ -0.2263 & 1.1653 & 0.0457 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.9182 \end{pmatrix}.

T is invertible, so the null spaces agree: metamers for XYZ = metamers for the cones.
The same holds for \bar r\bar g\bar b: a matching experiment measures A up to an invertible 3 \times 3 matrix. Negative entries of \bar r\bar g\bar b just mean a basis that is not inside the cone of real lights.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Chromaticity: forget the brightness




Twice the light, same colour: divide out the brightness.
x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}, \qquad y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}

Every colour becomes a point (x, y): the chromaticity diagram.
Monochromatic lights trace the horseshoe (the spectral locus, wavelengths marked); the straight purple line closes it.
All real colours lie inside. White (daylight D65) is near the middle, at (0.313, 0.329).



The colours of the figure are only approximate: outside the sRGB triangle the screen cannot show them, so they are drawn at the nearest colour the screen can show. That is also true on this projector. The axes are x and y, not the X and Y of XYZ: lower case = chromaticity.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: The math: a central projection, and mixtures on straight lines
text:
The math: a central projection, and mixtures on straight lines
(x, y, z) = (X, Y, Z)/(X+Y+Z) is the central projection of XYZ space onto the plane X + Y + Z = 1 (as homogeneous coordinates: scaling a colour does not move it).
Mixing two lights adds their XYZ: \mathbf C = \mathbf C_1 + \mathbf C_2. With S_i = X_i + Y_i + Z_i,
\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \frac{S_1}{S_1 + S_2}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ y_1 \end{pmatrix} + \frac{S_2}{S_1 + S_2}\begin{pmatrix} x_2 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix}.

A convex combination: the mixture lies on the segment between the two chromaticities, at a position weighted by S_i (not by luminance Y_i).
Three primaries: all non-negative mixtures fill the triangle they span. Monochromatic lights are the extreme points, so the horseshoe region is convex.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
section: Gamuts: a display is a triangle
text:
Gamuts: a display is a triangle
A display mixes three primaries R, G, B with amounts between 0 and 1: it reaches exactly the triangle of their chromaticities, its gamut.

sRGB (most screens, the web): a modest triangle. Display P3 (newer phones and laptops): a larger green and red. Rec. 2020 (ultra-HD video): primaries almost on the horseshoe, as only lasers can produce.
No triangle with real primaries covers the horseshoe: some colours (saturated cyans, spectral greens) no display can show.
A colour outside the gamut needs a negative amount of a primary: it must be clipped or mapped inwards.

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Try it: the chromaticity diagram




Tour: “mixing two lights”: A = 470 nm with Y = 0.3, B = 580 nm with Y = 0.6, share of B 0.5: the mixture sits at 0.189 of the way from A to B, not at 0.5, because A carries X+Y+Z = 5.28 against B’s 1.23. Ask: which share puts it halfway? (0.811.) Drag A or B around: the mixture stays on the line. Then “design a display”: “sRGB vs P3” (the test point T = (0.21, 0.71) is outside both), “a laser display” (T inside), “a primary outside the locus” (flagged: no light has that chromaticity).

From a spectrum to three numbers

title: From a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Summary

Light is a spectrum; the eye and the camera reduce it to three numbers by weighted sums: a linear map of rank 3.
Metamers: different spectra with the same three numbers. They make displays possible, and break for another camera, a colour-blind viewer or another lamp.
CIE XYZ: a standard basis with X, Y, Z \ge 0 and Y = luminance; a change of basis of the cones.
Chromaticity (x, y) drops the brightness. Mixtures lie on straight lines; a display reaches a triangle, its gamut.
Next unit: what the numbers stored in an RGB image mean, and why they are not proportional to light.

title: Quiz: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A spectrum s(\lambda) is the power of light at each wavelength; the eye’s three cone responses L, M, S are weighted sums of it; x = X/(X+Y+Z), y = Y/(X+Y+Z).

Q1. Why is colour three numbers, when a spectrum needs dozens?






Hint





What does each cone measure?









Answer





Because we have three kinds of cones, and each one reports a single number: the spectrum weighted by its sensitivity curve and added up. Whatever else is in the spectrum is lost before the brain sees it. A camera with three filters does the same with its own three curves.




Q2. Two lamps have very different spectra but look the same white. What are they called, and what does that say about the difference of their spectra?






Hint





What do the three cones see of the difference?









Answer





They are metamers. Their difference adds light at some wavelengths and removes it at others in a way that leaves all three cone responses unchanged: each cone sees zero net change.




Q3. A shirt and a skirt match in the shop. At home, under a light bulb, they no longer match. Did the light bulb change the fabric?






Hint





What reaches the eye from a surface?









Answer





No. What reaches the eye is lamp spectrum × reflectance. The two fabrics have different reflectances that happen to give the same three numbers under the shop’s lamp. The light bulb weights the wavelengths differently (more red, less blue), and the two products no longer give equal numbers: metameric failure.




Q4. A person without M cones (a deuteranope) compares colours. Do they see more pairs of lights as identical, or fewer? Why?






Hint





Two numbers instead of three.









Answer





More. Only two numbers (L and S) must agree for a match, so every pair that differed only in the M response now matches as well. The set of invisible changes is larger.




Q5. Light 1 has (X, Y, Z) = (10, 10, 10), light 2 has (30, 20, 10). Where is their sum on the chromaticity diagram?






Hint





Add XYZ first, then divide.









Answer





Sum (40, 30, 20), total 90: x = 0.444, y = 0.333. Light 1 is at (0.333, 0.333) with total 30, light 2 at (0.5, 0.333) with total 60: the sum lies on the line between them, two thirds of the way towards light 2, because light 2 carries twice as much X + Y + Z.




Q6. Why is the colour range (gamut) of a screen a triangle on the chromaticity diagram?






Hint





What do mixtures of two lights do on the diagram?









Answer





The screen makes every colour as a mixture of its three primaries with non-negative amounts. Mixtures of two lights lie on the straight line between them, and mixtures of three fill the triangle spanned by the three chromaticities. Nothing outside it can be made without a negative amount of a primary.




Q7. Can a screen with three primaries show every colour we can see?






Hint





What is the shape of the region of all colours?









Answer





No. All colours fill the horseshoe, which is curved, and any triangle of real primaries (inside the horseshoe) leaves parts of it uncovered, for example the saturated cyans and spectral greens. Primaries on the horseshoe itself (lasers) cover the most, but still not all.




Q8. (math) The eye is a 3 \times 36 matrix A of rank 3. What is the dimension of the set of differences \mathbf s_2 - \mathbf s_1 between metamers, and why can’t every vector of that set be added to a given spectrum?






Hint





Rank–nullity; and what values can a spectrum take?









Answer





The differences are exactly \ker A, of dimension 36 - 3 = 33. Adding \mathbf d \in \ker A keeps A\mathbf s, but the result must still be a physical spectrum, \mathbf s + \mathbf d \ge \mathbf 0 in every bin. So only a bounded piece of the null space (around \mathbf s) is allowed; a dark spectrum has few metamers.

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the three responses of an eye (or a camera) to a sampled spectrum,
construct a metamer of a spectrum and say when a match breaks (another camera, a colour-blind viewer, another lamp),
compute chromaticities, and locate a mixture of two lights on the chromaticity diagram,
decide whether a colour is inside a display’s gamut triangle.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Spectrum
power s(\lambda) at each wavelength; sampled, a vector \mathbf s


Cone (or filter) response
a weighted sum of the spectrum: L = \sum_\lambda \bar l(\lambda)\,s(\lambda); together \mathbf c = A\mathbf s


Metamers
spectra with the same three responses: A\mathbf s_1 = A\mathbf s_2


Surface under a lamp
the light is lamp × reflectance, wavelength by wavelength


CIE XYZ
a standard basis of the three responses; Y = luminance; X, Y, Z \ge 0 for real light


Chromaticity
x = X/(X+Y+Z), y = Y/(X+Y+Z): the colour without its brightness


Gamut
the triangle of a display’s three primaries on the (x, y) diagram






Cone sensitivities (left, each scaled to peak 1) and the CIE colour-matching functions (right).

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
By hand
B1. A toy eye sees 5 wavelength bins with three cones (rows L, M, S): A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Compute the responses A\mathbf s to \mathbf s_1 = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1), \mathbf s_2 = (0, 2, 0, 2, 0) and \mathbf s_3 = (2, 0, 1, 0, 2). Which of them look identical to this eye? (b) The vectors \mathbf v_1 = (3, -2, 1, 0, -1) and \mathbf v_2 = (2, -1, 0, 1, -2) satisfy A\mathbf v = \mathbf 0. Check one of them. What happens to the responses if you add \mathbf v_1 to a spectrum? (c) Find a third metamer of \mathbf s_1 that is non-negative in every bin, using \mathbf v_1 - \mathbf v_2. For which multiples t of \mathbf v_1 - \mathbf v_2 does \mathbf s_1 + t(\mathbf v_1 - \mathbf v_2) stay a physical spectrum?
B2. A toy camera looks at the same bins with the filters A_\text{cam} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Compute its responses to \mathbf s_1 and \mathbf s_2 of B1. Do eye and camera agree that the two are the same colour? (b) A dichromat has only the L and S cones of A. Compute its responses to \mathbf s_1 and to \mathbf s_4 = (2, 1, 0, 1, 2). Does it see a difference? Does the trichromat eye?
B3. Light 1 has (X, Y, Z) = (20, 30, 50) and light 2 has (30, 15, 5). (a) Compute the chromaticities (x, y) of both. (b) Compute the chromaticity of their sum. Check that it lies on the line between the two, and say where: at what fraction of the way from light 1 to light 2? (c) Which light is brighter? Why does the mixture lie closer to light 1 although light 1 is not brighter?
B4. The sRGB primaries have chromaticities R (0.64, 0.33), G (0.30, 0.60), B (0.15, 0.06). A point is inside the triangle if it can be written as p = \alpha R + \beta G + \gamma B with \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 and all three \ge 0 (barycentric coordinates). (a) Find \alpha, \beta, \gamma for p = (0.30, 0.50). Is it inside? (b) The same for p = (0.20, 0.70), a saturated green. Can an sRGB screen show it?
B5. Explain in two sentences each: (a) why a photo of two fabrics that match to your eye may show them as different; (b) why a white LED and daylight can look the same white although their spectra differ.






Solutions





B1. (a) A\mathbf s_1 = (4, 4, 4), A\mathbf s_2 = (4, 4, 4), A\mathbf s_3 = (3, 2, 3). \mathbf s_1 and \mathbf s_2 are metamers; \mathbf s_3 looks different. (b) A\mathbf v_1 = (1 + 0 - 1,\; -2 + 2 + 0,\; 3 - 4 + 1) = (0, 0, 0). Adding \mathbf v_1 does not change any response: the eye is blind to it. (c) \mathbf v_1 - \mathbf v_2 = (1, -1, 1, -1, 1), so \mathbf s_1 + t(\mathbf v_1 - \mathbf v_2) = (1 + t, 1 - t, 1 + t, 1 - t, 1 + t). It is non-negative for -1 \le t \le 1. For example t = 0.5 gives (1.5, 0.5, 1.5, 0.5, 1.5), with responses (4, 4, 4). t = -1 gives \mathbf s_2.
B2. (a) A_\text{cam}\mathbf s_1 = (3, 4, 3), A_\text{cam}\mathbf s_2 = (2, 4, 2). The camera sees two different colours where the eye sees one: its blind directions are different. (b) The dichromat’s responses (L, S): \mathbf s_1 \to (4, 4), \mathbf s_4 \to (0 + 0 + 0 + 2 + 2,\; 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 0) = (4, 4): no difference. The trichromat eye: A\mathbf s_4 = (4, 2, 4) against (4, 4, 4): the M cone sees it.
B3. (a) Light 1: total 100, (x, y) = (0.2, 0.3). Light 2: total 50, (0.6, 0.3). (b) Sum (50, 45, 55), total 150: (x, y) = (0.333, 0.3). Both lights have y = 0.3, so the line between them is y = 0.3, and x = 0.333 is (0.333 - 0.2)/(0.6 - 0.2) = 1/3 of the way from light 1. The weight of light 2 is its total divided by the sum of totals: 50/150 = 1/3. (c) Light 1 has luminance Y = 30, light 2 has Y = 15: light 1 is twice as bright. The position along the line is weighted by X + Y + Z (100 against 50), not by Y; here both ratios happen to be 2 : 1. In general they differ: a blue light has a large Z, so a little blue luminance pulls the mixture strongly.
B4. Solve \alpha(0.64, 0.33) + \beta(0.30, 0.60) + \gamma(0.15, 0.06) = p with \alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1 (three linear equations). (a) (\alpha, \beta, \gamma) = (0.067, 0.781, 0.152): all positive, inside. (b) (-0.308, 1.339, -0.031): two negative coordinates, outside. The screen would need negative red and blue light; it can only show a clipped, less saturated green.
B5. (a) The camera’s filters are different weighted sums of the spectrum from the cones; the two fabrics’ reflected spectra differ by something the cones cannot see but the camera’s filters can. (b) The LED spectrum (a blue peak plus a yellow hump) and daylight differ only by a change that all three cones are blind to: they are metamers, and LEDs are designed to be.




Math questions
B6. (math) Let A be 3 \times n with rank 3 and P = I - A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A. Show that AP = 0, that P^2 = P, and that P\mathbf v = \mathbf v for every \mathbf v \in \ker A. Why does AA^\top have an inverse?
B7. (math) Two lights have XYZ \mathbf C_1 and \mathbf C_2, totals S_i = X_i + Y_i + Z_i > 0 and chromaticities \mathbf p_i = (x_i, y_i). Show that their sum has chromaticity \frac{S_1}{S_1+S_2}\mathbf p_1 + \frac{S_2}{S_1+S_2}\mathbf p_2. Conclude that a mixture with non-negative amounts of three primaries lies inside their triangle.
B8. (math) The cones are \mathbf c = T\,\mathbf x with \mathbf x = (X, Y, Z) and an invertible 3 \times 3 matrix T; so A_\text{LMS} = T A_\text{XYZ}. Show that \ker A_\text{LMS} = \ker A_\text{XYZ}: metamers do not depend on the basis. Does the same argument work for a camera, A_\text{cam}?






Solutions (math)





B6. AP = A - AA^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A = A - A = 0. P^2 = I - 2A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A + A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}AA^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A = I - A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}A = P. If A\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 then P\mathbf v = \mathbf v - A^\top(AA^\top)^{-1}\mathbf 0 = \mathbf v. AA^\top is 3 \times 3 and \mathbf u^\top AA^\top\mathbf u = \|A^\top\mathbf u\|^2 > 0 for \mathbf u \ne \mathbf 0, because A^\top has rank 3 (independent columns): it is positive definite, hence invertible. So P projects onto \ker A, and \mathbf s + tP\mathbf v is a metamer of \mathbf s for any \mathbf v, t.
B7. The sum has XYZ \mathbf C_1 + \mathbf C_2 and total S_1 + S_2. Its chromaticity is (X_1 + X_2, Y_1 + Y_2)/(S_1 + S_2) = (S_1\mathbf p_1 + S_2\mathbf p_2)/(S_1 + S_2), since X_i = S_i x_i and Y_i = S_i y_i. The weights are non-negative and sum to 1: a convex combination, a point of the segment. For three primaries with amounts a_k \ge 0, the same argument gives \sum_k w_k\mathbf p_k with w_k = a_kS_k/\sum_j a_jS_j \ge 0, \sum w_k = 1: a point of the triangle.
B8. A_\text{LMS}\mathbf s = T A_\text{XYZ}\mathbf s = \mathbf 0 \iff A_\text{XYZ}\mathbf s = \mathbf 0 because T is invertible (T\mathbf u = \mathbf 0 \iff \mathbf u = \mathbf 0). So the null spaces agree. For a camera this works only if A_\text{cam} = T'A_\text{XYZ} for some invertible T', i.e. if the camera’s filter curves are linear combinations of the colour-matching functions (the Luther condition). Real cameras do not satisfy it exactly; that is why they see metamers differently.

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
section: Explore: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Explore: from a spectrum to three numbers
Top: one or two spectra A (black) and B (orange) from 380 to 730 nm, in 10 nm bins. Drag on the plot to draw (choose A or B under drag to draw). Middle: the three sensitivity curves of the chosen observer (eye: L, M, S cones; a synthetic camera: R, G, B; a deuteranope: L and S), each scaled to peak 1; the shaded areas are spectrum A times each curve, and their sums are the numbers. Right: the two colours as that observer sees them, and the numbers, each relative to the response to daylight (so daylight gives 1, 1, 1). In surfaces under a lamp, the curves are reflectances lit by the chosen lamp, and the numbers are relative to a white surface under the same lamp (the eye adapts to the lamp). Make a metamer adds a seeded random spectrum from the observer’s blind set.



E1. Preset daylight vs LED: same white. Describe the two spectra. What numbers does the eye give for each, and what chromaticity? Now choose camera: what does the camera report for the LED?
E2. Preset make a metamer. Click make a metamer a few more times. What changes, and what stays the same? Look at the shaded areas: how can the sums stay equal while the curves differ so much?
E3. Still with the metamer pair, choose camera. Give the camera’s numbers for A and B. Then choose deuteranope: does the pair still match?
E4. Preset metameric failure under tungsten. The curves are now reflectances. Compare the numbers for A and B under tungsten, then click daylight. Which lamp was the metamer made for? Try the fluorescent and white LED lamps: which one breaks the match most?
E5. Preset a dichromat sees more matches. Compare the numbers for the deuteranope, then for the eye. Which cone sees the difference, and how large is it?
E6. Preset 580 nm vs red + green: monochromatic yellow light (A) against a mixture of 540 nm and 640 nm light (B). Is it a match for the eye? Which number differs, and why can no mixture of these two lights fix it exactly?






Solutions





E1. Daylight is smooth (about 50 to 117 across the range); the LED has a sharp blue peak (245 at 450 nm), almost nothing below 420 nm and a broad hump in the yellow–red. The eye gives 1.000, 1.000, 1.000 for both, and both have chromaticity (0.313, 0.329): the two swatches are the same white. The camera gives 1.000, 1.000, 1.000 for daylight but 0.905, 0.962, 0.900 for the LED: in the photo the LED light is darker and slightly green.
E2. B jumps around (in the preset it ranges from 8.8 to 249 in different bins), but the numbers stay 1.022, 0.931, 0.591 for both and the chromaticity stays (0.379, 0.372). Each cone curve is broad: where B has more light than A in one part of a curve’s range, it has less in another part, so the weighted sums are equal. The button chooses exactly such a change for all three curves at once.
E3. Camera: A gives 1.161, 0.853, 0.600 and B gives 1.251, 0.865, 0.666: the camera sees two different colours. For the deuteranope (L and S only) the pair still matches: it only needs fewer equations to hold.
E4. Under tungsten (2800 K): A 0.602, 0.545, 0.353; B 0.589, 0.555, 0.302: the swatches differ: B has less S response, so it looks yellower. Under daylight both are 0.560, 0.500, 0.351: the metamer was made for daylight. Fluorescent: 0.587, 0.533, 0.351 against 0.635, 0.607, 0.475, the largest difference; white LED: 0.561, 0.509, 0.350 against 0.584, 0.537, 0.296. The spiky fluorescent lamp re-weights the wavelengths most unevenly.
E5. Deuteranope: both give L 0.955, S 0.812: a match. Eye: L 0.955 and S 0.812 as well, but M is 0.972 for A and 0.693 for B: the M cones see a difference of about 29 % of the largest number. B was built by removing light in the M cones’ range in a way that L and S cannot see.
E6. Not quite: L 0.140 and M 0.115 agree, but S is 0.000 for the 580 nm light and 0.002 for the mixture (the demo reports 1.1 % of the largest number). Two lights give only two amounts to tune, while there are three numbers to match; the 540 nm light stimulates the S cones a little and the 580 nm light not at all. The chromaticities are close, (0.513, 0.486) against (0.511, 0.482): on the diagram, 580 nm lies almost (but not exactly) on the line between 540 and 640 nm.

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Explore: the chromaticity diagram
The (x, y) chromaticity diagram with the spectral locus (wavelengths in nm) and the purple line, filled with approximate colours (outside the sRGB triangle a screen cannot show them, so they are clipped). Triangles: the gamuts of sRGB, Display P3 and Rec. 2020; the black dot is the D65 white. In mix two lights, drag A and B, set their brightness (luminance Y) and the share of B; the readout gives the mixture and its position on the line. In design a display, drag the primaries R, G, B, the white point W and a test colour T; the readout gives the display’s RGB → XYZ matrix and its inverse (see the next unit) and T’s barycentric coordinates.



C1. Preset mixing two lights (A = 470 nm, Y = 0.3; B = 580 nm, Y = 0.6; share of B 0.5). Where does the mixture lie on the line from A to B? Compute the share of B that puts the mixture halfway, then check it with the slider.
C2. Preset a dim blue and a bright yellow (Y_A = 0.1, Y_B = 1). Where is the mixture now, and what does it look like? Why is it so close to white?
C3. Drag A off the horseshoe, outside it. What does the demo say, and why?
C4. sRGB vs P3: is the test colour T = (0.21, 0.71) inside either gamut? Then a laser display (primaries at 635, 532 and 465 nm). Is T inside now? Compare the laser triangle with Rec. 2020.
C5. A primary outside the locus: what is wrong with this display? Drag G back inside the horseshoe and watch the matrix.






Solutions





C1. At 0.189 of the way from A, at (0.196, 0.138), a blue-violet. A carries X + Y + Z = 5.28, B only 1.23, so A dominates although B is twice as bright. Halfway needs w \cdot 1.23 = (1 - w)\cdot 5.28, w = 5.28/(5.28 + 1.23) = 0.811.
C2. X + Y + Z is 1.76 for A and 2.06 for B; at share 0.5 the mixture is 0.539 of the way, at (0.333, 0.288): close to the white point, a slightly pinkish white. 470 nm and 580 nm are nearly complementary: the line between them passes close to white, so a suitable mixture of the two looks white (as in the white LED: blue plus yellow).
C3. “A outside the locus: not a real light”. No spectrum has that chromaticity: every real light is a non-negative mixture of monochromatic lights, so it lies inside the region they span (the horseshoe closed by the purple line).
C4. T has barycentric coordinates (-0.29, 1.35, -0.06) in sRGB and (-0.12, 1.08, 0.04) in P3: outside both. For the laser display, (0.09, 0.85, 0.06): inside. The laser primaries lie on the locus, so their triangle is almost as large as Rec. 2020, whose primaries are themselves (nearly) monochromatic.
C5. The green primary (0.05, 0.90) is outside the horseshoe: no light has that chromaticity, so the display cannot be built. The matrix can still be computed (scales 0.307, 0.613, 0.080), which shows that the algebra does not know about physics: the check that primaries are real lights must be made separately.

title: Exercise: from a spectrum to three numbers
text:
Where this leads
The three numbers of a pixel depend on the camera’s curves and on the lamp. The next unit asks what the numbers stored in an RGB file are: values for a particular display, gamma-encoded, related to XYZ by a 3 \times 3 matrix, and how a diagonal matrix undoes the lamp (white balance). The spectral unmixing elective returns to the linear model \mathbf c = A\mathbf s with many channels instead of three.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
About this lecture
A threshold tells us which pixels belong to a bright object. Today we draw its boundary as a curve with sub-pixel precision, in 2D; the next unit does the same in 3D.

The boundary at level c: the level set \{I = c\}, an isocontour.
Marching squares: each 2 \times 2 cell on its own, 16 cases, crossing points by linear interpolation.
The two saddle cases, and the asymptotic decider that resolves them.
Measuring a contour: length, and the enclosed area by the shoelace formula.
Real images: noise, blur, and the choice of c.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit owns marching squares for the whole course: the level-set elective draws its zero contours with the same code (lib/marching.ts) and only recalls the idea. Prerequisites: bilinear interpolation from “Images as arrays”; thresholds (one line here; the thresholding day owns them).

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: A boundary is where the image crosses a value
text:
A boundary is where the image crosses a value

A bright object on a dark background: inside I > c, outside I < c. The boundary is where I = c.
The set of points \{(x, y) : I(x, y) = c\} is the level set of I at level c. In 2D it is a set of curves, an isocontour: the contour lines of a height map, with I as the height. In 3D it is a surface (next unit).
Thresholding at c labels whole pixels (the thresholding day). The level set lies between the pixel centres: where exactly between a pixel of 40 and one of 200 does I pass 120?
One c gives one boundary; a different c moves it, merges or splits pieces. Choosing c comes back in the last unit of the day.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: We only know the image at the pixels
text:
We only know the image at the pixels
Treat pixel centres as grid points and look at one cell of 2 \times 2 pixels at a time.


Mark each corner above (orange, I > c) or below c. Four corners, two states: a 4-bit case index, 2^4 = 16 cases. Corners 0, 1, 2, 3 = top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, bit k = corner k.
An edge whose two corners disagree is crossed by the contour, exactly once. The case says which edges are crossed and how to connect them.
Cases 0 and 15: no contour. Cases 5 and 10: four crossings, two ways to connect them (later).

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Where on the edge?
Along an edge from corner a (value I_a) to corner b (value I_b), assume I changes linearly. It reaches c at the fraction
t = \frac{c - I_a}{I_b - I_a}
of the way from a to b.

Example: I_a = 40, I_b = 200, c = 120: t = 80/160 = 0.5. With c = 80: t = 0.25, closer to the dark pixel.
Midpoint rule (t = \tfrac12 always): the contour of the thresholded image. It only knows above/below, so it is blocky, with steps of half a pixel.
Linear interpolation uses the grey values: a smooth contour, accurate to a fraction of a pixel when the image is smooth.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
The math: the crossing point
The straight line through (0, I_a) and (1, I_b) is f(t) = I_a + t\,(I_b - I_a). Setting f(t) = c:
t = \frac{c - I_a}{I_b - I_a} \in (0, 1)\quad\text{when } c \text{ lies strictly between } I_a \text{ and } I_b.

The point is \mathbf p = \mathbf p_a + t\,(\mathbf p_b - \mathbf p_a).
Computed from the same two values, it is the same point whichever of the two neighbouring cells computes it.
Along a cell edge the bilinear interpolant of images/ is this straight line, so the crossing points lie exactly on the level set of the bilinear interpolant.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Marching: every cell on its own
text:
Marching: every cell on its own

Visit the cells one by one (“marching” over the grid). Each cell needs only its 4 corners: no global step, every cell could be processed in parallel.
Two neighbouring cells share an edge, so they compute the same crossing point there: the segments join up. The result is a set of closed curves, or curves that end at the image border.
Pad the image with a frame of background pixels, and every contour closes.
Orientation: connect each segment so that the bright side is always on the same side. Then outer boundaries run one way round and the boundaries of holes the other way: that sign is what makes the area formula work.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Try it: marching squares by hand
text:
Try it: marching squares by hand




An 8 × 8 grid of values (one bump, maximum 9.1); case numbers in the cells, the selected cell’s arithmetic in the readout. Tour: move c from 5 down to 3 and up to 8: one closed contour that grows and shrinks. Click a cell on the contour, e.g. (2, 2): corners 4.7, 6.1, 8.8, 6.7, case 14, one crossed edge pair. Drag a corner value up or down and watch the crossing points slide. “All 16 cases”: find all of them; 5 and 10 are drawn in purple. “Midpoint vs linear” at c = 3: the midpoint contour is an octagon-like staircase; the dashed red curve is the exact level curve of the bilinear interpolant.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Saddle cells: two valid answers


Case 5 (corners 0 and 2 above) and case 10 (corners 1 and 3): diagonal corners above, the other two below. Four crossings, two ways to pair them:

separate the two bright corners (two small bright pieces), or
join them through the cell (one bright band, the dark corners cut off).

The corners alone cannot decide. A fixed rule (always separate) still gives closed, consistent curves, but sometimes the wrong topology: two objects where there is one, or the reverse.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
The asymptotic decider
Use the values, not only the signs. The bilinear interpolant inside the cell (from images/) has curved level lines: hyperbolas. In a saddle cell it has a saddle point with value f^\ast:

if f^\ast > c, the middle of the cell is above c: the bright corners are joined;
if f^\ast < c, the middle is below c: they are separated.

Example (corners clockwise from top-left: 8, 4, 7, 3, c = 5): f^\ast = (8 \cdot 7 - 4 \cdot 3)/(8 + 7 - 4 - 3) = 44/8 = 5.5 > 5: join. With 6 instead of 8 and 6.5 instead of 7: f^\ast = 27/5.5 = 4.91 < 5: separate.
Two neighbouring cells never disagree: the decision is made inside one cell (Nielson & Hamann, 1991).

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: The math: the saddle of the bilinear interpolant
text:
The math: the saddle of the bilinear interpolant
On the cell [0, 1]^2 with corner values I_{00}, I_{10}, I_{01}, I_{11} (first index x):
f(x, y) = I_{00}(1-x)(1-y) + I_{10}\,x(1-y) + I_{01}(1-x)\,y + I_{11}\,xy = A + Bx + Cy + Dxy,
with D = I_{00} + I_{11} - I_{10} - I_{01}. Setting \partial_x f = B + Dy = 0 and \partial_y f = C + Dx = 0 gives the saddle at x^\ast = -C/D, y^\ast = -B/D, with value
f^\ast = A - \frac{BC}{D} = \frac{I_{00}I_{11} - I_{10}I_{01}}{I_{00} + I_{11} - I_{10} - I_{01}}.

f - f^\ast = D\,(x - x^\ast)(y - y^\ast): the level lines are hyperbolas with asymptotes x = x^\ast and y = y^\ast (hence the name).
In a saddle case the two bright corners lie in opposite quadrants around (x^\ast, y^\ast); they are connected inside the cell exactly when the region \{f > c\} contains the centre point of the hyperbolas, i.e. when f^\ast > c.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Measuring a contour

Length: the sum of the segment lengths.
Enclosed area: the shoelace formula (from the labelling day’s shape features, restated here): for a closed polygon (x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n), A = \tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i\,y_{i+1} - x_{i+1}\,y_i), \qquad (x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1).
Example: the diamond (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1): \tfrac12\big[(1 - 0) + (4 - 1) + (1 - 0) + (0 - 1)\big] = 2.
Signed: one direction round gives +, the other -. With the orientation of marching squares, holes count negative automatically; summing over all contours gives the bright area.
Compare: counting pixels above c gives almost the same area, but the pixel boundary (a staircase) has the wrong length.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: The math: why the shoelace works
text:
The math: why the shoelace works

Each term \tfrac12(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i) = \tfrac12\det\begin{bmatrix} x_i & x_{i+1} \\ y_i & y_{i+1}\end{bmatrix} is the signed area of the triangle (origin, \mathbf p_i, \mathbf p_{i+1}). Summed around the polygon, the parts outside cancel.
Equivalently, Green’s theorem: A = \oint \tfrac12(x\,dy - y\,dx), evaluated exactly on straight segments.
This is the 2D version of the divergence theorem. The last unit of the day uses the 3D version to get the volume of a closed surface from its triangles.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Real images: noise and blur

Noise: every pixel that noise pushes across c starts a tiny contour of its own, and the boundary becomes ragged. Lengths explode; areas are almost unaffected (the specks inside and outside roughly cancel).
Blur first (Gaussian, kernels/): the noise is averaged away, contours become smooth and few. Too much blur rounds corners, moves the contour of small objects, and breaks or closes thin necks.
c decides the topology: two blobs joined by a valley are one contour below the valley’s height and two above it.

title: Level sets and marching squares
section: Try it: contours of an image
text:
Try it: contours of an image




128 × 128 test image (two Gaussian blobs, two discs joined by a 3-pixel neck, background 30) or the micrograph. Tour: “noise” (σ_n = 25, c = 120): 141 contours (111 outer, 30 holes), total length 935 px, yet enclosed area 2138 px² against 2212 pixels above c. “Blur first” (σ = 1.5): 3 contours, length 385 px. Raise the blur to 2.5: the neck breaks and the dumbbell falls apart (4 contours). “Two blobs merge as c drops”: lower c from 140; the two blobs join at about c = 96 (their saddle value). Then the micrograph.

title: Level sets and marching squares
text:
Summary

The boundary at level c is the level set \{I = c\}: curves in 2D, surfaces in 3D.
Marching squares: per cell, 4 corners → case index (16 cases) → crossed edges → segments. Shared edges make the curves close up.
Crossing points by linear interpolation t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a); the midpoint rule gives the blocky boundary of the thresholded image.
Saddle cases 5 and 10 are ambiguous; the asymptotic decider joins the bright corners when the bilinear saddle value exceeds c.
Length by summing segments, area by the shoelace formula; noise makes many tiny contours, blur first.

title: Quiz: level sets and marching squares
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A grid point is above when I > c; cell corners 0, 1, 2, 3 = top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left; case index = \sum 2^k over the corners above c.

Q1. What is the difference between thresholding an image at c and computing its level set at c?






Hint





One produces pixels, the other a curve.









Answer





Thresholding labels each pixel above or below c: a region made of whole pixels. The level set \{I = c\} is the boundary between those regions, a curve that passes between pixel centres at the interpolated position, with sub-pixel precision.




Q2. A cell has corners (top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left) = 2, 7, 8, 1 and c = 5. What is its case index, and which edges are crossed?






Hint





Which corners are above 5?









Answer





Corners 1 and 2 are above: case 2 + 4 = 6. The crossed edges are the top edge (2 → 7) and the bottom edge (8 → 1); the contour runs from top to bottom, like a vertical line.




Q3. On an edge from 30 to 90, where is the crossing for c = 45?






Hint





t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a).









Answer





t = 15/60 = 0.25: a quarter of the way from the corner with 30.




Q4. Why do the line segments of neighbouring cells always join up, although each cell is handled on its own?






Hint





What do the two cells have in common?









Answer





They share the edge between them, with the same two corner values: both find the same crossing point (or both find none). So every segment ending on that edge meets the segment of the neighbour there.




Q5. Which cases are ambiguous, and what are the two possible contours?






Hint





Look for diagonal corners.









Answer





Cases 5 and 10: two diagonal corners above, the other two below. The contour can separate the two bright corners (each cut off on its own) or join them (the two dark corners cut off instead). Both choices give closed curves; they differ in topology.




Q6. A saddle cell has corners 6, 2, 6, 2 (clockwise from top-left) and c = 4. What does the asymptotic decider do?






Hint





f^\ast = (I_0 I_2 - I_1 I_3)/(I_0 + I_2 - I_1 - I_3).









Answer





f^\ast = (36 - 4)/(12 - 4) = 32/8 = 4 = c: exactly the borderline (with the rule “join if f^\ast > c” it separates). Any change of a value tips the decision. This is the case where the bilinear interpolant’s level curve at c is a pair of crossing lines.




Q7. A noisy image gives 300 contours at c where you expect 5 objects. Name two things you could do, and their side effects.






Hint





Change the image, or filter the result.









Answer





Blur before extracting (fewer and smoother contours; but small objects shrink and thin necks break), or discard contours enclosing less than a minimum area (keeps the shapes; but real small objects go too, and the remaining boundaries stay ragged). Choosing c further from the noise level also helps.




Q8. (math) Show with the shoelace formula that the triangle (0, 0), (4, 0), (0, 3) has area 6, and that listing its corners in the opposite order gives -6.






Hint





A = \tfrac12\sum(x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i).









Answer





Terms: (0 \cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 0) + (4 \cdot 3 - 0 \cdot 0) + (0 \cdot 0 - 0 \cdot 3) = 12, so A = 6. Reversed, (0,0), (0,3), (4,0): (0 - 0) + (0 \cdot 0 - 4 \cdot 3) + (0 - 0) = -12, A = -6.

title: Exercise: level sets and marching squares
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run marching squares by hand: classify cells (16 cases), find the crossed edges, place the crossing points by linear interpolation, and draw the contour,
recognise a saddle cell and resolve it with the asymptotic decider,
measure a contour: length and enclosed area (shoelace), with holes counting negative,
predict what noise, blur and the choice of c do to the contours of a real image.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: level sets and marching squares
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Above / below
a grid point is above if I > c


Cell corners
0 = top-left, 1 = top-right, 2 = bottom-right, 3 = bottom-left; edge k joins corner k and k+1


Case index
\sum 2^k over the corners above c: 0 … 15


Crossing point
on an edge from a to b with I_a, I_b on opposite sides of c: t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a) of the way from a


Saddle cases
5 (corners 0, 2 above) and 10 (corners 1, 3 above)

f^\ast = \dfrac{I_0 I_2 - I_1 I_3}{I_0 + I_2 - I_1 - I_3} (corner values I_k); f^\ast > c: join the above corners, else separate


Shoelace
A = \tfrac12\sum_i (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1}y_i) around a closed polygon






The 16 cases (orange: above c; the saddle cases 5 and 10 in purple, drawn with the “separate” rule).

Mark the grid points above c. Give the case index of each of the 9 cells (cell (x, y) has its top-left corner at grid point (x, y)).
Which cell is a saddle? Compute f^\ast and decide with the asymptotic decider.
For every crossed edge, compute t and the crossing point in grid coordinates (x, y).
Draw the contour. How many pieces does it have, and where do they end?
Which piece changes if you use the rule “always separate” in the saddle cell?

B2. An edge runs from a pixel of value I_a = 40 to one of value I_b = 200, one pixel apart. (a) Where does the contour cross it for c = 120, for c = 60 and for c = 180? (b) Where does the midpoint rule put it? By how much can the midpoint rule be off on this edge, as c ranges over (40, 200)?
B3. The saddle cell with corners (clockwise from top-left) 8, 4, 7, 3. (a) For which values of c is it a saddle case at all? (b) Compute f^\ast. For which of these c does the decider join the bright corners, and for which does it separate them? (c) Replace the 8 by 6 and the 7 by 6.5. Recompute f^\ast. What changes at c = 5?
B4. (a) Compute the area and the perimeter of the closed polygon (1, 0), (2, 1), (1, 2), (0, 1) with the shoelace formula and the segment lengths. (b) Reverse the order of the points. What happens to the shoelace sum? (c) A bright ring is described by two closed contours, an outer one of area 50 and an inner one around the dark hole of area 12. Marching squares orients them oppositely. What is the sum of the signed areas, and what does it measure?
B5. Pad the grid of B1 with a frame of zeros (so every contour closes) and keep c = 5. (a) How many closed contours are there with the asymptotic decider, and how many with “always separate”? (b) Without computing: which rule gives the larger total length?
B6. A noisy image (noise standard deviation 25 grey levels) of bright objects (200) on a dark background (30), contoured at c = 120. (a) Why are there many tiny contours, and why do they barely change the total enclosed area? (b) What does a Gaussian blur before marching squares do to the number of contours? Name one thing that too much blur breaks.






Solutions
