title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
By hand
B1. Data 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10 (the k-means example). Start \mu = (2, 8), \sigma^2 = (4, 4), \pi = (0.5, 0.5). (a) Show that with equal variances and weights r_1(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-a}) with a = [(x - 8)^2 - (x - 2)^2]/8. Compute r_1(4) and r_1(7). (The others are 1.00, 0.99, 0.00, 0.00 for x = 1, 2, 9, 10; more precisely 0.998, 0.989, 0.002, 0.001.) (b) M-step: compute N_1, \mu_1, \mu_2 and \pi_1. (c) Compare with the k-means result (2.33, 8.67). Which point is “shared”, and how does that show in \mu_1 and \mu_2? (d) The log-likelihood over the first iterations is -14.94, -14.22, -14.03, -13.99. What would a decrease tell you?
B2. A smaller example: points 0, 2, 3; start \mu = (0, 4), \sigma^2 = (1, 1), \pi = (0.5, 0.5). (a) E-step: compute all responsibilities. (Use r_1(x) = 1/(1 + e^{-a}) with a = [(x - 4)^2 - x^2]/2.) (b) M-step: N_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2, \pi_k.
B3. Two groups of points overlap in the middle. A point lies exactly halfway between the two current means; both components have the same variance and weight. (a) What does k-means do with it, and what does EM do? (b) In the M-step, how much does the point pull on each mean in k-means, and in EM?
B4. BIC and AIC. You fitted 1D mixtures to n = 1000 pixel intensities and got \log p(\mathcal D) = -4210, -4020, -4012, -4010 for K = 1, 2, 3, 4. (a) Give the number of parameters p for each K. (b) Compute BIC and AIC. Which K does each choose? (c) Explain in words why they differ.
B5. Choosing the covariance type. Two components fitted to n = 200 points in 2D give \log p(\mathcal D) = 273.0 with diagonal covariances and 274.7 with full covariances. Compute both BICs. Which model does BIC prefer, and what does that say about the shape of the groups?
B6. Predict and explain: you start EM with one component placed exactly on an outlier point, far from the rest, with a small variance. What happens in the next few iterations? What would you see in the log-likelihood plot? How do you fix it?






Solutions





B1. (a) With equal \sigma^2 and \pi, the constants cancel: r_1 = \frac{e^{-(x-2)^2/8}}{e^{-(x-2)^2/8} + e^{-(x-8)^2/8}} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-[(x-8)^2 - (x-2)^2]/8}}. At x = 4: a = (16 - 4)/8 = 1.5, r_1 = 0.82. At x = 7: a = (1 - 25)/8 = -3, r_1 = 0.05. (b) N_1 = 0.998 + 0.989 + 0.818 + 0.047 + 0.002 + 0.001 = 2.85; \mu_1 = (0.998 + 2 \cdot 0.989 + 4 \cdot 0.818 + 7 \cdot 0.047 + \dots)/2.85 = 2.31; N_2 = 3.15, \mu_2 = 8.39; \pi_1 = 2.85/6 = 0.48. (Variances: \sigma^2 = (1.87, 2.83).) (c) The point 4 is shared: 82 % of it goes to component 1, 18 % to component 2. It pulls \mu_2 down from 8.67 to 8.39 and \mu_1 slightly down (2.31 instead of 2.33, since 4 counts only 0.82 while 7 adds a little). After convergence EM ends at (2.34, 8.66): close to k-means, because the groups are well separated. (d) A bug (or a modified algorithm): exact EM can never decrease the log-likelihood.
B2. (a) x = 0: a = 8, r_1 = 0.9997. x = 2: a = 0, r_1 = 0.5. x = 3: a = -4, r_1 = 0.018. (b) N_1 = 1.518, N_2 = 1.482; \mu_1 = (0 + 1 + 0.054)/1.518 = 0.69, \mu_2 = (0.001 + 1 + 2.946)/1.482 = 2.66; \sigma_1^2 = 0.94, \sigma_2^2 = 0.23; \pi = (0.51, 0.49).
B3. (a) k-means gives it fully to one of the two (whichever wins the tie). EM gives it responsibility 0.5 to each. (b) k-means: weight 1 on one mean, 0 on the other. EM: weight 0.5 on each; it pulls both means a little towards the middle.
B4. (a) p = 3K - 1: 2, 5, 8, 11. (b) BIC = -2\log p + p\ln 1000 (\ln 1000 = 6.91): 8433.8, 8074.5, 8079.3, 8096.0: K = 2. AIC = -2\log p + 2p: 8424, 8050, 8040, 8042: K = 3. (c) Going from 2 to 3 components improves -2\log p by 16 at the cost of 3 parameters. AIC charges 2 \times 3 = 6 and accepts; BIC charges 3 \times 6.91 = 20.7 and refuses. BIC’s penalty grows with n, so for large data sets it prefers simpler models.
B5. p = 9 (diagonal: 1 + 4 + 4) and p = 11 (full: 1 + 4 + 6); \ln 200 = 5.30. BIC: -546.0 + 47.7 = -498.3 (diagonal) and -549.4 + 58.3 = -491.1 (full). BIC prefers the diagonal model: the two extra covariance numbers improve the fit by only 1.7 in \log p. The groups are (close to) axis-aligned ellipses; their correlations are not needed.
B6. The component owns the outlier with responsibility close to 1 and almost nothing else. The M-step puts its mean on the outlier and its variance becomes (almost) zero; its density at the outlier explodes and the log-likelihood shoots up to a huge value in one or two iterations, then stays there (in practice limited by a numerical minimum variance). The plot shows a sudden jump, not a gentle rise. Fix: a variance floor, removing or restarting the component, starting from k-means(++) or from several starts, or a robust model (heavy-tailed components).




Math questions
B7. (math) Starting from \log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_i\log\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i \mid \boldsymbol\mu_k, \Sigma_k), derive the M-step for \boldsymbol\mu_k (set the gradient to zero) and for \pi_k (with a Lagrange multiplier for \sum_k\pi_k = 1).
B8. (math) Prove Jensen’s bound \log p(\mathbf x_i) \ge \sum_k q_i(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{q_i(k)} for any distribution q_i, show that it is tight for q_i(k) = r_{ik}, and use it to show that one EM iteration cannot decrease \log p(\mathcal D).
B9. (math) Take \Sigma_k = \sigma^2 I for all k, fixed, and \pi_k = 1/K, fixed. Show that as \sigma \to 0 the responsibilities become 0 or 1 (for points with a unique nearest centre), and that EM becomes k-means.
B10. (math) Show that the likelihood of a 1D mixture with two components is unbounded: put \mu_2 = x_1 and let \sigma_2 \to 0 while component 1 is fixed. Why does this not happen with a single Gaussian (unless all points are equal)?






Solutions (math)





B7. \partial/\partial\boldsymbol\mu_k of \log\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N_j(\mathbf x_i) is \frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N_j(\mathbf x_i)}\Sigma_k^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k) = r_{ik}\Sigma_k^{-1}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k). Summing over i and setting to zero (multiply by \Sigma_k): \sum_i r_{ik}(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k) = 0, so \boldsymbol\mu_k = \sum_i r_{ik}\mathbf x_i/N_k. For \pi_k: \partial/\partial\pi_k[\log p(\mathcal D) - \lambda(\sum_j\pi_j - 1)] = \sum_i\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)/p(\mathbf x_i) - \lambda = \sum_i r_{ik}/\pi_k - \lambda = 0, so \pi_k = N_k/\lambda; \sum_k\pi_k = 1 and \sum_k N_k = n give \lambda = n. The r_{ik} depend on the parameters, so these are fixed-point equations; EM iterates them.
B8. \log is concave, so \log\sum_k q_k y_k \ge \sum_k q_k\log y_k for weights q_k \ge 0 summing to 1 (Jensen). With y_k = \pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)/q_i(k), the left side is \log p(\mathbf x_i). For q_i(k) = r_{ik}, y_k = p(\mathbf x_i) for all k, and both sides are \log p(\mathbf x_i). Write \mathcal L(q, \theta) = \sum_i\sum_k q_i(k)\log\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)}{q_i(k)}. E-step: q = r^{\text{old}}, so \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{old}}) = \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{old}}). M-step: \theta^{\text{new}} maximises \mathcal L(q, \theta) over \theta (only \sum_i\sum_k q_i(k)[\log\pi_k + \log\mathcal N_k(\mathbf x_i)] depends on \theta: weighted one-Gaussian fits). Then \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{new}}) \ge \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{new}}) \ge \mathcal L(q, \theta^{\text{old}}) = \log p(\mathcal D \mid \theta^{\text{old}}).
B9. r_{ik} = \frac{\exp(-\lVert\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_k\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)}{\sum_j\exp(-\lVert\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu_j\rVert^2/2\sigma^2)} (the constants and equal weights cancel). Divide numerator and denominator by the term of the nearest centre k^*: r_{ik} = 1/\sum_j\exp(-(d_j^2 - d_k^2)/2\sigma^2). For k = k^* all other exponents are negative and \to -\infty: r_{ik^*} \to 1; for k \ne k^* the term j = k^* has a positive exponent \to +\infty: r_{ik} \to 0. The M-step mean with 0/1 weights is the mean of the points nearest to \boldsymbol\mu_k: exactly k-means’ update.
B10. p(x_1) \ge \pi_2\mathcal N(x_1 \mid x_1, \sigma_2^2) = \pi_2/(\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_2) \to \infty, and for i \ne 1, p(x_i) \ge \pi_1\mathcal N_1(x_i) > 0, a fixed positive number. So \prod_i p(x_i) \to \infty. With one Gaussian, shrinking \sigma to fit x_1 makes every other point’s density go to zero (like e^{-(x_i - \mu)^2/2\sigma^2}, much faster than 1/\sigma grows), so the likelihood goes to 0, not infinity; its maximum is at the sample variance, which is positive unless all points are equal.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Explore: EM step by step
The demo shows 6–12 points on a line (drag them) and the current mixture: each weighted component \pi_k\mathcal N(x \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2) dashed, their sum in black, the means as vertical lines. Points are coloured by their responsibilities. The tables give r_{ik} for every point and N_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2, \pi_k per component; the readout gives \log p(\mathcal D) after every M-step. E-step and M-step do one half-step each. Options: hard assignments, equal variances and weights, and a variance floor \varepsilon = 0.1.



P1. Preset the by-hand example. Do one E-step and one M-step and compare the tables with B1. Then alternate until nothing changes. Is \log p always increasing? Where does it end?
P2. Preset an ambiguous point in the middle. What is the responsibility of the point 5.5 at the start and at the end? Why does it not change?
P3. Preset collapse: one component on one point. Alternate E and M. Write down \log p after each M-step. What happens to \sigma_2^2? Now tick variance floor and repeat (reset first).
P4. Preset hard EM = k-means. Run to convergence. Compare the means with B1 of the k-means unit. Untick hard assignments (keep equal variances and weights), reset and run again: does the result change?






Solutions





P1. After the E-step: r_{i1} = 1.00, 0.99, 0.82, 0.05, 0.00, 0.00; after the M-step N = (2.85, 3.15), \mu = (2.31, 8.39), \sigma^2 = (1.87, 2.83), \pi = (0.48, 0.52). \log p: -14.94 \to -14.22 \to -14.03 \to -13.99, always increasing, and it converges at -13.99 with \mu = (2.34, 8.66), \sigma^2 = 1.57 for both, \pi = (0.5, 0.5).
P2. 0.50 at the start and 0.50 at the end. The data and the start are symmetric about 5.5 (points 1, 2, 3 and 8, 9, 10; means 2 and 9; equal variances and weights), so every iteration keeps the symmetry: the point is always exactly halfway, with equal densities and equal weights. EM ends at \mu = (2.50, 8.50), \sigma^2 = 2.08 for both.
P3. Without the floor: \log p = -16.59 \to -14.58 \to -14.24 \to -12.97 \to -2.13. Component 2 sits on the single point 10; its variance shrinks from 8 to 10^{-10} (the demo’s numerical minimum) and the spike makes \log p jump. With a smaller numerical minimum the jump would be larger still: the likelihood is unbounded. With the floor \varepsilon = 0.1: -16.59 \to -14.59 \to -14.27 \to -13.20 \to -12.50, and \sigma_2^2 stops at 0.1: still a narrow component on one point, but with finite likelihood. (Is one point a “group”? Unit 4 calls such points anomalies.)
P4. The means end at (2.33, 8.67), exactly the k-means answer. \log p goes -29.41 \to -16.40 \to -15.27 \to -13.99. With soft assignments (equal variances and weights still fixed to be equal) EM ends at (2.34, 8.66), \log p = -13.99: almost the same here, because the groups are well separated; it takes more iterations (13 M-steps instead of 4), since the start (1, 2) makes both components share all points at first.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Explore: EM in 2D
The main demo of the day. The points come from a dataset (seeded); click to add points, drag them, or remove them. Choose K, the covariance type (spherical, diagonal, full, tied) and the start (random points, k-means, k-means++ seeds, or by hand: drag the centres). E-step, M-step, step and run fit the mixture; points are coloured by their responsibilities, ellipses are 1σ (solid) and 2σ (dashed), and the background shows the regions of the most probable component (or the density). Right: \log p(\mathcal D) per iteration (a red ring would mark a decrease), 20 restarts (histogram of the final \log p), BIC / AIC for K = 1..6, and the variance floor \varepsilon. k-means (hard) switches to Lloyd’s algorithm for comparison.



E1. Preset well separated. Press run. What are the final \log p and weights? Press 20 restarts: do all runs end at the same value?
E2. Preset elongated: k-means fails, full GMM works. It starts in k-means mode: run and describe the groups. Switch to EM (soft) and run. Compare the groups, and look at the ellipses.
E3. Preset one big, one small: weights matter. Run. Where is the boundary (background) compared with the k-means bisector? What are the weights?
E4. Preset bad start: local maximum. Run. What is the final \log p, compared with E1 (same data)? Describe the solution. Press new start, then run.
E5. Preset collapse (floor off). Run and watch the \log p plot and the readout. Then set the floor to 10^{-4} (reset and run). Compare.
E6. Preset K too large: BIC says no. Read the BIC and AIC bars. Which K does each choose? Relate to B4.
E7. Presets diagonal is enough and diagonal is not enough. In each, compare the BIC values for diagonal and full covariances (switch Σ and press BIC / AIC). When are the extra parameters worth it?
E8. Preset heavy overlap: soft labels near 0.5. Run. Which points have mixed colours? Would a hard label be trustworthy there?






Solutions





E1. \log p(\mathcal D) = 179.7 with weights 0.33, 0.33, 0.33 (three blobs of 50 points). (The log-likelihood is positive because the points live in the unit square, where densities are larger than 1.) Of 20 restarts from k-means, 19 end at 179.7 and one at 140.4, a local maximum.
E2. k-means cuts across both cigars (J = 3.079; only 125 of 160 points grouped as in the cigars). EM with full covariances ends at \log p = 245.6 with two long, thin, tilted ellipses, one per cigar: 146 of the 160 points are grouped as in the two cigars. The covariance lets each component follow the shape of its group.
E3. Weights 0.80 and 0.20; the wide component’s region extends around the small, tight group, and the boundary lies close to the small group, not halfway between the centres. All 150 points get the label of the group they came from (k-means: 138).
E4. \log p = 123.4, far below 179.7: one component covers two blobs (weight 0.67), the other two share one blob (0.08 and 0.25). No single EM step can move a component across the empty gap. A new start (k-means) finds 179.7 again.
E5. Without a floor the third component sits on the outlier at (0.88, 0.15): after one iteration \log p jumps from -62.0 to 203.1 and then 203.9; its variance is at the numerical minimum 10^{-10}, and the readout reports a collapse. With \varepsilon = 10^{-4}, \log p = 190.1 and the component is a small circle (variance 10^{-4}, i.e. σ = 0.01) on the outlier: finite, and visibly an “outlier component” with weight 0.01.
E6. BIC is smallest at K = 2 (the two blobs), AIC at K = 4. As in B4, AIC’s penalty (2 per parameter) is smaller than BIC’s (\ln 100 = 4.6 per parameter), so AIC accepts extra components that improve the fit only slightly.
E7. Diagonal is enough (axis-aligned clouds): BIC at K = 2 is -498.3 for diagonal and -491.0 for full: the two correlations are not worth their cost. Diagonal is not enough (tilted cigars): with diagonal covariances BIC is smallest at K = 4 (-361.1): it needs a staircase of axis-aligned blobs to cover each tilted cigar. With full covariances BIC is -439.9 at K = 1 and -435.3 at K = 2: far better than any diagonal model, and one tilted ellipse (or two) suffices. (BIC slightly prefers one big ellipse around both cigars here: the cigars are close together.)
E8. The points in the overlap region, between the two centres, have mixed colours: 26 of the 100 points have responsibilities between 0.3 and 0.7. A hard label there is close to a coin toss; the soft label says so honestly.

title: Exercise: fitting a mixture with EM
text:
Where this leads
EM fits mixtures to any points: pixels in a feature space, or objects in a feature table. Unit 4 applies it to images: mixtures of grey levels (the thresholding day’s minimum-error threshold for K classes), colour segmentation, populations of cells, and anomalies.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: one deep tree fits its training data perfectly but is unstable: change a few points and the whole tree changes. Today we turn that into a strength (Breiman, 1996 and 2001).

Grow many trees, each on a bootstrap sample, and let them vote: bagging.
Averaging helps only as far as the trees make different mistakes.
Random forest: each split looks at a random subset of the features, so the trees differ more.
Out-of-bag error: a validation estimate for free.
Vote fractions as probabilities, and where they mislead.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: One tree: low bias, high variance
text:
One tree: low bias, high variance

A tree grown fully follows every training point: on average it is in the right place (low bias), but it moves a lot with the particular sample of data (high variance).
Measurements have the same problem, and the same cure: average several of them.
But we have only one training set. How do we get many trees?


Recall from the decision-trees unit: on the noisy-overlap data one full tree has 0 % training error and 28.8 % test error. A shallower tree (depth 4) has 21.0 %: less variance, more bias. Averaging tries to get the low bias of deep trees with less of their variance.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
The bootstrap

Draw n points from the n training points with replacement.
Some points are drawn twice or three times, about a third are not drawn at all.
Each draw is a new, slightly different training set from the same data.
Bagging (bootstrap aggregating): grow one tree per bootstrap sample, let all trees vote.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: one in three is left out
text:
The math: one in three is left out
The chance that one particular point is not chosen in one draw is 1 - \tfrac1n; the n draws are independent: P(\text{point not in the sample}) = \left(1 - \frac1n\right)^n \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} e^{-1} \approx 0.368 . n = 5: 0.328; n = 20: 0.358; n = 1000: 0.368. The expected number of distinct points in a bootstrap sample is n\,(1 - (1 - 1/n)^n) \approx 0.632\, n.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Try it: bootstrap samples




With n = 20 the first sample (seed fixed) leaves out 6 points and draws 4 points more than once (two of them three times). “draw 1000”: the out-of-bag fraction has mean 35.6 %, close to (1 − 1/20)^20 = 0.358; for large n it approaches 1/e = 0.368. With n = 5 the fraction jumps around a lot (standard deviation 13.9 percentage points over 1000 samples).

title: Bagging and random forests
section: Averaging helps only if the trees differ
text:
Averaging helps only if the trees differ

Average B predictions, each with the same spread.
If they are independent, the spread of the average shrinks without limit as B grows.
If they are correlated (they make similar mistakes), it shrinks only down to a floor set by the correlation.
Bagged trees on the same data are alike: the strongest feature is chosen at the root of almost every tree.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: the variance of an average
text:
The math: the variance of an average
B predictors f_1, \dots, f_B, each with variance \sigma^2, every pair with correlation \rho: \operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_b f_b\Big) = \frac{1}{B^2}\Big(\sum_b \operatorname{Var} f_b + \sum_{b \ne c}\operatorname{Cov}(f_b, f_c)\Big) = \frac{B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2}{B^2} = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\,\sigma^2 .

B \to \infty leaves \rho\sigma^2: more trees cannot beat the correlation.
\sigma^2 = 1, \rho = 0.3: 1, 0.370, 0.307 for B = 1, 10, 100; floor 0.3.
To lower the floor, lower \rho, even at some cost in each tree’s own accuracy.
Squared error = bias² + variance + noise. Averaging leaves the bias unchanged and lowers only the variance.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Try it: averaging correlated predictors




Dots: simulated variance of the average of B predictors (2000 runs, fixed seed); line: the formula; dashed: the floor ρσ². With σ² = 1, ρ = 0.3: 0.370 at B = 10, 0.307 at B = 100 (simulated 0.375 and 0.312). With ρ = 0 the line keeps falling (0.010 at B = 100); with ρ = 0.5 it stops at 0.5.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Random forests: decorrelate the trees

At each split, look only at a random subset of m features (out of d) and choose the best split among those.
A typical choice: m \approx \sqrt d for classification.
The strongest feature is not always available, so other features get their turn: the trees become less alike, and their average better.
Everything else as in bagging: bootstrap samples, deep trees, vote.

m = d is plain bagging; m = 1 makes every split’s feature a coin toss.

title: Bagging and random forests
section: Try it: a forest in the plane
text:
Try it: a forest in the plane




Tour: “one deep tree overfits”: 0 % training, 28.8 % test error, hard edges everywhere. “100 bagged trees”: the map softens (colour strength = confidence), test 23.4 %, OOB 26.0 %; the error-vs-trees curve flattens after a few dozen trees. The six small maps are individual trees: each on its own bootstrap sample. “m = d: trees look alike” (two moons with the extra features x + y, x − y, d = 4): tree correlation 0.68, test 8.7 %. “m = 1”: correlation 0.62, test 9.2 % — lower correlation, but each tree is weaker; here the trade does not pay. “noise features”: 4 pure-noise features added; the forest’s test error is 1.9 % (3.2 % without them) and a single tree 3.0 %. “confident far from the data”: the corners are coloured with probability 1.00. “uncertainty on the boundary”: pale colours along the boundary between the moons.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Out-of-bag (OOB) error

Each training point was left out by about a third of the trees.
Let only those trees vote on it: that is a prediction for a point they never saw.
The error rate of these votes is the out-of-bag error: a validation estimate for free, without setting data aside.
It assumes the training points are independent. Pixels in a painted stroke are not: the pixel-classification unit shows how OOB then fools you.


In the demo the OOB error (solid curve) and the test error on 1000 fresh points (dashed) track each other: 26.0 % and 23.4 % for the bagged overlap data, 10.6 % and 8.7 % for the moons.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Probabilities from votes

70 of 100 trees say “nucleus”: P(\text{nucleus}) \approx 0.7. (Each tree votes with its leaf’s class shares; fully grown leaves are pure, so this is a vote count.)
The probability map: confident inside the classes, uncertain near the boundary. Useful for deciding where to look or where to label more.
Caveat: far from all training data, every tree extends its outermost rectangles, so the forest can be confident where it has never seen anything. A vote fraction is not a calibrated certainty.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
The settings

Number of trees B: more never hurts accuracy, only time. The OOB error curve flattens; stop there.
Depth / leaf size: forests usually grow deep trees; averaging takes care of the variance.
m: the one that matters most, but often fine at the default.
No feature scaling, little tuning: a reason forests are a common first choice for tables of measurements and for pixel classification.

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Bagging vs boosting









bagging / random forest
boosting




trees
deep, grown independently
shallow (often stumps), grown in sequence


each new tree
sees a bootstrap sample
focuses on the points the previous trees got wrong


combination

weighted sum


reduces
variance
bias



Boosting is the subject of the integral-images day (AdaBoost and the face-detector cascade).

title: Bagging and random forests
section: The math: a forest as adaptive neighbours
text:
The math: a forest as adaptive neighbours
The forest’s class probability at \mathbf x is the average of the trees’ leaf shares, \hat p_k(\mathbf x) = \frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B \hat p_{k,b}(\mathbf x) . Each leaf share is an average over the training points in the leaf of \mathbf x. So \hat p_k(\mathbf x) is a weighted vote of training points, with weight high for points that often share a leaf with \mathbf x: a nearest-neighbour rule whose notion of “near” is learned from the labels (it ignores features that never help to split).

title: Bagging and random forests
text:
Summary

Bootstrap: n draws with replacement; about 1/e \approx 37\,\% of the points are left out of each sample.
Bagging: many deep trees on bootstrap samples, averaged: less variance, same bias.
Averaging B correlated predictors: variance \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B; the correlation sets the floor.
Random forest: a random subset of m features at each split lowers the correlation.
OOB error for free; vote fractions as probabilities, but confident far from the data.
Boosting is the sequential, bias-reducing relative.

title: Quiz: bagging and random forests
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A bootstrap sample of 1000 training points is drawn. About how many distinct points does it contain?






Hint





About 37 % are left out.









Answer





About 1000 \cdot (1 - 0.368) \approx 632. The sample still has 1000 entries: the missing ones are made up by points drawn two or more times.




Q2. Why does bagging use deep trees rather than stumps?






Hint





Which part of the error does averaging reduce?









Answer





Averaging reduces the variance but leaves the bias unchanged. Deep trees have low bias and high variance: exactly what averaging fixes. Averaging stumps would give an average of biased, simple models that are all wrong in the same way (that is what boosting addresses, by growing them in sequence).




Q3. Your forest’s OOB error stops improving after 80 trees. You add 400 more. What happens to the error, and to the training and prediction time?






Hint





More trees never hurt accuracy.









Answer





The error stays about the same (it does not get worse: a forest does not overfit by adding trees). Training and prediction take six times longer.




Q4. What does the random subset of m features per split do that bootstrap samples alone do not?






Hint





What does every bagged tree ask first?









Answer





With all features available, every bagged tree picks the same strong feature at the root and similar splits below: the trees are highly correlated, so averaging them gains little. A random subset forces other features in, the trees differ more, and the correlation floor \rho\sigma^2 of the average drops.




Q5. 63 of 90 trees vote “mitotic” for a cell. What does the forest report? Is it 70 % sure the cell is mitotic?






Hint





Where do vote fractions go wrong?









Answer





P(\text{mitotic}) = 63/90 = 0.7, label mitotic. It is a vote share, not a calibrated probability: trees are correlated, and far from the training data they can all agree for no good reason. Use it as a ranking of confidence, and check calibration on held-out data before reading it as “70 % of such cells are mitotic”.




Q6. Why is the out-of-bag error an honest estimate for independent samples, without a separate validation set?






Hint





Which trees vote on a training point?









Answer





Each training point is predicted only by the trees whose bootstrap sample did not contain it: for those trees it is new data. If the samples are independent, that is like a validation set of the full size (with a forest of about a third of the trees).




Q7. (math) \sigma^2 = 4, \rho = 0.25. What is the variance of the average of 15 such predictors, and the smallest variance reachable with many?






Hint





\rho\sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B.









Answer





0.25 \cdot 4 + 0.75 \cdot 4/15 = 1 + 0.2 = 1.2. The floor is \rho\sigma^2 = 1.




Q8. Bagging or boosting: which grows its trees independently, and which reduces mainly the bias?






Hint





Boosting looks at the previous trees’ mistakes.









Answer





Bagging (and random forests) grow trees independently, each on its own bootstrap sample, and reduce the variance. Boosting grows shallow trees one after the other, each focusing on what the previous ones got wrong, and reduces mainly the bias.

text:

title: Exercise: bagging and random forests
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Bootstrap sample
n points drawn from n with replacement


Out of bag
the points a bootstrap sample did not draw: about (1 - 1/n)^n \approx 37\,\%


Bagging
one deep tree per bootstrap sample; the trees vote


Random forest
bagging + a random subset of m of the d features at every split


Variance of an average
B predictors, variance \sigma^2, pairwise correlation \rho: \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B


Vote fraction
share of the trees that vote for a class: the forest’s probability


OOB prediction / error
for each training point, the vote of the trees that did not see it; their error rate









The math: why correlation sets the floor





For B predictors with variances \sigma^2 and covariances \rho\sigma^2, \operatorname{Var}(\sum_b f_b) = B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2. Divide by B^2 for the average: \rho\sigma^2 + (1-\rho)\sigma^2/B. The second term vanishes as B grows; the first does not, because the shared part of the errors is the same in every predictor and survives any amount of averaging.

title: Exercise: bagging and random forests
text:
By hand
B1. A training set has n = 5 points. (a) What is the probability that point 1 is not in a given bootstrap sample? (b) Three trees are grown on three independent bootstrap samples. What is the probability that point 1 is in none of them? In at least one? (c) A forest has 100 trees. About how many of them can give an OOB vote on point 1, if n is large?
B2. Predictors with \sigma^2 = 1 and pairwise correlation \rho = 0.3. (a) Compute the variance of the average of 1, 10, 100 and infinitely many of them. (b) A different way of growing trees gives \rho lower. How low must \rho be so that the average of only 10 trees beats 100 trees at \rho = 0.3? (c) In a forest, what do you change to lower \rho, and what does it cost?
B3. Five trees vote on a training pixel: N, N, B, N, B. Trees 2, 3 and 5 did not have the pixel in their bootstrap sample. (a) What is the forest’s probability of N, and its label? (b) What is the OOB vote, and the OOB label? The pixel is truly B: does it count as an OOB error?
B4. Ten features, one of which (texture) separates the classes much better than all others. (a) With m = 10 (plain bagging), which feature does nearly every tree use at its root? What does that mean for \rho? (b) With m = 3, in what fraction of the trees can the root split use texture?
B5. A forest separates nuclei from background using intensity (0–255). The training nuclei have intensities 140–200, the background 20–80. A new image has a bright artefact at intensity 250. What probability will the forest give it, and why is that misleading?
B6. A forest with 300 trees has OOB error 8.0 %; with 500 trees, 7.9 %. A colleague suggests 5000 trees. Will it help? What would help more if the error is still too high?






Solutions





B1. (a) (1 - 1/5)^5 = 0.8^5 = 0.328. (b) Independent samples: 0.328^3 = 0.8^{15} = 0.035. In at least one: 1 - 0.035 = 0.965. (c) About 100 \cdot 0.368 \approx 37 trees.
B2. (a) B = 1: 1. B = 10: 0.3 + 0.7/10 = 0.370. B = 100: 0.3 + 0.007 = 0.307. B \to \infty: 0.300. (b) \rho + (1 - \rho)/10 < 0.307 \iff 0.9\rho < 0.207 \iff \rho < 0.23. (c) Lower m (fewer features tried per split), or more randomness (random thresholds, smaller bootstrap samples). The cost: each tree is a little worse on its own (\sigma^2 and the bias may rise), so too much randomness also hurts.
B3. (a) 3 of 5 votes for N: P(\text{N}) = 0.6, label N. (b) Trees 2, 3, 5 vote N, B, B: OOB P(\text{N}) = 1/3, OOB label B. The true class is B, so it is not an OOB error, although the full forest (which includes trees that saw the pixel) gets it wrong.
B4. (a) Texture: whenever it is among the candidates it wins, and with m = 10 it always is. All trees start with the same question and look alike: high \rho. (b) The root’s 3 candidates are a random subset of the 10 features; texture is among them with probability 3/10 = 30\,\%. In the other 70 % of the trees the root uses another feature (texture comes in lower down), so the trees differ more.
B5. Every tree’s last split on intensity sends 250 to the “bright” side (above the largest threshold, somewhere between 80 and 140), where all leaves say nucleus. All trees agree: probability close to 1. But the forest has never seen anything at 250: the agreement comes from all trees extending the same last rectangle, not from evidence. Vote fractions are not calibrated far from the training data.
B6. No: the OOB curve has flattened, so more trees only cost time (the variance part that averaging removes is already gone). What remains is the correlation floor and the bias: better features, more (and more varied) training data, or a different m / leaf size help more.




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive \operatorname{Var}\big(\tfrac1B\sum_b f_b\big) = \rho\sigma^2 + \tfrac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2 from \operatorname{Var}(\sum_b f_b) = \sum_b\operatorname{Var}f_b + \sum_{b\ne c}\operatorname{Cov}(f_b, f_c).
B8. (math) Show that (1 - 1/n)^n \to 1/e as n \to \infty, and that the expected number of distinct points in a bootstrap sample is n\,(1 - (1 - 1/n)^n). Evaluate it for n = 5.
B9. (math) Show that a negative pairwise correlation is possible for two predictors, but that for B predictors with the same pairwise correlation \rho one must have \rho \ge -1/(B - 1). What does that say about using negative correlation to beat the floor?






Solutions (math)





B7. There are B variance terms \sigma^2 and B(B-1) ordered pairs b \ne c with covariance \rho\sigma^2: \operatorname{Var}(\sum f_b) = B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2. The average divides by B, the variance by B^2: \frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{B-1}{B}\rho\sigma^2 = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2.
B8. \ln(1 - 1/n)^n = n\ln(1 - 1/n) = n(-1/n - 1/(2n^2) - \dots) \to -1, so the limit is e^{-1}. Let Z_i = 1 if point i is drawn at least once: E[Z_i] = 1 - (1 - 1/n)^n; by linearity the expected number of distinct points is \sum_i E[Z_i] = n(1 - (1-1/n)^n). For n = 5: 5(1 - 0.328) = 3.36.
B9. Two predictors f and -f have correlation -1. For B predictors, \operatorname{Var}(\sum f_b) = B\sigma^2(1 + (B-1)\rho) \ge 0 requires \rho \ge -1/(B-1). For many predictors the bound tends to 0: a large set of predictors cannot all be negatively correlated with each other, so in practice the floor \rho\sigma^2 with \rho \ge 0 is what we work against.

title: Exercise: bagging and random forests
text:
Explore: bootstrap and averaging
Left: n numbered training points. draw a bootstrap sample shows how often each was drawn (grey with “–”: never, out of bag); draw 1000 collects the out-of-bag fraction of 1000 samples in a histogram. Right: the variance of an average of B predictors with variance \sigma^2 and correlation \rho, simulated (dots, 2000 runs, fixed seed) and by the formula (line), with the floor \rho\sigma^2 (dashed). Both axes are logarithmic.



E1. With n = 20 the first sample is already drawn. How many points are out of bag, how many were drawn more than once, and what is the largest count? Press draw 1000: what is the mean OOB fraction, and how does it compare with (1 - 1/n)^n?
E2. Set n = 5 and press draw 1000. Mean OOB fraction, and the shape of the histogram compared with n = 20? Then n = 100.
E3. With \sigma^2 = 1 and \rho = 0.3, read the formula values for B = 10 and 100 and the simulated ones. Then choose \rho = 0 and \rho = 0.5. For which \rho is it worth growing 100 rather than 10 trees?






Solutions





E1. Sample 1: 6 of 20 out of bag (30 %), 4 points drawn more than once, the largest count is 3 (two points). Over 1000 samples the mean OOB fraction is 35.6 %, close to (1 - 1/20)^{20} = 0.358.
E2. n = 5: mean 32.5 % (formula 0.328), but the histogram is wide and lumpy: only 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 of 5 points can be out of bag (standard deviation 13.9 percentage points). n = 20: 6.9 points; n = 100: mean 36.6 % (formula 0.366), narrow (3.2 points).
E3. \rho = 0.3: formula 0.370 (B = 10) and 0.307 (B = 100); simulated 0.375 and 0.312. \rho = 0: 0.100 and 0.010 (simulated 0.098, 0.010): ten times better. \rho = 0.5: 0.550 and 0.505. Going from 10 to 100 trees pays off when the correlation is low; with high correlation the floor is reached early.

title: Exercise: bagging and random forests
section: Explore: a forest in the plane
text:
Explore: a forest in the plane
Left: the training points (click to add, drag, remove points) with the forest’s class probabilities behind them: the colour is the mix of the class colours, the strength the confidence. Middle: the first six trees, each grown on its own bootstrap sample, and the out-of-bag error (solid) and the error on 1000 hidden test points (dashed) against the number of trees. Sliders: number of trees B, features per split m, maximum depth, minimum leaf size; bootstrap samples on/off. add x + y and x − y gives the trees two extra (derived) features; noise features adds features that are pure random numbers. The readout gives the number of features d, the errors, and \hat\rho: the average correlation between the trees’ maps.



E4. Preset one deep tree overfits (one tree, no bootstrap). Training and test error? Then preset 100 bagged trees: training, OOB and test error. Read the error curve at 1, 10, 50 and 100 trees.
E5. On 100 bagged trees, compare the six small maps with the forest’s map. Where do the single trees disagree? Then set trees B to 200: does anything improve?
E6. Preset m = d: trees look alike (two moons, d = 4, m = 4). Note \hat\rho and the test error. Preset m = 1: diverse trees: the same numbers. Did lowering \rho help here? Set trees B to 1 in both presets and compare the single trees’ test errors. Explain.
E7. Preset noise features (two blobs plus 4 noise features, d = 6). Test error of the forest? Untick bootstrap samples and set B = 1: test error of one tree? Set noise features to 0 and compare both again.
E8. Preset confident far from the data (three blobs). How confident is the forest in the four corners of the square, where there are no training points? Add a point of a new colour in an empty corner and watch.
E9. Preset uncertainty on the boundary (two moons, minimum leaf size 5). Where is the map pale? How do OOB and test error compare? Set minimum leaf size to 1: what happens to the training error and to the map?






Solutions





E4. One deep tree: training error 0 %, test error 28.8 %. 100 bagged trees: training 0 %, OOB 26.0 %, test 23.4 %. Error curve, OOB / test: 1 tree 35.0 / 35.4 % (one tree on a bootstrap sample sees only 63 % of the points), 10 trees 29.9 / 24.9 %, 50 trees 26.0 / 24.6 %, 100 trees 26.0 / 23.4 %. Most of the gain comes in the first tens of trees.
E5. The single trees have hard, blocky boundaries that differ wherever the two clouds overlap: each follows the noise of its own bootstrap sample. Where they disagree the forest’s map is pale; where they agree it is strong. With 200 trees the test error stays at 23.5 % and the OOB error at 26.0 %: the curve has flattened, so more trees change nothing but the time.
E6. m = 4: \hat\rho = 0.68, test error 8.7 % (OOB 10.6 %). m = 1: \hat\rho = 0.62, test error 9.2 % (OOB 11.3 %). The trees are a little less alike, but the forest is not better: the difference of half a percentage point is within what another seed would give. A single tree: 11.9 % with m = 4 and 12.0 % with m = 1, about equally good. With only 4 features, all of them informative, there is no dominant feature that m = d would put at every root, so a small m has little to decorrelate. The gain from a small m is largest with many features, a few of them dominant (B4).
E7. Forest with noise features: test error 1.9 % (OOB 2.0 %). One tree without bootstrap: 3.0 %. Without noise features: forest 3.2 %, one tree 3.3 %. The noise features do not hurt the forest (here they even help slightly: they make the trees more different), because splits on noise are averaged away. The noise features do make the single tree’s map speckled, since the map’s grid points get their own random noise values.
E8. The corners get probabilities of 1.00 (e.g. class 1 at the bottom-left corner, class 3 at the top-left): every tree extends its outermost rectangles to infinity, so far from the data all trees agree. A new point in an empty corner changes the map only around that corner: the forest had no reason to be confident there before.
E9. The map is pale along the curved boundary between the moons, where they overlap, and strong inside each moon. Training error 4.4 %, OOB 11.3 %, test 8.5 %: OOB is close to the honest test error, slightly pessimistic (each OOB vote uses only about a third of the trees). With minimum leaf size 1: training error 0 %, OOB 11.3 %, test 9.0 %; the map gets more small islands around single points and is confident in more places.

title: Exercise: bagging and random forests
text:
Where this leads
The next unit uses forests on tables of object measurements and asks which features matter (feature importance). The last unit of the day classifies every pixel from a few painted strokes, where the OOB error will turn out to be misleading.

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
About this lecture
Segment the cells, measure each one, classify the rows of the table: mitotic or not, cell or debris. A forest is the usual first choice for such tables. Then the question every biologist asks: which measurements matter?

Why forests suit tables of object measurements.
Impurity importance: how much each feature’s splits purified the nodes.
Permutation importance: how much worse the forest gets when a feature is shuffled.
The trap: correlated features (area, perimeter, diameter).
Importance describes the model, not the biology.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
From objects to a table

Segment the image (thresholding, watershed, …) and label the objects.
Measure each object: area, perimeter, mean intensity, texture, shape (the measurements day).
One row per object, one column per feature; a few rows get a class from an expert.
Train a forest on the labelled rows; it classifies all the others.

The table, not the image, is now the data. Everything from the last two units applies: trees, bagging, OOB error.

Measurements (day 11) owns the feature catalogue; here we only use the table. Example in the demo: 400 cells, two phenotypes (interphase / mitotic), eight features.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Why forests for tables?

Mixed units, no scaling: area in µm², intensity in counts, solidity between 0 and 1; a tree only compares each feature with its own thresholds.
Irrelevant features are mostly ignored: a split on noise rarely wins.
Little tuning: number of trees and m are forgiving.
OOB error for free, fast prediction.
Some interpretability: which features did the forest use?
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Which features matter? Two answers
Impurity importance (mean decrease in impurity):

Every split purifies its node by some amount (the impurity decrease of the decision-trees unit), weighted by the share of the points that reach the node.
Add these up per feature, over all splits and all trees.
Free (comes out of training), but measured on the training data.

Permutation importance:

Shuffle one column among the out-of-bag (or held-out) objects, so that it no longer belongs to its object.
Predict again: how much does the error rise?
Honest about prediction, but costs extra predictions.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
The math: the two importances
Impurity importance of feature j, for a forest of B trees and n training points: \mathrm{MDI}_j = \frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B\;\sum_{\substack{\text{nodes } t \text{ of tree } b\\ \text{split on } j}} \frac{n_t}{n}\,\Delta I_t , often reported as shares of \sum_j \mathrm{MDI}_j. In each tree the sum over all features telescopes to the root impurity minus the weighted leaf impurities.
Permutation importance, with \pi a random permutation of the (OOB) objects: \mathrm{PI}_j = \operatorname{err}\big(\text{data with column } j \text{ replaced by } x_{\pi(i),j}\big) - \operatorname{err}(\text{data}), averaged over several permutations. It can be slightly negative by chance.

section: Try it: importance on a cell table
text:
Try it: importance on a cell table




400 synthetic cells, 100 trees, m = 3. Bars: impurity importance (share of the total Gini decrease, blue) and permutation importance (rise of the OOB error in percentage points, orange). Tour: “texture decides”: texture 48 % / +24.0 points; everything else small; the size features get 9–13 % each by impurity but slightly negative permutation importance. “duplicate area”: area alone 42 %, with an exact copy 28 % + 23 %. “size block”: without texture, the three size features share the credit by impurity (19, 22, 16 %) but each has permutation importance near zero (−0.7 to +1.8); “permute the block together” gives +14.9. “noise”: the continuous noise feature gets 4 % by impurity, the yes/no “coin” 1 %; both ≈ 0 by permutation.

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
section: Correlated features: who gets the credit?
text:
Correlated features: who gets the credit?
Area, perimeter and equivalent diameter all measure size (correlations 0.99 in the demo’s cells).

Impurity importance splits the credit: whichever of them a split happens to use gets the decrease. An exact duplicate of a feature roughly halves its importance.
Permutation importance can hide all of them: shuffle area, and perimeter still carries the size information, so the error hardly rises. Each looks unimportant; together they matter.
Shuffling one of them also creates impossible objects (a huge area with a tiny perimeter), on which the forest was never trained.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Remedies and the right question

Group correlated features (look at their correlations first, e.g. the correlation blocks of the measurements day) and permute each group together.
Remove duplicates you do not need, and compare the OOB error with and without a group.
Importance answers “what does this forest use to predict?” It does not say which measurement is biologically causal, nor that a feature with low importance carries no information (another feature may carry the same).
Use it to choose which measurements to keep, not as proof.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Biases of impurity importance

Computed on the training data: deep trees split on anything, even noise, to purify small nodes.
Features with many distinct values (continuous noise) offer many thresholds and win more of these small splits than yes/no features. In the demo, a continuous noise feature gets 4–14 % of the impurity importance, a random yes/no feature 1–3 %.
Permutation importance on OOB data does not have this bias: both noise features stay near 0.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
section: The math: an exact copy halves the credit
text:
The math: an exact copy halves the credit
Let feature j' be an exact copy of j. Wherever a split on j is best, the same split on j' is equally good; with random candidate subsets (or random tie-breaking) each is chosen about equally often. The total decrease credited to the pair stays what j alone would have got, so in expectation \mathrm{MDI}_j \approx \mathrm{MDI}_{j'} \approx \tfrac12\,\mathrm{MDI}_j^{\text{(without copy)}} . Permutation importance of j with the copy present: the trees that split on j' are unaffected by shuffling j, and many trees use both; the error rises much less than without the copy. In the limit where every split can use either, \mathrm{PI}_j \to 0.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Summary

Object classification: segment → measure → table → forest. Mixed units, no scaling, OOB error for free.
Impurity importance: sum of the weighted impurity decreases per feature; free, but on training data and biased towards features with many values.
Permutation importance: rise of the OOB (or held-out) error after shuffling a column; honest, slower.
Correlated features share or hide their importance: group them and permute the group.
Importance describes the model, not the biology.
crumbs: Forests on feature tables, and feature importance

title: Quiz: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Your table has area in µm², intensity in camera counts (0–4095) and solidity (0–1). Do you need to standardise the columns before training a forest?






Hint





What does a split compare?









Answer





No. Each split compares one feature with its own threshold; the units and ranges of the other features play no role. (Distance-based classifiers such as nearest neighbour or the SVM do need it.)




Q2. How is the impurity importance of a feature computed, in one sentence?






Hint





Every split purifies its node a little.









Answer





Add up the impurity decreases of all splits that use the feature, each weighted by the fraction of the training objects reaching that node, and average over the trees.




Q3. Why is permutation importance usually computed on out-of-bag or held-out objects rather than on the training objects?






Hint





What is the training error of a forest of deep trees?









Answer





On the training objects the forest is almost perfect and partly memorised; shuffling a column measures how much the memorisation depends on it, not how much prediction on new objects does. On OOB or held-out objects the error rise is about generalisation.




Q4. Area has permutation importance 0.1 points, perimeter 0.3, equivalent diameter −0.2. Can you drop all three?






Hint





What happens when you shuffle one of three features that carry the same information?









Answer





Not without checking: the three are strongly correlated, so each can be shuffled without loss because the other two still carry the size. Shuffle them together (or drop all three and compare the OOB error). If that hurts, size matters, and one of them (any) should be kept.




Q5. A random noise column gets 8 % of the impurity importance. How can that be?






Hint





Where in the tree do these splits happen?









Answer





Deep trees split small nodes until they are pure. In a small node, a continuous noise feature with many distinct values offers many thresholds and often purifies the node best by chance. These decreases are counted on the training data, so noise collects a share. Its permutation importance on OOB data stays near zero.




Q6. Shuffling the area column creates cells with a large area and a small perimeter. Why is that a problem for permutation importance?






Hint





Did the forest ever see such cells?









Answer





Such objects do not exist in the data; the forest’s predictions for them are extrapolations that were never trained. The error rise then partly measures the behaviour on impossible objects, not the value of the feature. Permuting correlated features as a group avoids this.




Q7. (math) In a tree, a node with 40 objects and Gini 0.48 is split into children of 30 objects (Gini 0.2) and 10 objects (Gini 0). The training set has 200 objects. What does this split add to its feature’s impurity importance?






Hint





\tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta G.









Answer





\Delta G = 0.48 - \tfrac{30}{40}0.2 - 0 = 0.33; weighted by 40/200 = 0.2: 0.066.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature table
one row per segmented object, one column per measurement


Impurity importance (MDI)
per feature: sum of \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t over its splits, averaged over the trees


Permutation importance
rise of the OOB (or held-out) error when the feature’s column is shuffled


Correlated features
carry (almost) the same information: area, perimeter, equivalent diameter


Group permutation
shuffle several columns with the same permutation, so they stay consistent with each other









The math: the impurity importance of one tree adds up





Each split replaces the weighted impurity \tfrac{n_t}{n}I_t of a node by the weighted impurities of its two children; the difference is \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t. Summed over all splits of a tree, the inner nodes cancel: the total importance is the root impurity minus \sum_{\text{leaves}}\tfrac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell. For a tree grown until its leaves are pure, it is just the root impurity, shared among the features that did the splitting.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
By hand
B1. A depth-2 tree on 100 cells, 50 interphase (I) and 50 mitotic (M). Node counts are written (I, M).

Root: split on texture into (45, 10) and (5, 40).
Left child (45, 10): split on area into (40, 2) and (5, 8).
Right child (5, 40): split on texture into (5, 5) and (0, 35).


Compute the Gini impurity of every node.
Compute \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta G for each of the three splits.
Give the impurity importance of texture and area, and their shares of the total.

B2. A forest is tested on 10 held-out cells: 1 is misclassified. Shuffling the texture column among the 10 cells (several times, on average) gives 4 errors; shuffling area gives 2; shuffling the noise feature gives 1. What are the permutation importances (as rises in error rate)?
B3. A table has area and equivalent diameter d = 2\sqrt{A/\pi}, and size matters for the classes. (a) Is equivalent diameter new information? Will a tree that splits on it ever separate cells differently than a split on area? (b) Predict the impurity importance of area when both are in the table, compared with area alone. (c) Predict the permutation importance of area when both are in the table. What happens to it if you remove the diameter column?
B4. You add a column of random numbers (uniform between 0 and 1) to the table and grow deep trees. Will its impurity importance be zero? Its permutation importance? Why the difference?
B5. The forest says texture is by far the most important feature for “mitotic”. A colleague concludes that texture is what causes or defines mitosis. What can and cannot be concluded?






Solutions





B1. (a) Root (50, 50): G = 0.5. (45, 10): 1 - (45/55)^2 - (10/55)^2 = 0.298. (5, 40): 0.198. (40, 2): 0.091. (5, 8): 0.473. (5, 5): 0.5. (0, 35): 0. (b) Root: \Delta G = 0.5 - 0.55 \cdot 0.298 - 0.45 \cdot 0.198 = 0.247; weight 100/100: 0.247. Left: \Delta G = 0.298 - \tfrac{42}{55}0.091 - \tfrac{13}{55}0.473 = 0.116; weight 55/100: 0.064. Right: \Delta G = 0.198 - \tfrac{10}{45}0.5 - 0 = 0.086; weight 45/100: 0.039. (c) Texture: 0.247 + 0.039 = 0.286 (82 %); area: 0.064 (18 %).
B2. Base error 0.1. Texture: 0.4 - 0.1 = 0.3. Area: 0.2 - 0.1 = 0.1. Noise: 0.1 - 0.1 = 0. (With only 10 cells these numbers are very noisy; in practice use many objects and several shuffles.)
B3. (a) No: d is an increasing function of A, so any split on d separates exactly the same cells as some split on A (B5 of the decision-trees exercise). It is the same feature in other units. (b) The trees use area or diameter about equally often for the same splits, so area gets roughly half of what it had alone (and diameter the other half). (c) Small: when area is shuffled, the trees that split on diameter still see the true size, and size is not lost. Remove the diameter column, and the forest has to use area; its permutation importance rises to the full importance of size.
B4. Impurity importance: not zero. Deep trees keep splitting small nodes until they are pure, and among the candidate features the noise column, with its many distinct values, often offers the best split in a small node by chance; the decreases are counted on the training data. Permutation importance on OOB data: about zero (possibly slightly negative), because shuffling the noise column does not change how well the forest predicts new objects.
B5. Only that this forest, on this data, relies on texture to tell the classes apart. Texture may be a consequence of mitosis (condensed chromatin), it may stand in for another, correlated feature, and features with low importance may carry the same information (they were simply not needed). Importance is a property of the model; causation needs experiments.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that the impurity importances of all features in one tree add up to the root impurity minus \sum_{\text{leaves}}\frac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell.
B7. (math) Feature j' is an exact copy of feature j. At each split the candidate features are a random subset of size m, and ties are broken at random. Argue that the expected impurity importances of j and j' are equal, and that their sum is about the importance j would have alone.
B8. (math) Show that permutation importance can be negative, and give a reason why a small negative value should be read as zero.






Solutions (math)





B6. Write W_t = \tfrac{n_t}{n}I_t. A split of node t into L and R contributes \tfrac{n_t}{n}\Delta I_t = W_t - W_L - W_R. Summing over all splits, every inner node other than the root appears once with + (as the parent of its split) and once with - (as a child of its parent’s split); the root appears only with +, the leaves only with -. The sum is W_{\text{root}} - \sum_{\text{leaves}} W_\ell = I_{\text{root}} - \sum_\ell \tfrac{n_\ell}{n}I_\ell.
B7. j and j' are interchangeable: every split on one has an identical split on the other with the same decrease, and the random candidate subsets treat them symmetrically. So any tree has the same probability as the tree with j and j' swapped, and the expected importances are equal. With the copy present, a split that j would have made alone is made by j or by j' (when at least one is a candidate), with the same decrease, so their sum is about \mathrm{MDI}_j alone. (Not exactly: with the copy, size is a candidate more often, which changes the trees a little. In the demo: area alone 42 %, area + copy 28 % + 23 %.)
B8. It is a difference of two error rates measured on a finite set; shuffling a useless column can by chance fix a few predictions as easily as break them, so the difference can be negative. Its size is about the sampling noise of the error rate (for n objects and error e, roughly \sqrt{e(1-e)/n}, 1.7 points for e = 0.13, n = 400): values within that range mean “no detectable importance”.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Explore
400 synthetic segmented cells, 200 interphase and 200 mitotic, with eight measured features: area, perimeter and equivalent diameter (three measures of size), intensity, texture, solidity, a continuous noise feature and a random yes/no feature (coin). Left: a scatter plot of any two features (choose x and y). Middle: for each feature in use, the impurity importance (share of the total Gini decrease, blue) and the permutation importance (rise of the OOB error in percentage points when its column is shuffled, orange; average of 5 shuffles). The forest has 100 trees; m is the number of features tried per split. Tick features on or off; add an exact copy of area appends a duplicate column; permute the size block together adds a bar for shuffling area, perimeter, diameter (and the copy) with one permutation.



E1. Preset texture decides. Read the OOB error and both importances of texture. Plot area against texture: why is texture so useful? Which features have a negative permutation importance, and what does that mean?
E2. Preset duplicate area: credit splits (area, intensity, solidity and the two noise features, plus an exact copy of area). Note both importances of area and of its copy. Untick add an exact copy of area: what are area’s importances now?
E3. Preset size block: permutation hides it (texture removed; area, perimeter, diameter in). Read the three impurity and permutation importances of the size features. Then tick permute the size block together. What does the block bar show? Is size important?
E4. Preset noise: impurity vs permutation. Compare the noise and coin features under both measures. Then remove texture: what happens to the noise feature’s impurity share, and why?
E5. With all eight features, set m to 1 and to 8 and compare the impurity importances of the three size features. Explain the 0 % of equivalent diameter at m = 8.






Solutions





E1. OOB error 12.8 %. Texture: impurity 48 %, permutation +24.0 points. In the scatter plot the classes overlap strongly in area but are almost separated by texture (class means 8.2 and 14.1). Negative permutation importance: area −0.7, perimeter −0.4, diameter −0.4, noise −0.1, coin −0.2. Shuffling these columns did not make the forest worse (by chance even slightly better): no detectable importance, here partly because the size information is held three times.
E2. With the copy: area 28 % and copy 23 % by impurity (51 % together); by permutation +5.9 and +3.3 points. Without the copy: area 42 % and +13.6 points. The impurity credit is split roughly in half; each permutation importance drops even more, because when one copy is shuffled the other still carries the size.
E3. Impurity: area 19 %, perimeter 22 %, diameter 16 %: together 57 %, the largest group. Permutation: −0.7, +1.8, +1.5 points: each looks almost useless. The block bar: +14.9 points. Size is important (with texture removed it is the main information); each single size feature is redundant given the other two. OOB error 24.0 %, almost twice that with texture.
E4. Texture decides: noise 4 % and coin 1 % by impurity, −0.1 and −0.2 by permutation. Without texture (the “size block” settings): noise 10 %, coin 2 % by impurity; +1.1 and +0.5 by permutation. Without a strong feature, the trees need many more splits to purify the nodes; in the small nodes deep in the trees the continuous noise feature, with 400 distinct values, often wins by chance. The yes/no coin offers only one threshold and wins rarely. Permutation stays near zero for both.
E5. m = 1: area 15 %, perimeter 12 %, diameter 15 % (the feature is a coin toss at every split, so the three share almost equally). m = 8: area 12 %, perimeter 6 %, diameter 0 %. With every feature a candidate at every split, area and diameter always offer exactly the same best split; the tie goes to the feature listed first (area), so diameter is never used. The split of credit between duplicates depends on details like this; it says nothing about the features themselves.

title: Exercise: forests on feature tables, and feature importance
text:
Where this leads
The last unit of the day applies the forest to every pixel of an image, with features computed by filters at several scales, and trains it from a few painted strokes. Feature importance returns there as “which filters does the forest use?”, and the OOB error meets a new trap: neighbouring pixels are not independent.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
About this lecture
Paint a few strokes on an image, “this is nucleus, this is background”, and let a forest label every pixel: semantic segmentation without deep learning.

Every pixel becomes a point in feature space; the painted pixels are the training set.
The feature stack: filters at several scales describe each pixel’s neighbourhood.
The interactive loop: paint, train, look at the result and the uncertainty, correct.
The traps: neighbouring pixels are not independent, label imbalance, painting only the easy cases.
From probabilities to objects.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit owns the pixel feature stack and the paint – train – correct loop for the course. The SVM, integral-images and neural-network days recall it. The demo works on a synthetic test image with ground truth (so we can measure honestly) and on the course micrograph.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Every pixel is a point

Thresholding asked one question of one number: is the pixel bright?
Instead, describe each pixel by many numbers: its brightness at several blurs, how strong the edges near it are, whether it sits in a blob, a line or a texture.
The painted pixels, with their classes, are training points in this feature space.
The forest colours the whole feature space, and with it every pixel of the image.

Why not intensity alone? Two kinds of cell in the test image have the same mean brightness: smooth nuclei and granular cells. Only their texture differs: exactly the situation of the eight pixels in the decision-trees unit.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
The feature stack

Each filter family at each scale \sigma gives one image, a channel; a pixel’s feature vector is its value in every channel. Above (test image, left to right, top row then bottom): smoothed at \sigma = 1 and 5, gradient magnitude (\sigma = 1.6), Laplacian of Gaussian (\sigma = 5), Hessian eigenvalue and structure-tensor eigenvalue (\sigma = 1.6).

Scales used in the demo: σ = 0.7, 1, 1.6 (small) and 3.5, 5, 10 (large). Five families: intensity (1 channel per σ), edges (1), blobs (1), ridges (2), texture (2): 7 channels per σ, 42 in all. The granular cells light up in the gradient and structure-tensor channels at small σ; the LoG at σ = 5 is a “blob of this size” detector.

The families (recall)

The filters come from the filtering unit (Gaussian, derivatives, Laplacian) and the edges, blobs and ridges day (LoG, Hessian, structure tensor). The forest takes the whole pile as it is: no scaling, and redundant channels do no harm. Box means and local variances are the cheap cousins (integral-images day).

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The math: the stack as formulas

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The loop: paint, train, look, correct
text:
The loop: paint, train, look, correct

Paint a few strokes per class.
Train the forest on the painted pixels (seconds, or less).
Look at the segmentation and at the uncertainty map (1 − the largest vote fraction).
Correct: paint where the result is wrong or uncertain, and train again.

Few strokes go a long way, because each stroke holds hundreds of pixels and the features describe their neighbourhoods. Interactive pixel-classification programs implement exactly this loop.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Try it: paint and classify




Synthetic test image: background (uneven illumination, brighter to the right), smooth nuclei (some dim), granular cells as bright as the nuclei. Tour: “two strokes” (nucleus + background): 87.4 % of the pixels right; the granular cells are called nucleus (8.5 % of the image). “intensity only” (three classes painted): 91.3 %, granular cells partly nucleus. “full stack”: 96.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.85, granular 0.86. “uncertainty”: without a granular stroke the granular cells are classified confidently as nucleus — the uncertainty map shows the object rims and the brighter background on the right, not the granular cells. Then “micrograph: nucleus” and “+ cytoplasm”.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Trap 1: neighbouring pixels are near copies
text:
Trap 1: neighbouring pixels are near copies

The pixels of one stroke are almost identical in every channel (the filters even mix them).
OOB error assumes independent samples. A pixel left out of a tree’s bootstrap sample has its neighbour inside it: the “unseen” pixel is not new. OOB accuracy is close to 100 % almost regardless of the result.
Honest evaluation: a held-out region (or another image) with its own labels: the confusion matrix and Dice of the thresholding day.
Even then: your strokes sit where labelling was easy. Accuracy on painted pixels overrates the result; a full annotation of a region is the honest test.

Rule: split by image or region, never by pixel. The evaluation day treats leakage and object-level evaluation in full.

“OOB vs held-out region”: training strokes only left of the yellow line. OOB accuracy 100.0 %; the held-out region’s painted pixels 99.8 % right (650 pixels); against the full ground truth in that region 95.9 %.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: The math: why OOB fails here
text:
The math: why OOB fails here
The bootstrap treats the n painted pixels as n independent draws. Pixels along a stroke are strongly correlated: the effective number of independent samples is close to the number of strokes, not the number of pixels. A tree that saw pixel p + 1 has, in effect, seen pixel p, so the OOB vote on p is not a prediction for new data. The OOB error is then an estimate of the error on pixels next to the strokes. Leaving out whole strokes (or regions) restores independence: the SVM day’s by-stroke cross-validation does exactly that.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Trap 2: label imbalance

A big background stroke has thousands of pixels; a nucleus stroke a few dozen.
Ambiguous pixels (dim nuclei, object rims) fall into leaves dominated by background: the probabilities lean towards the big class.
Fix: balance: weight each class by 1/n_c (or sample the same number of pixels per class).
Balancing moves errors from the small classes to the large one: the small classes are found more often, the background a little less. It cannot invent information the strokes lack.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
The math: class weights = resampling
With weight w_k for every sample of class k, the class shares in a node become p_k = \frac{w_k n_k}{\sum_l w_l n_l} , the same as if each sample of class k were copied w_k times. So weighted Gini picks the same splits as Gini on the resampled data. Balancing weights w_k = \dfrac{n}{K\, n_k} give every class the same total weight n/K. Example: 400 background and 20 nucleus pixels: w = 0.525 and 10.5 (ratio 20). A leaf with 8 background and 2 nucleus pixels: P(\text{nucleus}) = 0.2 unweighted, 0.83 weighted.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Trap 3: the forest knows only what it was shown
text:
Trap 3: the forest knows only what it was shown

Paint only the bright nuclei, and the dim ones look like nothing the forest knows: part of them become background.
Leave out a whole class (the granular cells) and its pixels are forced into the classes that exist, often confidently: the uncertainty map flags rims and new illumination, but not “something else that looks like a nucleus”.
Scale: channels much larger than the structures blur across boundaries; with only small scales the result is speckled and loses context.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
From probabilities to objects

Threshold the probability map of the class you want (0.5, or chosen with the ROC or precision–recall curve of the thresholding day).
Clean up with morphology: opening, filling holes, removing small pieces.
Or smooth with a graph cut: use -\log P(\text{class} \mid \text{features}) as the data term (the graph-cuts day).
Then label the connected components and measure them, and the measurement table may go into another forest (previous unit).

title: Pixel classification with a forest
section: Forests, SVMs and networks on the same pixels
text:
Forests, SVMs and networks on the same pixels

A forest on a hand-made stack is the strong baseline that works from a few strokes: no scaling, little tuning, fast.
An SVM on the same stack needs standardised features and a search over its settings (the SVM day plugs into the same demo).
A convolutional network (U-Net, the neural-networks day) learns its own filters instead of the stack, and needs many more labelled pixels.

title: Pixel classification with a forest
text:
Summary

Pixel classification = classification in a feature space whose axes are filter responses at several scales.
The feature stack: intensity, edges, blobs, ridges, texture; the forest needs no scaling.
The loop: paint, train, look at segmentation and uncertainty, correct.
OOB is optimistic for pixels (neighbours are near copies): evaluate on a held-out region with full labels.
Imbalance: weight or resample; the forest knows only what it was shown.
Probabilities → threshold, morphology or graph cut → objects.

title: Quiz: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is a pixel’s feature vector in pixel classification, and where do the training points come from?






Hint





One number per channel of the stack.









Answer





The values of the pixel in every channel of the feature stack (each filter family at each scale): typically a few dozen numbers describing its brightness, edges, blobs, ridges and texture around it. The training points are the painted pixels, with the class of the stroke they belong to.




Q2. Why use several scales σ for each filter family?






Hint





How large are the structures, and how far does a pixel need to “see”?









Answer





Structures come in different sizes: a 2-pixel membrane, a 30-pixel nucleus, a texture of fine grains. Small scales capture fine detail and texture; large scales capture context (is this pixel inside a large bright object?). The forest picks whichever channels help; it does not need to be told the right scale.




Q3. The OOB accuracy on your painted pixels is 99.9 %. Why should you not believe it?






Hint





What is next to an out-of-bag pixel?









Answer





Neighbouring pixels in a stroke are near copies; an OOB pixel’s neighbours were in the bootstrap sample, so the trees have effectively seen it. Moreover, the strokes are where labelling was easy. Evaluate on a held-out region (or image) with full labels.




Q4. The uncertainty map is dark (confident) inside a group of cells you never painted. Does that mean they are classified correctly?






Hint





What can the forest say about a class it has never seen?









Answer





No. The forest can only choose among the classes it was shown; if the unknown cells resemble one of them, all trees agree on it and the map is confident. Uncertainty is high where known classes meet, not where something new appears. Look at the image (or the truth) and add a class or strokes.




Q5. Name the feature family you would rely on to separate a granular region from a smooth region of the same mean brightness.






Hint





Smoothing removes the difference.









Answer





Texture (structure-tensor eigenvalues) or edges (gradient magnitude) at small σ: the granular region has strong local gradients everywhere, the smooth one does not. Smoothed intensity at large σ is the same for both.




Q6. You paint 5000 background pixels and 50 nucleus pixels. What happens to ambiguous pixels, and what are two remedies?






Hint





Who wins the majority in a mixed leaf?









Answer





Mixed leaves are dominated by background, so ambiguous pixels (dim nuclei, rims) are called background. Remedies: weight each class by 1/n_c (balance), or sample the same number of pixels per class; better still, paint more nucleus strokes on the hard cases.




Q7. How can a graph cut improve a pixel classification?






Hint





What does the forest ignore about neighbouring pixels’ labels?









Answer





The forest labels each pixel on its own, so its result can be speckled. A graph cut uses -\log P(\text{class} \mid \text{features}) as the data term and adds a smoothness term that makes neighbours prefer the same label: isolated wrong pixels disappear and boundaries become clean.




Q8. (math) 300 background and 30 nucleus pixels. Give the balancing weights w_k = n/(K n_k) and the weighted P(\text{nucleus}) of a leaf with 6 background and 3 nucleus pixels.






Hint





n = 330, K = 2.









Answer





w_{\text{bg}} = 330/600 = 0.55, w_{\text{nuc}} = 330/60 = 5.5. Leaf: P(\text{nucleus}) = 3 \cdot 5.5/(3 \cdot 5.5 + 6 \cdot 0.55) = 16.5/19.8 = 0.83 (unweighted: 3/9 = 0.33).

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Feature stack
filter responses at several scales σ; one channel per family and scale


Families
intensity (smoothed), edges (gradient magnitude), blobs (LoG), ridges (Hessian eigenvalues), texture (structure-tensor eigenvalues)


Training set
the painted pixels and their classes


Uncertainty
1 - \max_k P(k): high where the trees disagree


Held-out region
a part of the image whose labels are not used for training, only for evaluation


Confusion matrix, Dice
from the thresholding day: counts of (true, predicted) pairs; Dice = 2TP/(2TP + FP + FN)


Class weights
w_k = n/(K n_k) gives every class the same total weight









The math: the channels





With L_\sigma = G_\sigma * I: intensity L_\sigma; edges \|\nabla L_\sigma\|; blobs \sigma^2\nabla^2 L_\sigma; ridges: eigenvalues of \sigma^2 \mathbf H(L_\sigma); texture: eigenvalues of \sigma^2\, G_{\sigma/2} * (\nabla L_\sigma\nabla L_\sigma^\top). In the demo the derivatives are central differences of L_\sigma, at σ = 0.7, 1, 1.6, 3.5, 5 and 10: 42 channels.

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
By hand
B1. A 5 \times 5 patch; the pixel of interest is the centre (value 90):
\begin{pmatrix} 10 & 12 & 14 & 30 & 60 \\ 12 & 15 & 40 & 80 & 90 \\ 14 & 50 & \mathbf{90} & 95 & 92 \\ 40 & 85 & 96 & 98 & 94 \\ 70 & 92 & 97 & 99 & 96 \end{pmatrix}

Compute three features of the centre pixel: the 3 \times 3 box mean b; the gradient magnitude g from central differences, g_x = (I_{x+1} - I_{x-1})/2 and g_y = (I_{y+1} - I_{y-1})/2 (rows go down); and the 4-neighbour Laplacian $= $ (sum of the 4 neighbours) - 4 \cdot centre.
A forest of three stumps: tree 1: b \le 60 → background, else nucleus; tree 2: g \le 30 → nucleus, else background; tree 3: \ell \le -50 → nucleus, else background. What is P(\text{nucleus}), and the label?
Repeat for the pixel at row 2, column 2 (value 15).
Where does the centre pixel sit, and why do the trees disagree on it?

B2. A user paints 400 background pixels and 20 nucleus pixels. (a) A leaf of a tree holds 8 background and 2 nucleus training pixels. What does it vote for a pixel that lands there? (b) Give two ways to fix the imbalance. With balancing weights, what does the same leaf say? (c) Can balancing make the result worse somewhere?
