Give the confusion matrix (TP, FP, FN, TN with N as positive), the accuracy and the Dice coefficient of N and of B.
The forest’s OOB error on the painted pixels was 0.5 %. Why is it so much lower than the error here?

B4. Which feature family, at which scale, should separate: (a) nuclei (bright, about 30 px across) from background; (b) a thin bright membrane (2 px wide) from the cytoplasm on both sides; (c) a granular region from a smooth region with the same mean brightness; (d) a dim nucleus from slightly brighter background that ramps up across the image?
B5. A forest trained on strokes from image 1 reaches 97 % on a fully annotated region of image 1, and 81 % on image 2. Give two reasons, and what you would paint next.






Solutions





B1. (a) Box: the 3 \times 3 block 15, 40, 80, 50, 90, 95, 85, 96, 98 sums to 649: b = 72.1. g_x = (95 - 50)/2 = 22.5, g_y = (96 - 40)/2 = 28, g = \sqrt{22.5^2 + 28^2} = 35.9. \ell = 40 + 96 + 50 + 95 - 360 = -79. (b) Tree 1: 72.1 > 60 → N. Tree 2: 35.9 > 30 → B. Tree 3: -79 \le -50 → N. P(\text{N}) = 2/3, label N. (c) Pixel (row 2, column 2) = 15: box over rows 1–3, columns 1–3: 10 + 12 + 14 + 12 + 15 + 40 + 14 + 50 + 90 = 257, b = 28.6; g_x = (40 - 12)/2 = 14, g_y = (50 - 12)/2 = 19, g = 23.6; \ell = 40 + 12 + 50 + 12 - 60 = 54. Votes: B, N, B: P(\text{N}) = 1/3, label B. (d) The centre sits on the edge of a bright object (dark top-left, bright bottom-right): bright on average and brighter than its neighbours, but with a strong gradient. The edge tree reads “boundary” as background, the others “inside”. Boundary pixels are where the votes split and the uncertainty is high.
B2. (a) Majority background: P(\text{nucleus}) = 2/10 = 0.2. (b) Weight each class by 1/n_c (here w = 0.525 and 10.5, ratio 20), or sample the same number of pixels per class (e.g. all 20 nucleus pixels and 20 random background pixels, which throws data away). With the weights: P(\text{N}) = 2 \cdot 10.5/(2 \cdot 10.5 + 8 \cdot 0.525) = 0.83. (c) Yes: background pixels that resemble the 20 nucleus pixels are now called nucleus more often. Balancing trades errors of the small class for errors of the large one; it does not add information.
B3. (a) TP = 4, FP = 2 (row 1 column 3, row 3 column 2), FN = 1 (row 2 column 2), TN = 9. Accuracy 13/16 = 0.8125. Dice N = 8/(8 + 2 + 1) = 0.727; Dice B = 18/(18 + 3) = 0.857. (b) OOB votes are cast on painted pixels, whose neighbours (near copies) were in the bootstrap samples, and which sit where painting was easy. The held-out region contains boundaries, dim objects and other hard pixels that no stroke came near.
B4. (a) Intensity (smoothed) at a medium scale, or blobs (LoG) at σ ≈ 30/(2√2) ≈ 10. (b) Ridges (Hessian eigenvalue) at a small scale, σ ≈ 1: a bright line has a strongly negative eigenvalue across it. (c) Texture (structure tensor) or edges (gradient magnitude) at a small scale: smoothing removes the texture, so intensity at large σ cannot tell them apart. (d) Large-scale intensity to capture the ramp, together with small-scale intensity, so that the tree can compare the pixel with its surroundings; or paint background on both ends of the ramp.
B5. Image 2 may differ in staining, illumination or noise (the features shift), and it may contain structures never painted in image 1. Strokes from image 1 also share its specific neighbourhoods. Paint a few strokes on image 2 where it is wrong or uncertain, retrain on both images, and evaluate on a third, or on an annotated region not used for training.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that weighting every sample of class k by w_k in the Gini impurity gives exactly the impurity of the data in which each sample of class k is replicated w_k times (for integer w_k), so both choose the same splits. Which weights balance 400 background and 20 nucleus pixels?
B7. (math) A stroke of 200 pixels is so smooth that consecutive pixels have correlation \rho = 0.95 in every feature. Treating the correlation as that of an AR(1) sequence, the effective number of independent samples is about n\frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}. Compute it, and explain what it means for the OOB error.






Solutions (math)





B6. In a node with n_k samples of class k, the weighted shares are p_k = w_k n_k/\sum_l w_l n_l. Replicating each sample of class k w_k times gives w_k n_k samples of class k and the same shares. Gini depends only on the shares, and the weighted sizes \sum_l w_l n_l of the children are the sizes of the replicated children, so every split has the same impurity decrease in both settings: the same splits win. Balancing: w_k = n/(K n_k): 420/(2 \cdot 400) = 0.525 and 420/(2 \cdot 20) = 10.5 (any pair with ratio 20 works).
B7. 200 \cdot 0.05/1.95 \approx 5.1: the stroke is worth about 5 independent pixels, not 200. The bootstrap and the OOB estimate count 200; nearly every OOB pixel has near copies in the bag, so OOB measures the error on near copies of training pixels, and is far too optimistic.

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Explore
Left: the image with the painted labels. Choose a label and paint with the mouse (brush sets the size; erase, undo, clear). The forest retrains when you lift the mouse (untick train after each stroke to train only with train). Middle: the result: segmentation (colour = most probable class), probability of a chosen class, uncertainty (1 - \max P), one feature channel (step through all of them), or the ground truth (test image only). Right: presets, the classifier (random forest or single tree) and its settings, the feature families and scales used, balance classes, and hold out the right part (the strokes right of the yellow line are not used for training; the region is evaluated). The readout lists the painted (and used) pixels per class, the OOB accuracy on the painted pixels, and on the test image the accuracy, Dice per class and the confusion matrix against the ground truth (rows: truth; columns: prediction; in % of the pixels of the whole image or the held-out region).
The test image: background (illumination rising to the right), smooth nuclei (some dim) and granular cells that are as bright as the nuclei but textured. The micrograph has no ground truth.



E1. Preset two strokes (one nucleus stroke, one background stroke). How many pixels are painted? Accuracy and Dice of the nucleus class? What happens to the granular cells, and why can the forest not do otherwise? Paint one stroke of granular cell across a granular cell and watch the result.
E2. Preset intensity only (strokes for all three classes, only the intensity channels): accuracy, Dice of nucleus and granular cell, and the share of granular-cell pixels called nucleus. Then preset full stack (all 42 channels): the same numbers. Use the features view to find a channel in which the granular cells differ clearly from the nuclei.
E3. Preset small scales only (σ ≤ 1.6). Accuracy and Dice compared with the full stack? Look at the segmentation: where are the extra errors?
E4. Preset only bright nuclei painted. Compare the nucleus row of the confusion matrix (how much of the image is nucleus called background?) with the full stack preset. Look at the dim nuclei in the segmentation. Then paint a short nucleus stroke on one dim nucleus.
E5. Preset huge background strokes. How many pixels per class are painted, and how many are used (the training set is capped at 4000)? Read the nucleus row of the confusion matrix and the Dice of the nucleus. Tick balance classes: what changes in the nucleus row, in the background row and in the accuracy?
E6. Preset OOB vs held-out region (strokes on both sides; those right of the yellow line are held out). Compare the OOB accuracy, the accuracy on the painted pixels in the held-out region, and the accuracy against the ground truth in that region. Which number would you report? Untick hold out the right part: what does the accuracy in the right part (now trained on) become?
E7. Preset uncertainty: where to paint (no granular stroke). Where is the uncertainty high? Is it high on the granular cells? Paint where the map tells you to, and then where the truth view tells you to.
E8. Switch the classifier to single tree on the full stack preset. Accuracy and Dice compared with the forest? Look at the segmentation of the granular cells.
E9. Preset micrograph: nucleus (nucleus and background strokes). Describe the result: where is it wrong? Then preset micrograph: + cytoplasm. Which parts of the cell become cytoplasm? Where would you paint next?






Solutions





E1. 220 background and 116 nucleus pixels. Accuracy 87.4 %, Dice nucleus 0.57. The granular cells are classified as nucleus (8.5 % of all pixels: the granular row of the confusion matrix is 0.4 / 8.5 / 0.0): the forest only knows two classes and granular cells are bright like nuclei. A classifier can only output classes it was shown. A granular stroke adds the class; with the base strokes (E2) its Dice reaches 0.86.
E2. Intensity only (6 channels): accuracy 91.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.65, granular 0.68; 3.8 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus (granular row 0.0 / 3.8 / 5.1). Full stack (42 channels): 96.3 %, Dice nucleus 0.85, granular 0.86; granular row 0.1 / 0.0 / 8.7. Channels that separate them: the gradient or the structure-tensor eigenvalue μ1 at small σ (σ = 0.7–1.6): bright speckle inside the granular cells, nearly flat inside the nuclei.
E3. Small scales only (21 channels): 94.8 % (full stack 96.3 %), Dice nucleus 0.78 (0.85), granular 0.83 (0.86). The extra errors: an orange speckle of “nucleus” in the brighter background on the right (0.9 % of the image, against 0.2 %), and more nucleus pixels called granular (2.2 % against 1.6 %). Without the large scales a pixel only knows its immediate surroundings: a bright background pixel on the right looks like a dim nucleus pixel, and the forest cannot see that it lies far from any object.
E4. Only bright nuclei: nucleus row 1.2 / 6.4 / 2.0, i.e. 1.2 % of the image is nucleus called background (full stack: 0.7 %); Dice nucleus 0.80 (0.85). Parts of the dim nuclei (16 % of their interior, against 2 % with a dim stroke) become background: they are darker than anything painted as nucleus. One stroke on a dim nucleus brings them back.
E5. Painted: 4772 background, 37 nucleus, 45 granular; used (capped, same fraction per class): 3959, 30, 42. Without balancing: nucleus row 4.1 / 3.5 / 2.0 (more nucleus pixels called background than found), Dice nucleus 0.53, accuracy 92.6 %. Balanced: nucleus row 3.3 / 3.9 / 2.4, Dice 0.58; but the background row changes from 81.6 / 0.0 / 0.0 to 79.1 / 0.0 / 2.5, and the accuracy drops to 91.8 %. Balancing helps the small classes and costs the large one; the real cure is better strokes for the small classes.
E6. OOB accuracy 100.0 %; painted pixels in the held-out region 99.8 % right (650 pixels); full ground truth in the region 95.9 %. Report the last one: OOB is fooled by neighbouring pixels, and the painted pixels in the region are easy ones (stroke centres). Trained on all strokes: the accuracy in the right part rises to 96.9 %, but that number is no longer an independent test.
E7. High uncertainty on the rims of all objects and on the background in the right part of the image, which is brighter than any painted background (the background strokes are on the left). Not on the granular cells: they are classified confidently as nucleus (8.4 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus). The uncertainty map shows where the classes it knows meet, not what it has never seen. Paint background on the right; for the granular cells you need the truth (or your eyes) to add a class.
E8. Single tree: accuracy 94.6 %, Dice nucleus 0.78, granular 0.74 (forest: 96.3 %, 0.85, 0.86). Every granular cell gets a thick nucleus-coloured rim: 3.5 % of the image is granular cell called nucleus. One tree uses only a few channels (mean depth 3) and draws one hard boundary in them; the forest averages many trees that use different channels and gets the rims right.
E9. With nucleus and background only: the nucleus is found, but so is much of the cytoplasm and other dark material (it is neither the light background nor anything else the forest knows). With the cytoplasm strokes, the cytoplasm around the nucleus and the cell processes become cytoplasm; the nucleus is mostly nucleus, with its lower part and its envelope partly called cytoplasm. Paint nucleus in the lower part of the nucleus and cytoplasm or background where the result is uncertain (the uncertainty view).

title: Exercise: pixel classification with a forest
text:
Where this leads
The forest on a hand-made stack is the strong baseline from a few strokes. The SVM elective plugs a support-vector machine into the same demo, where feature standardisation and by-stroke cross-validation become essential. The neural-networks day replaces the hand-made stack by filters that a network learns itself (U-Net), at the price of many more labels. The evaluation day measures segmentations object by object and makes the “split by image” rule precise.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
About this lecture
The Fourier transform rewrites a signal as a sum of waves. Every wave runs over the whole signal, so the spectrum says which frequencies are present but not where. Today: a basis whose functions are short.

A spike and a step in the Fourier basis: every coefficient is busy.
The short-time Fourier transform, and why one window size cannot serve all frequencies.
The wavelet idea: short windows for high frequencies, long windows for low ones.
The Haar transform by hand: averages and differences, level by level, and back.
The Haar basis is orthonormal, and piecewise-constant signals are sparse in it.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the wavelets elective (group “Transforms”; the compression day follows and builds on it). Prerequisites: the Fourier unit (change of basis, orthogonality, Parseval) and the kernels unit (convolution). Everything today is on 1D signals of 8 to 256 samples; images come in unit 3.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Recall: the Fourier basis is global
text:
Recall: the Fourier basis is global
From Images in frequency space (day 1): the DFT is a change of basis to waves e^{2\pi i k n/N}, each of which extends over the whole signal. It is orthogonal, so nothing is lost and energies add up (Parseval).
That is perfect for signals that are periodic or smooth everywhere. Images are not: they are flat in most places, with edges and spots at a few positions.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: A spike and a step in the Fourier basis
text:
A spike and a step in the Fourier basis


A spike: every Fourier magnitude is exactly 1. Where the spike is lives only in the phases, spread over all coefficients.
A step: the magnitudes fall off slowly, like 1/k. Keep the 6 largest of 64 and the result rings everywhere (Gibbs).
6 coefficients in the Haar basis of this lecture (dashed blue) do much better: 12.5 % and 5.5 % error instead of 90 % and 19 %.


N = 64, spike at position 23, step from position 23 (positions from 0). Left: the signal; middle: |X_k| for k = 0..32 (the rest mirror these); for the step the dashed curve is 64/(πk), the envelope for small k. Right: keeping the 6 largest coefficients in a real orthonormal Fourier basis (cosines and sines) and in the Haar basis (6 levels). Relative errors: spike 90 % (Fourier) vs 12.5 % (Haar), step 19 % vs 5.5 %. In the Haar basis both signals have only 7 nonzero coefficients (log2 64 + 1), so 6 of them miss one small one. Ask: why can a single wave never say “here”?

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: spectra of a spike and a step
text:
The math: spectra of a spike and a step
DFT X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n e^{-2\pi i k n/N}.

Spike at n_0, x_n = [n = n_0]: \;X_k = e^{-2\pi i k n_0/N}, so |X_k| = 1 for every k. The position n_0 is only in the phase -2\pi k n_0/N.
Box of m ones starting at n_0 (a step up and a step down): a geometric sum, |X_k| = \left|\sum_{n=n_0}^{n_0+m-1} e^{-2\pi i k n/N}\right| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi k m/N)}{\sin(\pi k/N)}\right| \approx \frac{N}{\pi k}\,|\sin(\pi k m/N)| \quad (k \ll N).
So the coefficients of a jump decay only like 1/k: the energy beyond frequency K is \sum_{k > K} 1/k^2 \approx 1/K, which falls slowly. Cutting them off leaves an overshoot near the jump of about 9 % of the jump height that does not shrink as K grows (Gibbs phenomenon).

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Fix 1: the short-time Fourier transform
Cut out a piece of the signal with a smooth window (the tapers of the Fourier unit), take its DFT, slide the window along.

Now each coefficient belongs to a position (the window) and a frequency: a tile in the position–frequency plane.
A narrow window locates the step well, but a few samples contain too few cycles of a slow wave to tell its frequency.
A wide window resolves low frequencies, but smears the step over the whole window.
One window size serves either the edges or the slow variations, not both.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The math: the uncertainty relation
For a window w(t) with \int |w|^2 dt = 1, define its spread in time and in (angular) frequency: \Delta t^2 = \int (t - \bar t)^2 |w(t)|^2 dt, \qquad \Delta\omega^2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int (\omega - \bar\omega)^2 |\hat w(\omega)|^2 d\omega.

Heisenberg–Gabor: \Delta t\,\Delta\omega \ge \tfrac12, with equality only for a Gaussian window (Gabor 1946).
Squeezing the window in time by a factor s, w(t) \to \sqrt{s}\,w(st), multiplies \Delta t by 1/s and \Delta\omega by s: the area of a tile is fixed, only its shape can change.
The STFT uses the same tile shape everywhere. Wavelets change the shape with the frequency: \Delta t \propto 1/\omega, so each tile holds about the same number of cycles.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Fix 2: the wavelet idea
Short windows for high frequencies, long windows for low frequencies.

High frequencies (edges, spots, noise) change quickly: we want to know exactly where they are.
Low frequencies (slow shading) are spread out anyway: a long window gives their frequency precisely, and their position does not matter much.
So: tall, thin tiles at high frequency; short, wide tiles at low frequency (right panel of the tiling figure).

The simplest way to build such tiles is to keep halving the signal: pairs, then pairs of pairs, … This is the Haar transform (Haar, 1910).

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The Haar transform by hand
Replace each pair (a, b) by its average and half-difference: s = \frac{a + b}{2}, \qquad d = \frac{a - b}{2}. Keep the ds; repeat on the ss. For x = (4, 6, 10, 12, 8, 6, 5, 5):



level
averages s
differences d (kept)




1
5,\ 11,\ 7,\ 5
-1,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0


2
8,\ 6
-3,\ 1


3

1



Result (coarse to fine): (7 \mid 1 \mid -3,\ 1 \mid -1,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0). Eight numbers in, eight out: 1 overall average + 1 + 2 + 4 details, each detail tied to a place and a scale.

Do this on the board first, then with the demo. Point out that the level-1 details are small where the signal is locally flat (the last pair 5, 5 gives 0), and read the level-3 detail: the left half averages 8, the right half 6, so the left half lies 1 above the overall average 7 and the right half 1 below.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Try it: the Haar transform step by step
text:
Try it: the Haar transform step by step




Board example, N = 8. Press step three times: the brackets show which pairs are combined next; the grey blocks are the current averages drawn over the signal; the lower panel the coefficients coloured by level. Readout: Σx² = 446 but Σc² = 63 with the 1/2 normalisation. Switch to s = (a+b)/√2: now Σc² = 446. Keep K = 3 (orthonormal): kept 19.80, 2.83 and −6; the reconstruction (orange) is (5, 5, 11, 11, 6, 6, 6, 6), squared error 10 = sum of the dropped squared coefficients. Presets: spike (4 nonzero coefficients), step (a jump inside a pair: 4 nonzero), ramp (details everywhere: Haar only knows constants), constant (one coefficient). “Show basis” draws the transform matrix.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Going back: nothing is lost
Each step can be undone: from s and d, a = s + d, \qquad b = s - d.
Board example backwards: 7 \pm 1 \to (8, 6); 8 \pm (-3) \to (5, 11), 6 \pm 1 \to (7, 5); then 5 \pm (-1) \to (4, 6), … back to x.

The Haar transform is a change of basis, like the DFT: the same signal, described by different numbers.
The coefficient of a basis vector says how much of that pattern the signal contains. Which patterns?

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
The Haar basis vectors




Each coefficient multiplies one pattern; the signal is their sum.

One constant (the overall average),
one +/- square wave over the whole signal,
two over half the signal, four over a quarter.

Short patterns for fine detail, long ones for coarse: the wavelet tiling. They are all the same shape, shifted and squeezed: that shape is the Haar wavelet.
With 1/\sqrt2 in place of 1/2 at each step the patterns all have length 1 and are perpendicular: an orthonormal basis.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: the Haar matrix is orthogonal
text:
The math: the Haar matrix is orthogonal
Normalised step: s = (a + b)/\sqrt2, d = (a - b)/\sqrt2, i.e. each pair is multiplied by \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}, an orthogonal matrix (a rotation by 45° and a reflection).

One level on N samples is block-diagonal in these 2 \times 2 blocks (after reordering): orthogonal. A product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal, so the whole transform c = Hx has H H^\top = I.
N = 4: \;H = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 \\ \tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 \\ \tfrac1{\sqrt2} & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \tfrac1{\sqrt2} & -\tfrac1{\sqrt2}\end{pmatrix}, rows of length 1, mutually perpendicular.
Hence Parseval: \|c\|^2 = x^\top H^\top H x = \|x\|^2, and the inverse is the transpose, x = H^\top c.
With 1/2 the rows are still perpendicular but have lengths 2^{-j/2}: invertible, not orthonormal. Board example: \|x\|^2 = 446, but \sum c^2 = 63 with 1/2 and 446 with 1/\sqrt2.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Why this pays off: sparsity
A coefficient is zero when its pattern sees a flat signal.

A piecewise-constant signal has nonzero details only where a jump falls inside a pattern: at most one per level, near each jump.
A spike touches only the patterns that contain it: one per level plus the average, \log_2 N + 1 coefficients (4 of 8, 9 of 256).
A ramp gives nonzero details everywhere: Haar patterns only see constants as “nothing to report”. Better wavelets in the next unit.

Few large coefficients and many (near-)zero ones = sparse. Keeping only the large ones then loses little.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: Try it: sparsity in two bases
text:
Try it: sparsity in two bases




256 samples; Haar with 5 levels (periodic). One slider K keeps the K largest coefficients in both bases. Tour: “step”: at K = 8 Fourier has 16.5 % error, Haar 2.8 %; 1 % error needs 176 Fourier and 11 Haar coefficients. “spike”: Fourier needs 247 of 256, Haar 6 (5 levels + the approximation). “sine”: one Fourier coefficient; Haar needs 218. “Doppler” (frequency changes along the signal): both need many, Fourier 231 and Haar 196. Switch the lower-left panel to “wavelet coefficients by level”: the large coefficients sit where the signal jumps.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
section: The math: error of keeping K coefficients
text:
The math: error of keeping K coefficients
Orthonormal basis \{\mathbf u_i\}, coefficients c_i = \mathbf u_i^\top x, so x = \sum_i c_i \mathbf u_i. Keep a set S of K indices: \hat x = \sum_{i \in S} c_i \mathbf u_i. Then \|x - \hat x\|^2 = \Big\|\sum_{i \notin S} c_i\mathbf u_i\Big\|^2 = \sum_{i \notin S} c_i^2.

The error is the sum of the dropped squared coefficients (Pythagoras), so the best S keeps the K largest |c_i|.
The error curve against K depends only on the sorted magnitudes |c|_{(1)} \ge |c|_{(2)} \ge \dots: a basis is good for a signal when they fall fast.
This only holds in an orthonormal basis. With the 1/2 normalisation, coefficients at different levels are not comparable: a level-j coefficient counts 2^j times in the error.

title: Localised basis functions and the Haar transform
text:
Summary

The Fourier basis is global: a spike or a step spreads over all coefficients, and truncation rings.
A window trades position against frequency resolution; one window size cannot fit all frequencies. Wavelets use short windows for high frequencies, long for low.
Haar transform: pairwise averages and differences, repeated on the averages; inverse a = s + d, b = s - d.
With 1/\sqrt2 it is an orthonormal change of basis: energy is preserved, and the error of dropping coefficients is the sum of their squares.
Piecewise-constant signals are sparse in the Haar basis; ramps are not: next unit, wavelets with more vanishing moments.

title: Quiz: the Haar transform
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. By hand, a Haar step replaces a pair (a, b) by s = (a+b)/2 and d = (a-b)/2; the orthonormal version uses 1/\sqrt2 instead of 1/2.

Q1. A signal is zero except for one spike. Its Fourier magnitudes are all equal. Where in the Fourier coefficients is the position of the spike?






Hint





Magnitudes and phases.









Answer





In the phases: a spike at n_0 has X_k = e^{-2\pi i k n_0/N}, magnitude 1 for every k, phase -2\pi k n_0/N. The position is spread over all coefficients together; no single coefficient says “here”.




Q2. Why can a short-time Fourier transform with one window size not resolve both a sharp edge and a slow wave well?






Hint





What does a short window contain of a slow wave? What does a long window do to the edge?









Answer





A short window locates the edge, but contains only a fraction of a cycle of the slow wave, so its frequency cannot be determined. A long window contains many cycles, but smears the edge over the window length. Position and frequency resolution trade off against each other (uncertainty relation); wavelets use short windows for high frequencies and long windows for low ones.




Q3. Compute the Haar transform (by hand, 1/2) of (3, 5, 5, 3).






Hint





Two levels: averages and differences of the pairs, then of the two averages.









Answer





Level 1: averages (4, 4), differences (-1, 1). Level 2: average 4, difference 0. Result (4 \mid 0 \mid -1, 1). Check: 4 \pm 0 = (4, 4); 4 \pm (-1) = (3, 5), 4 \pm 1 = (5, 3).




Q4. Invert the by-hand Haar transform (10 \mid 2 \mid 1, -1).






Hint





a = s + d, b = s - d, coarse to fine.









Answer





10 \pm 2 = (12, 8); then 12 \pm 1 = (13, 11) and 8 \pm (-1) = (7, 9): x = (13, 11, 7, 9).




Q5. Which of these signals of 8 samples has the fewest nonzero Haar coefficients: a constant, a spike, a ramp, a step between samples 4 and 5?






Hint





A Haar pattern gives zero when it sees a constant.









Answer





The constant: 1 (only the average). The step exactly in the middle: 2 (the average and the coarsest detail). The spike: 4 (\log_2 8 + 1). The ramp: all 8, because every pattern sees a slope.




Q6. With the orthonormal Haar transform, a signal has coefficients (10, -4, 3, 0, 1, 0, -1, 0). You keep the two largest. What is the squared error, without reconstructing?






Hint





In an orthonormal basis the error is the sum of the dropped squares.









Answer





Keep 10 and -4; drop 3, 1, -1 (and the zeros): 9 + 1 + 1 = 11.




Q7. Why does the by-hand normalisation s = (a+b)/2 not preserve \sum x^2, while (a+b)/\sqrt2 does?






Hint





Compare s^2 + d^2 with a^2 + b^2 for one pair.









Answer





With 1/2: s^2 + d^2 = \tfrac14\big((a+b)^2 + (a-b)^2\big) = \tfrac12(a^2 + b^2), half the energy per step. With 1/\sqrt2: \tfrac12\big((a+b)^2 + (a-b)^2\big) = a^2 + b^2. The normalised step is an orthogonal 2\times2 matrix, a rotation plus a reflection.




Q8. (math) Show that the Haar basis vectors (1, 1, -1, -1)/2 and (1, -1, 0, 0)/\sqrt2 are orthogonal, and explain in words why any two Haar patterns at different levels are orthogonal.






Hint





Where the short pattern is nonzero, what does the long one look like?









Answer





Dot product: \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}(1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot (-1) + 0 + 0) = 0. In general, a finer pattern lies entirely inside one half of a coarser pattern, where the coarser one is constant. The dot product is then that constant times the sum of the finer pattern, which is zero (+ and - halves cancel). Two patterns at the same level do not overlap.

title: Exercise: the Haar transform
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why a spike or a step is spread over all Fourier coefficients, and what a window trades off,
compute a full Haar transform of 8 samples by hand, and invert it,
check that the normalised Haar matrix is orthogonal, and use it to compute the error of keeping only some coefficients,
predict which signals are sparse in the Haar basis.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: the Haar transform
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Haar step (by hand)
pair (a, b) → average s = (a+b)/2 and half-difference d = (a-b)/2


Inverse step
a = s + d, b = s - d


Full transform of N = 2^J samples
repeat on the averages J times; result (s \mid d_J \mid \dots \mid d_1), coarse to fine


Orthonormal version
s = (a+b)/\sqrt2, d = (a-b)/\sqrt2: energy \sum x^2 = \sum c^2 (Parseval)


Keeping K coefficients
in an orthonormal basis: squared error = sum of the dropped squared coefficients


Sparse
few large coefficients, the rest zero or nearly zero

title: Exercise: the Haar transform
text:
By hand
B1. Compute the full Haar transform (averages and half-differences) of x = (6, 2, 5, 7, 9, 9, 4, 0), level by level. Write the result as (s \mid d_3 \mid d_2, d_2 \mid d_1, d_1, d_1, d_1). Then invert it and check that you get x back.
B2. The board example x = (4, 6, 10, 12, 8, 6, 5, 5) has the orthonormal Haar coefficients (19.80 \mid 2.83 \mid -6,\ 2 \mid -1.41,\ -1.41,\ 1.41,\ 0). (a) Check that \sum c^2 = \sum x^2. (b) Keep only the 3 largest coefficients (in magnitude) and set the rest to 0. What is the squared error \sum (x - \hat x)^2, without reconstructing anything? (c) Reconstruct \hat x and check (b). (d) In the by-hand version the coefficients are (7 \mid 1 \mid -3, 1 \mid -1, -1, 1, 0). Why is “keep the largest” not a good rule there?
B3. Write down the orthonormal Haar matrices for N = 2 and N = 4 (rows = basis vectors, coarse to fine). Check that every row has length 1 and that any two rows are perpendicular.
B4. A spike at position 5 of 8: x = (0, 0, 0, 0, 8, 0, 0, 0). Compute its Haar transform. How many coefficients are nonzero? How many would a spike have in a signal of 1024 samples? And in the Fourier basis?
B5. Two steps: x = (2, 2, 2, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10) and y = (2, 2, 2, 2, 10, 10, 10, 10). Compute both Haar transforms. Which has fewer nonzero coefficients, and why?
B6. The ramp x = (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8). Compute its Haar transform. Which details are zero? What does this tell you about the Haar basis?
B7. The 8-point DFT X_k = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i k n/8} of a spike at position 0, x = (1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0), and of a spike at position 3. What are |X_k| in both cases? Where is the position of the spike stored?
B8. A signal sampled at 1000 samples per second contains a slow wave of 4 Hz and, at one moment, a sharp step. You analyse it with a short-time Fourier transform. (a) With a window of 50 ms, how many cycles of the slow wave fit in one window? Can you tell its frequency? (b) With a window of 2 s, over how many samples is the step smeared? (c) What would a wavelet analysis do differently?
