title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Separable 2D DWT
one level of the 1D filter bank on every row, then on every column


Subbands
LL approximation; V high-pass along x (vertical edges); H high-pass along y (horizontal edges); D high-pass along both


2 \times 2 Haar block \begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}
LL = \tfrac12(a+b+c+d), V = \tfrac12(a-b+c-d), H = \tfrac12(a+b-c-d), D = \tfrac12(a-b-c+d)


Pyramid (Mallat layout)
repeat on LL; L levels on N \times N give N^2 coefficients


Orthonormal transform
\mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\text{dropped}} c^2


PSNR (8 bits)
10\log_{10}(255^2/\mathrm{MSE}) (camera noise unit)

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
By hand
B1. Compute the four Haar subband values of each 2 \times 2 block: \text{(a)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 5\\ 5 & 5\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(b)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 8\\ 2 & 8\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(c)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 8 & 8\end{pmatrix} \qquad \text{(d)}\ \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 2\\ 2 & 8\end{pmatrix} Which band responds to which kind of edge?
B2. A 4 \times 4 image with a horizontal edge: the first three rows are all 1, the last row is all 9. (a) Compute one level of the 2D Haar transform (four 2 \times 2 subbands). Which bands are nonzero? (b) Now the edge lies one row higher: the first two rows are 1, the last two are 9. Which bands are nonzero after one level? After two levels? (c) What does this say about how the transform reacts to moving an edge by one pixel?
B3. A 256 \times 256 image, 4 levels. (a) How large is each subband at each level, and how many coefficients are there in total? (b) What fraction of the coefficients is in the final LL?
B4. Keeping a fraction of all coefficients of the micrograph (4 levels) gives these PSNR values (dB):



kept
Haar
db4
CDF 9/7
Fourier
8\times8 DCT




1 %
18.2
18.6
18.8
18.4
10.5


5 %
20.9
21.5
21.8
21.0
21.2


20 %
25.7
26.4
26.7
25.0
26.2




Which basis would you use, and how much better is it than Fourier at 5 %, in dB and as a ratio of MSEs?
Why does the DCT collapse at 1 %? (Hint: 655 coefficients for 1024 blocks.)
For the synthetic disc at 2 %, the values are Haar 47.6, db4 40.5, DCT 34.9, Fourier 29.8. Why is the ranking different from the micrograph?

B5. In an orthonormal transform of a 256 \times 256 image, the dropped coefficients have a total squared value of 10^6. What are the MSE and the PSNR? What happens to the PSNR if twice as much energy is dropped?
B6. You keep 5 % of the coefficients of a 256 \times 256 8-bit image. Estimate the number of bits if each kept coefficient is stored as an 8-bit value plus its position. What compression ratio is that? Name two things a real codec does to do better.






Solutions





B1. (a) LL = 10, V = H = D = 0. (b) LL = 10, V = \tfrac12(2 - 8 + 2 - 8) = -6, H = D = 0: a vertical edge (change along x) lights V. (c) LL = 10, H = \tfrac12(2 + 2 - 8 - 8) = -6, V = D = 0: a horizontal edge lights H. (d) LL = 10, D = \tfrac12(8 - 2 - 2 + 8) = 6, V = H = 0: a checkerboard (diagonal) pattern lights D. The sign tells the direction (here: brighter on the right gives a negative V, because V is left minus right).
B2. (a) Blocks (rows 1–2) are flat 1s: LL = 2, details 0. Blocks in rows 3–4 are \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 9 & 9\end{pmatrix}: LL = 10, H = \tfrac12(1 + 1 - 9 - 9) = -8, V = D = 0. Subbands: LL = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 10 & 10\end{pmatrix}, H = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0\\ -8 & -8\end{pmatrix}, V = D = 0. Only H has details. (b) Every 2 \times 2 block is flat (rows 1–2 all 1, rows 3–4 all 9): all level-1 details are 0, LL = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 2\\ 18 & 18\end{pmatrix}. At level 2, LL is one block \begin{pmatrix}2 & 2\\ 18 & 18\end{pmatrix}: LL = 20, H = \tfrac12(2 + 2 - 18 - 18) = -16. (c) The same edge, moved by one row, appears at a different level with different values: the transform is not shift-invariant. Where an edge falls relative to the even–odd grid decides which coefficients see it.
B3. (a) Level 1: three bands of 128 \times 128 = 16\,384; level 2: three of 64 \times 64 = 4096; level 3: three of 1024; level 4: three of 256; final LL 16 \times 16 = 256. Total 3(16\,384 + 4096 + 1024 + 256) + 256 = 65\,536 = 256^2. (b) 256/65\,536 = 1/256 = 0.39\,\% (= 4^{-4}).
B4. (a) CDF 9/7 (or db4, 0.3 dB behind): 21.8 against 21.0 dB for Fourier, 0.8 dB, i.e. an MSE ratio of 10^{0.08} = 1.20: 20 % less squared error. The differences are small on this textured image; what you see differs more (blocks, ringing). (b) 655 coefficients for 1024 blocks: at least 369 blocks keep nothing, not even their average (DC), and become 0 (black). Real codecs always code every DC coefficient. (c) The disc is piecewise constant: flat regions and one smooth edge. Wavelets (Haar best: no smooth part needs vanishing moments) describe it with few coefficients along the edge; Fourier needs all frequencies for the edge. The micrograph is full of fine texture that no basis compresses well, which pulls all bases together.
B5. \mathrm{MSE} = 10^6/65\,536 = 15.26, \mathrm{PSNR} = 10\log_{10}(65\,025/15.26) = 36.3 dB. Twice the dropped energy doubles the MSE: 36.3 - 10\log_{10}2 = 33.3 dB (3 dB less).
B6. 0.05 \cdot 65\,536 = 3277 coefficients; each 8 bits of value plus \log_2 65\,536 = 16 bits of position: 3277 \cdot 24 = 78\,648 bits, against 65\,536 \cdot 8 = 524\,288 for the raw image: ratio 6.7. Real codecs quantise the values coarsely (fewer bits per value), code the positions jointly (large coefficients cluster along edges and across levels), and entropy-code the result. (Compression day.)




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive the four 2 \times 2 Haar formulas by applying the 1D step (a, b) \mapsto ((a+b)/\sqrt2, (a-b)/\sqrt2) first to both rows, then to both columns.
B8. (math) Let W be an orthogonal N \times N matrix (one 1D level or a full 1D transform). Show that X \mapsto WXW^\top preserves \sum_{ij} X_{ij}^2, and derive \mathrm{MSE} = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{\text{dropped}} c^2.
B9. (math) Show that an L-level pyramid of an N \times N image (N divisible by 2^L) has exactly N^2 coefficients, using a geometric sum.
B10. (math) Show that a circular shift of an image by one pixel changes only the phases of its DFT coefficients. Then give a 1D two-sample example showing that the Haar detail coefficients are not invariant to a shift by one sample.






Solutions (math)





B7. Rows: (a, b) \mapsto \big(\tfrac{a+b}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{a-b}{\sqrt2}\big), (c, d) \mapsto \big(\tfrac{c+d}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{c-d}{\sqrt2}\big). Columns: the left column \big(\tfrac{a+b}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{c+d}{\sqrt2}\big) gives LL = \tfrac{a+b+c+d}{2} (top) and H = \tfrac{a+b-c-d}{2} (bottom); the right column gives V = \tfrac{a-b+c-d}{2} and D = \tfrac{a-b-c+d}{2}.
B8. \sum_{ij}X_{ij}^2 = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X), and \operatorname{tr}\big((WXW^\top)^\top WXW^\top\big) = \operatorname{tr}(W X^\top X W^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X W^\top W) = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X) (cyclic trace, W^\top W = I). The map is linear, so the error image X - \hat X maps to the dropped coefficients C - \hat C; its energy is preserved: \sum (x - \hat x)^2 = \sum_{\text{dropped}} c^2; divide by N^2.
B9. Level j has three bands of (N/2^j)^2 = N^2/4^j; the final LL has N^2/4^L. Total 3N^2\sum_{j=1}^{L} 4^{-j} + N^2 4^{-L} = 3N^2\cdot\frac{1 - 4^{-L}}{3} + N^2 4^{-L} = N^2.
B10. y_{m,n} = x_{m, n-1} (indices mod N) gives Y_{k,l} = e^{-2\pi i l/N}X_{k,l}: |Y_{k,l}| = |X_{k,l}|. Haar on 4 samples (0, 8, 8, 8): details \big(\tfrac{0-8}{\sqrt2}, 0\big) = (-5.66, 0). Shifted by one (circularly) to (8, 0, 8, 8): (5.66, 0). Shifted by two, (8, 8, 0, 8): (0, -5.66). The same edge moves between coefficients and changes sign; there is no simple relation like a phase factor, because the downsampling keeps only even positions.

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Explore
A 256 \times 256 image (the micrograph or a synthetic one) and its 2D wavelet transform. Panels: the image, the subbands (Mallat layout: grey LL in the corner, detail bands in blue/red, each scaled to its own largest value; with log |w| all bands in grey on a log scale), the reconstruction, and the error. keep K largest keeps a percentage of all coefficients (dropped ones are faded in the subband panel); zero bands lets you click subbands to remove them. compare shows the reconstructions from the same number of coefficients in the wavelet basis, the global Fourier basis and the 8 \times 8 block DCT. The plot gives PSNR against the percentage kept for the three. shift by 1 px moves the image one pixel to the right.



E1. Preset one level: three orientations (oriented bars, Haar, 1 level). In which band does each bar appear, and where? Compare with B1. Then set levels to 3.
E2. Preset pyramid of the cell (db2, 4 levels). Which band looks like a thumbnail? Which bands are the brightest in log |w| display, and which level has the most coefficients?
E3. Preset keep 3 %: Haar blocks. Read the PSNR and look at the reconstruction. Then select db4 and db8. What changes in the numbers and in the look of the errors?
E4. Preset wavelets vs Fourier vs DCT at 5 %. Read the three PSNRs. Move keep % to 1. What happens to the DCT reconstruction, and why (B4b)? Then choose CDF 9/7.
E5. Still in compare, choose the image disc and keep % = 2. Read the PSNRs. Select Haar: what is special at 3 %?
E6. Preset drop the finest level = blur (db4, 3 levels, the three level-1 bands removed). How many coefficients are kept, and what is the PSNR? Bring back V and H, keeping only D removed: PSNR? And only V removed? Then remove levels 1 and 2 entirely and compare with keep K largest at a similar percentage.
E7. Preset shift variance (square, Haar, 2 levels). By how much do the detail coefficients change? And the band energies? Choose the micrograph and db4, 3 levels.






Solutions





E1. The vertical bar’s left and right sides appear in V (top right), as two vertical lines of opposite colour; the horizontal bar’s top and bottom in H (bottom left); the diagonal bar in all three detail bands, strongest along its edges. Flat areas are white (0) everywhere. With 3 levels the coarser bands show the same structures at lower resolution, and only the edges that fall inside a coarser pattern appear there.
E2. The top-left LL (16 \times 16) is the thumbnail. In log |w| the LL and the coarse bands are brightest (largest values): the energy sits at coarse scales. Level 1 has the most coefficients (3 \times 128^2 = 49\,152, three quarters of all), mostly small.
E3. Haar at 3 %: 19.9 dB, and the reconstruction is made of visible rectangular blocks. db4: 20.4 dB, db8: 20.5 dB; the blocks disappear and the error turns into a smooth blur with faint ringing near strong edges.
E4. At 5 %: db4 21.5, Fourier 21.0, DCT 21.2 dB; Fourier rings everywhere, the DCT shows 8 \times 8 blocks. At 1 %: db4 18.6, Fourier 18.4, DCT 10.5 dB, with many black blocks: those blocks kept no coefficient, not even their average. CDF 9/7: 21.8 dB at 5 %, 18.8 at 1 %.
E5. Disc at 2 %: Haar 47.6, db4 40.5, DCT 34.9, Fourier 29.8 dB (with the demo’s 4 levels). With Haar at 3 % the readout says “∞ (exact)”: the disc (with its antialiased edge) has fewer than 3 % nonzero Haar coefficients, so keeping 3 % keeps all of them.
E6. 16 384 of 65 536 coefficients (25 %), 23.9 dB: the fine texture is gone, the image is blurred. Only D removed: 31.5 dB; only V removed: 27.5 dB (vertical edges become soft): the diagonal band carries the least energy. Levels 1 and 2 removed: 4096 coefficients (6.3 %), 20.3 dB, worse than keeping the largest 5 % (21.4 dB with 3 levels): choosing coefficients by size beats choosing them by band.
E7. Square, Haar, 2 levels: the detail coefficients change by 68 % (\|c_{\text{shifted}} - c\|/\|c\|), but the level-1 band energies stay the same (1.27 \cdot 10^6 in V). Micrograph, db4, 3 levels: 92 %, with level-1 V energy 7.58 \cdot 10^6 \to 7.35 \cdot 10^6. The energy per band hardly changes; the individual coefficients do.

title: Exercise: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Where this leads
Sparsity is useful beyond compression. Noise does not become sparse in any basis: an orthonormal transform spreads white noise evenly over all coefficients. The next unit uses this to denoise by keeping the large coefficients and shrinking the small ones.

title: Quiz: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Hard threshold: keep w if |w| > t, else 0. Soft threshold: \operatorname{sign}(w)\max(|w| - t, 0).

Q1. Why does thresholding wavelet coefficients separate signal from noise?






Hint





How are signal and noise spread over the coefficients?









Answer





The image is sparse: its energy sits in a few large coefficients. White noise, in an orthonormal basis, puts noise of the same standard deviation \sigma_n into every coefficient. So small coefficients are mostly noise and large ones mostly signal; killing the small ones removes most of the noise and little of the signal.




Q2. Soft-threshold (4, -0.5, -2.5, 1) with t = 1. Then hard-threshold it.






Hint





Soft subtracts t from the magnitude of the survivors.









Answer





Soft: (3, 0, -1.5, 0). Hard: (4, 0, -2.5, 0) (|1| = t is not above t, so it is killed).




Q3. Which threshold rule tends to leave isolated blips, and which lowers the contrast of edges? Why?






Hint





What happens to a noise coefficient just above t, and to a large signal coefficient?









Answer





Hard thresholding leaves blips: a noise coefficient just above t survives at full size and shows up as a small wavelet-shaped spot. Soft thresholding shrinks every survivor by t, including the large coefficients at edges, so edges lose contrast; a surviving noise coefficient becomes tiny instead of a blip.




Q4. What is the universal threshold for a 512 \times 512 image with \sigma_n = 10?






Hint





\sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N} with N = 512^2 = 2^{18}.









Answer





\ln N = 18\ln 2 = 12.48, \sqrt{2 \cdot 12.48} = 5.00, so t \approx 50 grey levels.




Q5. Why is \sigma_n estimated with the median of the finest D band and not with its standard deviation?






Hint





What else is in that band besides noise?









Answer





The band also contains a few large signal coefficients at edges and corners. They inflate the standard deviation a lot, but barely move the median. For pure Gaussian noise the median of |w| is 0.6745\,\sigma_n, hence the divisor.




Q6. Why is the coarsest approximation (LL) not thresholded?






Hint





How large are LL coefficients compared with \sigma_n?









Answer





LL coefficients are averages over large blocks: large compared with \sigma_n, so they would survive anyway, and soft thresholding would only shift the brightness. The noise per pixel in the block average is small; the noise to remove sits in the details.




Q7. What is cycle spinning, and which artefact does it reduce?






Hint





The decimated transform is shift-variant.









Answer





Shift the image, denoise, shift back, and average over many shifts. Thresholding errors of the decimated transform are tied to its grid (blocks with Haar, small ringing patterns with Daubechies); for different shifts they fall in different places and average out.




Q8. (math) For which energy is soft thresholding with t = \lambda the exact minimiser, and why does the problem split into one scalar problem per coefficient?






Hint





Orthonormal transforms preserve distances.









Answer





\tfrac12\|y - x\|^2 + \lambda\|Wx\|_1 with W orthonormal. Since \|y - x\| = \|Wy - Wx\|, with c = Wx and w = Wy the energy is \sum_i\big(\tfrac12(w_i - c_i)^2 + \lambda|c_i|\big), a sum of independent terms; each is minimised by c_i = \operatorname{sign}(w_i)\max(|w_i| - \lambda, 0).

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

apply hard and soft thresholding by hand and say what each does to edges and to noise,
compute the universal threshold and the robust noise estimate \hat\sigma_n,
explain why the threshold is applied to the details only, and what cycle spinning fixes,
connect soft thresholding to an energy “data + λ · prior”.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Model
y = x + n, independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n (camera noise unit)


Noise in an orthonormal basis
every coefficient gets noise of the same \sigma_n


Hard threshold
\eta_H(w) = w if |w| > t, else 0


Soft threshold
\eta_S(w) = \operatorname{sign}(w)\max(|w| - t, 0)


Universal threshold
t = \hat\sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N} for N coefficients


Noise estimate
\hat\sigma_n = \operatorname{median}(|w|)/0.6745 over the finest diagonal band D


Cycle spinning
shift, denoise, shift back, average over shifts

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
By hand
B1. Apply hard and soft thresholding with t = 2 to w = (5, -1.5, 0.4, -3, 2.1, -0.2).
B2. Compute \sqrt{2\ln N} for N = 256^2 and for N = 1024, using \ln 2 \approx 0.693. For \sigma_n = 20 and a 256 \times 256 image, what is the universal threshold?
B3. Nine D coefficients of a noisy image: (0.8, -2.1, 0.3, 14.0, -1.2, 0.5, -0.9, 1.6, -25.0). (a) Estimate \hat\sigma_n with the median rule. (b) Compute the root mean square of the nine values. Why is it a bad noise estimate here?
B4. An edge in its simplest form: two pixels (0, 100), one level of orthonormal Haar: s = (a+b)/\sqrt2, d = (a-b)/\sqrt2. (a) Compute s and d. (b) Soft-threshold d with t = 20 (leave s alone) and transform back. What is the new contrast b - a? (c) And with hard thresholding at t = 20? At t = 80?
B5. An image has \sigma_n = 20. In a flat region, what standard deviation do the orthonormal detail coefficients have? And the LL coefficients after 4 levels, in grey-level units of the 16 × 16-pixel average they represent? (An LL coefficient after L levels is 2^L times the average of its 2^L \times 2^L block.)
B6. For pure noise and N = 65\,536 coefficients, the probability that one coefficient exceeds 4.71\,\sigma_n in magnitude is 2.5 \cdot 10^{-6}. How many noise coefficients do you expect above the universal threshold? What happens to real image coefficients of size 3\sigma_n?
B7. A Haar-denoised image shows faint square blocks aligned to an 8-pixel grid. Explain where they come from, and how averaging over shifts removes them.






Solutions





B1. Hard: (5, 0, 0, -3, 2.1, 0). Soft: (3, 0, 0, -1, 0.1, 0). Hard keeps the survivors at full size; soft subtracts 2 from each survivor’s magnitude.
B2. \ln 65\,536 = 16\ln 2 = 11.09, \sqrt{2 \cdot 11.09} = \sqrt{22.18} = 4.71. \ln 1024 = 10\ln 2 = 6.93, \sqrt{13.86} = 3.72. Universal threshold for \sigma_n = 20: 4.71 \cdot 20 = 94.2 grey levels.
B3. (a) Sorted |w|: 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 1.2, 1.6, 2.1, 14, 25; median 1.2; \hat\sigma_n = 1.2/0.6745 = 1.78. (b) \sqrt{\tfrac19\sum w^2} = 9.6. The two edge coefficients (14 and -25) dominate the sum of squares; the median ignores them.
B4. (a) s = 100/\sqrt2 = 70.7, d = -100/\sqrt2 = -70.7. (b) Soft: d \to -50.7. Back: a = (s + d)/\sqrt2 = 14.1, b = (s - d)/\sqrt2 = 85.9: contrast 71.7 instead of 100, i.e. reduced by \sqrt2\,t = 28.3. (The mean, 50, is unchanged.) (c) Hard at 20: |d| = 70.7 > 20, kept: contrast 100, unchanged. Hard at 80: d killed, both pixels become 50: the edge vanishes completely.
B5. Details: \sigma_n = 20 (orthonormal). LL after 4 levels: also standard deviation 20 as a coefficient; the corresponding block average is the coefficient divided by 2^4 = 16, with standard deviation 20/16 = 1.25 grey levels (averaging 256 pixels divides by \sqrt{256} = 16). Thresholding LL would mostly change real brightness, not noise.
B6. 65\,536 \cdot 2.5 \cdot 10^{-6} = 0.16: usually none. Real coefficients of size 3\sigma_n are below the threshold and are killed too: the universal threshold over-smooths faint structure.
B7. With the decimated Haar transform, each coefficient covers a fixed square of the grid (at level 3: an 8 \times 8 square). When a noisy coefficient is killed or shrunk, its square pattern is missing in the result, so the error is made of grid-aligned squares. Shifting the image moves the grid relative to the content; the squares land in different places for each shift, and their average is smooth. Averaging over all shifts equals the undecimated transform.




Math questions
B8. (math) Show that if n has independent \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2) entries and W is orthogonal, then Wn also has independent \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2) entries.
B9. (math) Show that \eta_S(w) minimises f(c) = \tfrac12(w - c)^2 + \lambda|c| with t = \lambda, and that \eta_H(w) minimises g(c) = \tfrac12(w - c)^2 + \tfrac{t^2}{2}[c \ne 0]. Then show that for orthonormal W, soft thresholding the coefficients of y minimises \tfrac12\|y - x\|^2 + \lambda\|Wx\|_1.
B10. (math) Using P(|Z| > u) \le \frac{2}{u\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2} for standard normal Z, show that the expected number of N pure-noise coefficients beyond \sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N} goes to 0 as N \to \infty.
B11. (math) Show that the median of |Z| for Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) is 0.6745\,\sigma.






Solutions (math)





B8. Wn is a linear transform of a Gaussian vector, hence Gaussian, with mean W\,\mathbb E[n] = 0 and covariance W(\sigma_n^2 I)W^\top = \sigma_n^2 I. For Gaussian vectors, zero covariance means independence.
B9. f is convex. For c \ne 0, f'(c) = c - w + \lambda\operatorname{sign}(c). A minimiser c > 0 needs c = w - \lambda > 0, i.e. w > \lambda; c < 0 needs c = w + \lambda < 0, i.e. w < -\lambda. If |w| \le \lambda, then c = 0: the subdifferential at 0 is -w + [-\lambda, \lambda] \ni 0. This is \eta_S with t = \lambda. For g: with c \ne 0 the best is c = w, cost t^2/2; with c = 0 the cost is w^2/2. Keep w if w^2/2 > t^2/2, i.e. |w| > t: \eta_H. For the vector problem: \|y - x\|^2 = \|W(y - x)\|^2 = \sum_i (w_i - c_i)^2 with w = Wy, c = Wx, so the energy is \sum_i f_i(c_i), minimised coefficient by coefficient.
B10. With u = \sqrt{2\ln N}, e^{-u^2/2} = 1/N, so N\,P(|Z| > u) \le \frac{2}{u\sqrt{2\pi}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{2\ln N}} \to 0. (For N = 65\,536 the bound is 0.17; the exact value is 0.16.)
B11. The median m of |Z| satisfies P(|Z| \le m) = \tfrac12, i.e. 2\Phi(m/\sigma) - 1 = \tfrac12, \Phi(m/\sigma) = \tfrac34, m/\sigma = \Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6745.

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Explore: denoising an image
A 256 \times 256 image with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n (fixed seed). It is transformed, the detail coefficients are thresholded (hard or soft) at t, set in units of \hat\sigma_n, and transformed back. Panels: the noisy image, the denoised one, the removed part (noisy − denoised; should look like noise) and the error (denoised − truth). The plot shows PSNR against t for hard and soft (filled in gradually), with the universal threshold and the current t marked; below, the histogram of the finest D coefficients with \pm t. cycle spinning averages over 4 or 16 shifts.



E1. Preset universal threshold, soft (shapes, \sigma_n = 20, db4, 4 levels). Compare \hat\sigma_n with the true \sigma_n. Read the PSNR before and after and the percentage of details kept. From the plot, which t would be best for soft, and for hard?
E2. Preset hard vs soft at the same t (t = 3\hat\sigma_n). Compare hard and soft: PSNR, and what the removed part and the error look like near the edges.
E3. Presets threshold too low (hard, t = 1.5) and too high (soft, t = 6). Describe what goes wrong in each. Switch the first to soft: what changes?
E4. Preset Haar blocks, then … with cycle spinning (and try 4 shifts). Read the PSNRs. What do the artefacts look like before and after?
E5. Preset micrograph: texture vs noise (\sigma_n = 40, soft, t = 1.25). How much does denoising help, and what is lost? Look at the removed part.
E6. Preset σ̂ fooled by texture (micrograph, \sigma_n = 10). Compare \hat\sigma_n with \sigma_n and read the PSNR. Then switch to the shapes image at the same \sigma_n. Explain.






Solutions





E1. \hat\sigma_n = 20.26 for \sigma_n = 20. t = 4.75\hat\sigma_n = 96: PSNR 22.1 \to 27.0 dB with 0.7 % of the details kept. The curves peak near t = 1.75\hat\sigma_n for soft (30.5 dB) and 3.25\hat\sigma_n for hard (30.4 dB): the universal threshold is far too high for soft here and over-smooths (with hard at the same t: 29.3 dB).
E2. Hard 30.2 dB, soft 28.8 dB. With soft, the removed part shows the outlines of the shapes (edge contrast taken away, B4) and the error is concentrated along the edges; with hard the edges stay sharp and the removed part looks more like pure noise.
E3. Too low (hard, 1.5\hat\sigma_n): 24.6 dB; many noise coefficients survive at full size and appear as isolated blips (small wavelet-shaped spots). Soft at the same t: 30.4 dB: the surviving noise coefficients are shrunk almost to zero. Too high (soft, 6\hat\sigma_n): 26.1 dB; smooth but blurred, edges have low contrast and the removed part shows the shapes.
E4. Haar, soft, t = 3\hat\sigma_n: 29.1 dB, with visible square blocks along the edges and in flat regions. 4 shifts: 30.3 dB; 16 shifts: 31.0 dB; the blocks average out into smooth transitions.
E5. 16.1 \to 20.2 dB. The noise is reduced, but the fine texture of the micrograph is removed as well: the removed part contains texture, not only noise. Texture and noise both live in the small fine-scale coefficients, and thresholding cannot tell them apart.
E6. \hat\sigma_n = 15.7 for a true \sigma_n = 10: the D band contains the image’s own texture (on the clean micrograph \hat\sigma_n would be 11). The threshold is too high, and the result (21.1 dB) is worse than the noisy input (28.1 dB). On the shapes image \hat\sigma_n matches \sigma_n closely (D has almost no signal there).

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Explore: denoising a 1D signal
The same method on a 1D test signal of 1024 samples (standard deviation 7) with noise of standard deviation \sigma_n: noisy samples (grey dots), truth (black) and the estimate (blue). The plot on the right gives the RMSE against t.



E7. Preset Blocks, Haar (soft, universal threshold). RMSE before and after? Switch to hard. Which is better here, and why?
E8. Preset HeaviSine, db4. RMSE? What happens near the two jumps?
E9. Preset Doppler, hard vs soft (db8, t = 3): compare hard and soft. Preset Bumps: too high: what is lost?






Solutions





E7. Soft: RMSE 1.004 \to 0.703; hard: 0.320. Blocks has a few very large Haar coefficients at the jumps; hard keeps them at full size, soft shrinks every one of them by t and so lowers every jump.
E8. RMSE 1.004 \to 0.389, with 0.2 % of the details kept. The smooth parts are clean; near the jumps there is some ringing and the jumps are slightly rounded.
E9. Doppler: hard 0.492, soft 0.695. The fast oscillations at the left are lost by both, but soft also damps the oscillations it keeps. Bumps with soft t = 6: RMSE 1.986, worse than the noisy signal (1.004): the narrow bumps have their tops cut off; at the universal threshold it is 1.398, still worse than doing nothing. Spiky signals need lower thresholds.

title: Exercise: denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Where this leads
This was the last core unit of the wavelets day. The compression day (next in this elective) turns sparse coefficients into bits: quantisation, entropy coding, JPEG and JPEG 2000. Denoising with other priors and the general comparison of denoisers are on the deconvolution day; total variation and MRF priors on the Ising day.

title: Quiz: marching cubes
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Corner k of a cube has offsets (x, y, z) with k = x + 2y + 4z; the case index is \sum 2^k over the corners above c.

Q1. Corners 1, 2 and 4 are above c, the others below. What is the case index? How many corners are below?






Hint





Add the powers of two.









Answer





2 + 4 + 16 = 22; five corners are below.




Q2. Why does marching cubes produce a closed surface, although every cube is processed on its own?






Hint





What do neighbouring cubes share?









Answer





Neighbouring cubes share edges and faces. A crossing point on a shared edge is computed from the same two values, so it is the same point; and if both cubes cut each shared face in the same way (a consistent face rule), their triangles meet edge to edge. The surface can only end where it leaves the volume.




Q3. How do the 256 cases reduce to 15?






Hint





Two kinds of symmetry.









Answer





The 24 rotations of the cube map a case to another case with the same (rotated) surface: 23 classes. Swapping above and below (complement) gives the same surface with flipped normals: together 15 classes.




Q4. What is a crack, and how can the 15-case table produce one?






Hint





Think of an ambiguous face shared by two cubes.









Answer





A hole in the surface along a face where the two neighbouring cubes connected the crossing points differently (one separated the bright corners, the other joined them). The 15-case table uses the complement for some cases, which swaps “separate” for “join” on their ambiguous faces; when only one of the two neighbours is complemented, they disagree.




Q5. Why is marching tetrahedra never ambiguous, and what is its price?






Hint





What does the interpolant look like inside a tetrahedron?









Answer





Linear interpolation of 4 corner values is an affine function, whose level set is a plane: it cuts a tetrahedron in a single triangle or quadrilateral, and there are no diagonal corners on its (triangular) faces. The price: more triangles (typically 2–4 times), thinner triangles, and a slight dependence on how the cubes were split.




Q6. A vertex lies on the surface of a bright nucleus where \nabla I = (0, 0, -12). Which way does the outward normal point?






Hint





\mathbf n = -\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert for a bright object.









Answer





\mathbf n = (0, 0, 1): I decreases towards +z, so outside (darker) is in the +z direction.




Q7. You extract a surface from a binary mask (0/1) at c = 0.5 and shade it with gradient normals. Why does it look blocky, and what helps?






Hint





Where are the vertices, and which values can the central differences take?









Answer





Every crossed edge goes from 1 to 0, so every vertex sits at an edge midpoint (terraces), and central differences of 0/1 values point in only a few directions (combinations of -1, 0, 1): the normals are blocky too. Blurring the mask slightly before extraction gives grey values that place the vertices and normals smoothly.




Q8. (math) Why does the number of triangles grow like n^2, while the running time grows like n^3, for an n^3 volume containing one blob of size proportional to n?






Hint





Which cubes produce triangles, and which cubes are visited?









Answer





All (n-1)^3 cubes are visited (each in constant time), so the time is O(n^3). Only the cubes the surface passes through produce triangles; their number is proportional to the surface area in voxel units, \propto n^2 for a blob whose size grows like n.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
About this lecture
Images are sparse in a wavelet basis: a few large coefficients carry the structure. Noise is not sparse in any basis. Today we use that difference to remove noise.

In an orthonormal basis, white noise stays white noise with the same standard deviation in every coefficient.
Hard and soft thresholding: keep or kill, kill and shrink.
How large the threshold should be (the universal threshold), and how to estimate the noise level from the image itself.
Artefacts tied to the grid, and cycle spinning.
A third view of denoising: a sparsity prior in a basis.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Fourth unit of the wavelets elective. Needs the 2D DWT unit. The noise model and PSNR are recalled from the camera noise unit; total variation from the Ising day; the general comparison of denoisers (median, bilateral, non-local means, learned) belongs to the deconvolution day.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Recall: the noise model
From Camera noise, SNR and PSNR (day 3): we model the observed image as y = x + n, the true image x plus independent Gaussian noise of standard deviation \sigma_n in every pixel, and measure quality by the PSNR in dB (higher is better).
Goal: estimate x from y alone.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
section: Signal and noise in the wavelet basis
text:
Signal and noise in the wavelet basis


The clean signal has 37 nonzero detail coefficients of 496, all large (circles).
The noise puts a small value, of the same size \sigma_n = 1 everywhere (dots).
So: small coefficients are mostly noise, large ones mostly signal. Keep the large, drop the small.


Piecewise-constant test signal (Donoho–Johnstone “Blocks”, 512 samples, scaled to standard deviation 7), noise σ = 1, Haar, 5 levels. The dashed lines are ±σ√(2 ln N) = ±3.53 (next slides). 36 noisy coefficients exceed it, all at positions where the clean signal is nonzero; none at a pure-noise position. The standard deviation of the noisy details where the clean signal is zero is 0.95, close to σ = 1.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
section: The math: white noise stays white
text:
The math: white noise stays white
Noise vector n with independent \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2) entries: \;\mathbb E[n] = 0, \operatorname{Cov}(n) = \sigma_n^2 I.
For an orthogonal transform W (WW^\top = I), the coefficients Wn are again Gaussian (linear combinations of Gaussians) with \operatorname{Cov}(Wn) = W\,\sigma_n^2 I\,W^\top = \sigma_n^2\,WW^\top = \sigma_n^2 I.

Same standard deviation \sigma_n in every coefficient, and still independent.
Geometrically: the noise is a round (isotropic) Gaussian cloud in \mathbb R^N, and a rotation leaves a round cloud round.
The signal, by contrast, is concentrated on few coordinates. Thresholding works coordinate by coordinate.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Hard and soft thresholding


Hard: keep w if |w| > t, else 0. Large coefficients are untouched (low bias), but a noise coefficient that just passes t survives at full size: isolated blips.
Soft: kill if |w| \le t, otherwise shrink towards 0 by t. Smoother results, no blips, but every kept coefficient is too small by t: edges lose contrast.
Example, t = 2: (5, -1.5, 0.4, -3, 2.1) → hard (5, 0, 0, -3, 2.1), soft (3, 0, 0, -1, 0.1).

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
How large should t be?
Pure noise must be killed: t should exceed (almost) every noise coefficient.

The largest of N independent Gaussian values of standard deviation \sigma_n is about \sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N}.
Universal threshold (VisuShrink, Donoho & Johnstone 1994): t = \sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N}. For N = 256^2: \sqrt{2 \cdot 16 \cdot \ln 2} = 4.71, so t \approx 4.7\,\sigma_n. For N = 1024: 3.72\,\sigma_n.
With N = 256^2, on average only 0.16 pure-noise coefficients exceed it.
It kills noise reliably but tends to over-smooth: it also kills real coefficients below 4.7\sigma_n. Level-dependent thresholds chosen from the data (SureShrink, BayesShrink) usually do better; the idea is the same.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
section: The math: the maximum of N Gaussians
text:
The math: the maximum of N Gaussians
For Z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1) and u > 0, the Gaussian tail bound \;P(|Z| > u) \le \dfrac{2}{u\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-u^2/2}.

With u = \sqrt{2\ln N}: e^{-u^2/2} = 1/N, so the expected number of the N noise coefficients beyond u\sigma_n is N\,P(|Z| > u) \le \frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sqrt{2\ln N}} \to 0 \quad (N \to \infty).
N = 65\,536: u = 4.71, P(|Z| > u) = 2.5 \cdot 10^{-6}, expected count 0.16.
Donoho & Johnstone showed that soft thresholding at this t has a risk within a factor \approx 2\ln N of an ideal “oracle” that knows which coefficients are signal.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Estimating \sigma_n from the image
\sigma_n is usually unknown. Use the finest diagonal band D (level 1): it is almost all noise, with a few large signal coefficients at edges.
\hat\sigma_n = \frac{\operatorname{median}(|w|)}{0.6745} \quad \text{over the level-1 D coefficients.}

For pure Gaussian noise, the median of |w| is 0.6745\,\sigma_n.
The median barely moves when a few values are huge; the standard deviation would be dragged up by the edges.
Example: D coefficients (0.8, -2.1, 0.3, 14, -1.2, 0.5, -0.9, 1.6, -25): median |w| = 1.2, \hat\sigma_n = 1.78; the standard deviation is 9.6.
Caveat: fine texture also lives in D. On a textured image \hat\sigma_n comes out too large.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Leave the approximation alone
Threshold only the detail bands; keep LL as it is.

LL is small (here 16 \times 16 of 256 \times 256) and holds almost all the energy: every LL coefficient is large compared with \sigma_n and would survive anyway, but soft thresholding would shift the brightness.
The noise in LL is averaged over 2^L \times 2^L pixels; it is the details that carry most of the noise.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Try it: wavelet shrinkage




Synthetic shapes, σn = 20, db4, 4 levels. “universal threshold, soft”: t = 4.75 σ̂ (σ̂ = 20.26): 22.1 → 27.0 dB, 0.7 % of the details kept. The plot shows PSNR against t for hard and soft (computed in the background): soft is best near t = 1.75 σ̂ (30.5 dB), hard near 3.25 σ̂ (30.4 dB). The universal threshold over-smooths, especially with soft. “hard vs soft at the same t” (t = 3): hard 30.2, soft 28.8. “threshold too low” (hard, t = 1.5): 24.6 dB with noise blips. “too high” (soft, 6): 26.1 dB, blurred, edges lose contrast. “removed” panel: should look like pure noise; where it shows edges, signal was removed.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Artefacts and cycle spinning
The decimated transform is shift-variant (previous unit), so the errors of thresholding are tied to the grid: Haar leaves blocks, Daubechies wavelets small ringing patterns next to edges.
Cycle spinning (Coifman & Donoho 1995):

shift the image by (\Delta x, \Delta y),
denoise,
shift back,
average over many shifts.

The grid artefacts land in different places for each shift and average out. Shapes image, Haar, soft, t = 3\hat\sigma_n: 29.1 dB → 30.3 dB (4 shifts) → 31.0 dB (16 shifts). Averaging over all shifts equals the undecimated (translation-invariant) wavelet transform.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
section: A third view: a prior on the coefficients
text:
A third view: a prior on the coefficients
Other units denoise by minimising data + λ · prior:

Ising/MRF elective: a prior on neighbouring pixels; total variation (TV) penalises \sum |x_{p+1} - x_p|.
Wavelet shrinkage: a prior on coefficients in a basis: soft thresholding with t = \lambda is the exact minimiser of \tfrac12\|y - x\|^2 + \lambda\,\|Wx\|_1 \qquad (W \text{ orthonormal}), “close to the data, few large coefficients”. A sparsity prior.



Same noisy step-and-ramp profile (σ = 0.1, 256 samples), each method with the weight that minimises the error. TV keeps the step sharp and turns the ramp into a staircase (RMSE 0.027); wavelet soft thresholding (db4, 5 levels, 16 shifts) keeps the step with small ringing and follows the ramp (RMSE 0.042). On this profile TV has the lower error; on textured images the ranking can flip. Regularisation of inverse problems in general: the deconvolution day.

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
section: The math: soft thresholding minimises an \ell^1 energy
text:
The math: soft thresholding minimises an \ell^1 energy
Since W is orthonormal, \|y - x\|^2 = \|Wy - Wx\|^2. With c = Wx, w = Wy: \tfrac12\|y - x\|^2 + \lambda\|Wx\|_1 = \sum_i \Big(\tfrac12(w_i - c_i)^2 + \lambda|c_i|\Big): one independent scalar problem per coefficient.

Minimise f(c) = \tfrac12(w - c)^2 + \lambda|c|. For c > 0: f' = c - w + \lambda = 0 \Rightarrow c = w - \lambda, valid if w > \lambda. For c < 0: c = w + \lambda if w < -\lambda. Otherwise the minimum is at the kink c = 0 (subgradient 0 \in [-\lambda, \lambda] + (0 - w), i.e. |w| \le \lambda).
Together: c = \operatorname{sign}(w)\max(|w| - \lambda, 0), the soft threshold with t = \lambda.
Hard thresholding minimises \tfrac12(w - c)^2 + \tfrac{t^2}{2}[c \ne 0]: an \ell^0 penalty (count of nonzeros).

title: Denoising by wavelet shrinkage
text:
Summary

An orthonormal transform maps white noise to white noise of the same \sigma_n; the signal is sparse. Small coefficients: noise; large ones: signal.
Hard thresholding keeps or kills (blips); soft kills and shrinks (smooth, loses contrast).
Universal threshold t = \sigma_n\sqrt{2\ln N} (4.7\sigma_n for 256^2) kills pure noise but over-smooths.
Estimate \hat\sigma_n = \operatorname{median}|w|/0.6745 on the finest D band; texture inflates it. Leave LL alone.
Cycle spinning averages away grid artefacts.
Soft thresholding = minimiser of data + \lambda\|Wx\|_1: a sparsity prior, beside TV and the MRF priors.

title: Quiz: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why is there no single “best” σ for analysing a micrograph?






Hint





How large are a nucleus, a granule and the texture inside the nucleus?









Answer





Different structures have different sizes: membrane texture is visible at σ ≈ 1, granules at a few pixels, the nucleus at σ ≈ 10 or more. A σ that suits one structure blurs away a smaller one or sees only the inside of a larger one. Scale space keeps all σ and lets each structure pick its own.




Q2. You blur an image with σ = 3 and then blur the result with σ = 4. Which single blur gives the same image?






Hint





Variances add.









Answer





A Gaussian of \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5. The squared widths (variances) add, as for sums of independent random variables.




Q3. Why is the Gaussian preferred over a box kernel for building a scale space?






Hint





What can a box blur do to a bright line in a dark band?









Answer





Gaussian blurring never creates new structure (in 1D: no new bumps, dips or zero crossings) as σ grows, and successive blurs chain into one Gaussian. A box blur can create new extrema: a bright line in a dark band can split into two bumps. Then a “structure” in scale space could be an artefact of the kernel.




Q4. Without normalisation, the LoG response over all σ always peaks at the smallest σ for most blobs. Why, and what does multiplying by σ² fix?






Hint





What does blurring do to the curvature of the brightness?









Answer





Blurring spreads and flattens everything, so second derivatives shrink roughly as 1/\sigma^2: the raw response falls with σ and small σ always wins, so a large blob loses to a small one. Multiplying by σ² measures the curvature in units of σ (scale-invariant), and each blob’s response then peaks at a σ matched to its size.




Q5. A spot is detected at σ = 3 pixels. What is its radius? At 0.1 µm per pixel, what is its diameter?






Hint





Radius ≈ √2·σ.









Answer





r = \sqrt2 \cdot 3 = 4.24 pixels; diameter 8.49 pixels = 0.85 µm.




Q6. An elongated blob (a short thick line) gives several small detections along it rather than one large one. Why?






Hint





Which dimension does the Mexican hat “fit”?









Answer





The LoG responds most strongly when its centre fits the blob in all directions. Across the line that happens at a σ set by the width; along the line there is nothing to fit, the response is almost constant, and noise picks several local maxima along it. The LoG measures the width of elongated objects, not their length.




Q7. Why is the difference of two Gaussian blurs a good replacement for the scale-normalised LoG?






Hint





What are the two blurs needed for anyway?









Answer





G_{k\sigma} * I - G_\sigma * I \approx (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 L: it is already normalised by σ², up to a constant. And the blurred images are computed anyway to build the scale space, so the DoG costs one subtraction per pixel.




Q8. A Gaussian pyramid of a 2048 × 2048 image down to 1 × 1: how many pixels does it hold in total, roughly? Why must each level be blurred before downsampling?






Hint





1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots









Answer





About \tfrac43 \cdot 2048^2 \approx 5.59 million pixels (the image itself has 4.19 million). Without blurring, detail finer than the new pixel spacing would alias into false coarse patterns (moiré); the blur removes it first.




Q9. (math) Show that G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2} = G_{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}} using the Fourier transform.






Hint





The Fourier transform of G_\sigma is e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}; convolution becomes multiplication.









Answer





\widehat{G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2}}(\omega) = e^{-\sigma_1^2\omega^2/2}\,e^{-\sigma_2^2\omega^2/2} = e^{-(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)\omega^2/2}, the transform of a Gaussian with variance \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2. The inverse transform is unique, so the convolution is that Gaussian.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run one cube of marching cubes by hand: case index, crossed edges, vertices by linear interpolation, triangles,
decide whether two cases are rotations of each other, and count the cases of a tetrahedron,
explain how an ambiguous face leads to a crack, and how a consistent rule or the asymptotic decider prevents it,
compute a normal from the image gradient, with the voxel spacing, and say which way it points.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

text:

Corner and edge numbering of a cube (y up, z towards you).

Normal

The 15 classes (orange: corners above c; one representative case each).

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
By hand
B1. A cube has the corner values I_0, \dots, I_7 = 7, 3, 2, 1, 6, 4, 1, 0, and c = 5. (a) Which corners are above c? What is the case index? (b) Which edges are crossed? (Use the edge list.) (c) Compute t and the vertex position (x, y, z) in the unit cube for each crossed edge. (d) How many triangles does the cube get, and what shape do they form? Which of the 15 classes is it?
B2. (a) Case 3 (corners 0 and 1 above) and case 10 (corners 1 and 3 above): show that a rotation of the cube maps one to the other. Which rotation? (b) Is case 9 (corners 0 and 3 above) a rotation of case 3? Why or why not? (c) Case 1 and case 254 (all corners except 0 above) give the same surface with opposite normals. Are they in the same class of 23? Of 15?
B3. Marching tetrahedra. A tetrahedron has 4 corners, so 16 cases. (a) List the cases by the number of corners above c (0 to 4). How many cases has each group? (b) Group them into classes: what does the surface look like in each? How many triangles? (c) Why is no tetrahedron case ambiguous?
B4. Take case 1 (only corner 0 above, all values 0.8 or 0.2, c = 0.5). (a) How many triangles does marching cubes produce? (b) The 6-tetrahedron split cuts the cube into 6 tetrahedra that all share the diagonal from corner 0 to corner 7. How many of them contain corner 0, and how many triangles do they produce in total? (Each contains corner 0 and three corners below.) (c) What does this say about the size of tetrahedral meshes?
B5. Gradient normal. Around a grid point, the six face neighbours have the values I(x \pm 1) = 80, 40, I(y \pm 1) = 60, 60, I(z \pm 1) = 90, 30 (the “+” neighbour first). (a) With spacing (1, 1, 1): compute \nabla I by central differences and the outward normal \mathbf n of a bright object. (b) The same with spacing (1, 1, 2) (the z neighbours are 2 units away). How much does the normal tilt? (c) The object is dark on a bright background. Which way does the outward normal point now?
B6. Cracks. Two cubes share a face whose corners (going round) have the values 8, 4, 7, 3, and c = 5. (a) Why is this face ambiguous? What does each of the two rules (separate, join) draw on it? (b) The left cube uses “always separate”, the right cube “always join”. What happens along the shared face? (c) Both use the asymptotic decider. What do they draw, and why can they not disagree?
B7. A smooth surface extracted from a volume has about 3 triangles per unit of area (in voxel units) and 2 triangles per vertex. Estimate the number of triangles and vertices for a sphere of radius 20 voxels. How many voxels does the ball contain?






Solutions





B1. (a) Corners 0 (value 7) and 4 (value 6). Case 2^0 + 2^4 = 17. (b) Edges with one corner above: from corner 0 to 1 (e0) and to 2 (e4); from corner 4 to 5 (e2) and to 6 (e6). Edge e8 (0–4) is not crossed: both ends are above. (c)

One loop of 4 vertices, a quadrilateral cutting off the edge 0–4: 2 triangles. It is the “edge” class (class 2 of 15, representative case 3), rotated.

B2. (a) A 90° rotation about the z axis (through the centres of the front and back faces) maps corner 0 → 1, 1 → 3, 3 → 2, 2 → 0 (and 4 → 5 → 7 → 6 → 4): the edge 0–1 goes to the edge 1–3. So case 3 becomes case 10. (b) No. Corners 0 and 1 are joined by a cube edge (distance 1), corners 0 and 3 by a face diagonal (distance \sqrt2). Rotations keep distances, so they cannot map one pair to the other. Case 9 is in another class (the “face diagonal” class, 3 of 15), and it has an ambiguous face. (c) Under rotations alone, no: one corner above and seven corners above are different classes of the 23 (rotations do not change the number of corners above). With the complement, yes: both are class 1 of the 15.
B3. (a) 0 corners above: 1 case; 1: 4; 2: 6; 3: 4; 4: 1. Total 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16. (b) Three classes: nothing (0 or 4 above: 2 cases); one corner different from the other three (1 or 3 above: 8 cases): a triangle cutting off that corner; two and two (6 cases): a quadrilateral, 2 triangles. (c) Every pair of corners of a tetrahedron is joined by an edge, so there is no diagonal pair on a face, and the interpolant inside is linear (its level set is a plane), so there is only one way to cut.
B4. (a) 1 triangle. (b) All 6 tetrahedra contain corner 0 (it is on the shared diagonal), each with three corners below: 6 triangles. (c) Tetrahedral meshes are larger (here 6 against 1; on whole surfaces typically 2–4 times), with smaller and thinner triangles.
B5. (a) \nabla I = \big((80 - 40)/2,\; (60 - 60)/2,\; (90 - 30)/2\big) = (20, 0, 30), length 36.06. \mathbf n = -\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert = (-0.555, 0, -0.832). (b) \partial_z I = (90 - 30)/(2 \cdot 2) = 15: \nabla I = (20, 0, 15), length 25, \mathbf n = (-0.8, 0, -0.6). The angle from the z axis goes from \arctan(0.555/0.832) = 33.7° to \arctan(0.8/0.6) = 53.1°: a tilt of about 19°. (c) For a dark object the inside has low values, so outward is the direction of increasing I: \mathbf n = +\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert = (0.555, 0, 0.832) (spacing 1).
B6. (a) The corners with 8 and 7 (diagonal) are above 5, the ones with 4 and 3 below: a 2D saddle. “Separate” draws two segments, each cutting off one bright corner; “join” draws two segments cutting off the two dark corners. (b) The left cube’s triangles end on the face along the “separate” segments, the right cube’s along the “join” segments. The crossing points are the same four, but they are connected differently: the triangle edges on the face do not match, and the surface has a hole there, a crack (each of those edges belongs to one triangle only). (c) Both compute f^\ast = (8 \cdot 7 - 4 \cdot 3)/(8 + 7 - 4 - 3) = 5.5 > 5 from the same four values and both join. The decision depends only on the face, so neighbours agree.
B7. Area 4\pi \cdot 20^2 = 5027 voxel²: about 3 \cdot 5027 \approx 15\,000 triangles and 7\,500 vertices. The ball has \tfrac43\pi \cdot 20^3 \approx 33\,500 voxels: the mesh grows with the area (r^2), the voxel count with the volume (r^3).




Math questions
B8. (math) Count the 23 classes with Burnside’s lemma: list the 24 rotations of the cube by type, the cycles of the corner permutation of each type, and the number of cases each fixes. Then extend to the 48 symmetries “rotation, optionally followed by complement” and show you get 15.
B9. (math) Show that the gradient of I is perpendicular to the level set \{I = c\}, and that for a bright object -\nabla I points outwards. What goes wrong when \nabla I = 0 on the surface?
B10. (math) Show that the linear interpolant f = \sum_i \lambda_i I_i on a tetrahedron is an affine function of \mathbf x, that its level set is a plane, and that a plane meets a tetrahedron in a triangle or a convex quadrilateral (or nothing). Why does the trilinear interpolant on a cube not have this property?






Solutions (math)





B8. Burnside: classes = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g}|\mathrm{Fix}(g)|, and a case is fixed by g when every cycle of g’s corner permutation is all above or all below: 2^{\#\text{cycles}} cases.
