Sum 256 + 24 + 48 + 128 + 96 = 552, and 552/24 = 23. With complement: “rotate, then complement” fixes a case when every cycle alternates above/below, which needs every cycle to have even length; then each cycle has 2 alternating patterns. The identity, the 120° rotations (cycles of length 1 and 3) fix nothing; 90° rotations fix 2^2 = 4 each (24), face 180° fix 2^4 = 16 each (48), edge 180° fix 16 each (96): 168 in total. (552 + 168)/48 = 720/48 = 15.
B9. For a curve \mathbf x(s) in the level set, \frac{d}{ds}I(\mathbf x(s)) = \nabla I \cdot \mathbf x'(s) = 0, so \nabla I is perpendicular to all tangent directions. \nabla I points to increasing I; inside a bright object I > c, so +\nabla I points inwards and -\nabla I outwards. Where \nabla I = 0 the level set need not be a smooth surface (a saddle or a plateau) and the direction is undefined: normalising divides by (nearly) zero, and noise decides the result.
B10. The barycentric weights are the solution of the linear system \mathbf x = \sum\lambda_i\mathbf p_i, \sum\lambda_i = 1, so they are affine functions of \mathbf x, and so is f: f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf x + b. Its level set \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf x = c - b is a plane (if \mathbf a \ne 0). A plane splits the 4 corners into two groups (1 + 3 or 2 + 2) and cuts the 3 or 4 edges between the groups: a triangle or a quadrilateral, convex as the intersection of two convex sets. The trilinear interpolant on a cube contains the terms xy, yz, xz, xyz: its level sets are curved (hyperbolic on the faces), and can be disconnected inside one cube, so the corner signs do not determine the topology.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
Explore: one cube
One marching-cubes cell, drawn with the corner numbering of the figure above (drag to rotate; front, side, top and 3/4 view buttons). Click a corner to flip it to the other side of c (orange = above) and select it; the first slider sets the selected corner’s value. The readout gives the bits, the case index, the class among the 15 and the 23 and the rotation to the class representative (rotate to its representative animates it). Ambiguous faces are tinted purple; the face rule decides how they are cut. 5 / 6 tetrahedra show the tetrahedral split and its triangles. Neighbour cube adds a second cube on the +x side with its own face rule; cracks are drawn in red.



C1. Preset one corner. Read the case and class. Click corner 1: what are the case and the class now? Click rotate to its representative and describe the rotation.
C2. Preset values: vertices slide. Which corners are above c = 0.5, and what is the case? Check the vertex on edge 0–1 by hand (I_0 = 0.9, I_1 = 0.35) and the one on edge 0–4 (I_4 = 0.45). Move c up to 0.55: which vertex moves furthest along its edge, and why?
C3. Preset the 15 classes: step through all of them. Which classes have 4 triangles? Find the class whose single loop is a hexagon. Which classes have an ambiguous face?
C4. Preset an ambiguous face (case 9). How many triangles do separate and join give? What does decider choose, and why exactly that? Now click corner 0 twice (it flips and flips back, and is selected) and set its value to 0.9: what does the decider do now?
C5. Preset a crack. How many crack edges are there? Set the neighbour’s rule to separate; then set both cubes to decider. When is the surface closed?
C6. Preset tetrahedra instead (case 9 with 6 tetrahedra). How many triangles? Switch to 5 tetrahedra and to marching cubes. Then load one corner and compare the three algorithms again (B4).






Solutions





C1. Case 1, class 1 of 15 and of 23 (already the representative). With corner 1 also above: case 3, class 2 (representative 3 itself, so no rotation). (Other edges need a rotation: with corners 1 and 3 above, case 10, the demo turns the cube by 120° about a body diagonal to reach case 3; a 90° turn about the z axis would do as well, B2.)
C2. Corners 0 (0.9) and 2 (0.6): case 1 + 4 = 5, the edge class (2 of 15), 2 triangles. Edge 0–1: t = (0.5 - 0.9)/(0.35 - 0.9) = 0.727, vertex (0.73, 0, 0). Edge 0–4: t = (0.5 - 0.9)/(0.45 - 0.9) = 0.889, vertex (0, 0, 0.89). At c = 0.55 the case stays 5; a vertex moves by \Delta t = \Delta c/|I_b - I_a|, so the one on the edge with the smallest difference of values moves furthest: edge 2–6 (0.6 → 0.3), from t = 0.33 to 0.17. Edge 0–1 moves only from 0.73 to 0.64.
C3. Classes 9 to 14 have 4 triangles (with the “separate” rule). Class 9 (case 23: corner 0 and its three neighbours 1, 2, 4) has a single hexagonal loop. Classes 3, 6, 7, 12, 13, 14 (representatives 6, 22, 25, 30, 60, 105) have at least one ambiguous face: 6 of the 15.
C4. Separate: 2 triangles (two corner pieces). Join: 4 triangles (one band across the cube). The decider computes f^\ast = (0.8 \cdot 0.8 - 0.2 \cdot 0.2)/(0.8 + 0.8 - 0.2 - 0.2) = 0.5 = c, the borderline, and does not join (it joins only for f^\ast > c): 2 triangles. With I_0 = 0.9: f^\ast = (0.72 - 0.04)/1.3 = 0.523 > 0.5: it joins, 4 triangles.
C5. 4 crack edges (red). With the neighbour on “separate” (the same as the left cube) the crack closes: 0. With both on “decider” it closes too. The surface is closed whenever both cubes cut the shared face the same way, which a rule that depends only on the face’s own values guarantees.
C6. Case 9 with 6 tetrahedra: 8 triangles; with 5 tetrahedra: 2; with marching cubes (“separate”): 2. For one corner (case 1): marching cubes 1, 5 tetrahedra 1 (corner 0 is cut off by one corner tetrahedron), 6 tetrahedra 6. The count depends on how the corners sit relative to the split.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
section: Explore: marching cubes on a volume
text:
Explore: marching cubes on a volume
Marching cubes on a whole volume (48³ voxels, or the nuclei stack), recomputed on every change; drag to rotate. Choose the volume, c (slider or histogram), blur \sigma (voxels) and noise; face normals shade each triangle flat, gradient normals use -\nabla I; ignore the z spacing treats the voxels as cubes; cubes / 6 / 5 tetrahedra switch the algorithm; the face rule (decider, separate, complement as in the 15-case table) applies to cubes. Red lines are boundary edges (cracks). Show an xy slice adds a slice with its marching-squares contour at the same c. The readout gives vertices, triangles, area, volume, components and the Euler characteristic \chi = V - E + F (2 for each closed surface without holes, 0 for a torus; more in the next unit).



M1. Preset two blobs merge (c = 0.6). How many components? Lower c in steps of 0.01. At which c do the two surfaces become one? What happens to \chi? (The blobs are two Gaussians with value 1 at their centres, 20 voxels apart, \sigma = 6: what is the value halfway between them?)
M2. Preset a torus has a hole. Read \chi and the number of components. Compare the area and volume with the true torus (tube radius 5.5, centre-line radius 13: area 4\pi^2 R r, volume 2\pi^2 R r^2). Switch to 6 tetrahedra: how many triangles, and how does the area change?
M3. Preset noise: many tiny surfaces. How many components and triangles? Compare the area with the noise-free sphere (switch noise to 0). Then preset blur first: what happens to components, area and volume? Why is the blurred volume smaller than the true \frac43\pi \cdot 15^3?
M4. Preset faceted vs gradient normals. With wireframe on, switch between face and gradient normals. Are the triangles different? Explain what the gradient normals add.
M5. Preset wrong z spacing (an ellipsoid sampled with \Delta z = 2.5 voxels). Compare area and volume with “ignore the z spacing” on and off. By what factor does the volume change, and why exactly that factor?
M6. Preset cracks from inconsistent faces. How many cracks are there with the complement rule? Switch to decider and to separate. Then try 6 tetrahedra.
M7. Preset a slice is a contour (torus). How many contours does the slice show, and how do they relate to the surface? Move the slice to the top of the torus and above it.
M8. Preset nuclei stack (the volume of volumes3d/, values scaled so that background ≈ 0.05 and nuclei ≈ 1). How many components are there, and what is the total volume in µm³? (The true volumes of the four ellipsoids add up to 79.2 µm³.) Lower c to 0.3: what happens to the volume?






Solutions





M1. 2 components (\chi = 4: two sphere-like surfaces). At c = 0.50 still 2, at c = 0.49 one component with \chi = 2. Halfway between the centres each Gaussian has the value e^{-10^2/(2 \cdot 36)} = 0.249, together 0.499: the saddle value, where the two surfaces touch.
M2. \chi = 0, 1 component: a closed surface with one hole. Area 2816.0 and volume 7698.4 (voxel units) against the true 4\pi^2 \cdot 13 \cdot 5.5 = 2822.7 and 2\pi^2 \cdot 13 \cdot 5.5^2 = 7762.4: −0.2 % and −0.8 % (the tube’s edge is a smooth ramp, which shifts the half-way level slightly). With 6 tetrahedra: 24 216 triangles instead of 7680 (3.2 times), area 2828.8, still \chi = 0.
M3. Noise: 4324 components and 56 054 triangles; the area is 7351.7 against 2824.6 without noise (the true sphere: 2827.4): the many tiny surfaces and the roughness add area. Blur first (\sigma = 1.5): 1 component, area 2772.3, volume 13 670.9 against \frac43\pi \cdot 15^3 = 14\,137.2. Blurring a convex object moves its half-way level inwards (a curved edge loses more brightness to the outside than it gains), so the surface shrinks; the effect grows with \sigma and with the curvature.
M4. The triangles are identical; only the normals used for shading differ. Face normals are constant per triangle (facets visible); gradient normals vary smoothly from vertex to vertex because they come from the image, so the same coarse mesh looks like a smooth sphere.
M5. With the correct spacing: area 1976.7, volume 7608.9 (true \frac43\pi \cdot 17 \cdot 9 \cdot 12 = 7690.6). Ignoring it: area 1184.6, volume 3043.6. The volume changes by exactly 1/2.5 = 0.4: every vertex’s z is scaled by 1/2.5, and volume scales with the product of the three scale factors. The area changes by a factor between 0.4 and 1 (here 0.60), depending on how the surface is oriented.
M6. Complement rule: 296 crack edges (red), and many more components and a jumpy \chi. Decider and separate: 0 cracks. 6 tetrahedra: 0 cracks, but about 3 times the triangles.
M7. Two closed contours, the outer and the inner circle of the torus’ cross-section in that plane: the slice of an isosurface is an isocontour, and the yellow curve lies on the surface. Moving up, the two circles approach each other (the ring-shaped cross-section gets thinner) and vanish together at the top of the tube; above the torus, none.
M8. 4 components (A, B, C, D), volume 77.8 µm³ (area 146.6 µm²), against 79.2 µm³ for the ideal ellipsoids. At c = 0.3: 95.9 µm³, larger, because the surfaces move out into the blurred edges. Which c is “right” is the subject of the next unit.

title: Exercise: marching cubes
text:
Where this leads
The mesh is a measurement instrument: the next unit computes areas and volumes from it, compares them with counting voxels, and looks at the choice of c, smoothing, anisotropic voxels and mesh size. Rendering the mesh (projection, rasterisation, Lambert and Phong shading) is the 3D-graphics day.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: one σ for the whole image. But a nucleus is a blob at σ ≈ 10 pixels and texture at σ ≈ 1. Today: look at all scales at once.

Scale space: the stack of all blurred versions of an image.
Why the Gaussian: blurring removes structure, never invents it.
Second derivatives: zero crossings mark edges; the Laplacian of Gaussian finds blobs.
Scale normalisation (× σ²): each blob picks its own scale, and the scale gives its size (radius ≈ √2·σ).
The difference of Gaussians and image pyramids: the cheap versions.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Structures exist at a scale


At σ = 1 we see texture and membranes; at σ = 4 the granules and the nuclear envelope; at σ = 16 only the nucleus and the cell as a whole.
There is no single “right” σ for a whole image: each structure has its own.
A leaf vein is an edge pair at a fine scale and a line at a coarser one.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Scale space
Compute the blurred image L(x, y; \sigma) = G_\sigma * I for every σ: a stack, with σ as a third axis.

For a 1D signal the stack is a 2D picture: position x across, σ up (on a log scale, so each doubling of σ gets the same height).
Follow a feature (a bump, an edge) as σ grows: it traces a curve in this picture, and the curve ends where the feature merges into a coarser one.
Fine noise lives only at the bottom (small σ); a large structure survives up to large σ.

The demo shows the stack of L, of the slope and of the curvature, with the features traced.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Why the Gaussian?
What we want from blurring: as σ grows, structure should only disappear, never appear.

In 1D, Gaussian blurring never creates a new extremum (bump or dip) or a new zero crossing as σ grows. Curves in scale space end; they never start.
Blurring by σ₁ and then by σ₂ is one blur by \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}: the scales form a chain, so any level can be computed from a finer one.
Among smoothing kernels, the Gaussian is the only one with both properties (Babaud et al. 1986; Lindeberg).
A box kernel of the same width can create new bumps: try it in the demo.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
section: The math: scale space as diffusion
text:
The math: scale space as diffusion

L = G_\sigma * I solves the heat equation \partial_t L = \tfrac12\nabla^2 L with “time” t = \sigma^2 and L(\cdot, 0) = I: blurring is heat flowing from bright to dark.
Semigroup: in Fourier space a Gaussian is a Gaussian, \widehat{G_\sigma}(\omega) = e^{-\sigma^2\omega^2/2}, so

\widehat{G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2}} = e^{-\sigma_1^2\omega^2/2}e^{-\sigma_2^2\omega^2/2} = e^{-(\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)\omega^2/2} \;\Rightarrow\; G_{\sigma_1} * G_{\sigma_2} = G_{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}}.

Causality (Koenderink 1984): by the heat equation, a local maximum can only decrease and a minimum only increase as t grows, so in 1D extrema can merge and vanish but not be created.
Honest note: in 2D, new local extrema can appear in rare configurations; the exact statement is about level sets (a weaker causality). It does not matter in practice.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Try it: a 1D scale space




Top: the signal (three box bumps of half-widths 2, 6 and 18) and its blur. Middle: the scale-space image, x across, σ up from 0.5 to 32 (log); the dots trace the extrema of L. Bottom: the response at the clicked x against σ. Tour: “three bumps” (L): each bump’s maximum survives up to a σ that grows with its width, then merges with the dip next to it. “Box kernel creates structure”: the bright line in a dark band; at σ = 8 the box blur (27 pixels wide) splits the line into two bumps (5 extrema instead of 3); the Gaussian never does. “Noise lives at small σ”: noise 10, L has 143 extrema at σ = 0.5, 45 at σ = 2, 18 at σ = 3.9. Then the curvature presets, which belong to the next slides.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Second derivatives and zero crossings
The Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) \nabla^2 L = L_{xx} + L_{yy} (the Laplacian from the filtering unit, applied to the blurred image):

At an edge it is positive on the dark side and negative on the bright side: it crosses zero exactly at the edge, where the slope is steepest.
Zero crossings of the LoG are edges (Marr & Hildreth, 1980). They always form closed contours.
Compared with Canny: no thresholds on a ridge and no thinning needed, but many weak spurious contours, and corners are badly rounded. Canny won for edges.
The LoG is much better at something else: blobs.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Blobs: the Laplacian of Gaussian



A bright blob gives a strongly negative LoG at its centre (brightness curves down in every direction).
We use -\nabla^2 L, so bright blobs are positive. As a kernel, -\nabla^2 G_\sigma is the “Mexican hat”: a positive centre and a negative ring.
The response is strongest when the hat’s centre fits the blob: too small a σ sees only the flat inside, too large a σ averages the blob away.
So the best σ tells us the size of the blob.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Why scale-normalise?


Blurring flattens the image, so raw derivatives shrink as σ grows: the raw LoG always prefers small σ, and a large blob loses to a small one.
Multiply by σ² (σ per derivative): this measures distances in units of σ, making scales comparable.
Now each blob’s response, plotted against σ, has a maximum at its own scale: automatic scale selection (Lindeberg).

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Size from scale
For a disc of radius r, the normalised LoG at its centre peaks at \sigma = r/\sqrt2.

So a detection at scale σ is drawn as a circle of radius \sqrt2\,\sigma.
Example: a blob detected at σ = 5 pixels has radius \sqrt2 \cdot 5 = 7.1 pixels; at 0.2 µm per pixel its diameter is 2 \cdot 7.1 \cdot 0.2 = 2.8 µm.
A Gaussian spot of width s peaks at \sigma = s.
1D: a box of half-width a peaks at \sigma = a (the demo’s three bumps: σ = 2, 6.14 and 17.67 on its grid of scales, for a = 2, 6 and 18).

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
section: The math: normalisation and blob size
text:
The math: normalisation and blob size

1D box of half-width a, height 1: L(x) = \Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x + a}{\sigma}\big) - \Phi\!\big(\tfrac{x - a}{\sigma}\big), so \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -2\,\tfrac{a}{\sigma}\,\varphi\!\big(\tfrac{a}{\sigma}\big) \propto -\tfrac{a}{\sigma}e^{-a^2/2\sigma^2}, maximal in size where \tfrac{d}{du}\big(u e^{-u^2/2}\big) = 0: u = a/\sigma = 1.
2D disc of radius r: by the divergence theorem, \nabla^2 L(0) = \oint \nabla G_\sigma\cdot\mathbf n\,ds over the circle, so \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{r^2}{\sigma^2}\,e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2},\qquad \text{maximal in size at } r^2/\sigma^2 = 2,\; r = \sqrt2\,\sigma.
Gaussian blob of width s: \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) \propto -\sigma^2/(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2, maximal at \sigma = s.
Why exactly σ²: for derivatives of order m, normalise by \sigma^{\gamma m}; \gamma = 1 makes the response of a scaled copy of the image identical at the scaled σ (scale invariance). Other γ are used for ridges and edges (Lindeberg 1998); stated, not derived here.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Detection: maxima in (x, y, \sigma)
Compute -\sigma^2\nabla^2 L for a range of σ (e.g. 16 levels from 1 to 16) and look for local maxima in 3D: larger than all 26 neighbours (8 in the same scale, 9 above, 9 below), and above a threshold. Draw each as a circle of radius \sqrt2\,\sigma.
What goes wrong:

Touching blobs: one big blob or two small ones, depending on the scales.
Elongated blobs: respond at their width, not their length; several small detections along them.
Edges give weak responses along their sides (about a third of a blob’s): a threshold, or the Hessian test of the next unit, rejects them.
Uneven background: the LoG ignores constant and linear brightness changes, an advantage over thresholding.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Try it: blobs over scales




256 × 256 synthetic: discs of radii 2–20, Gaussian spots, a touching pair, an elongated blob, uneven background, noise 6. The scale space (16 levels, σ = 1 … 16) is computed once; the σ slider only indexes it. Tour: “one σ finds one size” (σ = 4.39): 13 maxima, 8 of 15 blobs, all circles the same size. “All scales, normalised” (threshold 26): 28 detections, 14 of 15 blobs, circles of the right size; click the disc at (146, 30): its curve peaks at σ = 3.65, radius 5.2 (true 6). “Raw LoG”: every detection sits at σ = 1; the big discs are missed. “Radius = √2·σ” with the truth: the r = 20 disc is found at σ = 13.3, radius 18.8. “Touching blobs”: two circles at σ = 6.35 plus one big one around both (σ = 11.1). “Elongated blob”: a row of small detections along it. “DoG matches LoG” (k = 1.2): almost the same result (21 detections, 13 of 15 blobs, against 28 and 14 for the LoG at threshold 26).

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Difference of Gaussians
Subtract two blurs: \text{DoG} = G_{k\sigma} * I - G_\sigma * I (with k = 1.2 to 1.6).

It looks like (minus) a Mexican hat: a narrow positive centre minus a wider bump.
\text{DoG} \approx (k - 1)\,\sigma^2\,\nabla^2 L: already scale-normalised.
The blurs are needed anyway for scale space, so neighbouring levels give the DoG for free.
Example (1D, a Gaussian bump of width 3 and height 100, σ = 2, k = 1.2): at the centre the two blurs are 83.21 and 78.09, DoG = −5.12; (k - 1)\sigma^2 L_{xx} = 0.2 \cdot 4 \cdot (-6.40) = -5.12.

Pointer: scale-invariant keypoints (SIFT, Lowe 2004) are DoG extrema in a pyramid, plus an orientation from the gradient.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
The math: DoG ≈ LoG
The Gaussian satisfies the heat equation in the form \partial_\sigma G_\sigma = \sigma\,\nabla^2 G_\sigma (check by differentiating \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}). A finite difference in σ:
G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k\sigma - \sigma)\,\partial_\sigma G_\sigma = (k - 1)\,\sigma^2\,\nabla^2 G_\sigma.

The factor σ² appears by itself: the DoG is the normalised LoG, up to the constant k - 1.
The error is of order (k - 1)^2: for k = 1.2 a few percent, for k = 1.6 (Marr’s choice) noticeably more, but the shape is the same.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Image pyramids
After blurring by σ there is no detail finer than about σ: we can keep fewer pixels.

Gaussian pyramid: blur, keep every second pixel in each direction, repeat. Each level has ¼ of the pixels of the one before: total 1 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{16} + \dots = \tfrac43 of the image.
Blur before downsampling, or fine detail aliases into false coarse patterns (recall the Fourier unit).
Laplacian pyramid: each level minus the (upsampled) next level, a DoG; the coarsest level is kept as it is. Adding the levels back up gives the image exactly.
Uses: coarse-to-fine search (registration, active shape models), fast large filters, image blending, mipmaps in computer graphics.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
section: The math: the Laplacian pyramid is exact
text:
The math: the Laplacian pyramid is exact
Let g_0 = I, g_{i+1} = \text{down}(G * g_i) and l_i = g_i - \text{up}(g_{i+1}) for i < n, l_n = g_n.

Reconstruction from the top: g_n = l_n, and g_i = l_i + \text{up}(g_{i+1}) for i = n-1, \dots, 0.
This is a telescoping sum: whatever \text{up} and \text{down} are, g_0 = l_0 + \text{up}(l_1 + \text{up}(l_2 + \dots)) holds exactly, because each l_i was defined as the difference.
The pyramid has \tfrac43 as many numbers as the image, but most l_i values are near zero: the basis of early image compression (Burt & Adelson 1983).

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Where this leads

Hessian (next unit): the LoG is the trace of the Hessian; its two eigenvalues tell a blob from a ridge, and reject edges.
Wavelets (transforms elective): the Mexican hat is a wavelet; à trous spot detection.
Integral images (detection elective): box filters as fast approximations of Gaussians and DoG.
Spot detection in fluorescence images: LoG/DoG at a known spot size, then local maxima.

title: Scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Summary

Scale space: all blurred versions L(x, y; \sigma) at once. The Gaussian is the kernel that never creates structure; scales chain: \sigma^2 adds.
LoG: zero crossings = edges (Marr–Hildreth); -\nabla^2 L = blob detector (Mexican hat).
Normalise by σ², then each blob’s response peaks at its own σ; radius ≈ √2·σ.
Detect blobs as maxima in (x, y, σ); watch touching, elongated blobs and edges.
DoG ≈ (k − 1)·normalised LoG; pyramids: 4/3 of the pixels, Laplacian pyramid exactly invertible.

title: Quiz: the 2D wavelet transform
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Subbands: LL (approximation), V (high-pass along x: vertical edges), H (high-pass along y: horizontal edges), D (diagonal).

Q1. How is the 2D wavelet transform computed from the 1D one?






Hint





As for the 2D DFT.









Answer





Separably: one level of the 1D filter bank on every row (low-pass half left, high-pass half right), then on every column of the result (low top, high bottom). This gives the four subbands; further levels repeat this on LL only.




Q2. An image shows a single vertical line. Which detail band at level 1 lights up?






Hint





Along which axis does the image change?









Answer





V: the image changes along x (across the line), so the band that is high-pass along x responds. Along y the line is constant, so H and D stay near 0 (except at the line’s ends).




Q3. Compute the Haar subbands of the block \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 4\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}.






Hint





LL = \tfrac12(a+b+c+d), V = \tfrac12(a-b+c-d), H = \tfrac12(a+b-c-d), D = \tfrac12(a-b-c+d).









Answer





LL = 4, V = 0, H = 4, D = 0: a horizontal edge (bright top, dark bottom) lights only H.




Q4. A 512 \times 512 image is transformed with 5 levels. How big is the final LL, and how many coefficients are there in total?






Hint





Each level halves both sides of LL.









Answer





512/2^5 = 16: LL is 16 \times 16. Total: still 512^2 = 262\,144 coefficients, a change of basis.




Q5. Why are the detail coefficients of a photograph or micrograph mostly small, with a few very large ones?






Hint





What does a detail coefficient see in a flat region, and at an edge?









Answer





Most of an image is smooth or flat locally, where the high-pass filters give near-zero output. Large details appear only where the filter covers an edge or a small structure, which is a small part of the image. The histogram is sharply peaked at 0 with heavy tails: the image is sparse in the wavelet basis.




Q6. With 3 % of the coefficients, a Haar reconstruction looks blocky and a db4 reconstruction blurred. Why?






Hint





What do the basis functions look like?









Answer





A reconstruction is a sum of the kept basis functions. Haar basis functions are piecewise-constant squares, so missing details leave square steps; db4 basis functions are smooth bumps, so missing details leave a smooth blur (with slight ringing from their small side lobes).




Q7. Keeping 5 % of the coefficients is not a compression ratio of 20. Why not?






Hint





What else must be stored?









Answer





The decoder also needs the positions of the kept coefficients (16 bits each for a 256 \times 256 image), and the values need bits too. With 8 bits per value and 16 per position, 5 % gives a ratio of about 6.7. Real codecs quantise and entropy-code to do better (compression day).




Q8. (math) Show that the 2D Haar subbands of a 2 \times 2 block form an orthonormal change of basis, by writing the four “basis images”.






Hint





Each subband value is \langleblock, basis image\rangle.









Answer





The basis images are \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\1 & 1\end{pmatrix} (LL), \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\1 & -1\end{pmatrix} (V), \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\-1 & -1\end{pmatrix} (H), \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\-1 & 1\end{pmatrix} (D). Each has squared entries summing to 4 \cdot \tfrac14 = 1, and any two have an entrywise product summing to 0 (two + and two - products). So they are orthonormal in \mathbb R^4, and the block is the sum of the subband values times its basis images.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

read a scale-space picture and explain why the Gaussian never creates structure,
find the best scale of a blob from its normalised response, and turn a scale into a size (radius ≈ √2·σ),
compute a difference of Gaussians and compare it with the LoG,
work out the size and cost of an image pyramid,

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Scale space
L(x, y; \sigma) = G_\sigma * I for all σ; blurs chain: \sigma^2 adds


LoG
\nabla^2 L = L_{xx} + L_{yy}; zero crossings at edges; -\nabla^2 L large at bright blobs


Normalised LoG
-\sigma^2\nabla^2 L: comparable across scales; peaks at the blob’s own scale


Size from scale
disc of radius r: peak at \sigma = r/\sqrt2 (draw radius \sqrt2\,\sigma); Gaussian spot of width s: \sigma = s; 1D box of half-width a: \sigma = a


Detection
local maxima of -\sigma^2\nabla^2 L in (x, y, \sigma) (26 neighbours) above a threshold


DoG
G_{k\sigma} * I - G_\sigma * I \approx (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 L


Pyramids
Gaussian: blur, keep every 2nd pixel, repeat (total 4/3 of the image); Laplacian: level − upsampled next level, exactly invertible

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids

Compute the DoG row (σ = 2.4 minus σ = 2). (b) Compute (k - 1)\sigma^2 L_{xx}. How close are they? (c) Where is the DoG most negative, and what does a negative value mean here?

B4. Pyramids. (a) List the side lengths of the Gaussian pyramid of a 1024 × 1024 image down to 1 × 1, and the total number of pixels. Compare with \tfrac43 \cdot 1024^2. (b) A Gaussian blur with σ = 16 (kernel cut at 4σ) applied separably to the full image: how many multiplications? The same smoothing is roughly a σ = 1 blur at level 4 (64 × 64): how many multiplications there? (Building levels 1–4 with σ = 1 blurs costs about 25 million.) (c) Why must each level be blurred before taking every second pixel? What would go wrong with a fine stripe pattern?
B5. Predict. You run blob detection over σ = 1 … 16 on an image, then on the same image enlarged ×2 (each pixel becomes 2 × 2). (a) What happens to the scale and the radius of each detection? To the normalised response values? To the number of detections? (b) What would happen to the raw (unnormalised) response values?
B6. A row of LoG values across an edge: 3.1, 2.4, 0.9, −0.9, −2.4, −3.1 (pixels 0 to 5). Where is the edge (Marr–Hildreth)? Which side is brighter?






Solutions





B1. (a) σ = 3 (48.4) wins: the half-width is 3, as expected for a box (\sigma = a). (b) Half-width 6, so width 12. (c) Divided by σ²: 2.7, 9.7, 5.4, 2.8, 1.0: σ = 2 would win, too small. Without normalisation the curve is pushed towards small σ (here it still has a maximum, at a/\sqrt3 \approx 1.7 for a box; for a disc in 2D at r/2).
B2. (a) r = \sqrt2 \cdot 5 = 7.07 pixels; diameter 14.1 pixels = 2.83 µm. (b) Diameter 10 µm = 50 pixels, radius 25 pixels, so \sigma = 25/\sqrt2 = 17.7: just above the range; σ should go up to about 20 (or the image should be shrunk ×2 first, i.e. one pyramid level down).
B3. (a) DoG: 0.45, −3.15, −5.12, −3.15, 0.45. (b) (k - 1)\sigma^2 = 0.2 \cdot 4 = 0.8, so 0.8\,L_{xx} = 0.64, −3.04, −5.12, −3.04, 0.64. At the centre they agree to two decimals; in the tails the DoG is a little smaller (the approximation has an error of order (k - 1)^2). (c) Most negative at the centre, x = 0: blurring more lowers the peak (the bump flattens), which is what a negative curvature means. With the sign flipped, -\text{DoG} is the Mexican-hat response, largest at the blob’s centre.
B4. (a) 1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: 11 levels, 1\,398\,101 pixels in total, = \tfrac43 \cdot 1024^2 = 1\,398\,101.3 (the geometric series stops at 1 × 1). (b) σ = 16: 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 16 + 1 = 129 taps, 2 \cdot 129 = 258 multiplications per pixel, 258 \cdot 1024^2 \approx 271 million. At level 4: 9 taps, 18 \cdot 64^2 = 73\,728; with the 25 million for building the levels, about 10 times cheaper, and the other levels come for free. (c) Taking every second pixel can only represent detail coarser than 2 pixels (Nyquist, Fourier unit). Finer detail is not removed but aliased: a fine stripe pattern turns into false coarse stripes (moiré). The blur removes the fine detail first.
B5. (a) Every detection moves to σ × 2 and radius × 2, at position × 2; the normalised responses stay the same (scale invariance), and the number of detections stays the same, provided 2σ is still inside the scale range (detections near σ = 16 drop out; new ones at σ < 2 may appear only from finer detail, of which there is none). (b) Raw values drop by a factor of 4 (second derivatives scale as 1/\text{length}^2): the same blobs would look weaker, which is why the raw LoG cannot compare scales.
B6. The zero crossing is between pixels 2 and 3, halfway (0.9 and −0.9): the edge is at 2.5. The LoG is positive on the dark side and negative on the bright side, so the brighter side is towards pixel 5.




Math questions
B7. (math) (a) For a 1D box of half-width a, show that \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -2\frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi\big(\frac{a}{\sigma}\big) (\varphi = standard normal density) and that its size is maximal at \sigma = a. (b) For a 2D disc of radius r and height 1, use \nabla^2 L(0) = \oint_{|\mathbf u| = r}\nabla G_\sigma\cdot\mathbf n\,ds to show \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{r^2}{\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, maximal in size at r = \sqrt2\,\sigma.
B8. (math) Show that the 2D Gaussian G_\sigma(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2\sigma^2} satisfies \partial_\sigma G_\sigma = \sigma\,\nabla^2 G_\sigma, and conclude G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 G_\sigma.
B9. (math) A Gaussian blob of width s: I = A\,e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2s^2}. Show that L = G_\sigma * I = \frac{A s^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}e^{-(x^2 + y^2)/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)} (semigroup), compute \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) and find the σ where it is largest in size.






Solutions (math)





B7. (a) L(x) = \int_{-a}^{a} g_\sigma(x - u)\,du = \Phi\big(\frac{x + a}{\sigma}\big) - \Phi\big(\frac{x - a}{\sigma}\big). Differentiating twice: L_{xx}(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big[\varphi'\big(\frac{x + a}{\sigma}\big) - \varphi'\big(\frac{x - a}{\sigma}\big)\big] with \varphi'(t) = -t\varphi(t), so L_{xx}(0) = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big[-\frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi(\frac a\sigma) - \frac{a}{\sigma}\varphi(\frac a\sigma)\big] and \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -2u\varphi(u) with u = a/\sigma. \frac{d}{du}u e^{-u^2/2} = (1 - u^2)e^{-u^2/2} = 0 at u = 1: \sigma = a. (b) \nabla^2 L(0) = \int_{\text{disc}}\nabla^2 G_\sigma(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u (the Gaussian is symmetric), and the divergence theorem turns this into the flux of \nabla G_\sigma through the circle. On the circle \nabla G_\sigma\cdot\mathbf n = \partial_r G_\sigma = -\frac{r}{\sigma^2}\frac{1}{2\pi\sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, constant, times the length 2\pi r: \nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{r^2}{\sigma^4}e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}, so \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -v\,e^{-v/2} with v = r^2/\sigma^2, largest in size at v = 2: r = \sqrt2\,\sigma.
B8. \partial_\sigma G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(-\frac{2}{\sigma} + \frac{x^2 + y^2}{\sigma^3}\big). And \partial_{xx}G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(\frac{x^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\big), likewise in y, so \nabla^2 G_\sigma = G_\sigma\big(\frac{x^2 + y^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{2}{\sigma^2}\big) and \sigma\nabla^2 G_\sigma = \partial_\sigma G_\sigma. A first-order Taylor step in σ: G_{k\sigma} - G_\sigma \approx (k\sigma - \sigma)\,\partial_\sigma G_\sigma = (k - 1)\sigma^2\nabla^2 G_\sigma.
B9. I = 2\pi s^2 A\,G_s, so L = 2\pi s^2 A\,G_{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}} = \frac{A s^2}{s^2 + \sigma^2}e^{-r^2/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)}. With v = s^2 + \sigma^2, \nabla^2 e^{-r^2/2v} at r = 0 is -2/v, so \sigma^2\nabla^2 L(0) = -\frac{2As^2\sigma^2}{(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2}. Maximise \sigma^2/(s^2 + \sigma^2)^2: the derivative in \sigma^2 is \frac{(s^2 + \sigma^2) - 2\sigma^2}{(s^2 + \sigma^2)^3} = 0 at \sigma = s, where the value is -A/2.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Explore: a 1D scale space
A 1D signal of 256 pixels: three box bumps of half-widths 2, 6 and 18 (at x ≈ 40, 100, 180); a step and a ramp; a bright line in a dark band; or a line through the micrograph. Top: the signal and its blur at the current σ. Middle: the scale-space image (x across, σ from 0.5 to 32 upwards on a log axis) of L, the slope or the curvature, with features traced as dots. Bottom: the response at the clicked x against σ, normalised (red) and raw (grey). Click the scale-space image to choose both x and σ.



S1. Preset noise lives at small σ (noise 10, L). Count roughly how many dots (extrema of L) there are along the bottom row of the scale-space image and how many survive at σ ≈ 4. Where do the surviving curves lead?
S2. Preset raw LoG prefers small σ (curvature, not normalised, x = 99, the centre of the bump with half-width 6). At which σ does the grey (raw) curve peak, and at which the red (normalised) one? Click the centres of the other two bumps: compare the heights of their raw and of their normalised peaks.
S3. Preset normalised: each bump picks its σ. Read the peak σ for the three bumps and compare with their half-widths 2, 6 and 18.
S4. Preset edges and bumps as curves (step and ramp, slope \sigma L_x). Click on the step (x = 69) and on the middle of the ramp (x = 170). How does \sigma L_x change with σ at each? Why does the step give the same value at every scale?
S5. Preset box kernel creates structure (σ = 8). What happens to the bright line in the blurred signal? Untick box kernel: what does the Gaussian of the same σ do? Find the σ at which the box blur first splits the line.






Solutions





S1. At σ = 0.5 the noisy signal has 143 extrema; at σ ≈ 1, 93; at σ = 2, 45; at σ ≈ 3.9, only 18. The noise extrema form short curves at the bottom that end quickly; the curves that continue upwards belong to the three bumps (and the dips between them). Curves end as σ grows; none starts.
S2. Raw: peak at σ = 3.39 (value 2.57); normalised: σ = 6.14 (value 48.3). Raw peaks are 23.77 (half-width 2), 2.57 (6) and 0.29 (18): the small bump wins by far, although all three have the same height. Normalised peaks are 46.5, 48.3 and 48.6: equal, as they should be for the same shape at different sizes.
S3. σ = 2.00, 6.14 and 17.67, close to the half-widths 2, 6 and 18 (the demo’s 64 scales are spaced by 7 %, so 6 and 18 fall between grid points).
S4. At the step \sigma L_x = 43.3 (σ ≈ 1), 46.9 (2), 47.6 (3.9), 47.8 (8), 47.9 (15.5): constant. A step looks the same at every scale; normalised, its response is 120/\sqrt{2\pi} = 47.9 for a step of 120. At the ramp centre (slope 100/60 per pixel): −1.6, −3.3, −6.5, −13.3, −24.5, i.e. \sigma times the slope, growing until σ is comparable to the ramp’s length (60 pixels). A ramp is an edge at a coarse scale.
S5. With the box (27 pixels wide at σ = 8) the line becomes two bumps with a dip in between (5 extrema instead of 3: at the centre L = 46.7, at x = 118 it is 51.1). The Gaussian keeps one maximum at the centre (54.9). On the demo’s grid of scales the box first splits the line at σ = 8.00 (27 pixels wide); at σ = 7.49 (25 pixels) it still has 3 extrema. The Gaussian never does, at any σ.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Explore: blobs over scales
A 256 × 256 synthetic image (discs of radii 2–20 px, Gaussian spots, a touching pair, an elongated blob, a faint disc, on an uneven background with noise; the truth is known) or the micrograph. The normalised response -\sigma^2\nabla^2 L (or the DoG) is computed for 16 scales σ = 1 … 16. Detections are circles of radius \sqrt2\,\sigma, coloured by scale. The middle panel shows the response at the current σ (0 = grey), the plot below it the response at the clicked pixel against σ. The readout scores detections against the truth (a hit is within max(3, r/2) pixels of a true centre). Pyramid shows the Gaussian and Laplacian pyramids.



E1. Preset one σ finds one size (σ = 4.39, maxima at this σ only). How many detections, how many of the 15 blobs are hit? Which are missed? Move σ to 1.45 and to 9.19: which blobs are found now?
E2. Preset all scales, normalised (threshold 26). How many detections and hits? Which blob is missed, and which false alarms remain? Click the disc at (146, 30) (true radius 6): at which σ does its curve peak, and what radius does that give?
E3. Preset raw LoG: only the small spots (normalise off, threshold 12). At which σ are all detections? Which blobs are found? Click the centre of the disc at (120, 92) and compare the grey and red curves.
E4. Preset radius = √2·σ (truth overlay). Compare the circles with the dashed truth for the discs of radius 3, 9 and 20. Are the radii right? What about the Gaussian spots?
E5. Presets touching blobs and elongated blob. Describe what is detected in each case and why.
E6. Preset low threshold: edges respond too (threshold 18). Where do the extra detections appear, and at which scales? Compare the response of an edge with that of a blob.
E7. Preset DoG matches LoG (k = 1.2). Compare detections with all scales, normalised. Increase k to 1.6: what changes?
E8. Preset uneven background does not matter (σ = 16). Look at the response map: does the bright patch in the lower right (no blobs) give a strong response? Why not?
E9. Preset the pyramid. How many pixels does the Gaussian pyramid hold, and what is the reconstruction error of the Laplacian pyramid? Why is it not exactly 0 in the readout?
E10. Preset dark granules in the micrograph (dark blobs, threshold 50). What is detected? Click the dark granule near (106, 68): at which σ does it respond best?






Solutions





E1. At σ = 4.39: 13 detections, 8 hits, 5 false alarms; missed are the smallest discs (r = 2, 3) and the large ones (r = 12, 16, 20), the elongated blob and the faint disc. All circles have the same radius \sqrt2 \cdot 4.39 = 6.2. At σ = 1.45 only the small blobs are hit (4 hits, 12 detections); at σ = 9.19 the large ones (8 hits, 12 detections) but not the small. One σ finds one size.
E2. 28 detections, 14 hits, 14 false alarms; missed is the elongated blob (its centre is not a maximum; detections lie along it). Of the false alarms, 9 sit along the elongated blob, 2 in the notch of the touching pair, and 3 at the rims of discs. The disc at (146, 30) peaks at σ = 3.65: radius \sqrt2 \cdot 3.65 = 5.2 (true 6; the scales are 20 % apart, and the predicted σ = 4.24 lies between 3.65 and 4.39).
E3. Every detection is at the smallest scale, σ = 1 (radius 1.4): 146 detections, mostly noise, and only 5 hits (the discs of radius 2, 3, 4 and the two small Gaussian spots). At (120, 92) the raw curve is tiny and peaks at σ = 7.64; the normalised one peaks at σ = 11.06 with value 36.1 (radius 15.6, true 16).
E4. Radius 3: σ = 2.09, circle 3.0; radius 9: σ = 6.35, circle 9.0; radius 20: σ = 13.30, circle 18.8. Within one scale step (20 %) of the truth, slightly small for the largest. Gaussian spots of width 2, 4, 7 are found at σ = 2.09, 3.65, 7.64, close to their widths; their dashed circles are drawn at \sqrt2 s.
E5. Touching pair (two discs of radius 10 touching at (54, 215)): two circles at σ = 6.35 (radius 9.0) on the discs, plus one large circle at σ = 11.06 around both (and a small false alarm in the notch): the pair is also a blob at a coarser scale. Elongated blob (26 × 5): a row of small detections along it at σ = 1.2 to 5.3: the LoG fits the width (5), not the length.
E6. 102 detections (88 false alarms): small circles along the rims of the larger discs (35 on the disc of radius 20 alone), along the elongated blob and around the touching pair, almost all at small σ (1.2 to 3.65). The normalised response of a straight edge is at most 0.24 \times its contrast, that of a blob of the same contrast 0.74 \times: about a third. A threshold between the two separates them, as long as blob contrasts are not too different.
E7. At k = 1.2: 21 detections, 13 hits (8 false alarms), nearly the same blobs as the LoG; the smallest disc (r = 2) is missed. At k = 1.6: 17 detections, 12 hits; the faint disc also goes. Larger k smooths over a wider range of scales: fewer false alarms, but the response is less selective and weak or tiny blobs drop below the threshold.
E8. Hardly: at the centre of the patch (180, 192) the noise-free response at σ = 16 is only 5.0, far below the threshold. A smooth background is almost linear over the width of the Mexican hat, and the LoG of a constant or linear function is 0. A global threshold on the image itself would be thrown off by the same patch.
E9. 87 296 pixels for 256² (65 536) and its levels: 4/3 as many. The reconstruction error is about 10^{-6}: exact up to the rounding of 32-bit floating-point numbers (the telescoping sum is exact in real arithmetic).
E10. Dark granules, vesicles and dark spots in the fibrous background: 144 detections at threshold 50 (no truth for this image). The granule near (106, 68) responds best at σ = 3.65 (radius 5.2). The nucleus itself, about 45 pixels in radius, would need σ ≈ 32, outside the range.

title: Exercise: scale space, blobs and pyramids
text:
Where this leads
The LoG is the trace of the Hessian: it adds the curvatures in two directions and cannot tell a blob from a line. The next unit uses both curvatures separately: blobs, ridges and saddles, and vesselness.

title: Continuous MRFs: quadratic smoothing and total variation
section: Quadratic versus TV on a noisy profile
text:
Quadratic versus TV on a noisy profile


Quadratic (\lambda = 10): noise gone, but the step is spread over about 15 samples and the narrow peak drops from 2 to 0.9.
TV (\lambda = 1): the step stays sharp, the flat parts are flat, the ramp becomes a staircase, the peak drops to 1.4.
Error against the truth (RMSE): noisy data 0.29, quadratic 0.24, TV 0.14.

title: Marching cubes
text:
About this lecture
Marching squares drew the boundary \{I = c\} of a 2D image as curves. The same idea in a volume gives a surface made of triangles: marching cubes (Lorensen & Cline, 1987), the standard way to turn a 3D image into a 3D model.

A cell is a cube of 8 voxels: 256 cases, which symmetry reduces to 23 or 15.
The triangle table, and how to generate it from marching squares on the cube’s faces.
Ambiguous faces, cracks, and how to avoid them; marching tetrahedra.
Normals from the image gradient: smooth shading for free.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Builds directly on the previous unit (marching squares, crossing points, saddle cells, the asymptotic decider) and on volumes3d/ (spacing, trilinear interpolation). Rendering (projection, shading) is the 3D-graphics day’s; here it is a pointer. Corner numbering convention of the course: k = x + 2y + 4z, printed on the exercise sheet.

title: Marching cubes
section: The same idea, one dimension up
text:
The same idea, one dimension up





A cell = the cube between 8 neighbouring voxel centres. Corner k = x + 2y + 4z.
Each corner above or below c: an 8-bit case index, 2^8 = 256 cases.
An edge with corners on opposite sides is crossed once; the crossing point by linear interpolation, t = (c - I_a)/(I_b - I_a), as in 2D.
The crossing points are connected by triangles: up to 5 per cube.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Shared edges: one closed mesh

A cube edge is shared by up to 4 cubes, and each computes the same crossing point. Store the point once per grid edge and let all triangles index it: a mesh with shared vertices, not a soup of loose triangles.
With a consistent rule on every face, the triangles of neighbouring cubes meet edge to edge: the surface is closed (watertight), apart from where it leaves the volume. Pad the volume with background to close it.
One pass over the cells: n^3 cubes for an n^3 volume. The output grows with the area of the surface, about n^2 triangles, not with the volume.
For a smooth surface: about 2 triangles per vertex, and about 3 triangles per unit of area (in voxel units).

title: Marching cubes
text:
256 cases, but only 15 shapes


Rotations: turning the cube turns the case into another case with the same surface, turned. The cube has 24 rotations; they group the 256 cases into 23 classes.
Complement: swapping inside and outside gives the same surface with the normals flipped. Rotations + complement: 15 classes (the table of Lorensen & Cline). As we will see, the complement step is not innocent.

title: Marching cubes
text:
The math: counting classes (Burnside)
The number of classes = the average number of cases left unchanged by a rotation. A case is unchanged when all corners in each cycle of the corner permutation have the same state: 2^{\#\text{cycles}} cases.

With the complement as well (48 symmetries; a complement-rotation fixes a case when every cycle has even length and alternates), the same count gives 15.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Generating the triangle table
The table lists, for each of the 256 cases, which edges the triangles connect. We do not copy it; we generate it:

The surface meets each face of the cube in a marching-squares contour: run marching squares on the 6 faces (with a rule for saddle faces).
Every crossed edge belongs to two faces, so the face segments chain into closed loops around the cube.
Triangulate each loop as a fan (a polygon of m points gives m - 2 triangles).


Case 1 (one corner above): one loop of 3 points, 1 triangle. Case 3 (an edge): a loop of 4, 2 triangles.
The face rule is all the table “knows”: change the rule, and you get a different table.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Try it: one cube




Click corners to flip them (orange = above c). Readouts: bits, case index, class among 15 and among 23, the rotation to the representative (“rotate to its representative” animates it). Tour: “one corner” (case 1, one triangle); click corner 1 too: case 3, two triangles, a quad. “Values: vertices slide”: corners 0.9, 0.35, 0.6, … with c = 0.5; move c and the selected corner’s value: the vertices slide along the edges (on edge 0–1, t = 0.73). “The 15 classes”: step through them; class 9 (case 23) is a hexagon. “An ambiguous face”: case 9, face −z tinted; switch separate/join: 2 triangles or 4.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Ambiguous faces and cracks

A face with diagonal corners above is a 2D saddle: the surface may separate or join the two bright corners on that face. 6 of the 15 classes contain such a face (120 of the 256 cases).
The face is shared with the neighbouring cube. If the two cubes choose differently, their triangles end at different points on that face: a crack (a hole) in the surface.
The 15-class table makes exactly this mistake (Dürst, 1988): using the complement swaps “separate” for “join” in cases with many corners above, so neighbours can disagree.
Fixes:

one consistent rule for all faces (e.g. always separate; 23 classes, no complement): closed, but sometimes the wrong topology;
the asymptotic decider on each face (Nielson & Hamann, 1991): consistent, because both cubes see the same 4 face values, and usually the right topology;
ambiguities inside the cube (tunnels) need more cases (Chernyaev’s 33 cases, 1995; Lewiner et al., 2003).

title: Marching cubes
text:
Try it: a crack




Two cubes share the +x face of the left one, which is ambiguous (corners 1 and 7 above). The left cube separates, the right cube joins: their segments on the shared face differ, and the red lines are the 4 crack edges (edges with a triangle on one side only). Set the neighbour’s rule to separate, or both to decider: the crack closes. Then “tetrahedra instead”.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Marching tetrahedra

Split each cube into tetrahedra (5 or 6) and run the same idea per tetrahedron: 4 corners, 2^4 = 16 cases.
Up to symmetry only 3: nothing (all in or all out), one corner separated (1 triangle), two and two (a quad, 2 triangles).
Never ambiguous: no tetrahedron has a face with diagonal corners (its faces are triangles).
Costs: more triangles (often 2–4 times), thin triangles, and a directional bias from the chosen diagonals; the split must match between neighbouring cubes (the 5-tetrahedron split alternates between neighbours).

title: Marching cubes
section: The math: why a tetrahedron is unambiguous
text:
The math: why a tetrahedron is unambiguous

Inside a tetrahedron with corners \mathbf p_0, \dots, \mathbf p_3 every point is \sum \lambda_i \mathbf p_i with barycentric weights \lambda_i \ge 0, \sum\lambda_i = 1. The natural interpolant is f = \sum \lambda_i I_i, which is linear (affine) in \mathbf x.
The level set \{f = c\} of an affine function is a plane. A plane cuts a tetrahedron in nothing, a triangle or a quadrilateral, always connected: no choice to make.
On a shared triangular face, f is the same affine function seen from both sides, so neighbours agree automatically.
The cube’s trilinear interpolant is not affine (its xy, yz, xz, xyz terms bend the level set): that is where the ambiguity comes from.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Normals from the image
To shade a surface we need its normal at every vertex. A level set has one for free:

Moving along the surface, I stays equal to c; moving across it, I changes fastest. So the normal points along the gradient \nabla I.
For a bright object, \nabla I points inwards (towards higher values): the outward normal is \mathbf n = -\nabla I / \lVert\nabla I\rVert.
Compute \nabla I at the voxels by central differences (or Sobel, kernels/), interpolate it trilinearly to each vertex, normalise.
Result: smooth shading from a coarse mesh, because the normals come from the image, not from the facets.

title: Marching cubes
text:
The math: gradient normals

If \mathbf x(s) is any curve on the surface, I(\mathbf x(s)) = c, so \nabla I \cdot \mathbf x'(s) = 0: the gradient is perpendicular to every tangent direction.
Central differences with spacing: \partial_x I \approx \dfrac{I[i+1] - I[i-1]}{2\Delta x}, and likewise with \Delta y, \Delta z. Divided by voxels instead, the z component is \Delta z/\Delta x times too large and the normals tilt.
At a vertex \mathbf v on an edge: \nabla I(\mathbf v) \approx trilinear interpolation of the 8 voxel gradients around it (or linear along the edge).
Face normals instead: \mathbf n = (\mathbf b - \mathbf a) \times (\mathbf c - \mathbf a) per triangle; constant per facet, so the mesh looks faceted. Shading with normals (Lambert, Phong) is the 3D-graphics day.

title: Marching cubes
text:
When gradient normals fail

Noise: the gradient of a noisy image points in random directions; the surface looks speckled. Blur first.
Flat regions: where \lVert\nabla I\rVert \approx 0 (a plateau touching c), the direction is undefined.
Binary images (a 0/1 mask): central differences give only a few directions (combinations of -1, 0, 1), so the normals are as blocky as the mask. Blur the mask slightly first (last unit).
Wrong spacing in the differences: tilted normals, wrong lighting.

title: Marching cubes
section: Try it: marching cubes on a volume
text:
Try it: marching cubes on a volume




48³ volumes, extracted on every change. Tour: “two blobs merge”: lower c from 0.6; at c = 0.49 the two components become one (their saddle value is 0.499); χ drops from 4 to 2. “A torus has a hole”: 1 component, χ = 0. “Noise”: 4324 components (thousands of tiny surfaces); “blur first” (σ = 1.5): one surface again. “Faceted vs gradient normals” with wireframe: the same triangles, shaded two ways. “Wrong z spacing”: the ellipsoid volume drops by 0.4 (7609 → 3044). “Cracks”: the complement rule on a noisy sphere gives 296 boundary edges (red); the decider gives none. Switch to 6 tetrahedra: about 3 times the triangles.

title: Marching cubes
text:
Summary

Marching cubes: per cube of 8 voxels, case index (256) → crossed edges → triangles; vertices by linear interpolation, shared between cubes: a closed, indexed mesh in one pass.
Symmetry: 24 rotations → 23 classes; with the complement → 15.
The triangle table = marching squares on the 6 faces + chaining into loops + fans; the face rule decides it.
Ambiguous faces must be resolved the same way by both neighbours (consistent rule or asymptotic decider), or the surface cracks. Marching tetrahedra is never ambiguous, at the cost of more triangles.
Normals \mathbf n = -\nabla I/\lVert\nabla I\rVert from the image give smooth shading; blur noisy and binary images first.

title: Rectangle features
text:
About this lecture
What simple numbers describe “what is around this pixel” or “what is in this window”, and are cheap enough to compute millions of times?

Haar-like features: the sum over one rectangle minus the sum over its neighbour. Edges, lines, diagonals, blobs.
Each costs 6 to 9 table lookups, whatever its size.
The pool of all such features in a small window is huge, far larger than the number of pixels.
Their relation to the Haar wavelets, and why detection does not need a basis.
The box group of a pixel feature stack: every scale at the same cost.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Builds on the integral image (unit 1) and the local SD (unit 2). The feature stack, the painting loop and the classifier belong to the random forests day; here only the box group and “why large boxes are free”. The next unit selects a few of these features with boosting.

title: Rectangle features
text:
A feature from two rectangles
Place two equal rectangles side by side and take sum(white) − sum(black).

On a flat region: 0. On a vertical edge (dark left, bright right): large and negative; mirrored: positive.
It is a box-smoothed derivative: like the Sobel kernel of the filtering unit, but of any size.
With the integral image the two sums cost 4 lookups each, but they share two corners: 6 lookups in all.

A cartoon face: the band of the eyes is darker than the band of the cheeks below. A two-rectangle feature over both bands gives a strongly negative number on almost every face, whatever the person looks like.

title: Rectangle features
text:
The templates


Edge (two rectangles, across or down): 6 lookups. Line (three rectangles; the centre counts twice so that a flat region gives 0): 8. Diagonal (four rectangles): 9. Centre − surround (a box minus the mean of a larger box): 8.
Any position, any width and height: the cost stays the same.

title: Rectangle features
section: Try it: features on an image
text:
Try it: features on an image




Drag the template (inside: move; yellow handle: resize). Dots: the table entries read, green + and red −, numbered; the readout lists the coefficients (shared corners get 2 or −2). Tour: “eyes are darker than cheeks”: a 90 × 30 two-rectangle feature, response −13 230 (−9.8 per pixel), 6 lookups instead of 2700 pixels. Drag it down to the mouth: the sign changes. “eyes darker than the bridge of the nose”: three rectangles, 8 lookups. “vertical edge on a cell boundary”, with the response at every position: red and blue lines follow the membranes. “centre − surround”: red blobs at cells about as large as the centre box.

title: Rectangle features
text:
Normalising for lighting
The raw response grows with the contrast of the image: a face in dim light gives a smaller number than the same face in bright light.

Divide by the standard deviation of the window (from the two tables of unit 2): the response no longer depends on contrast.
Subtracting the mean is not needed: every template has weights that sum to zero, so adding a constant to the image changes nothing.
Dividing by the area of one rectangle makes features of different sizes comparable (a difference of mean grey levels).

title: Rectangle features
text:
The pool is huge
A detector looks at a 24 \times 24 window. How many features can we place in it?

One template type, e.g. the edge across with rectangles of width w and height h: it covers 2w \times h pixels and fits at (24 - 2w + 1)(24 - h + 1) positions. Summed over all w, h: 43 200.
All five classic types: 162 336 features. Our six types: 170 800.
A 24 \times 24 window has 576 pixels: the pool is about 280 times larger. It is overcomplete: far more features than needed to describe the window.
Each costs 6–9 lookups. Which few are worth computing? The next unit lets boosting choose.

title: Rectangle features
section: The math: features as inner products
text:
The math: features as inner products
A rectangle feature is an inner product with a piecewise-constant mask: f = \langle w, I\rangle = \sum_{x,y} w(x,y)\, I(x,y), \qquad w \in \{-1, 0, 1\} \text{ (or } 2, -\tfrac19\text{)}, \quad \textstyle\sum w = 0. Zero sum: \langle w, I + c\rangle = \langle w, I\rangle, so constant offsets do not matter; normalising by the window SD removes the contrast.
Lookups = the number of distinct corners with a non-zero coefficient: each rectangle adds +1, -1, -1, +1 (times its weight) at its corners; shared corners add up.
Pool size for a template of a \times b cells in a W \times H window: \sum_{w=1}^{\lfloor W/a\rfloor}\ \sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor H/b\rfloor} (W - aw + 1)(H - bh + 1). For the edge across (a = 2, b = 1) in 24 \times 24: (23 + 21 + \dots + 1)(24 + 23 + \dots + 1) = 144 \cdot 300 = 43\,200.

title: Rectangle features
section: The math: an edge feature on a ramp
text:
The math: an edge feature on a ramp
Let I(x, y) = ax + b (a ramp of slope a). An edge feature with two w \times h rectangles, left minus right:
Each pixel on the right is aw brighter than its partner on the left, and there are wh pairs: f = \text{sum(left)} - \text{sum(right)} = -a\,w^2 h. Divided by the rectangle area wh: -aw, the slope times the distance between the two rectangle centres. The edge feature measures the gradient, smoothed over a box: a box version of the Gaussian derivative of the edges day.

title: Rectangle features
text:
Rectangle features and Haar wavelets
The 2D Haar wavelets (wavelets elective) are also differences of rectangle sums: one level of the Haar transform gives the edge features across and down (H and V) and the diagonal one (D), plus the mean (LL).









Haar wavelet transform
Haar-like features




sizes, positions
powers of two, on a fixed grid
every size, every position


number
as many as pixels
hundreds of times more


structure
orthonormal basis: invertible
overcomplete: no inverse


purpose
represent and reconstruct (compression)
discriminate (detection)



A detector does not need to rebuild the image, only to tell faces from background: it can afford a redundant, overcomplete set and pick the useful features.

title: Rectangle features
text:
Feature stacks for pixel classification
Recalled from the random forests day: a pixel classifier gets a feature vector for every pixel, a stack of filtered images at several scales (Gaussian smoothing, derivatives, …).
This day adds the box group, each from the tables of I and I^2:

box mean and box standard deviation (texture), scales 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 px;
centre − surround: mean of a box minus the mean of a box twice as large; a blob detector, the box version of the difference of Gaussians (edges day);
edge features across and down: box-smoothed derivatives.

With the integral image every scale costs the same: large context is free. Gaussian stacks are the usual choice; box stacks are their fast approximation (repeated boxes ≈ Gaussian, unit 2).

title: Rectangle features
section: Try it: a box feature stack
text:
Try it: a box feature stack



Thumbnails: 5 feature types × 5 scales of the micrograph. Paint class A (orange) and B (blue); the scatter plot shows any two features (click a thumbnail: x, red frame; tick y and click: y, green frame) and a threshold on x. Preset “nucleus or cytoplasm?”: with the box mean at 4 px the classes overlap (best single threshold 82 %); click the box SD at 16 px: 99 %. The nucleus is uniformly fine-grained, the cytoplasm has membranes and vesicles: texture at a large scale separates them. That large-scale feature cost the same as the small one. “inspect”: click a pixel to see its 25-number feature vector. No classifier here: day 14 trains a forest on such vectors; the next unit trains a boosted one on rectangle features.

title: Rectangle features
text:
Summary

A rectangle feature is a difference of rectangle sums: edges (6 lookups), lines (8), diagonals (9), centre − surround (8), at any size and position.
Divide by the window’s standard deviation to remove contrast; the weights sum to zero, so offsets do not matter.
The pool in a 24 \times 24 window has about 160 000 features: overcomplete; something must choose.
Haar wavelets are a dyadic, orthonormal subset; Haar-like features drop the basis property because detection needs discrimination, not reconstruction.
The box group of a feature stack gets every scale at the same cost. (Per-object intensity and texture features: the measurements day.)

title: Quiz: rectangle features
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A two-rectangle feature (left − right) is placed on a flat region of grey level 120. What is its response? And on a region that is 120 on the left and 80 on the right, with rectangles of 10 \times 10 pixels?






Answer





Flat: 100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 120 = 0. Edge: 100 \cdot 120 - 100 \cdot 80 = 4000 (a mean difference of 40 grey levels).




Q2. Two rectangle sums cost 4 lookups each. Why does the two-rectangle feature need only 6?






Answer





The two rectangles share a side, so two of their corners are the same table entries. Their coefficients are added (giving \pm 2) and each shared entry is read once: 8 - 2 = 6.




Q3. Which template would you use to find (a) a thin bright vertical line, (b) a horizontal edge, (c) a round dark spot of about 10 pixels?






Answer






The three-rectangle line template across, with the centre rectangle about as wide as the line (positive response). (b) The two-rectangle edge template top − bottom. (c) Centre − surround with a centre box of about 10 pixels: a strongly negative response (the centre is darker than its surroundings).





Q4. Why is the feature response divided by the standard deviation of the detection window?






Answer





To remove the effect of contrast (lighting, camera gain): with twice the contrast every difference doubles, and so does the SD. Dividing makes the response the same. A brightness offset needs no correction, because the weights of every template sum to zero.




Q5. A 24 \times 24 window holds about 160 000 rectangle features but only 576 pixels. Is the feature set a basis? Does that matter for detection?






Answer





No: the features are far more numerous than the pixels, so they are linearly dependent (overcomplete), and the image cannot be uniquely rebuilt from them in a stable way. For detection that does not matter: the aim is to discriminate faces from background, not to reconstruct. The redundancy offers many candidate features; learning picks the useful few.




Q6. How do the 2D Haar wavelets differ from Haar-like features?






Answer





Haar wavelets use only dyadic sizes (powers of two) at fixed grid positions and form an orthonormal basis (the transform is invertible, useful for compression). Haar-like features take every size and position: an overcomplete set, with no inverse, for detection.




Q7. In a box feature stack, why does the box SD at 16 px cost the same as at 1 px?






Answer





Both come from four lookups in the table of I and four in the table of I^2, whatever the window size. Computed directly, the 16 px box (33 \times 33, 1089 pixels) would read 121 times as many pixels per window as the 1 px box (3 \times 3, 9 pixels).




Q8. (math) An edge feature of two w \times h rectangles (left − right) lies on the ramp I(x, y) = 3x + 40. What is its response divided by the area of one rectangle?






Answer





The response is -a w^2 h = -3w^2h; divided by wh: -3w, the slope times the distance w between the centres of the two rectangles.
