title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Rectangle feature
weighted sum of rectangle sums; the weights sum to zero


Edge (two rectangles)
sum(white) − sum(black), side by side or one above the other: 6 lookups


Line (three rectangles)
2\cdotsum(centre) − sum(left) − sum(right): 8 lookups


Diagonal (four rectangles)
top-left + bottom-right − top-right − bottom-left: 9 lookups


Centre − surround
sum(small box) − sum(large box)/9 (large = 3 × 3 small): 8 lookups


Lookups
the distinct table corners with a non-zero coefficient; shared corners are read once


Normalisation
divide by the window’s standard deviation (contrast) and by the rectangle area (size)


Box feature stack
box mean, box SD, centre − surround, edge across, edge down, at scales 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 px



As before, pixels are numbered from 1, x = column, y = row, and S(x, y) is the sum over columns 1..x and rows 1..y (zero for x = 0 or y = 0).

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
By hand
The 6 \times 6 image (row y = 1 on top) and its integral image:
I = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&1&5&5&5 \\ 1&2&1&6&5&5 \\ 1&1&2&5&6&5 \\ 2&1&1&5&5&6 \\ 1&1&1&5&5&5 \\ 1&2&1&5&6&5 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad
S = \begin{bmatrix} 0&0&0&0&0&0&0 \\ 0&1&2&3&8&13&18 \\ 0&2&5&7&18&28&38 \\ 0&3&7&11&27&43&58 \\ 0&5&10&15&36&57&78 \\ 0&6&12&18&44&70&96 \\ 0&7&15&22&53&85&116 \end{bmatrix}
(S has rows y = 0..6 and columns x = 0..6.)
B1. An edge feature, left − right, over rows 2–5: the left rectangle is columns 2–3, the right one columns 4–5. (a) Write each rectangle sum with four lookups. (b) Combine them. Which corners are shared, and what coefficients do they get? How many distinct lookups remain? (c) Compute the response and check it by adding the pixels. What does its sign say about the image?
B2. A line feature, 2\cdotcentre − left − right, over rows 2–5 with one column per rectangle: left = column 3, centre = column 4, right = column 5. (a) List the 8 lookups with their coefficients. (b) Compute the response and check it directly.
B3. Which template? A 6 \times 6 image is 1 everywhere except columns 3 and 4, which are 9 (a bright vertical bar). Four features cover the whole image: (i) edge across (columns 1–3 minus 4–6), (ii) edge down (rows 1–3 minus 4–6), (iii) line across with rectangles 2 columns wide (2\cdotcolumns 3–4 − columns 1–2 − columns 5–6), (iv) diagonal with 3 \times 3 quarters. Predict which respond, then compute all four responses.
B4. Counting. (a) How many edge-across features (two rectangles of w \times h side by side, any w, h \ge 1, any position) fit in an 8 \times 8 window? (b) The same window has 64 pixels. Why does a detector want so many more features than pixels?
B5. Lighting. A face is photographed twice, the second time with twice the contrast and 50 grey levels brighter. What happens to the raw response of the eyes-versus-cheeks feature? What happens after dividing by the window’s standard deviation?
B6. Scales for free. A box feature stack has 5 feature types at 5 scales (1 to 16 px) on a 1000 \times 1000 image. About how many table lookups does the whole stack take? How would the cost of the box mean at 16 px compare if it were computed directly (33 \times 33 window)?






Solutions





B1. (a) Left: S(3,5) - S(3,1) - S(1,5) + S(1,1) = 18 - 3 - 6 + 1 = 10. Right: S(5,5) - S(5,1) - S(3,5) + S(3,1) = 70 - 13 - 18 + 3 = 42. (b) Left − right = 2S(3,5) - 2S(3,1) - S(1,5) + S(1,1) - S(5,5) + S(5,1). The corners S(3,5) and S(3,1) on the shared side appear in both sums and get coefficients +2 and -2: 6 distinct lookups. (c) 36 - 6 - 6 + 1 - 70 + 13 = -32. Directly: left 2+1+1+1 + 1+2+1+1 = 10, right 6+5+5+5 + 5+6+5+5 = 42, difference -32. Negative: the right side is brighter, a dark-to-bright edge from left to right.
B2. (a) Corners lie at x = 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 1, 5: S(2,5) - S(2,1) - 3S(3,5) + 3S(3,1) + 3S(4,5) - 3S(4,1) - S(5,5) + S(5,1). At x = 3 the left rectangle’s right side (-1) meets the centre’s left side (-2): coefficient \mp 3; at x = 4 the centre’s right side (+2) meets the right rectangle’s left side (+1): \pm 3. Eight lookups. (b) -54 + 9 + 12 - 2 + 132 - 24 - 70 + 13 = 16. Directly: column 3 rows 2–5: 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 5; column 4: 6 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 21; column 5: 5 + 6 + 5 + 5 = 21; 2 \cdot 21 - 5 - 21 = 16.
B3. Only (iii) responds. (i): both halves contain one bright column (column 3 left, column 4 right): 0. (ii): the bar runs through both halves equally: 0. (iv): each quarter contains the same amount of bar: 0. (iii): centre columns 3–4: 12 pixels of 9 = 108; each side 12 pixels of 1 = 12; 2 \cdot 108 - 12 - 12 = 192, positive: a bright line on a dark background.
B4. (a) Rectangle width w = 1..4 (the feature is 2w wide), height h = 1..8: \sum_w (9 - 2w) \cdot \sum_h (9 - h) = (7 + 5 + 3 + 1)(8 + 7 + \dots + 1) = 16 \cdot 36 = 576, nine times the number of pixels. (b) The detector does not know in advance which differences of regions matter. A large, redundant pool contains features tuned to every part, size and orientation of the object; the learning step then picks the few that discriminate.
B5. The raw response doubles (twice the contrast); the offset of 50 does not change it, because the weights sum to zero. After dividing by the window SD (which also doubles) the response is the same in both photos.
B6. 25 maps of 10^6 pixels each, each with 4 lookups for a box mean (8 for an SD, which uses two tables; 8 for centre − surround, 6 for an edge): roughly 25 \times 6 \times 10^6 \approx 1.5 \cdot 10^8 lookups, the same at every scale. The box mean at 16 px directly: 33^2 = 1089 pixels per window, about 270 times the 4 lookups.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the edge feature needs 6 distinct corners and the diagonal feature 9, by adding the corner coefficients (+1, -1, -1, +1 times the rectangle’s weight) of all its rectangles. Why does the centre − surround feature need 8 and not fewer?
B8. (math) Let I(x, y) = ax + b. Show that the edge feature “left − right” with two w \times h rectangles gives -a w^2 h, independent of its position and of b. What does an edge feature “top − bottom” give on the same image?
B9. (math) Show that the number of placements of a template of a \times b cells in a W \times H window is \sum_{w=1}^{\lfloor W/a\rfloor}\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor H/b\rfloor}(W - aw + 1)(H - bh + 1), and compute it for the edge across (a = 2, b = 1) in 24 \times 24.






Solutions (math)





B7. A rectangle with weight c puts +c at its top-left and bottom-right corners and -c at the other two. Edge: on the shared side x = x_0 + w, rectangle 1 (c = +1) contributes its top-right (-1) and bottom-right (+1) corners, and rectangle 2 (c = -1) its top-left (+c = -1) and bottom-left (-c = +1) corners. The shared corners get -2 (top) and +2 (bottom): they do not cancel, and with the four outer corners there are 6. Diagonal: the corners form a 3 \times 3 grid. Each outer corner belongs to one rectangle (\pm 1); each edge midpoint to two rectangles of opposite weight, whose contributions have the same sign (\pm 2); the centre to all four, each contributing +1: +4. All 9 are non-zero. Centre − surround: the small box lies strictly inside the large one, so they share no corner: 4 + 4 = 8.
B8. Pair each pixel (x, y) of the left rectangle with (x + w, y) of the right one: their difference is -aw. There are wh pairs, so the response is -aw \cdot wh = -aw^2h; b cancels and the position does not appear. “Top − bottom” pairs pixels with the same x: every difference is 0, so the response is 0. The feature responds to the component of the gradient across its two rectangles.
B9. For cell sizes w (width) and h (height) the template covers aw \times bh pixels and its top-left corner can be at W - aw + 1 horizontal and H - bh + 1 vertical positions; w ranges over 1..\lfloor W/a\rfloor and h over 1..\lfloor H/b\rfloor. For a = 2, b = 1, W = H = 24: \sum_{w=1}^{12}(25 - 2w) = 144 and \sum_{h=1}^{24}(25 - h) = 300, product 43\,200.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Explore: rectangle features on images
Drag the template over the image: inside it to move it, the yellow handle to resize it. White rectangles count +, black -; the dots are the table entries read (green +, red -), numbered, and the readout lists their coefficients, the response (also per pixel of one rectangle), the number of lookups and the number of pixels a direct sum would add. response at every position shows the response with its centre at each pixel (red positive, blue negative).



E1. Preset eyes are darker than cheeks. Read the response, the response per pixel, the lookups and the pixels a direct sum adds. Drag the feature down over the mouth, then onto the background. What happens to the sign and size?
E2. Preset eyes darker than the bridge of the nose. How many lookups? Compare with B2. Explain the sign of the response.
E3. Choose each template in turn and count the dots. Do they match 6, 8, 9 and 8?
E4. Preset vertical edge on a cell boundary. In the response map, where are the strongest red and blue responses? Switch the template to edge — (top − bottom): which membranes light up now?
E5. Preset centre − surround finds cells of its size. Which cells give the strongest red response? Make the template smaller (resize to about half) and then larger. Which objects respond now?






Solutions





E1. Response -13\,230, per pixel -9.8 (the eye band is about 10 grey levels darker on average); 6 lookups instead of 2700 pixels. Over the mouth the upper band (cheeks) is brighter than the lower one (mouth): the sign flips to positive (about +18.6 per pixel 40 pixels lower). On flat background the response is small (about 3 per pixel).
E2. 8 lookups (three rectangles in a row, corners at four x positions and two y positions, as in B2). The response is large and positive (+59\,329, 114 per pixel): the centre rectangle, on the bridge of the nose between the eyes, is bright skin, the two side rectangles contain the dark eyes.
E3. Edge across and edge down: 6; both line templates: 8; diagonal: 9; centre − surround: 8.
E4. The strongest responses lie along nearly vertical boundaries: the left and right sides of the nucleus and the dark membranes of the cytoplasm, red where the left side is brighter, blue where the right side is. With top − bottom the vertical boundaries fade and the upper and lower boundaries of the nucleus and the horizontal membranes light up.
E5. With a 16 \times 16 centre box (48 × 48 in all) the strongest red responses sit on the centres of the larger bright cells, whose size matches the centre box (52 per pixel on the cell under the template). Smaller templates respond to small bright debris and to the bright rims inside cells; larger ones only to the biggest cells, and more weakly. Like the difference of Gaussians on the edges day, centre − surround is a blob detector tuned to one size.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Explore: a box feature stack
The 25 thumbnails are the box group of a feature stack: rows box mean, box SD, centre − surround, edge across, edge down; columns scales 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 px. Paint pixels of class A (orange) and B (blue) on the image. The scatter plot shows the painted pixels in two features: click a thumbnail to choose x (red frame); tick y and click to choose y (green frame). The slider puts a threshold on x; the readout counts A and B on each side and gives the best share any single threshold on x gets right. inspect shows the 25 features of one pixel (as z-scores over the image) in the bar plot.


E6. Preset nucleus or cytoplasm? (x = box mean at 4 px, y = box SD at 2 px). How well does a single threshold on x separate the classes? Look at the image: is the nucleus darker or brighter than the cytoplasm?
E7. Click through the thumbnails as x and note the best single-threshold share. Which feature and scale separates best? Why does the scale matter so much here?
E8. Preset cell or background? on the synthetic cells. Find a feature that separates perfectly. Is that problem easier or harder than E6, and why?
E9. Use inspect on a pixel in the nucleus and one in the cytoplasm. Which groups of bars differ most?






Solutions





E6. Poorly: the best threshold on the box mean at 4 px gets 82 % right (at the slider’s 50 % position only 61 %). The nucleus is on average a little brighter than the cytoplasm around it, but the grey levels overlap; so do the clouds along x.
E7. The box SD at 16 px is best (99.2 %), followed by the box SD at 8 px (92.6 %) and centre − surround at 16 px (91.6 %); the box SD at 4 px gets 86.5 %. The nucleus is uniformly fine-grained, the cytoplasm is full of membranes and vesicles; that difference in texture shows only when the window is large enough to contain several membranes. With the integral image the 16 px features cost exactly as much as the 1 px ones.
E8. The box mean at 8 px separates the painted cell and background pixels perfectly (100 %), as do several others: the synthetic cells are much brighter than their surroundings. Easier: here the mean grey level differs; in E6 only the texture does.
E9. For example at (140, 120) in the nucleus and (80, 30) in the cytoplasm: the box SD at 8 and 16 px is low in the nucleus (z about -1.5 to -1.9) and higher in the cytoplasm; centre − surround at 16 px is near 0 in the nucleus and strongly negative in the cytoplasm (-2.3); the box means differ less. The edge features are small and change sign from pixel to pixel.

title: Exercise: rectangle features
text:
Where this leads
Out of about 160 000 rectangle features in a 24 \times 24 window, which should a detector compute? The next unit lets boosting pick a few, one at a time, and arranges them in a cascade so that most windows are rejected after one or two of them.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
About this lecture
We can fit a mixture of Gaussians to any cloud of points with EM. Now the points are pixels and objects.

Grey-level mixtures: K classes from the histogram; labels and probability maps.
Colour and feature-space segmentation: why a full covariance keeps a shadowed object whole.
Populations: fractions of cells or spots from the component weights.
Anomalies: pixels or objects that no component explains.
Mixtures as the data term of a graph cut (GrabCut).

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Mixtures on images
section: Recall: two Gaussians and a threshold

title: Mixtures on images
text:
A mixture of grey levels


Every pixel’s grey value is a point in 1D. Fit K Gaussians with EM: each class gets a mean, a width and a weight (its share of the pixels).
EM on the histogram: pixels with the same grey value have the same responsibilities, so each of the 256 bins is one point with weight = its count. One iteration costs 256 \times K evaluations, whatever the image size.
Synthetic image above: three classes (background, cytoplasm, organelles; 49 %, 39 %, 12 % of the pixels). EM finds weights 0.49, 0.40, 0.12 and the Bayes boundaries at grey values 100 and 160.

title: Mixtures on images
section: The math: EM on a weighted histogram
text:
The math: EM on a weighted histogram
Grey values g_j (bin centres) with counts h_j, n = \sum_j h_j. All pixels in bin j have the same responsibilities r_{jk}, so every sum over pixels becomes a sum over bins with weight h_j:
N_k = \sum_j h_j r_{jk}, \qquad \pi_k = \frac{N_k}{n}, \qquad \mu_k = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_j h_j r_{jk}\,g_j, \qquad \sigma_k^2 = \frac{1}{N_k}\sum_j h_j r_{jk}\,(g_j - \mu_k)^2,
\log p(\mathcal D) = \sum_j h_j \log\sum_k \pi_k\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2).
The result is identical to EM on all pixels (exactly, for integer grey values). For numerical safety compute \log\sum_k e^{a_k} as a_{\max} + \log\sum_k e^{a_k - a_{\max}} (log-sum-exp): a pixel far from every mean would otherwise give \log 0.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Labels, probability maps, boundaries

Label image: every pixel gets its most probable class. Because the label depends only on the grey value, it is a multi-level threshold at the Bayes boundaries.
Probability map: the responsibility of one class at every pixel, a soft segmentation. Values near 0.5 mark pixels the model cannot decide on (edges, overlapping classes).
K = 2 with free variances: the minimum-error threshold again, now found by EM.
Equal variances (tied): the boundaries are halfway between neighbouring means, shifted by the weights. Close to multi-level Otsu (thresholding day), which also assumes equally wide classes.
The weights matter: a rare class gets a smaller region; its boundary moves towards its own mean.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
The math: the two-class boundary
Two classes with \sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = \sigma: the boundary \pi_1\mathcal N_1(x) = \pi_2\mathcal N_2(x) is
x^* = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2},
the thresholding day’s equal-variance formula. With \sigma_1 \ne \sigma_2, taking logs gives a quadratic equation in x,
\frac{(x - \mu_1)^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{(x - \mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} = 2\ln\frac{\pi_1\sigma_2}{\pi_2\sigma_1},
with two roots: the narrower class wins only between them (unit 2). Example: the synthetic image’s small bright class has \pi_3 = 0.04 against \pi_2 = 0.48: x^* = 155 + \frac{13^2}{51.5}\ln 12 \approx 163 instead of the midpoint 155.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: a histogram mixture




Course micrograph, 128 × 128. “K = 3 on the micrograph”: weights 0.50, 0.34, 0.16; means 122, 204, 240; Bayes boundaries 173 and 229. “K = 2”: boundary 183, multi-level Otsu 164: the dark class is much wider (σ 39 against 22), so the minimum-error boundary moves towards the narrow bright class. Synthetic image “equal variances: Otsu-like”: boundaries 101 and 160, Otsu 100 and 155; 97.4 % of pixels as in the truth. “K too large”: K = 6 splits the background peak into three; press BIC: smallest at K = 3. “noise”: noise 22, 85.7 % correct, salt-and-pepper labels. “small bright class”: π3 = 0.04, posterior view; the boundary is at 163.

title: Mixtures on images
section: The histogram forgets where pixels are
text:
The histogram forgets where pixels are
A label that depends only on the grey value cannot use the neighbours:

with noise, the classes overlap in the histogram and the label image is speckled (single wrong pixels everywhere);
a smooth intensity gradient (uneven illumination) shifts the classes and no single mixture fits the whole image.

Fixes that keep the mixture as the data term and add the neighbours:

graph cuts with a smoothness term (graph-cut day);
a hidden Markov random field (a Potts prior on the labels), with the mixture re-estimated by EM: the Ising elective.

title: Mixtures on images
section: Colour: a feature space with shape
text:
Colour: a feature space with shape
A colour pixel is a point in 3D (RGB or L*a*b*). The colour day segmented colours with thresholds and distances (and one slide of k-means); a mixture adds shape.

A shadowed object is not a ball of colours: its pixels lie along a line from bright to dark (in RGB, towards black; in Lab mostly along L*).
k-means describes every group by a round blob: to cover the long shadow line it splits the object, and to make room it merges two other colours.
A full-covariance component is a long ellipse along the shadow line: the object stays whole.
More features: colour + local mean (texture), or colour + position (x, y) with a weight: groups become spatially compact regions.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: colour segmentation




Synthetic scene: a red ball lit from the left, a green block, a blue ellipse on a beige table; features RGB, K = 4. “shadowed ball”: k-means (start 5) splits the ball into two clusters and merges the green block with the blue ellipse (Dice green 0.68, blue 0.00; J = 1.086 × 10⁶). “best of 6 starts”: k-means’ best J is this split (1.086 × 10⁶, against 1.462 × 10⁶ for the correct grouping): the split is what k-means wants. Switch to “Gaussian mixture” (full): from start 5 it keeps the ball whole and finds all four objects (Dice 1.00), log p = −137 740; best of 6 starts: the same. Spherical covariances split the ball again. “RGB vs Lab”: in Lab, k-means is already right (the shadow mostly changes L*). “add position”: Lab + xy, K = 6: the table breaks into compact patches.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Relatives: mean shift and superpixels

Mean shift: put a small Gaussian on every point (a kernel density estimate); move every point uphill to the nearest peak of the density. Points that reach the same peak form a group. K is not chosen; the kernel width is.
SLIC superpixels: k-means on (colour, x, y) with many small groups (K in the hundreds), each centre searching only a local window. The result is an over-segmentation into compact, colour-coherent patches.
Superpixels make later steps cheaper: a graph cut on 500 superpixels instead of 250 000 pixels.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Populations: counting by mixture weights
The points are objects now (one point per nucleus or spot), with features from the measurements day.

DNA content (integrated nuclear intensity): cells in G1 have one copy (2N), in G2 two copies (4N), in S phase something in between. The histogram is a mixture of a G1 peak, a G2 peak at twice the intensity, and an S-phase plateau. The fitted weights are the fractions of cells in each phase.
Spot brightness: a spot holds 1, 2 or 3 fluorophores, so its intensity is a mixture of peaks at 1×, 2×, 3× the single-molecule brightness. The weights count the molecules.
Constraints help: tie the G2 mean to twice the G1 mean, or the spot means to multiples of one brightness. EM still works (the M-step changes).

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Anomalies: what no component explains
Fit a mixture to “normal” pixels or objects. A new point is an anomaly when

its density p(\mathbf x) is below a threshold \tau, or
its Mahalanobis distance is above (say) 3 to every component.

Examples: dust or debris in a field of cells, an out-of-focus object, a rare cell type, a stain artefact.

Unlike a classifier, this needs no examples of the anomalies: it only knows what normal looks like.
The threshold is a trade-off: for a Gaussian in 3D, 1 normal point in 150 lies beyond d_M = 3.5 anyway (1 in 34 beyond 3, 1 in 6600 beyond 4.5).
The VAE day uses the reconstruction error of an autoencoder for the same purpose.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Try it: an odd object




The scene with a small yellow object; Lab, K = 4, full covariances, start 2. The four mixture components describe the table, ball, block and ellipse (Dice 0.99–1.00). View “d_M > t to all” with t = 4.5: 119 pixels are flagged, the 113 pixels of the odd object and 6 noise pixels. Lower t to 3.5: many more noise pixels on the table. Other starts may give a component to the yellow object: then it is no longer an anomaly, but a class.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Mixtures as data terms: GrabCut
The graph-cut day’s energy needs a data term D_p(\ell) = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell): how well pixel p’s value fits label \ell. A fitted mixture per label provides it.
GrabCut (Rother, Kolmogorov & Blake, 2004), for colour images:

The user draws a box: outside = background, inside = unknown.
Fit a colour mixture (about 5 components) to the background pixels and one to the current object pixels.
Graph cut with these data terms and contrast-sensitive smoothness.
Refit the mixtures to the new labels; cut again; repeat until it settles.

The same loop as EM: a labelling step and a model-fitting step, alternating.

title: Mixtures on images
text:
Summary

Histogram mixtures: EM on the bins, weighted by their counts; K classes, labels = multi-level thresholds at the Bayes boundaries; responsibilities = probability maps.
K = 2: the minimum-error threshold; equal variances: close to multi-level Otsu; weights move the boundaries.
The histogram ignores neighbours: noise gives speckle (fix: graph cuts, hidden MRF).
In colour, a full covariance follows a shadow; k-means splits it.
Weights count populations; low likelihood or large Mahalanobis distance flags anomalies.
Fitted mixtures are the data terms of graph cuts: GrabCut alternates fitting and cutting.

title: Quiz: mixtures on images
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why can EM for a grey-level mixture run on the 256 histogram bins instead of on the 1 000 000 pixels of a large image, and give exactly the same result?






Hint





What do two pixels with the same grey value have in common in the E-step?









Answer





Pixels with the same grey value have the same responsibilities, and they enter the M-step sums identically. So each bin can be treated as one point with weight equal to its count: every sum over pixels becomes a sum over bins times counts.




Q2. A histogram mixture with K = 3 assigns each pixel its most probable class. Why is the resulting label image the same as thresholding with two thresholds?






Hint





On what does the label of a pixel depend?









Answer





The label depends only on the grey value; the most probable class changes at a few grey values (the Bayes boundaries). Between two boundaries the label is constant, so the label image is a multi-level threshold at those boundaries (with equal or similar variances, two boundaries for three classes ordered by their means).




Q3. What does a probability map (posterior of one class) show that the label image does not?






Hint





Think of pixels near the boundary grey value.









Answer





How sure the model is: values near 1 or 0 are clear, values near 0.5 mark pixels whose grey value fits two classes equally well (edges, blurred regions, overlapping classes). The label image hides this uncertainty.




Q4. You fit a two-class mixture to a noisy micrograph; the label image is full of isolated wrong pixels. Will more EM iterations or more components help? What would?






Hint





What information does the histogram not contain?









Answer





No: the problem is not the fit but the model. The histogram ignores where pixels are, so a noisy pixel whose value falls on the wrong side of the boundary is labelled wrongly whatever its neighbours are. Use the mixture as a data term and add a smoothness term between neighbours (graph cuts, or a Markov random field prior), or denoise first.




Q5. A red object lies half in shadow. In RGB its pixels form a long line towards black. Why does k-means with $K = $ (number of objects) tend to fail, while a mixture with full covariances does not?






Hint





What shape does each method assume for a group?









Answer





k-means assumes round groups of similar size; covering a long line with round groups needs two of them, so it splits the object and merges two other colours to stay at K groups. A full-covariance component can be a long, thin ellipse along the shadow line and keeps the object whole.




Q6. A mixture fitted to the integrated DNA intensity of 2000 nuclei has weights 0.58 (G1 peak), 0.14 (S plateau) and 0.28 (G2 peak). How many cells are in G2? What should the ratio of the two peak means be?






Hint





G2 cells have doubled their DNA.









Answer





About 0.28 \times 2000 = 560 cells. The G2 mean should be twice the G1 mean (4N versus 2N); a fitted ratio far from 2 suggests a measurement problem (saturation, background, segmentation errors) or a poor fit.




Q7. How would you use a fitted mixture to flag debris in a field of normal cells, and what number do you have to choose?






Hint





What do normal cells have that debris does not?









Answer





Fit the mixture to features of (mostly) normal cells. Flag an object when its density is below a threshold, or when its Mahalanobis distance to every component exceeds a threshold such as 3. That threshold sets the trade-off between missed debris and normal cells flagged by chance.




Q8. In GrabCut, what plays the role of the E-step and what of the M-step?






Hint





One step finds labels, the other refits the colour models.









Answer





The graph cut finds a labelling given the colour models (like the E-step, but hard and with a smoothness term); refitting the object and background mixtures to the new labels is the M-step. Alternating them lowers the energy until the labelling settles.




Q9. (math) Write the M-step for \mu_k of a histogram mixture with counts h_j at grey values g_j.






Hint





Replace the sum over pixels by a sum over bins.









Answer





\mu_k = \sum_j h_j r_{jk} g_j \big/ \sum_j h_j r_{jk}, with r_{jk} = \pi_k\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)/\sum_l\pi_l\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_l, \sigma_l^2).

Exercise: mixtures on images
Exercise: mixtures on images
text:
Background







Word
Meaning

title: Exercise: mixtures on images
text:
By hand
B1. A grey-level mixture with three classes: \pi = (0.50, 0.35, 0.15), \mu = (70, 130, 185), \sigma = (12, 13, 13). (a) Compute the posteriors of the three classes for the grey values 95, 155 and 165, and give their labels. (b) Between classes 2 and 3 the variances are equal. Compute the Bayes boundary, and compare it with the midpoint of the means. Why are they different? (c) Which grey value near 100 is the most “uncertain”? What would a posterior map of class 1 look like there?
B2. Populations. A mixture fitted to the integrated DNA intensity of 1500 nuclei (in units of the G1 peak) has components G1 (\pi = 0.55, \mu = 1.00), S (\pi = 0.15, \mu = 1.48, wide) and G2 (\pi = 0.30, \mu = 1.97). (a) How many cells are in each phase? (b) Is the G2 mean plausible? What would you suspect if it came out at 1.6? (c) Why must the S component be wide?
B3. Anomalies. Two 2D components: \mathcal N_1 with \boldsymbol\mu_1 = (0, 0), \Sigma_1 = I; \mathcal N_2 with \boldsymbol\mu_2 = (5, 0), \Sigma_2 = \operatorname{diag}(4, 1). Using the rule “anomaly if d_M > 3 to every component”, classify the points (2.5, 2.5) and (0, 4).
B4. Predict, with a sketch of the colour space and of the label image: a red ball whose right half is in deep shadow, a green and a blue object, and a beige background; K = 4. (a) k-means in RGB. (b) A Gaussian mixture with full covariances in RGB. (c) Which of the two achieves the lower J (the k-means objective) in (a), the “correct” grouping or the split one? What does that tell you?
B5. A noisy image with two classes (means 80 and 160, σ = 30 each, equal weights). (a) Where is the Bayes boundary? What fraction of each class’s pixels ends up on the wrong side? (b) How does this show in the label image, and why do more EM iterations not help?






Solutions





B1. (a) At 95: (0.87, 0.13, 0.00), class 1. At 155: (0.00, 0.84, 0.16), class 2. At 165: (0.00, 0.17, 0.83), class 3. (b) x^* = \frac{130 + 185}{2} + \frac{13^2}{55}\ln\frac{0.35}{0.15} = 157.5 + 2.6 = 160.1. The midpoint is 157.5; class 2 is more than twice as frequent, so it gets the grey values just above the midpoint too. (c) Around 100 the posteriors of classes 1 and 2 are about equal (at 100: 0.49 and 0.51): the posterior map of class 1 passes through 0.5 there, a band of intermediate values along the edges between the two classes.
B2. (a) G1: 0.55 \times 1500 = 825, S: 225, G2: 450. (b) Yes: G2 cells have twice the DNA of G1 cells; 1.97 is close to 2. A G2 mean of 1.6 would suggest saturation of bright nuclei, a wrong background subtraction, or a poor fit (for instance the S and G2 components swapped roles). (c) S-phase cells are spread over all DNA contents between 1 and 2: the S component has to cover the whole plateau between the peaks.
B3. (2.5, 2.5): d_1 = \sqrt{12.5} = 3.54, d_2 = \sqrt{(2.5/2)^2 + 2.5^2} = 2.80: within 3 of component 2, not an anomaly. (0, 4): d_1 = 4, d_2 = \sqrt{(5/2)^2 + 16} = 4.72: beyond 3 of both: an anomaly.
B4. (a) In RGB the ball’s pixels form a long streak from bright red towards black. k-means needs two round groups to cover it, so the ball is split into a lit and a shaded half; with only four groups, the green and the blue object (or the table and another object) share one group. (b) One long ellipse along the red streak: the ball is one group, and the four objects are separated. (c) The split grouping has the lower J (in the demo: 1.09 \times 10^6 against 1.46 \times 10^6): k-means converges to it because it is better by its own measure. The objective, not the optimiser, is the problem.
B5. (a) At 120 (the midpoint). A class pixel is wrong if it is more than 40 = 1.33\sigma beyond its mean towards the other class: P(Z > 1.33) = 0.09, about 9 % of each class. (b) As scattered single wrong pixels (speckle) in both regions. The fit is already correct: the classes simply overlap in grey value, and a label that depends only on the grey value cannot do better. Neighbours (smoothing, graph cuts, an MRF prior) are needed.




Math questions
B6. (math) Write the EM updates (N_k, \pi_k, \mu_k, \sigma_k^2) for a histogram with counts h_j at grey values g_j, and show that they equal per-pixel EM.
B7. (math) Show that for two classes with equal variances the Bayes boundary is x^* = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}. Check it with B1(b).
B8. (math) Why compute \log\sum_k e^{a_k} as a_{\max} + \log\sum_k e^{a_k - a_{\max}}? Give an example where the direct formula fails in double precision.






Solutions (math)





B6. All h_j pixels with value g_j have the same responsibilities r_{jk} = \pi_k\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_k, \sigma_k^2)/\sum_l\pi_l\mathcal N(g_j \mid \mu_l, \sigma_l^2). The per-pixel sums \sum_i r_{ik}, \sum_i r_{ik}x_i, \sum_i r_{ik}(x_i - \mu_k)^2 group by grey value: N_k = \sum_j h_jr_{jk}, \pi_k = N_k/\sum_jh_j, \mu_k = \sum_jh_jr_{jk}g_j/N_k, \sigma_k^2 = \sum_jh_jr_{jk}(g_j - \mu_k)^2/N_k. Identical results, at a cost of (number of bins) instead of (number of pixels) per iteration. (The demos’ test file checks this numerically.)
B7. \ln\pi_1 - \frac{(x - \mu_1)^2}{2\sigma^2} = \ln\pi_2 - \frac{(x - \mu_2)^2}{2\sigma^2} (the normalisers cancel). (x - \mu_2)^2 - (x - \mu_1)^2 = 2x(\mu_1 - \mu_2) + \mu_2^2 - \mu_1^2, so 2\sigma^2\ln\frac{\pi_2}{\pi_1} = 2x(\mu_1 - \mu_2) + (\mu_2 - \mu_1)(\mu_2 + \mu_1). Dividing by 2(\mu_2 - \mu_1): x = \frac{\mu_1 + \mu_2}{2} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\mu_2 - \mu_1}\ln\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_2}. B1(b): 157.5 + \frac{169}{55}\ln\frac73 = 160.1.
B8. The terms a_k = \log\pi_k + \log\mathcal N_k(x) can be very negative for a point far from every component (e.g. -800): e^{-800} underflows to 0 in double precision (the smallest positive double is about e^{-745}), so the direct formula gives \log 0 = -\infty and the responsibilities 0/0. Subtracting the maximum makes the largest term e^0 = 1: \log(e^{-800} + e^{-802}) = -800 + \log(1 + e^{-2}) = -799.87. The identity holds because \sum_k e^{a_k} = e^{a_{\max}}\sum_k e^{a_k - a_{\max}}.

title: Exercise: mixtures on images
text:
Explore: grey-level mixtures
Left: the image with the label of each pixel, the posterior of one class, or the pixels with p(I) < \tau (low p(I)). Right: the histogram with the fitted weighted components (dashed), their sum (black), the Bayes boundaries (black vertical lines) and, optionally, the multi-level Otsu thresholds (dotted purple); next to it BIC for K = 1..6 (button). Images: the course micrograph (128 × 128) and a synthetic image of three classes with known truth (noise and blur sliders). step EM does one iteration; changing K re-fits to convergence.



H1. Preset K = 2: the minimum-error threshold again. Read the two components and the Bayes boundary. Compare it with the Otsu threshold. Why do they differ?
H2. Preset K = 3 on the micrograph. Which structures does each class contain? Look at the posterior map of class 2 (choose posterior, then class 2): where is it uncertain?
H3. Preset equal variances: Otsu-like. Compare the Bayes boundaries with the Otsu thresholds and read the fraction of correctly labelled pixels. Untick equal variances: what changes?
H4. Preset K too large: components split a peak. How are the six components distributed over the three peaks? Press BIC for K = 1..6: which K does BIC choose?
H5. Preset noise: speckle in the label image. Describe the label image. Read the fraction of correct pixels. Lower the noise to 12 and compare.
H6. Preset small bright class: weights matter. Read the weight and the boundary of the bright class, and compare the boundary with the midpoint between the means of classes 2 and 3.






Solutions





H1. Component 1: \pi = 0.55, \mu = 127.9, \sigma = 39.1; component 2: \pi = 0.45, \mu = 218.8, \sigma = 22.1. Bayes boundary 183; Otsu 164. The dark class is much wider than the bright one: the minimum-error boundary moves towards the narrow class (the wide one wins further out), while Otsu assumes equally wide classes.
H2. Weights 0.50, 0.34, 0.16; means 122, 204, 240; boundaries 173 and 229. Class 1: the dark cell material (nucleus, cytoplasm, membranes); class 2: the light grey background; class 3: the brightest regions. The posterior of class 2 is uncertain (intermediate values) along the edges of the cell and in textured grey areas, where the grey values sit near 173 or 229.
H3. Bayes boundaries 101 and 160, Otsu 100 and 155; 97.4 % of the pixels are labelled as in the truth. The fitted means are 70.7, 129.9, 181.9 with σ = 12.7 for all. Otsu’s second threshold is lower than the mixture’s because the mixture takes the small weight (0.12) of the bright class into account. With free variances the fit hardly changes (boundaries 100 and 160, again 97.4 %): the true classes have equal widths.
H4. Three components share the background peak (means 64, 69, 81), two the middle peak (126, 133), one the bright peak (182); the extra boundaries cut through peaks. BIC is smallest at K = 3.
H5. Salt-and-pepper: isolated pixels of the wrong class inside every region. With noise 22, 85.7 % of the pixels are correct (boundaries 101 and 157); with noise 12, 97.4 %. The classes overlap in the histogram, and a per-pixel label cannot use the neighbours.
H6. Weight 0.04, mean 180.8; Bayes boundary 163, while the midpoint between 129.3 and 180.8 is 155: the rare bright class gets a smaller range of grey values (98.0 % correct pixels overall).

title: Exercise: mixtures on images
text:
Explore: colour segmentation
Left: a synthetic colour image (a scene with a shadowed ball, the same scene with an odd object, or a stained tissue section), all with known truth. Middle: its pixels as a 2D histogram in two feature dimensions, with the fitted components as 2σ ellipses (k-means: its centres). The readout gives Dice per class (each cluster mapped to the class it overlaps most).



E1. Preset shadowed ball: k-means splits it, full GMM keeps it. Look at the label image and the Dice values. Press best of 6 starts: which J is the lowest, and which grouping has it? Then choose Gaussian mixture (full) and run. Compare with B4.

E6. Preset an odd object has low likelihood. How many pixels are flagged at t = 4.5, and where? Lower t to 3.5. Explain the difference with the χ² tail numbers from the lecture.






Solutions





E1. k-means (start 5) splits the ball into a lit and a shaded half (both mapped to “red ball”), and the green block and the blue ellipse share one cluster: Dice green 0.68, blue 0.00, mean 0.67, J = 1.086 \times 10^6. Best of starts 1–6: one start reaches the correct grouping with J = 1.462 \times 10^6, five reach the split with J = 1.086 \times 10^6, the lowest: the split is k-means’ own optimum. The full Gaussian mixture from start 5 converges to the correct grouping: all four objects found (Dice 1.00), \log p = -137\,740. Its ellipse for the ball is long and thin, along the shadow streak.
E2. With spherical covariances the mixture behaves like k-means: the ball is split again and the green and blue objects merge (Dice 0.68 and 0.00). Round components cannot follow the streak.
E3. No: k-means in Lab finds all four objects (Dice 1.00). The shadow mostly lowers L* and changes a* and b* less, and the other colours are far apart in a*b*: the ball’s cloud is elongated mainly along L*, which is short compared with the distances between the colour groups.
E4. With Lab + position, K = 6 and weight 1, the clusters are compact patches: the large table is split into several regions (three clusters map to “table”), each object gets its own cluster or shares one with a nearby table patch (Dice green 0.80). At weight 0.5 colour dominates again and all four objects are found (Dice 1.00 for all); at weight 2 position dominates and the clusters become blocks of the image that cut through objects (Dice of green and blue fall to 0). This is the idea behind superpixels.
E5. Full covariances: matrix 0.99, nuclei 1.00, lumen 0.87. Diagonal: 1.00 for all three. Spherical: the lumen is lost (Dice 0.00; matrix 0.96). The lumen is a very tight cluster of near-white pixels and the matrix a wide, elongated one (its stain density varies); diagonal covariances describe this with fewer parameters and get it right here, while one round width per component cannot.
E6. At t = 4.5: 119 pixels, the 113 pixels of the yellow object and 6 noise pixels elsewhere. At t = 3.5 many more noise pixels on the table and objects are flagged (for a 3D Gaussian about 1 in 150 normal pixels lies beyond 3.5, against 1 in 6600 beyond 4.5; with 16 384 pixels that is about 100 against 2).

title: Exercise: mixtures on images
text:
Where this leads
The mixture models in this unit label each pixel from its own value. The graph-cut day adds the neighbours through a smoothness term, with -\log of a fitted mixture as the data term (GrabCut alternates the two). The Ising elective does the same with a Markov random field and re-estimates the mixture by EM. Generative models of whole images, rather than of single pixels, are the subject of the VAE day.

title: Exercise: neural networks
text:
Explore: classifying points
The demo trains a small network to classify points in the plane. The points are coloured by class; the background shows the network’s decision (colour = predicted class, stronger = more confident). Choose the number of hidden layers (0–2), the units per layer and the activation \varphi. Each thumbnail shows one hidden unit: orange where it is active (strong = large output). play trains, step takes one gradient step, reset goes back to the start weights, new start draws other start weights. Click to add points of the chosen class, drag points to move them. With no hidden layer and two classes the network is one neuron: drag the round handle to move its line and the dark tip to turn it (the arrow is \mathbf w).



P1. Preset one neuron, by hand. The line starts vertical through the centre (\mathbf w = (1, 0), b = 0). Read the loss and accuracy. Turn and move the line so that it separates the two blobs as well as possible. Then drag the tip further out without moving the line: what happens to the loss, and why? Finally press play: where does training put the line, and what happens to \|\mathbf w\|?
P2. Preset one neuron on XOR fails. Press play. What loss and accuracy does the neuron reach? Compare the loss with \ln 2 = 0.693.
P3. Preset 2 hidden units solve XOR. Press play and watch the two thumbnails. What does each hidden unit do, and what does the output region look like? Then press new start a few times (play each time). Does training always succeed?
P4. Preset no nonlinearity: still a line: 8 hidden units, but no bend, on a circle inside a ring. Train. What does the boundary look like and what accuracy is reached? Explain with the collapse argument.
P5. Preset circle: 3 ReLU units. Train and describe the shape of the region inside. Why 3 units at least? Try 2 units.
P6. Preset spiral needs depth (two layers of 8). Train and compare the thumbnails of layer 1 with those of layer 2. Then set hidden layers to 1 and train again.
P7. Preset 3 classes with softmax, no hidden layer. What do the boundaries between the regions look like? Why?






Solutions





P1. The start line splits the blobs fairly well already: loss 0.535, accuracy 98 %. A line between the blobs, perpendicular to the line joining their centres, does about as well in accuracy. Making \mathbf w longer without moving the line makes every probability more confident: the loss falls while all points are on the right side (for example \mathbf w = (1, 1): 0.461, (4, 4): 0.154, (8, 8): 0.070, same line through the centre), but a point on the wrong side is punished harder and harder, so with overlapping classes the loss eventually rises again. Training puts the line between the blobs (accuracy 98 %, loss 0.032 after 1000 steps) and keeps growing \mathbf w, to about (16.8, 6.5) after 1000 steps: the few points in the overlap stay wrong, and the rest become ever more certain.
P2. The loss drops to 0.691 and stays; accuracy 50 %. 0.693 = \ln 2 is the loss of always answering “50 : 50”. The best a single line can do here is to give up: whatever line it draws, half of each class is on the wrong side.
P3. After about 50 steps the loss is below 0.03 and the accuracy 100 % (0.002 after 1000 steps). Each hidden unit is a half-plane (a ReLU of one line); the output region of one class is the band between the two lines (as in B11), which contains the two corners of that class. With other start weights (new start: start seeds 2 to 6) the network gets stuck at 75 % every time: one corner stays wrong. With the second start, one hidden unit is off on every point (“dead”: its gradient is zero, so it never comes back); with the others, both units are active but their lines sit where they can only fix three of the four corners, and no small step improves the loss. Small networks are sensitive to the start; larger ones much less (try 4 units).
P4. The boundary stays a straight line; accuracy 74 % (the line cuts off part of the ring), loss 0.569. Without a bend, W^{(2)}(W^{(1)}\mathbf x + \mathbf b^{(1)}) + \mathbf b^{(2)} is a single affine function of \mathbf x, however many units: one line.
P5. The inner region is a rounded triangle: three lines, one per hidden unit, cut off the corners; accuracy 100 % after about 200 steps (loss 0.016). A bounded region needs at least 3 lines in the plane (two lines give a wedge or a band, which is open on one side). With 2 units the accuracy stays around 74 %.
P6. Layer-1 thumbnails are half-planes (one line each). Layer-2 units combine them: their thumbnails are polygons and stripes. Together they follow the spiral: 100 % after about 500 steps. With a single layer of 8 units the network needs much longer and stays around 75–90 % (it oscillates between these values for thousands of steps): 8 lines are too few to cut the spiral into the right pieces.
P7. The boundaries are straight lines meeting in a point: with no hidden layer each class score is linear, z_k = \mathbf w_k^\top\mathbf x + b_k, and the boundary between classes k and j is where z_k = z_j, a line. Softmax only turns the scores into probabilities; it does not bend the boundaries.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Recall: a classifier draws a line
text:
Recall: a classifier draws a line
Thresholding (day 6) decides “nucleus if intensity > t”: a cut on one measurement. Day 14 put objects as points in a feature space and let a classifier carve it up.

Two measurements per object (say area and mean intensity): each object is a point in the plane.
The simplest rule that uses both: a straight line, w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b > 0 means “nucleus”.
The numbers w_1, w_2, b are what we will learn from examples.


One slide of recall from thresholding and from the random-forest day, which owns feature space and the train/test vocabulary. A forest carves feature space into boxes; a neuron cuts it with a line; a network combines many lines.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
One neuron


A neuron adds its inputs with weights, adds a bias, then bends the result with an activation \varphi:
\text{out} = \varphi(w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + b)

Step \varphi: a hard yes/no, the perceptron (1958).
Sigmoid \varphi(s) = 1/(1 + e^{-s}): a probability between 0 and 1.
ReLU \varphi(s) = \max(0, s): the workhorse of today’s networks.

The weights point across the line, to the positive side; the bias moves the line.


\mathbf w = (2, 1), b = -4: (2, 1) and (3, 0) are positive.


Compute two points with the class: (1, 1) gives 2 + 1 − 4 = −1, negative; (2, 1) gives +1, positive. With the sigmoid the outputs are 0.27 and 0.73: a neuron with a sigmoid is exactly logistic regression. Doubling w and b keeps the line but makes the probabilities sharper.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: The math: a neuron is a half-plane
text:
The math: a neuron is a half-plane
\text{out} = \varphi(\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b)

The decision boundary \mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b = 0 is a line (a hyperplane in \mathbb R^n) with normal \mathbf w.
Its distance from the origin is |b|/\|\mathbf w\|; the signed distance of a point is (\mathbf w^\top\mathbf x + b)/\|\mathbf w\|.
With the sigmoid, the output is an S-shaped function of that signed distance times \|\mathbf w\|: larger \|\mathbf w\|, steeper transition, same line.
Example: \mathbf w = (2, 1), b = -4: distance 4/\sqrt5 = 1.79.

text:
AND, OR, but not XOR
Inputs x_1, x_2 \in \{0, 1\}, step activation (1 if the sum > 0):

XOR wants (1,0) and (0,1) on one side, (0,0) and (1,1) on the other: no single line does that.
This observation (Minsky and Papert, 1969) stalled neural networks for a decade. The answer: more than one neuron.

Each hidden unit is a neuron with its own line; the output combines them.
The hidden layer has turned the four corners into points that one line can separate.


Do the table on the board. In the playground, preset “2 hidden units solve XOR” shows the two hidden units as two half-planes (thumbnails) and the output region as the band between two lines.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
section: Try it: a network classifies points
text:
Try it: a network classifies points




Tour: “one neuron, by hand”: drag the handle and the tip, read the loss (lower when the line separates the blobs and w is long). “one neuron on XOR fails”: play, the loss stays at 0.69 (= ln 2, a coin toss), accuracy 50 %. “2 hidden units solve XOR”: play, the two thumbnails become two half-planes, loss below 0.01 after a few hundred steps; “new start” with other seeds often gets stuck at 75 %: the start matters. “no nonlinearity: still a line”: 8 units, no bend, the circle cannot be separated (74 %). “circle: 3 ReLU units”: a triangle-like region. “spiral needs depth”: 8 + 8 units. “3 classes with softmax”.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
Many classes: softmax
One output score z_k per class; turn the scores into probabilities:
p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}

All p_k are positive and sum to 1; the largest score gets the largest probability.
Scores (2, 1, 0) → probabilities (0.67, 0.24, 0.09). The predicted class is the largest.
Two classes with softmax are the same as one sigmoid output.

title: Neural networks: matrix, bend, matrix
text:
The math: softmax

Adding a constant to all scores does not change p: e^{z_k + c}/\sum_j e^{z_j + c} = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}. So (102, 101, 100) gives the same (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), and computers subtract \max_k z_k first to avoid overflow.
Two classes: p_1 = e^{z_1}/(e^{z_0} + e^{z_1}) = 1/(1 + e^{-(z_1 - z_0)}), the sigmoid of the score difference.
Universal approximation (Cybenko 1989 for sigmoids; the same holds for ReLU): one hidden layer with enough units approximates any continuous function on a bounded region as closely as we like. It says nothing about how many units, or whether training finds them.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: a snake moves its beads downhill on an energy, and explodes when the step is too large. Today we look at the update as linear algebra, and give the snake a longer reach.

The internal forces of all beads at once: one matrix A, the same for x and y.
A is a circular convolution, so its eigenvectors are waves around the curve: wiggles are expensive, the overall shape is cheap.
Why the plain step explodes, and the semi-implicit step that never does.
The capture range: larger \sigma, a balloon force, gradient vector flow.
What snakes cannot do, and where that leads.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: The snake as a linear system
section: All beads at once: a matrix
text:
All beads at once: a matrix
Put the x coordinates of the n beads in one vector \mathbf x = (x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}) (and the y’s in another). The internal force on every bead is a fixed weighted sum of its neighbours: force = -A\,\mathbf x, the same A for \mathbf y.
With \alpha = 1, \beta = 0 and n = 6:
A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}

Row i: 2x_i - x_{i-1} - x_{i+1}, minus the elastic force. The corner entries are the wrap-around: bead 0 and bead 5 are neighbours.
With \beta > 0 every row is [\beta,\; -\alpha - 4\beta,\; 2\alpha + 6\beta,\; -\alpha - 4\beta,\; \beta] around the diagonal: cyclic pentadiagonal.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
What the matrix tells us

Rows sum to 0: A\mathbf 1 = 0. Moving the whole snake (all x_i by the same amount) costs nothing.
Symmetric, and the energy \tfrac12\mathbf x^\top A\mathbf x \ge 0: A is positive semidefinite.
Each row is the same stencil, shifted: A\mathbf x is a circular convolution of \mathbf x with [-1, 2, -1] (Filtering & convolution).
So, as in Images in frequency space: the waves around the curve are its eigenvectors. The alternating pattern (1, -1, 1, -1, 1, -1): A maps it to (4, -4, 4, -4, 4, -4), four times itself.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Waves around the curve
Wave number k = how many times the pattern goes up and down around the curve. k = 0: a shift; k = 1: once around, the round shape itself (its size and how elongated it is); high k: wiggles.


Left: the eigenvalue \lambda_k is the cost of mode k. Low modes are almost free, wiggles are expensive. \beta (red) penalises wiggles much more steeply than \alpha (blue).
Under the internal forces alone, every mode shrinks independently, the expensive ones fastest: the snake first smooths, then slowly shrinks.

title: The snake as a linear system
section: The math: the eigenvalues of a circulant matrix
text:
The math: the eigenvalues of a circulant matrix
Try v_j = e^{2\pi i kj/n} (indices mod n, so the wrap-around is automatic). Row j of A\mathbf v for the elastic part:
\alpha(2v_j - v_{j-1} - v_{j+1}) = \alpha\big(2 - e^{-2\pi ik/n} - e^{2\pi ik/n}\big)v_j = \alpha\big(2 - 2\cos\tfrac{2\pi k}{n}\big)v_j = 4\alpha\sin^2\!\tfrac{\pi k}{n}\;v_j.
The rigid stencil is the elastic one applied twice, so its eigenvalue is the square:
\lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2\frac{\pi k}{n} + 16\beta\sin^4\frac{\pi k}{n}, \qquad k = 0, \dots, n - 1.

Real eigenvectors: \cos(2\pi kj/n) and \sin(2\pi kj/n) (same \lambda_k = \lambda_{n-k}). The DFT diagonalises every circulant matrix.
\lambda_0 = 0 (translation). Largest at k = n/2 (alternating signs, n even): \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta.
Low modes: \lambda_k \approx \alpha(2\pi k/n)^2 + \beta(2\pi k/n)^4, the continuous \alpha and \beta terms.
n = 6, \alpha = 1, \beta = 0: \lambda_k = 0, 1, 3, 4, 3, 1.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Why the explicit step explodes
One step with the internal force: new \mathbf x = \mathbf x - \tau A\mathbf x. Mode k is simply multiplied by 1 - \tau\lambda_k.

Small \tau: every factor lies between 0 and 1. Every mode shrinks.
The stiffest mode (the alternating zig-zag, \lambda_\text{max} = 4\alpha + 16\beta) gets the most negative factor. Once \tau\lambda_\text{max} > 2 its factor is below -1: the zig-zag flips sign and grows every step.
Unit 1’s snake: \alpha = 0.1, \beta = 0.05, \lambda_\text{max} = 1.2: stable for \tau < 1.67, and \tau = 2 (factor -1.4) exploded.
A large \beta makes it much worse: \beta = 2 gives \lambda_\text{max} = 32.4, so \tau < 0.06: thousands of tiny steps.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
The semi-implicit step
Kass et al.: evaluate the internal force at the new position, the image force at the old one.
(A + \gamma I)\,\mathbf x_\text{new} = \gamma\,\mathbf x + \mathbf f(\mathbf x), \qquad \gamma = 1/\tau.

Each step solves a linear system instead of a multiplication. Mode k is now multiplied by \frac{\gamma}{\gamma + \lambda_k} = \frac{1}{1 + \tau\lambda_k}: always between 0 and 1. No \tau makes it explode.
With huge \tau the internal part jumps straight to its smoothest state in one step: stable, but the image force then dominates each step.
A + \gamma I does not change while \alpha, \beta, \tau, n stay fixed: factor it once, reuse it every step. It is banded (plus two corners), so solving costs a few operations per bead.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
The math: the semi-implicit step
Gradient descent \mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t - \tau(A\mathbf x_t - \mathbf f_t) is an explicit Euler step of \dot{\mathbf x} = -A\mathbf x + \mathbf f. Taking the stiff linear part at t + 1:
\mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t - \tau(A\mathbf x_{t+1} - \mathbf f_t) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (I + \tau A)\mathbf x_{t+1} = \mathbf x_t + \tau\mathbf f_t \;\Longleftrightarrow\; (A + \gamma I)\mathbf x_{t+1} = \gamma\mathbf x_t + \mathbf f_t.

A + \gamma I has eigenvalues \lambda_k + \gamma \ge \gamma > 0: always invertible.
Without \mathbf f: \mathbf x_{t+1} = (I + \tau A)^{-1}\mathbf x_t, and in the eigenbasis mode k gets 1/(1 + \tau\lambda_k) \in (0, 1]. Explicit: 1 - \tau\lambda_k, inside [-1, 1] only for \tau\lambda_k \le 2.
A fixed point satisfies A\mathbf x = \mathbf f(\mathbf x) for either step: the same balance, only the path differs.

title: The snake as a linear system
section: Try it: the modes of a snake
text:
Try it: the modes of a snake




No image: internal forces only, n = 16, noisy circle. Top plot: λ_k; middle: the factor per step (green inside ±1, red outside); bottom: the size of each mode in the current contour (grey bars: at the start). Tour: “α only” (α = 0.2, semi-implicit τ = 1): the wiggles (modes 4–8, factors 0.71–0.56) disappear in a few steps, mode 1 (factor 0.970) shrinks the circle with a half-life of 23 steps. “β only” (β = 0.2): wiggles go even faster (mode 8: 0.24) but mode 1 has factor 0.995, half-life 150 steps. “explicit at the limit” (α = 0.25, τ = 1.95): mode 8 factor −0.95, the zig-zag flips sign every step and fades slowly. “just beyond” (τ = 2.1): factor −1.1, it grows and explodes. “semi-implicit, huge τ” (τ = 50): mode 8 factor 0.02, mode 1 0.34: stable, the circle collapses in a few steps. “n = 6”: the matrix by hand (show matrix A).

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Capture range
The edge force w\nabla f is only non-zero within a few \sigma of an edge. A snake that starts further away feels nothing. Three remedies:

Larger \sigma, then smaller: a coarse-to-fine schedule. Wide pull first, accurate edge later.
Balloon force (Cohen, 1991): push every bead along its outward normal with strength \kappa. The snake inflates through flat regions until an edge stops it (\kappa < 0 deflates).
Gradient vector flow (Xu & Prince, 1998): spread the edge force out into the flat regions, so that every pixel points towards some edge.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
The balloon force

A bead’s normal: perpendicular to the line through its two neighbours, pointing out of the curve.
Start a small circle inside the object: the balloon inflates it until the edge force at the boundary is stronger than \kappa.
\kappa too small: stops on noise inside. \kappa too large: pushes through weak parts of the edge and keeps going.
The balloon cancels part of the shrinking by \alpha, so the snake’s size is no longer biased towards small.

Demo (unit 1’s disk, w = 2, \sigma = 2): \kappa = 0.3 stops at radius 30.3; \kappa = 1 escapes. On a disk whose right edge fades out, \kappa = 0.3 already leaks through the weak side.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Gradient vector flow
Make a force field \mathbf v that equals the edge force near edges and varies smoothly everywhere else. Start from \mathbf v = 
abla f and repeat:
\mathbf v \leftarrow \mathbf v + \Delta t\, ig[\,\underbrace{\mu\,
abla^2\mathbf v}_{	ext{smooth it}} - \underbrace{|
abla f|^2(\mathbf v - 
abla f)}_{	ext{stay at }
abla f	ext{ near edges}}\, ig]


abla^2 is the Laplacian kernel of Filtering & convolution: each step diffuses the field a little, like heat. Where |
abla f| is large, the second term keeps \mathbf v \approx 
abla f.
After many steps, flat regions are filled with arrows pointing towards edges, also into concavities, where the plain edge force points sideways.

title: The snake as a linear system
section: The math: GVF as an energy
text:
The math: GVF as an energy
GVF minimises, over vector fields \mathbf v = (u, v),
\mathcal E(\mathbf v) = \iint \mu ig(|
abla u|^2 + |
abla v|^2 ig) + |
abla f|^2\,|\mathbf v - 
abla f|^2 \;dx\,dy.

Its Euler–Lagrange equations: \mu
abla^2 u - |
abla f|^2(u - f_x) = 0, the same for v. The update above is gradient descent on \mathcal E (a diffusion equation run to steady state).
Explicit diffusion with the 5-point Laplacian is stable for \Delta t \le 1/(4\mu). The field spreads about \sqrt{4\mu t} pixels in t steps: a far reach needs many steps (the demo first iterates on a half-size grid).
The snake itself is unchanged: \mathbf v simply replaces 
abla f as the image force.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Try it: balloon and GVF




Same snake demo with GVF and the balloon enabled, and the matrix A + γI on the right (n = 100 is too large to read: lower n to 8 to see the band and the orange wrap-around corners). Tour: “U: GVF enters the concavity” (n = 100, α = 0.03, β = 0.01, resample every 10): tick field to see the GVF arrows pointing down into the slot; after 800 steps the snake reaches the bottom of the slot (y = 77.5); “concavity” with the edge force stays at y = 15.6. Without resampling the GVF snake also stops early (y = 38): the beads in the slot are pulled apart and need re-spacing. “balloon from inside”: κ = 0.3 from radius 8, stops at radius 30.3. “leaks”: the weak-edge disk with κ = 0.6 escapes to the right; even κ = 0.3 leaks (beads up to x = 129). “far start: GVF captures it”: α = 0.01 from radius 58: radius 29.85 after 100 steps (with the edge force: 56.4).

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
What snakes cannot do

Initialisation: a snake is a local method; it refines a curve you give it.
Topology is fixed: one snake = one closed curve. It cannot split around two objects, nor merge two snakes. Two objects need two snakes.
Self-intersection: nothing prevents the curve from crossing itself.
Parameters: \alpha, \beta, \sigma, w, \kappa depend on the image and the number of beads.
No idea of shape: any smooth curve is allowed. A missing piece of edge is bridged by a straight line, not by what the object should look like.

Representing the curve implicitly, as the zero level of a function on the image grid, removes the topology problem (and gives edge- and region-based versions of the snake): the level set day. Learning which shapes are plausible: the next two units.

title: The snake as a linear system
text:
Summary

Internal forces of all beads: -A\mathbf x with the cyclic pentadiagonal A; A\mathbf 1 = 0, symmetric, positive semidefinite, circulant.
Its eigenvectors are waves around the curve; \lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n): wiggles expensive, shape cheap.
Explicit step: mode k times 1 - \tau\lambda_k; explodes for \tau(4\alpha + 16\beta) > 2.
Semi-implicit step (A + \gamma I)\mathbf x_\text{new} = \gamma\mathbf x + \mathbf f: mode k times 1/(1 + \tau\lambda_k), always stable; factor once.
Capture range: coarse-to-fine \sigma, balloon \kappa\mathbf n, GVF (diffused edge force, enters concavities).
Fixed topology and no shape knowledge: level sets, and shape models.

title: Quiz: the snake as a linear system
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A is the snake matrix (internal force = -A\mathbf x), with eigenvalues \lambda_k = 4\alpha\sin^2(\pi k/n) + 16\beta\sin^4(\pi k/n).

Q1. Why does every row of A sum to zero?






Answer





The internal energy depends only on differences between bead positions. Moving the whole snake by the same amount changes nothing, so it creates no force: A\mathbf 1 = 0, and the eigenvalue of the constant mode is \lambda_0 = 0.




Q2. What do the corner entries of A (top right, bottom left) represent?






Answer





The wrap-around of the closed curve: the last bead is a neighbour of the first. Without them A would be banded and describe an open chain with free ends.




Q3. Why are the eigenvectors of A sampled cosines and sines?






Hint





Every row is the same stencil, shifted by one.









Answer





A\mathbf x is a circular convolution of \mathbf x with a fixed stencil. Convolution turns into multiplication in the Fourier basis (Images in frequency space): a wave going k times around the curve comes out as the same wave times a number, \lambda_k.




Q4. \alpha = 0.5, \beta = 0.25. What is the largest step \tau for which the explicit update is stable?






Answer





\lambda_\text{max} = 4 \cdot 0.5 + 16 \cdot 0.25 = 6; stable for \tau\lambda_\text{max} < 2, i.e. \tau < 1/3.




Q5. Which pattern of the beads is the first to explode when \tau is too large, and what does it look like?






Answer





The mode with the largest eigenvalue, k = n/2: alternate beads displaced in opposite directions, a zig-zag. Its factor per step 1 - \tau\lambda_\text{max} drops below -1 first, so it flips sign and grows every step.




Q6. The semi-implicit step costs a linear solve per step. Why is that cheap?






Answer





The matrix A + \gamma I is the same in every step as long as \alpha, \beta, \tau and n do not change: it can be factored (or inverted) once. It is banded with five diagonals plus corners, so a solve costs a few operations per bead, and x and y use the same factorisation.




Q7. A balloon snake inflates nicely inside a cell but escapes where the membrane is faint. Name two things you could change.






Answer





Lower \kappa (but then it may stop early on the strong side or on texture), raise the edge weight w or lower \sigma where the faint edge needs sharpening, switch to GVF without a balloon, or add shape knowledge (a shape model). No single \kappa fits a strong and a weak edge at once.




Q8. What does gradient vector flow add that a larger \sigma does not?






Answer





GVF spreads the edge force into flat regions without blurring the edges themselves: near edges the field stays equal to the sharp edge force. It also points into concavities, where the plain edge force points sideways. A larger \sigma widens the pull but blurs and shifts the edges and merges nearby ones.




Q9. Two touching nuclei, one snake around both. Can GVF or a balloon make the snake separate them?






Answer





No. One snake is one closed curve; no force changes that. It needs two snakes (one started in each nucleus), or an implicit representation that can split (level sets).




Q10. (math) Show that the semi-implicit factor \gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k) lies in (0, 1] for every \gamma > 0.






Answer





A is positive semidefinite, so \lambda_k \ge 0. With \gamma > 0: 0 < \gamma \le \gamma + \lambda_k, hence 0 < \gamma/(\gamma + \lambda_k) \le 1, with 1 only for \lambda_k = 0 (translation).

title: Exercise: the snake as a linear system
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write the snake matrix A for a small n and read its properties,
give the eigenvalues of A and say which shapes of the curve each one belongs to,
find the largest stable step of the explicit update, and the factor per step of the semi-implicit one,
explain the capture range and choose between a larger \sigma, a balloon force and GVF,

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations.
