title: Exercise: active shape models
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Profile
2k + 1 samples of the image derivative along the normal at a landmark, normalised by \sum\lvert g\rvert


Profile model
mean \bar{\mathbf g}_j and covariance S_j of the training profiles at landmark j


Matching
try offsets -m, \dots, m; cost: -(edge strength), or the Mahalanobis distance (\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}_j)^\top S_j^{-1}(\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}_j)


Pose
the similarity T: \mathbf p \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a\end{pmatrix}\mathbf p + \mathbf t, fitted by Procrustes


Projection
\mathbf b = \Phi^\top(T^{-1}(\mathbf Y) - \bar{\mathbf x}); clamp \lvert b_j\rvert \le 3\sqrt{\lambda_j}


Pyramid
blur and halve the image; search the coarsest level first

title: Exercise: active shape models
text:
By hand
B1. The derivative profile along the normal at one landmark, at offsets -4, \dots, 4, is (0.0, 0.6, 0.0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.0, 0.1). The model profile (3 samples, centred on the landmark) is (0.3, 0.5, 0.2). (a) Which offset does the strongest edge rule choose? (b) Slide the model over the profile: compute the sum of squared differences for the offsets -3, \dots, 3. Which offset is best? (c) Which of the two would you trust, and why? What could the spike at -3 be?
B2. A tiny shape model of a triangle, in the model frame: mean \bar{\mathbf x} = (-1, 0,\ 1, 0,\ 0, 1) (three landmarks (x, y)), two orthonormal modes \boldsymbol\phi_1 = (0, 0,\ 0, 0,\ 0, 1) (apex height) and \boldsymbol\phi_2 = (-1, 0,\ 1, 0,\ 0, 0)/\sqrt2 (base width), with \lambda_1 = 0.04, \lambda_2 = 0.02. (a) Give the limits 3\sqrt{\lambda_j}. (b) Suggested points, already in the model frame: \mathbf y = (-1.2, 0.1,\ 1.2, -0.1,\ 0, 1.3). Compute \mathbf b, b_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j}, the model shape and what the model cannot represent. (c) The same for \mathbf y = (-1.8, 0,\ 1.8, 0,\ 0, 2.5), then clamp. Give the clamped shape.
B3. Pose. The mean triangle of B2 is found in the image at (5, 3), (5, 7), (3, 5) (same order; y pointing up as in the maths). (a) Compute both centroids, then a and b of the Procrustes fit of the mean onto these points. Scale and angle? (b) The translation \mathbf t. Check that T maps (-1, 0) onto (5, 3).
B4. Pyramid. The search uses m = 6 and profiles with k = 3, on three levels (full size, half, quarter). (a) How far (in full-size pixels) can a landmark move in one iteration on each level? How long is the profile? (b) Why is the profile model trained separately for each level? (c) The start is 25 pixels off. What happens with one level, and with three?
B5. Predict the result of the search, and explain briefly: (a) strong noise, with and without the shape constraint; (b) a bar across the object that hides part of its edge; (c) an object whose shape is far outside the training set; (d) a good start, but the profile model trained on images with the opposite contrast (dark objects).
B6. Why are the training profiles normalised by \sum|g|? What would go wrong otherwise when the test images are darker than the training images?






Solutions





B1. (a) The largest value, 0.6, at offset -3. (b) Offsets -3 to 3: 0.14, 0.35, 0.26, 0.17, \mathbf{0}, 0.17, 0.27. Best: +1, where the profile is exactly the model. (c) The profile match: it uses the whole shape of the profile (an edge of this width and asymmetry), not just its height. The spike at -3 is narrow and isolated: noise, a small bright speck of clutter, or the edge of a neighbouring object.
B2. (a) 3\sqrt{0.04} = 0.6 and 3\sqrt{0.02} = 0.424. (b) \mathbf y - \bar{\mathbf x} = (-0.2, 0.1, 0.2, -0.1, 0, 0.3). b_1 = 0.3, b_2 = (0.2 + 0.2)/\sqrt2 = 0.283; b_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j} = 1.5 and 2.0: plausible. Model shape \bar{\mathbf x} + 0.3\boldsymbol\phi_1 + 0.283\boldsymbol\phi_2 = (-1.2, 0,\ 1.2, 0,\ 0, 1.3). Left over: (0, 0.1,\ 0, -0.1,\ 0, 0), a tilt of the base: no mode does that (a rotation is the pose’s job). (c) \mathbf y - \bar{\mathbf x} = (-0.8, 0, 0.8, 0, 0, 1.5): b_1 = 1.5 (7.5\sqrt{\lambda_1}), b_2 = 1.6/\sqrt2 = 1.131 (8\sqrt{\lambda_2}): both implausible. Clamped: b_1 = 0.6, b_2 = 0.424; shape (-1.3, 0,\ 1.3, 0,\ 0, 1.6): the tallest and widest triangle the model allows.
B3. (a) Centroids (0, 1/3) and (13/3, 5). Centred mean: (-1, -1/3), (1, -1/3), (0, 2/3), \sum|\mathbf p|^2 = 8/3; centred image points: (2/3, -2), (2/3, 2), (-4/3, 0). \sum\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q = -2/3 + 2/3 - 2/3 + 2/3 + 0 + 0 = 0, so a = 0; \sum(p_xq_y - p_yq_x) = (2 + 2/9) + (2 + 2/9) + (0 + 8/9) = 16/3, so b = 2. Scale 2, angle 90°. (b) \mathbf t = (13/3, 5) - \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -2 \\ 2 & 0\end{pmatrix}(0, 1/3) = (13/3 + 2/3, 5) = (5, 5). T(-1, 0) = (0, -2) + (5, 5) = (5, 3). ✓
B4. (a) Level 0: 6 pixels, profile \pm3; level 1: 12 and \pm6; level 2: 24 and \pm12 full-size pixels. (b) A profile of 7 samples covers a different stretch of the image at each level, and blurring changes how an edge looks: the trained mean and covariance must match the level they are used on. (c) One level: most landmarks do not see the edge within 6 pixels; the search moves to whatever it finds (or stays), and ends in a wrong place. Three levels: on the coarsest level the edge is within reach (24 pixels), the search gets the shape roughly right, and the finer levels refine it.
B5. (a) With the constraint: the outline fits, because wrong suggestions are outvoted by the many correct ones and the shape stays plausible. Without: every landmark follows its own noisy suggestion and the outline becomes ragged. (b) The landmarks behind the bar get bad suggestions, but the model fills the outline in from the visible part. Without the constraint they stick to the bar’s edges. (c) The search finds a compromise inside the plausible range: close where the shape is typical, wrong where it is unusual (the parameters hit their limits). (d) Every profile match prefers an edge of the wrong polarity: the landmarks move to the wrong side of the object or onto other edges; the model cannot repair systematically wrong suggestions.
B6. So that profiles compare by shape, not by contrast: an edge twice as strong gives the same normalised profile. Without normalisation a darker test image has smaller derivatives everywhere, its profiles are far from the trained mean at every offset, and the Mahalanobis distance prefers whatever offset happens to have the strongest derivative.




Math questions
B7. (math) Assume the profiles at landmark j are Gaussian, \mathbf g \sim \mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf g}_j, S_j). Show that maximising the likelihood over the offsets is the same as minimising the Mahalanobis distance. What does the rule become for S_j = \sigma^2 I?
B8. (math) (a) Show that \mathbf b = \Phi^\top(\mathbf y - \bar{\mathbf x}) gives the model shape closest to \mathbf y. (b) Show that clamping each b_j separately gives the point of the box |b_j| \le 3\sqrt{\lambda_j} closest to \mathbf b, both in the shape distance \sum_j(b_j - b'_j)^2 and in \sum_j(b_j - b'_j)^2/\lambda_j. Scaling \mathbf b down until \sum_j b_j^2/\lambda_j = 9 gives the closest point of that ellipsoid in the second distance only. Compute both for B2(c) and compare their \sum_j b_j^2/\lambda_j.
B9. (math) Suppose the suggested points are exactly a model shape in some pose: \mathbf Y = T(\bar{\mathbf x} + \Phi\mathbf b^*) with |b^*_j| \le 3\sqrt{\lambda_j}, and the current shape is the mean in another pose. Show that one iteration (pose by Procrustes of the mean onto \mathbf Y, then projection) does not in general give \mathbf b^* exactly, but that repeating pose and projection converges to it. Why does the pose fit not recover T in one step?






Solutions (math)





B7. \log p(\mathbf g) = -\tfrac12(\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}_j)^\top S_j^{-1}(\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}_j) - \tfrac12\log\det(2\pi S_j). The last term is the same for every offset, so the most likely offset minimises the Mahalanobis distance. With S_j = \sigma^2 I the distance is |\mathbf g - \bar{\mathbf g}_j|^2/\sigma^2: the sum of squared differences of B1, scaled.
B8. (a) As in the previous unit: with \Phi^\top\Phi = I the gradient of |\mathbf y - \bar{\mathbf x} - \Phi\mathbf b|^2 is -2(\Phi^\top(\mathbf y - \bar{\mathbf x}) - \mathbf b). (b) Both distances are sums of one term per mode, and the box constrains each b'_j separately, so each term is minimised on its own: the closest allowed b'_j is b_j clipped to \pm3\sqrt{\lambda_j}, whatever the weights. In the coordinates c_j = b_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j} the second distance is Euclidean and the ellipsoid is the sphere |\mathbf c| = 3, whose closest point is the radial projection: scaling. In the shape distance (weights 1 instead of 1/\lambda_j) the sphere becomes an ellipsoid again, and its closest point is not a scaled \mathbf b when the \lambda_j differ. B2(c): c = (7.5, 8). Box: c = (3, 3), \mathbf b = (0.6, 0.424), shape (-1.3, 0, 1.3, 0, 0, 1.6), \sum c^2 = 18. Ellipsoid (scale by 3/10.97): c = (2.05, 2.19), \mathbf b = (0.410, 0.309), shape (-1.219, 0, 1.219, 0, 0, 1.410). The box allows both modes at their extreme at once (\sum c^2 = 18 > 9); the ellipsoid rule keeps the shape within 3 standard deviations overall.
B9. Procrustes fits the mean to \mathbf Y, but \mathbf Y is a different shape (\mathbf b^* \ne 0): the best similarity between two different shapes is not the T that produced \mathbf Y (part of the shape difference is absorbed as an apparent rotation or scaling, as in the mislabelled landmark of the previous unit). Projecting with this slightly wrong pose gives a \mathbf b close to \mathbf b^*. Fitting the pose again to the new model shape \bar{\mathbf x} + \Phi\mathbf b is more accurate, and so on: alternating pose and shape is a block-coordinate descent on |T(\bar{\mathbf x} + \Phi\mathbf b) - \mathbf Y|^2, whose minimum, 0, is at (T, \mathbf b^*) (unique if no mode is itself a similarity). This is why Cootes et al. alternate pose and shape a few times per iteration.

title: Exercise: active shape models
text:
Explore
A 128 \times 128 synthetic image of a nucleus (or a hand) of a shape the model has not seen. The model: 40 training shapes, aligned, PCA. Before the first step you can drag the square (move) and the ring (rotate and scale) to place the mean shape. 1 suggest, 2 pose, 3 project, 4 clamp run one iteration step by step (the next step is framed); iteration runs a whole one, play runs them all (12 per pyramid level). Blue lines: the normals and their search range; red dots: suggested points. Click a landmark: the top plot shows its cost for every offset (the red line marks the best). The bottom plot shows b_j/\sqrt{\lambda_j} (red bars: at the \pm3 limit; red dots: before clamping). The readout gives the RMS distance of the landmarks to the true ones. truth draws the true outline; snake too runs a snake from the same start (green).



A1. Preset clean image, good start. Run one iteration step by step and describe what each step does to the outline. Then play. What is the final RMS error? Tick truth: is the outline as good as the RMS error suggests? Why could the two differ?
A2. Click a landmark on the left side and look at its cost curve, at the start and after a few iterations. Where is the minimum at the end? Switch to strongest edge: how does the curve change?
A3. Preset noise: constraint saves it (noise 0.25). Play. Then switch to strongest edge (reset), and then back to the profile model with the shape constraint off. Compare the three final errors.
A4. Preset occlusion: model fills in. Play with and without the shape constraint. What happens to the landmarks behind the bar?
A5. Preset far start: single level fails, pyramid works. Play with 1, 2 and 3 pyramid levels (reset after changing). Watch the caption: which level is searched when?
A6. Preset shape outside the training set (snake too ticked). Compare the ASM outline (blue) and the snake (green) with the truth. Look at the \mathbf b plot. Raise the number of modes to 5: does it help?
A7. Preset hands: coarse to fine (3 levels). Play. Then set the pyramid levels to 1 and reset. Why is the hand harder than the nucleus with one level?
A8. Back to clean image, good start, tick clutter. Compare the profile model and the strongest edge. Then set modes to 1 on the clean image: is the result worse?






Solutions





A1. Suggest: each landmark proposes a point on the edge along its normal (red); some are good, some wander. Pose: the mean shape moves, turns and scales towards the red points. Project: the shape deforms (modes) to match the red points better; the red dots in the \mathbf b plot show the raw values. Clamp: values beyond \pm3 are cut back. Final RMS error 1.61 px (from 11.79). With truth the outline lies almost exactly on the true one: the landmarks’ distance to the outline is about 0.5 px, but they are shifted a little along it (the pose angle ends at 8.1° against the true 4.6°). On a smooth, nearly elliptical outline, sliding along the curve hardly changes the image, so the search cannot see it; the RMS landmark error counts it.
A2. At the start the cost curve has its minimum somewhere along the normal, where the edge is (often near the end of the search range); after a few iterations the minimum sits at offset 0: the landmark is on the edge and stays. With the strongest edge the curve is -|edge strength|: a sharp dip at the edge, but also dips at noise, and no preference for the right polarity or width of the edge.
A3. Profile model with constraint: 2.85 px. Strongest edge with constraint: 12.20 px, worse than the start (11.79): with this much noise the strongest derivative along a short normal is usually noise. Profile model without the constraint: 10.48 px: suggestions alone follow the noise and the outline becomes ragged.
A4. With the constraint: 3.63 px. The landmarks behind the bar get poor suggestions (on the bar’s edges), but the pose and the three mode values are fitted to all landmarks; the model fills in a nucleus outline behind the bar. Without the constraint: 11.12 px, the hidden landmarks stay on the bar’s edges or wander.
A5. One level: 20.30 px after 12 iterations: the true edge is mostly outside the 6-pixel search range and the shape is pulled the wrong way. Two levels: 1.22 px; three levels: 0.60 px. The caption shows the level: with three levels the first 12 iterations run on the 32-pixel image (level 2), the next 12 on 64 pixels, the last 12 at full size. At level 2 the search reaches 24 full-size pixels.
A6. The snake follows the unusual outline closely (0.21 px from the true outline). The ASM outline is good where the shape is typical but misses the deep dent and the elongation (0.98 px from the outline, RMS landmark error 3.32 px): in the \mathbf b plot mode 1 sits at the limit -3 and the others near it. With 5 modes the RMS error is 3.95 px, not better: the extra modes describe the training set’s small variations, not this shape. The model can only produce shapes like its training shapes; unclamping them would also remove its robustness.
A7. Three levels: from 10.31 px to 0.44 px. One level: 8.48 px. The fingers are about 7 pixels wide and close together: from a start 8 px and 8° off, many finger landmarks see the edge of the neighbouring finger within their search range and lock onto it. On the coarse levels the fingers merge into a blob and the pose is found first; the fine levels then separate the fingers.
A8. With clutter blobs (and the 10 px start), the profile model ends at 1.80 px and the strongest edge at 1.99 px: here both work, because the blobs are mostly outside the search range. With one mode only, the clean image gives 1.38 px, even slightly better than 3 modes (1.61): fewer modes means fewer ways to follow wrong suggestions, as long as the object needs no more.

title: Exercise: active shape models
text:
Where this leads
Shape models learn what an object class looks like from examples. The same idea grows into active appearance models (shape and grey levels together), 3D shape models of organs, and shape priors inside graph cuts and level sets. Level sets, the next day in this elective, take the other road: no landmarks and no training, but curves that can split and merge.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
About this lecture
A segmentation is usually used to count and measure objects. Pixel scores (the thresholding day) do not see objects. Today we score objects:

IoU of two objects, and what an IoU of 0.5 looks like.
Matching predicted to true objects, one to one, at an IoU threshold \tau: true positives, false positives, false negatives.
Precision, recall, F1 of objects, and F1 as a function of \tau.
Splits and merges: the errors that cost most.
Scored predictions: the precision–recall curve and average precision, and a naming trap.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Recall: pixel scores cannot see objects
text:
Recall: pixel scores cannot see objects
From the thresholding day: compare a predicted mask with the true mask pixel by pixel. TP, FP, FN pixels; Dice = 2\,TP/(2\,TP + FP + FN), IoU (Jaccard) = TP/(TP + FP + FN).

Two touching nuclei predicted as one object: almost every pixel is right (Dice 0.96), but the count is 1 instead of 2, and the area of “the nucleus” is doubled. We have to decide which predicted object is which true object.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
IoU of two objects
The intersection over union of a true object G and a predicted object P: the overlap divided by the area covered by either.


IoU 1: identical. IoU 0: no overlap.
IoU 0.5 is already sloppy: the same disc shifted by about half its radius.
Small objects lose IoU fast: a one-pixel shift of a disc of radius 3 px gives IoU 0.65; of radius 20 px, 0.94.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: IoU and Dice
For pixel sets A (truth) and B (prediction):
\text{IoU}(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}, \qquad \text{Dice}(A, B) = \frac{2|A \cap B|}{|A| + |B|}.
With |A \cup B| = |A| + |B| - |A \cap B|, writing J for IoU and D for Dice:
D = \frac{2J}{1 + J}, \qquad J = \frac{D}{2 - D}.
Both are monotone in each other, so they rank results the same way; IoU is the stricter number (IoU 0.5 ⇔ Dice 0.67, IoU 0.9 ⇔ Dice 0.95).
Disc of radius r shifted by d: |A \cap B| = 2r^2\arccos\frac{d}{2r} - \frac d2\sqrt{4r^2 - d^2}. For d \ll r the overlap loses about 2rd and the union gains 2rd, so IoU \approx 1 - \frac{4d}{\pi r}: the loss per pixel of shift scales with 1/r.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: The math: matching is forced above 0.5
text:
The math: matching is forced above 0.5
Claim. If B_1 \cap B_2 = \emptyset, then IoU(A, B_1) > \frac12 and IoU(A, B_2) > \frac12 cannot both hold.
Proof. IoU(A, B) > \frac12 means |A \cap B| > \frac12|A \cup B| \ge \frac12|A|. Two disjoint predictions would cover more than \frac12|A| + \frac12|A| = |A| pixels of A: impossible. \square
The same holds with the roles of truth and prediction swapped (true objects do not overlap either). So for \tau > \frac12 each row and each column of the IoU table has at most one entry \ge \tau, and the matching is unique.
At exactly \frac12 it fails: A cut into two equal halves B_1, B_2 gives IoU \frac12 with both.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Below 0.5: greedy can lose a match
text:
Below 0.5: greedy can lose a match


Greedy: take the largest IoU first, then the next largest among free objects, … Here: G1–P1 (0.44); then G2 and P2 have no free partner. 1 match.
Optimal: the assignment with the most matches (then the largest total IoU): G1–P2, G2–P1. 2 matches.
Image libraries call the optimal solver the “Hungarian algorithm”. Above \tau = 0.5 both give the same answer.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: The math: matching as a linear assignment problem
text:
The math: matching as a linear assignment problem
Unknowns x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}: true object i is matched to prediction j. Weights
M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 + \varepsilon\,\text{IoU}_{ij} & \text{IoU}_{ij} \ge \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad (\varepsilon \text{ small: count matches first, then IoU}).
\max_x \sum_{i,j} M_{ij}\,x_{ij} \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_j x_{ij} \le 1,\ \ \sum_i x_{ij} \le 1,\ \ x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}.

The constraint matrix is totally unimodular: the linear-programming relaxation 0 \le x_{ij} \le 1 already has an integer optimum (stated without proof).
The Hungarian algorithm solves it exactly in O(n^3) for n objects (pad the table with zeros to a square).
With M_{ij} = \text{IoU}_{ij} instead, it maximises the total IoU; that can prefer fewer, better matches.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: Precision, recall and F1 of objects
text:
Precision, recall and F1 of objects
The pixel formulas, but each object counts one, big or small:
\text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} \quad \text{("how many of my objects are real")} \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \quad \text{("how many real objects did I find")} \text{F1} = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}
The table above at \tau = 0.5: precision 2/4 = 0.5, recall 2/3 = 0.67, F1 = 4/7 = 0.57. At \tau = 0.3: G2–P2 also matches, F1 = 6/7 = 0.86.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
F1 as a function of \tau

Sweep \tau from 0.1 to 0.95. Sloppy outlines (blue): F1 0.88 at 0.5, 0.25 at 0.8. Merged pairs (red): a lower plateau (0.69 at 0.5) but tight outlines, so 0.38 at 0.8. Their pixel Dice says the opposite (0.86 vs 0.97). Report the curve, or at least two \tau values, never one number.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: F1 against \tau
Write n_G and n_P for the numbers of true and predicted objects. Every object is either matched or not, so FP = n_P - TP and FN = n_G - TP:
\text{F1}(\tau) = \frac{2\,TP(\tau)}{2\,TP(\tau) + FP(\tau) + FN(\tau)} = \frac{2\,TP(\tau)}{n_G + n_P}.
The denominator does not depend on \tau; F1 is the number of matches, scaled. Raising \tau only removes allowed pairs, so the largest possible number of matches cannot grow: \text{F1}(\tau) is non-increasing. (Also for greedy matching: at a higher \tau it walks the same list of pairs, just stops earlier.)
The matching accuracy TP/(TP + FP + FN) = TP/(n_G + n_P - TP) moves with F1: \text{acc} = \text{F1}/(2 - \text{F1}), the same relation as IoU and Dice.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Splits, merges, misses, specks
Read from the IoU table:

Split: one true object, two predictions with IoU around 0.4 each. At \tau = 0.5: 1 FN + 2 FP.
Merge: two true objects, one prediction. At best 1 TP + 1 FN; often (IoU < 0.5 with both) 2 FN + 1 FP.
Missed dim objects: FN. Spurious specks: FP.

One merge costs more F1 than many slightly wrong outlines. Count splits and merges and report them on their own: they say what to fix (the seeds of a watershed, a threshold, a minimum size).
Watershed segmentation (the watershed day) produces exactly these errors when its markers are wrong.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Try it: matching objects




Synthetic nuclei, 16 true objects (white outlines). Predictions are filled green (TP) or red (FP); missed true objects have dashed orange outlines. Tour: “a typical result” at τ = 0.5: TP 12, FP 2, FN 4, F1 0.80, pixel Dice 0.86; two merges are labelled. “Dice high, count wrong”: Dice 0.97, but 5 merges, F1 0.69. “Sloppy outlines”: F1 0.88 at 0.5, drag τ to 0.8: 0.25. “One split”: TP 15, FP 2, FN 1. “Greedy loses a match” (τ = 0.3): switch the IoU table on the exercise page, or compare greedy (TP 15) and optimal (TP 16) with the buttons. “Specks”: precision 0.57, F1 0.73, but the PR tab shows AP 1.00: the specks have low scores. “vs a second annotator”: the grey band is above annotator B’s agreement with A.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Scores and average precision
Many methods give each object a confidence score. Sort the predictions by score and walk down the list; each one is a TP or an FP (at \tau). After each step write down (recall, precision).


4 true objects, 5 predictions by score: TP, TP, FP, TP, FP.

Average precision (AP) = area under the precision–recall curve, with precision made “never decreasing from the right”: 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 1 + 0.25 \cdot 0.75 = 0.6875.



Low-scored specks come last: they lower precision at the end of the list but hardly change AP. Averaging AP over \tau = 0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95 also rewards good outlines.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
The math: average precision
Predictions sorted by decreasing score; after the first k of them, P_k = TP_k / k and R_k = TP_k / n_G.
Interpolated precision: P^{\text{interp}}(R_k) = \max_{k' \ge k} P_{k'} (the best precision at this or a higher recall).
\text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\,P^{\text{interp}}(R_k), \qquad R_0 = 0.
Only steps that add a TP raise the recall, so FPs at the end of the list (R_k = R_{k-1}) add nothing. AP over thresholds: \frac{1}{10}\sum_{\tau \in \{0.5, 0.55, \dots, 0.95\}} \text{AP}(\tau).
For AP the matching is done in score order: each prediction takes the free true object with the largest IoU \ge \tau.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
section: A naming trap: “AP” is two different things
text:
A naming trap: “AP” is two different things
Many cell-segmentation papers report “AP at \tau” meaning
\frac{TP}{TP + FP + FN} \quad \text{at one } \tau, \text{ without any scores.}
That is not the area under a precision–recall curve. In the example: AP (area) = 0.6875, but TP/(TP+FP+FN) = 3/(3 + 2 + 1) = 0.5.
In this course we call TP/(TP + FP + FN) the matching accuracy, and say that papers sometimes call it AP. Always check the definition before comparing numbers between papers.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Two practical rules

Border objects: an object cut by the image border cannot match well. Decide once whether objects touching the border count, and apply the same rule to truth and prediction (the unbiased counting frame of the labelling day is one consistent choice).
Report enough to reproduce: \tau (or the F1-vs-\tau curve), the matching rule, how many objects, and the numbers of splits and merges, next to any single score.

title: Matching objects: IoU, F1 and average precision
text:
Summary

IoU of two objects: overlap / union. IoU 0.5 is already sloppy; small objects lose IoU fast.
Matching: one to one, IoU \ge \tau. TP = matched pairs, FP = unmatched predictions, FN = unmatched true objects; no TN.
Above \tau = 0.5 the matching is forced; below, use the optimal assignment, not greedy.
Object precision, recall, F1: the pixel formulas, counting objects. Report F1 against \tau.
Splits and merges cost most; count them.
AP = area under the precision–recall curve of scored predictions; TP/(TP+FP+FN) is the matching accuracy, which some papers also call AP.

title: Quiz: matching objects
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. IoU = overlap / union of two objects; matching is one to one at an IoU threshold \tau; TP = matched pairs, FP = unmatched predictions, FN = unmatched true objects.

Q1. Why is there no “true negative” when we count objects, and what does that mean for accuracy and ROC curves?






Hint





What would a true-negative object be?









Answer





A true negative would be “background correctly not predicted as an object”, but the background is not made of countable objects. So object-level scores use only TP, FP and FN: precision, recall, F1, matching accuracy. Accuracy (TP + TN)/\text{all} and the false-positive rate FP/(FP + TN) of a ROC curve are undefined; precision–recall curves take their place.




Q2. A nucleus of radius 3 px is predicted one pixel off; a nucleus of radius 20 px too. Which prediction is more likely to fail at \tau = 0.5, and why?






Hint





Compare the lost overlap with the area of the object.









Answer





The small one. A one-pixel shift loses a strip of about one pixel times the diameter: a large fraction of a small object (IoU about 0.65 for radius 3 px) and a small fraction of a large one (about 0.94 for 20 px). With a little extra outline error the small object falls below 0.5. Small objects need a lower \tau or a different criterion (e.g. distance between centres).




Q3. At \tau = 0.6, can one true object have two predictions with IoU \ge \tau?






Hint





How much of the true object must each of them cover?









Answer





No. IoU above 0.5 means the prediction overlaps more than half of the true object. Two non-overlapping predictions cannot both cover more than half of it. So above 0.5 every object has at most one candidate, and the matching is forced: no greedy-versus-optimal question.




Q4. A true nucleus is split by the method into two halves, each with IoU 0.4 with it. What are its contributions to TP, FP and FN at \tau = 0.5? And at \tau = 0.3?






Hint





One to one: at most one half can be matched.









Answer





At \tau = 0.5: no half matches, so 0 TP, 2 FP, 1 FN. At \tau = 0.3: one half matches (TP), the other is an FP: 1 TP, 1 FP, 0 FN.




Q5. Method A has F1 0.92 at \tau = 0.5 and 0.30 at \tau = 0.8; method B has 0.80 and 0.75. Which would you use to count cells, and which to measure their areas?






Hint





What does a high \tau demand?









Answer





A finds more objects (better at 0.5) but with sloppy outlines (collapses at 0.8): better for counting. B’s outlines are tight (holds up at 0.8), but it misses or merges more objects: better for measuring areas and shapes of the objects it finds. One F1 at one \tau would have hidden this.




Q6. A method predicts 20 objects with scores; 4 low-scored specks at the end of the list are false positives. Why does removing them change F1 but hardly change AP?






Hint





Where in the sorted list are they, and what happens to recall there?









Answer





F1 counts all predictions at the chosen cut-off: 4 fewer FP raise precision and F1. AP is the area under the precision–recall curve built by walking down the list by score; the specks come after all true objects are found, so they do not increase recall and add (almost) no area. AP rewards a good ranking; a method can have a high AP and still need a good score cut-off.




Q7. Paper X reports “AP_{0.5} = 0.80” for nucleus segmentation, paper Y “AP_{0.5} = 0.88” for detection. Can you conclude that Y is better?






Hint





The same name is used for two quantities.









Answer





No. Cell-segmentation papers often write AP for TP/(TP + FP + FN) at one \tau (the matching accuracy in this course); detection papers mean the area under a precision–recall curve of scored predictions. The two numbers are on different scales even for the same result (in the lecture’s example: 0.5 versus 0.69). Besides, they are measured on different data.




Q8. (math) Show that the object F1 equals 2\,TP/(n_G + n_P), where n_G and n_P are the numbers of true and predicted objects. Why does this make F1(\tau) non-increasing?






Hint





Every predicted object is either TP or FP.









Answer





n_P = TP + FP and n_G = TP + FN, so 2\,TP + FP + FN = n_G + n_P, which does not depend on \tau. Raising \tau removes allowed pairs, so the number of matches can only stay or drop; F1 is that number divided by a constant.

title: Quiz: active shape models
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. One ASM iteration: suggest points along the normals, fit the pose, project onto the modes, clamp.

Q1. Which step of an ASM iteration is “a snake without internal forces”, and which steps replace \alpha and \beta?






Answer





The suggestion step: every landmark moves towards a better image position on its own. Fitting the pose, projecting onto the modes and clamping replace the smoothness terms: instead of “be smooth”, the points must form a shape like the training shapes.




Q2. Why does the search look along the normal of the outline, not in every direction?






Answer





Along the outline the image hardly changes, so a move along it cannot be judged from the image; across it (along the normal) the edge is visible. Searching only along the normal also makes the search one-dimensional and cheap. Sliding along the outline is left to the shape model (which is why landmarks can end up slightly shifted along a smooth outline).




Q3. The profile model at a landmark expects a dark-to-bright step. Along the normal there is a strong bright-to-dark edge 4 pixels out and a weaker dark-to-bright edge 1 pixel in. Which does each matching rule choose?






Answer





The strongest edge (by magnitude) chooses the strong edge 4 pixels out, although it has the wrong polarity. The profile model (Mahalanobis distance to the trained profile) chooses the weaker edge 1 pixel in, whose profile looks like the trained one.




Q4. After projection, b_2 = 5\sqrt{\lambda_2}. What happens in the clamp step, and why?






Answer





b_2 is set to 3\sqrt{\lambda_2}: 5 standard deviations is far outside the range of the training shapes, so the suggested points are more likely wrong than the shape is real. The clamp keeps the shape plausible.




Q5. Part of the object is hidden behind another object. Why can an ASM still give a sensible outline there, and a snake not?






Answer





The ASM fits pose and a few mode parameters to all landmarks at once; the visible ones determine them, and the model draws the hidden part as the training shapes look there. A snake only knows “smooth”: it either follows the occluder’s edge or bridges the gap with a smooth curve that has nothing to do with the object.




Q6. Why does searching first on a coarse pyramid level increase the capture range?






Answer





On a level halved twice, a search of m pixels covers 4m full-size pixels, and the blurred image has broad edges that are visible from further away. The coarse level finds the rough pose and shape; the finer levels refine it. It is also faster: few pixels, few iterations.




Q7. You need to outline cells of an unusual mutant whose shapes are not in your training set. Snake or ASM?






Answer





A snake (or retrain the shape model with the mutants). The ASM can only produce shapes like its training shapes and will force the mutant’s outline towards a normal cell; the snake follows whatever edge it is near.




Q8. (math) Why is the Mahalanobis distance to the mean profile a sensible matching cost?






Answer





If the training profiles at a landmark are modelled as Gaussian \mathcal N(\bar{\mathbf g}, S), then $-2p(g) = (g - {g})S{-1}(g - {g}) + $ const: the smallest distance is the most probable profile. It also weighs each sample by how much it varied in training, unlike a plain sum of squared differences.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: erosion (where the SE fits) and dilation (where it hits). Erosion removes small things but shrinks everything; dilation fills small gaps but grows everything. Combined, they filter by size and shape without changing what is large enough.

Opening = erode, then dilate: removes what the SE does not fit into. Closing = the same for the background.
Their properties: increasing, idempotent (like a projection), dual.
Granulometry: openings with growing discs measure a size distribution without segmenting a single object.
The distance transform: distance from each object pixel to the background. Erosion by a disc of radius r is a single threshold of it.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: Opening: roll the SE around inside
text:
Opening: roll the SE around inside
A \circ B = (A \ominus B) \oplus B .

The erosion keeps the positions where B fits; the dilation puts a copy of B back on each of them.
So the opening is the union of all copies of B that fit inside A: roll the SE around inside the object, keep every pixel it can reach.
What it removes: specks, thin protrusions and bridges, corners sharper than B. What it keeps: everything B fits into, unchanged.


A 9 \times 9 image opened and closed by the 3 \times 3 square. Red: removed by the opening; green: added by the closing.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: Closing: roll the SE around outside
text:
Closing: roll the SE around outside
A \bullet B = (A \oplus B) \ominus B .

The same for the background: roll B around outside the object; every pixel it cannot reach becomes object.
What it fills: holes, gaps and narrow bays smaller than B. The rest of the outline stays where it was.
In the figure: the opening (20 → 12 pixels) removes the protrusion at the bottom and the two-pixel-wide part next to the hole; the closing (20 → 21) fills the hole and keeps everything else.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Properties









opening A \circ B
closing A \bullet B




compared with A
\subseteq A (removes only)
\supseteq A (adds only)


bigger input
bigger output (increasing)
bigger output


applied twice
no change: (A \circ B) \circ B = A \circ B
no change


duality
(A \circ B)^c = A^c \bullet \check B





Idempotent like a projection, P^2 = P: once every remaining part is a union of fitting copies of B, opening again finds the same copies.
Increasing + idempotent + only removes: such a filter is called an “opening” in general (an algebraic opening).

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: The math: why the opening is idempotent
text:
The math: why the opening is idempotent
A \circ B = \bigcup\{B_z : B_z \subseteq A\}: if x \in (A \ominus B) \oplus B then x = z + b with B_z \subseteq A, so x \in B_z; conversely every fitting B_z lies in the dilation of its own origin z \in A \ominus B.

Anti-extensive: a union of subsets of A is a subset of A.
Idempotent: every B_z \subseteq A also satisfies B_z \subseteq A \circ B (it is one of the sets in the union). So the fitting copies of B in A \circ B are the same as in A, and the union is the same.
Duality: (A \circ B)^c = \big((A \ominus B) \oplus B\big)^c = (A \ominus B)^c \ominus \check B = (A^c \oplus \check B) \ominus \check B = A^c \bullet \check B, using the erosion–dilation duality twice.
At the image border the properties need the adjoint pair: dilation ignores the outside, erosion treats it as object (the demo’s “ignored”).

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: Noise removal and what it costs
text:
Noise removal and what it costs

Opening removes bright specks (object pixels) smaller than B; closing fills dark holes smaller than B. A noisy mask has both: open, then close (or the other way).
Open-then-close ≠ close-then-open: a speck next to an object may be joined by the closing first and then survive the opening. Repeating with growing SEs (“alternating sequential filters”) treats both kinds of noise more evenly.
What is lost: corners are rounded (to the shape of B), thin necks are cut by the opening, thin gaps between two objects are bridged by the closing.

The SE size sets the scale: “noise” is whatever is smaller than B.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Try it: opening and closing




Same grid as last unit, with the border convention “ignored” (the adjoint pair). Tour: “opening removes the speck”: end → the speck and the thin arm are red, the block is unchanged (37 → 30). Step through: first the erosion pass, then the dilation brings back what the SE reaches. “closing fills the gap”: 65 → 70, the three one-pixel holes and the one-pixel gap between the two lower blocks are filled (green); the three-row gap above them stays. “open∘close ≠ close∘open”: open then close gives 36 pixels, the note says close-then-open differs in 31 pixels. “apply twice”: the second opening changes nothing (note: same as one opening).

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Size filtering and granulometry
Open with discs of growing radius r. Each opening is contained in the previous one: what a disc of radius r + 1 fits into, a disc of radius r fits into too.

The area left a(r) = |A \circ D_r| falls from |A| to 0: a cumulative size distribution.
The pattern spectrum a(r) - a(r + 1) counts the pixels that disappear between r and r + 1: a histogram of sizes, without segmenting or counting any object.
“Size” here = the radius of the largest disc that fits. A long thin object counts as small; two touching discs do not make one bigger object.
A line SE measures size in one direction only: openings with a horizontal line keep long horizontal structures (an orientation filter).

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
The math: granulometry
A family of openings \gamma_r is a granulometry if \gamma_r \gamma_s = \gamma_s \gamma_r = \gamma_{\max(r, s)}: the larger one wins.

For openings by B_r this holds when every B_s (s \ge r) is a union of translates of B_r, i.e. B_s \circ B_r = B_s. True for squares, diamonds, lines and Euclidean discs; digital discs only approximately, so in practice one uses the union of the openings by all discs of radius \ge r.
Then a(r) = |\gamma_r(A)| is non-increasing, a(0) = |A|, and the pattern spectrum \mathrm{PS}(r) = a(r) - a(r + 1) \ge 0 sums to |A|.
Each pixel p has a size s(p) = \max\{r : p \in \gamma_r(A)\} (the “opening function”); \mathrm{PS}(r) = |\{p : s(p) = r\}|.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Try it: granulometry




Left: the opening at radius r (dark), the removed pixels coloured by the radius at which they disappeared. Right: area left a(r) and the pattern spectrum. Tour: “two sizes, two peaks”: discs of radius 6 and 13 give peaks at r = 5 and r = 12 (the largest digital disc that fits in a disc drawn around a non-integer centre is one smaller); at r = 7, 64.7 % is left. “touching discs”: the spectrum has one peak at 7 for singles, pairs and chains alike. “lines”: horizontal line SE: the vertical bars vanish at r = 2, the horizontal ones between r = 12 and 24 according to their length. “square SE on discs”: peaks move to 3–4 and 8–9 (a square of radius r needs a disc of radius r√2).

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
The distance transform
For every object pixel p: the distance to the nearest background pixel,
\mathrm{DT}(p) = \min_{q \notin A} \|p - q\| \qquad (0 \text{ on the background}).





A mask and its city-block distance transform.




Picture it as a mountain over the object: low at the edge, high in the middle, with ridges along the centre lines.
The metric matters: city-block (steps to 4-neighbours), chessboard (8-neighbours), chamfer (weights 3 and 4 for straight and diagonal steps, \approx Euclidean), exact Euclidean.
By hand: count the steps outwards, ring by ring.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: The math: two passes are enough
text:
The math: two passes are enough
City-block DT by two raster scans, each “minimum over neighbours plus one step”:

Set d = 0 on the background, \infty on the object.
Forward (top-left to bottom-right): d(p) \leftarrow \min\big(d(p),\ d(\text{left}) + 1,\ d(\text{up}) + 1\big).
Backward (bottom-right to top-left): d(p) \leftarrow \min\big(d(p),\ d(\text{right}) + 1,\ d(\text{down}) + 1\big).


Why it works: after the forward pass, d(r) is the distance to the nearest background pixel above and to the left of r (paths of right and down steps). The backward pass then adds paths of left and up steps from such an r. Any background pixel q is reached through the corner pixel r in p’s row and q’s column (or p’s column and q’s row) chosen so that q is above-left of r and r below-right of p, with total length |\Delta x| + |\Delta y|.
Chessboard and chamfer: the same scheme with the diagonal neighbours (step weights 1, or 3 and 4).
The exact Euclidean DT is computed in linear time, separably: one 1D pass per column, then a lower envelope of parabolas per row (Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher); not derived here.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: Try it: the two-pass distance transform
text:
Try it: the two-pass distance transform




Left: the mask (click to edit); right: the distances. Step: the forward pass reads the neighbours above and to the left (the window on the right grid), the log writes min(…) for each pixel. “next stage” jumps a row. After the forward pass the bottom-right corner is too large (4); the backward pass fixes it. At the end the green cells are DT > r (slider r on the left) = the erosion by the diamond of radius r: for the 8 × 8 exercise mask, r = 2 leaves 3 pixels. Switch to chessboard: the green set becomes the erosion by the square.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
section: Erosion by a disc = a threshold of the DT
text:
Erosion by a disc = a threshold of the DT
A \ominus D_r = \{x : \mathrm{DT}(x) > r\}, \qquad A \oplus D_r = \{x : \mathrm{DT}_{A^c}(x) \le r\}
with D_r the disc of radius r and \mathrm{DT}_{A^c} the distance to A (the DT of the background).

The disc fits at x exactly when no background pixel is within distance r of x.
One DT gives the erosion by every radius; an opening by any disc is two distance transforms. Fast for large SEs.
Matching metrics: city-block DT ↔︎ diamond (the cross dilated by itself), chessboard DT ↔︎ square.
Level sets (elective): the boundary of A \oplus D_r is the outline moved outwards at unit speed for a time r, the zero level of the signed distance shifted by r.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
The math: the threshold identity
x \in A \ominus D_r \iff x + b \in A for all \|b\| \le r \iff no q \notin A with \|q - x\| \le r \iff \min_{q \notin A}\|q - x\| > r \iff \mathrm{DT}(x) > r.
For dilation, by duality: (A \oplus D_r)^c = A^c \ominus D_r = \{x : \mathrm{DT}_{A^c}(x) > r\}, since D_r is symmetric (\check D_r = D_r).
The same argument works for any norm and its “disc”: city-block (|\Delta x| + |\Delta y| \le r, a diamond), chessboard (\max(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|) \le r, a square). Pixels outside the image: the DT only sees background inside the image, which corresponds to erosion with the outside “ignored”.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Pointers

Skeletons (elective “Objects”): the centres of the largest discs that fit inside A lie on the ridges of the DT; they form the skeleton (medial axis). Hit-or-miss, thinning and skeletons are taught there.
Watershed (day 10): the DT of a mask of touching round cells has one peak per cell; flooding it splits them. Fill holes first (the reconstruction unit of this day).
Graph cuts (day 13): an opening/closing cleans a noisy threshold locally and cheaply, by size alone. A graph cut adds a smoothness term \lambda \cdot(boundary length) to an energy and finds the global best labelling; it uses the image values too, not only the mask.

title: Opening, closing and the distance transform
text:
Summary

Opening A \circ B = erode, then dilate = union of all copies of B inside A; removes what is smaller than B. Closing = the same for the background; fills what is smaller than B.
Both are increasing and idempotent; opening only removes, closing only adds; they are dual. Open-then-close ≠ close-then-open.
Granulometry: the area left after openings with growing discs, and its differences, the pattern spectrum: a size histogram without segmentation.
Distance transform \mathrm{DT}(p): distance to the background; two raster passes for city-block, chessboard and chamfer, linear time for exact Euclidean.
Erosion by a disc of radius r = \{\mathrm{DT} > r\}.

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
About this lecture
Two questions an analysis asks of colour: “find the red objects” and “how different are these two colours?”. Neither is easy in RGB.

The pixels of an image are a cloud of points in 3D; a colour space is a choice of coordinates for that cloud.
HSV: hue as an angle, saturation, value. Survives shading; singular at grey.
CIELAB: lightness and two opponent axes, built so that distance ≈ perceived difference (ΔE).
Segmentation: pick the space in which the wanted colours form a simple region.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Builds on the thresholding day (Otsu, isodata, Dice) and on the last two units (linear light, XYZ). The thresholds of day 6 work on one number per pixel; here each pixel has three, and the first job is to choose which numbers.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: Why RGB is awkward for analysis
text:
Why RGB is awkward for analysis

Shading changes all three channels. A red apple in shadow has small R, G and B: a threshold “R > 120” cuts the apple in half.
Equal RGB steps are not equal visible steps. Codes (255, 255, 0) and (255, 255, 40) are hard to tell apart; (0, 80, 0) and (0, 120, 0) are obviously different. Both pairs are 40 apart.
Hue, saturation and brightness are mixed in every channel. “Red” is not a range of one channel; it is a direction.

Better coordinates separate how much light from which colour, and measure differences as we see them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
The pixel cloud
Plot each pixel as a point at (R, G, B): an image becomes a cloud inside the RGB cube.

Greys lie on the diagonal from black to white.
An object under varying light lies on a ray from black: all three values scale together (in linear light exactly, in encoded values nearly).
A segmentation is a region of this space; a threshold on one channel is a slab with flat walls.
A good colour space bends the cube so that the wanted region becomes simple: a wedge, a disc, a ball.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
HSV: colour for picking colours
The RGB cube seen along its grey diagonal is a hexagon. HSV (Smith, 1978) uses it as a colour wheel:

V (value) = \max(R, G, B): how bright the strongest channel is.
S (saturation) = (\max - \min)/\max: how far from grey (0 = grey, 1 = pure).
H (hue): the angle around the grey axis: red 0°, yellow 60°, green 120°, cyan 180°, blue 240°, magenta 300°.

(200, 100, 50): V = 200/255 = 0.78, S = 150/200 = 0.75, H = 20° (orange).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: The math: computing H, S, V
text:
The math: computing H, S, V
With M = \max(R, G, B), m = \min(R, G, B), d = M - m (values in [0, 1]):
V = M, \qquad S = \begin{cases} d / M & M > 0 \\ 0 & M = 0 \end{cases}, \qquad H = 60° \times \begin{cases} \dfrac{G - B}{d} \bmod 6 & M = R \\[4pt] \dfrac{B - R}{d} + 2 & M = G \\[4pt] \dfrac{R - G}{d} + 4 & M = B \end{cases}

H is undefined for d = 0 (all greys): a singularity along the whole grey axis.
Piecewise linear on the hexagon, not a true angle; good enough to order the hues around a circle.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Hue is an angle

It wraps. Red sits at both 0° and 360°: “red” is the interval 340°–20°, a union of two intervals on the number line.
Averaging needs care. The mean of 350° and 10° is 0° (red), not 180° (cyan): average the unit vectors (\cos H, \sin H).
It is undefined at grey. Near the grey axis a tiny noise turns the hue anywhere: a hue mask of a noisy image speckles in grey and dark regions. Fix: require a minimum saturation (and value).
It ignores shading. Scaling all three channels by the same factor keeps H and S: a hue threshold survives shadows where an R threshold fails. The same idea: normalised rgb, r = R/(R+G+B), g = G/(R+G+B).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: The math: invariance and the circular mean
text:
The math: invariance and the circular mean
Shading: (R, G, B) \to (kR, kG, kB) with k > 0 scales M, m and d by k, so
S = \frac{kd}{kM} = \frac{d}{M}, \qquad H \propto \frac{kG - kB}{kd} = \frac{G - B}{d}: \quad \text{unchanged; } V \to kV.
(In encoded values a scaling of light is a scaling of codes only approximately, through the power law; in linear values it is exact.)
Circular mean of angles H_i: \bar H = \operatorname{atan2}\!\big(\sum_i \sin H_i, \sum_i \cos H_i\big), the direction of the mean unit vector. Its length \bar R = \|\frac1n\sum_i (\cos H_i, \sin H_i)\| is 1 when all hues agree and near 0 when they are spread out (e.g. noise around grey).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Try it: the colour cloud




WebGL: drag to rotate. Each point is a pixel in its own colour; the outline is the sRGB gamut (the cube’s edges) in the current space; the black line is the grey axis. Tour: “cube → HSV cone”: the chart of all hues fills the cube; it morphs into the cone (hue = angle, distance from the axis = S·V). Click “CIELAB”: the solid becomes lopsided (yellow high, blue low). “shadows are rays through black”: the red apple’s pixels in linear RGB lie along a line towards black (and a curve to white for the highlight). “grey pixels scatter in hue”: noise 0.03, the grey card’s pixels in HSV are a ball around the axis, every hue present. Click a pixel: its coordinates in all spaces; the ball around it selects similar colours, and their pixels light up in the image.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
CIELAB: a space for differences
CIELAB (1976) starts from XYZ and imitates perception:

L* (lightness, 0–100): a cube root of luminance, like the gamma curve. 18 % grey is L^* = 49.5: “middle grey” is not 50 % of the light.
a* (green − red) and b* (blue − yellow): opponent axes, as in the visual system. Greys have a^* = b^* = 0.
The white point is built in: everything is relative to the white (a simple white balance).
Polar form: chroma C^* = \sqrt{a^{*2} + b^{*2}} and hue angle h = \operatorname{atan2}(b^*, a^*): a perceptual version of HSV.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: The math: from XYZ to Lab
text:
The math: from XYZ to Lab
With the white (X_n, Y_n, Z_n) and
f(t) = \begin{cases} t^{1/3} & t > (6/29)^3 \\ \frac{t}{3(6/29)^2} + \frac{4}{29} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
L^* = 116\,f(Y/Y_n) - 16, \qquad a^* = 500\,\big[f(X/X_n) - f(Y/Y_n)\big], \qquad b^* = 200\,\big[f(Y/Y_n) - f(Z/Z_n)\big].

f compresses like the eye’s response; the linear piece avoids an infinite slope at black.
White: f = 1 everywhere, so (100, 0, 0). A grey kX_n, kY_n, kZ_n has equal f’s: a^* = b^* = 0.
CIELUV (same year) does the same with a different chromatic part; it is used where a more uniform chromaticity diagram is wanted.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: ΔE: colour difference as a distance
text:
ΔE: colour difference as a distance
\Delta E^*_{ab} = the Euclidean distance in Lab. About 1–2.3 is just noticeable.



pair (codes)
RGB distance
\Delta E^*_{ab}




(255, 255, 0) vs (255, 255, 40), yellows
40
4.6


(0, 80, 0) vs (0, 120, 0), dark greens
40
22.4




Lab is only approximately uniform: differences in saturated blues come out too large, and the just-noticeable “ellipses” (MacAdam) are not circles.
CIEDE2000 corrects this with weights for lightness, chroma and hue (formula not needed here; the demos offer it).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Choosing a space for segmentation
The pixels form a cloud; a class is a region of it. Choose the space in which the region is simple:

Hue wedge with a saturation (and value) floor in HSV: “red objects, in light and in shadow”.
Disc or box in a^*b^*: colour regardless of lightness.
Ball of radius ΔE around a reference colour in Lab: “everything that looks like this”.
A 2D histogram of the two chromatic coordinates (H–S, a^*–b^*, C_b–C_r, r–g) is where to see the clusters and draw the region.
One threshold is enough when one derived channel separates the classes: Otsu on a^* or on hue (the thresholding day’s Otsu, on a better number).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Clusters: isodata in 3D
The thresholding day’s isodata alternates between “split the pixels at the threshold” and “move the threshold between the two class means”. In 3D colour space the same loop is k-means:

pick k initial colours (centres);
give each pixel to its nearest centre;
move each centre to the mean of its pixels; repeat until nothing changes.


The result depends on the space (distances!) and on the start. In RGB the shadow and the lit side of an object may split into two clusters; in Lab the split follows colour more closely.
k-means as an algorithm (its objective, convergence, good starts) belongs to the Gaussian-mixture elective.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Try it: colour segmentation




Image (click: reference colour), 2D histogram (grey: all pixels, log counts; orange: the selected ones), result. Dice against the true apple (1810 pixels). Tour: “R threshold fails in the shadow”: R′ ≥ 120 keeps only the lit half, Dice 0.728. “hue survives the shadow”: hue 340°–20°, S ≥ 0.4: Dice 0.977. “red wraps around 0°”: the chart of all hues, both edges selected. “grey and dark pixels speckle”: noise 0.03, no saturation floor: 2096 table pixels selected, Dice 0.621; raise S to 0.4: 0.973. “ΔE ball”: radius 25 in Lab Dice 0.761, RGB distance 0.566. “k-means”: RGB best cluster 0.422 (shadow and light split), switch to Lab: 0.765.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
section: A colour model as a data term
text:
A colour model as a data term
Segmentation by colour alone treats every pixel separately: noise and shading leave holes and specks.

Fit a model of each class’s colours (a Gaussian in Lab, or a mixture): -\log P(\text{colour} \mid \text{class}) is a data term.
Add a smoothness term and minimise: graph cuts (day 13); interactive versions draw only a box around the object and learn both colour models (GrabCut).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Summary

An image’s pixels are a cloud in 3D; a colour space is a choice of coordinates, and a segmentation is a region.
HSV: hue is an angle (wraps, circular mean), undefined at grey (use a saturation floor), unchanged by shading.
CIELAB: lightness by a cube root, opponent axes a^*, b^*, the white built in; ΔE = Euclidean distance ≈ perceived difference (1–2 just noticeable; CIEDE2000 refines it).
Choose the space in which the class is simple: hue wedge, a^*b^* disc, ΔE ball, Otsu on one derived channel, or k-means (isodata in 3D).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute HSV coordinates, and handle hue as an angle (wrapping intervals, circular mean),
explain where hue is undefined and why a saturation floor is needed,
compute L^* and ΔE in CIELAB, and compare colour differences in Lab and in RGB,
choose a colour space and a rule (threshold, wedge, ball, clusters) for a colour segmentation.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.
