title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Pixel cloud
every pixel is a point in a 3D colour space; a segmentation is a region of it


HSV
V = \max(R, G, B), S = (\max - \min)/\max, H = angle (0° red, 60° yellow, 120° green, 180° cyan, 240° blue, 300° magenta)


Hue of a grey
undefined (\max = \min)


Circular mean
angle of the mean of the unit vectors (\cos H, \sin H)


Normalised rgb
r = R/(R+G+B), g = G/(R+G+B)


CIELAB
L^* = 116 f(Y/Y_n) - 16, a^*, b^* from f(X/X_n), f(Y/Y_n), f(Z/Z_n), f(t) \approx t^{1/3}


ΔE
\Delta E^*_{ab} = \sqrt{\Delta L^{*2} + \Delta a^{*2} + \Delta b^{*2}}; about 1–2.3 is just noticeable


k-means
assign each pixel to the nearest centre, move each centre to its pixels’ mean, repeat

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
By hand
B1. Compute H, S and V (with V in [0, 1]) of the codes (a) (255, 0, 0), (b) (0, 128, 0), (c) (200, 100, 50), (d) (128, 128, 128).
B2. (a) Compute the circular mean of the hues 350° and 10°, and their ordinary mean. Which colour is each? (b) What is the circular mean of 90° and 270°? What does that tell you? (c) Write the hue condition “red within ±20°” as one or two intervals of [0°, 360°).
B3. A surface has linear RGB (0.60, 0.10, 0.08) in the light and (0.30, 0.05, 0.04) in a shadow that halves the light. (a) Compute H, S, V for both. Which change? (b) Compute the normalised (r, g) for both. (c) Which of the rules “R > 0.4”, “H within ±20° of 0° and S > 0.4” keeps both?
B4. A grey wall has (R, G, B) = (0.50, 0.50, 0.50). Noise changes two pixels to (0.50, 0.52, 0.49) and (0.50, 0.49, 0.51). Compute their hue and saturation. What does this mean for a hue threshold?
B5. (a) Compute L^* for a grey with 18 % of white’s luminance, and for one with 50 %. (Use L^* = 116\,(Y/Y_n)^{1/3} - 16.) (b) Compute \Delta E^*_{ab} between (50, 20, 10) and (55, 17, 14). Visible? (c) In Lab, the yellow codes (255, 255, 0) and (255, 255, 40) are (97.1, -21.6, 94.5) and (97.2, -21.1, 89.9); the dark green codes (0, 80, 0) and (0, 120, 0) are (28.7, -37.2, 35.9) and (43.4, -49.4, 47.6). Compute the RGB distance and \Delta E^*_{ab} of each pair. What do you conclude?
B6. You must segment (i) yellow fruit on a table with soft shadows, (ii) all pixels that “look like” a reference skin colour, (iii) purple nuclei on a pink background. For each, propose a colour space and a rule, and say what could go wrong.






Solutions





B1. (a) H = 0°, S = 1, V = 1. (b) H = 120°, S = 1, V = 128/255 = 0.502. (c) \max = 200 (R), \min = 50, d = 150: V = 0.784, S = 150/200 = 0.75, H = 60° \cdot (100 - 50)/150 = 20° (orange). (d) S = 0, V = 0.502, H undefined (a grey).
B2. (a) Unit vectors (\cos 350°, \sin 350°) = (0.985, -0.174) and (0.985, 0.174): the mean is (0.985, 0), angle 0°: red. The ordinary mean is 180°: cyan, wrong. (b) The unit vectors (0, 1) and (0, -1) cancel: the mean vector is zero and the circular mean is undefined. Two opposite hues have no meaningful average (the length of the mean vector, 0, says the hues are maximally spread). (c) [340°, 360°) \cup [0°, 20°].
B3. (a) Light: \max = 0.60, \min = 0.08, d = 0.52: V = 0.60, S = 0.867, H = 60° \cdot (0.10 - 0.08)/0.52 = 2.3°. Shadow: V = 0.30, S = 0.867, H = 2.3°. Only V changes. (b) Both: r = 0.60/0.78 = 0.769, g = 0.10/0.78 = 0.128; the shadow gives 0.30/0.39 and 0.05/0.39, the same. (c) “R > 0.4” keeps the light part only. The hue/saturation rule keeps both.
B4. (0.50, 0.52, 0.49): \max = G, d = 0.03, H = 60°(0.49 - 0.50)/0.03 + 120° = 100°, S = 0.03/0.52 = 0.058. (0.50, 0.49, 0.51): \max = B, d = 0.02, H = 60°((0.50 - 0.49)/0.02 + 4) = 270°, S = 0.039. A noise of 1–2 % sends the hue from green to violet: on grey and dark pixels hue is meaningless, and a hue threshold selects some of them at random. A floor S > 0.2 (say) removes them.
B5. (a) 116 \cdot 0.18^{1/3} - 16 = 49.5; 116 \cdot 0.5^{1/3} - 16 = 76.1. A grey that looks halfway is only 18 % of the light. (b) \sqrt{5^2 + 3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{50} = 7.07: clearly visible. (c) Both pairs are 40 apart in RGB. Yellows: \sqrt{0.1^2 + 0.5^2 + 4.6^2} = 4.63; dark greens: \sqrt{14.7^2 + 12.2^2 + 11.7^2} = 22.40. The same RGB distance is a barely visible difference in the yellows and an obvious one in the dark greens: RGB distances do not measure perceived difference.
B6. (i) HSV: a hue wedge around yellow (about 40°–70°) with a saturation floor; robust to the shadows. Risk: the floor must be low enough for the shadowed fruit (in encoded values saturation drops slightly in deep shadow) and high enough to drop the table. (ii) Lab: a ball of radius ΔE around the reference; the radius sets what counts as “looks like”. Risk: lighting changes L^*, so a ball also rejects the same skin in shadow; a ball in a^*b^* only, or a larger radius along L^*, is more tolerant. (iii) Otsu on one channel that separates the stains (the red channel or a^*, see the colour-matrix demo of the last unit), or k-means with k = 2 or 3. Risk: unequal class sizes and stain variation between slides.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that in CIELAB any grey (X, Y, Z) = k\,(X_n, Y_n, Z_n), k > 0, has a^* = b^* = 0, and that the white has L^* = 100. Which property of f do you use?
B8. (math) Show that the circular mean \bar H = \operatorname{atan2}(\sum\sin H_i, \sum\cos H_i) minimises \sum_i \big(1 - \cos(H_i - \theta)\big) over \theta (the sum of squared chord lengths, up to a factor). When is the minimiser not unique?
B9. (math) One step of k-means on the 1D values \{0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10\} with centres starting at 0 and 1. Do the assignment and update steps until nothing changes. Then show, for general data, that the update step (centre = mean of its points) minimises the sum of squared distances of the points to their centre.






Solutions (math)





B7. With X/X_n = Y/Y_n = Z/Z_n = k, all three f values are f(k), so a^* = 500(f(k) - f(k)) = 0 and b^* = 0. White: k = 1, f(1) = 1, L^* = 116 - 16 = 100. Only that f is one and the same function for the three coordinates (and f(1) = 1).
B8. \sum_i(1 - \cos(H_i - \theta)) = n - \cos\theta\sum\cos H_i - \sin\theta\sum\sin H_i = n - R\cos(\theta - \bar H) with R\,(\cos\bar H, \sin\bar H) = (\sum\cos H_i, \sum\sin H_i). It is smallest when \cos(\theta - \bar H) = 1, at \theta = \bar H, provided R > 0. If R = 0 (the unit vectors cancel, e.g. 90° and 270°) every \theta gives the same value: no unique mean. And 1 - \cos\delta = \tfrac12\,(2\sin(\delta/2))^2 is half the squared chord.
B9. Centres 0 and 1. Assign: \{0\} to 0; \{1, 2, 8, 9, 10\} to 1. Update: centres 0 and 6. Assign: \{0, 1, 2\} to 0 (2 is closer to 0 than to 6), \{8, 9, 10\} to 6. Update: 1 and 9. Assign: unchanged. Done: centres 1 and 9. For a cluster with points \mathbf x_i, \sum_i\|\mathbf x_i - \mathbf c\|^2 is a convex quadratic in \mathbf c with gradient 2\sum_i(\mathbf c - \mathbf x_i); zero at \mathbf c = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbf x_i. So both steps lower (or keep) the total squared distance, and the algorithm stops after finitely many steps.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Explore: the colour cloud
Left: an image (synthetic); right: its pixels as a point cloud (WebGL), each point in its own colour, inside the outline of the sRGB gamut in the chosen space. The black line is the grey axis. Drag the cloud to rotate it; front, top, 3/4 view reset the view. Choose a colour space: the cloud morphs from the old coordinates to the new ones. Click a pixel to see its coordinates in all spaces; a ball of the chosen radius around its colour (in the current space) selects points, and their pixels stay bright in the image. Brush: paint over the image, and the painted pixels light up in the cloud. Noise adds noise to the stored codes; shading darkens the image from left to right.



E1. Preset cube → HSV cone. The image contains every hue at every saturation and value. Describe the cloud in sRGB (click sRGB (encoded)) and then in HSV. Where are the greys, the pure colours, black?
E2. Switch the same image to CIELAB and Y′CbCr. Which way is up? Why is the CIELAB solid lopsided: where are yellow and blue?
E3. Preset shadows are rays through black (the red apple, in linear RGB). What shape do the apple’s pixels make, and why? Set shading to 0.6: what happens to the clouds of the other objects?
E4. Preset grey pixels scatter in hue (noise 0.03, the grey card selected). Where are the card’s pixels in HSV? Switch to CIELAB: where are they now? Which space is better behaved near grey?
E5. Reset, then click the red apple at pixel (60, 55) (the readout shows the pixel you clicked). Note its HSV and Lab. With ball radius 0.08, compare how many pixels are selected in sRGB, linear RGB, HSV and CIELAB. Why is a ball not the natural shape in HSV?
E6. Preset H&E: two stains, a sheet (in sRGB). Rotate the cloud. Is it a 3D blob, a 2D sheet or a 1D line? What would you expect for an image stained with only one dye?






Solutions





E1. In sRGB the chart fills the surface layers of the cube: the top half of the image (white to pure colours) covers the faces around the white corner, the bottom half (pure colours to black) the faces around the black corner. Greys lie on the diagonal from black to white. In HSV the cube becomes a cone with black at the tip: the greys are on the vertical axis, the pure colours on the rim at the top, hue goes around.
E2. In CIELAB and Y′CbCr the lightness axis (L^*, Y′) points up and greys stay on it. The CIELAB solid is lopsided: yellow is light (high L^*, large b^*) while blue is dark (low L^*, negative b^*), and saturated blue reaches far from the axis. Y′CbCr is a linear map of the encoded cube, so it stays a (tilted, sheared) parallelepiped.
E3. A straight line from near black up to the lit red (plus a curve towards white from the specular highlight): every apple pixel is the same red times a different amount of light. With shading 0.6 every object’s cloud stretches along its own ray towards black. A threshold on one channel cuts across these rays; a hue (angle) does not.
E4. The card (mean code about 99, V \approx 0.39) has saturations up to 0.32 (mean 0.125) once noise is added, and hues all around the circle (about equally many in each 60° sector). In the HSV cone they form a ring-shaped smear around the axis: their hue is random. In CIELAB they form a compact ball around the L^* axis (chroma \sqrt{a^{*2} + b^{*2}} 7.3 on average): the noise is just noise, with no special behaviour near grey. CIELAB is smooth near grey; HSV is singular there.
E5. The pixel has codes (162, 20, 22), HSV (359.3°, 0.873, 0.634) and Lab (34.4, 54.2, 38.5). Of the apple’s 2809 pixels the ball selects 985 in sRGB, 810 in linear RGB, 976 in HSV and 1321 in CIELAB, and nothing from other objects. In the HSV cone, V is the height, so the shadowed part of the apple is far away even though its hue and saturation are the same: the natural region in HSV is a wedge (a hue interval with a saturation floor, at any V), not a ball. CIELAB selects the most because its lightness is compressed (a cube root) relative to its opponent axes.
E6. A thin, curved 2D sheet: the pixels are mixtures of two stains in different amounts (plus white), so they have two degrees of freedom. (It is curved because absorption multiplies the light; in optical density it becomes flat, see the spectral unmixing elective.) With one dye the cloud would be a single curve from white to the dye’s darkest colour.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Explore: colour segmentation
The image (click to set a reference colour), a 2D histogram of two chromatic coordinates (grey: all pixels, log counts; orange: the selected ones; the axes are written underneath), and the result: selected pixels at full brightness, or the k-means clusters in their mean colours. Methods: per-channel RGB thresholds; hue + floors (a hue interval that may wrap through 0°, minimum saturation and value); a ΔE ball around the reference colour (ΔE76 in Lab, ΔE2000, or plain RGB distance in code units); Otsu on one channel; k-means in RGB or Lab (step or run). Dice compares the result with the true red apple (1810 pixels) or the true nuclei of the synthetic scene.



S1. Preset R threshold fails in the shadow (R' \ge 120, G' \le 90, B' \le 90). Which part of the apple is found, and what is the Dice? Can you find RGB thresholds that do better?
S2. Preset hue survives the shadow. What is the hue interval, and the Dice? Where are the selected pixels in the H–S histogram?
S3. Preset red wraps around 0° (the chart of all hues). Which columns of the chart are selected, and why both edges?
S4. Preset grey and dark pixels speckle (noise 0.03, no floors). Which objects get selected by mistake? Raise S ≥ step by step: at which floor do the speckles disappear, and what is the Dice?
S5. Preset ΔE ball in Lab vs RGB distance (radius 25 around a lit apple pixel). Compare ΔE76, ΔE2000 and RGB distance at radius 25. Then increase the ΔE76 radius: what is the best Dice, and what happens if the radius is too large?
S6. Preset k-means in RGB vs in Lab (k = 4). Which clusters does RGB find, and what is the best cluster’s Dice? Switch to in Lab. Then try Otsu on a channel with a^*.






Solutions





S1. Only the lit upper half of the apple (1036 pixels): Dice 0.728. Lowering the thresholds to R' \ge 60 with G', B' \le 90 reaches 0.890 (1455 pixels, two of them table), but any fixed R' threshold trades the shadowed apple against dark non-red pixels: the shadow is a brightness change, and every RGB channel carries brightness.
S2. Hue in 340°–20° (shown as 0–20° ∪ 340–360°), S \ge 0.40, V \ge 0.10: 1728 pixels, Dice 0.977; only the specular highlight (white, low saturation) is missed. In the H–S histogram the selected pixels sit at the left and right edges (hue near 0° and 360°) and high saturation.
S3. The leftmost and rightmost columns of the chart (hues near 0° and near 360°), saturated rows only (1344 pixels). The interval wraps through 0°: it is the union of two intervals, which in the image are the two edges.
S4. With no floors, 3930 pixels are selected: 2096 table pixels (mostly in the dark shadow), 34 of the grey card and 17 of the dark stone, Dice 0.621. With S \ge 0.2: 456 table pixels remain, Dice 0.872. With S \ge 0.4: none, 1723 selected, Dice 0.973.
S5. At radius 25: ΔE76 Dice 0.761 (1111 pixels), ΔE2000 0.889 (1807, but 200 of them the dark stone), RGB distance 0.566 (715). ΔE76 at radius 60 reaches 0.986; at 80 the ball swallows the table (14 622 pixels, Dice 0.218). A ball in a lightness-including space must be wide enough to include the shadowed apple, which is far away in lightness; at some point it includes other things first.
S6. RGB, k = 4: clusters sized 5797, 968, 4119, 5500; the best matches the apple with Dice 0.422: the dark half of the apple joins the dark (shadowed) pixels, the lit half joins other bright saturated pixels. Lab: best cluster Dice 0.765: better, since a^* separates red, but L^* still splits by shadow. Otsu on a^*: threshold 21.2, Dice 0.943: one well-chosen number beats clustering in three.

title: Exercise: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Where this leads
Colour is now a set of coordinates in which a class can be a simple region. The next unit turns the question around: how to display data with colour (colour maps, channel merges, colour-blind viewers) and how PCA of the colour cloud brings out faint colour differences. A colour model per class becomes the data term of a graph cut (day 13), which adds smoothness to the pixel-wise decisions.

title: Quiz: HSV, CIELAB and colour segmentation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. HSV: V = \max, S = (\max - \min)/\max, H = angle around the grey axis (red 0°, green 120°, blue 240°). CIELAB: L^* lightness, a^* green–red, b^* blue–yellow; \Delta E^*_{ab} = Euclidean distance in Lab.

Q1. A red apple is half in shadow. Why does a threshold “R > 120” fail, while “hue near 0° and saturation > 0.4” works?






Hint





What does a shadow do to the three channels?









Answer





A shadow scales all three channels down by about the same factor. In the shadow R drops below 120, so the threshold cuts the apple in half. Hue and saturation depend only on the ratios of the channels, which the scaling keeps: the shadowed half has the same hue and saturation as the lit half.




Q2. What is the mean hue of two pixels with hues 350° and 10°? What does the ordinary average give?






Hint





Draw both on a circle.









Answer





Both are reds, 20° apart across 0°: the mean is 0°, red. The ordinary average (350 + 10)/2 = 180° is cyan, the opposite colour. Average the unit vectors (\cos H, \sin H) and take the angle of the result.




Q3. A hue mask for “red” applied to a noisy photo is full of speckles on a grey wall. Why, and what is the fix?






Hint





What is the hue of a grey pixel plus a little noise?









Answer





For grey the hue is undefined; with a little noise the channels differ slightly and the hue becomes the direction of the noise, which is random: some grey pixels get a “red” hue. Require a minimum saturation (and value): near-grey and dark pixels are then never selected.




Q4. Two colours differ by \Delta E^*_{ab} = 1. Two others differ by \Delta E^*_{ab} = 20. What do you expect to see?






Hint





What is a just-noticeable difference in Lab?









Answer





\Delta E \approx 1 is at the limit of what can be seen side by side: practically the same colour. \Delta E = 20 is an obvious difference. Lab was built so that distances roughly match perceived differences, so these statements hold anywhere in the space (approximately).




Q5. Two pairs of colours are each 40 code values apart in RGB: two bright yellows, and two dark greens. Which pair looks more different, and what does that say about distances in RGB?






Hint





Compare \Delta E: 4.6 and 22.4.









Answer





The dark greens (\Delta E = 22.4) look far more different than the yellows (\Delta E = 4.6). Equal distances in RGB are not equal visible differences, so a “ball” of fixed radius in RGB selects very different amounts of visible variation in different parts of the space.




Q6. What are a^* and b^* of any grey, and what is the Lab of the white point?






Hint





Lab is relative to the white.









Answer





Any grey has a^* = b^* = 0 (it is a scaled white, so the three ratios to the white are equal). The white is (L^*, a^*, b^*) = (100, 0, 0).




Q7. Why is “middle grey” (looks halfway between black and white) only about 18 % of white’s luminance?






Hint





L^* uses a cube root.









Answer





Perceived lightness grows roughly like the cube root of luminance. L^* = 50 (halfway) needs Y/Y_n with 116\,(Y/Y_n)^{1/3} - 16 = 50, i.e. Y/Y_n \approx 0.18. Conversely, 50 % luminance has L^* = 76: it looks fairly light.




Q8. k-means with k = 2 on the RGB values of a picture of a red apple half in shadow puts the shadowed half of the apple together with the dark background. Why might Lab do better, and why might it still fail?






Hint





What does the nearest-centre rule measure?









Answer





k-means gives each pixel to the nearest centre. In RGB the dark half of the apple is close to other dark pixels, because brightness dominates all three coordinates. In Lab the colour difference is carried by a^* (strongly positive for red), so the red pixels stay closer to each other. But L^* is still one of the three coordinates: a deep shadow can still move a pixel far from the lit apple. Dropping L^* (clustering in a^*b^* only) or using hue removes that.




Q9. (math) Show that HSV’s hue and saturation do not change when all three channels are multiplied by the same k > 0. What happens to V?






Hint





\max, \min and their difference all scale by k.









Answer





\max(kR, kG, kB) = k\max, likewise \min and d = \max - \min. S = kd/(k\max) = d/\max, and every case of H is a ratio like (kG - kB)/(kd) = (G - B)/d. Both unchanged; V = k\max scales by k.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
About this lecture
A marching-cubes mesh is not only a picture: it is a measurement. Today: what we can measure from it, how well, and which choices change the answer.

Area and volume from the triangles (the volume by the 3D shoelace formula).
Why counting voxel faces gets the area wrong at any resolution, and marching cubes does not.
Topology: components, holes, cracks, the Euler characteristic.
The choices: the iso-value c, smoothing, anisotropic spacing, surfacing a segmentation, and mesh size.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Last unit of the marching-cubes day. Builds on marching cubes (previous unit), the shoelace formula (isocontour unit; owned by the labelling day) and volumes3d/ (spacing). Choosing thresholds from histograms (Otsu) is the thresholding day’s; here it is one line.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Area and volume from the triangles
text:
Area and volume from the triangles

Area: the sum of the triangle areas. Each triangle’s area is half the length of the cross product of two of its edges.
Volume: pick any point, e.g. the origin. Each triangle and the origin form a tetrahedron; add up their volumes with sign (+ when the triangle faces away from the origin, − when it faces it). Parts outside the object cancel, and what is left is the volume inside: the 3D version of the shoelace formula.
This needs a closed, consistently oriented mesh (all normals pointing out). A surface that touches the border of the volume is open: pad the volume with background first.
Both are sums over triangles: cheap, even for millions of triangles.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: The math: area and the divergence theorem
text:
The math: area and the divergence theorem
For a triangle with corners \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c (counter-clockwise seen from outside):
\text{area} = \tfrac12\,\lVert(\mathbf b - \mathbf a) \times (\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\rVert, \qquad V = \sum_{\text{triangles}} \tfrac16\,\mathbf a \cdot (\mathbf b \times \mathbf c) = \sum \tfrac16 \det[\mathbf a\;\mathbf b\;\mathbf c].

\tfrac16\det[\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c] is the signed volume of the tetrahedron (\mathbf 0, \mathbf a, \mathbf b, \mathbf c).
Divergence theorem with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/3 (\nabla\cdot\mathbf F = 1): V = \iiint 1\,dV = \oiint \tfrac13\,\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n\,dA. On a flat triangle, \mathbf x \cdot \mathbf n is constant (= \mathbf a \cdot \mathbf n), and \tfrac13 (\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n)\cdot\text{area} = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c).
In 2D the same argument with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/2 gives the shoelace formula.
Translating the mesh adds \tfrac16\,\mathbf t\cdot\sum(\ldots) = 0 for a closed mesh: the origin does not matter.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
One bright voxel, by hand




One voxel of value 1, all neighbours 0, c = 0.5.

Each of the 6 edges to a neighbour is crossed halfway: t = 0.5.
The surface: an octahedron with vertices at distance 0.5 from the centre.
Area \sqrt3 \approx 1.73, volume \tfrac16.
Counting voxels: volume 1, area 6 (the voxel’s faces).

A single voxel is the extreme case; on large objects the two volume estimates agree, the areas do not (next slide).

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Counting voxels: fine for volume, wrong for area
text:
Counting voxels: fine for volume, wrong for area

Volume = number of voxels inside × voxel volume. Errors at the boundary go both ways and cancel: a good estimate for large objects.
Area = number of exposed voxel faces × face area. Always too large: a slanted surface becomes a staircase, and a staircase is longer than the slope.
For a sphere about 1.5 times too large, at any resolution: finer voxels make smaller steps, but just as many of them per unit of area.
In 2D, the pixel-edge perimeter of a disk is 4/\pi \approx 1.27 times too long (for a convex shape it equals the perimeter of its bounding box).
Marching cubes cuts the corners: its area converges to the true area as the voxels shrink.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: where 1.5 comes from

A small patch of area dA with unit normal \mathbf n, replaced by a voxel staircase, exposes faces whose total area is its projections onto the three coordinate planes: (|n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z|)\,dA.
Averaged over all directions on a sphere, \langle|n_x|\rangle = \tfrac12 (the mean of |\cos\theta| over the sphere), so the staircase area is 3 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac32 times the true area, independent of the voxel size.
In 2D: (|n_x| + |n_y|)\,ds, with \langle|\cos\phi|\rangle = 2/\pi on the circle: 4/\pi.
Weighting voxel configurations cleverly (Lindblad, 2005) reduces the bias to a few per cent without a mesh.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Try it: voxel faces vs marching cubes
text:
Try it: voxel faces vs marching cubes




Disk and ball of radius R, as a partial-volume grey image (each pixel ≈ the fraction of it inside) or a binary mask. At R = 6: voxel faces 674 against 4πR² = 452.4 (+49 %), marching cubes 449.4 (−0.7 %); pixel edges +27 %. Slide R up to 16: faces stay at +50 %, marching cubes at +0.07 %. Then “binary mask”: marching cubes now runs on 0/1 values, every vertex at an edge midpoint, and the area stays about 8 % too large at every R (terraces); volumes are fine either way.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Spacing, slices and topology

Anisotropic voxels: vertex positions use (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) (forgetting \Delta z scales every volume by \Delta x/\Delta z and distorts areas); gradient normals use them too (forgetting tilts the normals; recall volumes3d/).
Slice planes: the slice of an isosurface is an isocontour: the marching-squares contour of the slice lies on the mesh. A quick check of a surface against the image.
Topology: count connected components, boundary edges (edges with a triangle on one side only: cracks, or the volume border) and the Euler characteristic \chi = V - E + F.
For one closed surface, \chi = 2 - 2g with g the number of holes (handles): a sphere 2, a torus 0. Several components add up. Noise shows up as hundreds of components; a crack as boundary edges.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: Euler characteristic

Octahedron: V - E + F = 6 - 12 + 8 = 2. Any closed triangulated surface without holes: 2 (Euler’s polyhedron formula).
A torus made from an m \times n grid of quads, each split into 2 triangles: V = mn, E = 3mn, F = 2mn, \chi = 0.
\chi is a topological invariant: refining, decimating or deforming the mesh without tearing does not change it. For a closed surface with g handles \chi = 2 - 2g; for k components \chi = \sum_i(2 - 2g_i).
On a closed triangle mesh every edge has two triangles: 2E = 3F, so \chi = V - F/2 and F \approx 2V for large meshes (the “2 triangles per vertex”).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Choosing c

A blurred step edge between a dark level a and a bright level b, blurred symmetrically, passes the half-way value (a + b)/2 exactly at the true edge. Natural choice: c = (a + b)/2, from the two levels (read off the histogram).
On small or strongly curved objects the blur leaks brightness out of the object: at the true boundary the value is below half-way, the surface at c = (a + b)/2 lies inside, and the object looks too small (the partial-volume effect).
Plot the volume against c. A flat plateau: the measurement is robust. A steep curve: the result is mostly your choice of c; report it, or deblur/fit a model instead.
Thresholds from the histogram (Otsu and others) are the thresholding day’s tools; the same reasoning applies.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
The math: the half-way level

A step from a to b at x = 0, blurred by a symmetric kernel g (e.g. Gaussian): I(x) = a + (b - a)\,G(x) with G the cumulative distribution of g. Symmetry gives G(0) = \tfrac12: I(0) = (a + b)/2.
For a ball of radius R blurred by a Gaussian of width \sigma: at a boundary point, the ball covers less than half of the Gaussian’s weight (the boundary curves away), so I(R) < (a + b)/2. The error grows with \sigma/R.
Sensitivity: \dfrac{dV}{dc} = -\displaystyle\oiint \frac{dA}{\lVert\nabla I\rVert}. A sharp edge (large gradient) gives a flat volume curve; a blurred edge a steep one.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Try it: volume against c




A ball of radius 8 voxels (binary), blurred with σ, and the marching-cubes volume as a function of c. σ = 0.5: at c = 0.5 the volume is 2115.5 against the true 2144.7 (−1.4 %), and c ± 0.05 changes it by 2.3 %. “Heavy blur” (σ = 2.5): 1524.5 (−29 %), ± 14 % per ± 0.05 in c: the curve is steep and the partial-volume loss large. Then the nuclei stack (true total 79.2 µm³).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Smoothing: before or after?

Before extraction: Gaussian blur of the volume (in physical units, per axis). Removes noise, rounds corners, shrinks small and convex objects, removes thin structures. The surface stays a level set of a (smoothed) image.
After extraction: smooth the mesh, e.g. Laplacian smoothing (move each vertex towards the mean of its neighbours). Removes facets and terraces, but shrinks the whole surface step by step. Taubin’s two-step smoothing alternates a shrinking and an inflating step and keeps the size (mention only).
Either way, report what you smoothed: area is sensitive to it, volume less so.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Surfacing a segmentation

The output of thresholding, watershed (day 10) or graph cuts (day 13) is a mask (0/1) or a label image. Marching cubes at c = 0.5 on a mask puts every vertex at an edge midpoint: terraces, staircase normals, and an area that stays several per cent too large at any resolution.
Remedies: blur the mask slightly (σ ≈ 1 voxel) before extraction, or use a signed distance function (positive inside, negative outside, zero on the boundary; what the level-set elective works with): its zero level set is placed with sub-voxel accuracy.
Label images: one surface per label (mask of label \ell, then marching cubes). Two touching labels give two surfaces with a small gap or overlap between them; methods that produce one shared surface exist (multi-label marching cubes, dual methods), pointer only.

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Mesh size and decimation

Triangles ∝ surface area / voxel area: about 3 per voxel² of area. A skull in a 512³ CT has about 10^6 voxel² of surface: about 3 million triangles.
Storage: shared vertices (1.5 million × 12 bytes + 3 million × 12 bytes ≈ 54 MB) vs a triangle soup with every triangle storing its 3 vertices (108 MB).
Decimation reduces the count where the surface is flat:

vertex clustering: snap vertices to a coarser grid, merge each cell’s vertices into one, drop collapsed triangles. Simple and fast; the topology may break;
edge collapse with quadric error metrics (Garland & Heckbert, 1997): repeatedly merge the two ends of the edge whose removal changes the shape least. The standard; mention only.

Always check area and volume after decimating.

title: Measuring surfaces
section: Try it: binary masks and decimation
text:
Try it: binary masks and decimation




A tilted ellipsoid (semi-axes 16, 9, 11 voxels; true volume 6635) from a grey image, a binary mask, or the mask blurred with σ = 1. “Terraces”: the binary mask gives staircase surfaces and 8.6 % more area than the grey image (1932.9 against 1779.4). “Blurred mask”: smooth again, but 2.3 % too little volume. “Decimate 10×” (cell size 3): 508 triangles instead of 5332, area −2.1 %, volume −4.3 %. At cell size 6 the topology breaks (χ = 4, non-manifold edges).

title: Measuring surfaces
text:
Summary

Area = Σ triangle areas; volume = Σ ⅙ det[a b c] (divergence theorem, the 3D shoelace); needs a closed, oriented mesh: pad first.
Counting voxels gives good volumes; counting voxel faces overestimates area by about 1.5× at every resolution (4/π in 2D). Marching cubes converges.
Use the spacing in positions and normals; check topology with components, boundary edges and \chi = V - E + F.
c: half-way between the levels for a sharp edge; blur and small objects bias the size (partial volume); a volume-vs-c curve shows how much the choice matters.
Masks give terraces: blur slightly or use a signed distance. Decimate big meshes, and re-check area and volume.

title: Quiz: measuring surfaces
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Meshes are closed and oriented with outward normals unless said otherwise.

Q1. Why must a mesh be closed to compute its volume by summing signed tetrahedra?






Hint





What cancels in the sum?









Answer





The tetrahedra from the origin to the triangles overlap; only for a closed surface do the parts outside the object cancel between the near and far side, leaving exactly the enclosed volume. With a hole, part of the boundary is missing and the sum depends on where the origin is.




Q2. A sphere is digitised at a very fine resolution. Which estimate is good and which is bad: volume from the voxel count, area from the exposed voxel faces?






Hint





Does a staircase get closer to a slope when its steps get smaller?









Answer





The voxel count converges to the true volume. The face count stays about 1.5 times the true area at any resolution: smaller steps, but the same total length of steps per unit of slope.




Q3. A mesh has V = 1000, E = 3000, F = 2000. What is \chi, and what could the surface be?






Hint





\chi = V - E + F; a closed surface with g holes has \chi = 2 - 2g.









Answer





\chi = 0: for example one torus (one hole), or one sphere (+2) plus a surface with two holes (-2). Count the components to tell.




Q4. Two objects have the same true volume. Object A is large with sharp edges, object B small and blurred. Which one’s measured volume depends more on c?






Hint





How far does the surface move when c changes a little?









Answer





B. A blurred edge has a small gradient, so a small change of c moves the surface a long way, and a small object has a large fraction of its volume near the surface. A’s volume-against-c curve has a plateau; B’s is steep.




Q5. You smooth a mesh with many iterations of Laplacian smoothing. What happens to its volume, and why?






Hint





Where is the mean of a vertex’s neighbours on a convex surface?









Answer





It shrinks. On a convex surface the mean of a vertex’s neighbours lies inside the surface, so every step moves the vertices inwards; repeated, the whole mesh contracts (a sphere shrinks towards a point).




Q6. A confocal stack has \Delta z = 3\Delta x. The volume of a cell is computed from a mesh whose vertices were placed with \Delta z = \Delta x. By what factor is the volume wrong?






Hint





Only one coordinate is scaled.









Answer





All z coordinates are 3 times too small, so the volume is 3 times too small (a factor 1/3).




Q7. Why does a mesh from a binary mask (0/1) at c = 0.5 look terraced, and why does this inflate its area?






Hint





Where on each edge does the vertex go?









Answer





All edge values are 1 and 0, so every vertex is at an edge midpoint: the vertices follow the voxel staircase instead of the smooth boundary. The steps add area, like voxel faces but less (about 8 % for a sphere), at any resolution.




Q8. (math) Compute the signed volume \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) of the tetrahedron with \mathbf a = (1, 0, 0), \mathbf b = (0, 1, 0), \mathbf c = (0, 0, 1) and the origin. What happens if you swap \mathbf b and \mathbf c?






Hint





\mathbf b\times\mathbf c for two unit axis vectors.









Answer





\mathbf b\times\mathbf c = (1, 0, 0), so \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(1, 0, 0) = \tfrac16. Swapping \mathbf b and \mathbf c reverses the orientation: -\tfrac16.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the area and volume of a small triangle mesh, and compare them with voxel counts and voxel faces,
explain why voxel faces overestimate area at every resolution, and why marching cubes converges,
use the Euler characteristic and boundary edges to check a mesh’s topology,
reason about the choice of c, smoothing, anisotropic spacing, surfaces of binary masks, and mesh size.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Triangle area
\tfrac12\lVert(\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\rVert


Enclosed volume
\sum \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) over the triangles (closed, outward-oriented mesh)


Voxel estimates
volume = voxels inside × voxel volume; area = exposed voxel faces × face area


Euler characteristic
\chi = V - E + F; one closed surface with g holes: 2 - 2g; components add


Boundary edge
an edge with a triangle on one side only (a crack, or where the surface leaves the volume)


Half-way level
a symmetric blur of a step from a to b passes (a+b)/2 at the true edge

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
By hand
B1. One bright voxel. A voxel of value 1 has six face neighbours of value 0 (and all other voxels are 0); c = 0.5. (a) Where are the vertices of the marching-cubes surface? What shape is it, with how many triangles? (b) Compute its area. (Each triangle is equilateral; what is its side?) (c) Compute its volume, e.g. as 8 tetrahedra with a corner at the centre. (d) Compare with the voxel count (volume) and the exposed voxel faces (area).
B2. Same voxel. For which c does the octahedron have volume 1, the volume of the voxel? (The vertex on an edge from 1 to 0 lies at distance 1 - c from the centre.) What is its area then?
B3. Pixel edges in 2D. Take all pixels whose centres lie within distance 3 of the centre of one pixel (a digital disk of radius 3). (a) How many pixels are there? Compare with \pi \cdot 3^2. (b) Count the exposed pixel edges (each of length 1) and compare with 2\pi \cdot 3. (c) Show that for this convex shape the pixel-edge perimeter equals the perimeter of its bounding box. What does that give for a large disk of radius r, compared with 2\pi r?
B4. Euler characteristic. Compute \chi and say what it tells you: (a) the octahedron of B1; (b) the surface of a cube made of 12 triangles (8 vertices, 18 edges); (c) the octahedron with one triangle removed (how many boundary edges?); (d) a mesh of two separate spheres; (e) a torus made of a 6 \times 4 grid of quads, each split into two triangles.
B5. Choosing c. (a) A nucleus has grey value 200, the background 20, and the image is blurred symmetrically. Which c puts the surface at the true boundary of a large, flat part of the nucleus? (b) The nucleus is small (radius 2 voxels) and the blur is \sigma = 1.5 voxels. Will the surface at that c be too large or too small? Why? (c) Measuring the volume at c = 0.45, 0.5, 0.55 (normalised values) gives 2163, 2115, 2068 for one object and 1750, 1525, 1318 for another. Which measurement do you trust more, and why?
B6. Spacing. A spherical nucleus of radius 5 µm is imaged with \Delta x = \Delta y = 0.2 µm and \Delta z = 0.5 µm. (a) The vertex positions are computed with \Delta z = 0.2 µm by mistake. What shape do you get, and what are its volume and area? (The surface area of a flattened spheroid with semi-axes 5, 5, 2 is 200.0 µm².) Compare with the true sphere. (b) The positions are correct but the gradient normals ignore \Delta z. What is wrong now, and what is still right?
B7. Mesh size. A surface of area 10^6 voxel² is extracted (about 3 triangles per voxel², 2 triangles per vertex). (a) Estimate the number of triangles and vertices. (b) Each coordinate and each index takes 4 bytes. How much memory does the mesh need with shared vertices, and as a triangle soup (3 separate vertices per triangle)? (c) Vertex clustering with a cell of 3 voxels reduces the triangles about 10-fold on smooth surfaces. Why can it change the topology?
B8. Binary masks. A large flat surface tilted slightly against the voxel grid is extracted from a 0/1 mask at c = 0.5. (a) Where do all the vertices lie on their edges? What does the surface look like? (b) Why does its area stay too large however fine the voxels are? (c) Name two remedies.






Solutions





B1. (a) The 6 edges from the voxel to its face neighbours are crossed at t = 0.5: vertices at distance 0.5 from the centre along \pm x, \pm y, \pm z. They form an octahedron: 8 triangles. (b) Each side joins e.g. (0.5, 0, 0) and (0, 0.5, 0): length \sqrt{0.5} = 0.707. An equilateral triangle of side s has area \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2 = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\cdot 0.5 = 0.2165; times 8: \sqrt3 = 1.732. (c) Each of the 8 tetrahedra (centre plus one face) has three perpendicular edges of length 0.5: volume \tfrac16 \cdot 0.5^3 = \tfrac1{48}; total \tfrac{8}{48} = \tfrac16 = 0.167. (d) Voxel count: volume 1; voxel faces: area 6. The octahedron is much smaller (a single voxel is all boundary); for large objects the volume estimates agree.
B2. With vertices at distance r = 1 - c: volume 8 \cdot \tfrac16 r^3 = \tfrac43 r^3 = 1, so r = (3/4)^{1/3} = 0.909 and c = 0.091. Area 8 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}(r\sqrt2)^2 = 4\sqrt3\,r^2 = 5.72, still less than the 6 faces.
B3. (a) 29 pixels (rows of 1, 5, 5, 7, 5, 5, 1 pixels, i.e. offsets with x^2 + y^2 \le 9), against \pi \cdot 9 = 28.27. (b) 28 exposed edges, against 2\pi \cdot 3 = 18.85: 1.49 times too long. (c) Walking around a convex pixel shape, the boundary moves right as often as the bounding box is wide, and so on: the horizontal steps add up to twice its width, the vertical ones to twice its height. Here 2(7 + 7) = 28. For a large disk the box is 2r \times 2r: perimeter 8r, against 2\pi r, a factor 4/\pi = 1.27, at any resolution.
B4. (a) 6 - 12 + 8 = 2: one closed surface without holes. (b) 8 - 18 + 12 = 2: the same. (c) 6 - 12 + 7 = 1, with 3 boundary edges: the surface has a hole (a crack). (d) 2 + 2 = 4: two closed surfaces. (e) V = 24, E = 3 \cdot 24 = 72, F = 48: \chi = 0, one hole (a torus).
B5. (a) c = (20 + 200)/2 = 110. (b) Too small. At the boundary of a small ball the blur averages over a neighbourhood that lies mostly outside (the boundary curves away), so the value there is below 110, and the level 110 lies further inside: the partial-volume effect. (c) The first: changing c by ±0.05 changes its volume by about ±2 %, so the result hardly depends on c. The second changes by about ±14 %: its volume is mostly a choice of c (a heavily blurred or small object).
B6. (a) The z coordinates shrink by 0.2/0.5 = 0.4: a flattened spheroid with semi-axes 5, 5, 2 µm. Volume \tfrac43\pi \cdot 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 = 209.4 µm³ instead of 523.6 (exactly 0.4 times), area 200.0 µm² instead of 4\pi \cdot 25 = 314.2 (0.64 times). (b) The normals are tilted (their z component is 2.5 times too large before normalising), so the shading is wrong; the vertex positions, area and volume are still right.
B7. (a) About 3 \times 10^6 triangles and 1.5 \times 10^6 vertices. (b) Shared: vertices 1.5 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 B = 18 MB, triangles 3 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 B = 36 MB, together 54 MB. Soup: 3 \times 10^6 \cdot 3 \cdot 12 B = 108 MB, twice as much (and the connectivity is lost). (c) It merges all vertices in a cell, regardless of the surface: two sheets of the surface that pass through the same cell (a thin plate, two objects close together) are glued together, and small holes or thin parts collapse. The result can be non-manifold, and \chi can change.
B8. (a) Every crossed edge goes from 1 to 0, so t = 0.5: every vertex at an edge midpoint. The surface is a staircase of terraces following the voxels, with flat steps. (b) As with voxel faces, the steps get smaller with finer voxels but there are more of them; the excess area per unit of true area stays (in the demo about 8 % for a sphere). (c) Blur the mask slightly (σ ≈ 1 voxel) before extraction, or compute a signed distance function from the mask and extract its zero level; or smooth the mesh afterwards (which shrinks it).




Math questions
B9. (math) Derive V = \sum\tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) from the divergence theorem with \mathbf F = \mathbf x/3, and show that it does not depend on the choice of origin when the mesh is closed.
B10. (math) Show that replacing a surface patch with normal \mathbf n by voxel faces multiplies its area by |n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z|, and that the average of |n_x| over the unit sphere is \tfrac12. Conclude the factor \tfrac32 for a sphere, and derive 4/\pi in 2D.
B11. (math) (a) For a closed triangle mesh show 2E = 3F and hence F = 2(V - \chi). (b) Show that a torus built from an m \times n grid of quads (each split into 2 triangles, wrapping around in both directions) has \chi = 0.
B12. (math) (a) Show that a step from a to b, blurred by a symmetric kernel, passes (a + b)/2 at the step. (b) Use the coarea formula \frac{dV}{dc} = -\oiint_{\{I = c\}} \frac{dA}{\lVert\nabla I\rVert} to explain why a blurred edge makes the volume more sensitive to c.






Solutions (math)





B9. \nabla\cdot(\mathbf x/3) = 1, so V = \oiint \tfrac13\mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n\,dA. On a flat triangle with unit normal \mathbf n = (\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)/(2\,\text{area}), every point has \mathbf x\cdot\mathbf n = \mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n. So the triangle contributes \tfrac13\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf n\cdot\text{area} = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot\big((\mathbf b - \mathbf a)\times(\mathbf c - \mathbf a)\big) = \tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c) (the terms with \mathbf a\times vanish in the triple product). Shifting all points by \mathbf t adds \tfrac13\,\mathbf t\cdot\oiint\mathbf n\,dA = 0, because the vector area of a closed surface is zero.
B10. The voxel faces approximating the patch are its projections onto the three coordinate planes, with areas |n_x|\,dA, |n_y|\,dA, |n_z|\,dA. On the unit sphere with n_x = \cos\theta: \langle|\cos\theta|\rangle = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^\pi |\cos\theta|\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\phi = \frac{2\pi \cdot 1}{4\pi} = \tfrac12. Sum of three: \tfrac32. In 2D, (|\cos\phi| + |\sin\phi|) averaged over the circle: 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos\phi|\,d\phi = 2\cdot\frac{4}{2\pi} = \frac4\pi.
B11. (a) Every triangle has 3 edges and every edge of a closed mesh belongs to exactly 2 triangles: 3F = 2E. Then \chi = V - \tfrac32F + F = V - \tfrac12F, i.e. F = 2(V - \chi). (b) V = mn grid points; each quad contributes 3 new edges (one horizontal, one vertical, one diagonal) when the grid wraps around: E = 3mn; F = 2mn. \chi = mn - 3mn + 2mn = 0.
B12. (a) I(x) = a + (b - a)\int_{-\infty}^{x}g(s)\,ds; with g symmetric, \int_{-\infty}^0 g = \tfrac12, so I(0) = (a + b)/2. (b) Raising c by dc moves each surface point inwards by dc/\lVert\nabla I\rVert, removing a shell of volume \oiint dc/\lVert\nabla I\rVert\,dA. Blur lowers \lVert\nabla I\rVert at the edge (the same step spread over a wider distance), so the same dc moves the surface further: a steeper volume-against-c curve.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
section: Explore: voxel faces vs marching cubes
text:
Explore: voxel faces vs marching cubes
A disk (2D) and a ball (3D) of radius R pixels/voxels, as a grey image (each pixel ≈ the fraction of it inside, as a camera would record it) or a binary mask. Left: the disk with the pixels above ½, the pixel-edge boundary (red), the marching-squares contour (blue) and the true circle (dashed). Middle: relative errors against R on log–log axes, the dots at the current R. Right: the numbers.



R1. Preset voxel faces overestimate area (R = 6, grey). Read the area from voxel faces and from marching cubes, and the volume from voxel count and marching cubes. Compare with 4\pi R^2 and \tfrac43\pi R^3. Compare the 2D pixel-edge perimeter with B3.
R2. Preset marching cubes converges (R = 16). What happens to the four errors between R = 6 and R = 16? Which one does not improve, and why (B10)?
R3. Switch to binary mask and move R. What happens to the marching-cubes (and marching-squares) error now? Explain with B8.






Solutions





R1. Voxel faces 674 against 4\pi \cdot 36 = 452.4 (+49.0 %); marching cubes 449.4 (−0.7 %). Volume: 903 voxels (−0.2 %) and marching cubes 889.8 (−1.7 %) against 904.8. In 2D, 48 pixel edges against 37.7 (+27.3 %) = the bounding box 2(12 + 12), as in B3; marching squares 37.7 (−0.1 %).
R2. At R = 16: voxel faces still +50.1 %; marching cubes area +0.07 %, voxel count +0.09 %, marching-cubes volume −0.23 %. The face count does not improve: the staircase factor |n_x| + |n_y| + |n_z| does not depend on the voxel size. The other errors fall roughly like 1/R to 1/R^2 (the volume curves jump about because of how the boundary voxels happen to fall).
R3. With a binary mask every vertex sits at an edge midpoint. The marching-cubes area stays about 7–8 % too large (+7.4 % at R = 6, +8.3 % at R = 16), and the marching-squares perimeter about 6 % (+5.6 % and +5.8 %): the terraces do not go away with resolution. The volumes are still good: the mask has the right amount of inside.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Explore: volume against c
The volume enclosed by the marching-cubes surface as a function of c (click in the plot or use the slider), for a ball of radius 8 voxels that was binary and then blurred with \sigma, or for the nuclei stack of volumes3d/ (values scaled to background 0, nuclei about 1; true total volume 79.2 µm³). Right: a slice and its contour at the current c.



I1. Preset a plateau in volume vs c (\sigma = 0.5). Read the volume at c = 0.5 and the change for c \pm 0.05. How close is it to \tfrac43\pi\cdot8^3?
I2. Preset heavy blur: c decides the volume (\sigma = 2.5). The same questions. Why is the volume at c = 0.5 so much smaller now (B5)?
I3. Switch to the nuclei stack. Read the volume at c = 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7 and compare with 79.2 µm³. Which c would you report, and how would you justify it?






Solutions





I1. 2115.5 voxels³ against \tfrac43\pi\cdot512 = 2144.7 (−1.4 %); c \pm 0.05 changes it by about 2.3 %. A flat part of the curve: the measurement is robust.
I2. 1524.5 (−28.9 %), and c \pm 0.05 changes it by about 14 %. The blur (\sigma = 2.5 on a radius of 8) spreads the ball’s brightness outwards; at the true radius the value is well below 0.5, so the half-way surface lies inside (partial volume), and the gentle slope of the blurred edge makes the volume sensitive to c.
I3. About 94.4 µm³ at c = 0.3, 77.2 at c = 0.5 and 62.2 at c = 0.7 (blur 0.5 voxels). c = 0.5, half-way between background and nuclei, is closest to 79.2 (−2.5 %), as expected for objects much larger than the blur; report c together with the result, and the spread over a reasonable range of c.

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Explore: binary masks and decimation
A tilted ellipsoid (semi-axes 16, 9, 11 voxels; true volume 6635 voxels³) extracted from a grey image, a binary mask, or the mask blurred with \sigma = 1. The cluster cell size decimates the mesh by vertex clustering. Face normals, so facets and terraces show; drag to rotate.



D1. Preset terraces from a binary mask. Compare the area and volume with the grey-level image and the blurred mask. Which inputs agree on the volume, and which on the area?
D2. Preset decimate 10×. How many triangles are left, and how much do area and volume change? Increase the cell size to 6: what happens to \chi and the non-manifold edges?
D3. With a cell size of 3, compare the decimated binary mask with the decimated grey image. Does decimation remove the terraces?






Solutions





D1. Binary mask: area 1932.9, volume 6632.5. Grey image: area 1779.4, volume 6605.2. Blurred mask: area 1758.2, volume 6479.8. All three volumes are within 2.5 % of 6635; the binary mask’s area is 8.6 % larger than the grey image’s (terraces). Blurring the mask removes the terraces but shrinks the object (−2.3 % volume): blur rounds a convex object inwards.
D2. 508 triangles instead of 5332 (10.5 times fewer), area −2.1 %, volume −4.3 %: the coarse mesh cuts off the curved parts. At cell size 6: 138 triangles, area −7.2 %, volume −16.7 %, \chi = 4 and 3 non-manifold edges: vertices from different parts of the surface were merged into the same cell, and the mesh is no longer a single closed surface.
D3. With cell size 3 the binary mask gives 544 triangles and its area drops to 1759.5, close to the grey image’s decimated 1741.2: the merged vertices average over the steps, so the coarse mesh no longer follows the terraces. Decimation smooths at the scale of its cells (with the shrinkage seen in D2).

title: Exercise: measuring surfaces
text:
Where this leads
Optional further reading: dual methods (surface nets, dual contouring) place one vertex per cell instead of per edge, need no case table, and handle label images naturally. Instead of extracting a surface, a volume can also be rendered directly (projections, volume rendering with a transfer function): the 3D-graphics day, which also shows how the meshes of this day are drawn on the screen.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
About this lecture
Segmentation without labels: nobody tells us which pixels belong together. We look for groups of similar points.

Pixels and objects as points in a feature space.
k-means (Lloyd’s algorithm): assign every point to the nearest centre, move every centre to the mean of its points, repeat.
What it minimises, why it always stops, and why it can stop in the wrong place (local minima).
Initialisation: random starts, k-means++, restarts.
What k-means assumes: round groups of similar size, and units that mean something.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

First unit of the Gaussian-mixture day (elective, More learning). The day goes: k-means (this unit), one Gaussian and the mixture as a model (unit 2), fitting it by EM (unit 3), mixtures on images (unit 4). Everything here is unsupervised: no labelled examples, unlike the random-forests day and the SVM elective.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Every pixel is a point
Measure a few numbers per pixel (or per object) and draw each pixel as a point, one axis per number: a feature space.

Intensity: 1D. The histogram is the cloud of points along a line.
Colour: 3D (R, G, B or L*, a*, b*).
Intensity + local mean, or colour + position (x, y): 2D to 5D.
Every segmented object is a point too: (area, mean intensity, roundness, …).

Pixels of the same kind of material form a group (a cluster) in this space. Segmentation without labels = finding the groups. The feature space and the feature stack are the subject of the random-forests day; here we only need “a point per pixel”.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
section: Recall: isodata is two groups in 1D
text:
Recall: isodata is two groups in 1D
The thresholding day’s isodata threshold: start with a threshold t; take the mean grey value below t and the mean above; put the new t halfway between them; repeat.

That is exactly “two centres in 1D”: every pixel goes to the nearer of the two means, then each mean is recomputed.
The colour day ran the same loop on colour pixels (in Lab) as a quick colour segmentation.

Today: the algorithm itself, for any number of groups K and any dimension: what it optimises, and how it fails.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Lloyd’s algorithm
Choose K and K starting centres \mathbf m_1, \dots, \mathbf m_K. Then repeat:

Assign: every point goes to its nearest centre.
Update: every centre moves to the mean of the points assigned to it.

Stop when no assignment changes.

The assignment step cuts the space into Voronoi cells: the region closer to \mathbf m_k than to any other centre.
Between two centres the boundary is the perpendicular bisector: a straight line (a plane in 3D) halfway between them.
Each iteration costs one distance per point and centre: nK distances. Cheap even for every pixel of an image.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
section: By hand: six points on a line
text:
By hand: six points on a line

Points 1, 2, 4, 7, 9, 10, K = 2, start \mathbf m = (1, 2). The dashed line is the boundary halfway between the centres.

Assign: \{1\}, \{2, 4, 7, 9, 10\}. Update: m = (1, 6.4).
Assign: \{1, 2\}, \{4, 7, 9, 10\}. Update: m = (1.5, 7.5).
Assign: \{1, 2, 4\}, \{7, 9, 10\}. Update: m = (2.33, 8.67). Assign again: nothing changes, stop.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
What k-means minimises
The within-cluster sum of squares: every point’s squared distance to its own centre, added up:
J = \sum_i \lVert \mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)} \rVert^2 .

The assign step can only lower J: each point picks the centre that is nearest, so its term can only shrink.
The update step can only lower J: for a fixed group, the mean is the point with the smallest sum of squared distances.
There are finitely many ways to split n points into K groups, and J never goes up, so the loop must stop.
In the example: J = 142 \to 26.84 \to 15.50 \to 9.33.

But “stops” does not mean “best”: it stops when no single step helps, a local minimum. (The same objective with K = 2 appears as a region energy on the level-sets elective.)

title: Feature spaces and k-means
section: The math: why each step lowers J
text:
The math: why each step lowers J
Update. For a fixed group G_k, J_k(\mathbf m) = \sum_{i \in G_k} \lVert \mathbf x_i - \mathbf m \rVert^2 is a convex quadratic in \mathbf m:
\frac{\partial J_k}{\partial \mathbf m} = -2 \sum_{i \in G_k} (\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m) = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \mathbf m = \frac{1}{|G_k|}\sum_{i \in G_k} \mathbf x_i .
Moreover J_k(\mathbf m) = J_k(\bar{\mathbf x}) + |G_k|\,\lVert \mathbf m - \bar{\mathbf x} \rVert^2: any other centre costs more.
Assign. With the centres fixed, J = \sum_i \lVert \mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2 is minimised point by point by c(i) = \arg\min_k \lVert \mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_k\rVert.
Termination. J is non-increasing and takes one value per partition; there are at most K^n partitions, so no partition repeats once J strictly decreases: the loop ends. Finding the global minimum is NP-hard in general (already for K = 2 in many dimensions), which is why the starting point matters.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
section: Try it: k-means step by step
text:
Try it: k-means step by step




Tour: “by hand (1D)”: press assign / update alternately and read the centres and J off the readout: (1, 6.4), (1.5, 7.5), (2.33, 8.67); J 142, 26.84, 15.50, 9.33 in the plot. Then “three blobs” (k-means++, start 1): run; J goes 3.478 → 1.814 → 1.811 in two updates. Drag a centre into the middle of a blob and run again. Then “stuck”: centres (0, 1, 8) on the points 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11: J = 26 and nothing moves. “k-means++ avoids it”: the seeds land at 10, 0 and 5 and J = 1.5 after one update.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Stuck: a local minimum
Points 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11, K = 3, start \mathbf m = (0, 1, 8).

Assign: \{0\}, \{1\}, \{5, 6, 10, 11\} (5 is nearer to 8 than to 1). Update: 8 stays the mean of 5, 6, 10, 11. Nothing changes: stopped, J = 0 + 0 + (9 + 4 + 4 + 9) = 26.
The obvious answer \{0, 1\}, \{5, 6\}, \{10, 11\} has J = 6 \times 0.5^2 = 1.5.
Two centres share one group, and one centre has to cover two groups. No single assign or update step can fix this: one centre would have to jump across an empty gap.

This is typical: a bad start gives a bad answer, and k-means does not tell you.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Better starts: k-means++

Random points as centres: two of them often land in the same group.
k-means++ (Arthur & Vassilvitskii, 2007): choose the first centre at random; choose each next centre at random with probability proportional to D(\mathbf x)^2, its squared distance to the nearest centre chosen so far. Far-away points are much more likely: the centres spread out.
Restarts: run from several starts and keep the run with the smallest J.

The example with first centre 0: D^2 = 0, 1, 25, 36, 100, 121, sum 283.

P(\text{second centre} \in \{10, 11\}) = 221/283 = 0.78; P(\in\{5, 6\}) = 61/283 = 0.22; P(= 1) = 1/283.
Whichever group is picked, the third centre then most likely lands in the remaining far group.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Try it: restarts




The “100 restarts” histogram is the final J of 100 runs. On the points 0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 11 with K = 3 and random points as starts: 80 of 100 runs reach J = 1.5, 20 stop at J = 26. Press “k-means++” and “100 restarts” again: 100 of 100 reach 1.5. On “three blobs” with random starts: 94 of 100 reach the best J (1.811); the others stop between 7.6 and 8.4. With k-means++: 99 of 100.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
Feature spaces and k-means
section: The math: the boundary is a bisector
text:
The math: the boundary is a bisector
A point \mathbf x is equally far from \mathbf m_1 and \mathbf m_2 when
\lVert \mathbf x - \mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert \mathbf x - \mathbf m_2\rVert^2 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; 2\,\mathbf x^\top(\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1) = \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2 .
The quadratic terms \lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 cancel: a linear equation, a line (hyperplane) with normal \mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1 through the midpoint \tfrac12(\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2).

The cell of \mathbf m_k is an intersection of half-planes: a convex polygon (Voronoi cell).
Scaling feature j by s multiplies its squared differences by s^2: distances, and so the bisectors, change. k-means is not scale invariant.

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Try it: where k-means fails




“elongated: cut across”: two parallel cigars. k-means (run) ends with J = 3.079 and agrees with the true groups for only 125 of 160 points: it cuts both cigars across. The true split has a larger J (5.514): k-means does what it is told, the objective is wrong for these data. “big and small group”: 120 wide points and 30 tight ones; k-means gives 108 and 42: twelve points of the big group cross the bisector. “rescale the y axis”: two horizontal bands. At y × 1 k-means splits left/right; drag the slider to 1.5: the bands are separated (all 140 points right).

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
How many groups?

J always decreases with K: with K = n, every point is its own centre and J = 0. So “the smallest J” cannot choose K.
The elbow heuristic: plot the best J against K; look for the K after which adding a centre helps much less.
A principled answer needs a model of how the data arise, so that “fit” and “complexity” can be traded off: unit 3 (BIC, AIC).

title: Feature spaces and k-means
text:
Summary

Pixels or objects are points in a feature space; segmentation without labels looks for groups.
k-means: assign to the nearest centre, move centres to the means, repeat. Boundaries are perpendicular bisectors (Voronoi cells).
It minimises J = \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2; both steps lower J, so it stops, at a local minimum.
Starts matter: k-means++ seeds far apart; restarts keep the lowest J.
Assumes round, equally sized groups in comparable units; J cannot choose K.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
About this lecture
In 2001, Viola and Jones showed real-time face detection on an ordinary desktop computer. Three ideas, each worth a large factor:

Integral image: every rectangle feature costs a few lookups (units 1–3).
Boosting: out of about 160 000 features, choose a few hundred, one at a time, each time focusing on the examples still classified wrongly.
Attentional cascade: reject almost all background windows after one or two features; spend effort only on the promising ones.

We build such a detector for cartoon faces and for cells.
Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This day owns boosting; the random forests day owns trees, forests and classification basics and points here for boosting. The stump is defined in one slide below. Detection metrics (matching detections to the truth, precision–recall, AP) belong to the evaluation day; here only detection rate and false-positive rate.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
The detection task
Slide a 24 \times 24 window over every position and every scale of the image; for each window decide: face or not?

A 384 \times 288 image, scales growing by 1.25: about 670 000 windows.
Almost all are background; a few dozen overlap the faces.
So the detector must be very fast on background, and its false-positive rate per window must be tiny: 1 in 10^5 still gives several false detections per image.

Scales without an image pyramid: instead of shrinking the image, enlarge the features. With the integral image a rectangle of any size costs the same, so every scale costs the same. Each window is normalised by its own standard deviation (two tables, unit 2).

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Recall: classifiers, training and test
From the random forests day:

A classifier maps a feature vector to a label (here: face or background).
It is learnt from a training set of labelled examples and judged on a separate test set; its error rate is the fraction it gets wrong.
The training error alone is too optimistic (overfitting).

For a detector, two rates matter: the detection rate (faces found / faces present) and the false-positive rate (background windows called face / background windows).

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
section: The weak classifier: a decision stump
text:
The weak classifier: a decision stump
One feature, one threshold, one direction:
h(\text{window}) = \begin{cases} \text{face} & \text{if the feature value is above (or below) the threshold} \\ \text{background} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}

It is a decision tree of depth 1; the random forests day grows full trees from the same split search.
The best stump for a feature: sort the examples by feature value and try every threshold between neighbours.
Alone, a stump is weak: in our demo the first stump chosen has a weighted error of 6.9 %, the tenth 18.7 % (on the reweighted examples). But it is always better than guessing.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Boosting: many weak votes
AdaBoost (Freund & Schapire, 1997), as a picture:

Give every training example the same weight.
Pick the stump with the smallest weighted error.
Increase the weight of the examples it got wrong, decrease the others. The next stump must focus on them.
Repeat. The final classifier is a weighted vote of all stumps: good stumps get a larger vote.

Each round picks one feature: feature selection falls out. Of 160 000 features, a few hundred are ever used.
Viola and Jones’ first two features on real faces: “the eye region is darker than the cheeks” and “the eyes are darker than the bridge of the nose”: the two templates you tried in the last unit.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
section: Try it: boosting, one stump at a time
text:
Try it: boosting, one stump at a time




300 cartoon faces (random size, pose, lighting, hair, 30 % with glasses) and 600 background patches; feature pool 2769 (all six templates, stride 3, rectangles 2–8 px). Left: the chosen stump drawn on the mean face; below, the six examples with the largest weight in that round (orange frame: face). Top: training and test error and the bound. Bottom: every training example at its current score; dot area = weight. Tour: “first two stumps”: round 1 a centre − surround band at the top of the window (hair against forehead), ε = 0.069; round 2 an edge at the left side of the face. Add stumps one at a time: errors fall (training 0.2 % at 10 rounds, test 1.5 %). “boosting focuses on the hard examples”: the big dots sit close to 0 or on the wrong side; the heaviest examples are odd-looking background patches and unusual faces.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
The math: AdaBoost
Labels y_i = \pm 1, weights w_i = 1/n. For rounds t = 1, \dots, T:

choose the stump h_t with the smallest weighted error \varepsilon_t = \sum_i w_i\,[h_t(x_i) \ne y_i];
its vote \alpha_t = \tfrac12 \ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon_t}{\varepsilon_t} (positive whenever \varepsilon_t < \tfrac12);
reweight w_i \leftarrow w_i\, e^{-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i)} (wrong: \times e^{\alpha_t}, right: \times e^{-\alpha_t}), then divide by the sum.

Final classifier: H(x) = \operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_t \alpha_t h_t(x)\big).
After reweighting, the stump just chosen has weighted error exactly \tfrac12: the next round cannot pick the same information again.
Training error bound: \frac1n\#\{i : H(x_i) \ne y_i\} \le \prod_t 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1 - \varepsilon_t)}. Each factor is < 1 when \varepsilon_t < \tfrac12, so the training error falls exponentially fast.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
section: The math: the best threshold in one pass
text:
The math: the best threshold in one pass
For one feature, sort the n examples by value. With the threshold below all of them, every example is called positive: the error is the total weight of the negatives, E_0. Moving the threshold past example i (in sorted order) changes the error by +w_i if y_i = +1 and -w_i if y_i = -1: E_k = E_0 + \sum_{j \le k} y_{(j)} w_{(j)}. A prefix sum again. The opposite direction has error 1 - E_k. Sorting is done once per feature; each round costs one pass over n values per feature: O(\text{features} \times n).
Why \alpha_t: AdaBoost minimises the exponential loss \sum_i e^{-y_i F(x_i)}, F = \sum_t \alpha_t h_t, one term at a time; setting the derivative in \alpha_t to zero gives e^{2\alpha_t} = (1 - \varepsilon_t)/\varepsilon_t.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
The attentional cascade


A sequence of stages, each a small boosted classifier, tuned to keep almost all faces (detection about 99.5 %) and reject a fair share of background (about half or more).
A window is rejected at the first stage that says no. Only promising windows reach the expensive later stages.
Each stage is trained on the background windows that got through the earlier stages: harder and harder negatives.
On average only a few features are evaluated per window.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
The math: cascade rates
Stage i has detection rate d_i and false-positive rate f_i (on windows that reach it), and uses n_i features. A window must pass every stage, so D = \prod_i d_i, \qquad F = \prod_i f_i. Ten stages with d_i = 0.99, f_i = 0.3: D = 0.904, F = 5.9 \cdot 10^{-6}.
Expected features per background window, with p_j the pass rate of stage j: \bar n = n_1 + n_2 p_1 + n_3 p_1 p_2 + \dots = \sum_i n_i \prod_{j < i} p_j. The first stages dominate: make them tiny.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Try it: a cascade



The default cascade (8 stages, per-stage detection 0.995 and false positives at most 0.5) is precomputed; “build cascade” retrains with the slider settings (a few seconds). Table: stumps per stage, d and f on the stage’s own training set, and the share of random background windows that reach the stage. Bars: windows of the 256 × 256 test scene reaching each stage, log scale. Tour: 27 750 windows; stage 1 (2 features) rejects 20 597; after 8 stages 65 windows remain; 3.94 features per window on average although the cascade holds 37. Try fewer stages, or per-stage detection 0.95: faster but faces get lost.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Try it: detection



Sliding windows at 4 scales (24, 30, 36, 48 px) over the test scene; features are scaled, not the image. Left: merged detections (green: match a face, red: false), dashed: the true faces. Right: the windows at scale 1, coloured by the stage that rejected them. Preset “one strong classifier vs a cascade”: one boosted classifier of 50 stumps evaluates 50 features per window and gives 11 false detections; untick “no cascade”: 3.94 features per window, 2 false detections (its later stages were trained on hard background windows). “a rotated face is missed”: the face turned by 34° is not found. “training set without glasses”: one of the two faces with glasses is missed.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
section: Why it worked, and what fails
text:
Why it worked, and what fails

Three factors: cheap features (integral image), few features (boosting), few windows get many features (cascade). Overlapping detections of the same face are merged.
Rotation and profile: features are axis-aligned; a turned face is a different pattern. Fixes: rotated (45°) features, or separate detectors per pose.
Occlusion: a hand or a scarf breaks the rectangles the stumps rely on.
The training set decides who is detected. Faces unlike those in the training set (other skin tones, glasses, headscarves, ages) are detected less reliably. In our demo: train without glasses, and faces with glasses are missed.
Matching detections to the truth, precision and recall, average precision: the evaluation day.

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Beyond faces

The same detector, trained on other patches: cells, nuclei, mitoses in microscopy, pedestrians, number plates.
Modern detectors learn their features with convolutional networks (neural networks day, modern deep learning day). They are more accurate, but need much more computation and data.
The ideas live on: cascades (reject the easy cases cheaply), boosting (gradient-boosted trees are among the strongest classifiers on tabular data), and integral images wherever computation is tiny (cameras, embedded devices).

title: Boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Summary

Detection = classify hundreds of thousands of windows; almost all are background.
A stump (one feature, one threshold) is a weak classifier; AdaBoost reweights the examples so that each new stump fixes the old mistakes, and adds them as a weighted vote. It selects a few features from a huge pool.
The cascade rejects most windows after a few features: D = \prod d_i, F = \prod f_i; each stage trains on the background that got through.
Scale the features, not the image; normalise each window by its standard deviation.
What the training set lacks, the detector misses.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

find the best decision stump on a small weighted data set, and carry out AdaBoost rounds by hand: weighted error, vote \alpha, new weights,
compute the detection rate, false-positive rate and expected number of features of a cascade,
explain why a cascade is fast, why each stage trains on the background that got through, and what the training set does to the detector,
(math) derive the vote \alpha and the training-error bound.
