title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Stump
one feature, one threshold, one direction: a depth-1 decision tree


Weighted error
$= $ sum of the weights of the misclassified examples (weights sum to 1)


Vote
\alpha = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon}


Reweighting
misclassified: \times e^{\alpha}; correct: \times e^{-\alpha}; then divide by the sum


Strong classifier
sign of \sum_t \alpha_t h_t, with h_t = \pm 1


Training-error bound
\prod_t 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1-\varepsilon_t)}


Cascade
D = \prod d_i, F = \prod f_i; features per window \sum_i n_i \prod_{j<i} p_j

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
By hand
B1. AdaBoost on six numbers. One feature with values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and labels -, -, +, -, +, +. Start with equal weights \tfrac16. A stump says “+ if the value is above \theta” (or the opposite direction). (a) Find the best stump: its threshold, direction and weighted error. Compute its vote \alpha_1. (b) Reweight. What are the six new weights? Which example now carries half of the total weight? (c) Find the best stump for round 2 with the new weights, its error and \alpha_2. Compute the score \alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2 of every example. Which examples are still misclassified? (d) Round 3 finds the stump “+ if the value is below 3.5” with weighted error \tfrac29. Is the training error now 0? (Compute the final scores.)
B2. A three-stage cascade. The stages have detection rates 0.99, 0.98, 0.97, false-positive rates 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, and use 2, 5, 20 features. (a) What are the overall detection rate D and false-positive rate F? (b) How many features does a background window need on average? (Use the false-positive rates as the pass rates of background windows.) (c) Without a cascade, one classifier with all 27 features: how many per window? What is the speed-up?
B3. Ten stages. Each stage keeps 99 % of the faces and passes 30 % of the background. (a) Is D \ge 0.9? How small is F? (b) An image has 670 000 windows. How many false detections do you expect? (c) To halve the false detections, would you add a stage or make every stage stricter? What does each cost?
B4. Scales. A feature in the 24 \times 24 base window is a two-rectangle edge with rectangles of 4 \times 8 pixels at position (6, 2). (a) What does it become in a window of 36 \times 36 (scale 1.5)? How many lookups does it cost there? (b) Why divide the response by the window’s standard deviation, and by the rectangle area?
B5. Who is in the training set? A face detector is trained on 5000 faces, almost all without glasses and with light skin. (a) Predict how it behaves on faces with glasses or darker skin, and explain why with the cascade’s per-stage thresholds. (b) Why does a high detection rate on the test set not prove that the problem is absent?






Solutions





B1. (a) Threshold 2.5, “+ above”: only the value 4 (a -) is wrong. \varepsilon_1 = \tfrac16, \alpha_1 = \tfrac12\ln 5 = 0.805. (b) The mistake is multiplied by e^{0.805} = \sqrt5, the others by 1/\sqrt5; after normalising: 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1. The example with value 4 carries half the weight. (c) Threshold 4.5, “+ above”: only the value 3 (a +) is wrong, \varepsilon_2 = 0.1, \alpha_2 = \tfrac12\ln 9 = 1.099. (The old stump at 2.5 would now have error 0.5.) Scores: values 1, 2: -0.805 - 1.099 = -1.903; values 3, 4: 0.805 - 1.099 = -0.294; values 5, 6: +1.903. The value 3 (a +) is still wrong; training error \tfrac16. New weights: 0.056, 0.056, 0.5, 0.278, 0.056, 0.056. (d) \alpha_3 = \tfrac12\ln\frac{7/9}{2/9} = \tfrac12\ln 3.5 = 0.626. The stump says + for 1, 2, 3 and - for 4, 5, 6. Scores: values 1, 2: -1.903 + 0.626 = -1.277; value 3: -0.294 + 0.626 = +0.332; value 4: -0.294 - 0.626 = -0.920; values 5, 6: 1.903 - 0.626 = 1.277. All six correct: training error 0. (The bound is 0.745 \cdot 0.600 \cdot 0.831 = 0.372.)
B2. (a) D = 0.99 \cdot 0.98 \cdot 0.97 = 0.941; F = 0.5 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.2 = 0.03. (b) 2 + 5 \cdot 0.5 + 20 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 2 + 2.5 + 3 = 7.5 features. (c) 27 features per window; the cascade is 27/7.5 = 3.6 times faster. With many stages and a tiny first stage the factor grows much larger.
B3. (a) D = 0.99^{10} = 0.904: yes. F = 0.3^{10} = 5.9 \cdot 10^{-6}. (b) 670\,000 \times 5.9 \cdot 10^{-6} \approx 4 false detections per image (before merging). (c) An eleventh stage multiplies F by its own false-positive rate (0.3 would give a factor 3 fewer) and D by its detection rate (0.99): a small loss of faces, and a small extra cost, because few windows reach it. Making every stage stricter lowers D at every stage (ten times the loss) and makes the early stages, which see all windows, more expensive. Adding a stage is usually better.
B4. (a) Rectangles of 6 \times 12 pixels at (9, 3); still 6 lookups. (b) The SD makes the response independent of the contrast of this window (lighting, camera); the area makes responses at different scales comparable (the feature becomes a difference of mean grey levels). Without them, a threshold learnt at scale 1 in one lighting would not fit other scales and lighting.
B5. (a) Each stage’s threshold is set so that almost all training faces pass. Faces that differ systematically from the training faces (glasses hide the dark eyes; different contrasts between eyes, cheeks and skin) get lower scores and are rejected at some stage: they are detected less often. (b) If the test set is drawn from the same population as the training set, it lacks the same faces: the error on the missing groups is never measured. The test set must contain enough faces of every group the detector will meet, and the rates should be reported per group.




Math questions
B6. (math) After round t, AdaBoost multiplies the weights of the misclassified examples by e^{\alpha_t} and the others by e^{-\alpha_t}. Show that with \alpha_t = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1 - \varepsilon_t}{\varepsilon_t} the stump h_t has weighted error exactly \tfrac12 under the new weights. What does that mean for round t + 1?
B7. (math) Let Z(\alpha) = \sum_i w_i e^{-\alpha y_i h(x_i)} (the exponential loss after adding \alpha h). Show that Z(\alpha) = (1 - \varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha}, find the \alpha that minimises it, and show that the minimum is 2\sqrt{\varepsilon(1 - \varepsilon)}.
B8. (math) Show for two rounds that the training error of H = \operatorname{sign}(\alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2) is at most Z_1 Z_2 = \prod_t 2\sqrt{\varepsilon_t(1-\varepsilon_t)}. (Use [H(x_i) \ne y_i] \le e^{-y_i F(x_i)} with F = \alpha_1h_1 + \alpha_2h_2, and write the weights after two rounds in terms of F.) Check it on B1.






Solutions (math)





B6. Before normalising, the misclassified examples weigh \varepsilon e^{\alpha} in total and the correct ones (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha}. With e^{\alpha} = \sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} both equal \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}. So after normalising, the stump’s error is exactly \tfrac12: under the new weights it is no better than guessing, and round t + 1 must find a stump that carries new information (in B1, the stump at 2.5 has error 0.5 in round 2).
B7. Correct examples have y_i h(x_i) = 1, total weight 1 - \varepsilon; wrong ones -1, total \varepsilon: Z = (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha}. Z'(\alpha) = -(1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha} + \varepsilon e^{\alpha} = 0 gives e^{2\alpha} = (1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon, \alpha = \tfrac12\ln\frac{1-\varepsilon}{\varepsilon} (Z'' > 0: a minimum). Then Z = (1-\varepsilon)\sqrt{\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)} + \varepsilon\sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} = 2\sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}.
B8. Starting from w_i^{(1)} = 1/n, after two rounds w_i^{(3)} = \frac{1}{n}\frac{e^{-y_i\alpha_1h_1(x_i)}e^{-y_i\alpha_2h_2(x_i)}}{Z_1Z_2} = \frac{e^{-y_iF(x_i)}}{nZ_1Z_2}, where Z_t is the normaliser of round t (equal to the minimum of B7). The weights sum to 1, so \frac1n\sum_i e^{-y_iF(x_i)} = Z_1Z_2. A misclassified example has y_iF(x_i) \le 0, so e^{-y_iF(x_i)} \ge 1 \ge [H(x_i) \ne y_i]; hence the training error \le \frac1n\sum_i e^{-y_iF(x_i)} = Z_1Z_2. B1: Z_1 = 2\sqrt{\tfrac16\cdot\tfrac56} = 0.745, Z_2 = 2\sqrt{0.1 \cdot 0.9} = 0.6, bound 0.447 \ge \tfrac16. The same argument works for any number of rounds.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Explore: boosting and the cascade
The demo trains a detector on 24 \times 24 patches: 300 cartoon faces (random size, pose, lighting, hair; 30 % with glasses) and 600 background patches, with a test set of 200 faces and 400 background patches; switch target to cells for bright cells against debris. The feature pool has 2769 rectangle features (all six templates on a 3-pixel grid, rectangles 2 to 8 pixels). No real people are shown.

boost: add one stump / add 10. Left: the stump shown (slider) on the mean face (white +, black −), and the six examples with the largest weight in that round (orange frame: face, blue: background). Top plot: training and test error and the bound against rounds. Bottom plot: every training example at its score after that round; dot area = its weight for the next round.
cascade: the table lists the stages (stumps, detection and false-positive rate on the stage’s own training set, and the share of random background windows that reach the stage); the bars show how many windows of the test scene reach each stage. The default cascade (8 stages, per-stage detection 0.995 and false positives at most 0.5) is precomputed; build cascade retrains with your settings (a few seconds).
detect: the test scene with merged detections (green: a true face, red: false; dashed: the true faces) and, on the right, every window at the smallest scale coloured by the stage that rejected it.




E1. Preset first two stumps. Which features were chosen (template, position, size)? Read \varepsilon and \alpha of each (move the “show stump” slider). Do larger errors get smaller votes? What are the training and test errors after two rounds?
E2. add 10 until 10 rounds, then until 50. Note the training and test errors at 10 and 50 rounds, and the bound. Why can the training error reach 0 while the test error does not?
E3. Preset boosting focuses on the hard examples (10 rounds). Where are the big dots in the bottom plot? What kind of examples are the six heaviest?
E4. Tab cascade (preset a cascade: few features per window). How many windows does the test scene have, how many does stage 1 reject, and how many pass all stages? How many stumps does the cascade hold, and how many features does a window need on average? Compare with B2.
E5. Tab detect, preset one strong classifier vs a cascade. Compare features per window, faces found and false detections with and without the cascade (untick no cascade). Why does the cascade make fewer false detections, although it evaluates fewer features?
E6. Preset a rotated face is missed. Which face is missed by the cascade? Tick no cascade: what happens? What would you add to the training set?
E7. Preset training set without glasses. Which faces are missed? Compare with B5.
E8. Switch target to cells and look at the boost errors after 10 rounds and at the detection result. Which templates does boosting pick first for cells?






Solutions





E1. Round 1: centre − surround at (0, 3) with cells of 8 \times 2 pixels (a 24 \times 6 band near the top of the window: the hair against the forehead), \varepsilon_1 = 0.069, \alpha_1 = 1.30. Round 2: an edge (left − right) at (0, 15) with rectangles of 4 \times 8: the left side of the face against the background, \varepsilon_2 = 0.132, \alpha_2 = 0.94. Yes: the larger the weighted error, the smaller the vote. After two rounds: training error 6.9 %, test error 8.7 %. (The cartoon faces differ from real ones: here the hairline and the face outline are the most reliable cues; on real faces Viola and Jones found the eye features first.)
E2. 10 rounds: training 0.2 %, test 1.5 % (bound 3.2 %). 50 rounds: training 0.0 %, test 1.0 % (bound below 0.01 %). The training error measures the patches the stumps were chosen on; the test patches are new, and some of them (unusual faces, face-like background) fall on the wrong side of the learnt thresholds.
E3. The big dots lie near the decision boundary at 0 or on the wrong side: background patches with a high score and faces with a low one. The six heaviest examples in round 10 are four background patches and two faces: the examples the first nine stumps found hardest.
E4. 27 750 windows; stage 1 (2 stumps) rejects 20 597 (74 %); 65 windows pass all 8 stages. The cascade holds 37 stumps, but a window needs 3.94 features on average: as in B2(b), the first, tiny stages decide almost every window. Products of the stage rates on their training sets: D = 0.977, F = 2.4 \cdot 10^{-4}.
E5. No cascade (one classifier of 50 stumps, threshold 0): 50 features per window, 7 of 7 faces, 11 false detections. Cascade: 3.94 features per window, 7 of 7 faces, 2 false detections. Each later stage of the cascade was trained on the background windows that the earlier stages wrongly accepted (bootstrapping): hard, face-like background. The single classifier only saw 600 random background patches and never learnt to reject the face-like clutter.
E6. The large face right of the centre, turned by 34°, is missed by the cascade (6 of 7 found). Without the cascade the looser single classifier does find it (7 of 7, but with 11 false detections). Axis-aligned rectangle features expect upright faces; add rotated faces to the training set, use rotated (45°) features, or train separate detectors for several angles.
E7. One of the two faces with glasses is missed (6 of 7 found, no false detections). The glasses’ bright lenses and dark frames replace the dark eyes; trained only on faces without glasses, some stage rejects that window. In B5 terms: the training set decides whom the detector finds.
E8. After 10 rounds: training 0.2 %, test 0.8 %. On the test scene the cascade finds all 9 cells with no false detections (the single 50-stump classifier: 10 false detections). The first stumps are a three-rectangle line (a bright middle band between darker top and bottom), a four-rectangle diagonal and a three-rectangle line across: features that describe a bright round blob with a darker centre.

title: Exercise: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Where this leads
The detector is judged by its detection rate and false detections; matching detections to the truth, precision–recall curves and average precision belong to the evaluation day. The random forests day uses the same split search to grow full trees. Modern detectors learn their features with convolutional networks (neural networks, modern deep learning), but the cascade’s principle, spending computation only where it is needed, is still used wherever computation is scarce.

title: Quiz: phase correlation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Phase correlation divides every A_k\overline{B_k} by its size and takes the inverse FFT.

Q1. Why does the cross-correlation of two micrographs usually have a broad peak?






Hint





Which waves are strongest in a typical image, and how fast does their vote change with the shift?









Answer





Most of an image’s strength is in the slow waves (smooth brightness changes). Their votes are the largest, and a slow wave still agrees at shifts a few pixels away from the true one. The sum is a wide hill rather than a spike.




Q2. Which property of the Fourier transform makes phase correlation work?






Hint





What does a shift do to the sizes and to the phases of the waves?









Answer





The shift theorem: shifting an image multiplies each F_k by a phase factor e^{-2\pi i k t/N}; the sizes |F_k| do not change. All the information about the shift is in the phase differences, so the sizes can be thrown away.




Q3. Image B is a perfect circular shift of A by t_0. What does the phase-correlation surface look like?






Hint





After normalising, every frequency is a pure phase ramp.









Answer





A single spike of height 1 at t_0 and zero everywhere else: the inverse DFT of e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N} for all k is a delta.




Q4. B is A with twice the contrast and 50 grey levels brighter. How does the phase-correlation surface change? And the cross-correlation?






Hint





Which B_k does the offset change, and what does the gain do to the phases?









Answer





Phase correlation: not at all. The gain multiplies every B_k by 2 (same phase), the offset only changes B_0, and after normalisation R_0 has size 1 whatever B_0 is. Cross-correlation: the surface doubles (gain) and the mean term changes (offset); with the means subtracted, only the factor 2 remains, but an uneven brightness change would move CC’s peak.




Q5. Why does phase correlation suffer more from noise than cross-correlation?






Hint





Where in the spectrum is the noise as strong as the signal?









Answer





At high frequencies the image signal is weak and the noise is about as strong: the phase differences there are random. Cross-correlation gives these frequencies small votes (they are weak); phase correlation gives them the same vote as the strong low frequencies. Many random votes make a noisy floor that can be higher than the spike.




Q6. Name two ways to make phase correlation more robust to noise.






Hint





Change the weights of the frequencies.









Answer





Multiply the normalised spectrum by a low-pass weight that fades out the highest frequencies; or normalise only partly, dividing by |A_k\overline{B_k}|^p with 0 < p < 1, which keeps some of the strength information. (Also: an \varepsilon in the denominator, averaging or smoothing the images first.)




Q7. Without a taper, phase correlation of two crops often shows a false peak at shift (0, 0) and a bright cross in the spectrum. Why?






Hint





What does the DFT assume happens at the border of a crop?









Answer





The DFT treats each crop as periodic, so the left border meets the right one (and top meets bottom), usually with a jump in brightness. These jump lines produce strong waves along the axes (the cross) and they are at the same place in both crops: they do not move with the shift, so they vote for zero shift. A Hann taper brings both crops smoothly to zero at the border and removes the jumps.




Q8. Two tiles give a phase-correlation peak of 0.08 and a peak ratio of 1.05. What do you conclude?






Hint





What do the height and the ratio measure?









Answer





Do not trust this shift. A ratio of 1.05 means the second-best shift is almost as good; a height of 0.08 means very little shared content (or a lot of noise). Typical reasons: a nearly empty tile, a periodic texture, a very small overlap. A mosaic program should drop this pair or give it a small weight.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
About this lecture
The DP table needs an order: row after row, angle after angle. A boundary that may wander in any direction has no such order. Today the algorithm finds the order as it runs.

Pixels as a graph; the same Bellman equations, but no fixed order.
Dijkstra’s algorithm: the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost is final. A priority queue gives the order.
The result is a shortest-path tree: every pixel knows its best predecessor.
Live-wire (intelligent scissors): click a seed, and the cheapest path to the mouse follows in real time.
Same tree, other uses: length along a neurite, distances, watershed.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Prerequisites: the DP table and backtracking (first unit of this day), graphs from the graph-cut day (recalled in two lines), the gradient magnitude and the Laplacian of Gaussian from the filtering/edges units (used as costs, not re-taught). Watershed (day 10) is recalled on one slide.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
The detour
Recall the “detour” grid of the first unit: a cheap channel that runs down, right, up and down again.

The best monotone path (one cell per row) costs 24: it has to cross two expensive cells.
Following the channel costs 19, but that path goes up: not one cell per row.
Worse: the cheapest way to a cell in row 2 may come from row 5, which a row-by-row table fills later.

The same happened to the distance transform: one raster pass is wrong where the shortest path goes up or left. We need a method that works without a fixed order.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Pixels as a graph
Recall from the graph-cut day: a graph is a set of nodes and edges between them, each edge with a weight.

Node = pixel; edges to the 4 (or 8) neighbours.
Weight of a move u \to v: here the cost of the pixel entered, C(v) (times the step length 1 or \sqrt 2 for 8 neighbours).
A path from the seed s pays the sum of its weights. On the grids of this unit the seed’s own cost counts too, as in the first unit.

The question: the cheapest path from s to every pixel.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
The same equations, no order
The principle of optimality still holds: the best path to v ends with a step from some neighbour u, and its part up to u is the best path to u. So

d(v) = the smallest d(u) + w(u, v) over the neighbours u of v, and d(s) = its start value.

These are the same equations as the DP table. But now d(v) may depend on a neighbour below it, and that neighbour on v itself: the equations go round in circles. There is no row order in which every right-hand side is known first.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Dijkstra’s idea
All weights are non-negative. Keep a tentative cost for every pixel (∞ at first, the start value at the seed).

Take the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost. Its cost is final: any other route to it would pass through some unfinished pixel, which already costs at least as much, and can only add.
Update its neighbours: if going through it is cheaper, lower their tentative cost and remember it as their predecessor.
Repeat until every pixel is final.

A priority queue hands out the smallest tentative pixel quickly. This is DP where the order is discovered while the algorithm runs (Dijkstra, 1959).

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
section: The math: why the smallest is final
text:
The math: why the smallest is final
Let F be the set of final pixels, with d(u) correct for u \in F, and let v \notin F have the smallest tentative value \tilde d(v) = \min_{u \in F,\, u \sim v} d(u) + w(u, v).
Take any path from s to v. It leaves F somewhere: let y \notin F be the first pixel on it outside F, entered from x \in F. Its cost is at least
d(x) + w(x, y) + (\text{rest}) \;\ge\; \tilde d(y) + 0 \;\ge\; \tilde d(v),
because the rest has non-negative weights and v had the smallest tentative value. So no path beats \tilde d(v): it is final. Induction over the pops proves that every final value is correct.
With a binary heap, each pop and each update costs O(\log N): O(N \log N) for an image with N pixels and a fixed number of neighbours.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
section: Try it: Dijkstra step by step
text:
Try it: Dijkstra step by step




Left: the costs; right: the tentative cost d (∞ = not reached yet). “step” makes the smallest pixel of the queue final (blue, numbered in the order they become final) and updates its 4 neighbours (outlined); the queue, smallest first, is listed under the controls. Arrows point to each pixel’s predecessor (grey while tentative, orange when final). At the end “backtrack” follows the arrows from the target. Tour: by-hand grid (from the top-left corner; target bottom-right, cost 18). “the detour”: the same grid as in the first unit, now solved: 19. “a wall with one gap”: from the top-left to the bottom-left corner: the path goes right, through the gap and back left (16). Switch to “one raster pass”: the same grids with one top-to-bottom, left-to-right pass: wrong cells in red, with the true value as the small number.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
The shortest-path tree
When Dijkstra stops, every pixel has a final cost and a predecessor: the neighbour its best path comes from.

The predecessors form a tree rooted at the seed: following them from any pixel leads back to the seed.
The cheapest path to any pixel is read off by backtracking, as in the DP table: a few steps, no new computation.
Work: every pixel is made final once and updates its neighbours: about N \log N for N pixels. A 256 \times 256 image takes some tens of milliseconds.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
section: When Dijkstra fails, and when we don’t need it
text:
When Dijkstra fails, and when we don’t need it

A negative weight breaks the argument: a pixel declared final could still be reached more cheaply by a later detour through the negative edge. (Costs of pixels, which are \ge 0, are fine.)
If the moves only go forward (down, as in the first unit), the graph has no cycles, and a fixed order exists: the row-by-row table. Monotone-path DP is the special case where the order is known in advance.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
The math: the link cost
For a move from p to a neighbour q of length \ell = |q - p| (1 or \sqrt2):
w(p, q) = \ell\,\big(\varepsilon + w_G\, f_G(q) + w_Z\, f_Z(q)\big) + w_D\, f_D(p, q),
with f_G = 1 - G/G_{\max}, f_Z \in \{0, 1\}, and, for unit vectors \mathbf u_p, \mathbf u_q along the edge (the gradient turned by 90°) and the unit link \mathbf l (turned to agree with \mathbf u_p),
f_D(p, q) = \tfrac{2}{3\pi}\big(\arccos(\mathbf u_p \cdot \mathbf l) + \arccos(\mathbf l \cdot \mathbf u_q)\big) \in [0, 1].
Weights w_Z = w_G = 0.43, w_D = 0.14 (Mortensen & Barrett); \varepsilon = 0.02 keeps every step slightly expensive, so flat regions do not give free detours. All terms are \ge 0: Dijkstra applies.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Live-wire: how it is used

Click a seed on the boundary. One Dijkstra run computes the tree from the seed to every pixel.
Move the mouse: the wire is the backtracked path from the mouse to the seed. Only backtracking, so it follows in real time.
When the wire leaves the boundary, click to fix the good part: that point becomes an anchor and the seed of a new tree.
Close the contour by joining the last anchor to the first seed.

The user steers, the algorithm does the precise tracing. “Path cooling” fixes anchors automatically where the wire has been stable for a while.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Try it: live-wire




Click: seed / anchor; move the mouse, or drag the round handle (for touch and projectors), and the yellow wire follows; orange = fixed segments. “close” joins the last anchor to the first seed. Tour: “trace the nucleus” (micrograph, dark-line cost, 4 anchors, closed: 362.7 px). “weak edge”: seed at the top of the nucleus, free end at the bottom: the wire cuts straight through the nucleus (143.4 px for a straight line of 135.3 px): add an anchor on the left envelope. “no smoothing” (σ = 0.5) on the weak arc of the synthetic nucleus: the wire wanders; raise σ to 1.5. “the neighbour steals the path”: the wire runs around the outer edge of the brighter neighbour (195.2 px for 68.2 px straight); an anchor at the contact fixes it. “measure along a neurite”: bright-line cost, 240.1 px along the neurite against 188.4 px straight. View “distance from seed”: the tree’s costs with iso-lines.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
How live-wire behaves

Short-cuts: the cost is a sum along the path, so a long detour along a weak edge can cost more than a short cut across a uniform region. More anchors, or a stronger edge term, help.
The neighbour steals the path: a stronger edge nearby (another cell) is cheaper per pixel; the wire jumps over to it.
Smoothing: too little (\sigma small) and the noise makes cheap pixels everywhere; too much and the edge is displaced and nearby edges merge.
The user is part of the method: the result is as good as the anchors.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Same tree, other uses

Length along a structure: the distance along a neurite or a vessel between two points: the cheapest path with a cost that is low on the structure; its length counts steps of 1 and \sqrt2 (as on the skeleton day).
Distance from a point: with cost 1 per step, the tree gives the grid distance from the seed: city block with 4 neighbours, octagons with 8. Exact for the graph, not for the Euclidean plane (next unit).
Watershed (day 10) floods from markers with the same priority queue. It minimises the maximum height along the path (the lowest pass), where live-wire minimises the sum.
Fast marching, the next unit: Dijkstra’s order with a different update, for continuous, round fronts.

title: When there is no order: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Summary

When no fixed order exists, the Bellman equations d(v) = \min_u d(u) + w(u, v) still hold.
Dijkstra: the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative cost is final (non-negative weights); a priority queue gives the order; O(N \log N).
The result is a shortest-path tree: the cheapest path to any pixel by backtracking.
Live-wire: edge-following local costs, one tree per anchor, real-time backtracking to the mouse; watch for short-cuts and stronger neighbouring edges.
The monotone DP table is the special case with a known order; watershed uses the same queue with the maximum instead of the sum.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a short phase correlation by hand and explain why it is a spike,
show why gain and offset do not matter, and predict the effect of uneven illumination,
predict how noise affects phase correlation and choose a remedy (low-pass weight, exponent p),
explain the taper and read the peak height and peak ratio as a confidence.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a short phase correlation by hand and explain why it is a spike,
show why gain and offset do not matter, and predict the effect of uneven illumination,
predict how noise affects phase correlation and choose a remedy (low-pass weight, exponent p),
explain the taper and read the peak height and peak ratio as a confidence.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Cross-power spectrum
A_k\overline{B_k}: phase difference and strength of wave k in both images


Phase correlation
R_k = A_k\overline{B_k}/|A_k\overline{B_k}|, then the inverse FFT; a pure circular shift gives a spike of height 1


Exponent p
divide by |A_k\overline{B_k}|^p: p = 0 is cross-correlation, p = 1 phase correlation


Low-pass weight
multiply R_k by a smooth weight that fades out the highest frequencies


Hann taper
w(n) = \tfrac12\big(1 - \cos\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\big): 0 at both ends, 1 in the middle; in 2D w(x)w(y)


Peak height
about the fraction of content shared by the two images


Peak ratio
highest peak / second-highest peak; near 1: ambiguous

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
By hand
B1. A = (0, 1, 2, 0), B = (1, 2, 0, 0), A_k\overline{B_k} = (9, -5i, -1, 5i) (the previous unit). (a) Normalise every entry to size 1. (b) Take the inverse DFT, r(t) = \tfrac14\sum_k R_k\,i^{kt}. (c) Compare with the cross-correlation (2, 5, 2, 0).
B2. Same A, but B' = 2B + 1 = (3, 5, 1, 1). (a) Compute B'_k and compare with B_k = (3, 1 - 2i, -1, 1 + 2i). (b) Show that the normalised cross-power is the same as in B1. (c) What does the cross-correlation of A and B' look like (no means subtracted)?
B3. Two images share only one strong vertical edge (a long straight boundary, dark on the left, bright on the right); the rest is noise. Predict the shape of the phase-correlation surface. What can you measure, and what not?
B4. Two 128 \times 128 crops of one image, B’s frame (21, 13) pixels right and down of A’s, no noise. (a) What fraction of A’s pixels have a partner in B? Predict the phase-correlation peak height. (b) The same shift with 64 \times 64 crops? (c) Why does a Hann taper raise the peak a little in (a)?
B5. The Hann taper. (a) Write down w(n) for N = 5 and N = 8. (b) A 128 \times 128 tile overlaps its neighbour only in its last 24 columns. What is the average taper weight in those columns? What does that mean for registering mosaic tiles with a taper?
B6. A lattice of blobs 18 pixels apart is shifted by (21, 13). Which shifts give a high phase-correlation peak? What is the peak ratio likely to be?






Solutions





B1. (a) Sizes (9, 5, 1, 5): R = (1, -i, -1, i). (b) r(0) = \tfrac14(1 - i - 1 + i) = 0; r(1) = \tfrac14(1 + (-i)(i) + (-1)(-1) + (i)(-i)) = \tfrac14(1 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 1; r(2) = \tfrac14(1 + i - 1 - i) = 0; r(3) = \tfrac14(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0. A delta at t = 1. (c) The cross-correlation (2, 5, 2, 0) has its peak at 1 too, but with neighbours of 40 % of the peak; phase correlation leaves only the spike.
B2. (a) B'_k = (10, 2 - 4i, -2, 2 + 4i): for k \ne 0 exactly 2B_k; only B'_0 is not doubled (10 = 2\cdot3 + 4, the offset adds 4 \cdot 1 to the constant term). (b) For k \ne 0, A_k\overline{B'_k} = 2A_k\overline{B_k}, which has the same phase; for k = 0, A_0\overline{B'_0} = 30, normalised to 1 as before (9 → 1). So R and the delta are unchanged. (c) c'(t) = \sum_x A(x+t)(2B(x) + 1) = 2c(t) + \sum A = (4 + 3, 10 + 3, 4 + 3, 0 + 3) = (7, 13, 7, 3): same peak, twice as high, on a raised floor.
B3. A ridge: a line of high values along the edge direction. Shifting B along the edge (vertically) does not change how the edges line up, so every t_y scores the same for the right t_x. The horizontal shift is measured; the vertical shift is not determined at all (the “aperture problem”). In practice the noise picks a random point on the ridge.
B4. (a) (128 - 21)(128 - 13)/128^2 = 107 \cdot 115/16384 = 0.75: a peak of about 0.75, less in practice because the parts without a partner add noise; the demo gives 0.62. (b) (64 - 21)(64 - 13)/64^2 = 43 \cdot 51/4096 = 0.54; the demo gives 0.32, and the floor is relatively higher. (c) The taper weights the middle of each crop most; with a moderate shift, the middle of A is inside the overlap, so the shared fraction as weighted is higher (the demo: 0.67 instead of 0.62).
B5. (a) N = 5: (0, 0.5, 1, 0.5, 0). N = 8: (0, 0.19, 0.61, 0.95, 0.95, 0.61, 0.19, 0). (b) The average of w(n) over the last 24 of 128 samples is 0.10 (at most 0.29), against 0.5 over the whole tile: the overlap, the only part that the two tiles share, is almost switched off. Tapering is fine for crops that overlap mostly (drift, channels), but for mosaic tiles with small overlaps it removes the information: stitching registers the tiles without a taper and resolves the consequences (the four candidates) separately.
B6. Every shift that moves the lattice onto itself: (21 + 18m, 13 + 18n) for integers m, n, e.g. (3, -5), (3, 13), (-15, -5), (21, 13). All of these give about equally high peaks; which one wins depends on the crop borders and the noise. Peak ratio close to 1: ambiguous.




Math questions
B7. (math) (Sub-pixel shifts.) In 1D, let the normalised cross-power be an exact phase ramp for a non-integer shift t_0: R_k = e^{-2\pi i k t_0/N} for k = -\frac{N-1}{2}, \ldots, \frac{N-1}{2} (N odd). Show that r(t) = \frac1N\sum_k R_k e^{2\pi i kt/N} = \frac{\sin\big(\pi(t - t_0)\big)}{N\sin\big(\pi(t - t_0)/N\big)}, the Dirichlet kernel (“periodic sinc”) centred at t_0. What are the two largest samples for t_0 = 0.5 and large N?
B8. (math) (a) Show that the exponent p = 0 gives the cross-correlation. (b) Show that phase correlation of f and g equals the cross-correlation of the whitened images \tilde f, \tilde g with \tilde F_k = F_k/|F_k|, \tilde G_k = G_k/|G_k|. Why is whitening an edge-enhancing filter for typical images, whose |F_k| falls off with |k|?
B9. (math) Let g(x) = f(x + t_0) + \eta(x) with noise spectrum H_k. Write G_k = e^{2\pi i kt_0/N}(F_k + H'_k) with |H'_k| = |H_k|. Show that the phase error of R_k satisfies |\sin\delta_k| \le |H_k|/|F_k| when |H_k| < |F_k|. Where in the spectrum is the error large for a typical image with white noise?






Solutions (math)





B7. r(t) = \frac1N\sum_{k=-m}^{m}e^{2\pi i k(t - t_0)/N} with m = (N-1)/2, a geometric sum with ratio q = e^{2\pi i(t - t_0)/N}: \sum_{k=-m}^{m}q^k = \frac{q^{m+1/2} - q^{-m-1/2}}{q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}} = \frac{\sin(\pi(t - t_0))}{\sin(\pi(t - t_0)/N)}, since (m + \tfrac12)\cdot\frac{2\pi(t - t_0)}{N} = \pi(t - t_0). Dividing by N gives the formula; at t = t_0 it is 1 (limit). For large N, N\sin(\pi u/N) \approx \pi u and r(t) \approx \operatorname{sinc}(t - t_0) = \sin(\pi(t-t_0))/(\pi(t - t_0)). For t_0 = 0.5 the samples at t = 0 and t = 1 are equal, \approx 2/\pi = 0.64: the spike is split between two pixels. Fitting this shape locates t_0 (the stitching unit).
B8. (a) |A_k\overline{B_k}|^0 = 1: nothing is divided, the inverse FFT of A_k\overline{B_k} is the cross-correlation. (b) \tilde F_k\overline{\tilde G_k} = \frac{F_k\overline{G_k}}{|F_k||G_k|} = \frac{F_k\overline{G_k}}{|F_k\overline{G_k}|}, so the cross-correlation of the whitened images (the correlation theorem) is the phase correlation. Whitening divides each wave by its size; when |F_k| falls off with |k|, the high frequencies are amplified relative to the low ones, like a sharpening filter: what remains are edges, lines and texture.
B9. R_k \propto (F_k + H'_k)\overline{F_k}\,e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N}, whose phase differs from the ideal -2\pi kt_0/N by \delta_k = \arg\big(1 + H'_k/F_k\big). The point 1 + z with |z| = |H_k|/|F_k| < 1 lies in a disc of radius |z| around 1, so its angle satisfies |\sin\delta_k| \le |z|. White noise has about the same |H_k| at every frequency, while |F_k| of a typical image falls off with |k|: the error is small at low frequencies and large (random phase) at high frequencies, exactly where a low-pass weight helps.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Explore
Left: the micrograph with frame A (blue) and frame B (red); drag frame B, or set the shift with the sliders. Middle: the two crops (B with its degradations) and a small panel with the spectrum of A or the phase of A_k\overline{B_k} as a colour. Right: the correlation surface with shift (0, 0) in the centre; green ring: the true shift, cyan cross: the highest peak, white circles: the next ones. p blends from cross-correlation (p = 0) to phase correlation (p = 1). uneven light brightens the whole field from one corner to the other (both crops); ramp on B only crop B. brute force computes NCC for every shift directly and times it.



E1. Preset same image, shifted: delta: B is A rolled around by (21, 13). Read the peak height and the peak ratio. Show the cross-power phase panel: what pattern do you see, and how does it change if you change the shift?
E2. Preset CC: broad peak, then phase: sharp peak. Compare the peak heights, the next-highest peaks and the peak ratios. Which shift is second best for CC?
E3. Preset illumination ramp on B (CC, a ramp of 500 grey levels across B). Where is CC’s peak? Switch the method to phase, then to NCC. Which finds the shift? Then set the ramp to 0, gain 0.5 and offset 80 with phase correlation: does anything change?
E4. Preset noise: phase peak drowns (σ = 120 on both crops). Where is the highest peak, and how high is the surface at the true shift? Then preset noise + low-pass weight. Also try p = 0.5 without low-pass, and CC.
E5. Preset no taper: false (0, 0) peak (CC, uneven light 600, no taper). Where is the peak? Look at the spectrum panel, then tick Hann taper. Then untick the taper again and choose phase correlation: where are the false peaks now?
E6. Preset periodic texture. Where is the highest peak, and what is the value at the true shift? Explain with B6.
E7. Preset phase: sharp peak. Switch the crop size to 64. How do the peak height and the ratio change? Compare with B4.
E8. Preset overlap NCC, then press brute force. Compare the result, the number of multiply-adds and the time with the FFT route.






Solutions





E1. Height 1.00, peak ratio ∞ (everything else is zero up to rounding). The phase of A_k\overline{B_k} is a set of parallel stripes running through the whole spectrum: a phase ramp -2\pi(k_xt_x/128 + k_yt_y/128), wrapping around every 2\pi. Their direction and spacing are set by the shift: a larger shift gives more, narrower stripes.
E2. CC: peak at (21, 13), 4.03\cdot10^6; the second best (20, 10) still has 2.81\cdot10^6 (70 %), ratio 1.44. Phase: peak 0.67, next peaks 0.03 (at (-23, -6) and (-33, 16)), ratio 23.3.
E3. CC’s peak is at (54, 1): wrong. Phase correlation finds (21, 13) with the same height 0.67 and ratio 23.0. NCC (on the overlap) fails too, at (62, -57): NCC removes a constant offset and gain, not a ramp. With gain 0.5 and offset 80 the phase-correlation surface is exactly the same as without (0.671, ratio 23.26).
E4. The highest peak is at (-6, 7) (0.043, ratio 1.03), the true shift only 0.033: the spike has drowned. With the low-pass weight (sd 0.08 cycles per pixel) the peak is back at (21, 13), ratio 1.54. p = 0.5 gives (21, 14), CC also (21, 14): one pixel off, still close. The low-pass weight keeps the reliable low frequencies with equal votes and removes the noisy ones.
E5. The peak is at (0, 0) (the next ones on the line t_y = 0): the jumps at the crop borders do not move with the shift. The spectrum shows a bright horizontal and vertical cross. With the taper the cross disappears and CC finds (21, 13) (ratio 1.31). Phase correlation without taper finds (21, 13) (0.62), but the next peaks are at (15, 0) and (12, 0): still the axis line, only weaker.
E6. The highest peak is at (3, -5) (0.15), one lattice period from the truth in both directions; (3, 13) (0.10) and (-15, -5) (0.09) follow, and the true shift (21, 13) scores only 0.03. Peak ratio 1.58: not convincing. Every shift by a whole number of periods matches the lattice; only the crop borders make one of them a little better.
E7. At 64 \times 64 the peak drops from 0.67 to 0.32 and the ratio from 23 to 5.2: the shared fraction drops from 75 % to 54 % (B4), and there are fewer frequencies to vote, so the floor is relatively higher.
E8. NCC (through FFTs) finds (21, 13) with NCC 1.000; its second peak (20, 10) has 0.69. Brute force finds the same shift with 268 million multiply-adds and takes around a second or two in the browser (1.6 s in a test run), against tens of milliseconds for the FFT route; the readout shows the times on your machine.

title: Exercise: phase correlation
text:
Where this leads
The spike sits on whole pixels, and the circular FFT only knows the shift up to the size of the image. The next unit turns a peak into a usable shift (the four candidates, sub-pixel estimation), combines many pairwise shifts into a consistent mosaic, and corrects drift.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
About this lecture
Phase correlation gives a spike. Turning it into a usable shift, and many shifts into one consistent picture, takes three more steps.

The four candidates: a circular peak only knows the shift up to the tile size.
Sub-pixel shifts: parabola, centroid, and the upsampled DFT.
Global alignment of a mosaic: pairwise shifts do not add up around a loop; least squares on the graph of tiles.
Drift in a time-lapse and in localisation microscopy; channels; 3D stacks.
The limits: what a shift cannot describe.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Convention as before: the shift t of tile B relative to tile A is where B sits on A, B(x) = A(x + t); for a mosaic it is the position of B minus the position of A. The demos use 128 × 128 tiles cut from the course micrograph enlarged to 384 × 384; with only 256² pixels of real data, the mosaic is a teaching model, honestly labelled.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
A peak means four shifts
Without padding, the FFT treats each tile as periodic: a peak at (p, q) only says the shift modulo the tile size N.


t_x \in \{p,\ p - N\} and t_y \in \{q,\ q - N\}: four ways tile B can sit against tile A, with very different overlaps.
Decide by computing NCC on the actual overlap of each candidate and keeping the best; ignore candidates whose overlap is too small to judge.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Resolving the candidates

For each candidate, cut out the overlapping parts of A and B and compute their NCC (the matching unit): a direct, cheap check.
Require a minimum overlap: a few dozen pixels always correlate by chance.
In practice, check the candidates of the few highest peaks, not only the first: on small overlaps, the true peak is not always the highest.
The best NCC is also the pair’s confidence.
Alternative: zero-pad the tiles (the previous unit): no ambiguity, but FFTs four times as large, and the overlap gets a smaller share of the padded image. Stitching programs usually test candidates instead.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Sub-pixel shifts
Stages, drift and chromatic shifts are rarely whole pixels. A drift of 0.3 px matters when single molecules are localised to 0.1 px.

Parabola: fit a parabola through the peak and its two neighbours (in x, and separately in y); its top is the estimate. Cheap, but biased towards whole pixels: pixel locking.
Centroid of the peak and its neighbours: simplest, strongly biased for broad or narrow peaks.
Upsampled DFT: evaluate the inverse DFT of the (normalised) cross-power spectrum on a fine grid (e.g. 1/20 px) near the peak only. This is the exact interpolation of the correlation, without a huge padded FFT (Guizar-Sicairos et al., 2008).

To apply a sub-pixel shift: interpolate (bilinear, the images unit) or multiply the spectrum by a phase ramp (the shift theorem, backwards).

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
The math: sub-pixel peaks
Parabola. Through (-1, c_{-1}), (0, c_0), (1, c_{+1}): c(\delta) = a\delta^2 + b\delta + c_0 with a = \tfrac12(c_{-1} + c_{+1}) - c_0, b = \tfrac12(c_{+1} - c_{-1}); the vertex is at \delta = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})}. The true shape. For a non-integer shift, the phase-correlation peak is a Dirichlet kernel \frac{\sin(\pi(t - t_0))}{N\sin(\pi(t - t_0)/N)} (the phasecorr unit, B7), not a parabola: hence the bias. Fitting the kernel itself works too (Foroosh et al., 2002).
Upsampled DFT. c(x, y) = \frac{1}{N^2}\sum_{k_x,k_y} R_{k_y k_x}e^{2\pi i(k_xx + k_yy)/N} at U \times U points: C = E_y\,R\,E_x^{\top} with small DFT matrices E_x \in \mathbb C^{U\times N}, (E_x)_{jk} = e^{2\pi i k x_j/N}. Cost \mathcal O(N^2U) instead of an FFT of size (UN)^2.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: sub-pixel estimates




B is A shifted by 3.3 px through the Fourier phase ramp, so the truth is exact. Left: the correlation samples near the peak (dots), the parabola through the top three (red dashed), the upsampled-DFT curve (blue); vertical lines: truth (green), parabola, centroid, upsampled. Right: the error of each method for every fraction from 0 to 1. Tour: “parabola: pixel locking” (phase correlation): the parabola’s error is an S-curve, 3.262 instead of 3.300, at most 0.038 px; the centroid’s up to 0.065; the upsampled DFT is within its grid of 1/20 px (0.020). “a broad CC peak”: the parabola fits a broad peak well (0.004), the centroid is terrible (0.47). “upsampling too coarse” (U = 4): the upsampled estimate is quantised to 1/4 px, error up to 0.12. “noise sets the floor”: with noise all methods scatter.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: Many tiles: the mosaic as a graph
text:
Many tiles: the mosaic as a graph
A mosaic of tiles is a graph: one node per tile, one edge per overlapping pair, labelled with the measured shift and its confidence.

Stage positions alone: seams, off by several pixels.
Chaining pairwise shifts along a path: each step adds its error; tiles far down the chain inherit all of them, and one wrong pair moves everything after it.
Around a loop of four tiles, the measured shifts should add up to zero; with noise they do not.
Global alignment: find the tile positions that agree best with all measured shifts at once, weighting each by its confidence. One tile is fixed (the whole mosaic can be moved freely).

Pairs with low confidence (a blank tile, a repetitive pattern) are dropped or down-weighted; a pair whose shift disagrees strongly with the rest (a large residual) is suspicious.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: The math: least squares on a graph
text:
The math: least squares on a graph
Tile positions \mathbf x_1, \ldots, \mathbf x_n, measured shifts \mathbf d_{ij} \approx \mathbf x_j - \mathbf x_i with weights w_{ij}. Minimise, separately in x and in y, E(\mathbf x) = \sum_{(i,j)} w_{ij}\,(x_j - x_i - d_{ij})^2. Setting \partial E/\partial x_m = 0 gives the normal equations L\,\mathbf x = \mathbf b with L_{mm} = \sum_{j \sim m} w_{mj}, \quad L_{mj} = -w_{mj}, \qquad b_m = \sum_{(i,m)} w_{im}d_{im} - \sum_{(m,j)} w_{mj}d_{mj}. L is the weighted graph Laplacian. It is singular: adding a constant to every x_m changes nothing (L\mathbf 1 = 0). Fixing x_1 = 0 (deleting its row and column) makes it invertible when the graph is connected. The graph-cuts day meets the same matrix in normalized cuts.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: stitching a mosaic




3 × 3 tiles of 128², nominal overlap 24 px, stage error up to ±6 px, noise, a brightness change and vignetting per tile. Edges: green = trusted (overlap NCC ≥ 0.7), red dashed = not. Tour: “stage positions: seams”: errors up to 10.1 px (rms 6.4). Default noise: chain 0-1-2-5-4-3-6-7-8 max 1.66 px, global 0.60. “chained pairs: errors add up” (noise 12): max 1.94 at the end of the chain; “global: errors spread”: max 0.83. “an empty tile”: tile 4 is blank, its four pairs are untrusted (NCC 0.27–0.51); the chain runs through it and tiles 3–8 are off by ~130 px; global keeps every other tile within 0.9 px (tile 4 itself cannot be placed from its image). “a wrong pair”: the region shared by tiles 4 and 5 is empty, pair 4-5 measures nonsense (NCC 0.42); its residual after global alignment is 127.7 px, everything else below 0.8 px. “the four candidates”: click any edge to see its surface and candidates. Then blending.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Seams and blending
Even well-placed tiles show seams: each tile has its own brightness (exposure, bleaching) and darker corners (vignetting).

Feathering: in the overlap, blend the tiles with weights that fall off towards each tile’s border; the seam becomes a smooth transition.
Vignetting is better corrected before stitching: divide by a flat-field image (a picture of an empty, even sample).
Vignetting is also a registration hazard: the same dark corners in every tile do not move with the shift, like the border jumps of the phasecorr unit.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Drift in a time-lapse
Frame k is shifted by the drift \mathbf d_k since frame 1. Register every frame, then shift it back.

To the first frame: errors do not accumulate, but late frames may no longer look like the first one (the sample changes, cells move, bleaching makes them dim).
To the previous frame: neighbours look alike, but the drift is a sum of steps; each step’s error is added, and the error grows like a random walk (\sqrt{k} times one step’s error).
Key frames: register to a key frame every few frames, and the key frames to each other: a compromise.

Phase correlation ignores bleaching (a gain) and slow illumination changes; noise and real changes of the sample are the limit.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Try it: drift correction




40 frames (128²) with a random-walk drift of 0.6 px per frame (sd), ending at (6.2, 0.9). “bleaching: no problem”: the last frame keeps 20 % of the brightness, noise 10; to the first frame: max error 0.19 px. The corrected average is sharp, the uncorrected one blurred. “to the previous: errors add up” (noise 30): the error grows from 0.1 to 1.3 px by frame 30 and 5.1 px at the end, where the frames are dim; to the first frame instead: max 0.29. “sample changes: to the first fails” (the field slowly turns into its mirror image): to the first, max 8.4 px at frame 37; “key frames”: 0.44 px; to the previous: 0.76 px.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Localisation microscopy and other uses

Single-molecule localisation: there are no images, only lists of molecule positions over thousands of frames. Render the positions of each time block as an image, correlate all pairs of blocks, and solve for one drift per block by least squares, the same graph problem as the mosaic (redundant cross-correlation). Alternative: fiducial beads.
Colour channels: the channels show different structures, so register a calibration image (beads) instead; chromatic aberration also scales the image, so a shift is only a first approximation.
3D stacks: the same formula with a 3D FFT. Report the shift in µm with the voxel spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), which is usually larger in z (the 3D images unit of the marching-cubes elective).
Motion estimation: register small windows separately (particle image velocimetry, video coding).

title: From a peak to a mosaic
section: Try it: drift in localisation microscopy
text:
Try it: drift in localisation microscopy




7981 localisations of three rings and two lines over 4000 frames, precision 0.25 camera px, drift up to 6.2 px. 10 time blocks, 45 block pairs correlated, least squares for the 10 block drifts (block 0 fixed). The rendered image sharpens from a smear to thin rings. Drift error: max 1.57 px, rms 0.74 with 10 blocks (the drift changes within a block); with 40 blocks (780 pairs) max 0.43; with 3 blocks max 2.72. “strong drift” (35 px): blocks of 400 frames are far too long, error up to 15 px.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Limits of a shift

Translation only. Rotation and scale: the Fourier–Mellin method resamples the magnitude spectrum in log-polar coordinates, where they become shifts that phase correlation can find (Reddy & Chatterji, 1996; further reading).
Rigid only. Tissue deforms, cells move independently: non-rigid registration, optical flow and tracking are the Motion elective.
Features instead of pixels: match interest points (the edges day, structure tensor) and fit a transform; robust to large changes.
Empty or repeated texture gives no or many answers: check the confidence, use the stage positions as a fallback.

title: From a peak to a mosaic
text:
Summary

A circular peak at (p, q) means four shifts; test them by NCC on the overlap and keep the best (with a minimum overlap).
Sub-pixel: the parabola is quick but locks to pixels; the upsampled DFT evaluates the exact peak on a fine grid at little cost.
A mosaic is a graph; pairwise shifts are combined by weighted least squares (a graph Laplacian), which spreads errors instead of accumulating them and exposes wrong pairs by their residuals.
Drift: register to the first frame, to the previous one, or to key frames; the same graph solution corrects localisation microscopy.
A shift cannot describe rotation, scaling or deformation.

title: Exercise: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Grid graph
pixels are nodes, 4 (or 8) neighbours are edges


Path cost (by hand)
the sum of the costs of all pixels on the path, the start pixel included


Bellman equations
d(v) = \min_{u \sim v}\big(d(u) + C(v)\big), d(s) = C(s)


Dijkstra
repeatedly make the unfinished pixel with the smallest tentative d final, and update its neighbours


Predecessor
the neighbour the best path to a pixel comes from; all predecessors form the shortest-path tree


Live-wire cost
low on edges: gradient magnitude, zero crossings of the Laplacian of Gaussian, edge direction (weights w_G, w_Z, w_D), after smoothing with \sigma



Pixels are written (row, column), counting from 0; row 0 is the top.

B2. (a) d(1,1) = 10 (from the left: 2 + 8), d(1,2) = 17 (from (1,1)), and d(1,3) = 20: its best path now comes from below, from (2,3) with d = 15, a step up. The other distances do not change. The order of finalisation changes accordingly: \dots, (2,1)\ 6, (0,1)\ 8, (3,1)\ 9, (1,1)\ 10, \dots, (2,3)\ 15, (0,2)\ 16, (1,2)\ 17, (3,3)\ 18, (1,3)\ 20, (0,3)\ 25. (b) The pass computes d(1,3) = 5 + \min(d(0,3), d(1,2)) = 5 + \min(25, 17) = 22, but the true value is 20. When the pass reaches (1,3), the pixel (2,3) below it has not been computed yet: the best path to (1,3) comes from below, against the scan order. All other pixels are correct.
B3. Follow the channel: down column 1 to row 5, right along row 5 to column 3, up column 3 to row 2, right along row 2 to column 6, down column 6 to the bottom: 19 pixels of cost 1, total 19 (the best monotone path costs 24). Dijkstra makes pixels final in order of their distance: (5,1) has distance 6 (six 1s from the top), while (2,3) in the channel is reached only via row 5 and has distance 11. Pixels are not processed by row but by cost, so the far end of the detour comes later even though it is higher up.
B4. Dijkstra makes s final (0), then a with the smaller tentative value 2, then b with 3; when b is final, a is already final and is not updated. Result: d(a) = 2. True: s \to b \to a costs 3 - 2 = 1. The argument “any other route passes through an unfinished node that already costs at least as much and can only add” fails: the route through b costs 3 at b and then decreases.
B5. (a) 60 px of boundary cost 60 \cdot 0.40 = 24; the chord costs 40 \cdot 0.88 = 35.2: the wire follows the boundary. 100 px of boundary cost 40 > 35.2: the wire takes the chord. (b) Break-even at 40 \cdot 0.88 / 0.40 = 88 px. The user can add an anchor in the middle of the boundary (each piece is then much shorter than its chord’s alternative), increase the edge weights relative to the constant part, or smooth less so that the edge is stronger.
B6. (3, 4): 4 neighbours 3 + 4 = 7; 8 neighbours 3\sqrt2 + 1 = 5.243 (three diagonal steps and one straight); Euclidean 5. (5, 5): 10, 5\sqrt2 = 7.071, 7.071: on the exact diagonal 8 neighbours are exact, but between the axes and the diagonals they overestimate, and 4 neighbours overestimate by up to 41%. The next unit removes this error.




Math questions
B7. (math) Prove that Dijkstra’s algorithm is correct when all weights are non-negative: when a node is made final, its tentative value equals the true shortest distance. Point out where non-negativity is used.
B8. (math) Show that with a binary heap Dijkstra takes O((N + E)\log N) time for N nodes and E edges. What is that for an n \times n image with 8 neighbours? (The demo pushes a pixel again when its value improves, instead of decreasing its key; why is that still O(E \log E)?)
B9. (math) Suppose every edge goes from row i to row i + 1 (moves only downwards). Show that the rows give an order in which every Bellman equation can be evaluated once, that this order is a topological order of the graph, and that Dijkstra and the row-by-row DP table give the same distances.
B10. (math) Watershed-style flooding minimises the largest pixel value along a path (the lowest pass), d(v) = \min_{u \sim v} \max\big(d(u), C(v)\big). Show that the Dijkstra argument still works for this “bottleneck” cost.






Solutions (math)





B7. Induction over the pops. Suppose all final values are correct, and v is the unfinished node with the smallest tentative value \tilde d(v), which is the cost of an actual path (through final nodes), so d(v) \le \tilde d(v). Take any path P from s to v and let y be its first node outside the final set, entered from a final x. When x was made final, y was updated: \tilde d(y) \le d(x) + w(x, y). The rest of P from y to v has non-negative weight (here non-negativity is used), so \text{cost}(P) \ge d(x) + w(x, y) \ge \tilde d(y) \ge \tilde d(v). Hence d(v) = \tilde d(v).
B8. Each node is popped once as final and each edge relaxed at most once (from its final end): N pops and at most E decrease-key operations, each O(\log N) on a heap: O((N + E)\log N). An n \times n image with 8 neighbours: N = n^2, E \approx 8n^2, so O(n^2 \log n). With re-insertion instead of decrease-key, the heap holds at most one entry per successful relaxation, at most E + 1 entries; each push and pop costs O(\log E) = O(\log N) (since E \le N^2), and stale entries are skipped when popped.
B9. Every edge goes from a lower row index to a higher one, so evaluating row by row, every right-hand side d(u) (with u in the previous row) is final before it is used: a topological order (every edge points forward in it). The DP table computes exactly the Bellman equations in this order, so it gives the true shortest distances; Dijkstra also gives the true shortest distances (B7), so the two agree. (The test file of the demos checks this on random grids.)
B10. Replace “d(x) + w(x, y) + \text{rest}” by “\max(d(x), C(y), \dots)”. The cost of a path never decreases when the path is extended (\max with something can only grow or stay), which is all the argument needs: for the first non-final node y on any path to v, \text{cost}(P) \ge \max(d(x), C(y)) \ge \tilde d(y) \ge \tilde d(v). So the smallest tentative value is final, and the priority queue processes pixels in order of the flooding level, as in the watershed day.

title: Exercise: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Explore: Dijkstra step by step
The grid demo in Dijkstra mode: costs on the left, the tentative distances d on the right (∞ = not reached). step makes the smallest pixel of the queue final (blue, numbered in order) and updates its neighbours (outlined); the queue is listed under the controls, smallest first. Arrows point to the predecessors (grey while tentative, orange when final). After the last pixel, backtrack follows the arrows from the target (the bottom-right corner, the bottom-left corner, or the cheapest bottom-row pixel, depending on the preset). one raster pass runs a single top-to-bottom, left-to-right pass instead and marks the wrong cells in red (small number: the true value).



E1. Preset by-hand exercise grid. Step through and compare the order, the queue and the final distances with B1. Then raise the cost of (1, 1) from 5 to 8 (three clicks on its upper half) and check B2, in Dijkstra and in one raster pass.
E2. Preset the detour. Run all and backtrack. What does the path cost, and how many pixels become final before the first pixel of row 2 in the channel, (2, 3)? Then one raster pass: what is its value at the target, and how many cells are wrong?
E3. Preset a wall with one gap (from the top-left to the bottom-left corner). Predict the path before running. What is its cost, and what does one raster pass give at the target?






Solutions





E1. As in B1: final order (0,0) 1, (1,0) 2, (2,0) 3, (3,0) 4, (2,1) 6, …, (0,3) 25; the target (3,3) costs 18. With C(1,1) = 8: (1,3) gets 20 with its arrow pointing down to (2,3); one raster pass marks exactly one wrong cell, (1,3), with 22 instead of 20.
E2. Cost 19, along the whole channel. The pixel (2,3) is the 20th to become final (distance 11): before it come the channel cells of column 1 and row 5 (distances 1–8), the other seven top-row pixels (distance 9 each: they are sources), (4,3) and (3,3) (9 and 10), and (1,0) and (1,2), which also have distance 11 but entered the queue earlier. One raster pass gives 21 at the target (7,6) (true 19), and 30 cells are wrong: every cell whose best path goes up or left somewhere.
E3. The path runs right along the top, down through the gap in the last column, and back left along row 4: 16. Crossing the wall would cost 1 + 1 + 9 + 9 + 1 + 1 = 22. One raster pass gives 22 at the target (it can only come from above, through the wall); 12 cells are wrong.

title: Exercise: Dijkstra and live-wire
text:
Explore: live-wire
Click on the image to place a seed (red); one Dijkstra run computes the cheapest paths from it to every pixel. Move the mouse, or drag the round handle: the yellow wire is the cheapest path from the handle back to the last seed. Click again to fix an anchor (the wire up to it turns orange, and a new tree starts there); close joins the last anchor to the first seed; undo anchor and clear go back. Costs: edges (gradient, zero crossings and direction, with the three weights), bright line or dark line, after smoothing with \sigma. distance from seed shows the tree’s costs with iso-lines. The readout gives the length and cost of the wire, the straight-line distance, and the time of one Dijkstra run.



E4. Preset trace the nucleus (4 anchors). What are the length and the cost of the closed contour? Undo the last anchor and move the handle around the nucleus: where does the wire jump? Switch the view to distance from seed: what do the iso-lines look like along the envelope, and inside the nucleus?
E5. Preset weak edge: the wire short-cuts. Compare the wire’s length with the straight line. Now click an anchor on the left part of the envelope, near (103, 110) in image pixels (about the middle of the left edge), and drag the handle back to the bottom. Compare the total cost of the two-piece contour with the single short-cut. What does that tell you?
E6. Preset no smoothing: noise wins (\sigma = 0.5, along the weak lower-left arc of the synthetic nucleus). Describe the wire. Raise \sigma to 1.5 and 3. Which value would you use, and what is the price of a large \sigma?
E7. Preset the neighbour steals the path. Where does the wire go? Fix it in two ways: (a) with one anchor at the contact between the two nuclei, (b) without anchors, by changing a weight. Which works better?
E8. Preset measure along a neurite (bright-line cost). How long is the neurite between the two tips, compared with the straight line? Switch to the edges cost: what happens?






Solutions





E4. Closed, 4 segments, 362.7 px, cost 289.08. Without the last anchor, the wire follows the envelope only while the handle stays close to the previous anchor; moved further around, it soon takes a short-cut through the textured interior (as in E5) or runs along other dark lines nearby. The distance map grows slowly across the textured inside and quickly along the dark envelope: the iso-lines are stretched along the envelope.
E5. The wire is 143.4 px long against a straight line of 135.3 px: it cuts straight through the nucleus (cost 134.89). With an anchor at (103, 110) the contour follows the left envelope: 69.9 px (cost 60.81) to the anchor plus 99.2 px (cost 78.10) to the bottom, 169.1 px with a total cost of 138.91: more than the short-cut. The energy itself prefers the short-cut: a sum over a long path along a weak, interrupted line costs more than a short path across. The anchor is the user’s knowledge that the cost function lacks.
E6. At \sigma = 0.5 the wire zig-zags through the noise inside the wide, faint ramp of the weak arc, up to about 10 px from the true boundary (56.7 px, cost 19.63). At \sigma = 1.5 it is smooth and within about 4 px of the boundary (61.8 px, cost 22.79). \sigma = 1.5 to 2 is a good choice here; a large \sigma blurs nearby edges into each other (the contact with the neighbour) and rounds corners.
E7. The wire runs around the outer edge of the brighter neighbour: 195.2 px for a straight distance of 68.2 px, cost 24.14. Its edge is stronger than the nucleus edge, so it is cheaper per pixel even though the detour is long. (a) An anchor at the contact (the nucleus boundary at angle 0°, near (150, 128)) splits the wire into 45.3 px and 48.9 px pieces along the nucleus. (b) Raising w direction to 1 makes the turns of the detour expensive: the wire gets much shorter (94.9 px) but still bulges about 9 px off the nucleus boundary. The anchor works better: it is a hard constraint.
E8. 240.1 px along the neurite (through the soma), against a straight line of 188.4 px: a measurement along the structure, with steps of 1 and \sqrt2 as on the skeleton day. With the edges cost the wire follows the sides of the thin neurite (its edges) and wanders: 260.8 px. For thin lines, a line (ridge) cost is the right one.
