title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

list the four candidate shifts of a circular peak and choose between them,
estimate a sub-pixel shift with a parabola, and explain pixel locking and the upsampled DFT,
compute global tile positions by least squares on the tile graph and read the residuals,
choose a reference for drift correction, and convert a 3D shift to µm.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the three demos.

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Four candidates
an unpadded peak at (p, q) in N \times N tiles means t_x \in \{p, p - N\}, t_y \in \{q, q - N\}


Resolving them
NCC on the actual overlap of each candidate, with a minimum overlap; the best NCC is the pair’s confidence


Parabola
\delta = \dfrac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})} through the peak and its two neighbours


Upsampled DFT
the inverse DFT of the cross-power evaluated on a fine grid near the peak


Global alignment
positions minimising \sum w_{ij}(x_j - x_i - d_{ij})^2, one tile fixed; residual = x_j - x_i - d_{ij}


Drift
register each frame to the first, to the previous (and add up), or to key frames

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
By hand
B1. Four candidates. (a) 1D tiles of width N = 8 give a circular peak at p = 6. List the candidate shifts and their overlap widths. Which candidate would you test first if the stage says “about 6”? (b) 100 \times 100 tiles, peak at (80, 10): list the four candidates and their overlaps in pixels. Which is too small to judge with a minimum overlap of 1000 px?
B2. Sub-pixel. (a) Samples (c_{-1}, c_0, c_{+1}) = (0.5, 0.9, 0.7): the parabola estimate? The centroid estimate \frac{c_{+1} - c_{-1}}{c_{-1} + c_0 + c_{+1}}? (b) Samples (0.6, 0.9, 0.6): what do both give, and what does that tell you about the true peak? (c) The true shift is 3.5 px and the peak is sharp (phase correlation). What do the two middle samples look like? Why is that the hardest case for “take the highest sample”?
B3. Three tiles in a row, measured shifts d_{12} = 100, d_{23} = 102, d_{13} = 199 (pixels, x only). (a) Positions by chaining 1 → 2 → 3, and by chaining 1 → 3 directly? (b) Least squares with equal weights and x_1 = 0: write the energy, set its derivatives to zero, solve. What are the residuals? (c) Now the direct pair 1–3 is four times as trustworthy (w_{13} = 4). Predict whether x_3 moves towards 199 or 202.
B4. A square of four tiles: 1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom right, 4 bottom left. Measured x-shifts: d_{12} = 100, d_{43} = 102, d_{14} = 0, d_{23} = 0. (a) Do they add up around the loop? (b) Solve by least squares (x_1 = 0, equal weights) and give the residuals.
B5. Drift. A time-lapse of 200 frames drifts by about 0.1 px per frame. One registration has an error of about 0.05 px (standard deviation). (a) How large is the total drift? (b) Registering to the previous frame and adding up: how large is the expected error at frame 200? (c) When would you still prefer the previous frame?
B6. A 3D stack has voxels of 0.1 \times 0.1 \times 0.3 µm. Phase correlation gives a shift of (3, -2, 1.5) voxels. What is the shift in µm? Why must you not report it as “3.9 voxels”?
B7. Two colour channels are aligned with phase correlation on beads in the centre of the field. Near the corners the channels are still off. Why, and what kind of transform is needed?






Solutions





B1. (a) t = 6 (overlap 8 - 6 = 2) or t = 6 - 8 = -2 (overlap 6). The stage says about 6: test t = 6 first; but with an overlap of only 2 pixels the NCC is unreliable, so check both, and treat a 2-pixel overlap with suspicion. (b) (80, 10): 20 \cdot 90 = 1800 px; (-20, 10): 80 \cdot 90 = 7200; (80, -90): 20 \cdot 10 = 200; (-20, -90): 80 \cdot 10 = 800. The last two are below 1000 px and are not judged.
B2. (a) Parabola: \delta = \frac{0.5 - 0.7}{2(0.5 - 1.8 + 0.7)} = \frac{-0.2}{-1.2} = 0.167 px. Centroid: \frac{0.7 - 0.5}{2.1} = 0.095 px. (b) Both give 0: the samples are symmetric, so the peak is (as far as three samples can tell) exactly on the middle pixel. (c) The two middle samples (at 3 and 4) are equal, about 0.64 of the peak height for phase correlation (the Dirichlet kernel, the phasecorr unit B7): the spike is split between two pixels, and the highest sample is off by half a pixel, the largest possible error. The three samples around either of them give an asymmetric fit.
B3. (a) Chain: x_2 = 100, x_3 = 202. Directly: x_3 = 199. They disagree by 3. (b) E = (x_2 - 100)^2 + (x_3 - x_2 - 102)^2 + (x_3 - 199)^2. \partial E/\partial x_2 = 2(x_2 - 100) - 2(x_3 - x_2 - 102) = 0 \Rightarrow 2x_2 - x_3 = -2; \partial E/\partial x_3 = 2(x_3 - x_2 - 102) + 2(x_3 - 199) = 0 \Rightarrow -x_2 + 2x_3 = 301. Solution x_2 = 99, x_3 = 200; residuals 99 - 100 = -1, 200 - 99 - 102 = -1, 200 - 199 = +1. (c) Towards 199: the heavier pair pulls harder. (With w_{13} = 4: x_2 = 98.67, x_3 = 199.33; residuals -1.33, -1.33, +0.33.)
B4. (a) Around the loop 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 1: 100 + 0 - 102 - 0 = -2 \ne 0. (b) x_2 = 100.5, x_3 = 101, x_4 = -0.5. Residuals: x_2 - x_1 - 100 = +0.5, x_3 - x_4 - 102 = -0.5, x_4 - x_1 - 0 = -0.5, x_3 - x_2 - 0 = +0.5. The mismatch of 2 around the loop is shared equally by the four pairs.
B5. (a) About 200 \cdot 0.1 = 20 px. (b) The errors of 199 steps add up like a random walk: about 0.05\sqrt{200} = 0.71 px, fourteen times the error of one step. (c) When the sample changes over the experiment (cells move or divide, the field bleaches unevenly), so that late frames no longer resemble the first; a compromise are key frames every few frames.
B6. (3 \cdot 0.1,\ -2 \cdot 0.1,\ 1.5 \cdot 0.3) = (0.3, -0.2, 0.45) µm. Voxels are not cubes: one voxel in z is three times longer than in x or y. A length in voxels mixes different units; the shift in z is the largest one in µm although it is the smallest in voxels.
B7. Chromatic aberration makes the two colours focus at slightly different magnifications: one channel is a slightly scaled copy of the other, plus a shift. A scaling looks like a shift that grows with the distance from the centre. A shift measured in the centre is wrong in the corners; you need a transform with scale (an affine transform, fitted from beads all over the field).




Math questions
B8. (math) Derive the parabola formula: fit c(\delta) = a\delta^2 + b\delta + c through (-1, c_{-1}), (0, c_0), (1, c_{+1}) and find the vertex. When is the vertex a maximum? Show that |\delta| \le \tfrac12 when c_0 is the largest of the three samples.
B9. (math) For B3, write the normal equations of the full problem (all three positions free) as L\mathbf x = \mathbf b. Show that L is the graph Laplacian of the triangle, that L\mathbf 1 = 0, and that fixing x_1 = 0 gives the system of B3(b).
B10. (math) The upsampled DFT evaluates c(x, y) on a 31 \times 31 grid (1/20 px, \pm 0.75 px) around the peak of two 512 \times 512 images, as E_y R E_x^{\top}. Count the complex multiply-adds (first RE_x^{\top}, then E_y(\cdot)). Compare with zero-padding the cross-power spectrum to (20 \cdot 512)^2 and taking one FFT (5M\log_2M operations).






Solutions (math)





B8. c(0) = c = c_0; c(1) = a + b + c_0 = c_{+1}; c(-1) = a - b + c_0 = c_{-1}. So b = \tfrac12(c_{+1} - c_{-1}), a = \tfrac12(c_{+1} + c_{-1}) - c_0. The vertex c'(\delta) = 2a\delta + b = 0 is at \delta = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})}; it is a maximum when a < 0, i.e. c_0 > \tfrac12(c_{-1} + c_{+1}). If c_0 \ge c_{\pm1}, then -2a = (c_0 - c_{-1}) + (c_0 - c_{+1}) \ge |c_{+1} - c_{-1}| = 2|b|, so |\delta| = |b|/(-2a) \le \tfrac12.
B9. E = w_{12}(x_2 - x_1 - d_{12})^2 + w_{23}(x_3 - x_2 - d_{23})^2 + w_{13}(x_3 - x_1 - d_{13})^2 with all w = 1. The derivatives give \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -d_{12} - d_{13} \\ d_{12} - d_{23} \\ d_{23} + d_{13}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}-299\\-2\\301\end{pmatrix}. Diagonal = degree (2 neighbours each), off-diagonal -1 per edge: the Laplacian of the triangle. Each row sums to 0, so L\mathbf 1 = 0 (and the right-hand side sums to 0, so the system is consistent). Deleting row and column 1 (with x_1 = 0) leaves 2x_2 - x_3 = -2, -x_2 + 2x_3 = 301: B3(b).
B10. RE_x^{\top}: 512 \times 512 times 512 \times 31: 512^2 \cdot 31 = 8.1 \cdot 10^6 multiply-adds. E_y(\cdot): 31 \times 512 times 512 \times 31: 31^2 \cdot 512 = 4.9 \cdot 10^5. Total 8.6 \cdot 10^6 complex multiply-adds. The padded FFT: M = (10240)^2 = 1.05 \cdot 10^8, 5M\log_2M \approx 1.4 \cdot 10^{10} operations, and M complex numbers of memory (1.7 GB in double precision). The upsampled DFT is about a thousand times cheaper and evaluates only where it matters.

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Explore: stitching a mosaic
Nine 128 \times 128 tiles at jittered stage positions, each with noise, its own brightness and darker corners. The mosaic shows the tiles at the chosen positions (later tiles on top, or blended); the graph has one node per tile and one edge per overlapping pair, green if its overlap NCC is trusted (≥ the threshold), red dashed if not. Click an edge: the middle panel shows that pair’s phase-correlation surface (shift 0 in the centre; cyan circle: the peak used), its four candidates with overlap and NCC, and the residual after global alignment. The readout gives each tile’s distance from its true position.



E1. Preset stage positions: seams. What is the largest position error? Where are the seams most visible?
E2. Preset the four candidates: the pair 1-2 is selected. List its candidates with their overlaps and NCC. Which one is chosen, and why are two of them not scored? Click a vertical edge (e.g. 0-3) and compare.
E3. With the default noise, compare the position errors of chain 0-1-2-5-4-3-6-7-8, tree (most confident) and global least squares. Then preset chained pairs: errors add up (noise 12) and global: errors spread. Where along the chain are the errors largest?
E4. Preset an empty tile (tile 4 shows no sample). Which edges are untrusted, and with what NCC? Compare chain, tree and global. Which tiles are wrong in each case, and why can no method place tile 4?
E5. Preset a wrong pair: the region shared by tiles 4 and 5 is empty. What is the confidence of pair 4-5, and its residual after global alignment? Now set trust NCC ≥ to 0.3 so that the pair is trusted, and press drop worst edge. What happens?
E6. Preset global + blending. Compare with the unblended mosaic. Then raise vignetting to 0.5: what happens to the seams, and to the confidences?






Solutions





E1. Up to 10.1 px (tile 7), rms 6.4 px. The seams show as steps in structures crossing a tile border, and as brightness edges (each tile has its own brightness and dark corners).
E2. Pair 1-2: (107, 5), overlap 2583 px, NCC 0.96; (-21, 5), 13161 px, NCC −0.11; (107, -123) and (-21, -123) with 105 and 535 px: below the minimum overlap of 1000 px, not scored. (107, 5) is chosen (true shift (107.7, 4.9); with the sub-pixel parabola the measurement is (107.2, 5.0)). For the vertical pair 0-3 the roles of x and y swap: the winner is (-3, 105) with 2875 px and NCC 0.97.
E3. Default noise: chain max 1.66 px (rms 0.94), tree max 0.66 (0.35), global max 0.60 (0.42). Noise 12: chain max 1.94 px, growing along the chain (0.4 px at tile 1, 1.9 at tile 8, the end); global max 0.83. The tree uses only the most confident pairs and is about as good as global here; global uses all trusted pairs and spreads the errors.
E4. The four edges of tile 4 are untrusted: 3-4 and 1-4 with NCC 0.27, 4-5 with 0.43, 4-7 with 0.51. Chain: it runs through tile 4, so tiles 3 to 8 are all off by about 130–150 px. Tree: only tile 4 is wrong (37.7 px). Global: only tile 4 is wrong (81 px), all other tiles within 0.9 px. A blank tile has nothing to match: its position must come from the stage.
E5. Pair 4-5 has NCC 0.42 (untrusted, almost no weight); its residual after global alignment is 127.7 px, every other residual is below 1 px: the wrong pair stands out, and all tiles are within 0.74 px. At threshold 0.3 the pair is trusted and pulls the solution: tile 5 is now 21.5 px off, tiles 2 and 8 about 12 px, and the residuals of the good pairs grow to up to 10 px while 4-5 keeps the largest (100 px). drop worst edge removes 4-5, and the solution is as good as before (max 0.74 px). Dropping edges by residual works as long as the good pairs outnumber the bad ones around each loop. (With the threshold at 0.7 the button would drop the worst trusted pair, a good one: only drop edges whose residual is clearly out of line.)
E6. Feathering hides the seams: the brightness changes smoothly in each overlap. With vignetting 0.5 every tile has dark corners; blending cannot remove them, so the mosaic looks patchy. The confidences drop (the lowest pair from 0.85 to 0.70; at 0.5 vignetting several pairs are close to the threshold), because the same dark corners in both tiles do not move with the shift; the positions are still within 0.7 px here. Correct vignetting with a flat-field image before stitching.

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Explore: sub-pixel estimates
B is A shifted by 3 + f pixels through the phase ramp, so the truth is exact. Left: the correlation samples near the peak (dots), the parabola through the top three (red dashed) and the upsampled-DFT curve (blue); vertical lines: the truth (green), parabola (red), centroid (orange) and upsampled DFT (blue). Right: the error of each method for every true fraction f from 0 to 1 (the vertical line is the current f).



E7. Preset parabola: pixel locking (phase correlation, f = 0.3). Read the three estimates. Describe the parabola’s error curve: where is it zero, where largest? How large is the worst error of each method?
E8. Preset a broad CC peak. How well do the parabola and the centroid do now, and why so differently from E7?
E9. Preset upsampling too coarse (U = 4). What is the upsampled estimate, and its worst error? Raise U to 20, then 50.
E10. Preset noise sets the floor (CC, noise 10). Compare the errors. Then switch to phase correlation with noise 5. What happens, and why (the phasecorr unit)?






Solutions





E7. Truth 3.300; parabola 3.262 (−0.038), centroid 3.259 (−0.041), upsampled 3.300. The parabola’s error is an S-curve: zero at f = 0, 0.5 and 1, negative below 0.5 and positive above, at most 0.038 px: the estimates are pulled towards the nearest whole pixel. Worst errors: parabola 0.038, centroid 0.065, upsampled DFT 0.020 (limited by its grid of 1/20 px).
E8. Parabola 3.296 (worst 0.004 over all fractions): a broad, smooth peak is very close to a parabola near its top. The centroid gives 3.019 (worst 0.47): the three samples are almost equal, so their centroid stays near the middle sample. Which simple method works depends on the shape of the peak.
E9. With U = 4 the grid has steps of 1/4 px: the estimate is 3.500 (error −0.1), worst 0.12. With U = 20 the worst error is 0.020; with U = 50 it is 0.000 on this sweep, because the sweep’s fractions (steps of 0.02) lie exactly on the grid of 1/50 px; in general the error is at most half a grid step. The cost grows only linearly with U.
E10. With noise 10 (CC): parabola 3.449, centroid 3.018, upsampled 3.550; worst errors 0.17, 0.62 and 0.30. Noise moves the peak itself, and no interpolation can recover what the noise has changed: noise sets the floor. Phase correlation with noise 5: at f = 0.3 all estimates are off by about 0.3 px, and for fractions below about 0.2 the highest peak lands 7 px away (off the plot). The smooth test signal has almost no strength at high frequencies, so after normalising, the noise there gets full votes (the phasecorr unit).

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Explore: drift correction
Frames mode: 40 frames of the micrograph drifting by a random walk; noise, bleaching (the last frame keeps 1 − bleaching of its brightness) and a slow change of the sample (the field fades into its mirror image). The plot shows the true drift (lines; x blue, y red) and the estimate (dots); the images show one frame, frame 0, and the average of all frames before and after correction.



E11. Preset bleaching: no problem. How large is the largest error when registering to the first frame? Compare the two averages. Look at frame 39.
E12. Preset to the previous: errors add up (noise 30). How does the error develop over the frames? Switch to the first.
E13. Preset sample changes: to the first fails. Where does registration to the first frame go wrong? Try the previous and key frames.
Localisation-microscopy mode: blinking molecules on rings and lines, localised in 4000 camera frames while the sample drifts. Each time block is rendered as an image; every pair of blocks is correlated and the drift per block follows from least squares on the graph of pairs.



E14. Preset corrected localisations sharpen. How many localisations, block pairs, and how large is the drift error? Compare the two images.
E15. Try 3 blocks, 40 blocks and strong drift. Explain the errors. Why does correlating all pairs of blocks, rather than each block with the next, help?






Solutions





E11. Max error 0.19 px (frame 28), rms 0.08 px, although the last frame keeps only 20 % of the brightness: a gain does not change the phases. The uncorrected average is blurred over the 6 px of drift; the corrected average is sharp, and much less noisy than a single frame.
E12. The error grows over time: about 0.1–0.3 px in the first 15 frames, 0.6–0.8 px around frame 20–30, then 1.3 px and finally 5.1 px at frame 39, where the frames are dimmest (each step’s error adds to all later frames, and the last steps compare two dim, noisy frames). Registered to the first frame, the largest error is 0.29 px.
E13. Late frames: from about frame 35 on, the frame looks more like the mirror image than like frame 0, and the estimate jumps (max error 8.4 px at frame 37). Key frames every 10 frames: max 0.44 px; the previous frame: 0.76 px. When the sample changes, compare frames that are close in time.
E14. 7981 localisations, 10 blocks, 45 pairs; drift error max 1.57 px, rms 0.74 px (the drift reaches 6.2 px). The uncorrected image is a smear; the corrected one shows thin rings and lines.
E15. 3 blocks (3 pairs): max error 2.72 px: a single drift per block of 1333 frames cannot follow the drift. 40 blocks (780 pairs): max 0.43 px: finer time steps, and many redundant pairs make up for the fewer localisations per block. Strong drift (35 px): max 15 px; within one block the molecules move so far that the block images are smeared and the block drift is meaningless: use more, shorter blocks. All pairs: every block is compared with every other one, so each drift is determined by many measurements; one bad pair is outvoted, and errors do not add up along a chain (the mosaic’s least squares, in time).

title: Exercise: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Where this leads
A shift is the simplest transform. Rotation and scale can be turned into shifts in log-polar coordinates of the magnitude spectrum (the Fourier–Mellin method); deforming tissue and moving cells need non-rigid registration, optical flow and tracking (the Motion elective). The graph Laplacian of global alignment returns on the graph-cuts day, in normalized cuts.

title: Quiz: learning
text:
Short questions on losses, gradient descent, backpropagation and overfitting. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Cross-entropy is -\ln p_\text{true class}; a gradient step is \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L.

Q1. A network gives the true class probability 0.8 for one image and 0.05 for another. What is the cross-entropy of each?






Hint





-\ln p.









Answer





-\ln 0.8 = 0.22 and -\ln 0.05 = 3.00. The confident mistake costs about 13 times as much.




Q2. You train with full-batch gradient descent and the loss grows from step to step. What do you change first?






Hint





What sets the length of each step?









Answer





Lower the learning rate \eta: each step overshoots the valley and lands higher than it started.




Q3. 50,000 training images, mini-batches of 100. How many gradient steps is one epoch? What changes if you use batches of 10?






Hint





An epoch is one pass over all images.









Answer





500 steps. With batches of 10: 5,000 steps per epoch, each cheaper but noisier (the gradient estimate from 10 images varies more).




Q4. In the backward pass, a ReLU unit had z = -2 in the forward pass. What gradient does it pass back to its weights?






Hint





The local derivative of \max(0, z) at z < 0.









Answer





Zero: the ReLU’s local derivative is 0 for z < 0, so every gradient behind it is multiplied by 0. For this example the unit’s weights do not change. If that holds for every training example, the unit is dead.




Q5. Why is backpropagation so much cheaper than estimating each \partial\mathcal L/\partial w by changing w a little and recomputing the loss?






Hint





Count forward passes for a network with a million weights.









Answer





Finite differences need one extra forward pass per weight: a million forward passes. Backpropagation gets all million gradients from one forward and one backward pass, at about twice the cost of a forward pass, because it reuses the gradient of each node for everything behind it.




Q6. The training loss keeps falling, the validation loss has been rising for 50 epochs. What is happening, and which weights do you keep?






Hint





Learning curves.









Answer





The network is overfitting: it memorises the training examples, and gets worse on new ones. Keep the weights from the epoch with the lowest validation loss (early stopping), or regularise and train again.




Q7. Name three ways to reduce overfitting.






Hint





Penalty, noise, data.









Answer





Weight decay (a penalty on large weights), dropout (silence random units during training), more data or data augmentation. Also: a smaller network, early stopping.




Q8. (math) For softmax followed by cross-entropy, what is \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k? Evaluate it for \mathbf p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) when the true class is the second.






Hint





Predicted minus wanted.









Answer





\partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = p_k - y_k: (0.7, 0.2 - 1, 0.1) = (0.7, -0.8, 0.1). A step against it lowers z_1 and z_3 and raises z_2.

title: Quiz: box filters and local statistics
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A 41 \times 41 box filter. How many additions per pixel does it take directly, separably, and with the integral image?






Hint





Direct k^2 - 1, separable 2(k-1); the integral image does not depend on k.









Answer





Directly 41^2 - 1 = 1680, separably 2 \cdot 40 = 80, with the integral image 6 (3 to build the table, 3 for the four lookups).




Q2. The running sum costs 4 additions per pixel, fewer than the integral image’s 6. Give two situations in which you would still use the integral image.






Answer





Any two of: windows of many sizes from one table (a multi-scale feature stack); a window size that changes from pixel to pixel; rectangles that are not centred squares, at arbitrary positions and in any order (as a detector asks for them); several different rectangle sums per pixel (Haar-like features).




Q3. What is the shape of the filter after two passes of the same box? After many passes? Why?






Hint





Think of each pass as adding a random shift.









Answer





Two passes: a triangle (tent). Many passes: a Gaussian bell. Each pass adds an independent uniform random shift; the sum of many independent shifts is approximately normal (central limit theorem), and the variances add: n(k^2 - 1)/12.




Q4. Two tables, of I and of I^2, give the local mean and variance in any window. How many table lookups per pixel is that?






Answer





Four lookups in each table: 8 in total, whatever the window size. Then m = sum / n, s^2 = (sum of squares) / n - m^2.




Q5. Where in a micrograph is the local standard deviation large, and where small?






Answer





Large at edges (the window contains both sides) and in textured regions; small in flat regions, where it is just the noise level. That makes it a simple texture feature for every pixel.




Q6. In local contrast normalisation (I - m)/(s + \varepsilon), what does \varepsilon do? What happens in a flat, noisy background with \varepsilon = 0?






Answer





\varepsilon keeps the denominator from becoming small. In flat background s is only the noise SD, so with \varepsilon = 0 the noise is scaled up to SD about 1, as strong as real structure. \varepsilon of about the noise level suppresses that, and hardly changes regions with real contrast (s \gg \varepsilon).




Q7. An 8-bit image of 2048 \times 2048 pixels. How many bits does the integral image need? Does it fit in a 32-bit integer? In float32 exactly?






Hint





Bit depth + \log_2(number of pixels); float32 is exact for integers up to 2^{24}.









Answer





8 + 22 = 30 bits: fits a 32-bit integer. Float32 is exact only up to 2^{24}, so large entries are rounded: not exactly.




Q8. A program stores the integral image in unsigned 32-bit integers, and many entries wrap around. When are the rectangle sums still correct?






Answer





Whenever the true sum over the rectangle is below 2^{32}. The wrap-around errors are multiples of 2^{32} and cancel in D - B - C + A modulo 2^{32}.




Q9. Local variances computed as \overline{I^2} - m^2 from float32 tables come out negative in a bright, flat region. Why, and name two fixes.






Answer





Both terms are large and nearly equal (about 200^2), and the variance (about 1) is their small difference: the rounding errors of the large numbers are bigger than the answer (cancellation). Fixes: subtract an offset (e.g. the global mean) before building the tables, which does not change the variance; use integer tables; use float64.




Q10. (math) What is the variance of a box of width 7? How many passes of it give variance 16?






Answer





(49 - 1)/12 = 4. Variances add, so 4 passes give 16 (\sigma = 4).

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a cross-entropy loss and say why a confident wrong answer is expensive,
take gradient-descent steps by hand and say what the learning rate and the mini-batch size do,
run backpropagation by hand on a two-neuron network: forward values, gradients, one update,
read learning curves, choose where to stop, and name three defences against overfitting.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a cross-entropy loss and say why a confident wrong answer is expensive,
take gradient-descent steps by hand and say what the learning rate and the mini-batch size do,
run backpropagation by hand on a two-neuron network: forward values, gradients, one update,
read learning curves, choose where to stop, and name three defences against overfitting.

The questions under By hand and Explore are for everyone. The Math questions (derive, prove) are for students who want the full treatment.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Loss \mathcal L
squared error (\hat y - y)^2 for numbers; cross-entropy -\ln p_\text{true class} for classes; averaged over the examples


Gradient step
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,\partial\mathcal L/\partial w for every weight; \eta = learning rate


Mini-batch, epoch
the gradient is computed on a random batch of examples; an epoch is one pass over all of them


Forward pass
compute every node’s value, from the input to the loss


Backward pass
compute \partial\mathcal L/\partial(\text{node}) from the loss back: each node’s gradient = sum over the nodes it feeds of (their gradient × the local derivative)


Local derivatives
z = wx + b: \partial z/\partial w = x, \partial z/\partial x = w, \partial z/\partial b = 1; ReLU: 1 if z > 0, else 0; (\hat y - y)^2: 2(\hat y - y)


Learning curves
training and validation loss against the training step

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
By hand
B1. Cross-entropy. (a) The network gives the true class the probability 0.9, 0.5 and 0.01. Compute the loss for each. (b) Three classes, probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1). What is the loss if the true class is the first? The second?
B2. One weight, one data point: \mathcal L(w) = (y - wx)^2 with x = 2, y = 3 (the example of the previous unit). Start at w = 0 and take two steps with \eta = 0.1. Give w and \mathcal L after each step.
B3. Backpropagation by hand. The network z = w_1x + b_1, h = \text{ReLU}(z), \hat y = w_2h + b_2, \mathcal L = (\hat y - y)^2, with x = 2, y = 1, w_1 = 0.5, b_1 = 0, w_2 = 1.5, b_2 = 0. (a) Forward: compute z, h, \hat y and \mathcal L. (b) Backward: compute \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y, then \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h, \partial\mathcal L/\partial z, \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 and \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1. (c) Update all four weights with \eta = 0.1 and compute the new loss. Did it go down? Repeat with \eta = 0.05. (d) Now x = -1 (the rest unchanged). Forward and backward again. Which gradients are zero, and why? What does one update with \eta = 0.1 change?
B4. Learning curves of a small network (8 + 8 hidden units, 30 training and 30 validation points):


Which curve is which, and how can you tell without the labels?
At which step would you stop? What happens after it?
The validation set was used to choose the step. Which number do you report as the expected performance on new data, and on which data is it computed?

B5. 60,000 training images, mini-batches of 32. (a) How many gradient steps is one epoch? How many after 10 epochs? (b) Why not use all 60,000 images for every step?
B6. A sigmoid’s local derivative \varphi'(z) = \varphi(z)(1 - \varphi(z)) is at most 0.25 (at z = 0). (a) What is \varphi'(8)? Compare with ReLU’s local derivative for z = 8. (b) A gradient passes back through 10 sigmoid units in a chain (ignore the weights). By at most what factor is it multiplied? What does this mean for the first layers of a deep sigmoid network?






Solutions





B1. (a) -\ln 0.9 = 0.105, -\ln 0.5 = 0.693, -\ln 0.01 = 4.605. (b) -\ln 0.7 = 0.357; -\ln 0.2 = 1.609.
B2. \mathcal L'(w) = -2x(y - wx) = -4(3 - 2w). Step 1: \mathcal L'(0) = -12, w = 1.2, \mathcal L = (3 - 2.4)^2 = 0.36. Step 2: \mathcal L'(1.2) = -2.4, w = 1.44, \mathcal L = (3 - 2.88)^2 = 0.0144. Each step removes 80 % of the remaining distance to w = 1.5 (the factor 1 - 8\eta = 0.2).
B3. (a) z = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0 = 1, h = 1, \hat y = 1.5, \mathcal L = 0.5^2 = 0.25. (b) \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y = 2(1.5 - 1) = 1. \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = 1 \cdot h = 1, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2 = 1, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = 1 \cdot w_2 = 1.5. The ReLU is on (z > 0): \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 1.5. \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = 1.5 \cdot x = 3, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1 = 1.5. (c) \eta = 0.1: w_1 = 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.2, b_1 = -0.15, w_2 = 1.4, b_2 = -0.1. New forward pass: z = 0.25, h = 0.25, \hat y = 0.35 - 0.1 = 0.25, \mathcal L = 0.75^2 = 0.5625: worse. Every weight moved downhill on its own, but together they overshoot: \hat y went from 1.5 past the target 1 to 0.25. With \eta = 0.05: w_1 = 0.35, b_1 = -0.075, w_2 = 1.45, b_2 = -0.05, z = 0.625, \hat y = 0.856, \mathcal L = 0.021. (d) z = -0.5, h = 0, \hat y = 0, \mathcal L = 1. \partial\mathcal L/\partial\hat y = -2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_2 = -2, \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = -2 \cdot h = 0, \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = -2 \cdot 1.5 = -3, but the ReLU is off, so \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 0 and \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_1 = 0. Only b_2 changes: b_2 = 0.2, \hat y = 0.2, \mathcal L = 0.64. The hidden unit learns nothing from this example.
B4. (a) The blue curve is the training loss: it keeps falling, towards 0.002, because the network is fitted to exactly these points. The red curve is the validation loss: it falls at first, then rises. (b) At the lowest validation loss, step 126 (validation loss 0.169). After it the network fits the noise of the 30 training points: the training loss goes on falling, but the validation loss rises (0.377 at step 2000). (c) Neither of these curves: the validation loss at step 126 is optimistic, because the step was chosen on it. Report the loss or accuracy of the chosen network on a separate test set that played no part in any choice (as on the random-forest day).
B5. (a) 60{,}000/32 = 1875 steps; 18,750 after 10 epochs. (b) Every step would cost 60,000 forward and backward passes. The gradient of 32 random images points roughly in the same direction for 1/1875 of the cost, so in the same time we take 1875 (noisy) steps instead of one exact one.
B6. (a) \varphi(8) = 0.99966, \varphi'(8) = 0.00034. The ReLU passes the gradient unchanged (derivative 1). (b) At most 0.25^{10} \approx 10^{-6}. The first layers of a deep sigmoid network get gradients a million times smaller than the last: they hardly learn (vanishing gradients). ReLU units that are on pass the gradient with factor 1.




Math questions
B7. (math) Softmax p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} and cross-entropy \mathcal L = -\ln p_c for the true class c. Show that \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = p_k - y_k, where y_k = 1 if k = c and 0 otherwise.
B8. (math) A layer \mathbf z = W\mathbf a + \mathbf b followed by \mathbf a' = \varphi(\mathbf z). Given \boldsymbol\delta' = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z' of the next layer \mathbf z' = W'\mathbf a' + \mathbf b', derive \boldsymbol\delta = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta') \odot \varphi'(\mathbf z) and \partial\mathcal L/\partial W = \boldsymbol\delta\,\mathbf a^\top.
B9. (math) \mathcal L = \frac1N\sum_n\ell_n. A mini-batch B of m examples is drawn uniformly at random (without replacement). Show that \mathbf g_B = \frac1m\sum_{n\in B}\nabla\ell_n is an unbiased estimate of \nabla\mathcal L.
B10. (math) Show that gradient descent on \mathcal L(\mathbf w) + \lambda\|\mathbf w\|^2 multiplies the weights by 1 - 2\eta\lambda before the usual step (“weight decay”). For the one-weight loss of B2 with \lambda > 0, what is the minimiser?






Solutions (math)





B7. (math) \mathcal L = -z_c + \ln\sum_j e^{z_j}. Then \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_k = -[k = c] + e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j} = p_k - y_k.
B8. (math) z'_i = \sum_j W'_{ij}a'_j + b'_i, so \partial\mathcal L/\partial a'_j = \sum_i \delta'_i W'_{ij} = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta')_j. Since a'_j = \varphi(z_j) depends only on z_j: \delta_j = \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_j = (W'^\top\boldsymbol\delta')_j\,\varphi'(z_j). Finally z_j = \sum_k W_{jk}a_k + b_j gives \partial\mathcal L/\partial W_{jk} = \delta_j a_k, i.e. the outer product \boldsymbol\delta\mathbf a^\top, and \partial\mathcal L/\partial b_j = \delta_j.
B9. (math) Each example is in B with probability m/N. So \mathbb E[\mathbf g_B] = \frac1m\sum_n P(n\in B)\nabla\ell_n = \frac1m\cdot\frac mN\sum_n\nabla\ell_n = \nabla\mathcal L.
B10. (math) The gradient is \nabla\mathcal L + 2\lambda\mathbf w, so \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L - 2\eta\lambda\mathbf w = (1 - 2\eta\lambda)\mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L. For B2: \frac{d}{dw}[(3 - 2w)^2 + \lambda w^2] = -4(3 - 2w) + 2\lambda w = 0 gives w = 12/(8 + 2\lambda) = 6/(4 + \lambda): pulled from 1.5 towards 0.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Explore: backpropagation step by step
The network of B3 as a computational graph: orange boxes are weights, grey boxes are inputs, circles are operations. forward fills in every node’s value (blue), backward fills in \partial\mathcal L/\partial(\text{node}) from the loss back (red), with the local derivative on each edge. update takes one step with the learning rate \eta and shows the loss before and after. check compares each gradient with a finite difference. All numbers can be edited.



R1. Preset the by-hand exercise. Press forward, backward, update, and compare with your answers to B3. Press check: do backpropagation and finite differences agree?
R2. Preset dead ReLU (x = -1). Press backward. Which edges carry a zero, and where does the gradient stop? Press update a few times: what changes, and what never changes?
R3. Preset sigmoid saturates. Read the local derivative on the edge from z to h, and compare the gradients of w_1 and w_2. Press update: which weights move noticeably?
R4. Preset learning rate too large (\eta = 0.3). Press update once and read the loss. Then look at z: what has happened to the hidden unit? Press update four more times: does the loss go down, and how does the network now fit y?
R5. Preset 2–2–1 network. Press backward. Which weight has the largest gradient, and why? Press update with \eta = 0.05: what is the new loss?






Solutions





R1. The same numbers as B3: \mathcal L = 0.25; gradients w_1: 3, b_1: 1.5, w_2: 1, b_2: 1; after the update (\eta = 0.1) \mathcal L = 0.5625. The finite differences agree with backpropagation to many digits.
R2. The edge from z into the ReLU has local derivative ×0: \partial\mathcal L/\partial h = -3, but \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = 0, so w_1 and b_1 get 0. w_2 also gets 0, because its local derivative is h = 0. Only b_2 moves: 0 \to 0.2 (loss 0.64), then towards 1 with every further update. w_1, b_1, w_2 never change for this input.
R3. The edge z \to h has local derivative ×0.00034 (z = 8, the sigmoid is flat). \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_2 = 3.0 but \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_1 = 0.006, 500 times smaller. After one update with \eta = 0.1 the loss drops from 2.25 to 0.81, almost entirely through w_2 and b_2; w_1 moves by 0.0006.
R4. The loss goes from 0.25 to 1.69. The update made w_1 = -0.4 and b_1 = -0.45, so z = -1.25: the hidden unit is off (dead for this input). Further updates only change b_2: the loss falls (0.27, 0.043, 0.0069, 0.0011) because b_2 alone moves towards y = 1. The network now outputs a constant; the hidden unit no longer takes part.
R5. Loss 2.25 (\hat y = 3.5, y = 2). The largest gradient is \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_{22} = 12: it is \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_2 \cdot x_2 = 6 \cdot 2, where \partial\mathcal L/\partial z_2 = 3 \cdot v_2 = 6 (the output weight v_2 = 2 is the larger one) and x_2 = 2 is the larger input. After the update the loss is 1.3225.

title: Exercise: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Where this leads
Everything so far works for any input vector. For images, the next unit replaces the dense first layer by a convolutional layer: a bank of small kernels, learned with exactly this backpropagation, shared across the image. Data augmentation, the image-specific cure for overfitting, comes with it. The evaluation day (day 16) returns to the question of what makes a test set honest.

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
About this lecture
Dijkstra finds the cheapest path on the pixel graph. But the graph’s distances are not the distances of the plane: on a flat image the distance from a point grows in diamonds (4 neighbours) or octagons (8 neighbours), not circles.

The arrival time of a front that starts at a seed and moves with a given speed.
Fast marching: Dijkstra’s order, with a better update from two neighbours at once (Sethian, 1996).
One update by hand; why it approximates the Euclidean distance.
Costs from the image, and minimal paths by descending the arrival time.
How it relates to live-wire, geodesic active contours and watershed.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This unit moved here from the level-set day (it closes this day’s arc: grid DP → polar DP → Dijkstra → fast marching). Prerequisites: Dijkstra (previous unit); the level set equation (previous day of this chain) is recalled on one slide; the Euclidean distance transform is owned by the morphology day.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Distances on the grid are not round
text:
Distances on the grid are not round

The same flat cost (1 per pixel of length), the same seed: lines of equal distance every 10 pixels.

4 neighbours: the city-block distance. At 45° a point 100 px away gets 141: 41% too far.
8 neighbours: steps of 1 and \sqrt2. Exact on the axes and diagonals, up to 8% too far in between (at 22.5°).
Fast marching: circles, within about 1–2% here.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: The arrival time of a front
text:
The arrival time of a front
Light a fire at the seed. It spreads in every direction, with a speed that may depend on the place: fast on cheap pixels, slow on expensive ones.

T(x) = the time at which the fire reaches the point x. Lines of equal T are the successive fronts.
With speed 1 everywhere, T is the Euclidean distance from the seed: the fronts are circles.
With the speed low on edges, the fronts slow down there: T becomes a distance that “costs more” across edges.
Running time is a cost per unit of length: P = 1/\text{speed}. T is the cheapest total cost of a continuous path, measured along its length, not counted in pixel steps.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
The math: the Eikonal equation
Where the front passes x moving with speed F(x) > 0, it travels a distance F\,\Delta t in time \Delta t along the normal, so
|\nabla T(x)|\, F(x) = 1, \qquad \text{or}\qquad |\nabla T| = P,\quad P = 1/F, \qquad T = 0 \text{ at the seeds}.
This is the Eikonal equation. With P = 1 its solution is the Euclidean distance to the seeds (the distance transform of the morphology day, from the seed set). T(x) is also the minimal weighted length \min_\gamma \int_\gamma P\, ds over all curves \gamma from a seed to x.
Recall from the level-set day: a front moving with normal speed F is the zero level of \phi with \phi_t + F|\nabla\phi| = 0. When F never changes sign, each point is passed once, and \phi(x, t) = T(x) - t solves it: the arrival time is a level-set function that never needs to be updated in time.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Fast marching: Dijkstra with a better update
text:
Fast marching: Dijkstra with a better update
Keep everything of Dijkstra:

tentative values in a priority queue, the smallest is made final, then its neighbours are updated.

Change one thing, the update:

Dijkstra: d(v) = \min_u \big(d(u) + \text{cost}\big): the front arrives along one grid edge.
Fast marching: use the final neighbour along x and the final neighbour along y together, and solve for the time at which a straight front passing both would arrive. A front crossing the pixel diagonally is now seen as diagonal.

The values still only grow along the front, so “the smallest is final” still holds.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
The math: the upwind update
At pixel v (spacing 1), let a = the smaller final value of its left and right neighbours, b = the smaller final value of its upper and lower neighbours (∞ if none is final). Discretise T_x^2 + T_y^2 = P^2 with one-sided (“upwind”) differences towards the known side:
(T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = P^2, \qquad T \ge \max(a, b).
If |a - b| < P: \displaystyle T = \frac{a + b + \sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2}}{2}. Otherwise (only one useful neighbour): T = \min(a, b) + P, which is Dijkstra’s update.
Each T is larger than both a and b, so values never decrease along the front, and Dijkstra’s argument gives the order. Work O(N \log N), as Dijkstra.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
One update by hand
A pixel with known neighbours T = 2 on its left and T = 2.5 above, flat cost P = 1:

Dijkstra (4 neighbours): \min(2, 2.5) + 1 = 3.
Fast marching: |2 - 2.5| = 0.5 < 1, so T = \big(4.5 + \sqrt{2 - 0.25}\big)/2 = 2.911.
With only the left neighbour known: 2 + 1 = 3; with 2 and 3.2: too far apart, again 3.

From a seed at (0, 0): T(1, 0) = T(0, 1) = 1, then T(1, 1) = \big(2 + \sqrt 2\big)/2 = 1.707, against \sqrt2 = 1.414 exactly and 2 for 4-neighbour Dijkstra. Next to a point seed the first-order update is crude; implementations set the pixels within a few pixels of the seed to their exact distance first (the demo uses 3 px). Far from the seed the error is small.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Try it: fronts on a grid
text:
Try it: fronts on a grid




Left: fast marching, right: Dijkstra on 4 or 8 neighbours, same cost P and same seeds; colour = arrival time, white lines = fronts at equal time steps. Click places a target (or a seed, after “add seed”); orange = gradient descent on T, blue = Dijkstra’s pixel path. Tour: “flat cost”: circles against diamonds. “Dijkstra 4-nbr vs fast marching”: from the bottom-left to the top-right: T = 277.3 for a straight line of 275.8, Dijkstra 390.0 (city block); with 8 neighbours 275.8 on the exact diagonal. “two seeds”: the fronts meet on the perpendicular bisector (a Voronoi boundary). “neurite”: cost low on bright lines: the path follows the neurite. “edge cost”: P = 1 + (|∇I|/k)², the fronts slow down and bunch up at the nucleus boundary.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Costs from the image
As for live-wire, the cost P comes from the image:

Slow at edges: P = 1/g with the edge-stopping function g = 1/\big(1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2\big) of the level-set day: P \approx 1 in flat regions and large on strong edges. A front from a seed inside a nucleus fills it quickly and then stalls at its boundary.
Fast along lines: P small on a bright thin structure (a neurite, a vessel): the front runs along it, and T measures the cost along the structure.
k (contrast) sets which edges count, like \sigma in the contrast weights of the graph-cut day.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
section: Minimal paths: descend the arrival time
text:
Minimal paths: descend the arrival time
T has a single minimum, at the seeds, and no other local minima. So from any target:

Gradient descent on T (small steps against \nabla T) runs down to a seed. The curve it traces is the minimal path, at sub-pixel precision, not restricted to grid steps.
Dijkstra’s path follows the pointers: grid steps only, so a straight line at 30° becomes a staircase, longer than the line.

Same principle as before: compute the “table” (T) once, then read off any path by backtracking.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Three relatives









path
optimum




Live-wire (previous unit)
discrete, on the pixel graph
global (for its graph)


Fast marching + descent (today)
continuous
global (up to the discretisation)


Geodesic active contours (level-set day)
continuous
local, from a starting curve



The geodesic active contour minimises the same kind of weighted length \int g\, ds, but by moving a curve downhill: it can stop in a local minimum. Fast marching computes the global minimal path between two points directly, as live-wire does on the grid.
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Fronts, flooding and watershed
Recall from the watershed day: flooding from markers also processes pixels in the order of a priority queue, and the basins meet at the watershed lines.

Fast marching with several seeds: each pixel is reached first by one seed’s front; the fronts meet where the arrival times from two seeds are equal (with P = 1, the perpendicular bisector: a Voronoi diagram).
Watershed flooding uses the maximum height along the way, not the accumulated time; its basins meet at the ridges of the image.
Same machinery, different “cost of a path”: sum (Dijkstra, live-wire), integral of P (fast marching), maximum (watershed).
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths
text:
Summary

Dijkstra’s grid distances are blocky: diamonds with 4 neighbours, octagons with 8.
The arrival time T of a front with speed 1/P solves |\nabla T| = P; with P = 1 it is the Euclidean distance.
Fast marching = Dijkstra’s order + the upwind update from the smaller known neighbour along x and along y; O(N\log N); nearly round fronts.
Costs from the image (slow at edges, fast along lines); minimal paths by gradient descent on T, at sub-pixel precision.
The day’s arc: DP table (fixed order) → polar DP (closed curves) → Dijkstra (order found on the fly) → fast marching (continuous fronts).
crumbs: From Dijkstra to fast marching: continuous minimal paths

title: Quiz: fast marching
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. T is the arrival time of a front that starts at the seeds and moves with speed 1/P; fast marching computes it in Dijkstra’s order with the upwind update.

Q1. With a flat cost, why are 4-neighbour Dijkstra distances diamonds, and not circles?






Answer





Every path on the 4-neighbour grid is a staircase of horizontal and vertical steps. To reach a point at 45° it needs as many horizontal as vertical steps: the city-block distance |x| + |y|, whose level lines are diamonds. A point 100 px away on the diagonal gets about 141.




Q2. What is the arrival time T when P = 1 everywhere and there is one seed?






Answer





The Euclidean distance to the seed: the front moves with speed 1 in every direction, so its fronts are circles. With several seeds: the distance to the nearest seed (a distance transform of the seed set).




Q3. What does fast marching keep from Dijkstra, and what does it change?






Answer





It keeps the priority queue and the rule “the smallest tentative value is final”, so the order is found on the fly. It changes the update: instead of the best single neighbour plus a step, it combines the smaller known neighbour along x and along y and solves for the arrival time of a straight front passing both.




Q4. Left neighbour T = 5, upper neighbour T = 5, P = 1. What do Dijkstra (4 neighbours) and fast marching give?






Hint





T = \tfrac12\big(a + b + \sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2}\big) if |a - b| < P.









Answer





Dijkstra: 6. Fast marching: \tfrac12(10 + \sqrt2) = 5.707: a front arriving diagonally needs only 1/\sqrt2 to cross from the line through the two neighbours to the pixel.




Q5. The cost is P = 1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2. What happens to the fronts at a strong edge, and what does a larger k do?






Answer





At a strong edge P is large, so the front slows down and its iso-lines bunch up there; regions separated by edges are reached late. A larger k makes P smaller for the same gradient: only very strong edges slow the front, and T approaches the plain distance.




Q6. How is the minimal path found from T, and why is it not restricted to grid steps?






Answer





By gradient descent on T from the target: small steps against \nabla T (interpolated between pixels) lead down to a seed. The steps can go in any direction and the positions are real numbers, so the path is a smooth curve, not a chain of pixel steps.




Q7. Geodesic active contours (level-set day) and fast marching both deal with a weighted length \int P\, ds. What is the difference?






Answer





A geodesic active contour moves a curve downhill from a starting position and stops in a local minimum. Fast marching computes the arrival time from the seeds everywhere and finds the global minimal path between a seed and a target by descending it (up to the discretisation error).




Q8. (math) Show that T(x, y) = (x + y)/\sqrt2 satisfies the upwind update with P = 1 exactly.






Answer





The left and upper neighbours have a = b = T - 1/\sqrt2, so |a - b| = 0 < 1 and (T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12 = 1 = P^2. The update returns T = a + 1/\sqrt2, which is the exact value: plane waves are reproduced exactly.

title: Quiz: boosted detectors and the cascade
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why must a sliding-window detector have an extremely low false-positive rate per window?






Answer





Because it looks at hundreds of thousands of windows per image (every position and scale), and almost all are background. A false-positive rate of 1 % would give thousands of false detections per image; even 10^{-5} gives several.




Q2. What is a decision stump, and why is it called a weak classifier?






Answer





One feature, one threshold and a direction: “face if the feature is above (or below) \theta”. It is a decision tree of depth 1. Alone it is only somewhat better than guessing; boosting combines many of them into a strong classifier.




Q3. After an AdaBoost round, which training examples get more weight, and why?






Answer





The examples the new stump classified wrongly: their weights are multiplied by e^{\alpha}, the others by e^{-\alpha}. The next stump is chosen by its weighted error, so it must do well on exactly those examples: each round focuses on what is still wrong.




Q4. A stump has weighted error \varepsilon = 0.2. What is its vote \alpha? What would \varepsilon = 0.5 give?






Answer





\alpha = \tfrac12\ln(0.8/0.2) = \tfrac12\ln 4 = 0.69. With \varepsilon = 0.5: \alpha = 0, no vote; the stump is no better than guessing.




Q5. How does boosting select features?






Answer





Each round chooses the single stump, and hence the single feature, with the smallest weighted error out of the whole pool. After T rounds the classifier uses at most T features; the rest of the pool (often over 100 000 features) is never evaluated at detection time.




Q6. A cascade has 5 stages, each with detection rate 0.995 and false-positive rate 0.4. What are D and F?






Answer





D = 0.995^5 = 0.975; F = 0.4^5 = 0.010.




Q7. Why is the first stage of a cascade made as small as possible (one or two features)?






Answer





Every window passes through stage 1, so its cost is paid for every window; later stages are paid only by the few windows that reach them. Most background windows are easy and can be rejected by one or two features.




Q8. Why is each new cascade stage trained on background windows that the earlier stages accepted, rather than on random background?






Answer





Random background is already rejected by the earlier stages; training on it would teach nothing new. The windows that got through are the hard, face-like ones the cascade still gets wrong. Training each stage on those makes the cascade progressively better at exactly the cases that matter.




Q9. How does the detector handle faces of different sizes without an image pyramid?






Answer





It scales the features: in a larger window every rectangle grows by the same factor. With the integral image a larger rectangle costs the same four lookups. Dividing by the window’s standard deviation and the rectangle area keeps the responses comparable across scales.




Q10. A detector trained mostly on faces without glasses misses faces with glasses. Is this a bug in boosting?






Answer





No: boosting chose features and thresholds that fit the training set. If a group of faces is rare or absent there, the chosen features (e.g. “the eyes are dark”) may not hold for it, and the stage thresholds reject it. The fix is in the data: a training (and test) set that covers everyone the detector will be used on, with rates reported per group.




Q11. (math) Show that after reweighting, the stump just chosen has weighted error exactly \tfrac12.






Answer





Before normalising, the wrong examples weigh \varepsilon e^{\alpha} and the correct ones (1-\varepsilon)e^{-\alpha}. With e^{\alpha} = \sqrt{(1-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon} both are \sqrt{\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)}, so after normalising each part is \tfrac12.

title: Exercise: fast marching
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Arrival time T(x)
when a front that starts at the seeds (T = 0) reaches x, moving with speed 1/P


Eikonal equation
\lvert\nabla T\rvert = P; with P = 1, T is the Euclidean distance to the seeds


Fast marching
Dijkstra’s order (smallest tentative value is final) with the upwind update below


Upwind update
a = smaller final value left/right, b = smaller final value above/below; if \lvert a - b\rvert < P: T = \tfrac12\big(a + b + \sqrt{2P^2 - (a-b)^2}\big), else T = \min(a, b) + P


Dijkstra update (4 neighbours)
T = \min(a, b) + P


Minimal path
gradient descent on T from the target down to a seed



Pixel spacing is 1 throughout.

title: Exercise: fast marching
text:
By hand
B1. Updates with P = 1 unless stated. (a) Known neighbours: left T = 2, above T = 2.5. Compute the fast-marching update and Dijkstra’s update. (b) The same with P = 2. (c) Only the left neighbour (T = 2) is known. (d) Left T = 2, above T = 3.2.
B2. A seed at the corner (0, 0) of a 4 \times 4 quadrant, P = 1, T(0, 0) = 0 (no special treatment of the seed’s neighbourhood). Write T(x, y) with x the column and y the row. (a) Compute T on the whole quadrant with fast marching, in the order the pixels become final. (Use the symmetry T(x, y) = T(y, x).) (b) Compare with the Euclidean distance and with Dijkstra on 4 and on 8 neighbours. Where is fast marching worst, and why?
B3. A straight front crosses the grid at 45°: two neighbours of a pixel, one on the left and one above, both have T = t. (a) What does Dijkstra (4 neighbours) give the pixel, and what does fast marching give? (b) How far does a 45° front really travel from the line through those two neighbours to the pixel? Which update is right?
B4. Edge cost P = 1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2. At a nucleus boundary the gradient magnitude is about 40 per pixel over a band 4 px wide; elsewhere it is close to 0. (a) With k = 20: what is P in the band, and how long does the front need to cross it, compared with a flat region? (b) With k = 8? (c) What does that do to the fronts of a seed inside the nucleus, and to the minimal path from inside to a target outside?
B5. Two seeds at (70, 90) and (190, 170), P = 1. Where do the two fronts meet? What is T at the midpoint (130, 130)?






Solutions





B1. (a) |2 - 2.5| = 0.5 < 1: T = \tfrac12\big(4.5 + \sqrt{2 - 0.25}\big) = 2.911; Dijkstra \min(2, 2.5) + 1 = 3. (b) 0.5 < 2: T = \tfrac12\big(4.5 + \sqrt{8 - 0.25}\big) = 3.642 (Dijkstra: 4). (c) b = \infty: T = 2 + 1 = 3, the same as Dijkstra. (d) |2 - 3.2| = 1.2 \ge 1: the one-neighbour update, T = 3: the front clearly comes from the left; the upper neighbour is too late to matter.
B2. (a) Order: (0,0) 0; (1,0) and (0,1) 1; (1,1) 1.707; (2,0), (0,2) 2; (2,1), (1,2) 2.545; (3,0), (0,3) 3; (2,2) 3.252; (3,1), (1,3) 3.442; (3,2), (2,3) 4.048; (3,3) 4.755. For example T(2,1) from a = T(1,1) = 1.707 and b = T(2,0) = 2: \tfrac12\big(3.707 + \sqrt{2 - 0.086}\big) = 2.545. (b)

Fast marching is worst on the diagonal next to the seed: at (1,1) it is 0.29 too far, and this error is carried outward (0.51 at (3,3)). A point seed is the opposite of a straight front, which the update assumes. Far from the seed the fronts become nearly straight and the error grows only slowly; implementations set the seed’s neighbourhood to the exact distance first (the demo: within 3 px), after which the error at 100 px is about 1 px.
B3. (a) Dijkstra: t + 1. Fast marching: \tfrac12\big(2t + \sqrt 2\big) = t + 0.707. (b) The line through the two neighbours is at distance 1/\sqrt2 = 0.707 from the pixel (half the diagonal of a pixel): the front needs time 0.707. Fast marching is exact here; Dijkstra overestimates by 41%.
B4. (a) P = 1 + (40/20)^2 = 5: crossing 4 px takes 20 time units instead of 4. (b) P = 1 + (40/8)^2 = 26: 104 instead of 4. (c) The fronts spread quickly inside the nucleus and then bunch up at its boundary (many iso-lines close together) before continuing outside. The minimal path to an outside target crosses the boundary where the band is cheapest to cross (weak or thin edges) and as straight across as possible, because every pixel inside the band is expensive.
B5. On the perpendicular bisector of the two seeds: the points with equal distance to both (a straight line through the midpoint (130, 130), perpendicular to the line joining the seeds). T(130, 130) = \sqrt{60^2 + 40^2} = 72.11.




Math questions
B6. (math) Derive the upwind update from T_x^2 + T_y^2 = P^2 with one-sided differences T_x \approx T - a, T_y \approx T - b. Show that when |a - b| < P the larger root satisfies T > \max(a, b), and explain why that makes Dijkstra’s ordering argument work for fast marching.
B7. (math) Show that the update is exact for every plane wave T(x, y) = x\cos\varphi + y\sin\varphi with 0 \le \varphi \le 90° and P = 1, when the left and upper neighbours carry the exact values.
B8. (math) Grid distances from a point with cost 1 per unit length. For a direction at angle \varphi \in [0°, 45°] from the x-axis, show that 4-neighbour Dijkstra gives \cos\varphi + \sin\varphi times the Euclidean distance, and 8-neighbour Dijkstra \cos\varphi + (\sqrt2 - 1)\sin\varphi times. Find the worst angle and the worst factor for each.
B9. (math) With P = 1 and a single seed, show that gradient descent on T from any point follows the straight line to the seed. With a general P > 0, why can the descent not get stuck before reaching a seed?






Solutions (math)





B6. (T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = P^2 is 2T^2 - 2(a + b)T + a^2 + b^2 - P^2 = 0, with roots T = \tfrac12\big(a + b \pm \sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2}\big), real when |a - b| \le \sqrt2 P. The larger root minus \max(a, b) is \tfrac12\big(\sqrt{2P^2 - (a - b)^2} - |a - b|\big), which is positive exactly when 2P^2 - (a-b)^2 > (a-b)^2, i.e. |a - b| < P (the condition used). So every new value exceeds the final values it was computed from (and in the fallback, \min(a, b) + P > \min(a, b)). Values therefore increase along the front, and a pixel with the smallest tentative value cannot be lowered by updates from pixels made final later: the Dijkstra argument applies.
B7. With exact neighbours a = T - \cos\varphi, b = T - \sin\varphi (the left neighbour is one step back in x, the upper one step back in y), (T - a)^2 + (T - b)^2 = \cos^2\varphi + \sin^2\varphi = 1 = P^2, and |a - b| = |\sin\varphi - \cos\varphi| < 1 for 0 < \varphi < 90° (at 0° and 90° the fallback \min(a, b) + 1 is exact). So the exact T solves the update equation; it is the larger root since T > \max(a, b).
B8. A grid path to (r\cos\varphi, r\sin\varphi) with 4 neighbours needs r\cos\varphi horizontal and r\sin\varphi vertical unit steps: factor \cos\varphi + \sin\varphi, largest at 45°: \sqrt2 = 1.414. With 8 neighbours: r\sin\varphi diagonal steps of length \sqrt2 and r(\cos\varphi - \sin\varphi) straight steps: \cos\varphi + (\sqrt2 - 1)\sin\varphi; the derivative vanishes where \tan\varphi = \sqrt2 - 1, \varphi = 22.5°, with factor \sqrt{1 + (\sqrt2 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{4 - 2\sqrt2} = 1.082: 8.2% too far.
B9. T(x) = |x - s|, so -\nabla T = (s - x)/|x - s|: the unit vector towards the seed. Descent moves straight towards s. For general P > 0: |\nabla T| = P > 0 everywhere except at the seeds, so \nabla T never vanishes away from them: there are no other critical points, and T strictly decreases along the descent until a seed is reached (in the discrete version, plateaus and the grid’s corners can still stop small steps, which is why implementations fall back to the lowest neighbour).

title: Exercise: fast marching
text:
Explore
Left: the arrival time T by fast marching; right: Dijkstra on the 4- or 8-neighbour grid, with the same cost P and the same seeds. Colour = time; white lines = fronts at equal time steps. Click on either image to place a target (or a seed, after add seed): orange is the minimal path by gradient descent on T, blue is Dijkstra’s pixel path. Costs: P = 1, slow at edges (P = 1 + (|\nabla I|/k)^2, with the contrast k), fast on bright lines. show image puts the image under the paths. The readout gives T and d at the target, the straight-line distance (flat cost), the lengths of both paths and the times.



E1. Preset flat cost: circles, not diamonds. Describe the fronts on both sides. Switch Dijkstra to 8 neighbours: what shape now? In which directions is 8-neighbour Dijkstra exact, and where is it worst (compare B8)?
E2. Preset Dijkstra 4-nbr vs fast marching (seed bottom left, target top right). Read T, d, the straight-line distance and the two path lengths. Then switch to 8 neighbours. Explain the numbers.
E3. Preset two seeds: where fronts meet. Where do the fronts meet? Place a target near (130, 130) (the middle of the image, slightly right of and below the centre) and compare T with B5.
E4. Preset minimal path along a neurite. Compare the two paths and their lengths. Read T and d: which is smaller, and why might fast marching be slower than 8-neighbour Dijkstra on a structure only 2–3 pixels wide? Try 4 neighbours.
E5. Preset edge cost: front slows at the nucleus (k = 8, seed inside the nucleus, target outside, bottom right). Where do the fronts bunch up? Compare T with the flat cost (P = 1). Then try k = 20 and k = 60.
E6. With any image and P = 1, add a second and a third seed. What do the meeting lines of the fronts form? How does this relate to watershed basins (watershed day)?






Solutions





E1. Fast marching: circles. 4-neighbour Dijkstra: diamonds (squares turned by 45°), the city-block distance. 8 neighbours: octagons. 8-neighbour Dijkstra is exact along the axes and the diagonals, and worst halfway between them (22.5°), 8.2% too far (B8).
E2. T = 277.3 for a straight-line distance of 275.8 (0.5% too far; the descent path is the straight line, 275.8 long). 4-neighbour Dijkstra: d = 390.0, the city-block distance 195 + 195, and its path is a staircase of the same length 390.0 (here an L-shape). With 8 neighbours: d = 275.8 and a path of 275.8: the target lies exactly on a diagonal, where 8 neighbours are exact.
E3. On the perpendicular bisector of the two seeds: a straight line through the middle, from the lower left to the upper right, where the iso-lines of the two seeds meet in corners. At (130, 130) fast marching gives about 73.1, against 72.11 exactly (B5).
E4. Both paths follow the neurite from the tip at the bottom left, past the soma, to the tip at the top. Fast marching: T = 149.7, path length 250.1; Dijkstra (8): d = 123.9, path length 261.5 (a pixel path, with small zig-zags). Here fast marching is slower: its update uses only the 4 axis neighbours, so a fast lane only 2–3 pixels wide that runs diagonally looks like a staircase to it, and the front partly leaks into the slow background beside the lane. Dijkstra with 8 neighbours can step diagonally inside the lane. With 4 neighbours Dijkstra gives d = 159.5 and a 323.0 px path. For thin structures, the cost should be smoothed a little or the grid refined.
E5. The fronts bunch up along the nucleus boundary (many iso-lines close together), most where the edge is strong; through the soft lower-left part they pass more easily. T = 206.8 at the target, against 171.9 with P = 1: crossing the boundary costs about 35 time units. With k = 20: T = 177.7; with k = 60: 172.6, nearly flat: a large k makes only very strong edges slow.
E6. The meeting lines form a Voronoi diagram of the seeds (with P = 1): every pixel belongs to the seed whose front reaches it first, i.e. the nearest seed. With an image cost, the regions follow the image (fronts are slowed by edges), much like watershed basins grown from markers; watershed, however, uses the highest point along the way instead of the accumulated travel time.

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
About this lecture
The last unit built networks and said “training walks downhill”. This unit opens that box.

A loss says how wrong the network is: squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for classes.
Gradient descent steps downhill; the learning rate sets the step, a random mini-batch of examples estimates the slope.
Backpropagation computes the slope for every weight in one backward pass: the chain rule, organised.
Learning curves show overfitting; weight decay, dropout and more data fight it.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour: gdescent (presets “just right”, “zig-zag”, “diverges”, “SGD noise”, “two starts”), then backprop (the by-hand preset: forward, backward, update, check; then “dead ReLU” and “sigmoid saturates”), then the playground with the training controls (overfitting presets). Adam, used without explanation on the VAE day, gets its one line on the math slide about mini-batches.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: The loss: how wrong is the network?
text:
The loss: how wrong is the network?
One number for all training examples, averaged; training makes it small.

Numbers (a brightness, a size): mean squared error, (\hat y - y)^2 averaged.
Classes: the network gives probabilities; the loss is cross-entropy, -\log p_{\text{true class}}.




probability given to the true class
0.99

cross-entropy -\ln p
0.01
0.11

1.61
4.61



A confident wrong answer costs far more than a hesitant one. 0.69 = \ln 2 is “50 : 50, no idea”.

Cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of the labels under the network’s probabilities: minimising it is maximum likelihood. Squared error on probabilities would also work but gives tiny gradients when the network is confidently wrong; cross-entropy gives the largest push exactly there (next math slide).
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: softmax and cross-entropy
Scores \mathbf z, probabilities p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}, true class c (one-hot \mathbf y):
\mathcal L = -\log p_c = -z_c + \log\sum_j e^{z_j}, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial z_k} = p_k - y_k

The gradient is “predicted minus wanted”: no gradient when the network is right and sure, a gradient of almost -1 on the true score when it is sure and wrong.
Two classes with one sigmoid output p = 1/(1 + e^{-z}): \mathcal L = -[y\log p + (1 - y)\log(1 - p)], again \partial\mathcal L/\partial z = p - y.
Cross-entropy = negative log-likelihood of the training labels: minimising it is maximum likelihood.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Gradient descent: walk downhill
The loss is a landscape over all the weights. From the current weights, step a little in the steepest downhill direction; repeat.

Step length = learning rate \eta. Too small: it takes forever. Too large: it jumps across the valley, or out of it.
Recall the one-weight example of the last unit: \eta = 0.1, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5 gave losses 0.36, 0, 9, 81 after one step from 9.
A narrow valley makes a single \eta awkward: big enough for the gentle direction is too big for the steep one, so the path zig-zags.
Different starts can end in different valleys: different networks.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Try it: walking downhill




“too small” (η = 0.02): 192 steps to get within 0.001 of the minimum. “just right” (0.3): 11 steps. “zig-zag”: η = 0.6 in the narrow valley, the path bounces across the valley while it creeps along it. “momentum in the valley”: η = 0.03 with momentum gets there in about 115 steps; without momentum it is still far after 200. “diverges”: η = 0.8 on the bowl, the loss grows every step. “SGD noise”: batches of 4: a wandering path that ends jiggling around the minimum. “two starts, two minima”: the left start ends in the deeper minimum (loss −0.25), the right one in the shallower (+0.25). Click anywhere to add a path.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Mini-batches and epochs
The loss is an average over all training images, say 60,000. Its exact gradient needs all of them for every step: too slow.

Instead, take a random mini-batch (32 images), compute the gradient on it, step. A noisy but cheap estimate of the true slope.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD): one step per mini-batch. One epoch = one pass through all the data: 60{,}000/32 = 1875 steps.
The noise is not just tolerated: it shakes the weights out of flat regions and narrow dips.
Momentum: keep part of the previous step, like a ball rolling downhill; it smooths zig-zags.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: the update rules
\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\,\nabla_{\mathbf w}\mathcal L, \qquad \mathcal L(\mathbf w) = \frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N \ell_n(\mathbf w)

Mini-batch B of size m drawn uniformly: \mathbf g_B = \frac1m\sum_{n\in B}\nabla\ell_n has \mathbb E[\mathbf g_B] = \nabla\mathcal L (unbiased); its variance falls like 1/m.
Near a minimum the loss is a quadratic bowl with Hessian H; plain descent is stable only for \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}(H), and the slow direction needs \approx 1/(\eta\lambda_{\min}) steps: elongated bowls are slow.
Momentum: \mathbf v \leftarrow \beta\mathbf v + \mathbf g, \mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\mathbf v (typically \beta = 0.9).
Adam: momentum plus a separate step size per weight, dividing by a running average of \sqrt{g^2} (Kingma and Ba, 2015). The default in practice; the VAE day uses it.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Backpropagation: the network as a graph
text:
Backpropagation: the network as a graph


Forward: values flow left to right (blue): z = w_1x + b_1, h = \text{ReLU}(z), \hat y = w_2h + b_2, \mathcal L = (\hat y - y)^2.
Backward: from the loss, each node passes on its gradient times its local derivative (red). Every weight gets \partial\mathcal L/\partial w.


Every node only needs to know its own local derivative: the multiply node knows ∂(wx)/∂w = x, the ReLU knows it passes or blocks, the loss knows 2(ŷ − y). The chain rule does the rest. The forward values must be kept, because the local derivatives need them.

Every weight moved in its own downhill direction, but together they overshoot: ŷ goes from 1.5 to 0.25, past the target 1. A smaller step works. The demo’s “update” button shows exactly these numbers.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
The math: backpropagation
Chain rule on the graph: \partial\mathcal L/\partial w = \sum_{\text{paths } w \to \mathcal L}\ \prod_{\text{edges}} local derivatives. Organised layer by layer, with \mathbf z^{(l)} = W^{(l)}\mathbf a^{(l-1)} + \mathbf b^{(l)}, \mathbf a^{(l)} = \varphi(\mathbf z^{(l)}) and \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)} = \partial\mathcal L/\partial\mathbf z^{(l)}:
\boldsymbol\delta^{(l-1)} = \big((W^{(l)})^\top\boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}\big) \odot \varphi'(\mathbf z^{(l-1)}), \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial W^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}(\mathbf a^{(l-1)})^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\mathbf b^{(l)}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{(l)}

Start: \boldsymbol\delta^{(L)} = \mathbf p - \mathbf y (softmax + cross-entropy) or 2(\hat{\mathbf y} - \mathbf y) (squared error).
The backward pass is one matrix–vector product per layer, like the forward pass: the cost is about twice a forward pass, whatever the number of weights (Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, 1986). Finite differences would need one forward pass per weight.

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Try it: forward, backward, update




Press forward (values appear node by node), backward (gradients, with each edge’s local derivative), update (the loss goes from 0.25 to 0.5625 with η = 0.1), check (finite differences agree). Then the presets: “dead ReLU” (x = −1: z < 0, the ReLU blocks, w1 and b1 get zero gradient), “sigmoid saturates” (z = 8: the sigmoid’s local derivative is 0.0003, w1 gets almost nothing), “learning rate too large” (η = 0.3: the loss jumps to 1.69). “2–2–1 network” shows the same with two hidden units.
