title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: What the local derivatives tell us
text:
What the local derivatives tell us

ReLU passes the gradient (derivative 1) or blocks it (0). A unit that is off for every training example never gets a gradient again: a dead unit. A too large learning rate can kill many at once.
Sigmoid and tanh have derivatives near 0 when the input is large: a saturated unit passes almost nothing back. Through many such layers the gradient shrinks layer by layer: vanishing gradients.
That is why deep sigmoid networks were hard to train, and why ReLU took over around 2010.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Overfitting: recall, and learning curves

Day 14 (random forests): fit on training data, choose settings on validation data, report once on test data. A too flexible model fits the noise.

New here: plot the loss on both sets during training: the learning curves.
Training loss keeps falling. Validation loss falls, then rises: from there on the network memorises.
Early stopping: keep the weights from the step with the lowest validation loss.


The figure is the playground preset “overfitting”: 8 + 8 units on 60 noisy points, half of them for validation. The validation loss is lowest at step 126 (0.169); after 2000 steps the training loss is 0.002 and the validation loss 0.377. The test set must not be used for any of these choices, including when to stop.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Regularisation: making memorising harder

Weight decay: add \lambda\sum w^2 to the loss. Large weights make sharp, wiggly boundaries; small weights make smooth ones.
Dropout: during training, silence each hidden unit at random (say with probability 0.4). No unit can rely on a particular other unit; at test time all units are used.
More data, and data augmentation: train on shifted, rotated, brightened copies of the images (next unit).
And the simplest: a smaller network, or early stopping.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: The math: weight decay and dropout
text:
The math: weight decay and dropout

Weight decay: \mathcal L_\lambda(\mathbf w) = \mathcal L(\mathbf w) + \lambda\|\mathbf w\|^2, gradient \nabla\mathcal L + 2\lambda\mathbf w: every step also shrinks every weight by the factor 1 - 2\eta\lambda. The same penalty as ridge regression (Tikhonov regularisation, the deconvolution day).
Dropout: multiply each hidden output by m/(1 - q) with m \sim \text{Bernoulli}(1 - q); the expected output is unchanged, so nothing changes at test time (“inverted dropout”). It acts like averaging over the 2^{\#\text{units}} thinned networks (Srivastava et al., 2014).
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
section: Try it: overfitting and its cures
text:
Try it: overfitting and its cures




Hollow points are the validation set. “overfitting”: lowest validation loss 0.169 at step 126, then it rises while the training loss goes to 0.001. “weight decay smooths it”: the training loss stalls at 0.164 and the validation loss stays near 0.31: a smoother boundary. “dropout”: noisy training curve, the validation loss stays low much longer (0.18 at step 2000). “more data cures it”: 300 points, training and validation curves stay together. “mini-batches of 8”: a noisy curve. “learning rate too large”: the loss jumps, and 14 of the 16 hidden units die. “dead network”: η = 5, the loss sits at 0.693 = ln 2 for ever.
crumbs: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation

title: Learning: loss, gradient descent and backpropagation
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Loss
squared error for numbers, cross-entropy -\log p_\text{true} for classes


Gradient descent
\mathbf w \leftarrow \mathbf w - \eta\nabla\mathcal L; \eta too small is slow, too large diverges


Mini-batch SGD
the gradient on 32 random examples; an epoch is one pass over the data


Backpropagation
forward values, then gradients backward, each node times its local derivative


Dead / saturated units
ReLU blocks, saturated sigmoids pass almost nothing: vanishing gradients


Learning curves
training loss falls, validation loss turns up: stop there


Regularisation
weight decay, dropout, more data, augmentation



Next: networks for images, where the first layer is a bank of learned convolution kernels.

title: Quiz: colour for display
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A colour map turns a data value into a colour through a display range; L^* is the lightness of a colour (0 black, 100 white).

Q1. A smooth height map shown with the rainbow (“jet”) map seems to have sharp boundaries. Are they in the data?






Hint





How does jet’s lightness change along the map?









Answer





No. Jet’s lightness rises steeply from dark blue to bright cyan, stays high through green and yellow, and falls to dark red. Where lightness changes fast, small data changes look like edges; where it is flat, real changes are hidden. The boundaries are made by the map.




Q2. Which kind of colour map would you use for (a) a temperature difference to a reference, positive and negative; (b) photon counts; (c) cell labels 1–50?






Hint





Sequential, diverging, qualitative.









Answer






Diverging, centred at zero with a symmetric range. (b) Sequential with monotone lightness (viridis, magma, grey). (c) Qualitative: distinct colours without order, chosen so that neighbouring labels differ.





Q3. Signed data range from −3 to 7. You show them with a blue–white–red map and the display range −3 … 7. What value appears white, and what is wrong?






Hint





White is the middle of the map.









Answer





The middle of the range, (-3 + 7)/2 = 2, is white: values between 0 and 2 look blue, as if they were negative. Use the symmetric range −7 … 7 so that 0 is white (−3 is then light blue, at position 0.29 of the map).




Q4. A figure shows two fluorescence channels merged in red and green. Why is that a problem, and what is a better choice?






Hint





Who cannot tell red from green?









Answer





About 8 % of men have a red–green deficiency: for them red, green and their overlap (yellow) look like similar yellows, and the two channels cannot be told apart. Use magenta and green (overlap: white), and show each channel separately in grey as well.




Q5. Why do the viridis and cividis maps still work when printed in greyscale, while jet does not?






Hint





What does a greyscale print keep?









Answer





A greyscale print keeps (roughly) the lightness. Viridis and cividis increase lightness monotonically, so the order of values survives. Jet’s lightness goes up and down, so low and high values both print dark and the order is lost.




Q6. What does a decorrelation stretch do to the colour cloud of an image, and why do faint colour differences become visible?






Hint





Think of the cloud as a cigar along the grey axis.









Answer





It rotates the cloud to its principal axes, scales each axis to the same spread, and rotates back. The long axis (mostly brightness) is shrunk, the thin axes (colour differences) are stretched. Colour differences that were tiny compared with the brightness variation now span a large range of colours.




Q7. (math) A dichromat’s simulation matrix D satisfies D^2 = D and has rank 2. What does that mean geometrically, and which colour differences are invisible?






Hint





Projection; null space.









Answer





D is a projection onto a plane (its range, 2D): applying it twice changes nothing more. Every colour is mapped onto the plane along the direction of the null space (1D). Two colours look the same iff their difference lies in that null space; for a deuteranope, in LMS it is the direction of the M cone alone.

title: Exercise: colour for display
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

choose a sequential, diverging or qualitative colour map, and a display range, for a given kind of data,
check a map’s lightness profile and explain why the rainbow map invents edges,
simulate a dichromat as a projection and design figures that survive it,
compute the principal axes of a colour covariance and the factors of a decorrelation stretch.

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: colour for display
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Colour map
data value → position t \in [0, 1] (through the display range) → colour


Lightness profile
L^*(t) along the map; should be monotone for sequential data


Diverging map
neutral (lightest) at its centre; use a range symmetric around the meaningful value


Merge
coloured channels added; magenta + green rather than red + green


Dichromat
two cone types: a rank-2 projection of colour space


Decorrelation stretch
rotate to the principal axes, equalise the variances, rotate back






Lightness L^* along four maps, with the maps underneath (jet, viridis, cividis, grey).

title: Exercise: colour for display
text:
By hand
B1. The lightness L^* of jet and viridis at five positions:



t

0.25

jet
12.9

Which map is monotone? (b) With jet, which data value looks about as dark as the value at t = 0.25? (c) Between which positions does viridis change lightness fastest?

B2. Data range from −3 to 7. (a) With a diverging map and display range −3 … 7, which data value is shown white? (b) Which range puts zero at the centre? At what position t is −3 then shown, and at what position 7?
B3. In LMS, a toy deuteranope keeps L and S and replaces M by 0.5L + 0.5S: D = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 0 & 0.5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Apply D to a reddish (L, M, S) = (0.8, 0.4, 0.2) and a greenish (0.8, 0.9, 0.2). (b) What is the rank of D, and which vector does it send to zero? (c) Check that D^2 = D.
B4. The covariance of an image’s encoded colours (in units of 10^{-3}) is S = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. (a) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors (the matrix is block diagonal). (b) What share of the variance is along PC1? What does PC1 mean here? (c) A decorrelation stretch scales each axis to the standard deviation \bar\sigma = \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}S/3}. Give the three scale factors.
B5. Give a better design for each figure, in one sentence: (a) a fluorescence merge in red (nuclei) and green (membrane); (b) a map of cell speeds in jet with the range set to the 1st–99th percentile; (c) a map of the change in intensity between two time points, in viridis.






Solutions





B1. (a) Viridis: its lightness increases at every step. Jet rises to 90.6 and falls again. (b) t = 0.25 has L^* = 54.6; on the way down jet passes the same lightness between t = 0.75 (67.0) and t = 1 (25.4), near the dark red end: low and high values look equally light. (c) The steps are 18.2, 16.8, 16.6, 24.4: fastest between 0.75 and 1 (the map’s anchors are not perfectly uniform), slowest in the middle. Jet’s steps are +41.7, +36.0, −23.6, −41.6.
B2. (a) The centre of the range, (-3 + 7)/2 = 2, is white. (b) −7 … 7. Position t = 0.5 + v/14: −3 at t = 0.286 (light blue), 7 at t = 1 (full red); 0 at t = 0.5 (white).
B3. (a) Reddish: (0.8,\; 0.5 \cdot 0.8 + 0.5 \cdot 0.2,\; 0.2) = (0.8, 0.5, 0.2). Greenish: (0.8, 0.5, 0.2) as well: the two collapse to the same colour. (b) Rank 2 (the middle column is zero; the other two columns are independent). It sends (0, 1, 0) to zero: a change of M alone, exactly the difference of the two colours in (a). (c) Row 2 of D^2 is 0.5 \cdot (1, 0, 0) + 0.5 \cdot (0, 0, 1) = (0.5, 0, 0.5), rows 1 and 3 are unchanged: D^2 = D.
B4. (a) The upper 2 \times 2 block \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 3 \\ 3 & 4 \end{pmatrix} has eigenvalues 4 \pm 3: 7 with (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2 and 1 with (1, -1, 0)/\sqrt2; the third eigenvalue is 1 with (0, 0, 1). (b) 7/9 = 77.8\,\%. PC1 is “R and G together”: a brightness-like direction (in the R–G plane), the axis along which the image varies most. (c) \operatorname{tr}S = 9, \bar\sigma^2 = 3: factors \sqrt{3/7} = 0.655 along PC1, \sqrt{3/1} = 1.732 along the other two. The long axis shrinks, the thin ones grow.
B5. (a) Magenta for one channel and green for the other (overlap white), plus each channel separately in grey. (b) A sequential map with monotone lightness (viridis), with a colour bar that states the range and that values beyond it are clipped. (c) A diverging map centred at zero with a symmetric range, so that increases and decreases are told apart by hue and no change is neutral.




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that the decorrelation stretch \mathbf x' = \boldsymbol\mu + U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})U^\top(\mathbf x - \boldsymbol\mu) gives the covariance \bar\sigma^2 I, and that with \bar\sigma^2 = \operatorname{tr}S/3 the total variance is unchanged.
B7. (math) A deuteranope’s simulation in LMS is D with rows (1, 0, 0), (a, 0, b), (0, 0, 1), where a, b are chosen so that white \mathbf w and blue \mathbf q (both in LMS) are unchanged. Write the two equations for a and b. Show that D^2 = D for any a, b, and that the simulation in RGB, T^{-1}DT, is also a projection of rank 2.
B8. (math) A colour map is the curve \mathbf c(t) in Lab. Show that if L^*(t) is strictly increasing, then two different data values can never be shown with the same colour, and that the order of the values can be read from lightness alone. Is the converse true: does an injective map (no two values with the same colour) need monotone lightness?






Solutions (math)





B6. Let A = U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})U^\top (symmetric). \operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf x') = ASA = U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})\,\Lambda\,\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})U^\top = U(\bar\sigma^2 I)U^\top = \bar\sigma^2 I, using U^\top U = I. Total variance \operatorname{tr}(\bar\sigma^2 I) = 3\bar\sigma^2 = \operatorname{tr}S.
B7. Unchanged M-component: a\,w_L + b\,w_S = w_M and a\,q_L + b\,q_S = q_M (two linear equations; the L and S components are kept by construction). D^2: rows 1 and 3 are unit rows that pick L and S, which D keeps, so they stay; row 2 of D^2 is a\cdot(\text{row }1) + b\cdot(\text{row }3) = (a, 0, b). So D^2 = D. In RGB, (T^{-1}DT)^2 = T^{-1}D^2T = T^{-1}DT, and the rank is unchanged by the invertible T: a rank-2 projection.
B8. If L^* is strictly increasing, t_1 < t_2 implies L^*(t_1) < L^*(t_2): the colours differ (at least in lightness), and the larger value is always the lighter one, whatever the hue. The converse is false: a map can be injective without monotone lightness (jet is injective: no two positions have the same colour), but then the order cannot be read from lightness, and colours of very different values can have the same lightness (B1b).

title: Exercise: colour for display
text:
Explore: colour maps
A synthetic grey-level image through a colour map, with the colour bar and the map’s lightness profile L^*(t) (the readout says whether it is monotone). Images: a smooth height field (no edges at all), a fluorescence-like image, a signed difference (values −3 … 7). Choose the map and the display range. Simulate colour vision shows everything (image and bar) as a protanope, deuteranope or tritanope would see it. Merge two channels shows nuclei and filaments in red + green or magenta + green.



E1. Preset jet invents edges. Describe what you see in the height field. Where is the lightness maximum of jet, and what are L^* at both ends? Now viridis is monotone: compare.
E2. With the height field, try cividis, magma and hue circle. Which are monotone? Look at the hue circle’s ends: what goes wrong?
E3. Preset signed data needs a diverging map (viridis, range −3 … 7). Can you tell which regions are negative? Choose diverging: which value is white? Fix the display range so that zero is white.
E4. With viridis and the height field, simulate deuteranope, then do the same with jet. Which map still shows the order of values?
E5. Preset red/green merge for a deuteranope. Can you tell nuclei from filaments? Choose magenta + green. Then simulate normal vision again and compare the two merges.






Solutions





E1. Sharp-looking bands (a cyan ring, a yellow ring) around the bumps, although the field is smooth; the high peak looks dark red, darker than the middle. Jet’s lightness: 12.9 at t = 0, a maximum of 96.8 at t = 0.62, 25.4 at t = 1: not monotone. Viridis (14.9 → 90.9, monotone) shows smooth hills; the highest values are the lightest.
E2. Cividis (13.8 → 91.3) and magma (0.1 → 97.9) are monotone. The hue circle is not: it starts at L^* = 53.2 (red), peaks at 97.1 near t = 0.2 (yellow), dips to 32.3 (blue) and ends at 60.3 (magenta): both ends are similar reds, so the lowest and highest values look alike.
E3. With viridis, nothing marks zero: negative values are just “darker”. With diverging and the range −3 … 7, white is at 2. With the range −7 … 7 (move display min to −7), zero is white, the negative dip is blue and the positive peak red.
E4. Viridis keeps its order for the deuteranope: it becomes a blue-to-yellow ramp with the same rising lightness. Jet becomes dark blue → light blue → pale yellow → yellow → olive → dark olive, with lightness 13, 52, 87, 97 (at t = 0.62), 72, 31: both ends are dark, and the order is lost.
E5. For the deuteranope, red nuclei and green filaments both appear as yellows (pure red becomes about (156, 156, 0), pure green (214, 214, 46)): hard to tell apart, and the overlap is also yellow. With magenta + green, magenta becomes a blue (about (156, 156, 252)) and green a yellow: clearly different. For normal vision both merges are readable; magenta + green also shows the overlap as white rather than yellow.

title: Exercise: colour for display
section: Explore: PCA of the colour cloud
text:
Explore: PCA of the colour cloud
The pixels of a synthetic image in the sRGB cube, with the principal axes of the colour cloud (±2 standard deviations; orange PC1, purple PC2, green PC3). The readout gives the standard deviations along the axes, the share of PC1, its direction and the correlations of the channels (all before the stretch). Stretch applies a fraction of the decorrelation stretch: the cloud and the image change together.



P1. Preset H&E: a flat cloud. Give the standard deviations along the three axes and the share of PC1. What shape is the cloud, and why? Which pair of channels is most strongly correlated?
P2. Move stretch to 1 (preset decorrelation stretch). What happens to the cloud and to the image? Why do some colours look clipped?
P3. Preset objects: a cigar along grey. Where does PC1 point? What is its share? Compare with B4.
P4. Apply the stretch to the objects (preset objects, stretched). What becomes easier to see, and what would you not do with the stretched image?






Solutions





P1. Standard deviations 0.190, 0.070 and 0.002; PC1 carries 88.0 % of the variance. The cloud is a thin, flat sheet: every pixel is a mixture of two stains (and white), two degrees of freedom, so the third axis has almost no spread. R and B are the most correlated (0.99), then G–B (0.84) and R–G (0.74).
P2. The sheet swells towards a round blob: the thin directions are stretched by large factors, the third one most (its σ is tiny, so the gain is about 63). The image becomes garish, but nuclei and stroma now differ strongly in colour. Values pushed outside [0, 1] are clipped (14 % of the pixels), which is why some areas are flat saturated colours. A gain this large on the third axis would also amplify any noise along it.
P3. PC1 is (0.55, 0.64, 0.54), close to the grey diagonal (0.58, 0.58, 0.58): brightness (shading, shadow). It carries 77.2 % of the variance (standard deviations 0.309, 0.143, 0.088). As in B4, the correlated channels make one long axis along “all channels together”.
P4. The stretched image exaggerates colour differences: the table, the shadow and the objects separate more by colour, and subtle tints (such as the faint cast of the shadow) are easier to see. The colours are false and depend on the image’s own statistics: do not measure colours or intensities on it, and do not compare stretched images of different scenes as if their colours meant the same.

title: Exercise: colour for display
text:
Where this leads
The course’s colour maps (viridis for sequential data, a blue–white–red map for signed data, a label palette) are used in every later demo. The spectral unmixing elective continues the colour cloud: with more channels than three, mixtures of dyes form cones and simplices in channel space, and finding the dyes’ spectra is a geometric problem.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: colour is three numbers, a linear map of a spectrum. Today: what the three numbers in an RGB file are.

RGB is a device space: “full red” means this display’s red.
Stored values are gamma-encoded: not proportional to light. Blurring, resizing and averaging must be done on linear values.
Changing colour space is a 3 × 3 matrix: RGB → XYZ, → luminance, → Y′CbCr (with chroma subsampling).
White balance: undoing the lamp with a diagonal matrix, and when that fails.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Recall from the bit-depth day (highbit/): an 8-bit photograph stores sRGB codes, not light. Today explains why those codes exist. Everything here is linear algebra on 3-vectors, except the transfer curve, a function of one variable.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
RGB is a device space
“(255, 0, 0)” means: full drive of this display’s red primary. Without knowing the primaries and the white, it is not a colour.

sRGB fixes everything: the three primaries (the triangle of the last unit), the white point D65, and a transfer curve from stored values to light.
An untagged 8-bit image, a web page and the browser canvas are assumed to be sRGB.
A wide-gamut photo (Display P3) with the same numbers is a different, more saturated colour.
A camera’s raw data and a microscope’s detector are linear and in the camera’s own RGB: each sensor has its own three curves.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Gamma encoding




The stored value is not proportional to the light. The display decodes it with a curve close to a power 2.4.

Why: perceived lightness is roughly the cube root of light. Equal steps of stored value are roughly equal visible steps, so 8 bits suffice without banding in the darks.
Stored 128 is only 21.6 % of white’s light. Half of white’s light is stored as 188.
JPEG photos are encoded; raw camera data and microscope images are linear.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: the sRGB transfer function
text:
The math: the sRGB transfer function
Stored value C \in [0, 1] (the 8-bit code divided by 255), linear light C_\text{lin} \in [0, 1]:
C_\text{lin} = \begin{cases} C / 12.92, & C \le 0.04045 \\[2pt] \left(\dfrac{C + 0.055}{1.055}\right)^{2.4}, & C > 0.04045 \end{cases} \qquad C = \begin{cases} 12.92\,C_\text{lin}, & C_\text{lin} \le 0.0031308 \\[2pt] 1.055\,C_\text{lin}^{1/2.4} - 0.055, & \text{else.} \end{cases}

A short straight piece near black (no infinite slope at 0), then a power 2.4 with an offset. Overall it is close to a pure power 2.2.
128/255 = 0.502 \to 0.216; 188/255 = 0.737 \to 0.503; C_\text{lin} = 0.5 \to C = 0.735, code 187.5.
Decode with a 256-entry lookup table; encode by the formula (or a finer table).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Why it matters: light adds, codes do not
text:
Why it matters: light adds, codes do not
Blur, resampling, averaging and mixing add up light. Done on encoded values they are wrong:

Black + white: the average of 0 and 255 is 128 in codes, but the average light is 0.5, code 188. A fine black/white stripe pattern looks like 188 from a distance, not 128.
Blurred highlights lose their glow; small bright lights shrink and dim.
Red meets green: blurring on codes gives a dark, muddy seam (codes 111, 144, 0 at the border instead of 176, 198, 0).
Downsampling fine bright detail on a dark background darkens the image.

Rule: decode → operate → encode. In quantitative work, never measure intensities on gamma-encoded exports.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Try it: blur in linear light
text:
Try it: blur in linear light




Same blur twice: on the stored codes (middle) and decode → blur → encode (right); the profile is along the dashed row. Tour: “black + white = 128 or 188?”: the blurred stripes come out 128 (codes) and 188 (light). Squint at the input: which uniform patch matches the stripes? (On a well-behaved screen, the bottom one, 188; a projector may disagree.) Mean luminance: codes lose 32.9 %, linear keeps it. “red meets green”: a dark seam on codes (luminance profile dips to 107, below both the red at 127 and the green at 220). “blurred lights”: codes lose 62.8 % of the light. “downsampling ×4” on thin lines: −69.0 %.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Linear maps between colour spaces
In linear RGB a colour is a mix of the display’s three primaries:
\text{colour} = R \cdot \text{(red primary)} + G \cdot \text{(green primary)} + B \cdot \text{(blue primary)}.
So XYZ is a matrix times linear RGB; for sRGB:
\begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.4124 & 0.3576 & 0.1805 \\ 0.2126 & 0.7152 & 0.0722 \\ 0.0193 & 0.1192 & 0.9505 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} R \\ G \\ B \end{pmatrix}.

Columns: the XYZ of each primary at full drive. Middle row: the luminance weights; green carries 72 % of the brightness, blue only 7 %.
Display A → display B: M_B^{-1}M_A, a change of basis. Colours outside B’s gamut get components < 0 or > 1: they must be clipped (or mapped inwards).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: the matrix from primaries and white point
text:
The math: the matrix from primaries and white point
Primary k with chromaticity (x_k, y_k) has XYZ proportional to \mathbf p_k = (x_k/y_k,\; 1,\; (1 - x_k - y_k)/y_k). Unknown: its brightness s_k. Require that R = G = B = 1 gives the white \mathbf w (with Y_w = 1):
M = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf p_R & \mathbf p_G & \mathbf p_B \end{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(s_R, s_G, s_B), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf p_R & \mathbf p_G & \mathbf p_B \end{pmatrix}\mathbf s = \mathbf w .

One 3 \times 3 linear system for the three scales; the scales are the middle row of M (the luminance weights), since the middle entry of every \mathbf p_k is 1.
sRGB: primaries (0.64, 0.33), (0.30, 0.60), (0.15, 0.06), white (0.3127, 0.3290) give the matrix on the previous slide.
The display-design demo of the last unit computes exactly this.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Converting to grey is a choice
text:
Converting to grey is a choice
One colour image, four greys:

Luminance Y = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linear RGB: the physically right brightness.
Luma Y' = 0.299R' + 0.587G' + 0.114B' on encoded values: the video standard, an approximation.
Channel mean (R + G + B)/3: treats the eye as equally sensitive to blue. Simple, often wrong.
One channel: often the best for analysis. In stained tissue or fluorescence, pick the channel with the contrast you need.

Test: red letters on a green background of equal luminance vanish in the luminance image but not in the mean. “Greyscale” is a projection, and you choose its direction.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Opponent channels and Y′CbCr
The visual system recodes the cone signals into one brightness and two colour-difference channels (red–green, blue–yellow), and it sees the colour differences with less detail.
Y′CbCr (JPEG, video) does the same with a matrix on encoded R′G′B′:

Y′: luma; Cb ∝ B′ − Y′, Cr ∝ R′ − Y′, stored around 128.
Chroma subsampling (4:2:0): keep Cb and Cr at half resolution in both directions. Half the data, almost invisible. Subsampling Y′ the same way is obvious.
Same idea as the low-pass filtering in the Fourier unit: drop the detail the eye does not use.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: Y′CbCr as an affine map
text:
The math: Y′CbCr as an affine map
\begin{pmatrix} Y' \\ C_b \\ C_r \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.299 & 0.587 & 0.114 \\ -0.1687 & -0.3313 & 0.5 \\ 0.5 & -0.4187 & -0.0813 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} R' \\ G' \\ B' \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 128 \\ 128 \end{pmatrix}

Rows 2 and 3 are (to rounding) 0.564\,(B' - Y') and 0.713\,(R' - Y'): the coefficients of each row sum to zero, so every grey has C_b = C_r = 128.
Invertible: decoding is the inverse matrix after removing the offset. 4:2:0 stores 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac14 = 1.5 values per pixel instead of 3.
Because it acts on encoded values, Y′ is luma, not luminance.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: Try it: colour as a matrix
text:
Try it: colour as a matrix




Y′CbCr channels of the synthetic objects scene (Cb, Cr with 128 as mid-grey). Tour: “subsample chroma by 4”: hard to see any change; mean ΔE*ab 2.18, at 1.125 bytes per pixel. “subsample luma by 4”: blocky edges at once, although the mean ΔE is smaller (1.87): the eye is far more sensitive to brightness detail than mean ΔE suggests. Then “greyscale” → “the isoluminant test”: luminance gives 117.3 for both letter and background; switch to mean (78.8 vs 45.7). “any matrix” → “P3 → sRGB”: 15.3 % of the pixels fall outside [0, 1].

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
White balance: undoing the lamp
The same white paper is orange under a light bulb and blue in shade; our eyes adapt and still call it white (colour constancy). A camera does not.

Camera responses: \mathbf c = A\,\operatorname{diag}(\text{lamp})\,\mathbf r. We want the colours under a reference light (daylight, D65).
von Kries (1902): scale each channel separately, \mathbf c' = D\,\mathbf c with D = \operatorname{diag}(w_\text{ref}/w), where w is the response to a white under the current lamp. A diagonal matrix.
Apply it to linear values: on encoded values a scaling of light is not a scaling of codes.
Works best in a basis close to the cones (or “sharpened” cone-like channels, as in the Bradford transform).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Estimating the white
The correction needs w, the camera’s response to white under this lamp:

Grey world: assume the scene averages to grey; w = the mean of each channel. Fails when one colour dominates: a forest turns grey-magenta.
White patch (max-RGB): assume the brightest values are white. Fails with a clipped highlight, which is “white” whatever the lamp.
A grey card (or a known white area) in the image: the most reliable.
In microscopy: the blank-field reference (light with no specimen) is a per-pixel white balance; the same idea as flat-field correction.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
section: The math: diagonal in which basis?
text:
The math: diagonal in which basis?
Diagonal scaling in a basis given by an invertible B (rows: XYZ → cone-like channels), written in linear RGB:
\mathbf c' = M_{\text{XYZ}\to\text{RGB}}\,B^{-1}\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{B M\,\mathbf w_\text{ref}}{B M\,\mathbf w}\right) B\,M\,\mathbf c, \qquad M = M_{\text{RGB}\to\text{XYZ}} .

B = I (on RGB): the camera channels; B = cone matrix: von Kries; B = Bradford’s “sharpened” matrix: narrower channels, usually the most accurate diagonal.
Exact only if the lamp change acts diagonally in that basis, which needs narrow-band channels. Broad, overlapping sensitivities (and metameric failure) leave an error.
With a known chart: fit a full 3 \times 3 matrix by least squares, \min_M \sum_i \|M\mathbf c_i - \mathbf t_i\|^2, i.e. M = TC^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Try it: white balance




A chart of 24 patches with known reflectance spectra (synthetic), rendered under the lamp; truth = the same chart under daylight. ΔE*ab ≈ 2 is just noticeable. Tour: “tungsten 2800 K”: no correction, mean ΔE 44.1. Grey card (click the third grey), cones: 7.61; Bradford: 5.31; encoded: 14.99. “grey world in a forest”: 22.6 (magenta cast); white patch there: 6.08. “white patch fooled by a highlight”: 24.6. “narrow-band LED”: grey card 10.6, and even the 3×3 fit leaves 4.66.

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Forward pointer: stains absorb
Brightfield microscopy is different: stains absorb light. The transmitted light is I = I_0 \cdot 10^{-(\text{absorbance})}, a product, not a sum.

Take the optical density -\log_{10}(I/I_0) per channel: then two stains add up linearly again.
Separating hematoxylin and eosin is then a 3 \times 3 (or 3 \times 2) linear problem: the spectral unmixing elective (stain unmixing).

title: RGB: gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Summary

RGB numbers are device values; sRGB fixes the primaries, the white and the transfer curve.
Stored values are gamma-encoded: decode before blurring, resizing, averaging or measuring (128 + black/white: the light says 188).
Colour spaces are related by 3 × 3 matrices: RGB → XYZ (columns = primaries), luminance (its middle row), Y′CbCr (plus an offset; chroma can be subsampled).
White balance is a diagonal matrix on linear values, best in a cone-like basis; estimate the white by grey world, white patch or a grey card, and know how each fails.

title: Quiz: RGB, gamma, linear maps and white balance
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Stored 8-bit sRGB codes are gamma-encoded; “linear” values are proportional to light. Code 128 is 21.6 % of white’s light, code 188 is 50.3 %.

Q1. An image is half black (0) and half white (255), in fine one-pixel stripes. You shrink it by averaging 2 × 2 blocks of the stored codes. What value do you get, and what should it be?






Hint





Average the light, not the codes.









Answer





Averaging codes gives 127.5, i.e. 128, which is only 21.6 % of white’s light. The light averages to 50 %, which is stored as code 188. The naive result is much too dark.




Q2. Why are images stored gamma-encoded at all, if every computation has to undo it?






Hint





Where does the eye need small steps?









Answer





Perceived lightness grows roughly like the cube root of light, so the eye notices small absolute changes in the darks and only large ones in the brights. Encoding spends the 256 codes evenly in perceived lightness: with linear codes the darks would show banding and many bright codes would be wasted.




Q3. Two neighbouring regions, pure red and pure green, are blurred on the stored codes. Why does a dark band appear between them?






Hint





What light does a code of 128 in one channel stand for?









Answer





At the border each channel is about half its code: (128, 128, 0) in codes, which is only about 22 % of full red light plus 22 % of full green light. Blurring the light gives (0.5, 0.5, 0) in light, i.e. codes (188, 188, 0): as bright as its surroundings. Averaging codes loses light wherever values are mixed.




Q4. What do the three columns of the sRGB → XYZ matrix mean, and what does its middle row mean?






Hint





Multiply the matrix by (1, 0, 0).









Answer





Column k is the XYZ of primary k at full drive (the matrix times a unit vector). The middle row gives Y, the luminance: 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B on linear values, the brightness contributed by each primary.




Q5. A picture of red letters on a green background becomes a blank grey image when converted to luminance. Is the conversion broken?






Hint





What does greyscale keep, and what does it throw away?









Answer





No. The letters and the background have the same luminance, and luminance is a projection of the 3D colour onto one direction: everything else (here the red–green difference) is discarded. Another projection (the channel mean, or the R channel alone) keeps the letters. Choose the greyscale direction that keeps the contrast you need.




Q6. JPEG stores Cb and Cr at half resolution in both directions. Why is that hardly visible, while halving the resolution of Y′ would be obvious?






Hint





Where is the detail of a natural image, and how does the eye see colour detail?









Answer





Edges and texture are mostly changes of brightness, carried by Y′. The visual system resolves fine detail in brightness but only coarse detail in colour differences, so losing three quarters of the chroma samples costs little that we can see. It halves the data (1.5 instead of 3 values per pixel).




Q7. Grey world on a forest scene turns the green leaves grey-magenta. Why?






Hint





What does grey world assume about the scene?









Answer





Grey world assumes the average colour of the scene is grey, and scales the channels until it is. A forest is mostly green, so its average is green; the correction removes green from everything, and the leaves (and any truly grey objects) end up magenta-tinted.




Q8. Why should the white-balance gains be applied to linear values rather than to the stored codes?






Hint





A lamp multiplies light. What does that do to codes?









Answer





The lamp multiplies the light in each channel by a factor, so the right correction is a multiplication of linear values. Codes are a non-linear function of light: multiplying a code by a factor does not multiply the light by a factor, and different brightnesses get different, wrong corrections (the midtones go off while the white comes out right).




Q9. (math) Show that the middle row of the matrix M = (\mathbf p_R\;\mathbf p_G\;\mathbf p_B)\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf s) equals \mathbf s, where each \mathbf p_k = (x_k/y_k, 1, (1 - x_k - y_k)/y_k).






Hint





What is the middle entry of each \mathbf p_k?









Answer





M_{2k} = (\mathbf p_k)_2\,s_k = 1 \cdot s_k. So the luminance weights of the primaries are exactly the scales found from the white point; for sRGB they are 0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
About this lecture
The last units read colour from images. Now the other direction: using colour to show data.

Pseudocolour and channel merges for fluorescence: a choice, not a fact.
Colour maps for a scalar image: sequential, diverging, qualitative. Lightness must change monotonically; the rainbow map invents edges.
Colour-blind viewers: a dichromat sees a projection of colour space; check figures with it.
Decorrelation stretch: PCA of the colour cloud brings out faint colour differences.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Every demo in the course uses the colour maps of this unit (viridis for sequential data, the blue–white–red map for signed data, the label palette for labels). Recall from the bit-depth day: window/level and lookup tables for high-bit data; the display range is part of the map.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: Displaying a grey image is already a choice
text:
Displaying a grey image is already a choice
Recall (the bit-depth day): a lookup table maps each data value to a screen colour, after a display range (window/level).

The display range sets which values are black and white; values outside are clipped. Never let a display setting silently clip data that you measure.
A colour map is a lookup table with colours instead of greys: data value → position t \in [0, 1] → colour.
The data do not change; only how they look. But how they look decides what people see in them.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Fluorescence: channels are grey images
A fluorescence image has one grey image per filter set (per dye). Colour is added for display:

Pseudocolour: each channel through its own ramp (black → green, black → magenta, …).
Merge: add the coloured channels. Where both are present the colours mix (green + magenta = white; red + green = yellow).
The colour of a channel says nothing about the dye’s emission colour unless you choose it to.
Red/green merges are invisible to about 8 % of men (red–green colour blindness): red, green and their mixture become similar yellows. Use magenta/green (or cyan/magenta/yellow) and also show the channels separately, in grey.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Colour maps for scalar data








data
map
example




sequential (low → high)
lightness increases steadily
viridis, cividis, magma, grey


diverging (signed, around a centre)
lightest (or neutral) at the centre, two hues outwards
blue–white–red


qualitative (labels, classes)
distinct hues, no order
the label palette




The eye reads lightness as “how much”. A good sequential map has monotone lightness and roughly equal visible steps.
A diverging map puts its centre at the meaningful value (zero), so the display range must be symmetric around it.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Lightness must be monotone




Jet (the classic rainbow) goes dark blue → bright cyan/yellow → dark red: its lightness rises to L^* = 97 at t = 0.62 and falls to 25.

Bands of fast lightness change look like edges that are not in the data; flat stretches hide real structure.
High values (dark red) look darker than middle values: the order is lost in greyscale or for colour-blind viewers.
Viridis and cividis rise steadily (from about 14 to 91).
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: The math: what makes a map perceptually uniform
text:
The math: what makes a map perceptually uniform
A colour map is a curve \mathbf c(t) in Lab, t \in [0, 1]. Perceived contrast between neighbouring data values is about
\Delta E \approx \left\|\frac{d\mathbf c}{dt}\right\| \Delta t .

Uniform: \|\mathbf c'(t)\| constant, so equal data steps give equal visible steps (arc length proportional to t).
Ordered: L^*(t) strictly monotone, so “more” always looks lighter (or always darker), also without hue.
Jet: L^{*\prime}(t) changes sign twice, and \|\mathbf c'\| varies strongly: false edges where it is large, flat zones where it is small. A map built by interpolating in Lab between anchors with increasing L^* (as the course’s maps are) is ordered by construction.

Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Try it: colour maps




A smooth synthetic height field (no edges at all), the colour bar and its lightness profile. Tour: “jet invents edges”: sharp-looking boundaries at the cyan and yellow bands; L* from 12.9 up to 96.8 at t = 0.62 and down to 25.4. “viridis is monotone”: the same field reads as smooth hills. “signed data needs a diverging map”: data in [−3, 7] with viridis gives no clue where zero is; choose “diverging” and set the range to −7…7: zero is white. “red/green merge for a deuteranope”: both channels become yellows; choose “magenta + green”.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Colour-blind viewers
About 8 % of men and 0.5 % of women have a red–green deficiency; most common is a weak or missing M (deutan) or L (protan) cone.

A dichromat has two cone types: two numbers per colour instead of three. Colours that differ only in the missing cone’s response look the same.
For a deuteranope, red and green both look like yellows of different lightness; for the rarer tritanope (no S cones) blue and green merge.
Check figures by simulating: the simulation is one 3 \times 3 matrix in linear RGB. Use maps whose order is carried by lightness (viridis, cividis) and magenta/green rather than red/green.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: The math: a dichromat is a projection
text:
The math: a dichromat is a projection
In LMS a deuteranope does not have M. Replace it by a combination of the other two that keeps two anchor colours unchanged (white, and blue), i.e. M' = aL + bS with a, b from two equations:
D = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ a & 0 & b \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{in linear RGB: } S_\text{deutan} = T^{-1} D\, T,
with T = linear RGB → LMS.

D has rank 2 and D^2 = D: a projection onto a plane. Its null space is the direction (0, 1, 0) in LMS: changes of M alone are invisible.
Two colours look the same to the dichromat iff their difference lies in that null space, as in the metamers of the first unit.
(Brettel, Viénot and Mollon used two half-planes instead of one plane; a single matrix is the common simplification.)
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Decorrelation stretch
Recall PCA (day 1): the principal axes of a point cloud are the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix.

In most images R, G and B are strongly correlated: the colour cloud is a cigar along the grey axis. Brightness varies a lot, colour little.
Decorrelation stretch: rotate the cloud to its principal axes, equalise the variances, rotate back. The thin directions (colour differences) are stretched, the long one (brightness) compressed.
Faint colour differences become visible: faded stains, rock art, remote sensing. Colours become false; the stretch is for seeing, not for measuring.
PC1 alone is a data-driven greyscale: the direction in which this image varies most.
crumbs: Part II: From pixels to objects
Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
The math: decorrelation stretch
Colour vectors \mathbf x_i (encoded RGB), mean \boldsymbol\mu, covariance S = U\Lambda U^\top with eigenvalues \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \lambda_3.
\mathbf x_i' = \boldsymbol\mu + U\,\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\frac{\bar\sigma}{\sqrt{\lambda_k}}\right)U^\top(\mathbf x_i - \boldsymbol\mu), \qquad \bar\sigma^2 = \tfrac13(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3).

The new covariance is U\operatorname{diag}(\bar\sigma^2/\lambda_k)\Lambda U^\top = \bar\sigma^2 I: uncorrelated channels with equal variance, and the same total variance \operatorname{tr} S.
A tiny \lambda_3 means a huge gain \bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_3}: noise along that axis is amplified as much. Values outside [0, 1] are clipped.
A fraction t \in [0, 1] of the stretch uses factors (\bar\sigma/\sqrt{\lambda_k})^t.

Try it: PCA of the colour cloud




The pixels of the synthetic H&E image in the sRGB cube, with the principal axes (±2 standard deviations; orange PC1, purple PC2, green PC3). Readout: σ along the axes 0.190, 0.070, 0.002; PC1 has 88.0 % of the variance; correlations R–G 0.74, R–B 0.99, G–B 0.84. The cloud is a flat sheet (two stains). Move “stretch” to 1: the sheet swells, the image gets garish but nuclei and stroma separate in colour; 14 % of the pixels are clipped. Then “objects”: a cigar along grey (PC1 (0.55, 0.64, 0.54), 77.2 %).

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
section: A checklist for colour in figures
text:
A checklist for colour in figures

Sequential data: a map with monotone lightness (viridis, cividis, magma); never jet for quantities.
Signed data: a diverging map, centred on zero with a symmetric range.
Labels: a qualitative palette; neighbouring labels must differ.
Merges: magenta/green (not red/green), plus the single channels in grey.
Always show a colour bar with the display range, and say if anything is clipped.
Check the figure in greyscale and with a dichromat simulation.

title: Colour for display: colour maps, merges and decorrelation
text:
Summary

Showing data in colour is a lookup table: display range + map. It changes what viewers see, not the data.
Sequential maps need monotone lightness; the rainbow map invents edges and loses the order. Diverging maps need a centred, symmetric range; qualitative palettes are for labels.
A dichromat sees a rank-2 projection of colour; simulate it to check figures; avoid red/green merges.
Decorrelation stretch = PCA of the colour cloud, variances equalised: faint colour differences become visible (false colours, for looking only).

title: Quiz: feature spaces and k-means
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. k-means: assign every point to its nearest centre, move every centre to the mean of its points, repeat; J = \sum_i \lVert\mathbf x_i - \mathbf m_{c(i)}\rVert^2.

Q1. You segment a colour photograph by k-means on the pixels’ (R, G, B) values. What is a “point”, and what is a “cluster” here?






Hint





How many numbers describe one pixel?









Answer





Every pixel is a point in a 3D space with axes R, G and B; its position in the image plays no role. A cluster is a group of pixels with similar colours, wherever they are in the image. Mapping each pixel’s cluster back to its position gives the segmentation.




Q2. Points 0, 2, 3, 9, centres m = (1, 8). Do one assign step and one update step. What is J before and after the update?






Hint





3 is nearer to 1 than to 8.









Answer





Assign: \{0, 2, 3\} to 1, \{9\} to 8. J = 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 7. Update: m = (5/3, 9) = (1.67, 9). Now J = 2.78 + 0.11 + 1.78 + 0 = 4.67. Assigning again changes nothing: converged.




Q3. Why can k-means never run forever?






Hint





What happens to J in each step, and how many different assignments are there?









Answer





Neither step can increase J: each point picks the nearest centre, and the mean is the best centre for a fixed group. There are only finitely many ways to assign n points to K groups. If an iteration changes the assignment, it strictly lowers J, so no assignment can come back; after finitely many changes nothing changes any more and the algorithm stops.




Q4. k-means stopped with J = 26 on a data set where you know a solution with J = 1.5 exists. How can that happen, and what do you do?






Hint





“Stops” means “no single step helps”.









Answer





It stopped in a local minimum: for example two centres share one group while one centre covers two groups; no assign or update step can move a centre across the empty gap. Run again from other starts (preferably k-means++) and keep the run with the lowest J.




Q5. k-means++ has chosen its first centre. Point A is at distance 1 from it, point B at distance 4. How much more likely is B than A to become the second centre?






Hint





The probability is proportional to the squared distance.









Answer





4^2 / 1^2 = 16 times more likely. Squaring makes far-away points strongly preferred, so the seeds spread over the data.




Q6. Two long, parallel, cigar-shaped groups lie side by side. Sketch what k-means with K = 2 does, and explain why.






Hint





Compare J for “cut across both cigars” and “one cigar each”.









Answer





It tends to cut across the cigars: one centre near each end, with a straight boundary through the middle of both. Splitting a long group in half reduces the squared distances along its length a lot, more than separating two parallel groups that are close together. k-means only knows round groups; the boundary is always a perpendicular bisector between two centres.




Q7. You cluster nuclei by (area in µm², mean intensity in [0, 1]). The clusters follow the area only. Why, and what should you do?






Hint





How large are typical differences in each feature?









Answer





Areas differ by tens or hundreds of µm², intensities by a few hundredths. Squared distances are then entirely area differences, so k-means ignores intensity. Rescale the features first (for example divide each by its standard deviation), or choose units in which a “meaningful” difference has a similar size.




Q8. Your colleague picks the K that gives the smallest J. What goes wrong?






Hint





What is J with one centre per point?









Answer





The best J always decreases as K grows, down to J = 0 at K = n (every point its own centre). The smallest J always asks for the largest K. One needs a trade-off between fit and complexity: an elbow in the J-versus-K curve, or a criterion such as BIC once there is a probability model (unit 3).




Q9. (math) Show that the boundary between the cells of two centres is a straight line (in 2D).






Hint





Expand \lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf x - \mathbf m_2\rVert^2.









Answer





Expanding, \lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 - 2\mathbf x^\top\mathbf m_1 + \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2 = \lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 - 2\mathbf x^\top\mathbf m_2 + \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2. The \lVert\mathbf x\rVert^2 terms cancel: 2\mathbf x^\top(\mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1) = \lVert\mathbf m_2\rVert^2 - \lVert\mathbf m_1\rVert^2, a linear equation in \mathbf x: a line perpendicular to \mathbf m_2 - \mathbf m_1. The midpoint (\mathbf m_1 + \mathbf m_2)/2 satisfies it.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
About this lecture
The LoG of the last unit adds up the curvature in two directions. Today we keep the two curvatures apart: the second-derivative test from calculus, applied at every pixel.

The Hessian: a symmetric 2 × 2 matrix of second derivatives per pixel, at scale σ.
Its eigenvalues are the curvatures along two perpendicular directions; its eigenvectors are those directions.
Classification: bright or dark blob, ridge (line), saddle, flat.
Trace (the LoG) and determinant.
Vesselness (Frangi): a score for line-like structures, over several scales.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
The image as a landscape
Read the (smoothed) image as a height map: bright = high.


A bright spot is a hilltop: it bends down in every direction.
A bright line is a ridge: it bends down across the line, and not at all along it.
Two bright spots with two dark gaps between them make a pass (saddle): down one way, up the other.
A plain is flat. The question at each pixel: how does the surface bend, and in which directions?

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
The Hessian at every pixel
Three second derivatives of the Gaussian-smoothed image L at scale σ (separable kernels, as in the Canny unit):
H = \begin{pmatrix} L_{xx} & L_{xy} \\ L_{xy} & L_{yy} \end{pmatrix}


L_{xx}: curvature along x; L_{yy}: along y (down); L_{xy}: how the x-slope changes going down (the “twist”).
H is symmetric, so (recall the PCA unit) it has two real eigenvalues and two perpendicular eigenvectors.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Eigenvalues are curvatures

The curvature in a direction \mathbf u is a number that depends on \mathbf u. The eigenvectors of H are the directions of the largest and smallest curvature; the eigenvalues are those curvatures.
We order them by size: |\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2|. So \lambda_2 is the strongest bending, \lambda_1 the weakest, in the perpendicular direction.
Negative eigenvalue: the brightness bends down (a bright structure). Positive: bends up (a dark structure).

Example: f = -x^2 (a bright ridge along y). H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = 0 with eigenvector (0, 1), along the ridge; \lambda_2 = -2 with eigenvector (1, 0), across it.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
section: The math: curvature in a direction
text:
The math: curvature in a direction
Second-order Taylor expansion around a pixel \mathbf x:
L(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) \approx L(\mathbf x) + \nabla L^\top\mathbf h + \tfrac12\,\mathbf h^\top H\,\mathbf h.

Along a unit vector \mathbf u the second derivative (curvature of the profile) is \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u.
Maximise or minimise \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u subject to \mathbf u^\top\mathbf u = 1: Lagrange gives H\mathbf u = \lambda\mathbf u, and then \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u = \lambda (a Rayleigh quotient, the same algebra as PCA).
So the extreme curvatures are the eigenvalues, along the eigenvectors. At a critical point (\nabla L = 0) this is the second-derivative test: both negative = maximum, both positive = minimum, opposite signs = saddle.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
section: The math: eigenvalues in closed form
text:
The math: eigenvalues in closed form
For a symmetric \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix} (here a = L_{xx}, b = L_{xy}, c = L_{yy}):
\lambda_{\pm} = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\Big(\frac{a - c}{2}\Big)^2 + b^2}, \qquad \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2b,\; a - c)
where θ is the angle of the eigenvector of \lambda_+ (in image coordinates, y down).

Two numbers do not depend on how the image is rotated: the trace a + c = \lambda_+ + \lambda_- and the determinant ac - b^2 = \lambda_+\lambda_-.
Example: \begin{pmatrix} -8 & 4 \\ 4 & -8 \end{pmatrix}: \lambda = -8 \pm 4, i.e. -4 and -12; θ = ½·atan2(8, 0) = 45°: the eigenvector of -4 (the weak curvature) is (1, 1)/\sqrt2, along the diagonal.

section: Try it: the Hessian per pixel
text:
Try it: the Hessian per pixel




Left: the image (tabs: classes, λ1, λ2, trace, determinant, vesselness, best σ), with the glyph at the clicked pixel: two axes along the eigenvectors, length ∝ |λ|, red = negative curvature. Middle: the (λ1, λ2) plane with the class regions and a scatter of the pixels. Tour: “hilltop”: f = −(x² + y²), H = [−2 0; 0 −2] (the quadratic presets show H in the units of f). Drag c to 0: “ridge”, H = [−2 0; 0 0], the glyph is a single red bar across the ridge. Set c = +1: saddle (red across, blue along). Set a = c = −1, b = −2: f = −(x + y)², H = [−2 −2; −2 −2], λ = 0 and −4, a diagonal ridge. “An edge is not a ridge”: test scene, σ = 3, on the step at x = 25: flat on the edge itself (λ2 = −3.87, below the threshold 4), a bright ridge just inside (−10.76 at x = 26), a dark ridge just outside (+4.25 at x = 24). “The LoG cannot tell…”: trace tab: the blob and the thin line are both strongly negative (−31.3 and −28.8 at σ = 3); determinant tab: 245 for the blob, 2.7 for the line.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Trace and determinant
Two numbers per pixel that do not depend on the orientation:

Trace \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = L_{xx} + L_{yy}: the LoG of the last unit. A blob with λ = (−10, −10) and a ridge with λ = (0, −20) both have trace −20: the LoG cannot tell a blob from a line.
Determinant \lambda_1\lambda_2: 100 for the blob, 0 for the ridge. Large only when both curvatures are large: the “determinant of Hessian” blob detector.
Pointer: the integral-image elective computes the determinant of Hessian with box filters for speed (as in the SURF keypoint detector).

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Vesselness: a score for lines
Frangi et al. (1998): a number between 0 and 1 that is large on bright lines (vessels, filaments, membranes) and small elsewhere.

Reward: \lambda_2 strongly negative, i.e. a strong structure is present.
Penalise: |\lambda_1/\lambda_2| large, i.e. a blob, not a line.
Two knobs: β sets how strictly blobs are rejected; c sets what counts as “strong” (above the noise).
Example (β = 0.5, c = 15): a line with λ = (0, −20) scores 0.59; a blob with λ = (−10, −10) only 0.05.
Dark lines: flip the sign test.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
The math: Frangi’s vesselness (2D)
With |\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2| (for bright lines):
\mathcal V = \begin{cases} 0 & \lambda_2 > 0 \\[2pt] \exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{R_B^2}{2\beta^2}\Big)\Big(1 - \exp\!\Big(-\dfrac{S^2}{2c^2}\Big)\Big) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\qquad R_B = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2},\quad S = \sqrt{\lambda_1^2 + \lambda_2^2}.

R_B is 0 for a perfect line and 1 for a round blob; the first factor is the “blobness” penalty.
S (the Frobenius norm of H) is small in flat, noisy regions; the second factor is the “structureness” reward.
Example: H = \begin{pmatrix} -20 & 2 \\ 2 & -3 \end{pmatrix}: \lambda = -2.77, -20.23, R_B = 0.137, S = 20.42; \mathcal V = 0.963 \cdot 0.604 = 0.58.
In 3D (one line): a 3 × 3 Hessian with three eigenvalues; blob (all three large), tube (two large), sheet (one large).

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
section: Multi-scale: one σ is not enough
text:
Multi-scale: one σ is not enough

A line responds best when σ matches its width: a thin filament at small σ, a thick vessel at large σ.
Compute the Hessian at several σ, normalise by σ² (as in the scale-space unit, so the scales are comparable), take the maximum vesselness over σ.
The winning σ grows with the line width (for a line with a Gaussian profile of width s, \sigma^2\lambda_2 peaks at \sigma = \sqrt2\,s; exercise).
Failure: at junctions two lines cross, both curvatures are large, and the junction looks like a blob: vesselness fades exactly where branches meet.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Try it: vesselness over scales




Test scene at σ = 3: the blob at (28, 28) scores 0.10, the thin line 0.84, the thick line 0.40, the dark line 0 (bright mode). “One σ misses the thick line”: σ = 1.5, the thick line (Gaussian width 4.5) scores only 0.06. “Multi-scale” (σ = 1 … 8, 8 levels): the thick line reaches 0.70 at σ = 5.94, the thin line 0.87 at σ = 2.44; the “best σ” tab colours each line by its scale. “Membranes in the micrograph”: dark lines, σ = 2, c = 20: the nuclear envelope scores up to 0.97 at (94, 126); the texture also responds.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Ridges in practice

Microscopy: membranes, filaments (microtubules, actin), neurites, vessels.
Medical images: blood vessels in retinal photographs and angiograms (Frangi’s original use).
Other: roads in aerial images, cracks, the ridges of fingerprints.
Vessel and neuron networks (skeletonising them, measuring branches, junctions) are the subject of the skeleton elective; it builds on this unit.

title: The Hessian: blobs, ridges and saddles
text:
Summary

Hessian = the 2 × 2 matrix of second derivatives of the smoothed image, at every pixel.
Its eigenvalues are the extreme curvatures, its eigenvectors their (perpendicular) directions; order |\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2|.
Both negative: bright blob; \lambda_2 \ll 0, \lambda_1 \approx 0: bright ridge (along \lambda_1’s eigenvector); opposite signs: saddle; both ≈ 0: flat. Edges: weak half-ridges.
Trace = LoG (blob or ridge, cannot tell); determinant: blobs only.
Vesselness: rewards strong \lambda_2, penalises blob-like |\lambda_1/\lambda_2|; take the maximum over σ (normalised by σ²).

title: Quiz: the Hessian
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Eigenvalues are ordered |\lambda_1| \le |\lambda_2|; bright = high.

Q1. What do the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the Hessian at a pixel tell you, in words?






Hint





Think of the image as a landscape.









Answer





The eigenvalues are the strongest and weakest curvature (bending) of the brightness surface at that pixel; the eigenvectors are the two perpendicular directions in which they occur. Negative means bending down (a bright structure), positive bending up (a dark one).




Q2. At a pixel \lambda_1 = -0.5 and \lambda_2 = -12. What structure is this? In which direction does it run?






Hint





One strong curvature, one weak.









Answer





A bright ridge (line): it bends down strongly across one direction (\lambda_2) and hardly at all along the other. It runs along the eigenvector of \lambda_1.




Q3. Classify: (a) \lambda = (-8, -10); (b) \lambda = (6, -9); (c) \lambda = (0.2, 11); (d) \lambda = (0.1, -0.3) when the noise gives |λ| up to about 1.






Hint





Signs, and the ratio of the sizes.









Answer






Bright blob (both strongly negative, similar size). (b) Saddle (opposite signs, both large). (c) Dark ridge (one strong positive curvature, the other ≈ 0). (d) Flat (both within the noise).





Q4. Why can the Laplacian of Gaussian not tell a blob from a line, while the determinant of the Hessian can?






Hint





Trace and determinant in terms of the eigenvalues.









Answer





The LoG is the trace \lambda_1 + \lambda_2. A blob with λ = (−10, −10) and a line with λ = (0, −20) both give −20. The determinant \lambda_1\lambda_2 is 100 for the blob and 0 for the line: it is large only when both curvatures are large.




Q5. What does the Hessian report at a step edge?






Hint





Where is the second derivative across a step zero?









Answer





On the edge itself the curvature across it is zero (it is the zero crossing of the second derivative), so the pixel looks flat. Just inside the bright side the brightness bends down (a weak bright half-ridge), just outside it bends up (a weak dark half-ridge). The Hessian finds the centres of lines and blobs; edges are the gradient’s job.




Q6. Vesselness has two knobs, β and c. What happens if you make β very large? If you make c very large?






Hint





Look at which ratio each one divides.









Answer





β divides the blob ratio R_B = \lambda_1/\lambda_2: with a large β the blob penalty disappears and blobs score as high as lines. c divides the structure strength S: with a large c almost every structure counts as “weak”, so all vesselness values become small (only the strongest lines remain visible).




Q7. Why is vesselness computed at several σ and normalised by σ²? What fails at a junction of two vessels?






Hint





Which σ fits a thin line, and which a thick one?









Answer





Each line responds best at a σ matched to its width; a single σ misses thick lines (or broadens thin ones). Normalising by σ² makes the responses at different σ comparable, so the maximum over σ picks each line’s own scale. At a junction two lines cross: both curvatures are large, the pixel looks like a blob, and vesselness drops exactly where branches meet.




Q8. (math) Show that the curvature \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u along a unit vector \mathbf u is largest and smallest along the eigenvectors of H.






Hint





Write \mathbf u in the eigenvector basis.









Answer





H is symmetric, so it has orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2. Write \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2. Then \mathbf u^\top H\mathbf u = \lambda_1\cos^2\phi + \lambda_2\sin^2\phi, a weighted average of the two eigenvalues with weights summing to 1. It lies between them and reaches them exactly at \phi = 0 and \phi = 90°, i.e. along the eigenvectors.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Hessian
H = \begin{pmatrix} L_{xx} & L_{xy} \\ L_{xy} & L_{yy}\end{pmatrix} of the image smoothed at scale σ; x right, y down


Eigenvalues
the extreme curvatures, ordered \lvert\lambda_1\rvert \le \lvert\lambda_2\rvert; eigenvectors = their directions (perpendicular)


Closed form
\lambda = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2} for \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix}


Classes
(\lambda_1, \lambda_2) both ≪ 0: bright blob; \lambda_2 \ll 0, \lambda_1 \approx 0: bright ridge; opposite signs: saddle; both ≈ 0: flat; dark = signs flipped


Trace, determinant
\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 (= LoG), \lambda_1\lambda_2


Vesselness
\mathcal V = e^{-R_B^2/2\beta^2}\big(1 - e^{-S^2/2c^2}\big) if \lambda_2 < 0 (else 0), R_B = \lambda_1/\lambda_2, S = \sqrt{\lambda_1^2 + \lambda_2^2}


Second differences
L_{xx} \approx [1\;-2\;1] along a row, L_{yy} along a column, L_{xy} \approx \tfrac14\big[f(1,1) - f(1,-1) - f(-1,1) + f(-1,-1)\big]

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
By hand
B1. For each brightness pattern write the Hessian, its eigenvalues (ordered by size) with eigenvectors, and the class. Sketch the pattern as an image (bright = high). (a) f = -x^2; (b) f = -(x^2 + y^2); (c) f = x^2 - y^2; (d) f = -(x + y)^2.
B2. A 3 × 3 patch of a smoothed image (rows y = -1, 0, 1 from top to bottom, columns x = -1, 0, 1):

Estimate L_{xx}, L_{yy} and L_{xy} at the centre. (b) Find the eigenvalues and the eigenvector of the weaker one. (c) Classify the pixel. In which direction does the structure run? Does that match the picture?

B3. Trace, determinant and vesselness (β = 0.5, c = 15) for (a) λ = (−10, −10); (b) λ = (0, −20); (c) λ = (−2, −20). Which of the three numbers separates the line from the blob best?
B4. A bright disc of radius 10 (brightness 100 on 0). Predict the class (and the sign of the eigenvalues) at σ = 2: at the centre, 8 pixels from the centre (just inside the rim), 12 pixels from the centre (just outside) and 20 pixels from the centre. Then at σ = 7. Explain the difference.
B5. A Hessian at a pixel is \begin{pmatrix} -20 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{pmatrix}. Compute the eigenvalues, the class, and the vesselness for β = 0.5, c = 15. What happens to the vesselness if β = 0.1? If c = 50?






Solutions





B1. (a) H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = 0, eigenvector (0, 1) (along y); \lambda_2 = -2, eigenvector (1, 0). A bright ridge running vertically (along y). (b) H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = -2, every direction is an eigenvector. A bright blob (hilltop). (c) H = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda = 2 (eigenvector (1, 0)) and -2 (eigenvector (0, 1)), equal in size; a saddle: brightness rises left and right, falls up and down. (d) f = -(x^2 + 2xy + y^2), H = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2\end{pmatrix}: \lambda_1 = 0 with eigenvector (1, -1)/\sqrt2, \lambda_2 = -4 with eigenvector (1, 1)/\sqrt2. A bright ridge along the line x + y = 0; with y down, (1, -1) points up and to the right on the screen.
B2. (a) L_{xx} = 5 - 18 + 5 = -8; L_{yy} = 5 - 18 + 5 = -8; L_{xy} = \tfrac14(9 - 1 - 1 + 9) = 4. (b) \lambda = -8 \pm 4: \lambda_1 = -4, \lambda_2 = -12. The eigenvector of -4: \begin{pmatrix} -8 & 4 \\ 4 & -8\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} = -4\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}, so (1, 1)/\sqrt2. (c) |\lambda_1/\lambda_2| = 1/3: one curvature three times the other, both negative: a bright ridge (with this ratio threshold of ½), running along (1, 1), i.e. from top left to bottom right. The patch indeed has its bright values (9) on that diagonal.
B3.
