The trace cannot separate them at all; the determinant can, but it ranks the slightly curved line (c) between; vesselness separates lines (≈ 0.6) from the blob (0.05) clearly.
B4. At σ = 2 (much smaller than the disc): centre flat (λ ≈ 0: the inside of the disc is flat at this scale); 8 px: bright ridge (λ = −5.2, −22.9: the brightness starts to fall towards the rim); 12 px: dark ridge (λ = −3.4, +23.0: it bends up as it reaches the dark floor); 20 px: flat. The rim shows up as two parallel half-ridges, not as a blob. At σ = 7 (≈ r/√2): centre bright blob (λ = −36.9, −36.9); 8 px: bright ridge (−8.0, −26.3); 12 px: saddle (11.9, −16.5); 20 px: dark ridge (−3.1, +14.5). Only when σ matches the disc’s size is the disc seen as one blob.
B5. \lambda = \frac{-23}{2} \pm \sqrt{8.5^2 + 4} = -11.5 \pm 8.73: \lambda_1 = -2.77, \lambda_2 = -20.23. Ratio 0.14: a bright ridge. R_B = 0.137, S = 20.42: \mathcal V = e^{-0.137^2/0.5} \cdot (1 - e^{-20.42^2/450}) = 0.963 \cdot 0.604 = 0.58. With β = 0.1 the blob penalty becomes strict: e^{-0.137^2/0.02} = 0.39, \mathcal V = 0.24. With c = 50 the structure counts as weak: 1 - e^{-20.42^2/5000} = 0.080, \mathcal V = 0.08.




Math questions
B6. (math) Derive the closed-form eigenvalues of \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix} from the characteristic polynomial, and show that they are always real. When are they equal?
B7. (math) Show that trace and determinant of the Hessian do not change when the image is rotated. (Hint: rotating the image by R turns H into R^\top H R.)
B8. (math) A bright line with a Gaussian profile of width s: I(x, y) = A\,e^{-x^2/2s^2}. (a) Show that after smoothing with G_\sigma, L(x) = \frac{As}{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}}e^{-x^2/2(s^2 + \sigma^2)}. (b) Compute \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) and find the σ where its size is largest. (c) What does this mean for reading the width of a vessel from the best scale?






Solutions (math)





B6. \det\begin{pmatrix} a - \lambda & b \\ b & c - \lambda\end{pmatrix} = \lambda^2 - (a + c)\lambda + (ac - b^2) = 0, so \lambda = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\frac{(a + c)^2}{4} - ac + b^2} = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2}. The square root is of a sum of squares, so it is real. The eigenvalues are equal only if a = c and b = 0, i.e. H is a multiple of the identity (a perfectly round blob or a flat pixel).
B7. If L'(\mathbf x) = L(R\mathbf x), the chain rule gives H' = R^\top H R. Then \operatorname{tr}(R^\top H R) = \operatorname{tr}(H R R^\top) = \operatorname{tr}H (cyclic property, RR^\top = I), and \det(R^\top H R) = \det R^\top \det H \det R = \det H. Equivalently, H' has the same eigenvalues as H; only the eigenvectors rotate.
B8. (a) In x the profile is A\sqrt{2\pi}\,s\,g_s(x); convolving with g_\sigma gives A\sqrt{2\pi}\,s\,g_{\sqrt{s^2 + \sigma^2}}(x) (semigroup), which is the stated expression. (b) With v = s^2 + \sigma^2: L_{xx}(0) = -\frac{As}{\sqrt v}\cdot\frac1v, so \sigma^2 L_{xx}(0) = -As\,\frac{\sigma^2}{v^{3/2}}. Setting the derivative with respect to \sigma^2 to zero: v^{-3/2} - \tfrac32\sigma^2 v^{-5/2} = 0 \Rightarrow v = \tfrac32\sigma^2 \Rightarrow \sigma^2 = 2s^2, \sigma = \sqrt2\,s. (c) The best scale is proportional to the width, so multi-scale vesselness measures vessel width: width s \approx \sigma_\text{best}/\sqrt2 for this normalisation. (Other normalisations, \sigma^{2\gamma} with \gamma = 3/4, make the best scale equal s; the factor depends on the convention, the proportionality does not.)

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Explore: the Hessian per pixel
Images: an editable quadratic f = ax^2 + bxy + cy^2 (with contours; its Hessian is shown in the units of f), a test scene (a bright blob, a thin and a thick bright line, a dark line, a saddle of two bright and two dark spots, a step edge at the bottom left; noise 3), curved lines, or the micrograph (256 × 256). Tabs show the class map, λ1, λ2, trace, determinant, vesselness and the best scale. Click a pixel: the glyph shows the eigenvector axes (length ∝ |λ|, red = negative curvature), the readout the matrix, the eigenvalues and the verdict; its point is circled in the (λ1, λ2) plane.



E1. Presets hilltop, ridge, saddle: check your answers to B1(a)–(c) in the readout. Then set a = c = -1, b = -2 for B1(d). Where does the glyph point, and what does the image look like?
E2. Preset an edge is not a ridge (test scene, σ = 3). Click on the step at (25, 114), then one pixel to the left and one and three pixels to the right. Read λ1, λ2 and the class each time. Compare the size of λ2 with that of the thin line at (86, 27).
E3. Preset LoG cannot tell blob from ridge; det can. Compare the trace and then the determinant at the blob (28, 28) and on the thin line (86, 27). Look at the whole trace and determinant images: which structures light up in each?
E4. Preset vesselness: blob suppressed (σ = 3). Read the vesselness at the blob, the thin line and the thick line (30, 70). Untick bright lines: what lights up now? Change β and c and describe their effect.
E5. Preset one σ misses the thick line (σ = 1.5), then multi-scale. Compare the vesselness of the thick line in both. Which σ wins for the thin and for the thick line (best σ tab)? Compare with B8.
E6. Image curved lines, multi-scale, vesselness tab. Where does the vesselness drop along the lines? Why?
E7. Preset membranes in the micrograph (dark lines, σ = 2, c = 20). Which structures get high vesselness? Click on the nuclear envelope at (94, 126). What else responds, and how could you reduce it?






Solutions





E1. Hilltop: H = [−2 0; 0 −2], λ = (−2, −2), bright blob. Ridge: H = [−2 0; 0 0], λ = (0, −2), bright ridge; the glyph is one red bar across the ridge (the λ1 axis has length 0). Saddle: H = [2 0; 0 −2], λ = (2, −2), a blue and a red bar of equal length. With a = c = -1, b = -2: H = [−2 −2; −2 −2], λ = (0, −4), a bright ridge running from lower left to upper right; the red bar points across it, along (1, 1).
E2. At σ = 3: on the step (25, 114) λ = (−0.15, −3.87): flat (|λ2| below the threshold 4). One pixel left (24, 114): λ = (−0.02, +4.25): a weak dark ridge. One pixel right (26, 114): (−0.27, −10.76), three right (28, 114): (−0.39, −14.52): a bright ridge. The edge appears as a weak dark half-ridge outside, a bright half-ridge inside and nothing on the edge; λ2 there (−14.5) is half that of the thin line (−28.65), although the edge has the same contrast class.
E3. Trace: −31.3 (blob), −28.8 (thin line): almost the same. Determinant: 245 (blob), 2.7 (line). In the trace image all bright structures (blob, lines, the bright side of the edge) are dark (negative) and all dark structures bright; in the determinant image only the blob and the saddle’s spots stand out (the saddle centre itself is strongly negative, −96).
E4. Blob 0.10, thin line 0.84, thick line 0.40. With dark lines selected, the dark line lights up and the bright structures vanish; the dark side of the edge and the dark spots of the saddle respond a little. Larger β lets blobs through (the blob brightens); smaller β darkens everything that is not perfectly line-like. Larger c darkens weak structures first; smaller c brings up the noise.
E5. At σ = 1.5 the thick line scores only 0.06 (the kernel sees the flat top of the line); at σ = 3, 0.40; multi-scale (σ = 1 … 8) gives 0.70, won at σ = 5.94. The thin line wins at σ = 2.44 (0.87). The thick line has width 4.5 and the thin one 1.5: √2 × 4.5 = 6.4 and √2 × 1.5 = 2.1, both close to the winning σ on the 8-level grid, as B8 predicts.
E6. Vesselness drops where two lines cross or meet: there both curvatures are large, R_B approaches 1 and the blob penalty switches the response off. It also drops at line ends, and where a thin line passes near a thick one (they blend at the larger scale).
E7. The nuclear envelope and the membranes and fibres of the cytoplasm, which are dark thin lines; at (94, 126) the vesselness is 0.97. The dense granular texture inside the nucleus and the fibrous background also respond at σ = 2. A larger σ (or the multi-scale maximum with σ ≥ 2) and a larger c suppress the fine texture; but the Hessian alone cannot know which dark lines are “membranes”: that needs a classifier (random-forest day) or a model of the shape.

title: Exercise: the Hessian
text:
Where this leads
The Hessian measures second derivatives and finds the centres of blobs and lines. The next unit uses first derivatives, squared and averaged over a window: the structure tensor, which measures orientation and finds corners.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
About this lecture
Fibres, wood grain, fingerprints, muscle, collagen: what is the dominant orientation in a small window, and how sure are we? And where are the corners?

Averaging gradients fails; averaging \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top works.
The structure tensor J: a 2 × 2 matrix per pixel, with two scales σ and ρ.
J is the covariance matrix of the gradients in the window (recall PCA).
Its eigenvalues give orientation, coherence, and edge / corner / flat.
Corners (Harris) as interest points.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The question: orientation in a window
text:
The question: orientation in a window

At one pixel the gradient points across the local edge. But in a textured region, we want one orientation for a whole window, and a measure of how well defined it is.
Uses: fibre orientation maps (collagen, muscle, cytoskeleton), fingerprint ridge flow, wood grain, flow-like textures; also “is there an edge, a corner, or nothing here?”
First idea: average the gradient vectors in the window.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: First try: average the gradients. It fails.
text:
First try: average the gradients. It fails.


On a bright line the gradients on the two sides point in opposite directions (towards the line from both sides) and cancel: the average is ≈ 0, although the orientation is perfectly clear.
Same on stripes: every bright stripe has two sides.
Fix: average something that does not care about the sign. The outer product \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top is the same for \mathbf g and -\mathbf g: a direction counted as an axis, not an arrow.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
The structure tensor
J = G_\rho * \begin{pmatrix} L_x^2 & L_xL_y \\ L_xL_y & L_y^2 \end{pmatrix}

Two scales: the gradient is taken at scale σ (against noise, as in Canny); the products are averaged with a Gaussian window of width ρ (how large a region we summarise).
Every entry is an average of products of gradients: symmetric, 2 × 2, at every pixel.
It is the covariance matrix of the gradient vectors in the window (without subtracting the mean, which is the point): plot the window’s gradients as a point cloud, and J is its ellipse. The same picture as in the PCA unit.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: Reading J: three kinds of clouds
text:
Reading J: three kinds of clouds


Edge (or oriented texture): gradients all along one axis: a long thin cloud, one large eigenvalue \mu_1, \mu_2 \approx 0.
Corner: gradients in two directions in the same window: a round, large cloud, two large eigenvalues.
Flat: tiny cloud, both eigenvalues ≈ 0.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Orientation and coherence
With eigenvalues \mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0:

The eigenvector of \mu_1 is the dominant gradient direction, across the stripes. The structure’s orientation is perpendicular to it.
Coherence \Big(\dfrac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2}\Big)^2: 1 = perfectly oriented, 0 = no preferred direction (isotropic texture, or a corner).
Energy \mu_1 + \mu_2: how much is going on at all.
Display: hue = orientation, saturation = coherence, brightness = energy.

Example: J = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}: \mu = 3.5 \pm 2.5, i.e. 6 and 1; coherence (5/7)^2 = 0.51.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The math: why the outer product works
text:
The math: why the outer product works
The squared slope in a direction \mathbf u (unit vector) is
(
abla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^	op
abla L\,
abla L^	op\mathbf u, \qquad	ext{averaged over the window: } E(\mathbf u) = \mathbf u^	op J\,\mathbf u.

E(\mathbf u) is the energy of change in direction \mathbf u. Maximise over unit \mathbf u: J\mathbf u = \mu\mathbf u (Rayleigh quotient, the same algebra as PCA’s largest variance direction). The maximum \mu_1 is along the first eigenvector, the minimum \mu_2 along the second.
(
abla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 is the same for 
abla L and -
abla L: opposite gradients add instead of cancelling.
Without the window (ρ = 0), J = 
abla L\,
abla L^	op has rank 1: \mu_2 = 0 at every pixel. Every pixel is an “edge”; only the window can see two directions at once.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
The math: the doubled angle
Write the gradient as \nabla L = r(\cos\phi, \sin\phi). Then
J_{xx} - J_{yy} = \langle r^2(\cos^2\phi - \sin^2\phi)\rangle = \langle r^2\cos2\phi\rangle, \qquad 2J_{xy} = \langle r^2\,2\sin\phi\cos\phi\rangle = \langle r^2\sin2\phi\rangle.

So J averages the vectors r^2(\cos2\phi, \sin2\phi): the doubled angle. Opposite gradients (\phi and \phi + 180°) have the same doubled angle and add up.
The dominant gradient direction: \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2J_{xy},\, J_{xx} - J_{yy}) (image coordinates, y down); the orientation of the structure is \theta + 90°.
Coherence: \dfrac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2} = \dfrac{\sqrt{(J_{xx} - J_{yy})^2 + 4J_{xy}^2}}{J_{xx} + J_{yy}}, the length of the averaged doubled-angle vector relative to the average r^2.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Try it: the structure tensor




Left: the image with one ellipse of J per 16-pixel cell (tabs: orientation map, Harris corners). Middle: the window around the clicked pixel with its gradient arrows (yellow) and their mean (red), and the gradient cloud with the ellipse of J. Tour, square image, σ = 1, ρ = 3: “edge” (32, 64): J = [740 0; 0 0], μ2 = 0, coherence 1. “Corner” (32, 32): μ1 = 447, μ2 = 285, coherence 0.05, the cloud is a fan in two directions. “Flat”: nothing. “Averaging gradients cancels”: stripes at 30°, naive mode: the map is black; the mean gradient at (64, 64) is 0.48 against √μ1 = 32.1. “ρ = 0”: the corner pixel has μ2 = 0 and the Harris response is never positive: no corners. “Rotating stripes”: the hue follows the turning stripes; orientation 106°, 120°, 0°, 60°, 74° across the image at x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112.

Harris corner response: R = \det J - k\,(\operatorname{tr} J)^2 = \mu_1\mu_2 - k(\mu_1 + \mu_2)^2, k \approx 0.04 to 0.06: positive at corners, negative at edges, ≈ 0 in flat regions. No eigenvalues needed.
Förstner / Shi–Tomasi: the smaller eigenvalue \mu_2 itself.
Corners are local maxima of R above a threshold.
Example (k = 0.05): edge J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1): R = 1 - 0.05 \cdot 10.1^2 = -4.1; corner \mathrm{diag}(10, 8): R = 80 - 16.2 = 63.8; flat \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1): R = 0.008.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
section: The math: Harris from shifting a window
text:
The math: Harris from shifting a window
How much does a window change when shifted by a small \mathbf h?
E(\mathbf h) = \sum_{\mathbf x} w(\mathbf x)\,\big(I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x)\big)^2 \approx \sum_{\mathbf x} w(\mathbf x)\,(\nabla I^\top\mathbf h)^2 = \mathbf h^\top J\,\mathbf h \quad(\text{first-order Taylor}).

Flat: E \approx 0 for every shift. Edge: E large across the edge, ≈ 0 along it (\mu_2 \approx 0). Corner: E large for every direction of \mathbf h, i.e. \mu_2 large.
\det J = \mu_1\mu_2 and \operatorname{tr}J = \mu_1 + \mu_2, so Harris’s R is large only if both eigenvalues are, without computing them.
This is why corners are good interest points: a corner’s window cannot be shifted in any direction without changing, so it can be found again, uniquely, in a shifted image.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Interest points

A corner can be found again in a shifted or rotated image: that is what tracking and feature-based registration match.
Modern keypoint detectors and descriptors (SIFT, ORB and others) combine a detector (corners, or DoG blobs from the scale-space unit) with a description of the window around each point, so that points can be matched between images.
Pointer: the motion elective (registration, tracking) builds on this.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Try it: textures and corners




“ρ too small or too large”: two textures (30° and 120°) meeting at x = 64, noise 25, ρ = 1: the orientation map is speckled with noise; raise ρ to 3: clean; to 8: the boundary between the two textures becomes a wide band of low coherence (at x = 62 the coherence is 0.01 for ρ = 8). “Corners of a checkerboard” (ρ = 2): 35 corners: the 21 inner corners of the checkerboard, and corners of the square, the triangle and the checkerboard’s right border. Micrograph (σ = 1.5, ρ = 4): oriented membranes and fibres in colour, isotropic nucleus texture grey.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Uses

Orientation maps of fibres: collagen in tissue, actin, muscle; fingerprint analysis.
Coherence-enhancing diffusion and other anisotropic filters: smooth along the orientation, not across it (pointer).
Corners for registration and tracking.
A feature channel for pixel classifiers: the eigenvalues of J (and of the Hessian) at several scales are standard features on the random-forest day.

title: The structure tensor: orientation, coherence and corners
text:
Summary

Averaging gradients cancels on lines and stripes; averaging \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top does not.
Structure tensor J = G_\rho * (\nabla L\,\nabla L^\top): gradient at scale σ, window ρ; the covariance matrix of the window’s gradients.
Eigenvector of \mu_1: dominant gradient direction (orientation = perpendicular); coherence ((\mu_1 - \mu_2)/(\mu_1 + \mu_2))^2.
Flat: both small; edge: one large; corner: both large. Harris \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2, or \mu_2.
Corners are interest points: a window that changes under every shift.

title: Quiz: the structure tensor
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Eigenvalues of J: \mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0.

Q1. Why does averaging the gradient vectors in a window fail to find the orientation of a bright line?






Hint





Which way do the gradients point on the two sides of the line?









Answer





On both sides the gradient points towards the line (towards the brighter middle): on one side in direction \mathbf g, on the other in -\mathbf g. They cancel, and the average is about zero although the orientation is perfectly clear. The outer product \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top is the same for \mathbf g and -\mathbf g, so averaging it does not cancel.




Q2. The structure tensor has two scales, σ and ρ. What does each control?






Hint





One is applied before the products, one after.









Answer





σ is the scale of the gradient (the derivative of a Gaussian): it controls noise and which structures produce gradients at all. ρ is the width of the Gaussian window that averages the products: it controls how large a region is summarised by one tensor. Too small a ρ gives noisy orientations; too large a ρ blurs boundaries between differently oriented regions.




Q3. Classify the window: (a) \mu_1 = 900, \mu_2 = 5; (b) \mu_1 = 600, \mu_2 = 450; (c) \mu_1 = 2, \mu_2 = 1 (noise gives up to about 10).






Hint





How many large eigenvalues?









Answer






An edge or oriented texture (one large eigenvalue, coherence (895/905)^2 = 0.98). (b) A corner (or an isotropic, busy texture): two large eigenvalues, coherence (150/1050)^2 = 0.02. (c) Flat: both within the noise.





Q4. The structure tensor is “the covariance matrix of the gradients”. Describe the gradient point cloud of an edge, a corner and a flat region.






Hint





Plot every gradient in the window as a point (L_x, L_y).









Answer





Edge: the points lie along a line through the origin (all gradients parallel or antiparallel): a long thin ellipse. Corner: points along two different directions: a broad, roundish ellipse. Flat: all points near the origin: a tiny ellipse. The eigenvalues of J are the squared half-axes of the ellipse (up to a factor).




Q5. What is the Harris response \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2 (with k = 0.05) for J = \begin{pmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix} and for J = \begin{pmatrix} 16 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}? Which is the corner?






Hint





Both have the same trace.









Answer





First: 64 - 0.05 \cdot 256 = 51.2, a corner. Second: 0 - 0.05 \cdot 256 = -12.8, an edge (negative). Same trace (total gradient energy), but only the first has it in two directions.




Q6. Why are there no corners at all if the window is switched off (ρ = 0)?






Hint





What is the rank of \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top?









Answer





Without averaging, J = \nabla L\,\nabla L^\top at each pixel has rank 1: \mu_2 = 0 and \det J = 0. A single gradient has a single direction; two directions can only come from different pixels in a window. Every pixel looks like an edge, and the Harris response is never positive.




Q7. Hessian or structure tensor? (a) Find the centre line of a blood vessel. (b) Measure the dominant fibre direction in a patch of collagen. (c) Find points to track between two video frames.






Hint





Second derivatives, signed, at centres; or squared first derivatives, unsigned, in windows?









Answer






Hessian: the vessel’s centre is where the curvature across it is strongest (the gradient is zero there). (b) Structure tensor: orientation and coherence of a texture in a window. (c) Structure tensor: corners (Harris or \mu_2), which can be found again after a shift.





Q8. (math) Show that \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u is the average of (\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2 over the window, and explain why its maximum over unit vectors is \mu_1.






Hint





(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^\top\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u; then the Rayleigh quotient.









Answer





(\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf g)(\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u) = \mathbf u^\top(\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top)\mathbf u; averaging is linear, so \langle(\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2\rangle = \mathbf u^\top\langle\nabla L\nabla L^\top\rangle\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u. Writing \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2 in the orthonormal eigenvectors of J: \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u = \mu_1\cos^2\phi + \mu_2\sin^2\phi \le \mu_1, with equality along \mathbf e_1.

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Structure tensor
J = G_\rho * \begin{pmatrix} L_x^2 & L_xL_y \\ L_xL_y & L_y^2\end{pmatrix}: gradient at scale σ, window ρ (here, by hand: a plain average over the window)


Eigenvalues
\mu_1 \ge \mu_2 \ge 0; closed form \mu = \frac{a + c}{2} \pm \sqrt{\big(\frac{a - c}{2}\big)^2 + b^2} for \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix}


Orientation
eigenvector of \mu_1 = dominant gradient direction, angle \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2b, a - c) (image coordinates, y down); the structure runs at \theta + 90°


Coherence
\big(\frac{\mu_1 - \mu_2}{\mu_1 + \mu_2}\big)^2 \in [0, 1]


Verdict
both small: flat; one large: edge / oriented; both large: corner


Harris
R = \det J - k(\operatorname{tr}J)^2, k \approx 0.05: > 0 corner, < 0 edge, ≈ 0 flat

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
By hand
B1. A window contains four gradient vectors: (1, 0), (-1, 0), (1, 0), (-1, 0). (a) What is the average gradient? (b) Compute J as the average of \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top. (c) Eigenvalues, coherence and verdict. What kind of structure could produce these gradients?
B2. The same for (a) (1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1); (b) four zero vectors.
B3. A window has J = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}. (a) Compute \mu_1, \mu_2 and the coherence. (b) Compute θ, the angle of the dominant gradient direction in image coordinates. With y down, which way does it point on the screen? At what angle (counter-clockwise on the screen) do the stripes run?
B4. Harris responses with k = 0.05 for J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1), J = \mathrm{diag}(10, 8) and J = \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1). Which is the corner, the edge and the flat region? What does Förstner’s \mu_2 say?
B5. Predict the ellipse glyph of J (shape and orientation) for a window (a) on the straight top edge of a bright square, (b) on its top-left corner, (c) in its flat interior, (d) on vertical stripes, (e) on isotropic noise texture.
B6. You want an orientation map of collagen fibres about 4 pixels apart, in a noisy image, where regions of different fibre direction are about 40 pixels across. Suggest σ and ρ and explain the trade-off in each.






Solutions





B1. (a) (0, 0): the gradients cancel. (b) Each \mathbf g\mathbf g^\top is \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix} (also for (-1, 0)), so J = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}. (c) \mu_1 = 1, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1: an edge or oriented structure; the gradients are horizontal, so the structure is vertical. Opposite gradients in one window: a vertical line (or vertical stripes), bright or dark. The average gradient said “nothing here”; J says “perfectly oriented”.
B2. (a) Average (0, 0); J = \frac14\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix} + \begin{smallmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\big) = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = 0.5, coherence 0: two directions in one window, a corner (or isotropic texture). (b) J = 0: flat; coherence undefined (0/0; the demos show 0).
B3. (a) \mu = 3.5 \pm \sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = 3.5 \pm 2.5: \mu_1 = 6, \mu_2 = 1; coherence (5/7)^2 = 0.51. (b) \theta = \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(4, 3) = 26.6° in image coordinates: with y down the dominant gradient points to the right and down (−26.6° counter-clockwise on the screen). The stripes run perpendicular to it, at 90° - 26.6° = 63.4° counter-clockwise on the screen (from lower left to upper right, steeply).
B4. \mathrm{diag}(10, 0.1): 1 - 0.05 \cdot 10.1^2 = -4.10, an edge. \mathrm{diag}(10, 8): 80 - 0.05 \cdot 18^2 = 63.8, a corner. \mathrm{diag}(0.1, 0.1): 0.01 - 0.05 \cdot 0.04 = 0.008, flat (tiny). Förstner’s \mu_2: 0.1, 8, 0.1: large only at the corner; it does not distinguish edge from flat, but it does not need to: neither is a corner.
B5. (a) A thin ellipse, long axis vertical (across the edge: the gradients point up or down), short axis ≈ 0. (b) A large, roundish ellipse (gradients up and left). (c) A dot. (d) A thin ellipse with its long axis horizontal (across the stripes). (e) A roundish ellipse whose size reflects the texture’s contrast; coherence near 0.
B6. σ should be smaller than the fibre spacing so that the stripes produce gradients at all, but large enough to suppress pixel noise: σ ≈ 1 to 1.5 (σ = 4 would blur the fibres away). ρ should cover several fibres to average out noise (ρ ≈ 6 to 8, a window of about 25 to 30 pixels), but stay well below the 40-pixel regions, or the boundaries between directions blur into a band of low coherence.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u equals the window average of (\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2, and that over unit vectors it is largest along the eigenvector of \mu_1, with value \mu_1.
B8. (math) With \nabla L = r(\cos\phi, \sin\phi), show that J_{xx} - J_{yy} = \langle r^2\cos2\phi\rangle and 2J_{xy} = \langle r^2\sin2\phi\rangle, and that the dominant gradient angle is \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2J_{xy}, J_{xx} - J_{yy}). Why does the doubling make opposite gradients add?
B9. (math) Show that shifting a window by a small \mathbf h changes it by E(\mathbf h) = \sum w\,(I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x))^2 \approx \mathbf h^\top J\,\mathbf h, and use it to explain why a corner needs \mu_2 large.






Solutions (math)





B7. (\mathbf g\cdot\mathbf u)^2 = \mathbf u^\top\mathbf g\mathbf g^\top\mathbf u, and averaging over the window (with weights w) is linear: \langle(\nabla L\cdot\mathbf u)^2\rangle = \mathbf u^\top\langle\nabla L\nabla L^\top\rangle\mathbf u = \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u. J is symmetric with orthonormal eigenvectors \mathbf e_1, \mathbf e_2; with \mathbf u = \cos\phi\,\mathbf e_1 + \sin\phi\,\mathbf e_2, \mathbf u^\top J\mathbf u = \mu_1\cos^2\phi + \mu_2\sin^2\phi, at most \mu_1, attained at \phi = 0.
B8. L_x^2 - L_y^2 = r^2(\cos^2\phi - \sin^2\phi) = r^2\cos2\phi and 2L_xL_y = 2r^2\cos\phi\sin\phi = r^2\sin2\phi; averaging gives the two identities. From the closed form, the eigenvector of \mu_1 of \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c\end{pmatrix} has angle \tfrac12\operatorname{atan2}(2b, a - c), i.e. half the angle of the averaged vector \langle r^2(\cos2\phi, \sin2\phi)\rangle. A gradient and its opposite differ by 180° in φ, hence by 360° in 2\phi: they map to the same doubled-angle vector and add instead of cancelling.
B9. First-order Taylor: I(\mathbf x + \mathbf h) - I(\mathbf x) \approx \nabla I(\mathbf x)^\top\mathbf h. So E(\mathbf h) \approx \sum w\,(\nabla I^\top\mathbf h)^2 = \mathbf h^\top\big(\sum w\,\nabla I\nabla I^\top\big)\mathbf h = \mathbf h^\top J\mathbf h. For a fixed shift length |\mathbf h| this ranges from \mu_2|\mathbf h|^2 (shift along \mathbf e_2) to \mu_1|\mathbf h|^2. At an edge, shifting along the edge leaves the window unchanged (\mu_2 \approx 0); a window that changes under every shift, a corner, needs \mu_2 large.

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
Explore: the structure tensor
Images: synthetic textures (stripes with an angle and a frequency, rotating stripes, a “fingerprint”, two textures meeting at the middle, a checkerboard with a square and a triangle, a single square, isotropic noise) or the micrograph. The left panel shows the image with one ellipse of J per 16-pixel cell, the orientation map (hue = orientation of the structure, saturation = coherence, brightness = energy) or the Harris response with the detected corners. Click a pixel: the window (cyan), its gradient arrows (yellow) and their mean (red), the gradient cloud with the ellipse of J, and the numbers. Average gradients instead shows the naive orientation map from the mean gradient.



E1. Presets edge, corner, flat (square, σ = 1, ρ = 3). Read J, \mu_1, \mu_2 and the coherence in each case, and describe the gradient cloud. Compare with B1, B2 and B5.
E2. Preset averaging gradients cancels (stripes at 30°, naive mode). What does the naive orientation map look like, and why? Compare the mean gradient (red arrow) with \sqrt{\mu_1}. Untick the naive mode.
E3. Preset ρ = 0. Read \mu_2 at the corner (32, 32). Look at the corners tab: how many corners are found? Raise ρ slowly: from which ρ are the four corners of the square detected?
E4. Preset ρ too small or too large (two textures, noise 25, ρ = 1). Describe the orientation map. Then set ρ = 3 and ρ = 8. Read the coherence at (30, 64), (62, 64) (on the boundary) and (96, 64) each time.
E5. Preset rotating stripes. Click across the image at y = 64: x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112. Read the orientation each time. Does the hue follow?
E6. Preset corners of a checkerboard (ρ = 2). How many corners are found, and where? Raise the corner threshold and lower it; change Harris k. What happens on the triangle’s corners?
E7. Image fingerprint: describe the orientation map. Where is the coherence low, and why?
E8. Preset micrograph (σ = 1.5, ρ = 4). Which regions are oriented (saturated colours), which isotropic (grey)? Click on the nuclear envelope at (94, 126) and inside the nucleus at (150, 150): compare the coherence.






Solutions





E1. Edge (32, 64): J = [740 0; 0 0], \mu_1 = 740, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1.00, orientation 90° (the edge is vertical): the cloud is a short line along L_x. Corner (32, 32): J = [366 81; 81 366], \mu_1 = 447, \mu_2 = 285, coherence 0.05: the cloud spreads in two directions (a fan from the origin). Flat (64, 64): all zero. As in B1, B2 and B5: one large eigenvalue at the edge, two at the corner, none inside.
E2. The naive map is almost black: the average gradient is near zero everywhere on stripes. At (64, 64) the mean gradient has length 0.48, while \sqrt{\mu_1} = 32.1: the gradients are strong, they just cancel. With J the map is uniformly coloured (orientation 120°, coherence 1.00).
E3. With ρ = 0 the corner pixel has J = [1269 1269; 1269 1269]: \mu_1 = 2539, \mu_2 = 0, coherence 1: an “edge” (one diagonal gradient). The Harris response is never positive, so no corners are found. Already at ρ = 0.5 the four corners are back, at (32, 32), (95, 32), (32, 95) and (95, 95): a window of a few pixels is enough to contain gradients from both edges.
E4. ρ = 1: speckled colours and many grey pixels: each window is too small to average out the noise. Coherence at (30, 64), (62, 64), (96, 64): 0.98, 0.31, 0.97. ρ = 3: clean, uniform colours on both sides: 0.94, 0.05, 0.94. ρ = 8: still clean, but the boundary becomes a wide grey band of low coherence: 0.93, 0.01, 0.92 (the windows near the boundary mix both orientations). ρ trades noise against spatial resolution.
E5. Orientation 106°, 120°, 0°, 60°, 74° at x = 16, 32, 64, 96, 112 (coherence 0.92 to 0.99): the hue changes continuously across the image, following the turning stripes (0° = horizontal stripes in the middle).
E6. 35 corners: the 21 inner corners of the checkerboard (3 columns × 7 rows, where four squares meet), corners along the checkerboard’s right border, the four corners of the square and the three of the triangle. Raising the threshold to 0.5 changes nothing here: all corners of these clean shapes are strong. A larger k penalises the trace more; at k = 0.2 the triangle’s sharp top corner (51°) disappears first (34 corners): its two edges are close to parallel as axes, so \mu_2 is small compared with \mu_1. Right angles and the four-square corners of the checkerboard are the strongest corners.
E7. The colour turns around the centre (the orientation follows the rings), with high coherence (0.95 or more) everywhere except near the centre: 0.00 at the centre, 0.08 four pixels away, 0.49 eight pixels away. There the rings are small and strongly curved, and a window contains every orientation.
E8. Oriented: the membranes, the fibres in the cytoplasm and parts of the nuclear envelope; isotropic: the granular inside of the nucleus and the background texture. At (94, 126) on the envelope the coherence is 0.38 (the envelope is thin and curved, with texture around it); inside the nucleus at (150, 150) only 0.02.

title: Exercise: the structure tensor
text:
Where this leads
The day’s tools (Gaussian derivatives, LoG/DoG, Hessian and structure-tensor eigenvalues at several scales) come back as the feature stack of pixel classifiers on the random-forest day; corners and DoG blobs as interest points in registration; edges in the Hough elective.

title: Phase correlation
text:
About this lecture
Last unit: the cross-correlation of two images for every shift, as the inverse FFT of A_k\overline{B_k}. Its peak is broad, and uneven brightness can move it. Today: throw away the size of each wave and keep only its phase.

Why that gives a sharp spike at the shift (Kuglin & Hines, 1975).
What it buys: brightness does not matter, the spike is easy to find.
What it costs: noise gets the same vote as signal; low-pass weighting, partial normalisation.
The border of the image: a taper against the false peak at zero.
How much to trust a peak: peak height and peak ratio.

Recall: a complex number z = |z|e^{i\varphi} has a size |z| and a phase \varphi; z/|z| keeps the phase only.
Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Phase correlation
text:
The trouble with plain cross-correlation

Images are dominated by slow waves: smooth brightness changes carry most of the strength. Their votes are the biggest, and a slow wave agrees with many nearby shifts: the peak is broad.
A broad peak is hard to locate precisely and easily pushed sideways.
Uneven brightness (an illumination ramp, a bright region) changes the slow waves most, exactly the ones with the biggest votes. The peak can move to a wrong place.

In the demo: two 128 \times 128 crops of the micrograph, shifted by (21, 13). CC finds the shift, but the neighbouring shift (20, 10) still scores 70 % of the peak. Add a brightness ramp of 500 grey levels across B: CC’s peak jumps to (54, 1).

title: Phase correlation
text:
Keep only the phase
The shift theorem (the Fourier unit, exercise B4): a shift changes the phases of the waves, not their sizes. So the shift is in the phase differences alone.

Divide each A_k\overline{B_k} by its own size: every wave keeps its phase difference and gets a vote of exactly 1.
At the true shift all votes agree, and nothing else is left: the inverse FFT is a single spike, height 1 for a pure (circular) shift, zero everywhere else.
Picture: arrows on unit circles, all of the same length, each turning at its own rate as the shift changes. Only at the true shift do they all point the same way.

title: Phase correlation
text:
The math: why a delta
If B is A shifted circularly, g(x) = f(x + t_0), then (the shift theorem, the Fourier unit B9) G_k = e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot t_0/N}F_k \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R_k = \frac{F_k\overline{G_k}}{|F_k\overline{G_k}|} = e^{-2\pi i\,k\cdot t_0/N} for every k with F_k \ne 0. The inverse DFT of a pure phase ramp is a delta: r(t) = \frac1N\sum_k e^{2\pi i\,k\cdot(t - t_0)/N} = \delta(t - t_0) = \begin{cases} 1 & t = t_0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases} In 2D, k\cdot t means k_xt_x/N_x + k_yt_y/N_y (times N). In practice R_k = F_k\overline{G_k}/(|F_k\overline{G_k}| + \varepsilon), computed in floating point (the bit-depth day): the magnitudes can be tiny.

title: Phase correlation
text:
Try it: phase correlation




Left: the micrograph with frame A (blue) and frame B (red), which you can drag. Middle: the two crops and the spectrum of A. Right: the correlation surface, shift 0 in the centre; green ring = true shift, cyan cross = highest peak. Tour: “same image, shifted: delta” (B = A rolled around): a single spike of height 1.000, peak ratio ∞. “CC: broad peak”: a big blob, (20, 10) scores 70 % of the peak, ratio 1.44. “phase: sharp peak”: height 0.671 (the crops overlap by 75 %), next peaks 0.029, ratio 23. “illumination ramp on B” (CC): peak at (54, 1), wrong; switch to phase: correct again, still 0.671. Then slide p from 1 to 0 to go back from phase correlation to CC. Gain and offset on B do not change the phase-correlation surface at all.

title: Phase correlation
text:
What it buys

Brightness and contrast. A gain multiplies every B_k by the same number; an offset changes only the constant wave (k = 0). Neither changes any phase: the surface is identical.
Uneven illumination mostly changes the slow waves, which now get no more vote than any other.
A sharp spike: easy to locate, and two different shifts in one picture (two moving objects) give two separate spikes.
In words: phase correlation compares edges and texture; CC compares blobs of brightness. Normalising the spectrum is “whitening” the images: an edge-enhancing filter.

title: Phase correlation
text:
By hand: normalising the example
The last unit’s example: A = (0, 1, 2, 0), B = (1, 2, 0, 0), A_k\overline{B_k} = (9, -5i, -1, 5i).

Divide by the sizes (9, 5, 1, 5): R = (1, -i, -1, i).
Inverse DFT: r(t) = \tfrac14\sum_k R_k\,i^{kt}: r(0) = \tfrac14(1 - i - 1 + i) = 0, r(1) = \tfrac14(1 + 1 + 1 + 1) = 1, r(2) = r(3) = 0.
A delta at t = 1; the CC was (2, 5, 2, 0).

Now take B' = 2B + 1 = (3, 5, 1, 1): B'_k = (10, 2 - 4i, -2, 2 + 4i). Only B'_0 changed beyond a factor 2, and k = 0 is normalised to 1 anyway: R is unchanged.

title: Phase correlation
section: Partial overlap and the peak height
text:
Partial overlap and the peak height
Real tiles are not circular shifts: part of each crop has no partner.

The spike is still at the shift, but its height is roughly the fraction of shared content. Crops of 128^2 shifted by (21, 13) share \frac{107 \cdot 115}{128^2} = 75\,\%: the peak is 0.62 (0.67 with a taper, which favours the centre).
The rest of the surface is a low, noisy floor (here about 0.03).
Smaller crops, 64^2, share only 54 % with the same shift: the peak drops to 0.32, the ratio to the next peak from 23 to 5.

title: Phase correlation
text:
What it costs: noise
Normalising gives every frequency the same vote, including the ones that are mostly noise.

Fine detail (high frequencies) is weak in most images; there, the noise (the camera-noise unit’s \sigma_n) is as strong as the signal, and the phase difference is random.
There are many more high frequencies than low ones: their random votes add up to a noisy floor that can drown the spike.
Remedies:

low-pass weighting: normalise, then multiply by a smooth weight that fades out the highest frequencies;
partial normalisation: divide by |A_k\overline{B_k}|^p with 0 < p < 1 (p = 0: CC, p = 1: phase correlation);
a small \varepsilon in the denominator, so that nearly empty frequencies do not get a full vote.

title: Phase correlation
text:
Try it: noise and low-pass




“noise: phase peak drowns”: independent noise σ = 120 on both crops. The phase-correlation peak at the truth is only 0.033, below the highest noise peak at (−6, 7) (0.043), ratio 1.03: wrong. “noise + low-pass weight” (sd 0.08 cycles/pixel): the spike is back at (21, 13), ratio 1.54; the surface looks smoother because the fine detail is weighted down. Also try p = 0.5 without low-pass: (21, 14), one pixel off; CC (p = 0) also lands on (21, 14). Show the cross-power phase panel: with noise the hue is random at high frequencies.

title: Phase correlation
text:
Tapering: the border problem
The DFT assumes each crop repeats (the Fourier unit): the right border meets the left one, usually with a jump in brightness.

These jump lines belong to the frame, not to the sample: they are at the same place in A and in B and do not move with the shift.
They add strong vertical and horizontal waves (a bright cross in the spectrum) that vote for shift zero, and for shifts along the axes.
Cure: multiply both crops by a Hann taper, a smooth bump that is 1 in the middle and 0 at the border, after subtracting the mean. No jump, no cross.
Price: the content near the border counts less, so overlaps at the edge of a tile are weighted down (the stitching unit therefore does not taper).

title: Phase correlation
text:
Try it: no taper




“no taper: false (0, 0) peak”: the whole field is unevenly lit (brightness rising by 600 grey levels from corner to corner), CC, no taper. The crops’ borders jump strongly, the spectrum (small panel) shows a bright cross, and the highest peak is at (0, 0); the next peaks lie on the line t_y = 0. Tick “Hann taper”: the cross disappears and CC finds (21, 13) again (ratio 1.31). Phase correlation without a taper survives here (0.617), but shows the same line of small false peaks at (15, 0), (12, 0).

title: Phase correlation
text:
The math: tapers and noise
Hann taper of length N: w(n) = \tfrac12\big(1 - \cos\frac{2\pi n}{N - 1}\big), n = 0, \ldots, N-1; in 2D the product w(x)\,w(y). Multiplying by w convolves the spectrum with \hat w, a narrow bump: leakage is local instead of a 1/k tail along the axes.
Noise. With g(x) = f(x + t_0) + \eta(x): G_k = e^{2\pi i k t_0/N}F_k + H_k, \qquad \arg G_k = \frac{2\pi k t_0}{N} + \arg F_k + \delta_k, \quad |\delta_k| \lesssim \frac{|H_k|}{|F_k|}. The phase error \delta_k is small where the signal is strong and random where |F_k| \lesssim |H_k|, typically at high |k|. Phase correlation gives those frequencies full weight; a low-pass weight W_k (e.g. Gaussian in |k|) or |F_k\overline{G_k}|^{-p} with p < 1 reduces their share of the sum \sum_k W_k R_k e^{2\pi i k t/N}.

title: Phase correlation
section: How much to trust a peak
text:
How much to trust a peak

Peak height: about the shared fraction of the content (for phase correlation). A low peak means little overlap, or noise, or no match.
Peak ratio: highest peak divided by the second highest. A ratio near 1 means two shifts are about equally good: do not trust this pair.
Typical low-ratio cases: a blank tile (nothing to match), periodic texture (every period gives a peak), strong noise.
A mosaic program uses this confidence to decide which pairwise shifts to believe (the stitching unit).

In the demo, a lattice of blobs 18 pixels apart shifted by (21, 13): the highest peak is at (3, -5), one lattice period away in each direction; the true shift scores only 0.03.

title: Phase correlation
text:
Summary

Phase correlation: normalise A_k\overline{B_k} to size 1, inverse FFT. A pure shift gives a spike of height 1 at the shift.
Gains and offsets do not change it; uneven illumination hardly does. It compares edges and texture.
Noise gets a full vote too: weight down the high frequencies (low-pass) or normalise only partly (0 < p < 1).
The image border repeats with a jump: a Hann taper removes the cross in the spectrum and the false peak at zero.
Trust a peak by its height (shared fraction) and its ratio to the next one; periodic and empty images give ambiguous peaks.

title: Quiz: from a peak to a mosaic
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. The shift of tile B relative to tile A is where B sits on A; tiles are N \times N.

Q1. Two 100 \times 100 tiles give an unpadded phase-correlation peak at (80, 10). Which four shifts can it mean? Which overlaps do they have?






Hint





Subtract the tile size in x, in y, or in both.









Answer





(80, 10), (-20, 10), (80, -90) and (-20, -90). Overlaps: 20 \cdot 90 = 1800 px (18 %), 80 \cdot 90 = 7200 (72 %), 20 \cdot 10 = 200 (2 %), 80 \cdot 10 = 800 (8 %). NCC on each overlap decides; the 2 % candidate is too small to judge.




Q2. Why do stitching programs often test the four candidates instead of zero-padding the tiles?






Hint





Compare the cost of the two ways.









Answer





Padding makes every FFT about four times larger (in 2D) and the overlap becomes a smaller part of the padded image. Testing four candidates by NCC costs one small computation per candidate on the overlap pixels only, and also gives a confidence for the pair.




Q3. The correlation samples around a peak are (0.5, 0.9, 0.7). Estimate the sub-pixel position with a parabola.






Hint





\delta = \dfrac{c_{-1} - c_{+1}}{2(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_{+1})}.









Answer





\delta = \dfrac{0.5 - 0.7}{2(0.5 - 1.8 + 0.7)} = \dfrac{-0.2}{-1.2} = \tfrac16 \approx 0.17 px to the right of the middle sample, towards the larger neighbour.




Q4. What is “pixel locking”, and which method avoids it?






Hint





Plot the error of the parabola against the true fraction of a pixel.









Answer





The parabola (and the centroid) estimates are pulled towards whole pixels: their error is zero at fractions 0 and 0.5 and largest in between, an S-shaped curve, because the true peak is not a parabola. A histogram of many estimates then piles up near whole pixels. The upsampled DFT evaluates the exact interpolated correlation on a fine grid and has no such bias (only the grid spacing).




Q5. Three tiles in a row: measured shifts d_{12} = 100, d_{23} = 102, d_{13} = 199. Chaining gives x_3 = 202 from the first two, but the direct measurement says 199. What does least squares (equal weights, x_1 = 0) give?






Hint





Minimise (x_2 - 100)^2 + (x_3 - x_2 - 102)^2 + (x_3 - 199)^2.









Answer





Setting the derivatives to zero: 2x_2 - x_3 = -2 and -x_2 + 2x_3 = 301, so x_2 = 99, x_3 = 200. Each measurement is off by 1: residuals -1, -1, +1. The discrepancy of 3 around the loop is shared by all three pairs.




Q6. One pair of a mosaic was registered wrongly by 100 px. What happens with chaining along a path through that pair, and with global least squares?






Hint





Who depends on that pair in each case?









Answer





Chaining: every tile after the bad pair moves by 100 px. Global least squares: the other paths around the loop disagree with the bad pair, so the solution follows the majority; the bad pair is left with a large residual (here about 100 px), which flags it. If its confidence is low, it gets little weight in the first place. Then drop it and solve again.




Q7. A time-lapse drifts slowly while the cells inside change their shape. Register every frame to the first frame or to the previous frame?






Hint





What makes each choice fail?









Answer





To the first frame, errors do not accumulate, but late frames may no longer resemble the first one when the sample changes. To the previous frame, consecutive frames resemble each other, but the errors of all steps add up (a random walk). With a changing sample, register to the previous frame or to key frames, and keep the step errors small (sub-pixel estimation, low noise).




Q8. (math) Why is the matrix of the normal equations of global alignment singular, and how is that fixed?






Hint





What happens to the energy if every tile is moved by the same amount?









Answer





The energy depends only on differences x_j - x_i; adding the same constant to every position does not change it. So the graph Laplacian L has L\mathbf 1 = 0: the constant vector is in its null space. Fixing one tile (x_1 = 0, i.e. deleting its row and column) removes this freedom; for a connected graph the reduced matrix is invertible.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
About this lecture
Erosion and dilation were already written as a min and a max over the SE. Nothing in those formulas needs the image to be binary: applied to a grey image, they give the min filter and the max filter, and every construction of the last two units carries over.

A grey image as a landscape; erosion, dilation, opening and closing seen as a bar pushed up from below or down from above.
Top-hat: image minus its opening. Removes an uneven background, so that one threshold works.
Morphological gradient: dilation minus erosion. An edge detector without direction or ringing.
Rank filters: min, median, max as one family.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Min and max filters
With a flat SE B (a window, no weights), for a grey image I:
(I \ominus B)(x) = \min_{b \in B} I(x + b), \qquad (I \oplus B)(x) = \max_{b \in B} I(x - b).

Erosion: every pixel takes the darkest value in its window. Bright details narrower than B shrink or vanish, dark ones grow.
Dilation: the brightest value. Bright details grow, dark ones shrink.
Opening I \circ B and closing I \bullet B: as before, erode then dilate, or the other way round.
On a 0/1 image these are exactly the binary operations.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
The image as a landscape
Draw I as a profile (1D) or a relief (2D): height = grey level.

Opening: push the SE, a horizontal bar of width w, up from below as far as it goes. The top of the bar traces I \circ B. A bright peak narrower than the bar is cut off at the level where it becomes wider than the bar; a wide peak is kept.
Closing: push the bar down from above. Dark valleys narrower than the bar are filled.
The bar never goes above the profile (opening) or below it (closing): opening \le I \le closing.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Example: 12 samples, width 3

The opening of a 12-sample signal with a flat SE of width 3 (orange), and the white top-hat (green).I = 2\,2\,7\,2\,3\,3\,6\,6\,6\,1\,2\,2. Erosion (min over 3) = 2\,2\,2\,2\,2\,3\,3\,6\,1\,1\,1\,2; opening = 2\,2\,2\,2\,3\,3\,6\,6\,6\,1\,2\,2.
The one-sample peak (7) is cut down to 2; the three-sample plateau (6 6 6) survives. With width 5 it would be cut down to 3 too.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
section: The math: grey levels as stacked sets
text:
The math: grey levels as stacked sets
Threshold decomposition: for a flat SE, erosion commutes with thresholding,
\{x : (I \ominus B)(x) \ge t\} = \{x : I(x) \ge t\} \ominus B \quad \text{for every level } t,
because \min_b I(x + b) \ge t \iff I(x + b) \ge t for all b. The same holds for dilation, opening and closing. So grey-level morphology with a flat SE = binary morphology applied to every threshold of I, stacked again.

Opening keeps the part of each level set \{I \ge t\} that the SE fits into: a peak survives up to the level where it is still at least as wide as B.
The “landscape” is the umbra \{(x, t) : t \le I(x)\}; a flat SE is a horizontal segment pushed around in it.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
section: Try it: rolling the SE under and over a profile
text:
Try it: rolling the SE under and over a profile




The orange bar is the SE at the chosen position, pushed up under the profile (or down over it); “sweep” moves it along and leaves the trace, which is the opening (closing). Drag the round handles to change the profile. Tour: “narrow peak goes, wide peak stays”: w = 11; sweep: the trace runs under the narrow peak and over the plateau. Raise w past the plateau width (23): it goes too. “peaks on a slope”: opening (orange) follows the slope, the white top-hat (green) is flat with the peaks on it. “noise: min, median, max”: salt-and-pepper on a step; only the median removes both kinds and keeps the step sharp. “a line across the cell”: closing from above, black top-hat picks out the dark granules.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Top-hat: remove the background
White top-hat: the image minus its opening, \mathrm{WTH}(I) = I - I \circ B \ \ge 0 .

The opening is a background estimate: it follows everything wider than B and cuts off the bright details narrower than B.
The top-hat keeps exactly those details, on a flat zero background, whatever the background brightness was.
Black top-hat I \bullet B - I: the same for dark details (granules, cracks, dark spots).

Classic use: uneven illumination (a vignetted microscope field, a light gradient). On the raw image, no single threshold separates spots from background (the thresholding day showed this failure); on the top-hat, one threshold does.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Choosing the SE
B must be larger than the objects and smaller than the background variation.

Too small: the opening still follows the spots partly, the top-hat cuts their tops off; weak spots get lost.
Too large: the opening can no longer follow the background where it curves; part of the background (and the noise) leaks into the top-hat.
Spots of radius \approx 3 on a background that varies over 50 pixels: a disc of radius 5–8.

Some image programs offer this as “rolling-ball background subtraction”: an opening with a ball-shaped (non-flat) SE.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
The math: top-hat facts

\mathrm{WTH}(I) \ge 0 because the opening is anti-extensive, I \circ B \le I.
Adding a constant changes nothing: (I + c) \circ B = I \circ B + c, so \mathrm{WTH}(I + c) = \mathrm{WTH}(I).
A linear ramp is its own opening (in 1D, away from the ends): erosion of ax by a window of half-width k is a(x - k) for a > 0, and dilating that back gives ax. So slopes are background: their top-hat is 0.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
section: Try it: top-hat on an uneven background
text:
Try it: top-hat on an uneven background




Three panels: input, result of the chosen operation (disc radius r), threshold overlay (orange = above t). The threshold can act on the input or on the result; for the synthetic image the readout counts the true spots found and the false objects. Tour: “one threshold fails”: threshold the input at 150: 29 of 40 spots found and 250 false objects (the bright half of the background). “top-hat flattens the background”: white top-hat r = 6, threshold the result at 28: all 40 spots, no false objects. “SE too small” (r = 2): 37 of 40. “SE too large” (r = 20): still 40, but 148 false objects. “granules in the cell”: black top-hat. In the exercise page the profile line is shown below the panels.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Non-flat SEs: the rolling ball
A non-flat SE has a height s(b) at each offset (a cap, a paraboloid, a ball):
(I \oplus s)(x) = \max_{b} \big(I(x - b) + s(b)\big), \qquad (I \ominus s)(x) = \min_b \big(I(x + b) - s(b)\big).

Opening with a ball: roll a ball under the landscape; the highest points it reaches are the background. Narrow peaks and steep ridges are cut off more gently than with a flat bar.
Flat SE = all heights 0: the min and max filters again.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
The math: max-plus convolution
Replace (+, \times) by (\max, +) in a convolution \sum_b I(x - b)\,s(b) and you get the dilation \max_b \big(I(x - b) + s(b)\big).

It distributes over pointwise max like a convolution over sums: (I \vee J) \oplus s = (I \oplus s) \vee (J \oplus s), and it commutes with adding a constant, (I + c) \oplus s = (I \oplus s) + c.
It is shift-invariant and associative: (I \oplus s_1) \oplus s_2 = I \oplus (s_1 \oplus s_2) (a large parabola = several small ones).
There is no Fourier convolution theorem, but there is an analogue: the slope transform (Legendre–Fenchel) turns dilation into addition. Further reading only.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Morphological gradient
\nabla_B I = (I \oplus B) - (I \ominus B)
the largest minus the smallest value in the window: large at edges, 0 in flat regions.

Inner gradient I - (I \ominus B) and outer gradient (I \oplus B) - I: the two halves, on either side of the edge.
A step of height 10 with the 3-wide window: gradient 0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,0\,0\,0 (two samples wide). A ramp with slope 2: gradient 4 everywhere (2 × slope).
Compared with Sobel (the kernels unit): no sign and no direction, but the same response in every direction; thicker edges; no ringing or overshoot; and it is a range (max − min in the window), not a slope: on a smooth edge it grows with the SE size, a derivative does not.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Rank filters: min, median, max
Sort the values in the window. Take the smallest (erosion), the middle one (median), or the largest (dilation). Any other rank gives something in between.

Salt-and-pepper noise (isolated very bright and very dark pixels): the min removes the salt but spreads the pepper, the max the opposite. The median removes both and keeps steps sharp. (The median as a denoiser was introduced on the deconvolution day; here it is one member of the rank-filter family.)
All rank filters are nonlinear, shift-invariant, and commute with thresholding (a flat-SE property).
Example: 5\,5\,9\,5\,5\,0\,5\,5\,5\,9\,0\,5, window 3: the median gives all 5s.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Try it: gradient and noise




“gradient vs derivative”: a steep step (50 → 200 over two samples) and a ramp, w = 3. The gradient (pink) reaches the full step height, 150, at the middle sample and is 3 samples wide; |derivative| (dashed) peaks at 75. On the ramp the gradient is 9.3, twice the derivative (4.7). Raise w to 5 and 9: the gradient widens to 5 and 9 samples and grows on the ramp (18.7, 37.3); the derivative does not change. A morphological gradient is the range in the window, not a slope. “noise: min, median, max”: w = 5; min (blue) spreads the dark noise, max (red) the bright noise, the median (cyan) removes both.

title: Grey-level morphology: top-hat and gradient
text:
Summary

Grey-level erosion/dilation with a flat SE = min/max filters; opening pushes a bar up under the landscape, closing pushes it down.
Flat-SE morphology commutes with thresholding: it is binary morphology on every level set.
White top-hat I - I \circ B keeps bright details smaller than B on a flat background; black top-hat I \bullet B - I the dark ones. Choose B larger than the objects, smaller than the background variation.
Non-flat SEs (rolling ball) = dilation as a max-plus convolution.
Gradient (I \oplus B) - (I \ominus B): unsigned, isotropic edges. Median: the rank filter between min and max.

title: Quiz: grey-level morphology
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. With a flat SE B: erosion = min filter, dilation = max filter, opening I \circ B = erode then dilate, closing I \bullet B = dilate then erode; white top-hat I - I \circ B, black top-hat I \bullet B - I, gradient (I \oplus B) - (I \ominus B).

Q1. A fluorescence image has small bright spots (about 5 pixels across) on a background that gets brighter towards one side. Why does a single threshold fail, and which operation fixes it?






Hint





Compare the spot brightness on the dark side with the background brightness on the bright side.









Answer





A threshold low enough to catch the spots on the dark side is below the background on the bright side, and a threshold above the bright background misses the dim spots. A white top-hat with an SE larger than the spots (a disc of diameter 7–9) subtracts the opening, which follows the background but not the spots; on the top-hat the background is near 0 everywhere and one threshold works.




Q2. You open a 1D profile with a flat bar of width 9. A peak is 5 samples wide at its base. What is left of it? And of a plateau 12 samples wide?






Hint





Push the bar up from below.









Answer





The bar cannot enter the 5-sample peak at any height, so the peak is cut down to the level of its surroundings: it disappears. The 12-sample plateau is wider than the bar, so the bar reaches its top: the plateau is kept at full height (only its corners can be affected if its sides are sloped).




Q3. An image shows dark granules in a bright cytoplasm. Which top-hat do you use, and how do you choose the SE size?






Hint





Opening removes bright details, closing removes dark ones.









Answer





The black top-hat I \bullet B - I: the closing fills the dark granules (narrower than B) and follows everything else, so the difference is large exactly at the granules. B must be larger than the granules and smaller than the dark structures you want to ignore (and than the scale of brightness changes in the background).




Q4. What is the morphological gradient (window of 3) of the step 0\,0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,10\,10? How does it differ from a derivative filter such as Sobel?






Hint





Max minus min in each window of 3.









Answer





0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,0\,0\,0: the two samples next to the step see both levels. It has no sign (a rising and a falling step look the same) and no direction, it is as large as the full step (not the slope), and it never overshoots or rings. A derivative filter gives a signed value, proportional to the slope, with a direction (horizontal or vertical Sobel).




Q5. A signal has isolated bright and dark impulses (“salt and pepper”). Compare the min, the max and the median filter over a window of 3.






Hint





A single impulse in a window of 3 is either the smallest, the largest or the middle value?









Answer





The min filter removes the bright impulses but widens every dark impulse to 3 samples; the max does the opposite. The median takes the middle value: one impulse in a window of 3 is never the middle one, so both kinds disappear, and a step between two flat levels stays sharp. All three are rank filters of the same window.




Q6. Why does adding a constant brightness to the whole image not change its top-hat? Does multiplying by 2?






Hint





How do min and max behave under I \mapsto I + c and I \mapsto 2I?









Answer





\min(I + c) = \min I + c and \max(I + c) = \max I + c, so the opening shifts by c too and the difference is unchanged. Multiplying by 2 (a positive factor) also commutes with min and max, so the top-hat is multiplied by 2: the same details, twice as bright. A threshold on the top-hat must therefore scale with the image contrast, but not with an offset.




Q7. (math) Show that for a flat SE, \{x : (I \ominus B)(x) \ge t\} = \{x : I(x) \ge t\} \ominus B for every threshold t. What does it mean for “grey-level versus binary” morphology?






Hint





When is a minimum at least t?









Answer





\min_{b \in B} I(x + b) \ge t \iff I(x + b) \ge t for all b \in B \iff B_x \subseteq \{I \ge t\} \iff x \in \{I \ge t\} \ominus B. So grey-level erosion (and similarly dilation, opening, closing) with a flat SE is binary morphology applied to every level set of the image, and the results stack back into a grey image. It also means: thresholding and flat morphology can be done in either order.

title: Quiz: convolutional networks
text:
Short questions on convolutional layers, pooling, receptive fields and augmentation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A convolutional layer with C_\text{out} kernels of size k \times k on C_\text{in} channels has k^2C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out} weights; output size \lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1.

Q1. A convolutional layer has 32 kernels of size 3 \times 3 on an RGB image. How many weights does it have? How many for a 256 \times 256 image, and for a 2048 \times 2048 image?






Hint





Each kernel covers all 3 channels.









Answer





3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 32 + 32 = 896, for both image sizes: the same kernels are used at every position.




Q2. The input is shifted 5 pixels to the right. What happens to the feature maps of a convolutional layer (stride 1)?






Hint





Equivariance.









Answer





They shift 5 pixels to the right as well (apart from the border columns): the same kernel sees the same neighbourhoods, now 5 pixels further right.




Q3. A 64 \times 64 feature map goes through 2×2 max pooling, then a 3 \times 3 convolution with stride 2 and padding 1. What is the final size?






Hint





\lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1, twice.









Answer





Pooling: \lfloor(64 - 2)/2\rfloor + 1 = 32. Convolution: \lfloor(32 + 2 - 3)/2\rfloor + 1 = 16. So 16 \times 16.




Q4. What is the receptive field of four stacked 3 \times 3 convolutions (stride 1, no pooling)?






Hint





Each layer adds 2.









Answer





1 + 4 \cdot 2 = 9 pixels: a 9 \times 9 patch.




Q5. Why are the layer-1 kernels of a trained network worth looking at as pictures, but the layer-3 kernels hardly?






Hint





What does each kernel act on?









Answer





Layer-1 kernels act on pixels, so a kernel’s picture is the image pattern it responds to (an edge, a line, a blob). Layer-3 kernels act on feature maps of layer 2: their weights mix abstract channels, and only the feature maps, the most exciting image patches or occlusion experiments show what such a unit responds to.




Q6. You classify cells in microscope images whose orientation is arbitrary. Which augmentations would you use? Would you use the same for handwritten digits?






Hint





Which changes keep the label?









Answer





Cells: rotations by any angle, flips, small shifts, brightness and contrast changes, a little noise. Digits: small rotations and shifts only. A 6 rotated by 180° is a 9, and a mirrored 2 or 7 is not a digit at all.




Q7. (math) Two 3 \times 3 convolutions without a nonlinearity in between. Show that they are one convolution, and give its size.






Hint





Convolution is associative.









Answer





(x * k_1) * k_2 = x * (k_1 * k_2): one kernel k_1 * k_2 of size (3 + 3 - 1) \times (3 + 3 - 1) = 5 \times 5. Without the ReLU, depth adds no new kind of function, only a larger linear filter (the collapse argument of the first unit, in convolutional form).

title: Exercise: grey-level morphology, top-hat and gradient
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Flat SE of width w
a window of w samples (or a disc in 2D), no weights


Erosion / dilation
min / max over the window


Opening / closing
erode then dilate / dilate then erode; opening \le I \le closing


White top-hat
I - I \circ B: bright details narrower than B


Black top-hat
I \bullet B - I: dark details narrower than B


Gradient
(I \oplus B) - (I \ominus B); inner I - (I \ominus B), outer (I \oplus B) - I


Rank filters
sort the window, take the smallest (erosion), middle (median) or largest (dilation)



In 1D the window of width 3 at sample x is \{x - 1, x, x + 1\}; at the two ends only the samples inside the signal count.






The math: threshold decomposition





For a flat SE, \{I \ominus B \ge t\} = \{I \ge t\} \ominus B for every t (and the same for dilation, opening and closing): grey-level flat morphology is binary morphology on every level set, stacked again. Non-flat SEs s(b): (I \oplus s)(x) = \max_b I(x - b) + s(b), a convolution with (\max, +) in place of (+, \times).

title: Exercise: grey-level morphology, top-hat and gradient
text:
By hand
B1. I = 2\,2\,7\,2\,3\,3\,6\,6\,6\,1\,2\,2 (samples 0–11). With a flat SE of width 3, compute the erosion, the dilation, the opening and the white top-hat. Which bright detail does the top-hat show?
B2. Repeat the opening and the white top-hat with width 5. Which peaks survive now? What is the rule?
B3. With width 3, compute the closing and the black top-hat of I. Which dark detail is found? Why is the dip at sample 3 (value 2 between 7 and 3) only 1 deep in the black top-hat?
B4. Gradient. With width 3, compute the gradient, the inner and the outer gradient of the step 0\,0\,0\,0\,10\,10\,10\,10, and the gradient of the ramp 0\,2\,4\,6\,8\,10\,12\,14. Where is each half of the step’s gradient? What is the gradient of a ramp with slope a and width w, away from the ends?
B5. Impulse noise. J = 5\,5\,9\,5\,5\,0\,5\,5\,5\,9\,0\,5. Compute the min, the max and the median filter (width 3). Then compute the opening, the closing, and the closing of the opening. Which filter removes all impulses?

B7. On the raw image of B6, spots on the dark side have a peak brightness of 90 and the background on the bright side is 150. Explain why no threshold on the raw image separates spots from background, and why one does on the top-hat.
