The inverse multiplies the 1 % noise by 1/H: 1 %, 2 %, 10 %, 20 % and 100 %. At H = 0.01 the noise is as large as the image itself.
The Wiener gain peaks at H = 0.1 (where H^2 = 1/\mathrm{SNR}; there the gain is 1/(2H) = 5, half the inverse). Below that the frequency is mostly noise, and the filter damps it instead of amplifying it.

B2. Gains 1, 2, 5, 0, 0 (|H| = 0.1 is not larger than ε, so it is dropped). No noise is amplified by more than 1/\varepsilon = 10, and here by at most 5. Lost: everything at the two dropped frequencies, including the true signal there.
B3. (a) A(1,1)^\top = (1, 1)^\top and A(1,-1)^\top = (0.5, -0.5)^\top. \mathbf g = 0.75\,(1, 1) + 0.25\,(1, -1): sum part (0.75, 0.75), difference part (0.25, -0.25). (b) λ = 0: gains 1/1 = 1 and 1/0.5 = 2: \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.75, 0.75) + (0.5, -0.5) = (1.25, 0.25), the exact inverse. λ = 0.1: 1/1.1 = 0.909 and 0.5/0.35 = 1.429: (0.682 + 0.357, 0.682 - 0.357) = (1.04, 0.33). λ = 1: 1/2 = 0.5 and 0.5/1.25 = 0.4: (0.375 + 0.1, 0.375 - 0.1) = (0.48, 0.28). (c) The sum is 2 \times 0.75 \times (sum gain): 1.5, 1.36 and 0.75: the energy penalty shrinks it. A penalty on the difference only acts like the roughness penalty: it leaves the sum part alone (gain 1/1 = 1 for every λ) and damps only the difference.
B4. (a) Too little regularisation: SNR set too high (or λ too small, ε too small); noise at high frequencies is amplified. Lower the SNR. (b) PSF used is too wide (over-sharpening subtracts light around bright objects), or a sharp frequency cut (truncated inverse) rings. Check the PSF width; use a smooth filter. (c) Too much regularisation (SNR too low, λ too large), or a PSF that is too narrow. Raise the SNR or check the PSF.
B5. (a) H(0.1) = e^{-0.790} = 0.454, H(0.2) = e^{-3.16} = 0.0425, H(0.25) = e^{-4.93} = 0.0072. (b) Wiener gains 0.454/(0.206 + 0.01) = 2.10, 0.0425/(0.0018 + 0.01) = 3.60, 0.0072/(0.00005 + 0.01) = 0.72. Effective transfer WH: 0.954, 0.153, 0.005. (c) The restoration passes almost everything up to f \approx 0.15 (WH = 0.74 there) and some detail up to about 0.2; the optics alone fall below 0.5 already at f \approx 0.1. Beyond about 0.2 the noise wins and nothing is restored.
B6. Energy penalty: the gain at f = 0 is 1/(1 + \lambda) = 0.909, so the mean becomes 0.909 \times 0.1575 = 0.143. (The demo’s preset “too much regularisation” shows 0.1432.) Roughness penalty: gain 1 at f = 0, mean kept at 0.1575 (apart from the small effect of noise on the mean of the data).




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive the Wiener filter: with G = HF + N, F and N independent with zero mean and powers S_f, S_n, minimise E|F - WG|^2 over the complex number W. Show that the remaining error is S_f S_n/(|H|^2 S_f + S_n).
B8. (math) Derive the normal equations of \min_{\mathbf x}\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf g\|^2 + \lambda\|D\mathbf x\|^2. For a circular A and D, show that the solution in Fourier space is \hat X = H^* G/(|H|^2 + \lambda|\hat D|^2), and that it equals the Wiener filter when \lambda|\hat D|^2 = S_n/S_f.
B9. (math) Show that the roughness penalty with the 5-point Laplacian L keeps the mean of the image, while the energy penalty multiplies it by 1/(1 + \lambda) (assume the PSF sums to 1).






Solutions (math)





B7. E|F - WG|^2 = E|(1 - WH)F - WN|^2 = |1 - WH|^2 S_f + |W|^2 S_n, since the cross terms vanish (F, N independent, zero mean). Treat W and W^* as independent variables; the derivative with respect to W^* is -(1 - WH)H^* S_f + W S_n = 0, so W(|H|^2 S_f + S_n) = H^* S_f and W = H^* S_f/(|H|^2 S_f + S_n). Then 1 - WH = S_n/(|H|^2 S_f + S_n) and the error is \frac{S_n^2 S_f + |H|^2 S_f^2 S_n}{(|H|^2 S_f + S_n)^2} = \frac{S_f S_n}{|H|^2 S_f + S_n}.
B8. The objective J(\mathbf x) = (A\mathbf x - \mathbf g)^\top(A\mathbf x - \mathbf g) + \lambda\mathbf x^\top D^\top D\mathbf x has gradient 2A^\top(A\mathbf x - \mathbf g) + 2\lambda D^\top D\mathbf x; zero gives (A^\top A + \lambda D^\top D)\mathbf x = A^\top\mathbf g. A circular matrix is diagonalised by the DFT: A = F^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(H)F, A^\top = F^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(H^*)F (real A), and likewise for D. In Fourier space: (|H|^2 + \lambda|\hat D|^2)\hat X = H^* G at every frequency. Comparing with W = H^*/(|H|^2 + S_n/S_f) gives the condition \lambda|\hat D|^2 = S_n/S_f.
B9. The mean is the f = 0 coefficient divided by the number of pixels. At f = 0, H(0) = \sum h = 1. The Laplacian’s symbol is \hat L(f) = 4 - 2\cos 2\pi f_x - 2\cos 2\pi f_y, which is 0 at f = 0 (the Laplacian of a constant is 0). So the roughness gain at f = 0 is 1/(1 + 0) = 1. The energy penalty has \hat D = 1: gain 1/(1 + \lambda).

title: Exercise: linear deconvolution
text:
Explore
The demo blurs a test object with a PSF, adds noise (fixed seed) and restores it. Four images: truth, observed, restored, and the error restored − truth (blue negative, red positive). The upper plot shows, against frequency: the optics |H| (blue), the filter gain |W| (red), the effective transfer |WH| (green) and the noise floor (dashed), below which the data at that frequency are mostly noise. For motion blur the plot is a cut along x instead of a ring average. The lower plot shows the error (RMSE against the truth, image values 0..1) for 30 values of the method’s parameter, computed in the background: red line = the current value, green dot = the best. PSF used × makes the restoration PSF wider or narrower than the true one; borders chooses periodic or padded-and-tapered; realistic blur lets the scene continue past the border and blurs it on a finer grid.



E1. Preset 0.1% noise: inverse explodes. What are the RMSE and the share of negative pixels? Look at the gain plot: from which frequency is the red curve far above 1, and where does the blue curve cross the noise floor?
E2. Preset Wiener at the right SNR. Which SNR is best on the sweep, and with which RMSE? Compare it with the RMSE of the observed image (in brackets in the readout) and with the true SNR in the readout. Why is the best flat SNR so different from the true SNR?
E3. Preset Wiener with the wrong SNR (2000). Describe the image and give the RMSE and the share of negative pixels. Where on the gain plot do you see the problem?
E4. Preset 1/f² beats flat (Siemens star, motion blur of 9 pixels). Read the best RMSE for the 1/f^2 model from the sweep; then switch the signal model to flat and read its best RMSE. Which is better, and why does the motion blur make the difference large?
E5. Preset Tikhonov = Wiener with a flat spectrum. Compare the RMSE with E2. Then preset too much regularisation: blur: give the RMSE and the means of truth and restored image, and explain the ratio. Finally roughness penalty: RMSE and means.
E6. Preset wrong PSF width (beads, PSF used ×1.3). Describe what you see around the beads. Set PSF used to 1.00 and to 0.80 and compare the RMSE.
E7. Preset periodic borders ring. Where do the artefacts start, and what is the RMSE? Switch borders to padded + tapered.






Solutions





E1. RMSE about 1.0e6 and 50.5 % negative pixels: the image is pure amplified noise. With σ = 2 px the red curve (1/|H| for this method) passes 10 near f = 0.17 and leaves the plot (10⁴) near f = 0.34; the blue |H| drops below the noise floor at about f = 0.23 (where 1/|H| \approx 65). Beyond that every frequency is mostly noise, amplified 65 times and more.
E2. The best SNR on the sweep is 45.2 with RMSE 0.0244. The observed image has RMSE 0.0318: the restoration reduces the error by about a quarter. The true SNR in the readout is 537. One flat SNR must serve all frequencies: at low frequencies the real SNR is far higher (the image’s power sits there), at high ones far lower. The best compromise is the SNR around the frequencies where the filter decides, where |H| is about the noise floor, not the image-wide average.
E3. Fine bright and dark speckles everywhere; RMSE 0.0641 (worse than the observed 0.0318) and 14.4 % negative pixels. On the gain plot the red curve peaks near f = 0.22 with a gain of about 22, beyond the frequency (f \approx 0.16) where the blue curve fell below the noise floor: noise is amplified.
E4. 1/f^2: best RMSE 0.0714 (at SNR 304); flat: best 0.0817 (at SNR 161). The 1/f^2 model is better. The motion blur has near-zeros at many frequencies along x (every 1/9 cycle per pixel), also at high frequencies where a flat model with a high SNR would amplify noise. The 1/f^2 model trusts low frequencies more and high frequencies less, which matches both the image and the noise.
E5. λ = 1/45 gives RMSE 0.0244, exactly the Wiener result of E2: same gain at every frequency. Too much regularisation (energy, λ = 0.1): RMSE 0.0341, blurred, worse than the observed image; mean of the truth 0.1575, restored 0.1432: the ratio 0.909 is 1/(1 + \lambda), the energy penalty’s gain at f = 0. Roughness penalty (λ = 0.033): RMSE 0.0237, the best of the three linear methods here, and the mean is kept (0.1575).
E6. Dark rims around the bright beads, below the background level, and ripples: the restoration subtracts more blur than there was. RMSE 0.0465 at ×1.3, 0.0412 at ×1.00, 0.0445 at ×0.80. Too narrow is milder: it leaves blur (the beads stay wide) but makes no rims.
E7. Stripes start at the left and right borders and run into the image; RMSE 1.30 (the image is ruined). The step edge runs off the left and right borders and the blur brought light in from outside the field, neither of which the periodic model knows. Padded + tapered: RMSE 0.0497 and the stripes are gone.

title: Exercise: linear deconvolution
text:
Where this leads
Every method today had one number to choose: ε, the SNR, or λ. The next unit asks the general question: what is it we add to the data (the penalty, or prior knowledge), how much (choosing λ), and why stopping an iteration early does the same job. Unit 3 then replaces the linear filters by Richardson–Lucy, which knows that photons are counted and never negative.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
About this lecture
Every restoration of the last unit had one number to choose. This unit is the general lesson behind them, taught once for the whole course.

The pattern: fit the data + λ · look like what we expect.
What the penalty can say: small, smooth, never negative, piecewise constant, sparse.
Choosing λ: the discrepancy principle, the L-curve, a test image with known truth.
Filter factors: every linear method keeps a fraction of each frequency.
Stopping an iteration early regularises too: the number of iterations plays the role of λ.
A probabilistic reading: the most probable object.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

This day owns regularisation of inverse problems with continuous unknowns (course map). Later days recall it: the graph-cut day’s segmentation energy (data + λ · smoothness over labels), tomography (iterative reconstruction, early stopping), spectral unmixing, and the electives on Markov random fields (total variation) and wavelets (sparsity). The demo is 1D so that every λ is instant and the curves are exact: 256 samples, Gaussian blur σ = 3, noise σn = 0.02, fixed seed.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The pattern
Every restoration so far minimised
\underbrace{\text{misfit}(x, \text{data})}_{\text{how the image was made}} \;+\; \lambda \cdot \underbrace{\text{penalty}(x)}_{\text{what we know about the object}}

The data term encodes the forward model (blur) and the noise: it is small when the blurred estimate looks like the data.
The penalty encodes prior knowledge: it is small for objects we find plausible.
λ says how much we trust each: λ = 0 trusts only the data (the inverse filter); λ → ∞ only the prior.
The same pattern returns on the graph-cut day (each pixel takes one of two labels instead of a grey value), in tomography and in the electives.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
What the penalty can say









Penalty
prefers
keeps
destroys




energy \sum x_i^2
small values
shapes
the mean (shrinks everything)


roughness \sum (x_{i-1} - 2x_i + x_{i+1})^2
smooth
ramps, the mean
steps (rounded), narrow peaks


non-negativity x \ge 0
photons are not negative
everything positive
the dips and ripples below 0


total variation \sum \lvert x_{i+1} - x_i\rvert
piecewise constant
sharp steps
ramps (staircases), small bright spots (shrunk)


sparsity in a basis
few non-zero coefficients
what the basis describes well
what it does not




Non-negativity is a constraint, not a penalty: forbidden, not just expensive.
TV pays for the size of a jump, not its square, so one sharp step costs no more than a gentle ramp of the same height (owner: the Ising/MRF elective). Sparsity: the wavelets elective.
The prior is a modelling choice. Where the data are weak, it is the prior you see.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
section: Try it: what the penalty does
text:
Try it: what the penalty does




Top left: truth (dashed), data (thin blue), estimate (red). Tour: “roughness keeps the mean, energy shrinks it”: energy penalty, λ = 0.3: mean 0.256 against 0.331 in the truth (factor 1/1.3); switch the penalty to roughness: mean 0.333. “TV keeps the step, staircases the ramp” (λ = 0.01): the step is flat at 0.80 and sharp; the ramp comes out in small flat steps; error 0.0219 against 0.0537 for the best roughness λ. “TV shrinks the narrow peak” (profile with close peaks, λ = 0.02): the narrow peak (true height 1.0) comes out at 0.31. “Non-negativity removes the dips”: roughness λ = 1e-4 alone dips to −1.16 (error 0.323); with x ≥ 0 the minimum is 0 and the error 0.109. TV is computed iteratively (reweighted least squares), so its curves fill in after a moment.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Choosing λ
The question every student asks. Four answers:

By eye: common, not reproducible. Fine for a figure, not for a measurement.
Discrepancy principle: the residual (data − blurred estimate) should be as large as the noise, not smaller. A smaller residual means the estimate is fitting the noise. Needs the noise level σn (camera noise unit: offset frames, flat regions).
L-curve: plot the size of the residual against the size of the penalty for many λ, both on log axes. Pick the corner. Needs no σn, but the corner can be vague.
Known truth: a test image (beads, phantom) with the same microscope and noise; choose λ with the smallest error. The honest benchmark, if the test resembles the real data.

One line: generalised cross-validation (leave each pixel out, predict it) also exists; not taught here.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The discrepancy principle in numbers
An image of 256 × 256 pixels with noise σn = 2 grey levels.

The noise alone has root-mean-square 2, so the residual of a good estimate should have RMS ≈ 2: squared norm \approx 65\,536 \times 4 = 262\,144.
λ too small: the estimate follows the noise and the RMS residual drops below 2.
λ too large: the estimate is too smooth to explain the data, and the residual grows above 2, now containing image structure.
The residual grows steadily with λ, so there is exactly one λ with RMS residual = σn.

In the demo (1D, σn = 0.02): RMS residual 0.0151 at λ = 10⁻⁶, 0.0180 at 0.1, 0.0189 at 1, 0.0231 at 10: the discrepancy λ is about 2.6.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The L-curve
For each λ compute the residual norm \rho = \|A\hat x_\lambda - g\| and the penalty \eta = \|D\hat x_\lambda\|; plot \eta against \rho on log–log axes.

Small λ (top left): the penalty explodes (noise is fitted) for almost no gain in fit: a vertical branch.
Large λ (bottom right): the fit gets worse for almost no gain in smoothness: a horizontal branch.
The corner between them balances the two. Here: the point closest to the lower left corner of the plot (after scaling both log axes to the same length).

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The math: choosing λ
Discrepancy principle (Morozov): choose λ with \|A\hat{\mathbf x}_\lambda - \mathbf y\|^2 = N\sigma_n^2 (N data values). For Tikhonov, in the SVD basis (next slides) the residual is \sum_i \big(\tfrac{\lambda}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\big)^2 (\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y)^2, which increases with λ: one root, found by bisection on \log\lambda.
L-curve (Hansen): the parametric curve \big(\log\|A\hat{\mathbf x}_\lambda - \mathbf y\|,\ \log\|D\hat{\mathbf x}_\lambda\|\big). Its corner is defined as the point of maximal curvature
\kappa = \frac{\rho'\eta'' - \rho''\eta'}{(\rho'^2 + \eta'^2)^{3/2}} \quad (\text{derivatives of the logs with respect to } \log\lambda).
On sampled curves from iterative solvers (TV, non-negativity), which wiggle, the curvature is unreliable; the point nearest the lower-left corner of the normalised plot is a robust stand-in (used in the demo).

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Try it: choosing λ




Step-and-ramp profile, roughness penalty. Bottom right: error against the truth (orange) and RMS residual (blue) for 37 values of λ; dashed green: σn; dotted lines: discrepancy λ (green) and L-curve corner (orange). Tour: “λ too small” (10⁻⁶): error 2.29, the estimate is wild; residual 0.0151, below σn: it fits the noise. “λ too large” (100): smooth, rounded steps; error 0.0767, residual 0.0351, above σn. “Discrepancy principle”: λ = 2.57, error 0.0588. “L-curve corner”: λ = 0.178, error 0.0539; the best λ on the path is 0.1 (error 0.0537). Both rules are close to the best error here, the discrepancy principle a little on the smooth side. “The two rules disagree”: correlated noise (neighbouring samples related): the discrepancy λ jumps to 11.7 (error 0.0651), the corner gives 0.056 (error 0.0611), the best is 0.316 (error 0.0586). The discrepancy principle assumes white noise.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Filter factors
Every linear restoration keeps a fraction φ of each frequency (or, in general, of each singular direction of the blur), then divides by the blur’s gain s there.

The kept fraction φ against the blur’s gain s at that frequency, for Tikhonov (two λ), Landweber (two iteration counts, next slides) and the truncated inverse.
Inverse: φ = 1 everywhere. Truncated: φ = 1 or 0. Tikhonov: \varphi = s^2/(s^2 + \lambda), a smooth step at s^2 \approx \lambda.
Regularisation = choosing this curve. Numbers, λ = 0.01: s = 1 keeps 0.99, s = 0.5 keeps 0.96, s = 0.1 keeps 0.5.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The math: filter factors
Write the blur by its singular value decomposition A = U\Sigma V^\top (singular values s_i, singular vectors \mathbf u_i, \mathbf v_i). The inverse is \mathbf x = \sum_i \frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}\mathbf v_i. Any linear restoration is
\hat{\mathbf x} = \sum_i \varphi_i\,\frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}\,\mathbf v_i ,
with inverse \varphi_i = 1, truncated SVD \varphi_i \in \{0, 1\}, Tikhonov (energy) \varphi_i = \dfrac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}.

With \mathbf y = A\mathbf x + \mathbf n, term i carries the noise \varphi_i\,n_i/s_i (n_i = \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf n): small s_i amplifies, small \varphi_i suppresses.
For a circular blur the \mathbf v_i are the Fourier waves and s_i = |H(f)|: filter factors are gains per frequency, as in the last unit.
Tikhonov’s \varphi follows from the normal equations: (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf x = A^\top\mathbf y gives, in the SVD basis, (s_i^2 + \lambda)\,x_i = s_i\,(\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y).

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Stopping early regularises
An iterative method that starts from a flat (zero) image and improves the fit step by step:

picks up the strong frequencies (large s) first, the weak ones (small s, noisy) last;
after k steps it acts like a filter whose roll-off moves to smaller s as k grows: the number of iterations plays the role of λ (roughly \lambda \approx 1/k);
the error against the truth first falls, then rises again (semi-convergence), while the data fit keeps improving.

The simplest such method, Landweber: blur the estimate, subtract it from the data, blur the difference back (with the mirrored PSF), add it to the estimate. Filter factors 1 - (1 - s^2)^k:

s = 0.5: k = 1, 4, 16 keep 0.25, 0.68, 0.99.
s = 0.1: k = 16 keeps 0.15; k = 100 keeps 0.63. Weak frequencies need many iterations, which is why stopping early regularises.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The math: early stopping
Landweber: \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + \omega A^\top(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x_k), \mathbf x_0 = 0, 0 < \omega < 2/s_{\max}^2. In the SVD basis each component evolves alone: with c_i = \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y,
x_{k+1,i} = (1 - \omega s_i^2)\,x_{k,i} + \omega s_i c_i \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_{k,i} = \big(1 - (1 - \omega s_i^2)^k\big)\frac{c_i}{s_i}.
So \varphi_i^{(k)} = 1 - (1 - \omega s_i^2)^k. For small \omega s_i^2, (1 - \omega s_i^2)^k \approx e^{-k\omega s_i^2}, which falls from 1 to 0 around s_i^2 \approx 1/(k\omega): like Tikhonov with \lambda \approx 1/(\omega k).

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Try it: iterations as λ




“Restore by: stopping after k iterations” (Landweber, from zero). Top right shows the filter factors: as k grows the red step moves right to left across the frequencies. Bottom right: error (orange) falls to its minimum at k = 32 (0.0542), then rises: 0.0586 at k = 100, 0.143 at 1000, 0.375 at 10 000. The residual (blue) keeps falling. The discrepancy rule (first k with residual ≤ σn) stops at k = 6, early but safe. Tick “non-negative steps”: the iterate stays ≥ 0 and the late iterations are less wild.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
A probabilistic reading

Data term = how likely are these data if this were the object (the noise model: Gaussian noise gives squared differences).
Penalty = how likely is this object before we look (the prior: smooth objects are likely, wild ones unlikely).
Minimising data term + λ · penalty finds the most probable object given both (the maximum a posteriori, MAP, estimate).
λ is the ratio of how much we trust the data to how much we trust the prior: more noise → larger λ.
Modern deep learning (the last core day) replaces the hand-made prior by one learned from many images.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
The math: MAP
Gaussian noise \mathbf y = A\mathbf x + \mathbf n, \mathbf n \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma_n^2 I), and a Gaussian prior D\mathbf x \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2 I):
-\log p(\mathbf x \mid \mathbf y) = \frac{1}{2\sigma_n^2}\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|D\mathbf x\|^2 + \text{const}.
Multiplying by 2\sigma_n^2: Tikhonov with \lambda = \sigma_n^2/\tau^2. More noise or a tighter prior → larger λ.

A Laplace prior p \propto e^{-|t|/b} on the differences gives the total-variation penalty; on coefficients in a basis, the \ell^1 (sparsity) penalty.
Poisson noise instead of Gaussian changes the data term to \sum_i (A\mathbf x)_i - y_i\log(A\mathbf x)_i: the next unit.

title: Regularisation: what we add, and how much
text:
Summary

Restoration = data term + λ · penalty; the penalty is what we know about the object, λ how much we trust it.
Penalties: energy (shrinks the mean), roughness (smooth, keeps the mean), non-negativity (a constraint), TV (keeps steps, staircases ramps, shrinks spots), sparsity.
Choosing λ: discrepancy (residual = noise level, needs σn, assumes white noise), L-curve corner (no σn, can be vague), known truth on a test image.
Filter factors: every linear method keeps a fraction \varphi of each frequency; Tikhonov s^2/(s^2 + \lambda).
Early stopping regularises: Landweber’s factors 1 - (1 - s^2)^k; the error is U-shaped in k (semi-convergence).
MAP reading: λ = noise variance / prior variance.

title: Quiz: regularisation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A restoration minimises data term + λ · penalty; σn is the noise standard deviation.

Q1. In “data term + λ · penalty”, what does each of the three parts express?






Hint





One is about how the image was made, one about the object, one about trust.









Answer





The data term measures how well the blurred estimate explains the data (the forward model and the noise). The penalty measures how implausible the estimate is as an object (prior knowledge: small, smooth, non-negative, piecewise constant). λ sets how much the prior counts relative to the data.




Q2. A restoration with the roughness penalty turns a sharp step into a smooth S-curve. Which penalty would keep the step, and what would it do to a gentle ramp?






Hint





Which penalty charges a jump by its size rather than its square?









Answer





Total variation, \sum|x_{i+1} - x_i|: a single sharp step costs the same as a ramp of the same height, so it has no reason to round the step. But it prefers flat pieces, so a gentle ramp is turned into a staircase of small flat steps (and small bright spots are shrunk).




Q3. With the discrepancy principle the RMS residual should equal σn. What does it mean if the residual is much smaller than σn?






Hint





The residual is data minus the blurred estimate. What is left in it if it is smaller than the noise?









Answer





The estimate explains part of the noise as if it were signal: it is over-fitted, λ is too small. A good estimate leaves behind about the noise itself.




Q4. The noise level doubles. Should the best λ grow or shrink? By roughly what factor, according to the MAP reading?






Hint





λ = σn² / τ².









Answer





It should grow: the data deserve less trust. In the MAP reading λ = σn²/τ², so doubling σn multiplies λ by 4 (if the prior stays the same).




Q5. What are the two branches of the L-curve, and where is the good λ?






Hint





Log residual norm across, log penalty up.









Answer





For small λ the penalty explodes (noise is fitted) for almost no improvement of the fit: a steep, vertical branch. For large λ the fit gets worse for almost no gain in smoothness: a flat, horizontal branch. The good λ is at the corner where the two meet.




Q6. Tikhonov with λ = 0.01: what fraction of a frequency with blur gain s = 0.1 is kept? And with s = 0.5?






Hint





\varphi = s^2/(s^2 + \lambda).









Answer





s = 0.1: 0.01/(0.01 + 0.01) = 0.5. s = 0.5: 0.25/0.26 = 0.96. The roll-off sits where s^2 \approx \lambda, here s \approx 0.1.




Q7. An iterative restoration is run for 10 000 iterations “to be sure it has converged”. Why can that be worse than stopping at 30?






Hint





Which frequencies does the iteration add last?









Answer





Starting from a flat image, the iteration first restores the strong (low) frequencies and only later the weak (high) ones, which carry mostly noise. Running to convergence approaches the inverse filter, which amplifies that noise. The error against the truth is U-shaped in the number of iterations (semi-convergence): the number of iterations acts like λ.




Q8. (math) Show that for a Landweber step \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + A^\top(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x_k) from \mathbf x_0 = 0, the component along the i-th singular vector is multiplied by 1 - (1 - s_i^2)^k compared with the inverse.






Hint





Write x_{k,i} = \mathbf v_i^\top\mathbf x_k and use A^\top A\mathbf v_i = s_i^2\mathbf v_i.









Answer





With c_i = \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y: x_{k+1,i} = (1 - s_i^2)x_{k,i} + s_i c_i. The fixed point is c_i/s_i (the inverse); the distance to it shrinks by (1 - s_i^2) per step, from c_i/s_i at k = 0. So x_{k,i} = (1 - (1 - s_i^2)^k)\,c_i/s_i.

text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Restoration
minimise \lVert A x - y\rVert^2 + \lambda\cdot\text{penalty}(x)


Penalties
energy \lVert x\rVert^2; roughness \lVert D^2 x\rVert^2; total variation \sum\lvert x_{i+1} - x_i\rvert; constraint x \ge 0


Filter factor
fraction φ kept of a frequency (singular direction) with blur gain s; Tikhonov s^2/(s^2 + \lambda)


Landweber
x \leftarrow x + A^\top(y - Ax) from x = 0; after k steps \varphi = 1 - (1 - s^2)^k


Discrepancy principle
choose λ with RMS residual = σn


L-curve
log penalty against log residual norm for many λ; choose the corner


MAP
λ = σn² / τ² (noise variance / prior variance)

Math questions
B7. (math) With the SVD A = U\Sigma V^\top, show that the Tikhonov solution of \min\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf x\|^2 is \hat{\mathbf x} = \sum_i \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}\mathbf v_i. With \mathbf y = A\mathbf x + \mathbf n, what noise does term i carry?
B8. (math) Show that the squared residual \|A\hat{\mathbf x}_\lambda - \mathbf y\|^2 of B7 increases with λ (so the discrepancy equation has one solution).
B9. (math) Gaussian noise of variance σn² and a Gaussian prior D\mathbf x \sim \mathcal N(0, \tau^2 I): show that the most probable \mathbf x given \mathbf y is Tikhonov’s with λ = σn²/τ².
B10. (math) Show that for small s^2, Landweber after k steps keeps about the same fraction as Tikhonov with λ = 1/k: compare 1 - e^{-ks^2} with s^2/(s^2 + 1/k) at s^2 = 1/k and for s^2 \ll 1/k and s^2 \gg 1/k.






Solutions (math)





B7. The normal equations (A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf x = A^\top\mathbf y become, with A^\top A = V\Sigma^2V^\top and A^\top\mathbf y = V\Sigma U^\top\mathbf y, and \mathbf x = V\mathbf z: (s_i^2 + \lambda)z_i = s_i\,\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y. So z_i = \frac{s_i}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y = \frac{s_i^2}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\frac{\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y}{s_i}. With \mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y = s_i x_i + n_i, term i is \varphi_i x_i + \varphi_i n_i/s_i: the noise n_i is multiplied by \varphi_i/s_i = s_i/(s_i^2 + \lambda) \le 1/(2\sqrt\lambda), bounded however small s_i is.
B8. A\hat{\mathbf x} - \mathbf y = \sum_i (\varphi_i - 1)(\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y)\mathbf u_i plus the part of \mathbf y outside the range of A (independent of λ). So \|A\hat{\mathbf x} - \mathbf y\|^2 = \sum_i\big(\frac{\lambda}{s_i^2 + \lambda}\big)^2(\mathbf u_i^\top\mathbf y)^2 + \text{const}, and each \frac{\lambda}{s_i^2 + \lambda} increases with λ.
B9. p(\mathbf x\mid\mathbf y) \propto p(\mathbf y\mid\mathbf x)\,p(\mathbf x) \propto \exp\!\big(-\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2/2\sigma_n^2\big)\exp\!\big(-\|D\mathbf x\|^2/2\tau^2\big). Maximising it = minimising \frac{1}{2\sigma_n^2}\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{1}{2\tau^2}\|D\mathbf x\|^2; multiply by 2\sigma_n^2: \|A\mathbf x - \mathbf y\|^2 + \frac{\sigma_n^2}{\tau^2}\|D\mathbf x\|^2.
B10. (1 - s^2)^k = e^{k\ln(1 - s^2)} \approx e^{-ks^2} for small s^2. At s^2 = 1/k: Landweber 1 - e^{-1} = 0.63, Tikhonov 0.5. For s^2 \ll 1/k both are \approx ks^2; for s^2 \gg 1/k both are \approx 1. The two curves have the same position and similar shape (Landweber’s step is a little sharper).

title: Exercise: regularisation
text:
Explore
A 1D profile (256 samples) is blurred with a Gaussian (σ = 3 samples) and noise σn = 0.02 is added (fixed seed). Top left: truth (dashed), data (thin blue), estimate (red). Top right: the residual (data − blurred estimate) with the ±σn band, or (choose show) the filter factors with the blur’s |H|. Bottom left: the L-curve (penalty against residual norm, log–log) with the current λ (red), the corner (orange) and the discrepancy λ (green). Bottom right: error against the truth (orange) and RMS residual (blue) for 37 values of λ, with σn dashed; vertical lines: current, discrepancy and corner. Restore by switches between λ and stopping Landweber after k iterations. Total variation and non-negativity are computed iteratively; their curves fill in after a moment.



E1. Presets λ too small and λ too large. For each, give the error and the residual from the readout, and compare the residual with σn. Look at the residual panel: where does the residual of the large λ show structure?
E2. Presets discrepancy principle and L-curve corner. Which λ does each choose, with which error? Which λ is best on the path, and how much better is it?
E3. Preset the two rules disagree (correlated noise). Read the discrepancy λ, the corner λ and the best λ with their errors. Which rule is closer to the best, and why does the other fail?
E4. Presets roughness keeps the mean, energy shrinks it, TV keeps the step, staircases the ramp, TV shrinks the narrow peak and non-negativity removes the dips. For each, write one sentence on what the penalty kept and what it destroyed, with a number from the readout or the plot.
E5. Preset iterations as λ: semi-convergence. At which k is the error smallest? Give the error at k = 100, 1000 and 10 000. Which k does the discrepancy rule choose? Watch the filter factors while you move k.
E6. Set the penalty to energy (profile step and ramp, no correlated noise). Compare the discrepancy λ, the corner λ and the best λ, with their errors. Which rule does well here?






Solutions





E1. λ = 10⁻⁶: error 2.29, residual 0.0151, below σn = 0.02: the estimate fits the noise and oscillates wildly. λ = 100: error 0.0767, residual 0.0351, above σn; the residual shows bumps at the step edges and at the top and foot of the ramp: image structure the over-smooth estimate failed to explain.
E2. Discrepancy: λ = 2.57, error 0.0588. Corner: λ = 0.178, error 0.0539. Best on the path: λ = 0.1, error 0.0537. Both rules land near the best error; the corner is almost optimal, the discrepancy principle slightly over-smooths (9 % more error).
E3. Discrepancy λ = 11.7 (error 0.0651), corner λ = 0.056 (error 0.0611), best λ = 0.316 (error 0.0586). The corner is closer here. The discrepancy principle assumes white noise; correlated noise has little high-frequency power, so the residual stays below σn until the estimate is very smooth.
E4. Energy (λ = 0.3) shrinks the whole profile: mean 0.256 against 0.331 in the truth (factor 1/1.3); roughness keeps the mean (0.333). TV (λ = 0.01) keeps the step sharp and flat at 0.80 but turns the ramp into small flat steps; its error 0.0219 is far below the best roughness error (0.0537), because this profile is mostly flat pieces. TV on the narrow peak (λ = 0.02): the peak of height 1.0 comes out at 0.31; TV pays for every jump, and a narrow spot has two jumps for little area. Non-negativity: roughness with λ = 10⁻⁴ dips to −1.16 (error 0.323); adding x ≥ 0 removes the dips (minimum 0) and the error falls to 0.109.
E5. Smallest error at k = 32 (0.0542). At k = 100: 0.0586, at 1000: 0.143, at 10 000: 0.375 (semi-convergence). The residual keeps falling all the time. The discrepancy rule stops at k = 6: early, a little blurred, but safe. The filter-factor step moves from high |H| (low frequencies) towards low |H| as k grows.
E6. Discrepancy λ = 0.0189 (error 0.0552), corner λ = 0.0056 (error 0.0635), best λ = 0.0178 (error 0.0553). Here the discrepancy principle is almost exactly right and the corner too far to the left: the rules have no guarantee, and checking with a known-truth test is the honest way.

title: Exercise: regularisation
text:
Where this leads
The next unit takes the probabilistic reading seriously for photon counts: Richardson–Lucy maximises the Poisson likelihood with an iteration that keeps every pixel non-negative, and its number of iterations is the regularisation parameter, exactly like Landweber’s here. The same “data + λ · penalty” pattern returns on the graph-cut day (with labels instead of intensities) and in the electives on Markov random fields (total variation) and wavelets (sparsity).

title: Quiz: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. RL step: x \leftarrow x \cdot A^\top\big(y/(Ax + b)\big), with A = blur by a PSF that sums to 1 and b = background.

Q1. Why can a Richardson–Lucy estimate never become negative, if it starts positive and the data are non-negative?






Hint





What kind of operations does one step consist of?









Answer





One step multiplies each pixel by a sum of non-negative numbers (ratios of non-negative data to positive model values, weighted by the non-negative PSF). A product of non-negative factors stays non-negative. Linear filters subtract, and can go below zero.




Q2. RL starts from a flat image with the mean of the data. After one step, what is the total of the estimate (no background)?






Hint





Flux is kept every step.









Answer





The same as the total of the data: RL keeps the total number of photons at every iteration (for a PSF that sums to 1). The flat start already has this total, and each step keeps it.




Q3. You run RL on a noisy image and watch the error against a known truth. It falls for 20 iterations, then rises. What is happening, and what do you do with real data where the truth is unknown?






Hint





Which frequencies come in late?









Answer





Semi-convergence: early iterations restore the strong low frequencies, later ones the weak high frequencies, which are mostly noise, so the estimate starts fitting the noise (speckles). With real data: stop when the blurred estimate fits the data to the noise level (misfit about 1 per pixel), or choose the number of iterations on a test sample (beads, phantom) with the same noise, or add a penalty.




Q4. The same specimen is imaged once with 1000 and once with 100 photons per pixel. For which image should you stop RL earlier?






Hint





Where does the noise start to dominate?









Answer





For the 100-photon image: its relative noise is larger, so the frequencies that carry mostly noise start at a lower frequency, and RL reaches them after fewer iterations. In the demo’s bead image: best at 8 iterations with 100 photons, at 40 with 1000.




Q5. After RL the dark background of an image has become full of bright dots, and the camera offset had not been subtracted. Why?






Hint





What does RL do with light it cannot attribute to a background?









Answer





Without a background term, the constant offset must be explained as object light. RL’s estimates are built of sharp bright points (it maximises a Poisson likelihood with no smoothness), so the uniform level is concentrated into dots. Subtract the offset, and put the remaining background in the model (Ax + b).




Q6. In a deconvolved widefield stack, a thin membrane parallel to the coverslip is still smeared over a micrometre in z, while a filament running along z is sharp. Why?






Hint





Where are the frequencies of a horizontal sheet, and what does the widefield OTF miss?









Answer





A horizontal sheet is uniform in x and y, so all its frequencies lie on the k_z axis (k_x = k_y = 0). The widefield OTF is zero in a cone around that axis (the missing cone): those frequencies were never recorded, so no deconvolution can restore them. The vertical filament’s frequencies lie mostly in the k_x, k_y directions, which the OTF covers.




Q7. A deconvolution makes small beads look sharper and smaller than in any other image, with a dark ring around each. What do you suspect?






Hint





Which way was the PSF wrong?









Answer





The PSF used is too wide: the method removes more blur than there was, over-sharpening the beads (too small) and digging dark halos around them. A PSF that is too narrow does the opposite: it leaves blur and looks “safe”.




Q8. Why does blind deconvolution without constraints tend to return the blurred image itself?






Hint





Is there a PSF and an object that explain the data perfectly without any deblurring?









Answer





“PSF = a single point, object = the observed image” reproduces the data exactly, so the likelihood has no reason to prefer the true pair. Alternating updates drift towards this trivial solution. Constraints (limited size, smoothness, a parametric shape, a known width) are needed to rule it out, and even then a good starting PSF matters.




Q9. (math) Show that one RL step without background keeps the total, \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_i y_i, using A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1.






Hint





Write \sum_j x_j [A^\top r]_j = \sum_i r_i (A\mathbf x)_i.









Answer





With r_i = y_i/(A\mathbf x)_i: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j \sum_i A_{ij} r_i = \sum_i r_i \sum_j A_{ij}x_j = \sum_i \frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}(A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_i y_i. (A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1 is what makes the flat start’s total equal to the data total, and gives the update its fixed-point form.)

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
About this lecture
Last unit matched objects and counted them. Often what matters is not the match but the outline or the numbers we measure. And the “truth” we compare with is drawn by people.

Boundary metrics: Hausdorff distance and average surface distance, and what each is sensitive to.
Counts and measurements against manual values: why correlation is not agreement, and the Bland–Altman plot: bias and limits of agreement.
Ground truth is uncertain: the agreement between two annotators is the ceiling of any score.
How many annotated images an evaluation needs.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
When the outline matters
A tumour margin, the shape of a cell, the thickness of a membrane: here a good match is not enough.
For every point on the predicted outline, find the distance to the nearest point of the true outline, and the same the other way round. Then summarise all these distances:

Hausdorff distance: the largest of them (both directions). “Every point is within H pixels of the other outline.”
Average surface distance (ASD): the mean. “The typical outline error is ASD pixels.”
HD95: the 95th percentile, a compromise that ignores the worst 5 %.

In pixels, or in µm if the pixel size is known.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Three kinds of outline error


Uniform one-pixel offset: every distance is 1 px. Hausdorff = ASD = 1; IoU 0.95.
One thin spike, 14 px long: IoU hardly notices (0.994), Hausdorff jumps to 14; ASD stays small (0.40).
A tiny fragment far away: IoU 0.998, Hausdorff 38; HD95 0 (the fragment is less than 5 % of the outline).

IoU and Dice count pixels, the boundary metrics measure distances: choose by what matters.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
section: The math: Hausdorff and surface distances
text:
The math: Hausdorff and surface distances
Boundaries \partial A, \partial B (finite sets of boundary points), d(a, \partial B) = \min_{b \in \partial B}\|a - b\|.
h(A, B) = \max_{a \in \partial A} d(a, \partial B), \qquad H(A, B) = \max\big(h(A, B),\, h(B, A)\big)
\text{ASD} = \frac{\sum_{a \in \partial A} d(a, \partial B) + \sum_{b \in \partial B} d(b, \partial A)}{|\partial A| + |\partial B|}
The directed distance h is not symmetric: a fragment of B far from A raises h(B, A) but not h(A, B).
Fast computation with the distance transform (the morphology day): the distance transform of “not \partial B” gives d(x, \partial B) at every pixel x in one pass, O(N) for N pixels; read it on \partial A.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Try it: boundary distances




Grey: the true outline, blue: the prediction; drag the round handles to deform the prediction. Whiskers join boundary points to the nearest point of the other outline; the red whisker is the Hausdorff distance. Tour: “one thin spike”: IoU 0.994, Hausdorff 14.0, ASD 0.40, the histogram has a long thin tail. “one-pixel dilation”: everything 1.00, IoU 0.951. “a stray fragment”: drag the dashed circle around; Hausdorff follows it, IoU and HD95 do not move. “same error, small object” (radius 8 px): the same 1-px error now gives IoU 0.787. Move the radius slider: the pixel errors stay, IoU changes.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Counts and measurements
Often the outlines are only a means: the result is a number per image (cells per field, mean nuclear area, intensity per cell).
Then evaluate the numbers directly: for a set of images, measure the same quantity automatically and manually, and compare the two lists.
The first idea is a scatter plot of automated against manual, with the correlation r. It answers the wrong question.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Correlation is not agreement
A method that always reports 80 % of the manual count has correlation r = 1 and is wrong by 20 %.

Correlation measures whether the points lie on some straight line, not whether they lie on the identity line.
A wider range of values gives a higher r for the same errors: counts from 10 to 150 cells make almost any method look good.

We want to know how far apart the two measurements are, and whether that depends on the size of the value.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
The math: Bland–Altman
Pairs (x_i, y_i), i = 1, \dots, n (reference, method). Differences d_i = y_i - x_i, means m_i = (x_i + y_i)/2.
\text{bias} = \bar d, \qquad s_d = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{n-1}\textstyle\sum_i (d_i - \bar d)^2}, \qquad \text{limits} = \bar d \pm 1.96\, s_d
(95 % of differences inside, if they are roughly normal). Proportional bias: fit d_i = \alpha + \beta m_i; \beta \ne 0 means the error depends on the size.
Why correlation ignores bias: for y = a x + b with a > 0, r(x, y) = 1 for every a and b. And if y = a x + b exactly, then d = (a - 1)x + b and m = \frac{a + 1}{2}x + \frac b2, so the points lie on a line with slope \frac{2(a - 1)}{a + 1}: zero only for a = 1.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
section: Bias and scatter have different cures
text:
Bias and scatter have different cures

Bias (systematic): can be calibrated away if it is stable (multiply by 1/0.8, subtract the offset), measured on a calibration set.
Scatter (random): cannot be calibrated; only a better method, or averaging over more objects, reduces it.
For comparing two conditions measured the same way, a constant bias often cancels. But not if it depends on the condition: if treated wells are denser and merge more, the undercount is larger there and fakes (or hides) an effect.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
section: Measurements: small objects, large relative error
text:
Measurements: small objects, large relative error
Areas of objects, automated vs manual: a one-pixel outline offset is a fixed absolute error at the boundary, so a large relative error for small objects.

A disc of radius r drawn 1 px too large: area ratio (r + 1)^2 / r^2: 1.78 for r = 3, 1.21 for r = 10, 1.14 for r = 15.
In a Bland–Altman plot of areas the differences grow with the size, while the ratio plot shows the relative bias growing for small objects.
The same effect makes perimeters and small areas biased in the measurements day; the point spread function adds to it (the image formation day).
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Try it: agreement of counts




40 synthetic images with manual counts 17–146. Tour: “r = 0.99, still 20 % off”: r 0.997, bias −16.2, mean ratio 0.81. “merges at high density”: r 0.990, the Bland–Altman cloud slopes (slope −0.38), limits −41 to +9. “scatter only”: bias 1.2, limits −16.5 to 18.9, no slope. “small objects: area bias”: 150 objects, outline 1 px too large: the ratio is about 1.66 for objects below 50 px², about 1.17 above 400 px². “two annotators”: bias 0.55, limits −3.2 to 4.3: the ceiling.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Ground truth is uncertain
Annotators disagree: on boundaries (a few pixels, where exactly is the edge of a blurred nucleus?) and on objects (is this dim blob a nucleus? is this dividing cell one or two?).

The agreement between two annotators (their F1 against \tau, their Bland–Altman plot) is the ceiling of any score against one of them.
A method with F1 0.90 against annotator A, where annotator B scores 0.88 against A, is “as good as a human”, not “better than 0.88”.
Remedies: several annotators and a consensus; an “ignore” label for ambiguous objects; synthetic data where the truth is known by construction (but then the domain differs from real images).
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
How many annotated images?
A score from few objects wobbles. A recall of 0.9 measured on n independent objects has a standard error
\text{SE} = \sqrt{0.9 \cdot 0.1 / n}: \quad 0.055 \text{ for } n = 30, \quad 0.017 \text{ for } n = 300.
Roughly 95 % of the time the true recall lies within ±2 SE of the measured one.
But objects in one image are not independent: same illumination, same density, same staining. 300 objects from 2 images are closer to “2 measurements” than to 300. Evaluate per image, look at the spread across images, and collect images from several experiments. Units 3 and 4 make this precise.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
section: The math: standard error of a proportion
text:
The math: standard error of a proportion
A recall is a proportion: \hat p = X/n with X the number of found objects among n. If the objects are independent with the same p, X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p), \text{Var}(\hat p) = p(1 - p)/n:
\text{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \le \frac{1}{2\sqrt n}.
For a 95 % interval of half-width w: n \ge 1.96^2\, p(1-p)/w^2; in the worst case p = \frac12 and w = 0.05: n = 385.
With m objects per image and correlation \rho between objects of the same image, the variance grows by the design effect 1 + (m - 1)\rho: the effective number of objects is n / (1 + (m-1)\rho) (derived in the replicates unit).
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Summary

Hausdorff = the worst boundary distance (sensitive to one spike or a stray fragment); ASD = the typical one; HD95 in between. IoU and Dice hardly see thin errors.
Evaluate counts and measurements directly. Correlation is not agreement.
Bland–Altman: difference against mean; bias (calibratable), limits of agreement (scatter), slope = proportional bias (then use ratios).
A one-pixel outline error is a large relative error for small objects.
Inter-annotator agreement is the ceiling; use several annotators, consensus, “ignore” labels.
A score from n objects has SE \approx \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}, and objects within an image are not independent: count images and experiments.
crumbs: Boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run Richardson–Lucy by hand for two steps and check that it keeps the total and stays non-negative,
explain semi-convergence and choose when to stop, depending on the number of photons,
say what 3D deconvolution does for widefield and confocal stacks, and why it cannot fill the missing cone,
predict the effect of a wrong PSF, and why blind deconvolution needs constraints,

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the demo. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Data
photon counts y after removing the camera offset; Poisson noise


RL step
blur the guess, ratio y/(\text{blurred} + b), spread the ratio back with the mirrored PSF, multiply


Start
flat, every pixel = mean of y (minus the background)


Properties
never negative; total kept; the Poisson likelihood never decreases


Semi-convergence
error against the truth falls, then rises: the number of iterations is the regularisation parameter


Missing cone
the widefield OTF is zero in a cone around the k_z axis; confocal fills it


Wrong PSF
too narrow: blur left; too wide: halos, ringing, objects too small

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
By hand
B1. 1D, circular, 4 pixels, PSF (0.25, 0.5, 0.25), data \mathbf y = (0, 2, 2, 0), no background. (a) The flat start is \mathbf x_0 = (1, 1, 1, 1). Why 1? (b) Compute \mathbf x_1: blur \mathbf x_0, form the ratio, spread it back, multiply. (c) Compute \mathbf x_2. Check the sum after each step. (d) What does the estimate approach if you continue? Is that plausible for these data?
B2. In the demo’s bead image the error against the truth is smallest after 40 iterations with 1000 photons per unit brightness, and after 8 iterations with 100 photons. (a) Explain why fewer photons need fewer iterations. (b) The misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) falls to about 1 within the first 10 iterations at 100 photons and then only slowly. Why is “misfit ≈ 1” a reasonable place to stop?
B3. A widefield stack of a cell contains: round beads, microtubules running in all directions, the nuclear envelope (a closed surface), and a flat basal membrane on the coverslip. After 3D deconvolution, which of these is restored least in z, and why? What would change with a confocal stack?
B4. A bead of true FWHM 150 nm is imaged and deconvolved (a) with the correct PSF, (b) with a PSF 20 % too wide, (c) with a PSF 20 % too narrow. Which way is the measured FWHM biased in (b) and (c), and what else do you see around the bead?
B5. An image has a camera offset of 100 counts per pixel and a sample whose brightest spots reach 300 counts. You run RL on the raw image without a background term. Predict what happens to the dark areas, and to the total flux of the estimate.
B6. Blind deconvolution alternates RL steps on the object and on the PSF. (a) Show that “PSF = a point, object = the data” is a perfect fit. (b) Name three constraints that rule this out, and the price of each.






Solutions





B1. (a) The mean of the data: (0 + 2 + 2 + 0)/4 = 1. The flat start has the same total (4) as the data. (b) Blurred \mathbf x_0 = (1, 1, 1, 1); ratio (0, 2, 2, 0); spread back: pixel 1: 0.25 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 0 + 0.25 \cdot 2 = 0.5 (its neighbours are pixels 4 and 2), pixel 2: 0.25 \cdot 0 + 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.25 \cdot 2 = 1.5, pixel 3: 1.5, pixel 4: 0.5. \mathbf x_1 = (0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 0.5), sum 4. (c) Blurred \mathbf x_1: pixel 1: 0.25 \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot 0.5 + 0.25 \cdot 1.5 = 0.75, pixel 2: 0.25 \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 \cdot 1.5 + 0.25 \cdot 1.5 = 1.25, pixel 3: 1.25, pixel 4: 0.75. Ratio (0, 1.6, 1.6, 0). Spread back: (0.4, 1.2, 1.2, 0.4). \mathbf x_2 = (0.2, 1.8, 1.8, 0.2), sum 4. (A third step gives (0.071, 1.929, 1.929, 0.071).) (d) The outer pixels shrink towards 0 and the middle ones grow towards 2: (0, 2, 2, 0). Plausible for these noise-free data: blurring (0, 2, 2, 0) circularly gives (0.5, 1.5, 1.5, 0.5), and RL is undoing exactly such a blur. With noisy data the same sharpening would also amplify noise.
B2. (a) With fewer photons the relative noise is larger (1/\sqrt{\text{count}}), so the noise dominates already at lower frequencies. RL brings in the weak, high frequencies only after many iterations, so it starts fitting noise sooner. (b) A Poisson deviance of about 1 per pixel is what the noise alone produces: the blurred estimate explains the data as well as the noise level allows. Pushing it further fits the noise (a discrepancy principle for counts).
B3. The flat basal membrane: it is uniform in x and y, so its frequencies lie along the k_z axis, inside the widefield missing cone; it stays smeared in z. The horizontal parts of the nuclear envelope (top and bottom) suffer in the same way, its sides much less; beads and microtubules running at an angle are restored well. A confocal OTF has no missing cone, so the membrane is restored as well (with less contrast gain overall).
B4. (b) Too wide: over-sharpened, the measured FWHM is too small (below the value obtained with the right PSF), with a dark rim (halo) and possibly ringing around the bead. (c) Too narrow: under-restored, the FWHM stays too large; no halo. In the demo (beads, 1000 photons, k = 100): 2.57 px with a PSF 30 % too wide, 2.63 px correct, 3.25 px 30 % too narrow, and a rim down to 0.013 against a background of 0.05 for the wide PSF.
B5. The offset (100 counts everywhere) must be explained as object light. RL concentrates it into bright speckles in the dark areas, and the sharpening of real structure suffers. The total flux of the estimate equals the total of the raw data, including the offset: it is about 100 × (number of pixels) too large, so any intensity measurement is biased. Subtract the offset and model the remaining background.
B6. (a) With h = a single point (sum 1), h \ast x = x; with x = y the model reproduces the data exactly, the best possible fit. (b) A size limit (the PSF must be zero outside a radius; price: the true PSF may be larger), smoothness or a parametric shape such as a Gaussian of unknown width (price: real aberrations are not captured), a known width or a measured starting PSF that is changed only a little (price: it must be known). In the demo none of them stops the drift completely: unconstrained, the width falls from 7.1 px to 3.3 px in 300 iterations (true 4.8 px); with a Gaussian shape to 6.0 px.




Math questions
B7. (math) For y_i \sim \text{Poisson}((A\mathbf x)_i) write the log-likelihood, compute its gradient, and show that the RL update x_j \leftarrow x_j [A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j has the maximum-likelihood conditions as its fixed points (for x_j > 0), using A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1.
B8. (math) With a background, \mathbf y \approx A\mathbf x + b: show that the total of the new estimate is \sum_i y_i\frac{(A\mathbf x)_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i + b}. When is it equal to \sum_i (y_i - b)?
B9. (math) Show that RL can be written as a gradient step with a pixel-dependent step size: x_j^{\text{new}} = x_j + x_j\,\partial\ell/\partial x_j (no background). Why does this step size keep the estimate non-negative where a plain gradient step would not?






Solutions (math)





B7. \ell(\mathbf x) = \sum_i y_i\log(A\mathbf x)_i - (A\mathbf x)_i - \log y_i!. \partial\ell/\partial x_j = \sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i} - \sum_i A_{ij} = [A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j - 1, using \sum_i A_{ij} = [A^\top\mathbf 1]_j = 1. At a maximum with x_j > 0 the gradient is 0, i.e. [A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j = 1, which is exactly the condition x_j^{\text{new}} = x_j of the RL update. (Where x_j = 0 the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker condition only requires the gradient to be ≤ 0, and RL leaves the pixel at 0.)
B8. \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j\sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i + b} = \sum_i \frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i + b}(A\mathbf x)_i. It equals \sum_i(y_i - b) when the model fits the data exactly, (A\mathbf x)_i + b = y_i for every i; in general only approximately (in expectation at the right \mathbf x, since E[y_i] = (A\mathbf x)_i + b).
B9. x_j + x_j\,\partial\ell/\partial x_j = x_j + x_j([A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j - 1) = x_j[A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j: the RL update. The step size is proportional to x_j itself, so a pixel close to 0 moves only by a small amount; since [A^\top(\mathbf y/A\mathbf x)]_j \ge 0, the new value is never negative. A plain gradient step with a fixed step size can overshoot below 0 where the gradient is negative.

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
Explore: Richardson–Lucy step by step
A 128 × 128 test object is blurred (Gaussian PSF σ = 2 px, or Airy) and Poisson noise is drawn (fixed seed); “photons at 1” is the expected count where the object has value 1. RL runs in the background after every change and keeps about 30 snapshots; the iteration k slider scrubs through them. Panels: observed, RL estimate, error (estimate − truth, blue negative, red positive), and the true PSF next to the one used (or the current blind estimate). Right of them: a profile along row 24 (through the 1 : 4 bead pair and the edge), and the error (% of the largest true value) and the misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) against the iteration, with the best Wiener error dashed. The readout gives the peak and integrated ratio of the bead pair (truth 4.0) and the total flux.



E1. Preset noise: semi-convergence (100 photons). At which k is the error smallest, and how large is it? What are the error and the misfit at k = 10 and k = 1000? Compare with the best Wiener error.
E2. Preset no noise: keeps improving. Where is the error smallest now, and what happens to the misfit? Then fewer photons: stop earlier (20 photons): the best k and error. Set photons to 1000 (preset semi, then the slider): the best k?
E3. Preset 1000 iterations: speckles (cell phantom). Compare the error at k = 5 and k = 1000 and describe the background. Then forgot the background: what happens in the dark regions, and how does the total flux of the estimate compare with the data? Tick background in the model: the best k and error.
E4. Presets PSF too wide: halos and PSF too narrow: still blurred (k = 100). Describe the beads in each, and read the peak ratio of the bead pair. Which error is lower?
E5. Preset blind: the PSF shrinks to a point. Follow the FWHM of the blind PSF in the readout at k = 10, 100 and 300 (true 4.76 px). Then blind with a Gaussian-shape constraint. Which constraint helps, and does either give the true PSF?






Solutions





E1. Smallest error at k = 8: 2.20 %. At k = 10: error 2.20 %, misfit 0.98; at k = 1000: error 10.4 %, misfit 0.89 (below 1: noise is fitted). Best Wiener: 2.49 %, so RL at the right stopping point beats it.
E2. Without noise the error keeps falling to k = 1000 (1.22 %), and the misfit drops towards 0 (0.0002): nothing stops the deblurring but the iterations. With 20 photons: best at k = 3 (2.56 %). With 1000 photons: best at k = 40 (1.79 %).
E3. k = 5: 2.74 %; k = 1000: 18.7 %; the background is broken up into bright speckles and the cell interior is grainy. Forgot the background (30 photons per pixel, not in the model): the dark regions fill with speckles (up to 0.70 where the truth is 0.05), the error is never below 27.5 %, and the total flux of the estimate equals that of the data, background included (7.5e5). With the background in the model: best at k = 10, 3.18 %, and the flux of the estimate is the data minus the background (2.6e5).
E4. Too wide (×1.3): over-sharpened beads with dark rims, and the pair’s peak ratio is 9.1 instead of 4. Too narrow (×0.7): the beads stay round and wide (peak ratio 4.2, but only because both stay blurred). Error at k = 100: 2.58 % (wide) and 2.47 % (narrow); with the right PSF 1.87 %. Over-sharpening looks better and is not.
E5. No constraint: FWHM 6.44 px at k = 10, 4.90 at 100 (close to the true 4.76), 3.33 at 300: the PSF passes the right width and keeps shrinking towards a point. The Gaussian shape slows the drift (6.90, 6.34, 5.95) but does not find the true width either. The size limit (r ≤ 6 px) changes almost nothing here. Blind estimation needs strong constraints and a good starting PSF.

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
Explore: a 3D stack
A 3D volume of 64 × 32 × 32 voxels (100 nm across, 200 nm between planes) with two beads, a vertical filament, a horizontal sheet 200 nm thick and a hollow sphere, imaged with NA 0.8 in air (widefield or confocal 3D PSF), 1000 photons at value 1. Top row: xz slices (drawn to scale) of truth, observed and RL estimate; bottom row: xy slices at the middle plane. Right: the OTF magnitude in the (k_x, k_z) plane (log scale) with the missing cone dashed, and an axial profile (truth, the blurred stack before noise, and RL, each scaled to its own maximum so that the widths can be compared). The readout gives axial FWHMs, measured on the blurred stack before noise and on the RL estimate.



E6. Preset RL restores the bead in z. Read the bead’s axial FWHM before and after 100 iterations. Then the sheet stays smeared: the sheet’s axial FWHM in the truth, blurred and after 100 and 200 iterations. Explain with the OTF image.
E7. Preset confocal: less to gain, nothing missing. Compare the OTF image with the widefield one, and the FWHMs of bead and sheet with E6.
E8. Preset z-steps too large (800 nm between planes). What happens to the bead’s axial FWHM after RL, and why?






Solutions





E6. Bead: 1476 nm blurred, 526 nm after 100 iterations (444 nm after 200): a factor of about 3. Sheet: 200 nm thick, 4666 nm blurred, 1345 nm after 100 and 1111 nm after 200 iterations: still more than 5 times too thick. The sheet’s frequencies lie along the k_z axis, where the widefield OTF (dark region above and below the centre, inside the dashed cone) is zero: they were never recorded. The bead’s frequencies spread in all directions, and those outside the cone are restored.
E7. The confocal OTF covers the cone (no dark wedge above and below the centre). Bead: 854 nm blurred (already better than widefield) → 233 nm; sheet: 921 nm → 282 nm. Less blur to start with, and no missing information: the sheet is restored too.
E8. With 800 nm steps the bead goes only from 1178 nm to 808 nm (one plane is 800 nm). The stack samples the PSF axially below Nyquist: the fine axial structure is not in the data, and deconvolution cannot sharpen below the sampling.

title: Exercise: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF
text:
Where this leads
The next unit asks what to do when there is nothing to un-blur (classical denoisers compared by what they destroy) and, most importantly, what a restored image may be used for: which measurements survive deconvolution and which do not.

title: Quiz: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A predicted nucleus outline has one thin protrusion of 12 px; elsewhere it is perfect. Which changes most: IoU, average surface distance (ASD) or Hausdorff distance?






Hint





Which of them is a maximum, which an average, which counts pixels?









Answer





The Hausdorff distance: it is the worst boundary distance, so it becomes 12 px. The ASD averages over all boundary points and rises only a little; IoU counts pixels and a thin protrusion has very few.




Q2. You care about the typical error of a cell outline in µm, for objects of very different sizes. Why is IoU a poor choice, and what would you use?






Hint





What does a one-pixel error do to the IoU of a small and of a large object?









Answer





IoU mixes the outline error with the object size: the same 1-px error gives a much lower IoU for a small object. The average surface distance (in pixels or µm) measures the outline error directly and means the same for every size; add Hausdorff or HD95 if single large deviations matter.




Q3. An automated cell count has correlation r = 0.98 with the manual count over 50 images. Is the method accurate?






Hint





What does r say about the identity line?









Answer





Not necessarily. r only says the points lie close to some straight line; a method that always counts 70 % of the cells has r close to 1. Look at the Bland–Altman plot: the bias (mean difference), the limits of agreement, and whether the difference depends on the count.




Q4. In a Bland–Altman plot the differences (auto − manual) go from about 0 for sparse images to −30 for dense ones. Name a likely cause and a better way to report the agreement.






Hint





What goes wrong more often when nuclei touch?









Answer





A proportional bias: in dense images more nuclei touch and are merged, so the undercount grows with the count. One bias and one pair of limits do not describe it; report the ratio auto/manual (or the differences of logarithms) against the size, or the bias as a function of the count.




Q5. Your method undercounts every image by 8 %. Does this matter when you compare treated with control wells? When would it matter?






Hint





Does the bias depend on the condition?









Answer





A constant relative bias cancels when both conditions are measured the same way: the ratio treated/control is unchanged. It matters for absolute numbers (cells per mm²), and when the bias depends on the condition, e.g. if the treatment makes the cells denser and the method merges more of them there.




Q6. Two expert annotators agree with F1 0.85 at \tau = 0.5. A new method scores 0.87 against one of them. What is a fair summary?






Hint





What is the ceiling of any score against one annotator?









Answer





The method agrees with that annotator about as well as another expert does: “as good as a human annotator”, within the uncertainty of both numbers. It is not “better than humans”; it may have learned that annotator’s style. Evaluate against the other annotator or a consensus.




Q7. A recall of 0.9 is measured on 300 objects, all from 3 images. Is \pm 2\sqrt{0.9 \cdot 0.1/300} = \pm 0.035 a fair uncertainty?






Hint





Are the 300 objects independent?









Answer





No, it is too optimistic. The formula assumes 300 independent objects, but objects of one image share its illumination, density and staining. If the method does badly on one image, a whole block of objects fails at once. The real uncertainty is closer to that of a handful of images; evaluate per image and use more images and experiments.




Q8. (math) Show that if auto = 0.8 \cdot manual exactly, the Bland–Altman points lie on a line through the origin with slope -2/9.






Hint





Write the difference and the mean in terms of the manual value x.









Answer





d = 0.8x - x = -0.2x and m = (x + 0.8x)/2 = 0.9x, so d = (-0.2/0.9)\,m = -\frac29 m.

title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute directed distances, the Hausdorff distance and the average surface distance of two small point sets, and say which error each one reacts to,
draw and read a Bland–Altman plot: bias, limits of agreement, proportional bias,
explain why correlation is not agreement, and why a one-pixel outline error is a large relative error for small objects,

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.
