title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




d(a, \partial B)
distance from a boundary point a of A to the nearest boundary point of B


Directed distance h(A, B)
the largest d(a, \partial B) over the boundary points of A


Hausdorff H
\max(h(A, B), h(B, A)): the worst boundary distance


ASD
mean of all d(a, \partial B) and d(b, \partial A) together


HD95
like Hausdorff, but the 95th percentile instead of the maximum


Bland–Altman
difference (method − reference) against the mean of the two, per item


Bias, limits of agreement
mean difference \bar d; \bar d \pm 1.96\,s_d


SE of a proportion
\sqrt{p(1-p)/n} for n independent items

title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
By hand
B1. Two point sets (boundary points): A = \{(0,0), (1,0), (2,0)\} and B = \{(0,1), (1,1), (2,1), (1,4)\}. (a) For every point, the distance to the nearest point of the other set. (b) The directed distances h(A, B) and h(B, A), the Hausdorff distance and the ASD. Which point is responsible for the Hausdorff distance? (c) The ASD without the point (1, 4). If A and B were the outlines of two large regions and (1, 4) the tip of a thin spike, what would IoU say?
B2. Bland–Altman by hand. Manual counts of six images: 20, 35, 50, 65, 80, 100; automated counts: 19, 33, 46, 60, 72, 88. (a) Compute the differences (auto − manual) and the means. (b) Compute the bias, the SD of the differences and the limits of agreement (\pm 1.96 SD). (c) Sketch the plot. Why are these limits misleading here, and what would you plot instead? (d) Estimate the correlation of the two lists without computing it. What does it tell you about agreement?
B3. Two annotators reach an object F1 of 0.86 against each other at \tau = 0.5. Method X scores 0.84 against annotator A, method Y 0.91. (a) What can you conclude about X? (b) A paper presents Y as “better than human”. What would you check first? (c) Name two ways to make the ground truth less uncertain.
B4. A recall of 0.80 is measured on 25 objects. (a) Roughly how wide is its ±2 SE interval? (b) How many objects would you need for ±0.05? (c) Why could even that be optimistic if all objects come from two images?
B5. Predict, then explain. (a) An outline is 2 px too large everywhere. Hausdorff, ASD, and IoU for a nucleus of radius 8 px and one of radius 40 px? (b) An automated area measurement uses outlines that are 1 px too large. For which objects is the relative error largest, and what does the ratio auto/manual look like as a function of size? (c) Method A’s counts are always 10 % too low; method B’s are unbiased but scatter by ±10 %. Which one would you rather use to compare treated with control wells, and why?






Solutions





B1. (a) Each point of A is at distance 1 from the point of B above it: 1, 1, 1. From B: (0,1), (1,1), (2,1) at distance 1; (1, 4) is 4 from (1, 0). (b) h(A, B) = 1, h(B, A) = 4, Hausdorff H = 4, caused by (1, 4). ASD = (1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 4)/7 = 10/7 = 1.43. (c) Without (1, 4): ASD = 6/6 = 1. The spike adds one far point: it dominates the Hausdorff distance and raises the ASD a little, while IoU of the regions would hardly change (a thin spike has almost no area).
B2. (a) Differences: −1, −2, −4, −5, −8, −12. Means: 19.5, 34, 48, 62.5, 76, 94. (b) Bias = -32/6 = -5.33. SD = 4.08. Limits: -5.33 \pm 1.96 \cdot 4.08 = −13.3 to +2.7. (c) The differences fall steadily with the mean: the method undercounts more in dense images (proportional bias, typical of merges). The limits assume one spread for all sizes; here they are too wide for small counts and too narrow for large ones. Plot the ratio auto/manual (0.95, 0.94, 0.92, 0.92, 0.90, 0.88) against the mean, or the differences of logarithms; or report the bias as a function of the count. (d) Very close to 1 (it is 0.9995): the points lie almost exactly on a straight line, just not the identity line. Correlation says nothing about agreement.
B3. (a) X is about as good as a second human, within the uncertainty of both numbers (0.84 vs 0.86). It is not clearly worse. (b) Y agrees with annotator A better than annotator B does. Check whether Y was trained on (or tuned to) annotations by A, or by the same protocol: then Y has learned A’s style (where A draws boundaries, which dim objects A counts). Evaluate against B, or against a consensus. “Better than human” needs an independent truth. (c) Several annotators and a consensus (majority vote, or averaging the outlines); a clear annotation protocol; an “ignore” label for ambiguous objects; synthetic images where the truth is known by construction.
B4. (a) SE = \sqrt{0.8 \cdot 0.2/25} = 0.08: the interval is 0.80 \pm 0.16, from 0.64 to 0.96. (b) Need 2\,\text{SE} = 0.05, i.e. \text{SE} = 0.025: n = 0.16/0.025^2 = 256 objects. (c) The formula assumes independent objects. Objects of the same image share illumination, density and staining; if the method works badly on one of the two images, a whole block of objects fails together. The effective number of independent observations is much smaller (closer to the number of images), so the real uncertainty is larger.
B5. (a) Every boundary point is 2 px from the other outline: Hausdorff = ASD = 2 for both. IoU depends on the size: for a disc of radius r, r^2/(r+2)^2: 0.64 for r = 8, 0.91 for r = 40 (the demo’s nucleus-shaped outline gives 0.64 and 0.91). (b) Largest for the smallest objects: a disc of radius r gets the area \pi(r+1)^2 instead of \pi r^2, ratio (1 + 1/r)^2: 1.78 for r = 3, 1.21 for r = 10. The ratio falls towards 1 as the size grows, like 1 + 2/r. (c) Method A: a constant relative bias cancels when comparing two conditions measured the same way (a 10 % drop is still a 10 % drop), as long as the bias does not depend on the condition. B’s scatter adds noise to every well and needs more wells to see the same effect. (If treated wells are denser and A undercounts dense wells more, A’s bias would no longer cancel.)




Math questions
B6. (math) Show that the Hausdorff distance satisfies the triangle inequality H(A, C) \le H(A, B) + H(B, C) for non-empty finite (or compact) sets. Is the ASD a metric?
B7. (math) Suppose auto = a \cdot manual + b exactly. Show that the Bland–Altman points lie on a straight line and find its slope in terms of a. When is the slope zero? What is the correlation of auto and manual?
B8. (math) Show that \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} is largest at p = \frac12, and find the n needed for a 95 % interval of half-width 0.05 in the worst case.






Solutions (math)





B6. For a \in A, let b \in B be its nearest point: d(a, B) \le h(A, B). Then for any c \in C, \|a - c\| \le \|a - b\| + \|b - c\|, so d(a, C) \le \|a - b\| + d(b, C) \le h(A, B) + h(B, C). Taking the maximum over a: h(A, C) \le h(A, B) + h(B, C) \le H(A, B) + H(B, C). The same with the roles of A and C swapped gives h(C, A) \le H(C, B) + H(B, A); together H(A, C) \le H(A, B) + H(B, C). (H is also symmetric, and H(A, B) = 0 only if A = B for closed sets, so it is a metric.) The ASD is symmetric and zero for equal sets, but it is not a metric: it violates the triangle inequality. Example in 1D: A = \{0\}, B = \{0, 1\}, C = \{1\}: ASD(A, B) = (0 + 0 + 1)/3 = \frac13, ASD(B, C) = \frac13, but ASD(A, C) = 1 > \frac23.
B7. With y = ax + b: d = y - x = (a - 1)x + b and m = (x + y)/2 = \frac{a+1}{2}x + \frac b2. Eliminate x = (2m - b)/(a + 1): d = \frac{2(a-1)}{a+1}m + b\,\frac{2}{a+1}, a straight line with slope \frac{2(a-1)}{a+1}. The slope is zero only for a = 1 (then all points sit at d = b: a pure offset). For a = 0.8: slope -0.22. The correlation is r = 1 for every a > 0 and every b.
B8. f(p) = p(1 - p) has f'(p) = 1 - 2p = 0 at p = \frac12 and f'' = -2 < 0: a maximum, f(\frac12) = \frac14. So SE \le \frac{1}{2\sqrt n}. A 95 % interval of half-width w needs 1.96\,\text{SE} \le w: n \ge 1.96^2/(4w^2) = 384.1 for w = 0.05, so 385 objects (400 with the rule of thumb 2 SE). These are independent objects.

title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Explore: boundary distances
The grey outline is the truth, the blue one the prediction; drag the round handles to deform the prediction (each handle moves the outline locally). The square handle is the tip of an optional thin spike, the dashed circle an optional stray fragment. Whiskers join boundary points to the nearest point of the other outline, coloured by length; the red whisker is the Hausdorff distance. The object radius slider scales the object while the pixel errors stay the same.



C1. Preset one-pixel dilation. Read IoU, Hausdorff, HD95 and ASD. Why are the three distances equal?
C2. Preset one thin spike (14 px). Read the five numbers. Now drag the spike tip to make it about 28 px long, and then about 7 px. Which numbers change a lot, which hardly at all?
C3. Preset a stray fragment. Drag the fragment closer to the object, and then into the middle of the object. What happens to Hausdorff, HD95, ASD and IoU?
C4. Preset same error, small object (radius 8 px, 1 px too large). Compare IoU with C1. Move the radius slider from 5 to 50 and note IoU at a few sizes. Which metric would you use to compare outline quality across small and large objects?
C5. Choose a typical outline (radius 40 px) and read the numbers. Then set the radius to 10. Which numbers stay and which change?






Solutions





C1. IoU 0.951, Dice 0.975, Hausdorff 1.00, HD95 1.00, ASD 1.00. Every boundary point of either outline is exactly 1 px from the other outline, so the maximum, the 95th percentile and the mean of the distances are all 1.
C2. At 14 px: IoU 0.994, Hausdorff 14.0, HD95 7.48, ASD 0.40. At 28 px: IoU 0.987, Hausdorff 28.0, HD95 20.5, ASD 1.48. At 7 px: IoU 0.997, Hausdorff 7.0, HD95 0.93, ASD 0.12. Hausdorff follows the tip exactly; HD95 reacts once the spike is long enough to make up more than 5 % of the predicted outline; ASD grows with the spike’s length (it is an average over all points); IoU barely moves (the spike is 3 px wide).
C3. In its starting position: Hausdorff 37.8, HD95 0.00, ASD 0.87, IoU 0.998. Near the object (just outside): Hausdorff about 6 and ASD about 0.1; in the middle of the object Hausdorff is about 34 (its distance to the true outline) and IoU 1.000 (it lies inside the object anyway). HD95 stays 0: the fragment is less than 5 % of the outline points. Hausdorff measures the worst point, wherever it is.
C4. Radius 8 px: IoU 0.787, Dice 0.881, while Hausdorff = HD95 = ASD = 1.00 as in C1 (IoU 0.951 there). One pixel too large gives IoU 0.691 at radius 5, 0.787 at 8, 0.877 at 15, 0.905 at 20, 0.951 at 40, 0.960 at 50. To compare outline quality across sizes, a distance in pixels (or µm), such as ASD, says the same thing for every size; IoU mixes outline error and object size.
C5. Radius 40: IoU 0.940, Hausdorff 2.50, HD95 2.20, ASD 1.21. Radius 10: Hausdorff and ASD hardly change (2.50 and 1.23: the pixel offsets are the same), but IoU drops to 0.777.

title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Explore: agreement of counts
40 synthetic images with manual counts (annotator A) and automated counts from a model: scale (auto ≈ scale × manual), a constant offset, an undercount that grows with the count (density undercount, as from merges) and random scatter. Top left: automated against manual with the identity line (dashed) and the correlation r. Bottom left: the ratio auto/manual against the mean. Right: the Bland–Altman plot with the bias (red), the limits of agreement (orange) and a fitted line (green dots). Areas switches to one point per object (150 objects of radius 2.5–15 px) with an outline offset in pixels; annotator B compares a second manual annotation with annotator A.



A1. Preset r = 0.99, still 20 % off. Read r, the bias, the limits of agreement and the mean ratio. Why is r so high?
A2. Preset merges at high density. Describe the Bland–Altman cloud and read the slope of the fitted line. Why are the limits of agreement misleading here? What does the ratio panel show?
A3. Preset scatter only. Compare bias and limits of agreement with A1. Which of the two methods could you fix with a calibration factor, and which not?
A4. Preset small objects: area bias (outline 1 px too large). Read the mean ratio. In the ratio panel, what is the ratio for the smallest objects and for the largest? Set the outline offset to −1 px: what changes?
A5. Preset two annotators. Read the bias and the limits of agreement. What does this mean for the methods of A1–A3? Then tick areas: how well do two annotators agree on object areas?
A6. Start from a typical method, set density undercount and scatter to 0, and the scale to 1.1. Predict the Bland–Altman plot before you look (bias sign, slope sign). Compare the slope with B7.






Solutions





A1. r = 0.997, bias −16.2, limits of agreement −32.4 to 0.0, mean ratio 0.81. The automated counts are 80 % of the manual ones, so all points lie close to a straight line of slope 0.8: correlation measures closeness to a line, not to the identity line, and the wide range of counts (17 to 146) makes r high regardless.
A2. The differences fall with the mean: almost no error for small counts, an undercount of 30–45 for the densest images; the fitted slope is −0.38 (r = 0.990). The limits (−41.2 to +8.9) pretend that a sparse image can be off by −41, which never happens, and that a dense image is within the limits, which is only barely true. The ratio panel shows a ratio near 1 for low counts dropping to about 0.7 for the highest: report the bias as a function of the count, or as a ratio.
A3. Scatter only: bias 1.2 (almost none), but limits −16.5 to +18.9, wider than A1’s spread. A1 can be calibrated (multiply by 1/0.81, after checking that the factor is stable); A3’s random scatter cannot be calibrated away, only averaged over more images.
A4. Mean ratio 1.26 (bias +63.6 px²). Objects below 50 px² have a ratio of about 1.66, objects above 400 px² about 1.17: the same 1-px error is a much larger fraction of a small area. With −1 px the ratios fall below 1 (about 0.49 for objects below 50 px², 0.86 above 400 px²; mean 0.77): again the small objects suffer most.
A5. Two annotators: bias 0.55, limits −3.2 to +4.3. A method cannot be expected to do better than this; A1–A3 are far outside it, so they are clearly worse than a second human. For areas, the two annotators have bias 0.59 px² and limits −43.5 to +44.7 px²: their outlines differ by a fraction of a pixel, which on areas of 25–730 px² is a scatter of tens of px².
A6. Bias positive (+8.7: auto too high), and the cloud slopes up (slope 0.088): the overcount grows with the count. B7 predicts 2(a-1)/(a+1) = 0.095 for a = 1.1; the demo’s value is a little lower because the manual counts themselves have a small random error.

title: Exercise: boundaries, counts and the uncertain ground truth
text:
Where this leads
Every number in this unit came with an uncertainty that depends on how many independent images or experiments went into it. The next unit asks how to split data into training and test sets so that the test is honest; the last one how to turn measurements into claims about a treatment.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
About this lecture
A test score is only as good as the test. Today: how a validation can lie, and how to design one that does not.

The rule: the test set must be as new as the data you will work on later.
Why random pixel or patch splits leak: neighbouring pixels are near copies.
The hierarchy of splits: pixel, patch, image, specimen, experiment, day, site.
Other leaks: augmenting or normalising before the split, duplicates, tuning on the test set.
Domain shift: what a held-out day or site measures.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Recall: training and test sets
From the random-forest day: train on one set, measure on another; cross-validation rotates the test part through the data (k folds).
That day already met a trap: pixels of one stroke are near copies of each other, so a classifier “tested” on pixels next to its training pixels scores far too well (“out-of-bag 99 %, held-out region 85 %”).
Today turns this into a rule and climbs above the single image.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
The rule

The test set must be as new as the data you want to work on later.

If the method will be used on new images, from new experiments, on other days, then the test images must come from experiments and days it has never seen, not only from images it has not seen.
Every shortcut in the split is leakage: information about the test set reaches the training, and the score is optimistic. Leakage is not cheating on purpose; it is the default when data are split carelessly.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Why random pixel splits leak
Images are spatially autocorrelated: a pixel looks almost like its neighbours and has almost always the same label.


Random pixels: every test pixel has training pixels right next to it, with nearly the same features and the same label. The classifier only needs to remember, not to generalise.
Random blocks: only the pixels at block edges have close neighbours in training. Blocks with a buffer zone remove even those.
By image: no test pixel has a neighbour in training.

The same holds for patches cut from one image, frames of one movie, slices of one volume, cells of one well.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
section: The math: correlated samples count less
text:
The math: correlated samples count less
The autocorrelation of an image, C(\delta) = \text{corr}\big(I(\mathbf x), I(\mathbf x + \delta)\big), falls from 1 at \delta = 0 to about 0 beyond a correlation length \ell (the size of the structures, or of the smoothing in the features). Samples closer than \ell carry almost the same information.
n samples in clusters of m, with correlation \rho inside a cluster and 0 between clusters: the variance of their mean is that of
n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n}{1 + (m - 1)\rho}
independent samples (the design effect; derived in the replicates unit). For \rho \to 1, n_{\text{eff}} \to n/m: one sample per cluster.
For a test score: if test pixels sit within \ell of training pixels, the test is not a new sample at all; the error rate measures memory, not generalisation.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
The hierarchy of splits
Data come in nested levels; each level shares something the level below does not:
pixel < patch < image < specimen / well < experiment / day < site / microscope / lab

Split at the level you claim to generalise to: all data of one unit go to the same side. “Leave one experiment out” is k-fold cross-validation over experiments (group k-fold).
The test score then answers: how well does it work on a new experiment?
Only one big image (one slide, one scan)? Split it into spatial blocks with a buffer between training and test blocks wider than the correlation length.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
section: Try it: five ways to split
text:
Try it: five ways to split




12 synthetic images from 4 days, a k-nearest-neighbour pixel classifier on a feature stack, accuracy for five splits (4 folds each). Tour: “nothing to learn”: the labels are random blobs unrelated to the image. Random pixels: 78 %; random blocks 60 %; blocks + buffer 50 %; by image 48 %; by day 54 % (chance is 50 %). The prediction panel shows the blob shapes reproduced from neighbouring training pixels. “Random pixels look great” (real labels): pixels 97.8, blocks 96.9, buffer 94.5, image 92.2, day 86.8; always “background” gives 81.5. “A new day”: by day 80.5, no better than always “background”. “No day effect”: image 96.1, day 96.0. “Augment then split”: by image jumps to 99.1, by day stays 86.1.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Other leaks

Augment, then split: rotated or flipped copies of a test image end up in training. The classifier has seen the test image. Augment the training set after the split.
Normalise with statistics of the whole data set before splitting: the test set’s mean and SD shape the training data (usually mild, but avoid it).
Duplicates and near-duplicates: the same field imaged twice, overlapping tiles, the same patient under two names.
Selecting features on all data, then cross-validating the classifier: the selection has already looked at the test labels.
Shortcuts inside the data: a scale bar, a plate edge, a scanner mark that correlates with the label. Not a split error, but the same effect: the score measures something other than what you want.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Tuning on the test set
You try 50 settings (feature scales, a threshold, the network size, post-processing) and report the best test score. That reports luck.

A test score from n objects wobbles by about \sqrt{a(1-a)/n}: 0.04 for accuracy 0.8 and n = 100.
The maximum of many noisy scores lies above the true value, even if all settings are equally good: with 20 equal settings by about 1.9 SE, with 50 by about 2.2 SE.
50 settings, all with true accuracy 0.80, test set of 100 objects: the best reads 0.89 on average; on fresh data it scores 0.80.

Choosing the best-looking result after the fact is a leak from the test set into the method.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
section: The math: the optimism of the best of k
text:
The math: the optimism of the best of k
k settings with the same true accuracy a; test scores \hat a_j = a + \varepsilon_j, \varepsilon_j \sim N(0, \sigma^2) independent, \sigma = \sqrt{a(1-a)/n}.
E\big[\max_j \hat a_j\big] - a = \sigma\, E\big[\max_j Z_j\big], \qquad Z_j \sim N(0, 1).
E[\max Z] = 0.56 for k = 2 (exactly 1/\sqrt\pi), 1.54 for 10, 1.87 for 20, 2.25 for 50, 2.51 for 100. Bound: for any t > 0, by Jensen’s inequality,
e^{t\,E[\max Z]} \le E\big[e^{t \max Z}\big] \le \sum_j E\big[e^{t Z_j}\big] = k\,e^{t^2/2} \;\Rightarrow\; E[\max Z] \le \frac{\ln k}{t} + \frac t2 = \sqrt{2 \ln k} \text{ at } t = \sqrt{2\ln k}.
The optimism grows only like \sqrt{\ln k}, but it never stops growing, and it shrinks only like 1/\sqrt n.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
section: Try it: peeking at the test set
text:
Try it: peeking at the test set




Left: one run, the test score of each candidate (blue), the best one (red) and the same candidate on fresh data (green). Right: 1000 runs. Tour: “50 settings, 100 objects”: mean reported 89.1 %, fresh 80.1 %: optimism 9.0 points. “One method”: optimism about 0. “Bigger test set” (1000 objects): 2.9 points. “Validation set fixes it”: choose on a validation set, report the test score: optimism 0.0. “Real differences” (true accuracies spread by 0.03, 20 candidates): the choice now finds a better method (fresh 83.2) but still overstates it (reported 89.1).

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Training, validation, test

Training set: fit the model.
Validation set (or cross-validation inside the training data): make every choice: settings, features, when to stop, which model.
Test set: touch it once, at the end, for the number you report.

If you need the test set again after looking at it, it has become a validation set; a new test set is needed for an honest number. With little data, nested cross-validation: an inner loop chooses, an outer loop tests the whole procedure.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
The math: nested cross-validation
What we want to estimate is the error of the procedure “tune, then train”, applied to new data, not the error of one fitted model.

Outer loop over folds F_1, \dots, F_K: hold out F_k.
Inner loop on the rest: cross-validate every candidate setting; pick the best \theta_k^*; retrain on all of the rest with \theta_k^*.
Test that model on F_k. Average over k.

Every outer test fold is untouched by the choice of \theta_k^*, so the average is unbiased for the procedure (up to the smaller training sets). The inner CV score of \theta_k^* is the optimistic “best of k” from the previous math slide; the outer score is not.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Domain shift
A new microscope, a new stain batch, a new cell line, another lab: the input distribution changes (the neural-networks day calls this domain shift).

A test on held-out images of the same experiments measures interpolation. A test on a held-out day or site measures generalisation to new conditions.
The drop from “held-out image” to “held-out day” is the domain shift, and it is the number a user of the method cares about.
In the demo: by image 92.2 %, by day 86.8 %; with a strong day effect, by day 80.5 %, no better than always answering “background” (81.5 %).

Report the split level next to every score.

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
A checklist for a validation

What is the unit of the split (pixel, image, experiment, day, site), and is it the level of the claim?
Was anything done before the split (augmentation, normalisation, feature selection)?
What was tuned on what? Was the test set used once?
Are there duplicates or near-duplicates across the split?
What is the test domain: same microscope and protocol, or new ones?
Could a shortcut in the data explain the score?

title: Honest validation: leakage, splits and domain shift
text:
Summary

The test set must be as new as the data you will use the method on. Otherwise information leaks and the score is optimistic.
Neighbouring pixels, patches, frames and cells are near copies: random pixel splits leak. Split by image, experiment or day; for one big image use blocks with a buffer.
Augment and normalise after the split; beware duplicates and feature selection on all data.
Tuning on the test set reports luck: the best of k noisy scores is optimistic by about \sigma\sqrt{2\ln k} at most. Use a validation set or nested cross-validation; touch the test set once.
A held-out day or site measures domain shift, the number users care about.

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a median and a mean filter on a row by hand, and bilateral weights across a step,
choose a denoiser for a given image (outliers, thin lines, repetitive texture), judged by what it destroys,
read a method-noise image,
say which measurements survive restoration and which do not, and what to report,
show why the median ignores outliers and why restoration keeps the flux (math).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Gaussian
weighted mean of the neighbours by distance; linear


Median
middle value of the sorted window; a rank filter


Bilateral
weights e^{-\lVert p - q\rVert^2/2\sigma_s^2}e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2}: close and similar


Non-local means
weights e^{-d^2/h^2}, d^2 = mean squared difference of two patches


Method noise
noisy − denoised; should look like pure noise


Flux
total intensity; kept by RL, by roughness-penalised Tikhonov; shrunk slightly by Wiener


Restored image
an estimate: detect on it, measure on the raw image, validate, report the settings

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
By hand
B1. The row (10, 10, 10, 200, 10, 10, 50, 50, 50), window 3, ends mirrored (the value beyond the first pixel is the second pixel). (a) Compute the 3-point mean and median of every pixel. (b) What happened to the outlier and to the step in each? (c) Now the step is a 1-pixel line: (10, 10, 10, 10, 50, 10, 10, 10, 10). What does the median do to it?
B2. Bilateral weights in 1D, a centre pixel of value 10 with neighbours 10 (left) and 50 (right), all at distance 1, σs large (distance does not matter), σr = 10. (a) Compute the three range weights. (b) Compute the filtered value of the centre pixel. Compare with the plain mean. (c) How large must σr be for the 50 to get a weight of 0.5?
B3. Which denoiser would you choose, and which would you avoid, for: (a) an image with salt-and-pepper noise (dead and hot pixels); (b) thin filaments in moderate Gaussian noise; (c) a regular lattice of identical particles; (d) an image whose noise is as large as the contrast of its edges?
B4. A trust table. After RL deconvolution of a bead image, mark each measurement as kept, changed, or unknown (needs validation): (a) total intensity of a bead within a mask three times its size; (b) the peak value of a bead; (c) the ratio of the integrated intensities of two beads far apart; (d) the FWHM of a bead near the resolution limit; (e) the distance between two beads 1.2 Rayleigh distances apart; (f) the number of beads found by thresholding.
B5. A method-noise image shows (a) only fine grain everywhere, (b) bright and dark lines along all edges, (c) the dot lattice of the image, faint. What did the filter do in each case?
B6. A Wiener denoiser has an SNR of 100 at frequency 0. By how much does it change the total intensity of the image? What about Tikhonov with the roughness penalty?

B1. (a)

Mean: the outlier is spread over three pixels (73.3) and the step becomes a ramp (23.3, 36.7). Median: the outlier is gone and the step stays sharp.
Every window containing the 50 has two 10s: the median is 10 everywhere. The line is erased.

B2. (a) For the 10s: e^0 = 1 (both the centre and the left neighbour). For the 50: e^{-40^2/(2 \cdot 10^2)} = e^{-8} = 0.000335. (b) (10 + 10 + 50 \times 0.000335)/(1 + 1 + 0.000335) = 10.007. The mean is (10 + 10 + 50)/3 = 23.3: the bilateral filter does not average across the step. (c) e^{-1600/(2\sigma_r^2)} = 0.5: \sigma_r^2 = 1600/(2\ln 2) = 1154, \sigma_r = 34.
B3. (a) Median (3 × 3); avoid Gaussian, which spreads each outlier into a blob. (b) Bilateral, or non-local means with a small patch and h; avoid a median larger than the filament (it erases it) and a wide Gaussian (it blurs it into the background). (c) Non-local means: many similar patches; avoid a wide Gaussian. (d) None of the edge-preserving filters works well: the bilateral either keeps the noise or blurs the edges (cartoon); a modest Gaussian or Wiener is the honest choice, or better data.
B4. (a) kept (RL keeps flux; the mask is larger than the PSF); (b) changed (peaks rise with the iterations); (c) kept, approximately (both fluxes are kept); (d) changed (shrinks towards a floor set by the method); (e) changed or unknown (biased when the dip between them is weak; validate); (f) unknown (speckles can add false beads, merged pairs remove some; depends on the threshold and the iterations).
B5. (a) It removed noise only: good. (b) It blurred the edges (removed signal there). (c) It averaged the lattice partly away: the filter is too strong for the texture (or uses too large patches or h).
B6. Wiener’s gain at f = 0 is 1/(1 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}) = 1/1.01 = 0.990: the total intensity drops by 1 %. Tikhonov with the roughness penalty has gain exactly 1 at f = 0: unchanged.




Math questions
B7. (math) Show that the median minimises \sum_i |x_i - m|, while the mean minimises \sum_i (x_i - m)^2. Move one value of B1’s row from 200 to 2000: what happens to the mean and to the median of the window?
B8. (math) Non-local means with patch (2P + 1)^2 and search window (2S + 1)^2 on an n-pixel image. Count the operations of the direct method and of the per-offset method with integral images.
B9. (math) Show that RL keeps the total intensity at every iteration, and that a linear filter multiplies it by its gain at f = 0.






Solutions (math)





B7. \frac{d}{dm}\sum_i(x_i - m)^2 = -2\sum_i(x_i - m) = 0 gives m = \bar x. For the absolute deviations see Q8 of the quiz: the slope \#\{x_i < m\} - \#\{x_i > m\} changes sign at the median. Window (10, 2000, 10): the mean jumps from 73.3 to 673.3; the median stays 10, because the extreme value only counts as “one above”.
B8. Direct: for each of the n pixels and each of the (2S + 1)^2 candidates, a patch distance over (2P + 1)^2 pixels: n(2S + 1)^2(2P + 1)^2 operations. Per offset: for each of the (2S + 1)^2 offsets, the squared differences (n), their integral image (n) and one box sum per pixel (4 lookups): about n(2S + 1)^2 \cdot c with a small constant c, independent of P. For P = 2, S = 5: 25 times fewer.
B9. RL: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j\sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i} = \sum_i\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}(A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_i y_i. Linear filter: the total \sum_j x_j is the Fourier coefficient at f = 0; the filter multiplies each coefficient by its gain, so the total becomes W(0)\sum_j g_j (and with H(0) = 1 the data total equals the object total).

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Explore: denoisers
A 128 × 128 test image (top left a step, top right a ramp crossed by a 1-pixel line, bottom left a dot lattice, bottom right a flat area with one unique spot) or a crop of the micrograph, with Gaussian, Poisson or salt-and-pepper noise (fixed seed). Panels: noisy, denoised, method noise (noisy − denoised; blue negative, red positive) and the error against the truth. Compare with shows a second method (with its own last settings) next to the first. The plot shows the marked row (orange ticks in the noisy image); the readout gives the PSNR (peak 255).



E1. Preset Gaussian blurs the step (σn = 20, σ = 2). Read the PSNR of the noisy and the denoised image. Why is the denoised one worse? Find the σ with the best PSNR.
E2. Preset salt and pepper: median wins. Compare the median (3 × 3) with the Gaussian (σ = 1): PSNR and look.
E3. Preset median eats the thin line. Find the line in the profile (x = 96). What is its value before and after, and what does the PSNR do? Does a 3 × 3 median keep it?
E4. Preset bilateral keeps edges: compare with the Gaussian. Then bilateral at high noise: cartoon: describe the ramp.
E5. Preset non-local means on texture: compare it with the bilateral filter overall and on the lattice. Then non-local means smears the unique spot: what happens to the spot (row 98)?
E6. Preset method noise shows the removed edge (Gaussian σ = 3). What do you see in the method noise? Switch to the bilateral filter (σs 2, σr 30) and compare.
E7. Preset best PSNR, wrong look (micrograph crop, σn = 25). Compare the PSNR of the two methods and the images. Which would you use to show membranes, and what does that say about PSNR?






Solutions





E1. Noisy 22.1 dB, Gaussian σ = 2: 21.6 dB, worse than doing nothing. The dot lattice (period 6 px) is wiped out and every edge blurred: the error there outweighs the noise removed elsewhere. The best Gaussian is σ ≈ 0.6 (25.8 dB): it can only remove a little noise without destroying the lattice.
E2. Median: 15.3 → 22.7 dB, the image is clean with sharp edges. Gaussian σ = 1: 21.9 dB, but every hit pixel becomes a grey smudge.
E3. The line (true value 211 on the ramp at row 32) drops to 133 after the 5 × 5 median: it is erased; PSNR falls from 34.1 dB (noisy, σn = 5) to 21.6 dB. A 3 × 3 median erases it too (133): a 1-pixel line is only 3 of the 9 values.
E4. Bilateral (σs 2, σr 30) at σn = 15: 33.7 dB, edges sharp; Gaussian σ = 2: 21.7 dB. At σn = 50 with σr = 100 the ramp becomes a few flat patches with steps between them (a cartoon), and the lattice turns into blotches; 21.9 dB.
E5. Non-local means (patch 3 × 3, search 15 × 15, h = 25): 29.5 dB against 27.0 dB for the bilateral filter; on the lattice quarter 26.7 dB against 23.2 dB (noisy: 20.1 dB): the dots are kept because every dot has many similar copies. With patch 5 × 5 and h = 45, the unique spot (true value 220) falls to 129: it has no similar patch and is averaged with flat ones.
E6. The method noise shows the step as a bright and dark double line (up to +72 and −58 at the edge), the ramp’s line and the lattice; in flat regions it is plain noise (RMS 9.9, about σn = 10). The bilateral filter’s method noise has almost no edge in it.
E7. Wiener (SNR 3): 23.4 dB; bilateral (σs 1.5, σr 50): 23.3 dB. The Wiener result is blurred overall; the bilateral keeps the membranes and edges sharper but leaves flat patches. The PSNR prefers the blurred one by a hair: it measures pixel-wise error, not whether structures look right. Look at the images (and the method noise), not only at a number.

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Explore: what may be measured
A field with known truth, blurred by an Airy PSF (NA 1.0, Rayleigh distance 4.88 px) with Poisson noise: bead pairs at 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.5 Rayleigh distances (top), spots of flux 1 : 2 : 4 (middle), disks of radius 3, 5 and 8 px (bottom). Restore with Wiener, Tikhonov or RL; the table compares raw, restored and truth: the peak and integrated ratios of the flux-4 and flux-1 spots, the FWHM of the bright spot, the separation of the 1.2 × Rayleigh pair, and the number of local maxima above one fixed threshold in the top two rows (truth: 11). Green: within 10 % (counts: exact); yellow: within 30 % (counts: ±2); red: worse.



M1. Presets integrals hold and peaks lie (3000 photons, RL). Read the peak and integrated ratios at k = 100 and k = 316, and in the raw image. Which would you trust?
M2. Preset sizes shrink to a floor. Follow the FWHM of the bright spot from the raw image through k = 10, 32, 100, 316 and 1000. Where does it stop, and how does that compare with the truth?
M3. Preset close pairs: the separation is biased (1000 photons). Give the separation of the 1.2 × Rayleigh pair in the raw image, after 100 and after 1000 iterations.
M4. Preset 1000 iterations: extra spots. How many spots are detected in raw, restored and truth? Move k down: from which iteration does the count go wrong?
M5. Preset Wiener. Compare the five measurements with RL at k = 100 (same photons). What does Wiener do better, and what worse?






Solutions





M1. Raw: peak ratio 4.13, integrated 3.86. RL k = 100: peak 6.20, integrated 4.00; k = 316: peak 6.53, integrated 3.97. The integrated ratio stays close to 4 (light is moved, not created); the peak ratio rises with the iterations, because a bright spot is sharpened more than a dim one at the same noise. Trust integrals over a region larger than the PSF; never peaks after restoration.
M2. Raw 4.51 px; RL k = 10: 3.01, 32: 2.44, 100: 2.09, 316: 1.94, 1000: 1.93. It stops near 1.9 px, well above the true 1.45 px: the floor is set by the noise and the method (frequencies beyond those restored), not by the object. A FWHM measured after restoration is not the object’s size.
M3. Raw: 4.95 px (truth 5.92): the blur pulls the two maxima together. RL k = 100: 5.85 px; k = 1000: 5.62 px. Restoration reduces the bias but the result depends on the stopping point; at 3000 photons the raw value is 6.11 and RL gives about 6.0. Validate separations with pairs of known distance.
M4. Raw 11, restored (k = 1000) 259, truth 11. At k = 100 the count is still 11; at k = 316 it is 64: the noise has been turned into speckles above the threshold. Counting on restored images needs a stopping rule and validation.
M5. Wiener (SNR 300) at 1000 photons: peak ratio 3.66, integrated 4.27, FWHM 3.53 px, separation 5.82 px, 16 spots. RL at k = 100: 4.75, 4.38, 2.22 px, 5.85 px, 11 spots. Wiener sharpens much less (the FWHM stays large) and its ringing adds a few false maxima; RL sharpens more and keeps a correct count at this stopping point. Neither keeps peak ratios.

title: Exercise: denoising and what you may measure
text:
Where this leads
This ends Part I: images as numbers, from pixels and filters to the noise of the camera, the optics that blur and the restoration that undoes as much as the data allow. Part II starts from the restored or raw image and turns it into objects, beginning with thresholding, where the median returns in one line. Statistics of measurements, and how to compare them honestly, are the evaluation day’s.

title: Quiz: honest validation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A pixel classifier is trained on 75 % of the pixels of 10 images, chosen at random, and tested on the other 25 %. It scores 98 %. Why is this number not to be trusted?






Hint





Where is the nearest training pixel of a test pixel?









Answer





Every test pixel has training pixels right next to it, with almost the same features and the same label: the classifier can score well by remembering its neighbours, without generalising. The score says little about new images. Split by image (or by experiment or day).




Q2. The method will be used on images from future experiments in your lab. At which level should you split, and why not at a lower level?






Hint





The test set must be as new as the data you will work on.









Answer





By experiment (leave one or more experiments out). Images from one experiment share the staining, the cells, the day’s microscope settings; a test on held-out images of the same experiments is easier than the real use and gives an optimistic number.




Q3. You rotate and flip every image to get 8 times more data, then split the images at random into training and test. What goes wrong? What is the correct order?






Hint





Where do the copies of a test image end up?









Answer





Rotated copies of a test image end up in the training set, so the classifier has seen the test images (in rotated form). Split first, then augment only the training images.




Q4. You have one large whole-slide image. Why do random square tiles as test set leak, and what helps?






Hint





What is next to the edge of a test tile?









Answer





Pixels at the edge of a test tile have training pixels right across the edge: near copies. Use larger blocks (or stripes), and a buffer zone around test blocks, wider than the correlation length (structure size plus feature smoothing), that is used for neither training nor testing. It still says nothing about other slides.




Q5. You tried 40 post-processing settings and report the best test Dice. Why is it optimistic even if all 40 settings are equally good?






Hint





Each test score has some random error.









Answer





Each test score is the true value plus noise; the maximum of 40 noisy numbers lies above their common true value (about 2.1 standard errors above it for 40). You report the luckiest one. Choose on a validation set and report the test score of the chosen setting once.




Q6. A method scores 0.93 on held-out images and 0.81 on held-out days. What does the difference measure, and which number would a user care about?






Hint





What changes between days?









Answer





The drop measures the domain shift between days (staining, illumination, focus, cell state): how much the method relies on conditions of the days it was trained on. A user applies it to new days, so 0.81 is the relevant number.




Q7. Why does a larger test set reduce the optimism of picking the best of many settings, but never remove it?






Hint





How does the noise of one score depend on n?









Answer





The optimism is about (noise of one score) × (a factor that grows slowly with the number of settings). The noise shrinks like 1/\sqrt n, so a larger test set reduces the optimism, but as long as the test set is used for the choice, the chosen score still contains the luck of being chosen. Only an independent test set removes it.




Q8. (math) For two settings with equal true accuracy and independent normal errors of SD \sigma, what is the expected optimism of reporting the better one?






Hint





E[\max(Z_1, Z_2)] for standard normals.









Answer





\sigma\,E[\max(Z_1, Z_2)] = \sigma/\sqrt\pi \approx 0.56\,\sigma: \max(a, b) = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{|a-b|}{2}, and E|Z_1 - Z_2| = 2/\sqrt\pi.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
About this lecture
A classification network says what is in an image. For segmentation we want a class for every pixel.

An encoder–decoder: shrink the image to gain context, then upsample back to full size.
Skip connections (the U-Net) bring the fine detail back.
Train with a per-pixel loss: cross-entropy, or a Dice loss when the objects are a small part of the image.
Judge the result with Dice and IoU, by looking at the errors, and on images unlike the training ones.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour (unetseg): “a typical image” (Dice 0.986), “U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination” (0.987 vs 0.349), click the levels of the architecture to see feature maps; “no skips: small nuclei”; “touching nuclei merge”; “dimmer microscope” (domain shift: Dice 0.269, worse than Otsu). Day 6 owns Dice/IoU and the confusion matrix; recall them in one line. Instance segmentation by networks is day 18.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
From “what” to “which pixels”

Output: one class probability per pixel, an image of the same size as the input.
Naive way: classify a patch around every pixel with the network of the last unit. Slow (one network run per pixel), and the patch is small, so the context is small.
Better: a network that is convolutional all the way: no dense layer, so it takes any image size and gives a map out.
The problem: pooling made the maps small (64 \to 16 pixels). We need to get back to full resolution.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Encoder–decoder


Encoder (left): convolutions and pooling, as in the last unit. The maps get smaller and see more context.
Decoder (right): upsample (each pixel becomes 2 \times 2), then convolutions that sharpen the result. Back to 64 \times 64, one probability per pixel.


The figure is the network of the demo: two levels, 8, 16 and 32 channels, about 30,000 weights. Upsampling by nearest neighbour followed by a 3×3 convolution; the alternative is a transposed convolution, next math slide.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Upsampling by hand
1D signal (1, 2, 3), upsampled by 2:

Nearest neighbour: (1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3). Blocky; a following convolution smooths it, e.g. with (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14): (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75, 2.25) (zero beyond the ends).
Transposed convolution with stride 2: each input value stamps a weighted copy of the kernel into the output, 2 steps apart. With the kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12):

(0.5,\ 1,\ 1.5,\ 2,\ 2.5,\ 3,\ 1.5)
linear interpolation. With a learned kernel the network chooses its own way to upsample.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
The math: transposed convolution

A strided convolution is a matrix A (banded, rows s positions apart): \mathbf y = A\mathbf x maps n to about n/s values.
The transposed convolution applies A^\top: from n/s values back to n. Each input value adds the kernel, scaled by itself, to the output: “stamping”.
Output length (n - 1)s + k - 2p: for n = 3, s = 2, k = 3, p = 0: 7.
It is the same operation that backpropagation uses to send gradients back through a strided convolution. A^\top is not the inverse A^{-1}: it does not undo the convolution, it only goes back to the larger size.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Skip connections: the U-Net
A decoder that only gets the bottleneck knows what is where, roughly; the exact boundaries were lost in pooling.

U-Net (Ronneberger, Fischer and Brox, 2015): copy the encoder’s feature maps of each size across to the decoder and concatenate them with the upsampled maps.
Context comes from below (deep, coarse maps), detail from the side (shallow, sharp maps).
In the demo network: 32 upsampled channels + 16 copied = 48 channels into the decoder at 32 \times 32; 16 + 8 = 24 at 64 \times 64.

title: Segmentation networks
section: Try it: a U-Net segments nuclei
text:
Try it: a U-Net segments nuclei




Synthetic 64×64 images, generated with the same code as the training set; “new image” draws a new one. Errors: TP white, FP red, FN blue. “U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination”: the U-Net Dice 0.987, Otsu 0.349 (the bright right side is all “object”). Click “bottleneck”: 32 coarse maps. “no skips: small nuclei”: 0.936 against 0.954 with skips (same image). On the training distribution skips help little here (validation Dice 0.968 vs 0.965): these smooth blobs are easy to locate from 16×16 maps. “touching nuclei merge”: 7 nuclei, but the mask has 4 connected pieces.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Per-pixel loss

Cross-entropy per pixel, averaged over all pixels: every pixel is one classification example.
Class imbalance: if nuclei are 5 % of the pixels, “everything is background” is 95 % correct (recall “accuracy lies”, thresholding day). Its cross-entropy is not very large either.
Remedies: weight the object pixels more, or use the Dice loss: $1 - $ soft Dice, computed from the probabilities so that it has a gradient.
Recall (thresholding day): Dice = 2|P \cap G|/(|P| + |G|) of a predicted mask P and the truth G; IoU = |P \cap G|/|P \cup G|.

title: Segmentation networks
section: The math: soft Dice and its gradient
text:
The math: soft Dice and its gradient
With probabilities p_i \in [0, 1] and the true mask g_i \in \{0, 1\}:
D = \frac{2\sum_i p_ig_i}{\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i}, \qquad \mathcal L_\text{Dice} = 1 - D, \qquad \frac{\partial D}{\partial p_j} = \frac{2g_j\left(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i\right) - 2\sum_i p_ig_i}{\left(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i\right)^2}

For hard 0/1 predictions D is the usual Dice. The loss depends only on the object pixels and the predicted object area: the background count does not dilute it.
Weighted cross-entropy: -\frac1N\sum_i\big[w_1g_i\log p_i + w_0(1 - g_i)\log(1 - p_i)\big], with e.g. w_c \propto 1/(\text{share of class } c).
(Milletari, Navab and Ahmadi, 2016.)

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Evaluating a segmentation network

Dice and IoU against the ground truth, on held-out images (never seen in training or tuning).
Look at the errors, not only at the number: where are the false positives and negatives? Merged nuclei, missed dim nuclei and boundary pixels are different problems.
The number hides the distribution: a few failed images can disappear in an average over many good ones.
How to build an honest test set, and object-level scores (matched nuclei, F1): the evaluation day (day 16).

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Data: annotation is the bottleneck

Every training image needs a mask drawn by hand: hours per image for dense nuclei.
Small networks and augmentation (flips, rotations, brightness, noise, elastic deformation) go a long way with tens of annotated images: the original U-Net was trained on 30.
Synthetic images with known truth (as in the demo) are good for teaching and testing, but real images differ: blur, debris, textures the generator never made.
A network knows only its training range: a dimmer microscope, more noise, another stain can break it. The demo’s sliders show this; days 16 and 18 come back to it.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
After the mask

Touching nuclei come out as one blob: a semantic mask says “nucleus or not”, not “which nucleus”. Classic fix: a third class “boundary between nuclei”, then labelling or the watershed (days 9–10). Networks that output separate objects directly: day 18.
The probability map is a perfect data term for a graph cut (day 13): D_p(\ell) = -\log p_\ell, plus a smoothness term. The two ideas combine.
The baseline to beat: a random forest on the feature stack (day 14) with a few strokes of annotation. Often it is good enough, and it needs much less data.

title: Segmentation networks
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Encoder–decoder
shrink for context, upsample back to one probability per pixel


Upsampling
nearest + convolution, or transposed convolution (“stamping” the kernel)


U-Net
skip connections copy encoder maps to the decoder: context + detail


Per-pixel loss
cross-entropy per pixel; Dice loss or class weights against imbalance


Evaluation
Dice / IoU on held-out images, and look at the errors


Limits
needs annotations; only knows its training range; semantic, not instance masks



Next: evaluation and statistics (day 16): what makes a test set honest, and how to compare methods.

title: Exercise: honest validation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

decide whether a validation design leaks, and at which level,
choose the level of the split (image, specimen, experiment, day, site) that matches a claim, and design a split for a single large image,
estimate the optimism of reporting the best of many test scores,
explain what the drop from a held-out-image score to a held-out-day score measures (domain shift).

Do the pen-and-paper part first, then the two demos. Questions marked (math) are for those who want the derivations; the concept questions do not depend on them.

title: Exercise: honest validation
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Leakage
information about the test data reaches training or model choices; the score becomes optimistic


Unit of the split
everything of one unit (image, experiment, day) goes to the same side


Group k-fold
cross-validation where the folds are groups, e.g. “leave one experiment out”


Buffer
a zone around test blocks whose pixels are used neither for training nor for testing


Validation set
data used for choices (settings, features, stopping); the test set is used once at the end


Optimism of the best of k
\sigma\,E[\max_j Z_j]; E[\max Z] \approx 1.54 (k = 10), 1.87 (20), 2.25 (50), 2.51 (100); \sigma = \sqrt{a(1-a)/n}

title: Exercise: honest validation
text:
By hand
B1. For each design: does it leak, and at which level? What would you change? (1) 2000 tiles cut from 10 tissue slides; tiles split at random into training and test. (2) 40 images from 4 days; leave-one-day-out cross-validation. (3) Every image rotated in 8 ways, then the images split at random by image. (4) Intensities scaled by the mean and SD of the whole data set, then split by image. (5) The threshold of a segmentation chosen to give the best Dice on the test images. (6) Cells from 6 wells, classified per cell; cells split at random into training and test.
B2. You try 20 settings, all with the same true accuracy 0.80, on a test set of 100 objects, and report the best. (a) What is the standard error of one test score? (b) About what does the best of the 20 read? (c) The same with a test set of 1000 objects. (d) The same with 20 settings that are really different (one of them truly 0.85). Is the best one still optimistic?
B3. A pixel classifier scores 0.97 under a random pixel split, 0.91 when whole images are left out, and 0.78 when whole days are left out. (a) Which number goes in the paper, and for which claim? (b) What does each gap (0.97 → 0.91, 0.91 → 0.78) measure? (c) The always-“background” classifier scores 0.80 on these data. What does that change in your reading?
B4. You have one large image only: a whole-slide scan. (a) Design a validation that is as honest as possible. Draw it. (b) How wide should the buffer be? (c) What can such a validation not tell you?
B5. A colleague says: “I used a validation set to choose the network size, and then reported the validation score.” What is wrong, and how large could the problem be if 30 sizes were tried on 200 validation objects with accuracy around 0.9?






Solutions





B1. (1) Leaks at the tile level: tiles of one slide (neighbouring, even overlapping) are on both sides. Split by slide (group k-fold over slides). (2) Honest for the claim “works on a new day” (the strongest of these). (3) Leaks: rotated copies of a test image are in training; the classifier has seen it. Split first, then augment the training images only. (4) Mild leak: the test images’ statistics shaped the scaling. Compute mean and SD on the training images only (or per image). (5) Leaks: the test set was used to choose the threshold; the reported Dice is the best of many and optimistic. Choose it on a validation set. (6) Leaks at the cell level: cells of one well share the well’s conditions (and neighbours look alike); split by well. And with 6 wells, the test can only say something about wells like these.
B2. (a) \sqrt{0.8 \cdot 0.2/100} = 0.04. (b) 0.80 + 1.87 \cdot 0.04 \approx 0.875. (c) SE = 0.0126: 0.80 + 1.87 \cdot 0.0126 \approx 0.824, much less optimism. (d) Yes: the best-looking one is likely the good one, but its score still contains its own luck plus the luck of being picked. Selection then helps (you find a better method) but the reported number is still too high; re-test on fresh data.
B3. (a) For the claim “works on images from new days” (the normal use): 0.78. 0.91 is honest only for “new images from the same days”, 0.97 for nothing useful. (b) 0.97 → 0.91: the leakage of neighbouring pixels (memory, not generalisation). 0.91 → 0.78: the domain shift between days (staining, illumination, focus). (c) 0.78 is worse than predicting “background” everywhere (0.80): on a new day the classifier is useless. Accuracy with unbalanced classes needs this baseline (or use F1 or Dice of the object class).
B4. (a) Cut the slide into blocks larger than the structures (e.g. several cell diameters); assign blocks to k folds, preferably in contiguous groups (stripes or quadrants); for each test fold, leave out a buffer around the test blocks. (b) At least the correlation length of the features and labels: the largest smoothing scale of the features plus the size of the objects. In the demo, 3 px of buffer already brought blocks down to chance with features smoothed up to σ = 8. (c) Anything about other slides, patients, days or scanners: the domain shift is untested. Report it as “within-slide” performance.
B5. The validation score of the chosen size is the best of 30 and optimistic: SE = \sqrt{0.9 \cdot 0.1/200} = 0.021, E[\max] for 30 is about 2.04, so the optimism is up to about 0.04 if the sizes are about equally good. Report the score on a separate test set that was not used for the choice (or nested cross-validation).




Math questions
B6. (math) (a) Show that E[\max(Z_1, Z_2)] = 1/\sqrt\pi for two independent standard normal variables. (Hint: \max(a, b) = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{|a - b|}{2}.) (b) Show that E[\max_{j \le k} Z_j] \le \sqrt{2\ln k}, using Jensen’s inequality and E[e^{tZ}] = e^{t^2/2}.
B7. (math) A 1D signal has correlation length \ell; samples are taken every \Delta; the feature of a sample is a vector of d smoothed versions of the signal at scales up to \ell; the label is a smooth function of position, unrelated to the signal. Argue why the error of a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier under a random split goes to 0 as \Delta/\ell \to 0, and why it stays at chance under a split into contiguous blocks much longer than \ell.






Solutions (math)





B6. (a) E[\max] = \frac12 E[Z_1 + Z_2] + \frac12 E|Z_1 - Z_2| = \frac12 E|Z_1 - Z_2|. Z_1 - Z_2 \sim N(0, 2), and E|X| = \sigma\sqrt{2/\pi} for X \sim N(0, \sigma^2): E|Z_1 - Z_2| = \sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt{2/\pi} = 2/\sqrt\pi. So E[\max] = 1/\sqrt\pi = 0.564. (b) For t > 0, e^{t\,E[\max_j Z_j]} \le E[e^{t \max_j Z_j}] (Jensen, e^x convex) = E[\max_j e^{t Z_j}] \le \sum_j E[e^{t Z_j}] = k\,e^{t^2/2}. Take logarithms: E[\max Z] \le \frac{\ln k}{t} + \frac t2. The right side is smallest at t = \sqrt{2 \ln k}, where it equals \sqrt{2\ln k}. (For k = 20: 2.45, against the exact 1.87.)
B7. Random split: a test sample at x has training samples at distance of order \Delta (a fraction of all samples are in training, so the nearest one is a few steps away). Their features differ by about |\nabla f|\,\Delta, which goes to 0; a sample from far away matches all d smoothed features to within \varepsilon only with a probability that shrinks like \varepsilon^d. So for small \Delta/\ell the nearest neighbour in feature space is almost always a spatial neighbour, and its label differs from the test label only if a label boundary lies between them: probability of order \Delta/\ell_{\text{label}}. The error goes to 0, although the label has nothing to do with the signal. Block split: inside a test block of length \gg \ell, all spatial neighbours within \ell are test samples too; the nearest training sample in feature space is somewhere else, where the label is independent: the error is chance (0.5 for balanced labels). The demo shows exactly this: 78 % with random pixels, 50 % with buffered blocks or by image.

title: Exercise: honest validation
text:
Explore: five ways to split
Twelve synthetic 48 × 48 images from four days (rows), three per day; the task is “nucleus or background” per pixel. Each day has its own brightness, contrast and noise (day effect). The classifier is k nearest neighbours on a feature stack (smoothed intensities, gradient magnitude and blob filters at several scales), trained on all training pixels of a fold. Five ways to split into 4 folds are compared: the bars are the mean test accuracy over the folds, the whiskers the range. Thumbnails show the roles of the pixels in the fold that tests the selected image (red test, blue train, grey buffer); click a thumbnail to select an image, and a split button to show its folds. The right column shows the selected image with its true outline (yellow) and the prediction on its test pixels. The grey line is the accuracy of always answering “background” (or chance, 50 %, when the labels are random).



L1. Preset nothing to learn: the labels are random blobs, unrelated to the images. Read the accuracy of every split. Which ones would make you believe there is something to learn?
L2. Still nothing to learn, split random pixels: look at the prediction of the selected image. How can the classifier reproduce the blob shapes? Switch the split to by image.
L3. Still nothing to learn, split blocks + buffer: set the buffer to 0, 3, 6 and 12 px. What happens to the accuracy of “blocks + buffer”? Why is there still something left at 0?
L4. Preset random pixels look great (real labels). Read the five accuracies and the “always background” line. Rank the splits. Which number answers “how well does it work on a new day”?
L5. Preset a new day: domain shift (day effect 2). Compare “by image” and “by day” with L4. Select an image of day 1 and the split by day: what does the classifier do on that day? Then preset no day effect: compare “by image” and “by day”.
L6. Preset augment then split: every image is rotated by 90°, 180° and 270° before splitting, and each copy counts as an image. Which bars change compared with L4, and why does “by day” not jump?
L7. In nothing to learn, set k to 1 and to 15. How does the leakage of random pixels change? Why?






Solutions





L1. Random pixels 78.3 %, random blocks 59.9 %, blocks + buffer 50.4 %, by image 48.0 %, by day 54.0 % (chance is 50 %). Random pixels (and, less, random blocks) suggest the classifier has learned something. It has not: the labels are random.
L2. The prediction (78.7 % correct on the selected image) reproduces the blobs: every test pixel has training pixels next to it, with almost the same features and the same random label, and k-NN copies their label. By image the prediction is noise (51.5 %): no neighbour from the same image is in training.
L3. Buffer 0: 59.9 % (same as random blocks); 3 px: 51.1 %; 6 px: 50.4 %; 12 px: 52.4 % (around chance, the fold-to-fold scatter is a few percent). Without a buffer, the pixels at the edges of each test block have training pixels right across the edge, and they leak; the buffer removes those neighbours.
L4. Random pixels 97.8 %, random blocks 96.9 %, blocks + buffer 94.5 %, by image 92.2 %, by day 86.8 % (fold range 79.0–96.5 %); always “background” 81.5 %. The order is the order of how “new” the test pixels are. For new days: by day, 86.8 %, only 5 points better than the trivial classifier.
L5. Day effect 2: by image 91.4 %, by day 80.5 % (fold range 77.5–85.0 %), below the 81.5 % of always “background”. On day 1 (darker, higher contrast) the classifier trained on the other days predicts no nucleus pixel at all: the first image is 77.9 % correct only because 78 % of its pixels are background. No day effect: by image 96.1 %, by day 96.0 %: when days do not differ, leaving out a day costs nothing. The gap between image and day splits is the domain shift.
L6. Random pixels and random blocks rise to 99.1 %, by image jumps from 92.2 % to 99.1 %, blocks + buffer to 97.0 %. The rotated copies of every test image are in training, and the features are rotation invariant: each test pixel has an exact copy in training. By day stays at 86.1 %: all copies of an image belong to the same day, so they stay on the same side of the split.
L7. k = 1: random pixels 81.5 %; k = 15: 75.0 % (by image stays near 50 %). With k = 1 the classifier copies the label of the single nearest pixel, usually a direct neighbour; with 15 neighbours, more distant (and unrelated) pixels get a vote and dilute the leak. The leak is still large.

title: Exercise: honest validation
section: Explore: peeking at the test set
text:
Explore: peeking at the test set
k candidate methods (settings), each with the same true accuracy (grey dots, or spread around it), are scored on a test set of n objects. Left: one run: each candidate’s test score (blue), the best one (red, the number that would be reported) and the same candidate re-tested on fresh data (green). Right: 1000 runs: histograms of the reported best scores and of their fresh re-tests, with their means. Validation + test: the choice is made on a separate validation set (purple), and the test score of the chosen candidate is reported.



T1. Preset one method: honest. What are the mean reported and the mean fresh score over 1000 runs? Press run once again a few times: how much does a single test score wobble?
T2. Preset 50 settings, 100 objects. Read the mean reported score, the mean fresh score and the optimism. Compare with the formula \sigma\,E[\max Z] (Background table).
T3. Vary the number of candidates k (2, 10, 20, 100) at n = 100, and then n (30, 300, 3000) at k = 50. How does the optimism depend on k and on n?
T4. Preset validation set fixes it. What is the optimism now? Why?
T5. Preset real differences: 20 candidates whose true accuracies differ (spread 0.03). Is choosing the best still useful? Is the reported number still too high?






Solutions





T1. Reported 79.8 %, fresh 79.9 %: no optimism (−0.1 points, noise). A single score of 100 objects has an SE of 4 points: the first run, for example, reports 85.0 %, and a range of roughly 72–88 % (±2 SE) is normal.
T2. Reported 89.1 %, fresh 80.1 %: optimism 9.0 points. The formula: \sigma = 0.04, E[\max Z] = 2.25 for k = 50: 0.09, i.e. 9 points.
T3. At n = 100: optimism 2.1 points (k = 2), 6.2 (10), 7.6 (20), 10.0 (100): it grows with k, but slowly (like \sqrt{\ln k}). At k = 50: 15.0 points (n = 30), 5.2 (300), 1.6 (3000): it shrinks like 1/\sqrt n. A big test set helps, a small one with many trials is dangerous.
T4. Optimism 0.0 (reported 80.0 %, fresh 80.0 %). The validation scores decide which candidate is chosen; the test score of that candidate is a fresh, independent measurement, untouched by the choice.
T5. Yes: the chosen candidates are better than average (fresh 83.2 % against the mean true accuracy of 80 %). But the reported score (89.1 %) is still 5.9 points too high. Choose on validation data, report on test data.

title: Exercise: honest validation
text:
Where this leads
The same logic holds for the statistics of measurements: cells from one dish are not independent, just as pixels from one image are not. The next unit asks what the unit of replication is in an experiment, and how to report an effect honestly.

title: Quiz: segmentation networks
text:
Short questions on encoder–decoders, U-Nets, per-pixel losses and evaluation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Dice = 2|P \cap G|/(|P| + |G|), IoU = |P \cap G|/|P \cup G|.

Q1. Why can a classification network with a dense last layer not simply be used to segment an image?






Hint





What does it output, and for which input size?









Answer





It outputs one set of class probabilities for the whole image, and its dense layer fixes the input size. A segmentation network must output one probability per pixel, for any image size: it has to be convolutional all the way, with a decoder that returns to full resolution.




Q2. What do the skip connections of a U-Net carry, and what goes wrong without them?






Hint





What did pooling throw away?









Answer





They copy the sharp, full-resolution feature maps of the encoder to the decoder. Without them the decoder only has the coarse bottleneck maps: it knows roughly where objects are, but boundaries and small objects come out blurred or misplaced.




Q3. Nuclei cover 3 % of the pixels. A network predicts “background” everywhere. What are its pixel accuracy and its Dice?






Hint





|P| = 0.









Answer





Accuracy 97 %, Dice 0 (no true positives). Accuracy rewards the large background class; Dice looks only at the objects.




Q4. Upsample (4, 8) by a factor 2 with nearest neighbour, then with a transposed convolution with stride 2 and kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12).






Hint





Each input value stamps the scaled kernel, two positions apart.









Answer





Nearest: (4, 4, 8, 8). Transposed: 4 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 0–2 and 8 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 2–4: (2, 4, 2 + 4, 8, 4) = (2, 4, 6, 8, 4): linear interpolation between 4 and 8, with a half value at the far end.




Q5. A U-Net trained on images from one microscope gives Dice 0.95 on held-out images from it, and 0.6 on images from a new microscope. What is this called, and what would you do?






Hint





Training range.









Answer





Domain shift: the new images (brightness, noise, blur, stain) lie outside what the network has seen. Annotate a few images from the new microscope and add them to the training set (fine-tune), augment brightness and noise more strongly during training, and always test on images from the setting where the network will be used.




Q6. The U-Net gives a perfect mask of two touching nuclei. Why is the nucleus count still wrong?






Hint





Connected components of the mask.









Answer





A semantic mask only says “nucleus or not” per pixel: two touching nuclei form one connected component, which labelling counts as one object. They have to be split, for example with a “boundary” class, the distance transform and the watershed (days 8–10), or with a network that outputs separate objects (day 18).




Q7. (math) Soft Dice D = 2\sum p_ig_i/(\sum p_i + \sum g_i). A pixel outside the object (g_j = 0) has its probability p_j raised. Does D go up or down? Show it from the formula.






Hint





Only the denominator depends on p_j.









Answer





Down: with g_j = 0 the numerator does not change and the denominator grows, \partial D/\partial p_j = -2\sum_i p_ig_i/(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i)^2 \le 0. False positives are penalised, and more strongly the better the overlap already is.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
About this lecture
Image analysis turns images into measurements: areas, intensities, counts, hundreds of features per cell. The usual question behind them: does a treatment change a feature?

The new statistics, by simulation: standard error, p-value, confidence interval.
The unit of replication, and pseudoreplication: why 1000 cells from one dish are one replicate.
Do it right: aggregate per experiment, paired designs, the SuperPlot.
Effect sizes with confidence intervals; multiple comparisons across many features.
Batch and plate effects, and designs that are confounded beyond repair.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The data are hierarchical
A typical imaging experiment:
cells within images within wells within experiments (days, animals, patients)

Variation exists at every level: cells differ, fields differ, wells differ, and days differ: a new batch of cells, medium, stain, a refocused microscope.
The day-to-day variation is usually the largest, and it is shared by every cell measured that day.
Treatment and control are compared within this hierarchy. Which differences count as evidence?

title: From measurements to claims
section: A mean wobbles: the standard error
text:
A mean wobbles: the standard error
Measure n values with spread SD and take their mean. Repeat the whole experiment: the mean comes out a little different each time.

The wobble of the mean is its standard error: \text{SE} = \text{SD}/\sqrt n. Four times as many values halve it.
This holds for independent values. If they share a common deviation (the same day), it does not shrink below that shared part.

The difference of two means (treated − control) has \text{SE} = \sqrt{\text{SE}_1^2 + \text{SE}_2^2}.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The p-value, by simulation
Suppose the treatment does nothing. How often would chance alone give a difference at least as large as the one observed?

Four experiments per condition, experiment means with SD 1: the difference of the two means wobbles with SE 0.71. An observed difference of 1.6 or more (either sign) comes up in 2.3 % of the simulated null experiments: p = 0.023.
A small p says “chance alone rarely does this”. It says nothing about how large or important the effect is.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The confidence interval
Estimate ± 2 SE is a 95 % confidence interval: the range of true effects compatible with the data.

Observed 1.6 with SE 0.71: about 0.2 to 3.0. The effect is probably positive, but could be small or large.
The interval excludes 0 exactly when p < 0.05 (roughly); but it also shows the size and the uncertainty of the effect.
With few replicates the factor 2 is too small: it grows to 2.78 for 5 values and 4.30 for 3 (math slide).

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: t statistic and t-distribution
text:
The math: t statistic and t-distribution
One sample x_1, \dots, x_n with mean \bar x and sample SD s: \text{SE} = s/\sqrt n and
t = \frac{\bar x - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt n}.
If the x_i are independent and normal with mean \mu_0, t follows Student’s t-distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom: like the standard normal, but with heavier tails, because s is itself estimated from few values. 95 % interval: \bar x \pm t_{0.975,\,n-1}\, s/\sqrt n with $t_{0.975} = $ 4.30 (2 df), 2.78 (4 df), 2.07 (22 df), 1.96 (\infty).
Two groups (Welch): t = (\bar y - \bar x)/\sqrt{s_x^2/n_x + s_y^2/n_y}, degrees of freedom from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula. Paired data: a one-sample test on the differences d_i = y_i - x_i.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The unit of replication
The unit of replication is the level at which the treatment was applied independently: the experiment, the animal, the well if wells were treated separately. Not the cell.

1000 cells from one dish are 1000 measurements of one replicate: they share the dish, the day, the stain.
Treating cells as n (pseudoreplication) makes the SE far too small, and p-values tiny even when there is no effect.
In the demo below (3 experiments per condition, 100 cells each, day-to-day SD 1, cell-to-cell SD 2, no effect), the cells-as-n test gives p < 0.05 in 69 % of repeated experiments, instead of 5 %.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The math: the two-level model
y_{ec} = \mu + \tau\,T_e + u_e + \varepsilon_{ec} for cell c of experiment e, with u_e \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) (day) and \varepsilon_{ec} \sim N(0, \sigma^2) (cell), all independent.
Mean of the m cells of experiment e: \text{Var}(\bar y_e) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m. Mean of all E\,m cells of a condition:
\text{Var}(\bar y) = \frac{\sigma_u^2}{E} + \frac{\sigma^2}{E\,m}, \quad\text{while cells-as-}n \text{ assumes } \frac{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}{E\,m}.
Ratio = 1 + (m - 1)\rho, the design effect, with the intra-class correlation \rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2). Effective number of cells: n_{\text{eff}} = E\,m/(1 + (m-1)\rho) \to E/\rho as m \to \infty. More cells cannot beat the number of experiments.

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: how often cells-as-n is fooled
text:
The math: how often cells-as-n is fooled
Under no effect, the cells-as-n statistic z = (\bar y_1 - \bar y_0)/\sqrt{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em)} is normal with mean 0 but variance 1 + (m-1)\rho, not 1. It rejects when |z| > 1.96:
P(\text{false positive}) = 2\,\Phi\!\left(-\frac{1.96}{\sqrt{1 + (m - 1)\rho}}\right).
\rho = 0.1: m = 10: 0.16; m = 100: \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, 2\Phi(-0.59) = 0.55; m = 1000: 0.85. (Large-E approximation; with few experiments the t-test version behaves alike, as the demo shows.)

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Do it right

Aggregate per replicate: one number per experiment (mean or median of its cells), and test those E numbers. Correct false-positive rate, and the effect is unchanged.
Pair the design: control and treated in every experiment, compare within each. The day-to-day variation cancels; often far more power.
Mixed-effects models do the same with all cells kept (a pointer: they model u_e explicitly).
Show it as a SuperPlot: cells as small dots coloured by experiment, experiment means as big markers, the statistics on the big markers.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Try it: cells, experiments, pairs




Tour: “1000 cells, no effect” (3 experiments per condition, independent): cells as n: effect 0.65, p = 2.6e-31; experiments as n: same estimate, CI −2.27 to 3.57, p = 0.49. Over 1000 repetitions (exercise page): cells-as-n rejects in 89 %, experiments-as-n in 4 %. “More cells does not help” (true effect 1): power of the correct analysis 12.5 % with 1000 cells. “More experiments does”: 10 experiments of 20 cells: 46 %. “Paired design wins”: paired p = 0.023, unpaired means p = 0.43; power 84 % vs 14 %. “Confounded with the day”: no treatment effect, but all treated experiments in a later batch shifted by 1.5: estimate 2.53, even the experiment-level test gives p = 0.029.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
More cells or more experiments?
The SE of the effect, with experiments as the unit, against the number of cells per experiment (3 experiments per condition, day-to-day SD 1, cell-to-cell SD 2):
