Beyond a few dozen cells the true SE flattens out at \sigma_u\sqrt{2/E}: the day-to-day variation dominates.
More experiments shrink it like 1/\sqrt E. A paired design removes \sigma_u altogether.
Cells-as-n claims an SE that keeps shrinking: ever smaller p-values for the same evidence.

title: From measurements to claims
section: The math: pairing removes the day
text:
The math: pairing removes the day
Paired design: both conditions in each experiment e. Difference of the experiment means:
D_e = \bar y_{e,T} - \bar y_{e,C} = \tau + (u_e - u_e) + (\bar\varepsilon_{e,T} - \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}), \qquad \text{Var}(D_e) = \frac{2\sigma^2}{m}.
The day effect u_e cancels. Unpaired comparison of experiment means: \text{Var} = 2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m) per pair of experiments. Pairing wins whenever \sigma_u^2 > 0; it loses a little only through the degrees of freedom (E - 1 instead of 2E - 2) when \sigma_u is close to 0, or if the pairing is not real (control and treated not sharing the day).

title: From measurements to claims
section: Effect size and confidence interval first
text:
Effect size and confidence interval first
“Treated cells were significantly larger (p < 0.0001, n = 2400)” says nothing useful:

How much larger? “12 % larger (95 % CI 4 to 20 %)” says what matters.
What is n? “n = 4 independent experiments, 600 cells each” names the unit of replication.
p < 0.0001 with 2400 cells as n is pseudoreplication; with enough cells any tiny difference becomes “significant”.

For comparing features with different units, a standardised effect: the difference divided by the SD (of experiment means, or of cells, say which).

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Many features: multiple comparisons
Image-based profiling measures hundreds of features. Test 300 features with no real effect at \alpha = 0.05: about 15 “hits” by chance.


Under no effect, p-values are uniform: a flat histogram (left: 15 below 0.05, all false). Real effects add a spike near 0 (right: 30 real features).
Bonferroni: test each at \alpha/m. Controls the chance of any false hit. Strict: left 0 hits; right 13 hits, all real.
Benjamini–Hochberg (BH): controls the fraction of false hits among the hits (the false discovery rate). Right: 24 hits, 2 of them false.
Picking the best-looking feature after the fact is the same mistake as tuning on the test set.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
The math: Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg
m tests, all null, independent, level \alpha: P(\text{at least one false hit}) = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^m: 0.64 for m = 20, 0.99996 for m = 200.
Bonferroni. Reject when p_i \le \alpha/m. By the union bound, without any independence assumption: P\Big(\bigcup_{i \text{ null}} \{p_i \le \alpha/m\}\Big) \le \sum_{i \text{ null}} \frac{\alpha}{m} \le \alpha.
Benjamini–Hochberg at level q: sort p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}; find the largest k with p_{(k)} \le k\,q/m; reject the k smallest. Then E[\text{false hits}/\max(\text{hits}, 1)] \le q (for independent or positively dependent tests; stated without proof). Example: 0.001, 0.004, 0.012, 0.02, 0.03, 0.2, … with m = 10: lines 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, 0.025: k = 4.

title: From measurements to claims
section: Try it: many features on a plate
text:
Try it: many features on a plate




A 384-well plate, 300 features. Tour: “300 null features”: 15 uncorrected hits, Bonferroni and BH 0. “10 % real”: uncorrected 43 (14 false), Bonferroni 13 (all real), BH 24 (2 false). “gradient + treated on the left”: a left-to-right gradient, treated wells on the left half: 281 of 300 features “significant” at 0.05, 249 even after Bonferroni, none of them real. The plate map of the smallest-p feature shows the gradient. “Randomised layout”: the same gradient, random layout: no hits after correction (37 uncorrected).

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Batch and plate effects
Day, plate, row and column, the edge wells (evaporation), the order of imaging (focus drift, bleaching): all change the measurements.

If all controls are on day 1 and all treated on day 2, the treatment effect is confounded with the day: no statistics can separate them. More cells, more wells, any test: it stays an experiment about days.
The cures are in the design: every batch contains every condition; randomise the plate layout; controls on every plate; image in a randomised or balanced order.
Then normalise against the controls of each plate (the measurements day shows how) and analyse per plate or per experiment.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
A reporting checklist

n at every level (experiments, wells, images, cells), and which one is the unit of replication.
How values were aggregated (mean or median per well, per experiment).
Effect size with a confidence interval, not only a p-value.
Correction for multiple testing, and how many features were tested.
The design: pairing, randomisation, plate layout, batches.
How the image analysis was validated: the split (the leakage unit), who annotated (the agreement unit).
Images and analysis parameters available.

title: From measurements to claims
text:
Summary

Standard error = the wobble of an estimate; p-value = how often chance alone gives a result this extreme; 95 % CI ≈ estimate ± 2 SE.
The unit of replication is the independently treated unit (experiment, animal, well), not the cell. Cells as n gives false positives far above 5 %.
Aggregate per replicate, or pair the design; show a SuperPlot. More experiments help, more cells hardly.
Report effect sizes with CIs.
Many features: about \alpha m false hits; correct with Bonferroni (any false hit) or Benjamini–Hochberg (false discovery rate).
Batch and plate effects confounded with the treatment cannot be fixed afterwards: randomise and balance the design.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Encoder–decoder
convolutions and pooling down to small maps, then upsampling and convolutions back to full size


U-Net
an encoder–decoder with skip connections: encoder maps copied to the decoder and concatenated (channels add up)


Transposed convolution
each input value stamps a scaled copy of the kernel into the output, s positions apart: output length (n - 1)s + k - 2p


Per-pixel cross-entropy
-\frac1N\sum_i\big[g_i\ln p_i + (1 - g_i)\ln(1 - p_i)\big], g_i \in \{0, 1\} the true mask


Soft Dice
D = 2\sum_i p_ig_i/(\sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i); Dice loss = 1 - D


Dice, IoU (masks)
2\,\text{TP}/(2\,\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN}), \text{TP}/(\text{TP} + \text{FP} + \text{FN})

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
By hand
B1. A 3 \times 3 probability map and its true mask:
p = \begin{bmatrix} 0.9&0.8&0.1\\ 0.7&0.6&0.2\\ 0.1&0.2&0.1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad g = \begin{bmatrix} 1&1&0\\ 1&1&0\\ 0&0&0 \end{bmatrix}

Compute the mean per-pixel cross-entropy.
Compute the soft Dice. Then threshold at 0.5 and compute the ordinary Dice of the mask.
A 20 \times 20 image contains one nucleus of 20 pixels (5 %). A network outputs p = 0.01 everywhere. Compute the pixel accuracy (threshold 0.5), the cross-entropy, the soft Dice and the Dice of the mask. Which of these numbers notices that the network is useless?

B2. Upsampling the 1D signal (1, 2, 3) by a factor 2. (a) Nearest neighbour. (b) Nearest neighbour followed by the correlation with (\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac14) (zeros beyond the ends, keep 6 values). (c) A transposed convolution with stride 2 and kernel (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) (7 values). What kind of interpolation is it? (d) Which kernel, with stride 2, gives exactly nearest-neighbour upsampling?
B3. The U-Net of the demo on a 1 \times 64 \times 64 input (all convolutions 3 \times 3 with padding 1): encoder 1: conv 1→8, conv 8→8; pool; encoder 2: conv 8→16, conv 16→16; pool; bottleneck: conv 16→32, conv 32→32; upsample, concatenate with encoder 2, conv →16, conv 16→16; upsample, concatenate with encoder 1, conv →8, conv 8→8; 1 \times 1 conv 8→1. (a) Give the size (channels × height × width) after every block, including the two concatenations. (b) Count the weights of every layer and in total. (c) Without skip connections the two decoder convolutions after upsampling get only 32 and 16 channels. How many weights fewer?
B4. Receptive field of the same network. (a) Compute the receptive field of one bottleneck unit (conv, conv, pool, conv, conv, pool, conv, conv). (b) Can it see a whole nucleus of 20 pixels? (c) Upsampling does not enlarge the field, but the decoder’s convolutions do. Roughly how large is the field of one output pixel?
B5. A U-Net segments 7 nuclei perfectly, but 3 pairs of them touch. How many objects does connected-component labelling (day 9) find in the mask? Name two ways to get 7.
B6. The U-Net’s probability map as the data term of a graph cut (day 13): D_p(\ell) = -\ln p_p(\ell). Compute D_p(\text{object}) and D_p(\text{background}) for a pixel with p = 0.9, and for one with p = 0.5. What will the smoothness term decide?






Solutions





B1. (a) Object pixels: -\ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.7 - \ln 0.6 = 0.105 + 0.223 + 0.357 + 0.511; background pixels: -\ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.9 - \ln 0.8 - \ln 0.9 = 3 \cdot 0.105 + 2 \cdot 0.223. Total 1.958, mean over 9 pixels 0.218. (b) \sum p_ig_i = 0.9 + 0.8 + 0.7 + 0.6 = 3.0, \sum p_i = 3.7, \sum g_i = 4: D = 6/7.7 = 0.779. At threshold 0.5 the mask equals g exactly (TP 4, FP 0, FN 0): Dice 1. The soft Dice still rewards making the probabilities more confident. (c) Accuracy 380/400 = 95 %. Cross-entropy (380 \cdot 0.01005 + 20 \cdot 4.605)/400 = 0.240: below the 0.693 of a coin toss, so it does not look alarming. Soft Dice 2 \cdot 0.01 \cdot 20/(4 + 20) = 0.017; mask Dice 0. Only the Dice numbers show that not a single nucleus pixel is found.
B2. (a) (1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3). (b) (0.75, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 2.75, 2.25). (c) 1 \cdot (\tfrac12, 1, \tfrac12) at positions 0–2, 2 \cdot (\ldots) at 2–4, 3 \cdot (\ldots) at 4–6: (0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 1.5): linear interpolation (with half values at the open ends). (d) The kernel (1, 1) with stride 2: each value is stamped twice, side by side.
B3. (a) 8 \times 64 \times 64 → pool 8 \times 32 \times 32 → 16 \times 32 \times 32 → pool 16 \times 16 \times 16 → 32 \times 16 \times 16 → upsample 32 \times 32 \times 32 → concatenate 48 \times 32 \times 32 → 16 \times 32 \times 32 → upsample 16 \times 64 \times 64 → concatenate 24 \times 64 \times 64 → 8 \times 64 \times 64 → 1 \times 64 \times 64. (b) 9C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}: 80, 584, 1168, 2320, 4640, 9248 (encoder and bottleneck), 6928, 2320, 1736, 584 (decoder), 8 + 1 = 9 (the 1 \times 1 conv): 29,617. (c) 9 \cdot 16 \cdot 16 = 2304 fewer in the first (48 \to 32 input channels) and 9 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 = 576 in the second (24 \to 16): 2880 fewer, 26,737 in total.
B4. (a) r = 3, 5, 6, 10, 14, 16, 24, 32: 32 pixels (jump 4). (b) Yes, 32 > 20. (c) After the bottleneck, two convolutions at jump 2 add 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8, two at jump 1 add 4: about 44 pixels (the paths through the skip connections see less).
B5. 4 objects (3 merged pairs + 1 single). Split them: train with a third class “boundary between touching nuclei” and label the interiors; or use the distance transform and the watershed on the mask (days 8–10); or networks that predict separate objects directly (day 18).
B6. p = 0.9: D(\text{object}) = -\ln 0.9 = 0.105, D(\text{background}) = -\ln 0.1 = 2.303: a strong preference. p = 0.5: both \ln 2 = 0.693: no preference, so the neighbours (through the smoothness term) decide.




Math questions
B7. (math) Derive \partial D/\partial p_j for the soft Dice. Evaluate it for B1 at an object pixel and at a background pixel. Which pixels does a gradient step on the Dice loss push up, and which down?
B8. (math) Let A be the matrix of a 1D strided convolution (kernel k, stride s, no padding) and T the transposed convolution with the same kernel. Show that \langle A\mathbf x, \mathbf y\rangle = \langle\mathbf x, T\mathbf y\rangle for all \mathbf x, \mathbf y, i.e. T = A^\top.
B9. (math) Weighted cross-entropy with weights w_1 for object pixels and w_0 for background pixels. If the object share is f, show that choosing w_c \propto 1/(\text{share of class } c) makes both classes contribute equally to the loss of a network that outputs the constant p. Give the weights for f = 0.05, normalised so that w_0 = 1.






Solutions (math)





B7. (math) With I = \sum_i p_ig_i and S = \sum_i p_i + \sum_i g_i: D = 2I/S, \partial I/\partial p_j = g_j, \partial S/\partial p_j = 1, so \partial D/\partial p_j = (2g_jS - 2I)/S^2. For B1: S = 7.7, I = 3: object pixels (15.4 - 6)/59.29 = 0.159, background pixels -6/59.29 = -0.101. The Dice loss 1 - D has the opposite gradient: a step pushes object pixels up and background pixels down, with the same size for every object pixel, however confident it already is.
B8. (math) (A\mathbf x)_i = \sum_u k_u x_{is + u}, so \langle A\mathbf x, \mathbf y\rangle = \sum_i\sum_u k_ux_{is + u}y_i. The transposed convolution stamps: (T\mathbf y)_t = \sum_i\sum_u [is + u = t]\,k_uy_i, so \langle\mathbf x, T\mathbf y\rangle = \sum_t x_t\sum_{i,u}[is + u = t]k_uy_i = \sum_{i,u}k_ux_{is+u}y_i. The two sums are equal.
B9. (math) For a constant output p the loss is -\big[w_1f\ln p + w_0(1 - f)\ln(1 - p)\big]: the classes contribute with the factors w_1f and w_0(1 - f), equal when w_1/w_0 = (1 - f)/f. With w_c \propto 1/\text{share}: w_1 = c/f, w_0 = c/(1 - f), so w_1f = w_0(1 - f) = c. For f = 0.05: w_0 = 1, w_1 = 0.95/0.05 = 19. The minimum of this weighted loss over constant outputs is then at p = \tfrac12 instead of p = f.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Explore: a U-Net segments nuclei
A tiny U-Net (8, 16 and 32 channels, 29,617 weights) was trained on 4000 synthetic 64 \times 64 fluorescence-like images: nuclei of different sizes and brightness, some touching, an illumination gradient and noise. The demo draws new images from the same generator (new image). Panels: the input, the nucleus probability of every pixel, the mask at the threshold, the errors against the true mask (white = correct nucleus, red = false positive, blue = false negative) with Dice and IoU, and Otsu’s threshold (thresholding day) as the baseline. Click a block of the architecture to see its feature maps. The sliders move the input away from the training images: extra noise, a stronger illumination gradient, a brightness factor, larger or smaller nuclei. Weight sets: U-Net (trained with per-pixel cross-entropy), no skip connections, and trained with Dice loss.



U1. Preset a typical image. Read Dice, IoU and the error counts of the U-Net and the Dice of Otsu. Where are the U-Net’s errors? Move the threshold from 0.1 to 0.9: how much does Dice change?
U2. Preset U-Net vs Otsu on uneven illumination (the same image with an illumination gradient of 100 grey levels). Compare the two error images. Why does Otsu fail, and why not the U-Net?
U3. Click the five blocks of the architecture. How many maps of which size does each have? What do the bottleneck maps look like compared with those of encoder 1?
U4. Preset no skips: small nuclei (nuclei half the usual size). Compare the Dice of no skip connections and U-Net on this image, and the number of uncertain pixels (0.1 < p < 0.9). Then press back to training conditions and compare the two weight sets on a few new images. When do the skip connections matter?
U5. Preset touching nuclei merge. How many nuclei are there (readout), and how many separate white regions does the mask have? Is that an error of the network?
U6. Preset too noisy: outside the training range (extra noise with standard deviation 30). What happens to the U-Net and to Otsu? Try 15.
U7. Preset dimmer microscope: domain shift (the whole image ×0.5). Compare the U-Net with Otsu, and with the same image at brightness 1. Lower the threshold: does it help much? Then try brightness 2.
U8. Preset Dice loss: probabilities near 0 or 1. Compare the probability maps and the readouts (cross-entropy, soft Dice, uncertain pixels) of trained with Dice loss and U-Net. Move the threshold from 0.1 to 0.9 for both.






Solutions





U1. U-Net: Dice 0.986, IoU 0.972, TP 446, FP 2, FN 11; Otsu: 0.975. The few errors lie on the nucleus boundaries (blue rims: the U-Net’s nuclei are a little too small), where even the truth is a matter of half pixels. Dice is 0.980 at threshold 0.1, 0.986 at 0.5, 0.974 at 0.9: the probabilities are close to 0 or 1 except at the boundaries, so the threshold matters little.
U2. Otsu (threshold 81) labels the whole bright right side as nucleus: Dice 0.349 (a large red region). One global threshold cannot separate nuclei from a background that is brighter on one side than the dim nuclei on the other. The U-Net sees each nucleus in its neighbourhood (a bright blob is brighter than its surroundings) and was trained on images with gradients up to 100: Dice 0.987, the same as without the gradient.
U3. Encoder 1: 8 maps of 64 \times 64; encoder 2: 16 of 32 \times 32; bottleneck: 32 of 16 \times 16; decoder 2: 16 of 32 \times 32; decoder 1: 8 of 64 \times 64. Encoder-1 maps look like filtered versions of the image (edges, blobs, background); the bottleneck maps are coarse blobs that mark where the nuclei are, with blocky outlines.
U4. On this image: no skips Dice 0.936 (FP 27, 41 uncertain pixels), U-Net 0.954 (FP 19, 28 uncertain pixels): without skips the small nuclei come out too large and blurred. On typical images the difference is small (validation Dice 0.965 against 0.968): these smooth, fairly large blobs can be located from the 16 \times 16 bottleneck maps. Skip connections matter for small objects and fine boundaries; over 40 test images with half-size nuclei the Dice is 0.904 without and 0.925 with skips.
U5. 7 nuclei, but the mask has 4 connected regions: several nuclei touch. The network did what it was trained for (Dice 0.986): label pixels as nucleus or not. Separating touching nuclei needs another step (B5).
U6. Noise 30 (training noise was 3–10): the U-Net drops to Dice 0.943 and its mask breaks into 9 pieces (specks in the background, holes); Otsu drops to 0.729. At noise 15 both are still good (0.978 and 0.951). The network degrades gracefully here, but its errors are of a new kind (scattered specks).
U7. At brightness ×0.5 the U-Net misses most of the nuclei: Dice 0.269 (TP 143, FN 776), while Otsu still reaches 0.705. At brightness 1 the same image gives 0.951. Lowering the threshold to 0.1 helps little (0.335): the probabilities themselves are low, the network has never seen nuclei this dim. At brightness ×2: 0.930. A network can be beaten by a simple threshold as soon as the input leaves its training range; it gives no warning. Augmenting the brightness during training, or normalising the images, would help.
U8. The Dice-trained network gives almost only probabilities near 0 or 1: 16 uncertain pixels against 285 for the cross-entropy network. Its Dice hardly depends on the threshold (0.904–0.906 from 0.1 to 0.9); the cross-entropy network peaks at 0.5 (0.909) and drops to 0.851 at 0.1 and 0.856 at 0.9. The Dice-trained network’s cross-entropy is high (0.491 against 0.108): where it is wrong it is confidently wrong. Its probabilities are not calibrated: “0.99” does not mean “right 99 % of the time”.

title: Exercise: segmentation networks
text:
Where this leads
The evaluation day (day 16) asks how to measure segmentations honestly: object-level matching, test sets from new sources, and the statistics of comparing methods. Modern deep learning (day 18) splits touching nuclei with networks, uses pretrained models that need fewer annotations, and generates images; the VAE day (day 17) shows networks that learn to make images rather than label them. Learned image restoration (denoising, deconvolution with networks) is discussed on the deconvolution day.

title: Quiz: from measurements to claims
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You image 2000 cells from one treated dish and 2000 from one control dish, and a t-test on the cells gives p = 10^{-12}. What is n, and what can you conclude?






Hint





At which level was the treatment applied independently?









Answer





n = 1 per condition: one dish each. The cells share their dish, so the test compares two dishes, and any difference between two dishes (seeding, medium, position in the incubator, imaging day) looks like a treatment effect. Nothing can be concluded about the treatment; repeat the experiment independently several times and compare the dish (or experiment) means.




Q2. Explain a p-value of 0.03 in one sentence, without the word “probability of the hypothesis”.






Hint





Imagine the treatment does nothing.









Answer





If the treatment had no effect, a difference at least as large as the observed one would come up by chance in about 3 % of repeated experiments.




Q3. Why does measuring more cells per experiment hardly shrink the uncertainty of the treatment effect, while more experiments do?






Hint





Which variation do the cells of one experiment share?









Answer





All cells of one experiment share its day-to-day deviation. More cells average out the cell-to-cell variation but not that shared part; the uncertainty levels off at (day-to-day SD) × \sqrt{2/E}. Only more experiments average out the day-to-day variation.




Q4. In a paired design, control and treated are done on the same day in each of 4 experiments. Why is this usually much more powerful than 4 control and 4 treated experiments on 8 different days?






Hint





What happens to the day effect in the difference?









Answer





Within each day, the day effect is the same for both conditions and cancels in the difference treated − control. The paired test compares differences that only contain the (smaller) within-day variation; the unpaired test has to see the effect through the large day-to-day variation.




Q5. You measure 500 features and report the 12 with p < 0.05 as “affected by the treatment”. What is the problem, and what would you do?






Hint





How many hits would chance give?









Answer





With no real effect at all, 0.05 \cdot 500 = 25 features would be expected below 0.05; 12 hits are fully compatible with no effect. Correct for multiple testing: Benjamini–Hochberg to control the share of false discoveries, or Bonferroni (p \le 0.0001) to control the chance of any false hit; and confirm the hits in a new experiment.




Q6. All control wells were imaged on Monday and all treated wells on Tuesday. A colleague suggests a mixed-effects model with day as a random effect. Will it help?






Hint





Can any analysis separate the day from the treatment here?









Answer





No. Day and treatment are confounded: every difference between the conditions is also a difference between the days, and no model can split it. Only the design can: both conditions on every day (and every plate), randomised positions.




Q7. Report A: “p < 0.001”. Report B: “the area increased by 9 % (95 % CI 2 to 16 %), n = 5 experiments”. Why is B more useful?






Hint





What do you want to know about an effect?









Answer





B gives the size of the effect, its uncertainty, and the unit of replication with its n; the reader can judge whether 2–16 % matters biologically. A p-value alone says neither how large the effect is nor whether n counted cells or experiments; with enough cells any tiny difference gives p < 0.001.




Q8. (math) Cells within an experiment have intra-class correlation \rho = 0.1. What is the design effect for 100 cells per experiment, and what is the false-positive rate of a cells-as-n z-test at 5 %?






Hint





Design effect 1 + (m-1)\rho; the z statistic has that variance instead of 1.









Answer





1 + 99 \cdot 0.1 = 10.9. The z statistic has SD \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, so P(|z| > 1.96) = 2\Phi(-1.96/3.30) = 2\Phi(-0.59) = 0.55: 55 % false positives instead of 5 %.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Standard error (SE)
the wobble of an estimate between repeated experiments; SD/\sqrt n for a mean of n independent values


p-value
how often chance alone (no effect) gives a result at least this extreme


95 % CI
estimate \pm\, t_{0.975}\cdotSE (about ± 2 SE): the effects compatible with the data


Unit of replication
the level at which the treatment was applied independently (experiment, animal, well)


Pseudoreplication
treating dependent measurements (cells of one dish) as independent replicates


Paired design
both conditions in every experiment; compare within each


Bonferroni
reject when p \le \alpha/m (m tests)


Benjamini–Hochberg
sort the p-values; the largest k with p_{(k)} \le k\,q/m; reject the k smallest



Critical values of the t-distribution, t_{0.975}: 4.30 (2 degrees of freedom), 2.78 (4 df), 2.07 (22 df), 1.96 (very many).

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
By hand
B1. Three experiments (days), four cells per condition each:




control
treated




day 1
10, 11, 12, 11
12, 13, 14, 13


day 2
14, 15, 13, 14
15, 16, 14, 15


day 3
8, 9, 7, 8
10, 9, 11, 10




Compute the experiment means, and the paired differences treated − control per day.
Paired analysis: mean difference, SD of the differences, SE, t. Is it significant at 5 % (2 df)? Give the 95 % CI.
Unpaired analysis of the experiment means (3 against 3): the two means, their SDs, the SE of the difference and t (4 df). Significant?
Cells as n (12 against 12): the pooled two-sample test gives t \approx 1.65 (22 df). Now imagine 100 cells per experiment with the same spread: t becomes about 8.6. Which analyses are right, which is wrong, and why does the paired one win?

B2. 200 features, none with a real effect, each tested at \alpha = 0.05. (a) How many “hits” do you expect? (b) What is the probability of at least one (independent tests)? (c) What is the Bonferroni threshold?
B3. Ten sorted p-values: 0.001, 0.004, 0.012, 0.02, 0.03, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9. How many hits at \alpha = 0.05 (a) uncorrected, (b) with Bonferroni, (c) with Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.05?
B4. A plate: controls in columns 1–2, treatment A in columns 3–12, imaged from left to right over two hours while the focus drifts slowly. (a) What could go wrong? (b) How would you lay out and image the plate instead?
B5. Rewrite the sentence “Treated cells were significantly larger (p < 0.0001, n = 2400)” into a good report. What extra information do you need?






Solutions





B1. (a) Control means 11, 14, 8; treated 13, 15, 10. Differences 2, 1, 2. (b) Mean difference 5/3 = 1.67, SD 0.58, SE = 0.58/\sqrt3 = 0.33, t = 5.0 > 4.30: significant (p = 0.038). 95 % CI: 1.67 \pm 4.30 \cdot 0.33 = 0.23 to 3.10. (c) Means 11 and 12.67 (difference 1.67); SDs 3.0 and 2.52; SE of the difference \sqrt{(9 + 6.33)/3} = 2.26; t = 0.74 < 2.78: not significant. (d) Right: the paired analysis (the design is paired: both conditions every day), and the unpaired analysis of experiment means (valid, but it throws away the pairing). Wrong: cells as n. Its t = 1.65 is not “nearly significant evidence”; it treats 12 cells as 12 independent replicates. With 100 cells per experiment the same data would give t \approx 8.6 and a tiny p-value, although nothing about the evidence changed (still three days). The paired analysis wins because the day-to-day differences (means 8 to 14) are much larger than the treatment effect; comparing within each day removes them.
B2. (a) 200 \cdot 0.05 = 10. (b) 1 - 0.95^{200} = 0.99996: practically certain. (c) 0.05/200 = 0.00025.
B3. (a) Five p-values \le 0.05. (b) Bonferroni threshold 0.005: 0.001 and 0.004, 2 hits. (c) BH lines k \cdot 0.005: 0.005, 0.010, 0.015, 0.020, 0.025, … The largest k with p_{(k)} \le its line: k = 4 (0.02 \le 0.020; 0.03 > 0.025, and no later p-value is below its line). 4 hits.
B4. (a) The treatment is confounded with the plate position (edge columns, evaporation) and with time (focus drift, bleaching, cells changing during two hours): any difference between columns 1–2 and the rest could be position or time, not treatment. (b) Spread controls over the whole plate (e.g. in every row, also in the middle), randomise or balance the positions of the conditions, avoid or fill the edge wells, and image in a randomised (or interleaved) order; replicate on several plates and days, with controls on every plate.
B5. For example: “Treated cells were 12 % larger than controls (95 % CI 4 % to 20 %; mean of per-experiment medians, n = 4 independent experiments, 600 cells each; paired t-test, p = 0.02).” Needed: the effect size and its CI; the unit of replication and its n (experiments, not cells); how values were aggregated; the test; the number of features tested if this was one of many (and the correction).




Math questions
B6. (math) In the two-level model y_{ec} = \mu + u_e + \varepsilon_{ec} (E experiments, m cells each, u_e \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2), \varepsilon_{ec} \sim N(0, \sigma^2), independent), derive the variance of the grand mean and the design effect 1 + (m-1)\rho with \rho = \sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2). What is n_{\text{eff}} for m = 500, \rho = 0.2, E = 3?
B7. (math) Derive the false-positive rate of the cells-as-n z-test under no effect, 2\,\Phi\big(-1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big), and evaluate it for m = 10, 100, 1000 at \rho = 0.1.
B8. (math) Show that the paired difference of experiment means does not contain u_e. When does pairing lose power compared with the unpaired test of experiment means?
B9. (math) Prove that Bonferroni controls the family-wise error rate without any independence assumption. Show with B3 that Benjamini–Hochberg can reject a hypothesis with p > \alpha/m.






Solutions (math)





B6. \bar y_e = \mu + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_e with \text{Var}(\bar\varepsilon_e) = \sigma^2/m, so \text{Var}(\bar y_e) = \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m. The grand mean \bar y = \frac1E\sum_e \bar y_e averages E independent experiment means: \text{Var}(\bar y) = \sigma_u^2/E + \sigma^2/(Em). If all Em cells were independent with variance \sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2, it would be (\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em). Ratio: \frac{m\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2} = 1 + (m - 1)\frac{\sigma_u^2}{\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2} = 1 + (m-1)\rho. With m = 500, \rho = 0.2: design effect 1 + 499 \cdot 0.2 = 100.8; n_{\text{eff}} = 1500/100.8 = 14.9 cells’ worth of information, close to the limit E/\rho = 15. 1500 cells from 3 experiments are worth about 15 independent cells.
B7. Under no effect, \bar y_1 - \bar y_0 has variance 2(\sigma_u^2/E + \sigma^2/(Em)) = \frac{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)}{Em}\,(1 + (m-1)\rho) by B6. The cells-as-n statistic divides by \sqrt{2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2)/(Em)}, so z \sim N(0, 1 + (m-1)\rho). It rejects when |z| > 1.96: P = 2\,P\big(Z > 1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big) = 2\Phi\big(-1.96/\sqrt{1 + (m-1)\rho}\big). At \rho = 0.1: m = 10: \sqrt{1.9} = 1.38, 2\Phi(-1.42) = 0.155; m = 100: \sqrt{10.9} = 3.30, 2\Phi(-0.594) = 0.553; m = 1000: \sqrt{100.9} = 10.04, 2\Phi(-0.195) = 0.845.
B8. With both conditions in experiment e: \bar y_{e,T} = \mu + \tau + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_{e,T} and \bar y_{e,C} = \mu + u_e + \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}; the difference is \tau + \bar\varepsilon_{e,T} - \bar\varepsilon_{e,C}, without u_e, with variance 2\sigma^2/m instead of 2(\sigma_u^2 + \sigma^2/m). Pairing loses only when \sigma_u is about 0 (nothing to remove): then it has E - 1 degrees of freedom instead of 2E - 2, a larger critical value (t_{0.975} = 4.30 instead of 2.78 for E = 3), and slightly less power. It also loses if the “pairs” do not really share a day effect.
B9. Let N be the set of true null hypotheses, |N| \le m. Each null p-value is uniform, so P(p_i \le \alpha/m) = \alpha/m. P(\text{any false hit}) = P\big(\bigcup_{i \in N}\{p_i \le \alpha/m\}\big) \le \sum_{i \in N} \alpha/m \le \alpha, by the union bound, which needs no independence. In B3, BH rejects p = 0.012 and p = 0.02, both above \alpha/m = 0.005.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Explore: cells, experiments, pairs
A simulated experiment with two conditions: E experiments, m cells per experiment and condition, a day-to-day SD (shared by all cells of an experiment), a cell-to-cell SD and a true effect. Designs: independent (each experiment does one condition), paired (both conditions in every experiment), confounded (all treated experiments in a later batch, shifted by the batch shift). The SuperPlot shows cells as small dots coloured by experiment (at most 80 drawn per experiment) and experiment means as big markers. Three analyses: cells as n, experiment means as n, paired experiment means, each with the estimate, 95 % CI and p. The bars show the share of p < 0.05 over 1000 repetitions (the false-positive rate when the true effect is 0, the power otherwise). The last plot shows the SE of the effect against m: the true one, and what cells-as-n claims.



P1. Preset 1000 cells, no effect. Read the estimate, CI and p of the three analyses, and the shares of p < 0.05. Which analysis would you believe?
P2. Keep everything but set the cells per experiment to 10, then 100. Read the false-positive rate of cells as n. Compare with the formula of B7: here \rho = 1/(1 + 4) = 0.2.
P3. Preset more cells does not help (true effect 1, 1000 cells per experiment), then more experiments does (10 experiments of 20 cells). Compare the power of the experiments-as-n analysis, and look at the SE plot.
P4. Preset paired design wins. Compare the paired and the unpaired analysis of the same experiment means (p and CI), and their power over 1000 repetitions. What do the lines in the SuperPlot show?
P5. Preset confounded with the day: no treatment effect, but every treated experiment was done in a later batch. Read the estimate and the p-values. Increase the number of experiments to 10: does it help? What would?
P6. With the independent design and no effect, set the day-to-day SD to 0. What happens to the false-positive rate of cells as n? Why is this no excuse to analyse cells as n?






Solutions





P1. Cells as n: estimate 0.65 [0.54, 0.75], p = 2.6 \cdot 10^{-31}. Experiments as n: the same estimate, CI −2.27 to 3.57, p = 0.49. Over 1000 repetitions with no effect, cells as n gives p < 0.05 in 89 % (88.5 %) of them, experiments as n in 4.0 %. Believe the experiment-level analysis: the estimate is the same, but only its CI reflects the day-to-day variation.
P2. m = 10: 25 % false positives (25.1 %); m = 100: 69 % (68.8 %); m = 1000 (P1): 89 %. The formula with \rho = 0.2: 0.24, 0.67 and 0.89. It fits well even with only 3 experiments per condition.
P3. 1000 cells per experiment, 3 experiments per condition: power 12.5 %. 10 experiments of 20 cells (far fewer cells in total): 46 %. In the SE plot the true SE flattens out at about 0.82 beyond ~100 cells (for 3 experiments), while cells as n claims 0.06 at 1000 cells.
P4. Paired: estimate 0.87, CI 0.30 to 1.45, p = 0.023. Unpaired experiment means: the same estimate, CI −1.90 to 3.64, p = 0.43. Power over 1000 repetitions: 84 % paired, 14 % unpaired. The lines join the control and treated means of each experiment: they all go up by about the same amount, although the experiments sit at very different levels. Pairing compares the slopes, not the levels.
P5. Estimate 2.53 (no real effect; the batch shift is 1.5 and this run is a little lucky), and even the experiment-level analysis gives p = 0.029. Over 1000 repetitions it rejects in about 21 % of them instead of 5 %, and the estimate is always biased by the batch shift. More experiments do not help: with 10 experiments the estimate is 1.51 (the batch shift, now measured precisely), p = 0.005, and the experiment-level test rejects in 88 % of repetitions. More data make the batch difference more certain, not the treatment effect. Only the design helps: every batch must contain both conditions (or pair within a batch).
P6. With day-to-day SD 0, cells as n rejects in about 4 % of the null experiments, like the experiment-level test: cells are then really independent. But you cannot know beforehand that days do not differ (in practice they nearly always do), and aggregating first costs little when they do not. Analyse at the level of the unit of replication.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
section: Explore: many features on a plate
text:
Explore: many features on a plate
A 384-well plate (or 96), half treated, half control, with m features measured per well. A share of the features carries a real treatment effect (in SDs). Plate effects: a left–right and a top–bottom gradient and edge wells, which each feature feels with its own sensitivity. Layouts: treated on the left half, random, or random per row. Left: the plate map of one feature (treated wells outlined). Middle: the histogram of all p-values (grey: the null features). Right: the sorted p-values against their rank on log axes, with the uncorrected line \alpha, the Bonferroni line \alpha/m and the BH line k\alpha/m; green dots are real features, red dots null features (known from the simulation). The table counts the hits of each method and how many are false.



F1. Preset 300 null features. Read the hits of each method. Describe the histogram of p-values.
F2. Set m to 50 and to 500. How many uncorrected hits, and how many does \alpha m predict?
F3. Preset 10 % real: BH finds most. Read hits, false hits and true hits for each method. Where are the real features in the rank plot?
F4. Preset gradient + treated on the left. Read the hits. Look at the plate map of the smallest-p feature. Why does Bonferroni not help?
F5. Preset randomised layout fixes it (the same gradient). Read the hits. Then try random per row.
F6. Preset edge wells, row-blocked layout: edge effect, a top–bottom gradient and 10 % real features, with a balanced layout. How do the three methods do? Then untick 384 wells (96 wells, same settings): what happens, and why?






Solutions





F1. Uncorrected 15 hits (all false), Bonferroni 0, BH 0. The histogram is flat at about m/20 = 15 per bin: under no effect every p-value is equally likely.
F2. m = 50: 1 hit (\alpha m = 2.5); m = 500: 27 hits (\alpha m = 25). The number of false hits grows in proportion to the number of features.
F3. 30 real features. Uncorrected: 43 hits, 14 false, 29 true. Bonferroni: 13 hits, all true. BH: 24 hits, 2 false, 22 true. The real features have the smallest p-values (green dots at low ranks, below the BH line); the null ones continue as the uniform curve. BH finds most real features with few false ones; Bonferroni is safe but misses more than half.
F4. 281 of 300 features “significant” uncorrected, 249 after Bonferroni, 281 with BH; none of them real. The plate map shows the left–right gradient, and the treated wells are all on one side. Every feature that feels the gradient differs between the halves; the p-values are tiny, so no correction for the number of tests can remove them. The problem is bias (confounding), not chance.
F5. Random layout: 37 uncorrected hits, 0 after Bonferroni or BH. The gradient now hits both conditions alike on average; it only adds noise (and a little chance imbalance, which pushes many features together, hence 37 instead of 15 uncorrected). Random per row: 13 uncorrected hits, 0 corrected.
F6. 384 wells: uncorrected 32 hits (8 false), Bonferroni 8 (all true), BH 19 (1 false). With 96 wells: uncorrected 19 hits (6 false, 13 true); Bonferroni and BH find only 1. With a quarter of the wells the SE of each comparison doubles, and an effect of 0.35 SD hardly stands out from 300 tests.

title: Exercise: from measurements to claims
text:
Where this leads
The evaluation of a method (units 1–3) and the analysis of an experiment (this unit) share one lesson: count what is independent, and decide before you look. The modern deep learning day reuses the object matching and AP of unit 1 for detection.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
About this lecture
Linear filters do not know that light is counted in photons. Richardson–Lucy (RL) does.

The RL step in words, and by hand on four pixels.
Why it suits photon counts: never negative, keeps the total light.
The number of iterations is the regularisation parameter (semi-convergence).
3D widefield and confocal stacks, and the missing cone that no method fills.
The PSF you use: too narrow, too wide, and blind deconvolution.
A catalogue of artefacts.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Third unit of the deconvolution day. Recalls: the Poisson (shot) noise model and the camera offset (camera noise unit, day 3); the 3D PSF and the missing cone picture (image formation day); early stopping and filter factors (last unit). Notation: y = observed counts, x = estimate, h = PSF (sums to 1), b = background (counts per pixel), k = iteration.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Photons are counted

A fluorescence image counts photons (after removing the camera offset): never negative, Poisson noise whose variance equals the mean (camera noise unit).
Wiener and Tikhonov produce negative intensities next to bright objects (the last two units: up to 15 % of the pixels) and treat noise as equally large everywhere.
We want a restoration that keeps every pixel ≥ 0, keeps the total number of photons, and weights the data as Poisson counts.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Richardson–Lucy in words
Start from a flat guess (every pixel = the mean of the data). Then repeat:

Blur the guess with the PSF: what the microscope would show if the guess were true.
Compare with the data, pixel by pixel, as a ratio data / blurred guess. Where the guess is too dim the ratio is above 1, where it is too bright below 1.
Spread the ratio back with the PSF (mirrored): each object pixel collects the ratios of the image pixels it contributes to.
Multiply the guess by it.

Every factor is positive, so the guess stays non-negative; and (with a PSF that sums to 1) the total stays equal to the total of the data.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The math: RL from the Poisson likelihood
text:
The math: RL from the Poisson likelihood
Model: y_i \sim \text{Poisson}\big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big), A = convolution with h \ge 0, \sum h = 1, so A^\top\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1. Log-likelihood (dropping terms without \mathbf x):
\ell(\mathbf x) = \sum_i y_i \log\big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big) - \big((A\mathbf x)_i + b\big).
Gradient: \nabla\ell = A^\top\!\Big(\dfrac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x + b}\Big) - A^\top\mathbf 1. At a maximum with x_j > 0: A^\top\big(\mathbf y/(A\mathbf x + b)\big)_j = 1. RL is the fixed-point iteration
x_j \leftarrow x_j \cdot \Big[A^\top\Big(\frac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x + b}\Big)\Big]_j .

It is an EM algorithm (Shepp & Vardi 1982): the likelihood never decreases.
Non-negative: a product of non-negative factors. Flux: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_i y_i\frac{(A\mathbf x)_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i + b}, which is \sum_i y_i for b = 0.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: Try it: RL step by step
text:
Try it: RL step by step




Beads (a 1 : 4 pair, 6 px apart) next to an edge, Gaussian PSF σ = 2 px, Poisson noise with 100 photons at value 1 (the beads peak at 2.5). The iterations are computed in the background; the slider scrubs through ~30 snapshots. Tour: “no noise”: the error keeps falling up to 1000 iterations (1.22 % of the peak), the misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) drops to almost 0. “Noise: semi-convergence”: best at k = 8 (2.20 %), then rising (10.4 % at 1000); the misfit settles near 1, the noise level. Best Wiener: 2.49 %. “Fewer photons” (20): best at k = 3 (2.56 %). “1000 iterations: speckles” on the cell phantom: 18.7 % error against 2.74 % at k = 5; the background breaks up into bright dots. “RL vs best Wiener” (phantom, 1000 photons): RL 2.18 % at k = 25, Wiener 2.31 %.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The number of iterations is λ
text:
The number of iterations is λ
Recall from the last unit: an iteration from a flat image fills in strong (low) frequencies first and weak (high, noisy) ones last. RL does the same.

Semi-convergence: the error against the truth falls, then rises; the data fit keeps improving.
Fewer photons → stop earlier. In the demo (beads): best k = 40 at 1000 photons, 8 at 100, 3 at 20.
The misfit (Poisson deviance per pixel) reaches about 1 when the blurred estimate explains the data to the noise level: a discrepancy rule for RL.
Alternatives to stopping: add a penalty (e.g. total variation; one line here, the Ising/MRF elective owns TV).
Tomography’s MLEM (Radon elective) is the same algorithm with the projector instead of the PSF.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: The math: why stopping early regularises here too
text:
The math: why stopping early regularises here too
Write \mathbf x = \bar x(\mathbf 1 + \boldsymbol\delta) around the flat start \bar x, with small \boldsymbol\delta and b = 0. Then A\mathbf x = \bar x(\mathbf 1 + A\boldsymbol\delta) and
\frac{\mathbf y}{A\mathbf x} \approx \frac{\mathbf y}{\bar x}\big(\mathbf 1 - A\boldsymbol\delta\big), \qquad \mathbf x_{\text{new}} \approx \mathbf x + \mathbf x \cdot A^\top\Big(\frac{\mathbf y - A\mathbf x}{\bar x}\Big).
Near a flat image this is a Landweber step with \omega \approx 1 (in units of \bar x): \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + A^\top(\mathbf y - A\mathbf x). Per frequency the k-th iterate keeps about 1 - (1 - |H(f)|^2)^k of the inverse: strong frequencies early, weak ones after about 1/|H|^2 iterations.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Offset and background

RL needs counts: subtract the camera offset first (camera noise unit) but keep the photon scale; a negative pixel breaks the Poisson model.
Most images also have a background: out-of-focus haze, autofluorescence, a few photons per pixel everywhere.
Put it in the model, \mathbf y \approx A\mathbf x + b. If b is left out, RL must explain the background by the object, and it sharpens the background into speckles (the estimate is a sum of bright points).
In the demo (cell phantom, 100 photons at 1, background 30 photons): forgetting b gives at least 27.5 % error at every k; with b in the model 3.18 % at k = 10.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
3D: widefield stacks
Widefield 3D stacks are where deconvolution is most used. Recall (image formation day): the 3D PSF of a widefield microscope is elongated in z: an hourglass of out-of-focus light above and below each point, and its OTF has a missing cone around the k_z axis.

3D RL with the 3D PSF puts out-of-focus light back where it came from: contrast and axial resolution improve a lot. A bead’s axial FWHM in the demo: 1.48 µm blurred, 0.53 µm after 100 iterations.
But the missing cone is not filled: a thin horizontal sheet (all its frequencies along k_z) stays smeared in z: 200 nm thick, 4.7 µm blurred, still 1.3 µm after 100 iterations.
Vertical structures are restored better than horizontal ones.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
The math: the missing cone
The amplitude PSF of a lens is the inverse Fourier transform of the pupil: a cap of the sphere |\mathbf k| = n/\lambda with half-angle α (\sin\alpha = \mathrm{NA}/n). The intensity PSF is its squared magnitude, so the OTF is the autocorrelation of the cap: the set of differences \mathbf k_1 - \mathbf k_2 of two points on it.

The differences fill a torus-like region in (k_r, k_z): up to k_r = 2\,\mathrm{NA}/\lambda laterally.
Near the origin two nearby points on the cap differ in a direction tangent to the cap: at most at angle α to the k_r axis. So for small k_r only |k_z| \lesssim k_r\tan\alpha is reached: a cone around the k_z axis is missing.
A horizontal sheet, uniform in x and y, has only k_r = 0: of all its frequencies only k_z = 0 survives.
Confocal: excitation PSF × detection PSF, so the OTF is the convolution of two widefield OTFs, which fills the cone.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Try it: a 3D stack




64 × 32 × 32 voxels, 100 nm laterally, 200 nm between planes, NA 0.8 in air, 1000 photons at value 1. Top row: xz slices (drawn to scale), bottom: xy at the middle plane. Right: the OTF magnitude at ky = 0 (log), with the missing cone dashed; then axial profiles. 3D RL costs about 20 ms per iteration here, so 200 iterations take a few seconds. Tour: “widefield” (k = 0): blur above and below every object. “RL restores the bead in z”: bead axial FWHM 1476 nm blurred → 526 nm at k = 100 (444 at 200). “The sheet stays smeared”: 200 nm thick; 4666 nm blurred, 1345 at k = 100, 1111 at 200. “Confocal”: bead 854 → 233 nm, sheet 921 → 282 nm: the cone is filled. “z-steps too large” (800 nm): the bead only goes from 1178 to 808 nm; the stack under-samples the PSF in z.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Confocal, and depth

Confocal: the pinhole already rejects most out-of-focus light, and its OTF has no missing cone. Deconvolution gains less in contrast, but it works more reliably, and sheets are restored too.
Depth: the 3D PSF must match the depth. Imaging into water with an oil lens (refractive index mismatch) makes the PSF asymmetric in z and change with depth. A PSF measured at the coverslip is wrong 30 µm deeper.
Sampling: the z-step must resolve the PSF axially (Nyquist, image formation day); otherwise deconvolution has nothing to work with.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
The PSF you use








PSF used
result
looks




too narrow
leftover blur, under-restored
safe, but objects too large


right
best



too wide
over-sharpening, dark rims (halos) around bright objects, ringing, objects smaller than they are
crisp, wrong




Measured PSF (beads, image formation day): includes the real aberrations, but noisy and from one depth.
Computed PSF: clean but ideal.
Common compromise: fit a model PSF to measured beads.
In the demo (beads, 1000 photons, k = 100): the single bead’s FWHM is 3.25 px with a PSF 30 % too narrow, 2.63 px with the right one, 2.57 px with one 30 % too wide (truth 1.45 px); the too-wide PSF digs a rim down to 0.013 around it (background 0.05).

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Blind deconvolution
Estimate object and PSF together: alternate an RL step on the object (PSF fixed) with an RL step on the PSF (object fixed).

Very under-determined: the trivial answer “PSF = a point, object = the blurred image” explains the data perfectly.
So it needs constraints: PSF non-negative, sum 1, limited size, smooth, or a parametric shape (e.g. Gaussian with unknown width).
In the demo (start 50 % too wide, FWHM 7.1 px; true 4.8 px): unconstrained, the PSF width passes the true value near 100 iterations and keeps shrinking (3.3 px at 300). A size limit does not stop this; a Gaussian shape slows it (6.0 px at 300).
Use it when no PSF can be measured (motion, unknown aberration); otherwise prefer a measured or computed PSF.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
section: Try it: the PSF you use
text:
Try it: the PSF you use




Bottom right panel: the true PSF next to the one used (or the current blind estimate). Tour: “PSF too wide” (×1.3, 1000 photons, k = 100): dark rims around the beads; the peak ratio of the 1 : 4 pair is 9.1 instead of 4. “Too narrow” (×0.7): the beads stay round and wide. “Forgot the background”: speckles in the background (up to 0.70 where the truth is 0.05) and the total flux of the estimate equals that of the data including the background. “Ringing at the edge” (Airy PSF, 10 000 photons, 1000 iterations): the profile dips to 0.03 just before the edge (background 0.05) and overshoots to 0.56 after it (true 0.50). “Blind”: watch the PSF estimate shrink (readout: FWHM). “Blind with a Gaussian shape”: slower drift. Blind steps cost three times more, so the run stops at 300 iterations.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Artefacts

Cell phantom, Gaussian PSF σ = 2 px, 100 photons at value 1. From the left: truth, observed, RL after 5, 25 and 1000 iterations (RMSE against the truth 0.030, 0.039 and 0.205; the observed image 0.050; values 0..1).
Ringing: ripples next to sharp edges and around bright objects.
Speckling: noise turned into bright dots after many iterations (right image).
Halos: dark rims from a PSF that is too wide.
Border artefacts: the periodic FFT; pad and taper (unit 1).
Axial smearing of horizontal structures in widefield 3D: the missing cone.

title: Richardson–Lucy, 3D, and the PSF you use
text:
Summary

Richardson–Lucy: blur the guess, compare as a ratio, spread the ratio back, multiply. Never negative, keeps the photons, maximises the Poisson likelihood (EM).
Iterations = regularisation: semi-convergence; fewer photons → stop earlier; a misfit of about 1 per pixel means the noise level is reached.
Needs offset-corrected counts and a background term, or the background turns into speckles.
3D: puts out-of-focus light back; restores beads and vertical structures, but the missing cone keeps horizontal sheets smeared. Confocal has no missing cone.
PSF too narrow: leftover blur. Too wide: halos, ringing, objects too small. Blind estimation needs constraints and still drifts towards a point.
Artefacts: ringing, speckles, halos, borders, axial smearing.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
About this lecture
A network for images should know two things about images: neighbouring pixels belong together, and a nucleus is a nucleus wherever it is. A convolutional layer builds in both.

A convolutional layer = a bank of small kernels, learned instead of designed. Each gives a feature map.
The same kernel everywhere (weight sharing): few weights, and shifting the input shifts the maps.
Pooling shrinks the maps; stacked layers see ever larger parts of the image (the receptive field).
Early layers find edges, later ones parts and objects. Augmentation teaches the invariances we want.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Suggested demo tour: convlayer (hand-made vs learned bank, shift, pooling), receptive (presets “three 3×3 = 7”, “with pooling”, “how deep to see a whole nucleus?”), cnnviewer (a digit through the trained network; “a 6 rotated to a 9”, rotation with and without augmentation, occlusion). Convolution itself is from the kernels unit of day 1: recall it in one sentence, do not re-teach it.

title: Convolutional networks
section: From hand-made features to learned ones
text:
From hand-made features to learned ones
Day 14 (random forests) gave every pixel a feature stack: Gaussian, derivative, LoG, Hessian filters at chosen scales (the edges day), then a classifier on top.

The filters were designed by us: interpretable, no training data needed.
A convolutional network learns the filters, and further layers that combine them, from labelled examples.
The trade-off: learned features adapt to the task, but they need examples (and checking).

title: Convolutional networks
section: Dense layers do not suit images
text:
Dense layers do not suit images
A 64 \times 64 grey image into a dense layer of 100 units: 4096 \times 100 + 100 = 409{,}700 weights.

Too many weights: each unit has a separate weight for every pixel.
No neighbourhood: the pixel order could be shuffled and the layer would not notice.
No shift: a nucleus in the top-left corner and the same nucleus in the bottom-right use completely different weights. Every position has to be learned separately.

title: Convolutional networks
section: A convolutional layer: a bank of kernels
text:
A convolutional layer: a bank of kernels
Recall (the kernels unit, day 1): a 3 \times 3 kernel slides over the image; each output pixel is the weighted sum of the 3 \times 3 neighbourhood.

A convolutional layer applies several kernels, say 8, each giving one output image: a feature map.
Then a bias and the ReLU, as in any layer: each map says “my pattern is here, this strongly”.
The kernel values are weights, learned by backpropagation like any others.
Networks actually compute the correlation (no flip); with learned kernels the flip does not matter.


Show the convlayer demo next. The hand-made bank has Sobel x and y, two diagonals, the Laplacian, a Gaussian, and two line detectors. The learned bank is layer 1 of the small digit network of cnnviewer: several of its kernels look like edge or stroke detectors in some direction.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Try it: one convolutional layer




Start with the learned bank on a digit; switch to the hand-made bank and compare. Then “shift the input” (micrograph): every map shifts by the same amount. Then “pooling”: the maps at half size, still recognisable. Click a kernel and edit it (e.g. turn Sobel x into its negative: the other edge of each stroke lights up).

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Weight sharing
The same 9 weights at every position.

Weights per layer: 3 \cdot 3 \cdot C_\text{in} \cdot C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}, independent of the image size. One grey input, 8 kernels: 80 weights, for a 28 \times 28 or a 1000 \times 1000 image alike.
Translation equivariance: shift the input, and every feature map shifts the same way. A detector learned at one position works at all of them.
Compare: the dense layer of the last slide has 409,700 weights and no equivariance.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The math: a convolutional layer
With input channels x_c and output channels y_{c'}:
y_{c'}[i, j] = b_{c'} + \sum_{c}\sum_{u,v} w_{c',c}[u, v]\; x_c[i + u,\ j + v]

It is a dense layer whose matrix is sparse (each output depends on a k \times k patch) and repeated (every row is the same kernel, shifted): a banded Toeplitz matrix in 1D.
Equivariance: with T_s = shift by s, \text{conv}(T_sx) = T_s\,\text{conv}(x) (up to borders). The ReLU acts pixel by pixel, so it keeps this. Stride and pooling break it for shifts that are not multiples of the stride.
Backprop through a convolution is again a correlation: \partial\mathcal L/\partial w_{c',c}[u, v] = \sum_{i,j}\delta_{c'}[i, j]\,x_c[i + u, j + v].

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Channels

A colour image has 3 channels; the output of a layer with 8 kernels has 8 channels.
A kernel of the next layer covers all input channels: it is 3 \times 3 \times 8, with 72 weights.
So layer 2 combines features: “a vertical edge here and a bright blob next to it”. Each output channel has its own kernel stack.
Counting: layer 2 with 16 output channels on 8 input channels: 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 8 \cdot 16 + 16 = 1168 weights.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Pooling and stride

2×2 max pooling: keep the largest value of each 2 \times 2 block. The map shrinks to half width and height and keeps “the feature is somewhere here”, with a little tolerance to small shifts.
Stride 2: evaluate the kernel only at every second position: also halves the size.
Output size of a layer with kernel k, padding p, stride s on n pixels:

n_\text{out} = \left\lfloor\frac{n + 2p - k}{s}\right\rfloor + 1

n = 28, k = 3, p = 1, s = 1: 28 (padding keeps the size). k = 5, p = 0: 24. n = 64, k = 3, p = 1, s = 2: 32.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The receptive field
The part of the input that one unit can see.

One 3 \times 3 layer: 3 pixels wide. Two: 5. Three: 7.
Three 3 \times 3 layers see as much as one 7 \times 7 layer, with 27 instead of 49 weights per channel pair, and two more nonlinearities.
Pooling multiplies the growth: after a 2 \times 2 pool, each further 3 \times 3 layer adds 4 input pixels instead of 2.
Deep layers see whole objects: that is where “nucleus” or “digit 6” can be decided.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Try it: receptive fields




“three 3×3 layers = 7”, then “one 7×7 layer” (same field, readout shows 2320 weights per layer pair with 16 channels for 3×3, 12560 for 7×7: 6960 vs 12560). “with pooling”: conv, pool, conv, pool, conv sees 18 pixels (3, 4, 8, 10, 18). “how deep to see a whole nucleus?”: 8 layers with two pools see 32 pixels, more than a 20-pixel nucleus. “dilated: 1, 2, 4”: 15 pixels with only three layers. Click units in middle layers too.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
The math: receptive field recursion
Layer l with kernel k_l, stride s_l (pooling: k = s = 2), dilation d_l. Let r_l be the receptive field and j_l the jump: the distance in input pixels between neighbouring units of layer l.
r_l = r_{l-1} + d_l(k_l - 1)\,j_{l-1}, \qquad j_l = j_{l-1}\,s_l, \qquad r_0 = j_0 = 1

Conv 3, conv 3, pool, conv 3, conv 3: r = 3, 5, 6, 10, 14; j = 1, 1, 2, 2, 2.
Without pooling or stride, the field grows only linearly: r = 1 + 2L for L layers of 3 \times 3.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
What the layers learn


Layer 1 kernels: edges, lines, blobs in different directions. The only layer whose kernels can be looked at as pictures.
Deeper layers: corners and textures, then parts (a loop, a stroke ending), then whole objects (Zeiler and Fergus, 2014).
Ways to look inside: the feature maps for an input; the image patches that excite a unit most; occlusion: cover part of the image and watch the class probability.

title: Convolutional networks
section: A classification network, end to end
text:
A classification network, end to end
conv 3×3 (8) → ReLU → pool → conv 3×3 (16) → ReLU → pool → flatten → dense → softmax, trained with cross-entropy (previous unit).

9,098 weights, 98.7 % correct on 10,000 test digits. A dense 784 → 100 → 10 network has 79,510.

title: Convolutional networks
section: Try it: inside a trained network
text:
Try it: inside a trained network




Draw a digit or pick one; look at the layer-1 maps (strokes in different directions) and layer-2 maps; click a layer-2 map to see its 9 favourite test patches. “shifted digit”: maps shift, the prediction stays 6. “a 6 rotated to a 9”: at 180° the network says 9, correctly! “rotation 30°”: without augmentation it says 4 (0.55), with rotation augmentation 6 (1.00). Weight sets epoch 0, 1, 3: random kernels and 10 % accuracy at epoch 0, 94 % after one epoch. “what is the network looking at?”: occlusion map of a 2.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Data augmentation
Train on modified copies: shifted, rotated, flipped, brighter, darker, slightly deformed. The label stays the same.

The network learns the invariances we can name: “a rotated 2 is still a 2”.
Our digit network: on test digits rotated by 45°, 46.9 % correct without augmentation, 92.9 % with random rotations up to ±45° during training (and 97.2 % instead of 98.7 % on upright digits).
Choose with care: with full rotations a 6 and a 9 become the same class. For cells, rotations and flips are usually safe.
Compare the moments elective: there invariance is built into the features; here it is taught by examples.

title: Convolutional networks
text:
Summary







Idea
In one line




Convolutional layer
a bank of learned k \times k kernels, each giving a feature map; bias, ReLU


Weight sharing
same kernel everywhere: k^2C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out} weights, any image size


Equivariance
shift the input, the maps shift; pooling adds a little invariance


Output size
\lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1


Receptive field
grows by k - 1 per layer, faster after pooling


Hierarchy
edges → textures → parts → objects


Augmentation
teach invariances by training on modified copies



Next: from “what is in the image” to “which pixels belong to it”: segmentation networks.

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
About this lecture
Two questions to end the day:

When there is nothing to un-blur, only noise: the classical denoisers, each judged by what it destroys.

Gaussian, median, bilateral, non-local means; Wiener with no blur.
The method noise check: what did the filter remove?

A restored image is an estimate: which measurements survive restoration (total intensity), which do not (peaks, sizes, separations, counts), and what to report.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

Last unit of the deconvolution day. The median is introduced here as a denoiser (course map); the morphology day places it among the rank filters (min, median, max), and the thresholding day recalls it in one line. Noise models, PSNR and its peak: camera noise unit (day 3). All PSNR values here use peak 255 (8-bit grey levels). Statistics of measurements belong to the evaluation day (day 16).
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Nothing to un-blur
With PSF = a single point (H = 1), Wiener and Tikhonov become denoisers: gain 1/(1 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}(f)), a low-pass filter chosen by the SNR per frequency.
Classical denoisers differ in what they average:









method
averages over
keeps
destroys




Gaussian
neighbours, by distance
nothing in particular
edges and noise alike


median
the middle value of the window
steps, against outliers
thin lines, corners


bilateral
neighbours that are close and similar
edges
ramps (cartoon), detail at the noise level


non-local means
pixels whose whole patch looks similar, anywhere nearby
repeated texture
unique fine detail
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Gaussian and median
Gaussian: a weighted mean of the neighbours (the filtering unit). Linear: noise and edges are averaged alike, so every edge is blurred.
Median (a rank filter): sort the values in the window and take the middle one.
Row (10, 10, 10, 200, 10, 10, 50, 50, 50), window 3 (edges mirrored):



mean
10

The outlier 200 vanishes; the step 10 → 50 stays sharp. The mean smears both.
But a line thinner than half the window is a minority in every window and disappears; corners are rounded.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: The math: the median minimises the absolute deviation
text:
The math: the median minimises the absolute deviation
The mean minimises the sum of squared deviations \sum_i (x_i - m)^2; the median minimises the sum of absolute deviations
\operatorname*{arg\,min}_m \sum_i |x_i - m| .

The derivative of \sum_i|x_i - m| with respect to m is (\#\{x_i < m\}) - (\#\{x_i > m\}): zero (changing sign) when as many values lie below m as above it, the median.
An outlier moved from 200 to 2000 changes the squared cost hugely (and pulls the mean), but only adds to one side of the count: the median does not move.
This is the \ell^1 versus \ell^2 difference that also separates total variation from the roughness penalty (last unit).
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Bilateral: close and similar
Average the neighbours, but weight each by how close it is (σs, pixels) and how similar its value is (σr, grey levels):
w_{pq} = e^{-\|p - q\|^2/2\sigma_s^2}\; e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2} .

Across an edge the neighbours on the other side are dissimilar and get almost no weight: the edge stays sharp.
Three pixels 10, 10, 50 around a centre of 10, σr = 10: the 50 gets e^{-40^2/(2 \cdot 10^2)} = e^{-8} = 0.0003 of the weight of a 10.
Fails when the noise ≈ the edge height: noise then looks like edges and is kept, or σr is raised and edges blur. Large σr on a noisy ramp gives flat patches: a cartoon.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Non-local means: similar patches
Average pixels whose whole patch (say 3 × 3 or 5 × 5 around them) looks like the patch around the pixel being denoised, wherever they lie in a search window:

Repetitive structure (a lattice, a texture, many similar cells) finds many good matches: strong averaging without blurring the pattern.
Unique fine detail has no match; with a large h (tolerance), it is averaged with dissimilar patches and fades.
Cost: (search window) × (pixels), with box sums for the patch distances.


Test image (step, ramp crossed by a 1-pixel line, dot lattice, one unique spot), noise σn = 20. From the left: truth, noisy, Gaussian σ = 1.5, median 3 × 3, bilateral (σs 2, σr 30), non-local means (patch 5 × 5, search 11 × 11, h = 20).
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: The math: bilateral and non-local means weights
text:
The math: bilateral and non-local means weights
Both are weighted means \hat I_p = \sum_q w_{pq} I_q \big/ \sum_q w_{pq}, with different weights:

Bilateral: w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-\|p - q\|^2/2\sigma_s^2\big)\exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma_r^2\big) over a window of radius about 2\sigma_s.
Non-local means: w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-d^2(P_p, P_q)/h^2\big), with d^2 the mean squared difference of the patches P_p, P_q, over a search window.
Per-offset computation: for each offset \delta in the search window, the squared differences (I_r - I_{r + \delta})^2 are summed over every patch with an integral image; the cost does not depend on the patch size.
With noise σn, even identical patches differ by d^2 \approx 2\sigma_n^2; so h must be of the order of σn or larger.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Beyond these four

Total variation denoising: the TV penalty of the last unit with H = 1; keeps steps, staircases ramps (the Ising/MRF elective).
Wavelet shrinkage: a sparsity penalty, small coefficients set to zero (the wavelets elective).
Poisson noise depends on the signal: either use a method that knows it (Richardson–Lucy, Poisson data terms), or transform the image so the noise variance becomes constant first (camera noise unit).
Learned restoration: networks trained on noisy/clean pairs, or even on single noisy images, now beat all of these. Trained to “look right”, they can invent structure that was never in the data. The modern deep learning day shows when, with Wiener from this day as the honest baseline.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: Method noise: what did the filter remove?
text:
Method noise: what did the filter remove?
Method noise = noisy − denoised. If the filter removed only noise, it looks like pure noise: no structure.

An edge, a line or the lattice visible in the method noise = signal the filter removed.
Gaussian σ = 3 on the test image (σn = 10): the method noise has RMS 9.9 in flat regions (≈ σn, fine) but jumps to +72 and −58 at the step: the edge was blurred away.
PSNR against a clean truth needs the truth; the method noise needs only the noisy image. Use it on real data.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Try it: denoisers




PSNR (peak 255) noisy → denoised. “Gaussian blurs the step” (σn 20, σ 2): 22.1 → 21.6 dB, worse than doing nothing, because the lattice is wiped out; the best Gaussian σ is only 0.6 (25.8 dB). “Salt and pepper” (10 % of the pixels 0 or 255): median 3 × 3 15.3 → 22.7 dB, Gaussian σ 1: 21.9 dB, with grey smudges. “Median eats the thin line” (5 × 5, σn 5): the line pixel at (96, 32) drops from 211 to 133; PSNR falls from 34.1 to 21.6 dB. “Bilateral keeps edges” (σn 15, σs 2, σr 30): 33.7 dB, Gaussian σ 2: 21.7 dB. “Cartoon” (σn 50, σr 100): flat patches on the ramp. “Non-local means on texture” (σn 25, patch 3 × 3, search 15 × 15, h 25): 29.5 dB overall, 26.7 dB on the lattice quarter against 23.2 for bilateral. “Smears the unique spot” (patch 5 × 5, h 45): the spot falls from 220 to 129. “Method noise shows the removed edge”. “Best PSNR, wrong look” (micrograph crop, σn 25): Wiener SNR 3 23.4 dB, bilateral (1.5, 50) 23.3 dB: the PSNR prefers the blurred Wiener result by a hair.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: A restored image is an estimate
text:
A restored image is an estimate

It depends on the PSF, the method, λ or the stopping point. Change any of them and the image changes.
It improves contrast and separation, but cannot recover what lies beyond the cut-off (image formation day: invisible objects stay invisible).
Its noise is no longer independent between pixels, and no longer Poisson: the camera noise unit’s rules for error bars do not apply to it.
So: what happens to the numbers we measure on it?
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
What happens to measurements








measurement
after restoration
why




total intensity over a region larger than the PSF
kept (RL exactly; roughness-penalised Tikhonov exactly; Wiener and energy-penalised Tikhonov slightly shrink it)
flux is the f = 0 coefficient


peak intensity
rises, non-linearly, and depends on the iterations
light is moved into the centre


size (FWHM) near the resolution limit
shrinks with iterations to a floor set by the method, not by the object
restoration stops at the noise


separation of close objects
biased, most when the dip between them is weak



counts of objects
speckles and split objects add, ringing adds rims




In the demo (spots of flux 1 : 4, 3000 photons): RL after 100 iterations gives an integrated ratio of 4.00 but a peak ratio of 6.20; the raw image gives 3.86 and 4.13.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
The math: flux preservation
RL: \sum_j x_j^{\text{new}} = \sum_j x_j\sum_i A_{ij}\frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i} = \sum_i \frac{y_i}{(A\mathbf x)_i}\sum_j A_{ij}x_j = \sum_i y_i, every iteration (no background).
Linear filters: the total intensity is the f = 0 Fourier coefficient, \hat X(0) = \sum_j x_j, and the filter multiplies it by its gain at f = 0 (with H(0) = 1):

Wiener: \dfrac{1}{1 + 1/\mathrm{SNR}(0)}, slightly below 1;
Tikhonov, energy penalty: \dfrac{1}{1 + \lambda};
Tikhonov, roughness penalty: 1 exactly (\hat D(0) = 0).

Over a region rather than the whole image, flux is kept only approximately: light moves across the region’s boundary by about the PSF’s width, so the region must be larger than the PSF.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: Try it: what may be measured
text:
Try it: what may be measured




A field with known truth, Airy PSF NA 1.0 (Rayleigh distance 4.88 px): top row, bead pairs at 0.8, 1.0, 1.2 and 1.5 × Rayleigh; middle, spots of flux 1 : 2 : 4; bottom, disks. The table compares raw, restored and truth; green within 10 %, yellow within 30 %, red worse. Tour (RL): “integrals hold” (3000 photons, k = 100): integrated ratio 4.00, peak ratio 6.20. “Peaks lie” (k = 316): peak ratio 6.53, integral 3.97. “Sizes shrink to a floor” (k = 1000): FWHM 1.93 px (raw 4.51, truth 1.45): it stops shrinking around 1.9 whatever the object. “Close pairs” (1000 photons, k = 100): the 1.2 × Rayleigh pair is 4.95 px apart in the raw image (truth 5.92), 5.85 after RL. “Extra spots” (1000 photons, k = 1000): 259 local maxima above the threshold instead of 11. “Wiener” (SNR 300): integral 4.27, peak 3.66, FWHM 3.53.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
section: What to do, and what to report
text:
What to do, and what to report

Segment or detect on the restored image if it helps (better contrast, separated objects).
Measure intensities on the raw image (offset- and flat-field-corrected), inside the masks found.
Validate any measurement made on restored data with a known-truth test: beads, a phantom, the same microscope and noise.
Report the method, the PSF (measured or computed), λ or the number of iterations; show the raw data next to the result.
Never compare images restored with different settings, and keep the raw data.
Error bars and statistics of measurements: the evaluation day.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure

title: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
text:
Summary

With H = 1, Wiener and Tikhonov are low-pass denoisers. Gaussian blurs edges; median removes outliers, keeps steps, eats thin lines; bilateral keeps edges, cartoons at high noise; non-local means loves repetition, smears unique detail.
Method noise (noisy − denoised) should look like pure noise; structure in it is removed signal.
Learned restoration is better and can invent structure (modern deep learning day).
A restored image is an estimate: total intensity over a region larger than the PSF is kept; peaks, sizes, separations and counts change with the method and the stopping point.
Detect on the restored image, measure on the raw, validate with known truth, report everything.
crumbs: Denoising, artefacts, and what you may measure
